"To follow its flow" means that according to the conditions of defilement or purity,
it receives the designations of "ordinary being" or "sage."
What is meant by relying on the conventional?
A sutra states:
"A single dharma has many names."
Within the reality of dharmas, it does not exist,
because the nature of dharmas is non-forgetting;
yet it is disseminated throughout the world.
What is meant by "the time of the cause"?
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha-nature differs according to the stages of its causal development."
It explains the pure and the impure.
What is meant?
When [the mind] is in a state of defilement, it is called a "sentient being."
When abiding in purity, they are called the Buddhas.
How is this in terms of function?
It is like establishing phenomena based on the mind.
It is named according to its nature:
it is called "True" when abiding among the noble ones,
and designated as "Worldly" when dwelling among ordinary beings.
It is like gold fashioned into an object;
it receives its name according to the object.
When it is on a finger, it is called a ring.
An ornament for the arm is called a bracelet;
thus, with the mind unmoving in single-mindedness,
one grasps distinct designations and the myriad phenomena arise as differences.
Pure gold does not shift;
yet when recognized through different names, the thousand vessels appear unequal.
If one knows that every phenomenon is entirely made of the mind, [the distinctions vanish].
Every vessel is entirely made of gold;
names and forms cannot interfere,
and how could right and wrong cause delusion?
Furthermore, it is like a round vessel and a square vessel;
their names differ.
It is also like raw gold and refined gold.
Although verbal expressions differ,
when one traces them back to their origin and investigates their essence, all phenomena are empty.
There are only mental verbalizations (manojalpa) that differentiate names and meanings;
their movement constitutes the eight consciousnesses.
Concentrating into a single mind, one attains the essential meaning and forgets external conditions;
wherever one encounters the path, there is no place for attachment.
As stated in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra:
The Buddha said, "Good son,"
All the virtuous deeds of the Tathāgata are performed solely for the sake of taming all sentient beings; he is,
for example, like a king of physicians.
All medical prescriptions are intended solely for the healing of all suffering from illness,
O son of good family.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One,
acts for the sake of the land and for the sake of the season.
For the sake of speaking for others;
for the sake of individuals;
and for the sake of the faculties of the multitude.
Within a single dharma,
two types of explanations are made;
it is called "name" and "dharma."
It is said that there are immeasurable names;
within a single meaning,
immeasurable names are spoken.
Regarding immeasurable meanings,
immeasurable names are spoken.
How is it that a single name expresses immeasurable names?
It is like nirvana; it is called nirvana,
and it is also called non-arising.
It is also called "without emergence," "without action," and "unconditioned."
It is also called taking refuge;
it is also called a cave-dwelling;
it is also called liberation.
It is also called Radiance;
it is also called Lamp-Light;
it is also called the Other Shore.
It is also called fearlessness;
it is also called non-retrogression;
it is also called abiding securely.
It is also called tranquility;
it is also called signlessness;
it is also called non-duality.
It is also called "Single Practice," also called "Pure Coolness," and also called "Free from Darkness."
It is also called "unimpeded," it is also called "non-contentious," and it is also called "unturbid."
It is also called "Vast," it is also called "Nectar," and it is also called "Auspicious."
This is called giving immeasurable names to that which has but a single name.
How is it that a single meaning is expressed by immeasurable names?
It is, for example, like Śakra.
He is also named Śakra;
he is also named Kauśika; he is also named Vāsava.
He is also named Puraṃdara, also named Makha, and also named Indra.
He is also called Thousand-Eyed,
also called Lord of Śacī, and also called Vajra.
It is also called "Jewel Summit" and also called "Jewel Banner";
these are names for a single reality spoken of by infinite names.
How is it that infinite names are spoken for infinite meanings?
For example, the Buddha is named Tathāgata;
here the meaning differs and the name differs.
He is also called Arhat;
the meanings differ and the names differ.
He is also called Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The meaning differs and the names differ;
it is also called "mariner" and also called "guide."
He is also called the Perfectly Awakened One;
he is also called the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct;
he is also called the Great Lion King.
They are also called śramaṇas;
they are also called brāhmaṇas; they are also called those who have attained tranquility.
They are also called donors,
they are also called those who have reached the other shore,
and they are also called great kings of physicians.
He is also called the Great Elephant,
also called the Great Dragon King,
and also called the Giver of Eyes.
He is also named Mahābala (The Greatly Powerful One),
also named Mahāviśārada (The Greatly Fearless One),
and also named Ratnarāśi (The Heap of Jewels).
He is also called the Caravan Leader;
he is also called the One Who Has Attained Liberation;
he is also called the Great Man.
He is also called the Teacher of Gods and Humans;
he is also called the Great White Lotus;
he is also called the Solitary One Without Equal.
It is also called the Great Field of Merit;
it is also called the Ocean of Great Wisdom;
it is also called the Signless.
It is also called "endowed with the eight knowledges.
Thus, all these meanings have different names. Good son!
This is called the "Infinite Meanings.
Within it, infinite names are explained.
Furthermore, there is another sense in which infinite names are explained.
That which is called "like the aggregates" is also termed "the aggregates" and is also termed "inversion."
They are also called the Truths;
they are also called the Four Foundations of Mindfulness;
and they are also called the Four Nutriments.
It is also called the four stations of consciousness;
it is also called existence;
and it is also called the path.
It is also called time;
it is also called sentient beings;
it is also called the world.
It is also called the ultimate truth (paramārtha) and is also called the three cultivations,
namely: body, precepts, and mind.
It is also called cause and effect;
it is also called affliction;
it is also called liberation.
It is also called the twelve links of dependent origination;
it is also called śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
it is also called the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.
It is also called the past, the present, and the future;
this is what is meant by "one meaning expressed through immeasurable names. Good son!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One,
for the sake of sentient beings,
has explained the detailed in brief.
The brief is explained as extensive;
the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is explained as the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
To speak of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) as the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
What is meant by "explaining the concise within the extensive"?
As it was told to the bhikṣus:
"I shall now proclaim the twelve links of dependent origination.
What are they called the twelve links of dependent origination?"
Regarding what is called cause and effect:
how is it that a brief and intermediate statement is explained in detail?
It is as when [the Buddha] addressed the bhikṣus:
I now proclaim the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. As for suffering,
it refers to immeasurable varieties of suffering.
"Accumulation" refers to immeasurable afflictions;
"cessation" refers to—
What is called the path of immeasurable liberation refers to immeasurable skillful means.
What is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is spoken of as the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
as it was told to the bhikṣus:
This body of mine is subject to old age, sickness, and death;
how can it be called the conventional truth?
It is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya),
as when it was said to Kauṇḍinya:
"Because you have attained the Dharma."
He was named Ājñātakauṇḍinya. Therefore,
according to the person, the intention, and the time,
he is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowing the faculties of others.
"Good son, if I were to provide a definitive explanation regarding such meanings as these,"
Then one cannot rightly call me a Tathāgata who possesses the power of knowing the faculties. Good son,
a person of wisdom—
One should know that what a fragrant elephant can carry cannot be borne by a donkey;
so it is with all sentient beings.
The practices are immeasurable;
therefore, the Tathāgata explains them in various ways.
The Dharma is immeasurable. Why is this?
Because sentient beings possess many afflictions.
If the Tathāgata were to teach only a single practice,
he could not be said to have fully accomplished the knowledge of the powers of the faculties.
Therefore, one should know that dharmas are fundamentally nameless;
they are established by reason of the mind.
Therefore, the Great Sage conformed to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
accommodating various capacities and circumstances, such that his teachings were sometimes extensive and sometimes concise.
The one and the many have no fixed definition.
One will take that which can be spoken and subsume it into the unspeakable;
by employing that which has a name, one leads others into the nameless.
Ultimately, this causes all beings to reach the ground of quiescence within their own original mind.
Thus the Sūtra says:
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
You must be careful not to expound the Dharma extensively for those of sharp faculties;
[reserve it rather for] those of dull faculties.
This is a brief explanation of the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is established based on the substance of the cause;
the substance arises following the name.
The substance is empty, and thus names have no application;
names are illusory, and thus the substance has no arising.
Name and substance are mutually quiescent.
All phenomena are without arising;
there is only the single true mind,
and nothing else exists.
The *Yǒngjiā jí* states:
"Therefore, the essence is not without names, for it is through them that it is distinguished;
names are not without essence, for it is through it that they are applied."
To speak of an essence, one must rely upon its name;
to utter a name, one must rely upon its essence.
As for those who now apply names externally to an essence:
This is merely a name;
it has no substantial reality.
How could there be a substance that corresponds to its name?
It is like the case of a rabbit, which has no horns yet receives a name for them;
this name merely refers to its lack of horns.
How could there be actual horns corresponding to that name?
To bestow a name upon that which lacks substantiality is for the name to be a name without reality. That the name is a name without reality— this is what is meant.
Thus, that which is named has no name.
Since that which is named does not exist,
that which names it cannot exist either.
Why is this? A name is established precisely to designate its corresponding entity;
if there is no entity, how can it be designated by that name?
It is said that the substance fundamentally corresponds to its name;
yet if there is no name, how can it correspond to that substance?
To correspond to non-existence is not to correspond to the substance.
Names are nameless and yet not names.
Thus, how could it be that only the substance is primordially void?
It is also that names are fundamentally quiescent.
However, the fact that names correspond to non-existent entities has been so from the beginning; thus,
the correspondence of names is established.
What is meant by this? Now, a substance does not name itself;
it is through the provisional use of another's name that one names my own substance.
Names are not established by oneself;
one borrows the substance of another to bestow a name upon the self.
This applies even when the substance has not yet taken form.
Then what would the name name?
If the name has not yet been established,
then what would the essence manifest?
However, as for the luminous essence (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*),
although it is provisionally designated by that name,
it is not the case that it lacks an essence simply because it is not [inherently] named.
The designation is established by depending on its substance;
if there is no substance, then the designation is fundamentally non-existent.
Thus, the substance does not arise as a designation.
A name arises only from a substance;
the substance now exists prior to the name,
while the name follows after the substance.
As for "discrimination" (pravicaya): this is the establishment of a name to designate its essence;
thus, one knows the essence.
This is called the "origin.
Thus, that which names is caused to arise from the substance;
it is the primordial source of the substance.
What is its causal basis?
Its substance is not of the nature of a self;
it forms a substance only through the provisional convergence of conditions.
Conditions do not constitute a meeting;
it is through the substance of the meeting that conditions are formed.
If the substance has not yet manifested, there can be no meeting.
Then upon what would they depend?
If that which is depended upon has not yet met [with it],
then what form could its substance take?
The physical form is formed through the convergence of conditions;
when conditions converge, they assemble around the physical form.
Thus, the physical form assembles through conditions.
Thus it is clear that form has no separate meeting.
Since form has no separate meeting,
the meeting is fundamentally non-existent.
When conditions meet, form arises;
thus, when clarity meets, there is no distinct form.
When there is no distinct form, [formlessness prevails].
Thus, form is fundamentally non-existent.
Therefore, all phenomena arise from conditions and possess no intrinsic nature.
Because its substance lacks self-existence,
it is called "emptiness of nature. Since its nature is already empty, [it is so named].
Although they exist through the convergence of conditions, they are not inherently existent;
yet once the conditions have converged,
although their nature is empty, they are not non-existent.
Therefore, the existence of conditioned conjunctions is existence that is not existence;
the non-existence of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is [true] non-existence.
It is non-existent, yet not non-existent.
Why? Because when they are realized, their nature is empty.
Therefore, it is said that they are not existent;
yet because emptiness arises from the convergence of conditions,
it is said that they are not non-existent.
Now, when it is said that there is neither existence nor non-existence,
this does not mean that apart from existence there is a separate non-existence,
nor does it mean that apart from non-existence there is a separate existence.
Thus, it is clarified that dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent;
they are designated by the name "neither existent nor non-existent," yet they are not actually "neither existent nor non-existent."
Since it is neither existent nor non-existent,
and furthermore neither non-existent-nor-non-existent,
how could it be that only the path of language is cut off?
This is also the cessation of the sphere of mental activity.
Thus, when the substance is empty,
both speech and thought naturally cease.
It may be said that the myriad affairs of state have vanished their traces,
leaving only the true mind in solitary clarity.
Question:
The sublime principle of "Mind-Only" is entirely nameless;
even such designations as "sentient beings" are [merely conventional].
These names of the Buddhas are established through provisional designations;
how could they be established in vain?
Answer: It is because of ordinary beings that the noble ones are established;
yet, the noble ones are fundamentally nameless.
Manifesting the truth from within the conventional,
the truth itself fundamentally does not stand;
both rely entirely upon worldly words and letters.
They arise in dependence upon one another; yet words are empty,
and emptiness has no locus of reliance.
If one is a great being of superior capacity,
why rely on names and forms to bring forth [the truth]?
Facing objects, they know the fundamental source in every thought-moment.
When encountering conditions, mind after mind accords with the Way.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says,
as the Sūtra states:
In the buddha-field of the Buddha Siṃhaghoṣasvara,
it is adorned with jewel trees,
from which there constantly issue immeasurable sounds of the Dharma.
That is to say, all phenomena are ultimately empty,
without arising and without ceasing, and so forth;
such are the people of that land.
From birth, they have heard this sound of the Dharma;
therefore, they do not give rise to evil thoughts and attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
At this time, where could there be even the names of the Three Jewels?
One simply realizes the principle of non-arising.
The Three Jewels, which are naturally one essence,
are ever manifest in the world.
If one grasps at the names of specific distinctions,
one loses the principle of true permanence; rather,
one should thoroughly understand all phenomena.
Since there is no intrinsic nature, Buddhas appear in all places;
there is not a single dharma that is not the fundamental principle.
As the former masters have said:
"The appearance of a Buddha in the world" refers to the present manifestation of the Tathāgata.
All are entirely due to the lack of intrinsic nature in sensory objects;
they are the dependent origination of the dharma-realm, bodhi, and nirvana.
They regard it as the body of the Tathāgata.
This body pervades the three worlds;
therefore, throughout all lands, [it is present].
All sentient beings, all phenomena,
and all dependent origination.
All karmic retributions,
all atoms, hairs, and so forth,
each individually manifest bodhi, nirvana, and the like.
This is for the sake of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
If even one point is not fully understood,
one does not become a Buddha.
Nor does it appear.
Why? Because its locus is not understood.
It remains ignorance; therefore,
Buddhahood is not achieved,
and one does not appear [in the world].
Therefore, when the Buddhas appear in the world,
they discern the capacities and the timing of beings,
and stoop down to accommodate those of inferior faculties.
Manifesting birth during the kalpa of decrease;
using an empty fist to entice and lead;
holding up yellow leaves to awaken the mind.
If one is a person of the highest capacity,
then the Buddhas neither appear nor disappear;
thus, a sutra says:
Whether a Buddha appears or does not appear,
the nature and characteristics [of reality] abide eternally.
As a verse in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
As it is with the mind, so it is with all Buddhas;
as it is with the Buddhas, so it is with sentient beings. Thus, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings [are one].
These three are without distinction;
they are but a single dharma.
Their names differ, but their principle is the same.
Why is this? When one awakens to this mind— which is without support, without abiding, beyond dependence, and inconceivable— and it remains unmoving,
one enters the beginning of the ten stages of faith.
He is titled the Buddha Immovable Wisdom.
When he does not realize this absolute, non-referential true mind,
and fails to maintain his own nature as he follows conditions into differentiation, [he becomes a sentient being].
It is named the Dharma-body;
when it transmigrates through the five realms of existence,
it is called a sentient being.
There are merely the names of "delusion" and "awakening," which do not depart from the substance of the one mind.
What further dharma could there be to serve as the basis for designating the distinctions between ordinary beings and sages?
As stated in the Mañjuśrī-prajñā Sūtra:
The Buddha asked,
"Is the Buddha-dharma unsurpassed?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
"There is not a single dharma, even as small as a mote of dust, that can be called 'unsurpassed.
Furthermore, a sutra says:"
When the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma,
there was no bodhisattva who attained these samādhis and various dhāraṇī-doors,
nor were there any words, phrases, or meanings spoken by those Buddhas.
Not even a single word or phrase was spoken;
no one heard it, and no one understood it.
"No one attains Buddhahood.
Such teachings as these are the words of truth.
In the future final age,
during the period of five hundred years,
this dharma-gate of the sutra shall be propagated throughout Jambudvīpa.
It is universally disseminated,
blazing and unextinguished;
this is true speech.
Question:
Since the myriad affairs have vanished from view and the true mind alone shines with clarity, [how can there be any activity?]
How is it stated in the teachings:
"This is the dharma of ordinary persons;
this is the dharma of noble ones"?
Answer: Because all phenomena arise through conditions and lack intrinsic nature.
One does not attain the dharmas of ordinary beings,
nor does one attain the dharmas of noble ones,
because they arise through conditions and lack intrinsic nature.
Whether ultimate or conventional,
they do not become confused or intermingled,
as it is said:
All is one, and all are equally devoid of intrinsic nature;
one is all, yet cause and effect remain distinct and clear.
Although they are clearly manifest,
they do not lose the principle of being without intrinsic nature; although they are without intrinsic nature, [they remain manifest].
One does not destroy the way of dependent origination.
Furthermore, although one realizes that all is but the single mind,
regarding all phenomena...
Each and every one is thoroughly understood with clarity and without delusion,
as stated in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra:
The bodhisattva mahāsattva knows that all phenomena are of one and the same nature.
That which is called "absence of nature," "absence of manifold natures," and "absence of immeasurable natures."
It is beyond calculation, beyond measure,
formless, and signless.
Whether as one or as many,
none can be apprehended;
yet this is decisively and definitively known.
This is the Dharma of the Buddhas;
this is the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas;
this is the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas.
"This is the Dharma of the śrāvakas;
this is the Dharma of ordinary persons;
this is the wholesome Dharma."
This is an unwholesome dharma;
this is a worldly dharma;
this is a supramundane dharma.
This is a faulty dharma; this is a faultless dharma;
this is a dharma with outflows.
"This is an untainted dharma," up to "this is a conditioned dharma" or "this is an unconditioned dharma."
This is the seventh dwelling in accordance with reality.
Question:
Regarding the dharma of single-mindedness—
How is it that [this] is able to universally contain and encompass all,
giving rise to and fully perfecting all phenomena? Answer:
Now, as for the mind,
it is spiritual and subtle, without fixed form;
its ultimate principle is profound and remote.
Seeking through the three periods of time, nothing is found;
investigating through the two truths, nothing is known.
It is without form and without name.
Its depth and breadth cannot be measured;
being without dependence and without abiding,
its traces and footprints cannot be scrutinized.
It enters subtly into the midst of the infinitesimal,
such that its smallness cannot be described in words;
it encompasses broadly the realms beyond the celestial bodies, such that its vastness exceeds all bounds.
Its profundity cannot be expressed in words.
The Ultimate Way is void and mysterious;
who could cause it to exist?
The phantom does not fall;
who could cause it to cease?
Its traces divide the Dharma-realm, yet they are not many.
Its nature is united with true emptiness, yet it is not nothingness;
its essence coagulates as the One Way, yet it is not stasis;
its function encompasses the myriad things, yet it is not weary.
It is like the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), the supreme treasure of the heavens,
which, though the size of a mustard seed,
possesses great functional power.
Pure and exquisite objects of the five desires,
and a profusion of the seven treasures,
were not stored within.
It is not an external sense-field;
it does not deliberate on what precedes or follows,
nor does it discriminate between much and little.
It is neither coarse nor exquisite;
it accords with one's needs in terms of abundance or scarcity.
The rain falls in profusion, neither increasing nor diminishing.
The benefit and salvation are inexhaustible.
Since even this material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*) can be thus, how much more so for that which is not material!
How much more so for the spirit and mind, which are subtle and wondrous;
how could they not be endowed with all dharmas?
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
The Buddha said:
"All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas share this one wondrous path of pure purification."
All are identical to this single ultimate purity;
there is no second. It is on the basis of this that I [speak].
It was spoken with intentional meaning that there is only one vehicle,
even unto the analogy of space.
Pervading all places,
it is of a single uniform taste and does not obstruct any activities that are undertaken.
Thus it is, Blessed One;
based on these dharmas,
all are devoid of intrinsic nature.
All are of one single flavor,
and do not obstruct any śrāvakas,
pratyekabuddhas, or great beings.
Regarding the activities he practiced,
a poem by Hanshanzi says:
"My family resides here, known as Cold Mountain."
Dwelling among mountain crags, one is free from the clamor of worldly distractions;
when stilled, the myriad phenomena leave no trace.
When expanded, it flows everywhere throughout the great trichiliocosm.
Light and shadow soar in brilliance, illuminating the ground of the mind;
not a single dharma appears before one.
Only then does one know that it is but a single mani jewel.
Its wondrous function is inexhaustible and perfectly complete in every place.
The *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation on Returning to the Source) states:
"The light of samādhi manifests through the contemplation of non-thought."
This refers to the white, pure jewel-net within the teaching of the One Vehicle,
the precious gem of the Thousand-Syllable Wheel King;
the essential nature of this gem is transparently luminous.
Illuminating the ten directions simultaneously,
accomplishing deeds without thought.
As for "mindfulness":
All followed him;
although he manifested extraordinary feats,
his mind was free of thought or deliberation.
If a person enters this gate of great and wondrous śamatha-vipaśyanā,
they will be free from thought and deliberation,
and all tasks will be accomplished spontaneously.
Like that precious gem,
it illuminates both near and far equally,
appearing with distinct clarity.
Vast and transparent like empty space,
it cannot be obscured by the dust, mist, smoke, or clouds of the followers of the Two Vehicles or of external paths.
The *Qingliang shu* states:
"It is like the solar palace,
where a thousand rays shine simultaneously."
Although there are immeasurable approaches for each phenomenon that is cited,
there are nevertheless two fundamental meanings.
First, by way of similar categories:
for example, within the single category of impermanence,
there are birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Gathering and dispersing, union and separation;
gain and loss, formation and decay;
the three calamities and the four signs.
The external vessel-world and the internal body undergo arising and ceasing, as well as transformation, from moment to moment throughout the duration of a single lifetime.
Defilement and purity, concealment and manifestation—
all are gates of impermanence;
the same applies to all other cases as well.
Second, as for the fusion of their nature,
it is inexhaustible; that is to say,
the dharma-nature is tranquil and vast.
Although there are no marks,
the mark of marklessness does not obstruct the profusion of phenomena.
Therefore, it manifests universally based on its essence,
like the moon entering a hundred rivers; yet when one seeks the moon within those reflections, [it cannot be found].
The substance of the moon is undivided;
it is the function of that very substance,
and its function pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
Because essence and function interpenetrate,
it is inconceivable. — *Fuxingji* (Record of Aiding Practice).
Question: Since the single mind already possesses the causes and effects of the ten dharma realms,
one need only contemplate the mind.
Question: Why is it necessary to contemplate the [three] requisites? Answer:
This is the contemplative gate (guanmen) of our school.
It is eternally distinct from all other doctrines;
that it encompasses all causes and effects— whether mundane or sagely— of the ten directions and the three periods of time,
is truly due to the completeness of its contemplation.
That which is endowed is itself provisional;
that which is provisional is itself within emptiness.
Although the rational nature is endowed with all, it remains empty.
If one does not contemplate [the object] but merely speaks of "contemplating the mind," it does not accord with principle.
How could it be that the Hīnayāna has never contemplated the mind?
It is simply that they are deluded regarding the fact that the one mind contains all dharmas.
Question:
If one does not examine the details,
to which teaching does it belong? Answer:
Regarding the Path of Teaching in the Separate Teaching (biejiao),
from the initial stage of the mind onward,
it is simply said that one sequentially gives rise to the ten realms.
The severance [of afflictions] also occurs sequentially;
therefore, one does not contemplate them as being complete. Alternatively, this refers to those who follow the Shared Teaching (p’unggyo).
Emptiness is merely a principle;
or, following the Tripiṭaka,

while one thousand world-systems of the physical environment (*bhājanaloka*) belong to the basis.
Since the environment and its inhabitants already abide within the one mind,
how could that one mind be divided into subject and object?
Although there is no subject or object, [it is so].
The environment and its inhabitants are perfectly distinct; thus, within the rational nature, names, and contemplative practice,
there already exists the non-dual characteristic of the environment and its inhabitants.
Therefore, self and other, cause and effect, mutually encompass one another;
yet sentient beings remain within the fundamental principle.
Although the fruition has not yet been accomplished,
everything is none other than the wondrous realm of Vairocana;
nevertheless, one should further realize this.
The essence of the Buddhas' Dharma is non-pervasive yet pervasive; it is the fundamental nature of the capacity for enlightenment inherent in all sentient beings.
Not limited yet limited;
from beginning to end, it does not change.
There is no hindrance between the large and the small;
the principle of cause and effect is the same. What distinction, then, can there be between the primary and the secondary?
Therefore, in lands both pure and defiled,
and with bodies both superior and inferior,
the corporeal body and the Dharma-body are equal in measure.
The land of dust and the Land of Quiescent Light are no different.
Thus, every single atom-land is all lands;
every single atom-body is all bodies.
Its breadth and narrowness, its excellence and inferiority, are inconceivable;
its pure and impure locations are inexhaustible.
Were it not for the three thousandfold world as emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, [how could this be?]
How could such sovereign function be accomplished?
Only through this can one know that birth and Buddhahood are equal,
and that phenomena and principle mutually encompass one another.
This is established by way of the gate of the non-duality of defilement and purity.
Seventh, the gate of the non-duality of self and others:
benefiting others according to their capacities.
Matters depend upon the source;
the source is the single nature,
which fully encompasses both self and other.
Upon reaching the stage of fruition,
one benefits oneself and others;
this is like the three virtues and three truths of the principle-nature (*li-xing*).
Three thousand [miles].
Traveling by oneself,
one remains solely in mid-air.
To benefit others, he reaches out to sentient beings throughout the three thousandfold world system;
though the capacities of these beings are immeasurable, they do not exceed those within the three thousandfold world system.
Although the responsive manifestations are numerous,
they do not exceed the ten realms;
these ten realms undergo transformation and manifestation.
Without departing from a single thought,
lands arise in mutual succession;
yet they do not depart from the serene light.
Sentient beings are able to evoke [the response] because they inherently possess the three thousand realms according to principle;
the Buddhas are able to respond because they have fulfilled the three thousand realms according to principle.
Thus, the response is universal and the capacity is universal.
One proceeds with joy without error; otherwise,
how could it be like a mirror manifesting images?
A mirror possesses the principle of manifesting images;
a form possesses the nature of producing images.
If a single form faces it, it cannot manifest an image.
Then the mirror of principle would have its limits,
and forms and phenomena would remain unpenetrated,
as if separated from the reflected image.
Thus, there may indeed be such a principle:
there is no form that exists as a counterpart without being reflected.
It is like a mirror that has not yet manifested an image.
It is obscured by dust;
the removal of dust depends on the person who polishes,
yet the manifestation of the image does not pertain to the polisher.
By observing phenomena through these analogies,
the general principle can be understood.
One should know that although the principle is fully present within both self and other, [it is so].
One must rely upon the conditions (pratyaya) and the developmental aspect (pariniṣpanna) to constitute the merit of benefiting others.

Furthermore, it is only through the unification of these conditions and the developmental aspect with the fundamental nature (prakṛti) that one can, in accordance with that nature, establish the myriad phenomena.
Thus, there is no arising of self-nature,
and manifestations have no fixed location;
this is accomplished through the gate of the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants.
Regarding the eighth, the Gate of the Non-duality of the Three Karmas:
within the gate of transforming others,
the activities are divided into the three secrets.
Names are established in accordance with the nature of things;
they differ according to how the wheel of mind reflects upon capacities.
Establishing transformation through the two wheels,
he manifested his body and preached the Dharma without the slightest error.
Regarding the person, they are divided into the True and the Responsive;
regarding the Dharma, they are divided into the Expedient and the Real.
If these two bodies were different, [the following would ensue].
Why, then, do you say that this is precisely the Dharmakāya?
If these two statements were contradictory,
why would you say that all shall attain the Buddha-way?
If there were only the Dharma-body,
it would not descend into the world; if there were only the Buddha-way, [it would likewise not manifest].
Who bestows the Three Vehicles?
Even the body is no body;
what is taught is necessarily not taught.
Body and speech are equalized,
matching that wheel of mind;
mind and form are as one.
Transforming without deliberation,
they are perpetually in accord with the ultimate;
they act and provide for all things according to their nature.
Is it not that the hundred realms are one mind?
Within each realm, there are none that do not consist of the three karmas;
and since even a realm is but a single thought-moment.
How could the three karmas be different?
Since the efficacy of the fruit is unimpaired,
the cause must correspond to the fruit.
If one believes in cause and effect,
one will then know that the three mysteries have their source in the three karmas of the hundred realms.
Since [the three truths of] emptiness, the provisional,
and the middle are all present, they respond appropriately and universally to serve as fruits,
manifesting in accordance with each individual's physical form.
In each and every word and sound, there are no instances that do not encompass the hundred realms,
with the three karmas fully complete.
This is what is meant by "an emanation further creating another emanation. Thus,
it is the ordinary mind of a single thought-moment.
The ocean of the three mysteries of the fundamental principle already exists;
even a single atom of retributive form is identical to Vairocana in its original principle.
This is then called the non-differentiation of the three;
it is established by means of the gate of the non-duality of self and other.
Ninth, the clarification of the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real:
Equal and great wisdom constantly mirrors the dharma-realm;
this is also due to the nature of reality.
Nine are expedient means and one is the reality;
yet within that reality there are again nine realms,
and it is likewise with the expedient means.
The provisional and the real are mutually merged;
even the hundred realms within a single thought-moment cannot be differentiated.
Spontaneously and eternally so,
it reaches fruition precisely by accords with the fundamental principle of oneness.
Neither provisional nor real,
yet both provisional and real;
this is just as before.
The mind-wheel is sovereign,
enabling the body and speech to respond to the capacities of beings according to their provisional and ultimate needs.
The three karmas and a single thought do not conflict with the provisional and the real;
they bestow [benefits] without moving.
How could there be any separation or distinction?
It is explained that the designations are established precisely through the provisional and the real.
Regarding the body,
it is designated as "the true" and "the responsive";
the same principle applies to the three karmas.
The provisional and the ultimate are darkly unified;
this is accomplished through the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas.
Regarding the gate of the non-duality of the ten types of moisture:
In the fundamental nature of all phenomena,
the provisional and the ultimate are inherently present; yet, from time immemorial, they have been conditioned by habitual tendencies.
Whether expedient or ultimate,
these arise from habitual perfuming;
in principle, they are eternally equal.
Encountering the right conditions, they form habits;
these are what provide the support for aspiration and practice. If there were no fundamental cause, [they could not arise].
Perfuming would likewise be in vain;
for while that which encounters perfuming differs from itself,
this is not due to a difference in its intrinsic nature.
Although their nature is without distinction,
they must rely on illusion to manifest; it is through illusory capacity and illusory response that they arise.
The illusion responds and the illusion proceeds;
the transformer and the transformed are neither provisional nor ultimate.
However, because the causal endowments are neither provisional nor ultimate,
they constitute the capacity for the provisional and the ultimate;
likewise, the Buddha’s fruition is also neither provisional nor ultimate.
He manifests through provisional and ultimate truths in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings;
his bodies and lands are free from partiality.
It is identical to the Constantly Quiescent Light and there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm;
thus we know that the three thousand worlds are simultaneously present within the mind-ground.
It is no different from the Buddha’s mind-ground and the three thousand [worlds];
the substance of the four subtle elements is identical,
and the provisional and the real are equal in their benefit.
This is established by means of the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real.
All that precedes is an explanation based on the categories of principle and phenomenon, the provisional and the real, cause and effect, the subjective and the objective, and so forth.
Generally speaking, there are two gates: that of principle and that of phenomenon.
It is neither identical nor different.
As the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states:
"There are two kinds of gates."
First is the gate of ultimate emptiness;
second is the gate of discriminating between the good and the evil.
Now, we rely upon the gate of discrimination.
Thus, principle is the basis and is fundamental,
while phenomena are that which depend upon it and are derivative.
Furthermore, principle is subtle and difficult to know, and is therefore superior.
Matters that are coarse and easy to perceive are inferior;
for now, one should follow what is superior rather than conforming to what is inferior.
It is sufficient to attain the fundamental principle;
once the foundation is established, the Way arises,
and all affairs will naturally be accomplished.
Furthermore, in reality, one should take as an object the principle of unimpeded phenomena;
for phenomena are established by virtue of that principle.
There is nothing that contradicts reason;
those who today do not enter into perfect faith are all merely self-deprecating commoners.
To trace this back to the ultimate Sage is not only to lose sight of the facts;
it is also entirely devoid of principle.
One merely awakens to the principle of the single mind, which is unimpeded and sovereign;
therein, principle and phenomena naturally harmonize, and the ultimate and conventional truths mutually penetrate one another.
If one attends to the phenomena while being deluded regarding the principle,
one will sink into saṃsāra for eternal kalpas;
or if one awakens to the principle while neglecting the phenomena, [the same result follows].
This is not the perfect realization.
Why? Because principle and phenomena do not transcend one's own mind.
How could the nature and characteristics ever deviate from this single principle?
If one enters the Mirror of the Fundamental Teaching,
one will suddenly awaken to the true mind.
There is still no mention of what is neither principle nor phenomenon;
how, then, could there be any attachment to either principle or phenomenon?
Only after attaining the source is this so.
Nor does this neglect the perfect cultivation.
For instance, there was a student who asked Master Benjing,
"Does the Master still practice cultivation?"
He replied,
"My practice differs from yours.
You first practiced and later attained awakening."
I first attained awakening and subsequently engaged in cultivation.
Therefore, if one were to cultivate first and awaken later,
this would be a cultivation based on effort.
Merit belongs to the realm of arising and ceasing.
If one first attains awakening and subsequently practices,
this is the merit of no-merit.
Merit is never lost;
thus, Master Rong’s *Inscription on Faith in Mind* says:
"If you wish to attain purity of mind..."
There is no need for deliberate effort.
Furthermore, how could one who possesses the eye of wisdom allow themselves to give rise to such presumptuous arrogance?
How much more so for one who possesses clear vision,
who will never fall into a ditch or pit;
whereas those who are blind in their meditation and rely on dark, obscure realizations—
How can those of deluded wisdom who merely follow the literal text understand the six identities?
How could they recognize the single mind?
Now, simply first cause perfect faith to be free from doubt;
you will then naturally abide in the stage of contemplative practice.
As the ancients said:
"It can be accomplished in a single lifetime;
how could this be empty talk?
One must by no means delude one's nature while pursuing cultivation, or cling to expedient means to the detriment of the ultimate reality."
Abandoning the root to pursue the branches,
they recognize the delusory while neglecting the real;
they rely upon the conventional designations of worldly truth.
Grasping at beginningless habitual tendencies,
one attempts to establish definitive principles through words and sets forth interpretations to clarify the fundamental tenets.
It is consistently in accord with sensory objects and turned away from fundamental enlightenment,
as an ancient said:
How many years will it take for delusive sentiments to be drawn away?
One fails to repay the single point of light within the *lingtai*.
Furthermore, the Great Master Zhenjue sang:
Upon awakening, one immediately comprehends;
no effort need be exerted.
This is unlike all conditioned phenomena.
Giving with attachment to marks produces the merit for rebirth in heaven;
it is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the sky:
once its momentum is exhausted, [it falls].
The arrow falls back down,
bringing about an unfavorable future life;
how can this compare to the gate of the unconditioned true mark?
Leap directly into the stage of the Tathāgata.
Simply attain the root;
do not worry about the branches.
Like a pure lapis lazuli gem containing a precious moon,
one who can understand this wish-fulfilling jewel will never cease bringing benefit to oneself and others; such a person is like one of great merit in the world.
Within the hidden treasure,
he obtained a maṇi jewel;
it was naturally polished and refined by various means.
Thereupon, treasures naturally rain down;
how much more so for one who has awakened their mind and attained the Way—
it is likewise thus.
Having entered the stage of Buddhahood,
it is the natural law that one is adorned by the myriad practices,
and compassion and wisdom proceed in uninterrupted succession.
As stated in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
a Bodhisattva on the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā-bhūmi),
is like a great maṇi jewel.
There are ten kinds of natures.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Ten Stages":
"O Son of the Buddha..."
For example, there is a great maṇi jewel that possesses ten qualities and surpasses all other precious gems.
What are these ten?
First, they emerge from the great ocean.
Second, skillful craftsmanship;
third, governance.
Fourth, it is perfectly complete and without deficiency;
it is pure and free from defilement.
Fifth, his internal and external [body] is transparently clear. Sixth, [his body is perfectly proportioned].
Skillfully drilled through;
seventh, threaded with precious cords.
Eighth, place it atop a tall banner of lapis lazuli. Ninth, [place it atop a tall banner of crystal].
Tenth, they can universally emit all manner of various radiances and act in accordance with the King’s intentions.
They rain down various precious objects,
fulfilling the aspirations of sentient beings according to their respective minds.
O Son of the Buddha,
you should know that a bodhisattva...
It is likewise so.
There are ten matters that transcend all the holy ones.
What are the ten? First, generating the mind of omniscience.
Second, they maintain the precepts and practice the dhūtas,
their correct conduct being bright and pure.
Third, the various dhyānas and samādhis are complete and without deficiency.
Fourth, their conduct on the path is pure and white,
being free from all defilements and impurities.
Fifth, the supernormal power of skillful means,
which is transparently clear both internally and externally.
Sixth, they are well able to penetrate the wisdom of dependent origination. Seventh, [they are well able to penetrate the wisdom of the cessation of suffering].
It is threaded with the thread of various skillful means and wisdom. Eighth,
it is placed atop the high banner of sovereign mastery.
Ninth, observing the conduct of sentient beings,
he emits the light of hearing and retaining.
Tenth: having received the office of Buddha-wisdom, they fall within the number of Buddhas and are able to act for the sake of sentient beings.
Thus they extensively perform Buddha-works.
Therefore, we know that awakening to the Way is like obtaining a pearl;
how could there not be matters such as polishing, refining, and adorning it?
Question:
If one does not possess supernormal powers (ṛddhi),
by what means will one gather and transform sentient beings?
Answer: If one were to grasp solely at the phenomenal characteristics of supernatural powers,
it would contradict the true course.
As stated in the *Fuxingji* (Record of the Auxiliary Practice):
"One who cultivates samādhi may suddenly manifest supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)."
One must urgently abandon them,
for these tainted phenomena are false and illusory.
Therefore, the *Zhiguan* says:
"What is it that can obstruct prajñā? Why is this so?"
The Prajñā of the Knowledge of All Modes inherently possesses all dharmas and is able to dissolve all marks.
As long as one has not yet attained full realization,
one should simply rest in principle;
why must one seek correspondence with phenomena?
If one is exclusively intent upon penetration,
this constitutes an obstruction to principle;
moreover, it does not merely obstruct principle.
On the contrary, they will suffer calamity themselves,
just like the followers of Udraka Rāmaputra; such is their kind.
Now, as for what is called "true and real spiritual transformation," it is none other than the unfolding of the gateway of the One Vehicle and the discourse on the principle of non-arising.
A single word accords with the Way;
while facing birth and death, one realizes nirvana.
Witnessing it directly, one clarifies the fundamental principle.
One attains perfect enlightenment within the very midst of worldly afflictions;
in a single kṣaṇa, one transforms from an ordinary being into a sage;
in a mere moment, one changes existence so that it returns to emptiness.
Is such an activity not indeed a miraculous transformation?
Therefore, the Ratnakūṭa Sūtra says:
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
as for one who preaches the Dharma..."
This constitutes a great supernatural manifestation. As for those of inferior faculties and capacity:
The great compassion of all Buddhas does not allow anyone to be abandoned in isolation.
Their various skillful means are like using yellow leaves to stop a child's crying.
As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"One transforms ignorant sentient beings through the wisdom of supernormal powers;
as for those of the highest faculties,"
One is simply to contemplate the true mark of the body;
contemplating the Buddha is likewise so.
This was as when, in the past, Prince Pengcheng questioned various venerable masters.
If you would deign to realize the fruit and thus become a noble one (ārya),
let water flow from your left armpit for me.
From his right armpit, fire issued forth;
he soared into the void,
emitting light that shook the earth.
I immediately prostrated to you and took you as my teacher.
Great Master Niutou Rong replied,
"Excellent, excellent!"
This is inconceivable.
If I were now to be held accountable for attaining such a fruit of realization,
I fear it would deviate from the Way.
If it is truly so that one becomes a Buddha in this manner,
then even a magician could become a Buddha;
let the various virtuous ones and the assembled witnesses bear witness to this.
In the past, when Śākyamuni was among the Saṃgha expounding the unsurpassed path,
he was no different from the Saṃgha.
Vimalakīrti, while remaining in the secular world, expounded the fruit of liberation;
he was no different from the laity.
The woman Śrīmālā expounded the Mahāyāna Dharma.
The female characteristics do not change;
yet the bhikṣu Śunakṣatra practices the conduct of an icchantika.
The monastic characteristics do not shift.
This is based precisely on the distinction between whether one's inner mind understands or does not understand;
what concern has it with the physical body?
Regarding the physical appearances of men and women,
and the beauty or ugliness of their clothing:
if one says that form changes according to what is realized, [then this would be so].
If it were the case that one becomes a sage through the transformation of appearance as awakening progresses,
then Gautama’s physical form would have had to change before he could become Śākyamuni.
When Vimalakīrti passed away,
he became a Golden Grain Buddha;
thus we know that this realization is the realization of the mind itself.
It is not that the form has transmigrated;
it is the awakening that undergoes transformation.
It does not concern a difference in appearance.
For example, it is like a person in the world who has been appointed to an office;
when his rank is changed,
how could his appearance suddenly differ simply because his office is higher?
Furthermore, an ancient said:
"The person of former times is not changed;
only their conduct and practice are changed."
Even if forms are altered and substances transformed,
undergoing a thousand changes and myriad mutations,
all are produced by this single mind.
Even unto the exercise of supernormal powers,
they appear and disappear with mastery,
transforming the small into the large.
To expand the brief into the long—
how could this occur apart from within the single mind?
Thus we know that there is not a single thing among the myriad phenomena that does not arise from the mind.
One merely realizes one's own mind and becomes a sage in the instant; yet,
if one does not recognize the Way, [this will not occur].
What is the use of possessing the marks?
Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"If one were to view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks..."
The Wheel-Turning Sage King is none other than the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, a verse says:
Those who see me by means of form,
or seek me by means of sound,
these people follow a deviant path.
One cannot see the Tathāgata.
An ancient said:
"If one does not penetrate this principle..."
Even if one steps upon lotus flowers at every stride,
it is still the work of Māra.
As the Layman Pang said in verse:
Seeking the Buddha-way through forms and sounds results in becoming a demon instead.
If one were to resolutely grasp at the superior marks of supernatural powers to become a Buddha, [one would likewise fail].
Not only do illusory beings become sages;
even celestial Māras, non-Buddhist practitioners,
and malevolent foxes or spirits may do so.
Ghosts, spirits, dragons, and mist-dragons—
all shall attain Buddhahood;
they all possess the five supernormal powers resulting from karmic retribution.
Because they are all capable of transformation,
if one does not examine each one against the true mark (lakṣaṇa),
how can one distinguish the genuine from the counterfeit?
Provided that one first awakens to the Mirror of the Source (Zongjing),
so that the Dharma-eye becomes perfectly clear and bright,
what principle would not be penetrated?
What matter is not thoroughly penetrated?
All Buddha-activities, as gateways for gathering and transforming beings,
are spontaneously accomplished.
As stated in the *Huayan lun*:
The Sūtra says,
"Entering into profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)."
Those who have attained the supernormal powers of a Buddha accord their minds with the fundamental principle; thus,
they possess no essence of entering or exiting.
It has no essence of stillness or agitation;
it has no nature of contrivance;
it is spontaneously true in accordance with principle.
Neither arising nor ceasing,
its principle accords with true wisdom;
its nature is inherently all-pervasive.
Throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions,
he simultaneously and universally responds by manifesting his form-body.
He transforms the multitudes in accordance with their wisdom and capacities,
yet there is no coming or going,
nor is there any transformation.
This is called the Buddha’s supernormal power. Wisdom has no basis;
it is formless and colorless.
Its essence has no coming or going;
its nature is inherently all-pervasive;
it is not encompassed by the three periods of time.
To be able to universally respond to the dharmas of the three periods of time is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
Therefore, the sutra says:
Wisdom enters the three periods of time,
yet there is no coming or going,
because these three periods are falsely established by the sentiments of sentient beings.
Because it is not substantially existent,
its essence as wisdom is formless and colorless;
it neither constructs nor acts.
Responding to the various classes of beings,
it is called "spiritual" (shen);
it fills the ten directions in their entirety.
There is nothing that is not known;
there is no root that is not discerned.
This is called "penetration" (abhijñā).
Furthermore, it says:
The Lotus Sūtra states,
"The meanings of various natures and characteristics."
I and the Buddhas of the ten directions alone can know this matter;
the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot.
Even the non-regressive bodhisattvas are entirely unable to know them;
these are precisely the Three Vehicles at the gateway.

Because they have not yet understood that the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding, and that this is the established nature of phenomena (dharmasthititā) within the station of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
The three vehicles equally feel revulsion toward suffering and its origin,
and possess the desire to cultivate cessation and the path;
yet they have not yet clearly understood suffering and its origin.
Fundamentally, it is only the arising of wisdom;
it does not perceive cessation or the path.
Fundamentally, it is itself without cultivation, without creation, and without action.
They transform all classes of beings,
dwelling in the world like a phantom;
their nature is utterly free from ignorance.
Because this is precisely the Buddha:
"In a single thought-moment of correspondence, one is a Buddha;
in a single day of correspondence, one is a Buddha."
Why must one labor so hard for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*?
One need only personally realize the karma of the triple world and be able to empty the locus of that karma.
Spontaneously receiving and giving birth is itself the Buddha;
why must there be transformation?
If one becomes a Buddha through dialects,
and dragons and devas undergo transformation,
would they not then be Buddhas as well?
The persons of the three vehicles also undergo transformation;
why is it that they must wait for Buddhas over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before achieving [enlightenment]?
This is because above the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), [there is no further progress].
Only then can one see one's nature.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"If, by means of the great supernatural power of the nature of form..."
Yet those who desire to see the Tamer of Men possess clouded vision and distorted perception.
He does not recognize the most supreme Dharma; such a person is called a Buddha.
It is awakening.
Awakening to the true nature of karma,
one realizes that karma is without arising or ceasing.
There is nothing to be attained and nothing to be realized;
there is no emerging and no submerging;
its nature is without change.
Because the original suchness is itself the Buddha, it follows conditions to manifest within the six realms of existence.
Practicing the bodhisattva path,
he employs transformative supernatural powers to guide and lead those wandering in delusion.
The Buddha is not a transformation body.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"Although he has attained perfect enlightenment..."
They turn the wheel of Dharma without abandoning the path of the bodhisattva,
for this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
With this wealth of goodness, Sudhana,
at the beginning of the first stage of the ten stages,
[sought instruction] from the bhikṣu Meghashiri on Mount Sumerukalpa.
He attained the Dharma-door of the Wisdom-Light that Universally Perceives the Realms of All Buddhas through Mindfulness;
he then immediately attained Perfect Enlightenment.
Only thereafter did he go to his former friends to seek the Bodhisattva path.
When practicing the bodhisattva path,
one should know that at the moment of realizing the essence and function of perfect enlightenment,
the mind is in a state of non-action.
Since he is already a Buddha,
there is no need for cultivation; even if he were to fulfill his practice, it would be superfluous.
Nor does it shift to the present.
Thus, it is like when a transformation Buddha manifests the signs of attaining enlightenment,
such as practicing asceticism with hemp and wheat.
Shaving the hair, wearing the robes,
relinquishing all ornaments and finery,
and using grass mats for a seat— such matters.
In order to transform non-Buddhists,
the Buddha himself reconciled these matters within the sūtras;
it was not that the Buddha himself required such practices.
For one who is free from overweening pride,
why would such [effort] be necessary?
In a single thought-moment, rest in the nature of non-action.
When the Buddha’s wisdom manifests before one,
there is neither attainment nor realization;
this itself is the Buddha.
It is just as when Sudhana, after realizing awakening,
only then sought the path to bodhi and the practices of a bodhisattva.
The reason for this is that only after awakening to the Way is one able to enter the bonds of worldly entanglement and dwell among the laity without being fettered.
Only then can one preach the Dharma for sentient beings to untie their bonds;
if one is oneself bound,
how could one untie the bonds of others?
This is impossible, because when [the Buddha] speaks, the preceding and succeeding moments are of a single temporal nature.
One should know that if one wishes to practice the bodhisattva path,
one must first achieve perfect awakening.
Furthermore, a verse from a sutra says:
"Mañjuśrī’s Dharma is always thus" means that Mañjuśrī is the wisdom of all Buddhas,
