One does not crave attachment to the form-body,
nor does one cling to the dharma-body.
One who well knows all phenomena to be eternally quiescent like space,
and encourages others to practice accordingly.
If a person desires to attain wisdom as vast as the great ocean,
such that no one can act as their teacher, [they should practice this].
While sitting here, without exercising supernatural powers,
they see all the Buddhas and hear everything they preach.
One who is able to receive and uphold all of these constantly practices samādhi regarding all meritorious qualities.
This samādhi is the most supreme;
it is the mother of all Buddhas.
Buddha-eye. Buddha-father.
Unborn Great Compassionate Mother.
All Tathāgatas arise from these two dharmas;
they shatter the earth of the great trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, the grasses and trees are reduced to dust;
each particle of dust constitutes a single Buddha-field.
These worlds are filled with jewels.
The merit gained from practicing such giving is very great;
yet it does not equal that of hearing this samādhi without being startled or afraid.
How much more so for those who believe, accept, uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others;
how much more so for those who practice with a concentrated mind for even as long as it takes to milk a cow.
How much more so, then, can one accomplish this samādhi?
Therefore, it is immeasurable and boundless.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
The fires at the end of an eon, officials, thieves, and enemies;
venomous dragons, beasts, and various maladies—
none of these shall invade this person.
This is impossible. Such a person is constantly protected and remembered by the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings,
as well as by all the Buddhas, who all together praise them.
All desiring to see him together,
they came to his place;
if they hear this samādhi, [they shall likewise attain it].
One rejoices in all the merits of the four preceding instances.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time likewise rejoice.
Furthermore, there are four subsequent instances of even more supreme merit.
If one does not cultivate such dharmas,
one will lose immeasurable and precious treasures,
causing gods and humans to grieve and lament for them.
It is like a person with a nasal obstruction who holds sandalwood but cannot smell it;
or like a son of a farmer.
To trade a mani jewel for a single ox demonstrates that those who do not recognize their own mind as Buddha instead seek the Dharma elsewhere.
To turn one's back on the Way while practicing cultivation,
the fault is as described above;
it is precisely because ordinary beings do not realize the treasure of the mind.
They drink poison while feasting upon humans and devas;
the followers of the Two Vehicles distance themselves from the treasures of the household,
seeking instead the wages of a dung-remover.
Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says:
"If those with wisdom hear it,
they will be able to believe and understand."
If there is ignorance, doubt, or regret,
one will suffer eternal loss.
Question:
Now, regarding the gateway to attaining Buddhahood,
if one discusses the cultivation of goodness,
there is a sequence of before and after.
If it were inherently good,
the fundamental one mind would be equal;
yet since all Buddhas possess inherent evil, [it cannot be so].
Even icchantikas possess the nature of goodness;
since they share this same nature,
all shall together attain Buddhahood.
Why is it that icchantikas do not attain Buddhahood?
Answer: If one speaks of "Buddha by nature," [then they do not attain it].
Who is not equal? If judged by the accomplishment through cultivation,
the icchantika has not yet attained it.
Tiantai Teachings.
Question:
Regarding icchantikas and Buddhas.
What kind of wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas] are severed? Answer:
The icchantika severs all cultivated wholesome dharmas, though the innate wholesome [dharmas] remain.
The Buddha has severed all evil of cultivation,
yet the evil of nature remains.
Question:
The icchantika does not sever their inherent goodness,
and thus they can still be led to cultivate and give rise to wholesome qualities;
the Buddha does not sever his inherent evil.
Does this not cause them to cultivate evil and give rise to it?
Answer: The icchantikas do not realize that their nature is inherently good.
Because they do not understand this,
they are once again defiled by the wholesome; through the cultivation of the wholesome, [wholesome states] arise.
It extensively cures all evils.
Although the Buddha does not sever inherent evil,
he is able to penetrate it.
Because he has realized evil, he attains mastery over it;
therefore, he is not defiled by evil.
Because evil has been cultivated so as not to arise,
the Buddha is forever free from further evil;
this is due to his mastery.
He extensively employs various gates of unwholesome dharmas to transform and deliver sentient beings,
utilizing them throughout the entire day.
Throughout the day, one remains unstained.
Because one is unstained,
one does not give rise [to afflictions].
How can the icchantika be taken as an example?
If an icchantika were able to comprehend this distinction between good and evil,
they would no longer be called an icchantika.
If, relying on another person’s instruction, an icchantika who has severed all roots of goodness is perfumed by the ālayavijñāna,
they can once again give rise to wholesome states.
The ālaya is precisely the indeterminate ignorance that serves as the support for both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
It serves as the seed for all things;
because the icchantikas do not sever their indeterminate ignorance,
they are able to give rise to wholesome states once again.
The Buddha has severed and exhausted all indeterminate ignorance;
since there is nothing left to be perfumed,
evil no longer arises again.
If one wishes to transform beings through evil means,
one should merely manifest supernatural powers and transformations to deliver sentient beings.
Question: If,
in the stage of Buddhahood, all evil has been utterly severed,
how can one employ supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to transform sentient beings through that which is evil?
It is only through this mental attention that evil can arise;
it is not something that occurs spontaneously, just as when a person paints various forms and images.
Just as a bright mirror remains unmoving while forms and images appear of their own accord,
so too can this inconceivable principle respond to evil.
If one were to engage in mental attention [in this way],
how would it differ from that of the non-Buddhists? Answer:
Now it is clarified that the icchantika does not sever the goodness of their inherent nature;
when they encounter conditions, this goodness is activated.
Likewise, the Buddha also does not sever his inherent evil.
Stirred by karmic conditions and permeated by the power of compassion,
one enters Avīci.
One transforms sentient beings through all manner of evil deeds;
because there exists the nature of evil,
it is called "uninterrupted."
There is no further cultivation of evil;
this is called "not permanent.
If both cultivation and nature are exhausted, [it is called extinction].
This is then a cessation;
it cannot be characterized as neither-ceasing-nor-eternal.
It is the same with the icchantika.
The inherent goodness is uninterrupted,
and thus wholesome roots are regenerated.
The inherent evil of the Tathāgata is likewise uninterrupted.
Though they may still give rise to evil,
this mind of understanding remains undefiled;
it penetrates the limit of evil as being itself the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
One is able to attain liberation through the five heinous acts;
moreover, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
One traverses what is not the path yet penetrates the Buddha-way.
The icchantika is stained but does not penetrate;
this is what distinguishes them from the former.
What is meant by "not penetrating"?
Because they do not understand the absence of intrinsic nature,
all dharmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome,
have this very absence of intrinsic nature as their nature.
This nature is precisely the Buddha-nature;
it is the foundation of non-abiding.
Because it is the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
this nature of good and evil cannot be severed.
If one now investigates the nature of one's own mind, it cannot be apprehended;
thus, it has no place of abiding,
yet it is able to pervade all places.
This is the nature of good and evil.
The nature itself is neither good nor evil,
yet it is capable of producing both good and evil.
Good and evil can be severed,
but the nature cannot be severed.
Good and evil both take the mind-nature as their nature.
If one were to sever inherent evil,
one would thereby sever the nature of the mind;
yet, this nature cannot be severed.
Therefore, although icchantikas do not sever their innate goodness,
even if they fall into the three miserable realms,
their innate goodness does not diminish.
The inherent evil does not increase until one attains Buddhahood;
the inherent good likewise does not increase.
The inherent evil does not diminish;
this nature is itself the Dharmakāya,
just like a bright mirror.
Fundamentally, there are no images of beauty or ugliness;
yet it can manifest all manner of beautiful and ugly images,
and these images may increase or decrease.
The essence of luminous purity neither increases nor decreases;
the mirror originally has no images.
Therefore, it can manifest images.
Buddha-nature is neither good nor evil,
yet it can manifest both good and evil.
Sentient beings do not attain their true nature;
they merely attain good and evil,
and are thus constrained by good and evil.
They do not attain mastery.
Because their nature is good and indestructible,
the Buddha-realm arises from within hell as goodness.
The nature of evil is indestructible;
therefore, the Buddha can manifest the evils of the six realms of existence.
Furthermore, as for "nature":
This is the nature of all phenomena, such as good and evil,
which pervades all places throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, including sentient beings and their lands.
It is without change, neither increasing nor decreasing, yet it can manifest all things,
such as good and evil, ordinary beings and sages, defilement and purity, cause and effect, and so forth.
They arise from nature;
therefore, it is said that nature is both good and evil.
If [one asks] whether they are good, evil, or otherwise—
Thus, there is no fixed characteristic;
it is formed through conditioning according to conditions,
like a reflection in a mirror.
No substantial entity can be found.
If it encounters pure conditions, it is wholesome;
if it arises from defiled conditions, it is unwholesome.
They are obtained through cultivation;
therefore, they are called "cultivated good" and "cultivated evil.
If one discusses goodness by nature, however, [the case is different].
It is not only the icchantikas;
if one discusses the evil of nature,
it is not only the Buddhas.
Because this is the nature of all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas,
all sentient beings possess it in its entirety.
It is equal in its single limit.
If one awakens to and realizes this nature,
one immediately becomes a Buddha.
Therefore, they are able to manifest as sages or appear as ordinary beings with sovereign and unimpeded freedom.
If one discusses the cultivation of good or the cultivation of evil:
Regarding superior, middling, and inferior faculties,
these cannot be fixed; they depend on the thickness or thinness of one's cultivation and realization.
Depending on the depth or shallowness of one's capacity,
one receives worldly retribution and ascends or sinks through the six realms;
or one achieves supramundane fruition and ranks among the four types of noble beings.
Because they do not understand the nature of good and evil,
they are constrained by the karma of good and evil and lack self-mastery.
If one perceives the nature and penetrates the Way,
what Way would not be accomplished?
Thus, every dharma marks the fundamental principle.
If every particle accords with the ultimate principle,
how could it be that mastery is attained only through the two dharmas of good and evil?
Question:
The Three Jewels have the characteristic of space;
they are beyond the reach of seeing or hearing.
How is the path of seeing (darśanamārga) explained in the teachings?
Furthermore, it is also called "seeing the Buddha. Answer:
Revealed through the fundamental wisdom,
it is conventionally designated as "seeing," yet it is not something perceived by the physical eye.
Only through direct realization can one know it;
only by departing from both seeing and non-seeing is it called true seeing.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"A bodhisattva truly has nothing to see.
That which is 'nothing to see'..."
That is simply non-existence.
That which is non-existent is all phenomena.
Therefore, because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is non-existent,
the bodhisattva has nothing to perceive;
thus they accord with the principle of phenomena.
It is provisionally called "view," but in reality it is not a view;
the true nature is profoundly still and serene.
This is not a matter of seeing dharmas.
As the Sūtra says:
"One does not practice the seeing of dharmas."
That all Buddhas swiftly bestow upon one the prediction of enlightenment means that one has departed from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism,
and thus directly perceives the purity of one's own body.
To see the purity of the body is to see the purity of the Buddha,
and so on, up to seeing all dharmas.
All are entirely pure;
there is nothing that is not the Buddha,
and nothing that is not the Dharma.
Because the nature of one's own mind is unborn and conforms to all things throughout all places;
if even a single atom were not the Buddha, [it would contradict this].
This constitutes a veiling obstruction;
one does not enter the gateway of the Universal Eye,
but merely falls into the dualistic view of subject and object.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
Brahmā asked the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati,
"O son of good family..."
"Do you now clearly see the Buddha-dharma?
Brahmā replied,
"The Buddha-dharma is not form."
It cannot be seen.
How can you say that you see the Buddha-dharma clearly? All dharmas...
All are invisible.
That which is clearly understood is itself the Buddha-dharma.
There are no two distinct characteristics;
thus, their coming is like the moon reflected in water,
and their dispersal is like illusory clouds.
Seeing is like a dream-form;
hearing is like an echo in a valley.
They manifest immediately upon the arising of awareness.
It does not come from any direction;
it is inherently non-existent in the place of delusion.
It does not go from here.
As the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says:
"Perfect enlightenment shines universally;
it is quiescent and extinguished, without duality."
Within these hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of unspeakable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
they arise and perish in disorder, like flowers in the sky.
The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Verses on the Provisional Designation of Prajñā) states:
"The Tathāgata has the Dharma as his body;
one should contemplate only the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)."
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not an object of vision,
yet it cannot be known [as such] either.
As for this "nature of phenomena":
That which is called emptiness and the nature of non-arising is the ultimate body (paramārthakāya) of all Buddhas.
If one perceives this,
it is called seeing the Buddha.
As the sutra says:
To perceive emptiness is called seeing the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, it is the locus of the dharma-nature.
There is not a single thing that can be designated as an object of knowledge; therefore,
that wisdom, too, is unable to know.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
"Great King,
the nature of all phenomena..."
Just like space, it is equal toward all things and serves as their basis of reliance.
Yet its essential nature is neither a thing that exists nor a thing that does not exist.
To know that within this there is quiescent non-knowing is called "thorough understanding."
They are called "knowers" by way of conventional discourse;
they believe in and understand the merit of non-arising.
It is more meritorious than giving material wealth. As a verse says:
"If a person upholds the True Dharma..."
Even the generation of the bodhicitta is not worth even a sixteenth part of understanding emptiness.
Therefore, by resolving upon the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*),
one then accomplishes *prajñā* and perceives the self-nature of non-arising.
Thus one first realizes the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong):
because true emptiness does not destroy karmic retribution,
the distinctions between the noble and the humble remain perfectly distinct.
They are not the same; mere emptiness does not encompass all that exists.
As the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says:
"There is karma and there is its retribution."
Not perceiving a creator—
such dharmas as these are called the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Therefore, at the time of seeing one's nature,
the nature is fundamentally free from thought;
it is not something that can be cleared away by means of thought.
When contemplating things,
things are fundamentally formless;
it is not that there are things which can be dispensed with.
Therefore, it is said that the wisdom free from conceptual thought is equal to the realm of empty space.
As stated in the Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Great King of Teachings of the Thousand Bowls:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha entered the samādhi of the Vairocana Tathāgata’s Vajradharmagarbha-samādhi,
causing all bodhisattvas to [do so as well].
Together with all sentient beings, they shall cultivate and maintain this in common,
entering the Samādhi of the True Limit of the Dharma-Treasury of Innately Pure Suchness.
How should one practice to enter this contemplation?
The bodhisattva should then contemplate the ground of the mind and awaken the wisdom of mental activity.
Illuminating only the nature of the mind,
observe and perceive it subtly;
perceive and illuminate the essence of the mind.
Seeing that nature is immovable and realizing awakening as unmoving,
one is then able to employ it constantly.
By employing the wisdom of the essence through contemplation,
one perceives that the nature is pure;
this nature is inherently free from discursive thought.
Free from conceptualization, there is no object;
the mind is equal to empty space,
and one immediately realizes noble wisdom.
In accordance with suchness and the noble nature,
both are tranquil and still;
they are empty, identical, and without substance.
The essence of nature is empty and still;
this is called the Bodhisattva’s realization and entry into the seal of the nature of the *tathatā* dharmadhātu.
This is the gate of contemplation on the true limit (bhūtakoṭi) of the Dharma-treasury;
thus one knows that the nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is precisely the nature of the minds of sentient beings.
The nature of the minds of sentient beings is itself the nature of space; therefore,
the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states:
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abide in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, and great emptiness—

The emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the ultimate limit (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of that which has no beginning (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of dispersion (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena characterized by their own marks (*svalakṣaṇa-dharma-prakṛti-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the non-apprehensible (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of existence (*bhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of both non-existence and existence (*abhāva-bhāva-śūnyatā*).
"One should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
The commentary explains:
"Internal emptiness" means...
These are the internal phenomena, namely the six internal bases:
the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The eye is empty of self and of what belongs to self, and so forth.
As for external emptiness:
These are the external phenomena,
namely the six external sense bases:
forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
Form is empty, selfless,
and devoid of "mine," and so forth.
As for internal and external emptiness:
That is to say, the twelve internal and external bases (*āyatana*).
Within these twelve bases, there is no self,
no "mine," and so forth.
Regarding "emptiness of emptiness":
it uses emptiness to dismantle internal emptiness and external emptiness.
Internal-external emptiness.
Because it destroys these three kinds of emptiness,
it is called the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
The great emptiness is the emptiness of the ten directions;
the eastern direction is boundless.
Therefore it is called "Great.
Furthermore, because it exists in all places,
it is called "Great."
Regarding "emptiness of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*):
the ultimate truth is named the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena,
because it is neither broken nor destroyed.
This true nature of all phenomena is also empty.
Why? Because it is without grasping and without attachment.
If the true nature of all phenomena were existent,
it should be accepted and clung to; however,
because it lacks substantial reality, it is not so.
Do not accept, do not cling.
To accept or to cling is itself falsehood and deception.
Regarding conditioned emptiness and unconditioned emptiness:
conditioned phenomena [are empty].
They are called "arisen from the conjunction of causes and conditions," namely the five aggregates (skandhas) and the twelve bases (āyatanas).
The eighteen elements and so forth, as well as unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma),
are called "without causes and conditions" (ahetupratyaya).
It is eternally neither born nor extinguished,
like empty space. Question:
Conditioned phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions;
because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty.
This may indeed be so; unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) are not phenomena produced by causes and conditions.
It is without breaking or destruction,
eternally like empty space. Why is it empty?
The answer is:
If one excludes the conditioned,
then there is no unconditioned.
The true characteristic of the conditioned is itself the unconditioned;
it is just as the conditioned is empty.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is also empty,
because these two things are not different.
As for ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*):
All dharmas are ultimately empty;
this ultimate emptiness is also empty,
because emptiness has no dharma.
Furthermore, there is no mutual dependence between the false and the real.
Moreover, "ultimate emptiness" (atyanta-śūnyatā) negates all phenomena.
Because it leaves nothing remaining,
it is called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). If there were even the slightest remainder, [it would not be ultimate emptiness].
It is not called ultimate emptiness.
Regarding beginningless emptiness,
it is as stated in the sūtra:
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Sentient beings have no beginning;
they are shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving."
The beginning of coming and going within birth and death cannot be apprehended,
for it would entail the destruction of this principle of beginninglessness.
This is called the emptiness of the beginningless.
As for "dispersal-emptiness," "dispersal" refers to the characteristic of separation.
Just as all phenomena exist through combination— for example,
there is a chariot because of the spokes, the rim, the shaft, and the hub; it is through the assembly of these many parts that there is a "chariot."
If they were separated and each existed in its own place,
the designation "chariot" would be lost;
it is through the causal conditions of the harmony of the five aggregates that [the chariot exists].
Therefore, one is called a "person.
If one is separated from the five aggregates,
a person cannot be found.
Regarding "emptiness of nature":
the nature of all phenomena is eternally empty; it is only through the provisional coming together of conditions that they appear as a continuous succession.
It appears as if not empty;
for example, the nature of water is cold by itself,
yet it becomes hot through the presence of fire.
When the fire has been extinguished for a long time,
the water returns to being cold,
as stated in the sutras.
The eye is empty, without self,
and without what belongs to a self. Why is this?
Such is its very nature.
Regarding the emptiness of self-characteristics:
all phenomena possess two kinds of characteristics.
The general characteristic and the specific characteristic are these.
The two characteristics are empty;
therefore, it is called "emptiness of characteristics.
As for the general characteristic:
Regarding [the category of] specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa), such as impermanence and so forth: although all phenomena are indeed impermanent, [they differ in their specific modes].
Yet each has its own distinct characteristic;
for example, earth has the characteristic of solidity,
and fire has the characteristic of heat.
Regarding the emptiness of all phenomena:
among all phenomena, there are those that are beautiful and those that are ugly;
there are those that are internal and those that are external.
All phenomena arise from the mind;
therefore, they are called "existent.
Yet, they lack intrinsic nature.
Therefore, it is empty. Regarding "the emptiness of non-apprehension," it refers to all phenomena.
Even up to nirvana without remainder, nothing can be apprehended;
therefore, it is called the emptiness of non-apprehension and the emptiness of non-existence.
Regarding "the emptiness of phenomena" and "the emptiness of non-phenomena and phenomena": "non-phenomena" refers to that which is not a phenomenon.
When a phenomenon has already ceased,
because that cessation itself is non-existent,
it is called the emptiness of non-phenomena (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).
Regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*):
all phenomena arise through the combination of causes and conditions;
therefore, they exist as phenomena.
Because their substantial nature does not exist,
it is called the emptiness of existing phenomena (*bhāva-śūnyatā*). As for the emptiness of non-existent and existent phenomena (*abhāva-bhāva-śūnyatā*):
The marks of non-existence and existence cannot be apprehended;
this is the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*). It continues thus:
It is empty because it is devoid of self and what belongs to self;
it is empty because it arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions;
it is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Therefore it is called "emptiness.
Because its beginning and end cannot be apprehended, it is empty;
it is mind-only.
Therefore it is called "emptiness.
Thus one knows that all phenomena arise from the mind.
All lack intrinsic nature;
they are all termed "empty.
Therefore it is said:
If one abides in these eighteen gates of emptiness and studies Prajñā,
then there has never been a single dharma [that exists].
It is able to bring forth the wisdom-nature of my spiritual platform.
These eighteen kinds of emptiness extend downward even to the five aggregates of the conditioned world.
Reaching upward to the unconditioned ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
it encompasses all phenomena (*dharma*),
none of which are not empty.
If one does not study Prajñāpāramitā but instead adheres to other schools,
one regards the essence as existent yet fails to penetrate the source of existence.
Though one may exhaustively investigate emptiness, one does not yet fully realize the principle of emptiness;
one must return to the Mirror of the Source (Zongjing) to illuminate and manifest it through inward reflection.
Thus, externally there is not a single dharma remaining as a residue;
furthermore, this is like space.
It is not that the substance itself is empty;
rather, because the true mind is unimpeded,
it reflects and manifests the myriad dharmas.
Just as space does not reject the manifestation of various forms,
so within the true mind,
all things can appear.
All that appears, although lacking intrinsic substance as it depends upon the mind,
is seen through clear illumination to be empty in its five aggregates.
Nevertheless, one does not cling even to emptiness,
yet is able to perform the Buddha-work.
As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
All the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have fully realized all phenomena without exception;
though they know that all things are empty and quiescent, [they do not abandon sentient beings].
Yet they do not give rise to mental conceptions regarding emptiness;
they adorn all things with a single adornment,
and likewise do not produce discrimination regarding phenomena.
In this way, he awakens all sentient beings;
[he realizes that] all things lack intrinsic nature and there is nothing to be observed.
Question:
Regarding the principle of the Dharma-body:
is it established by means of existing dharmas,
or is it established by means of non-existing dharmas?
Is it established by means of a single dharma,
or is it established by means of distinct dharmas? Answer:
The school of the Mind of Innate Enlightenment,
the stage of the Dharma-body’s nature-ground:
when the mouth wishes to speak, words fail.
The mind desires to take it as an object of contemplation,
yet its deliberations vanish. The reason for this is that when one speaks of its existence, its wondrous essence is empty and profound.
If one speaks of non-existence, the Dao is omnipresent;
if one speaks of arising, there is nothing within the triple world;
if one speaks of extinction, the single essence is eternally numinous.
To speak of them as one, each assumes its own form;
to speak of them as distinct, they all ultimately converge in the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Thus we know that they cannot be measured or weighed.
It cannot be attained through mere aspiration.

Furthermore, these ten pāramitās can be attained through the mind;
they are the relinquishment of a single moment of thought in accord with reality.
Thus, one possesses the ten perfections.
To relinquish without grasping is giving;
to remain unsullied by all that is non-virtuous is discipline.
This is precisely morality.
To accept that which is non-conditioned is patience.
To be free from the marks of body and mind is diligence.
Quiescence and non-movement constitute *samādhi*;
the definitive realization of non-arising constitutes *prajñā*;
and while being empty, not obstructing the appearance of cognition constitutes *upāya*.
Aspiring for the fruit of Buddhahood is aspiration;
discerning without wavering is power;
and decisive clarity is wisdom.
In a single thought within the square inch of the heart,
the ten perfections are suddenly perfected.
Thus, it is said in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra:
The Bodhisattva of the seventh stage is fully endowed with the ten pāramitās in every thought-moment; thus,
when these ten perfections are perfected, [the eighth stage is attained].
The eighty-four thousand Dharma gates respond simultaneously and in unison;
such is what is called the ancestral teaching.
Whether shallow or deep,
as long as one applies it to the mind,
there is no principle that will not be fully exhausted.
If one acts with the mind directed toward external phenomena,
one grasps at signs and wanders in saṃsāra,
even if one passes through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
In the end, these become mere false imaginings. Therefore, the Youth said:
"In the past, throughout countless kalpas, I..."
To give away one's national wealth, body,
and life to others countless times with a mind of delusive conceptualization is not true giving.
Today, by offering five flowers with a mind of non-arising to the Buddha,
it is for the first time that this is truly called "giving.
Thus, a verse in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
Even if one were to offer wealth and treasures to the Buddha for incalculable eons,
yet remain ignorant of the Buddha’s true nature.
This also is not called giving.
Furthermore, it says:
"Regarding all roots of goodness..."
One gives rise to the perception of one's own roots of goodness;
even regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
one gives rise to the perception of one's own practice.
Now, as for all differentiated phenomena and appearances,
whether they be vertical or horizontal objects of experience,
if one observes them upon their manifest characteristics:
Then the sequential unfolding of phenomena is difficult to clarify;
yet, if they are dissolved within the essence of the body,
all are entirely equal.
Therefore, the former masters said:
"When the myriad phenomena are driven back to their fundamental source, they are level;
right and wrong naturally merge within the mind."
Therefore, Master Fu’s verse says:
"Returning to the source,
the nature of mind neither sinks nor floats."
Abiding in the King Samādhi,
the myriad practices are all fully encompassed.
Question:
The myriad practices are solely mind;
thus, practices arise from the mind.
Such is the Dharma of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
If one practices while remaining entirely within phenomenal appearances,
how can all the various paths be subsumed and unified within this single Way?
Answer: The wondrousness of this One Vehicle within our school relies solely upon the single thought-moment of mind.
Illuminating the ultimate truth and penetrating the conventional world,
one achieves unsurpassed enlightenment;
this is called the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Why is this? Illuminating the truth, there is no principle that is not encompassed;
penetrating the conventional, there is no phenomenon that is not perfected.
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"To know all dharmas in a single thought-moment is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
for it is the accomplishment of all-knowledge."
Dharma Master Shi’s commentary states:
"The vehicle of the Two Vehicles attains enlightenment through thirty-four moments of mind."
In the Mahāyāna, one attains decisive and great awakening in a single thought-moment,
becoming endowed with all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).
Master Zhao’s commentary explains:
The All-Knowing One is the pinnacle of wisdom;
his clarity is like the dawn.
It illuminates all darknesses together;
it is as clear and still as a deep abyss.
It reflects all forms simultaneously.
To be without knowledge yet to know all that there is to know—
this can only be the All-Knowing One (Sarvajña). Why is this?
Now, where there is a mind, there are boundaries;
where there are boundaries, there are frontiers. Once these boundaries and frontiers have taken form, [conflict arises].
Then their wisdom would have limits.
If their wisdom has limits,
then what it illuminates cannot be universal.
The Perfected Person has no mind.
Having no mind, there is no enclosure.
Having no enclosure, there are no boundaries.
Since there are no boundaries to his domain,
his wisdom is boundless; since his wisdom is boundless, [he is truly a sage].
Thus, that which is illuminated is boundless;
therefore, in a single thought-moment and at a single time,
one must necessarily know all dharmas.
Furthermore, as for the "site of practice" (dojō):
the principle of true reality (shissō) pervading all is the "field," and the universal realization through the myriad practices is the "path."
Thus, there is nowhere the Way does not reach,
and nowhere it is not present.
If one can embrace the site of enlightenment (dojang) within the breast, [the Way will be realized].
For one who has cast all worldly entanglements outside of themselves,
even though their physical form remains amidst the clamor and their traces are close to worldly affairs, [they remain detached].
Wherever one travels while riding upon movement,
there is nothing that is not a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Thus, the *Canyao jing* (Sūtra on the Essentials of Dhyāna) says:
The Bodhisattva Abandoning All Obscurations addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
I have heard that the Tathāgata sat at the site of enlightenment."
Where does the Way reside?
Is it near or far? And can it be seen?
The Buddha said,
"Good son, the Dharma-body is all-pervasive."
There is nothing that is not a Buddha-field;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
the five aggregates are the vihāras.
The emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself free from attachment; this is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Why, then, do you ask whether it is near or far?
Good son, if one can awaken to and understand that the Way resides within body and mind.
Such a person is said to have "vision.
As the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra* states:
Mañjuśrī said, "World-Honored One,
all sentient beings are the site of enlightenment."
This is the mark of immovability.
Mañjuśrī, why is this matter called the mark of immovability?
"Bhagavān, what is the meaning of 'place of enlightenment' (bodhimaṇḍa)?"
Mañjuśrī, all phenomena have the characteristic of quiescence; they are without characteristics.
The characteristic of non-arising;
the characteristic of non-existence;
the characteristic of being ungraspable.
This is the meaning of "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa),
World-Honored One.
All sentient beings...
"Do they not enter this maṇḍala?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
Therefore, World-Honored One,
all sentient beings are the site of enlightenment;
this is called the mark of immovability.
A verse from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"In this way, all these lords among men,
according to their respective spheres of experience..."
In a single thought-moment, one realizes all things,
yet does not abandon the practice of bodhi.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
In a single moment of mind,
one awakens to all phenomena,
exhaustively and without remainder.
This wondrous Bodhi is now likewise unimpeded by the phenomenal marks of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
for it is eternally true as the very Dharma itself.
Marks exist within the markless;
there is no phenomenon outside of principle.
The markless exists within marks.
Furthermore, when the signless resides within signs,
concealment and manifestation occur simultaneously;
when signs reside within the signless, [the same applies].
Thus, emptiness and existence are of one and the same limit.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"Although one cultivates the Pure Land..."
His mind is equanimous,
like empty space; though he practices at the site of enlightenment, [he remains thus].
Having understood that the three realms are without any distinct characteristics,
one thus acts in accordance with phenomena without losing the underlying principle.
Illuminating principle without abandoning phenomena;
phenomena and principle are without obstruction.
The Way lies in the middle.
Therefore, observing the Honored Master,
he established ten pure lands within the gateway of the one mind and accomplished ten kinds of Tathāgatas.
Seated at ten kinds of bodhimandas,
he expounds ten kinds of Dharma gates:
first, the Vajra Tathāgata.
Abiding in the Vajra Maṇḍala,
he is able to expound the Vajra Dharma-gate through his own mental wisdom.
Behold the nature of my mind:
from the very beginning, this mind has forever been devoid of all marks.
It is like space: serene and unmoving;
such is the mind that clearly perceives.
He is named Vajra Tathāgata.
Regarding the Vajra Dharma-gate he taught,
as it says in a verse of the sutra:
The bodhisattva’s mind of wisdom is as pure as space;
it is without intrinsic nature and without a place of dependence.
All things are unattainable.
Regarding what are called the ten pure lands,
as the sutra says:
The lands of the ten directions are all like empty space;
these are the two Tathāgatas of Liberation.
Abiding in the place of non-attachment,
they are able to expound the dharma-gate of non-attachment regarding both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The characteristics of all phenomena arise entirely from the mind;
there is nothing that is not the mind.
If that which arises from the mind itself lacks even a substantial essence or characteristic,
how could the various phenomena arising in dependence upon the mind possess them?
There is a substantial reality;
that is, essence and attributes are of one flavor, without distinction.
What is there to be attached to?
This is called the Tathāgata’s teaching on the Dharma-gate of non-attachment.
As the treatise states:
"All phenomena arise from the mind."
All conceptualizations are merely conceptualizing one's own mind;
the mind does not perceive the mind.
No marks can be apprehended.
The Tathāgatas of the three types of prajñā abide in the bodhimaṇḍa of non-abiding.
One is able to expound the dharma-gate of non-abiding.
As the sutra says:
"Entering into the three worlds."
The place where one dwells oneself,
and whatever places one seeks,
are forever devoid of intrinsic nature.
Therefore, one cannot abide in signs.
For this reason, it should be known that all signs [are empty].
In the dharma of non-abiding,
when following conditions,
appearances are immediately interfused.
From the root of non-abiding,
all dharmas are established;
one is thus able to understand the mind that does not abide.
The Tathāgata named Prajñā constantly expounds the Dharma-gate of Non-abiding.
The fourth is the Mahāyāna Tathāgata.
In the unimpeded place of enlightenment,
he preached the Dharma-gate of non-obstruction;
it was like space, unmoving.
It gives rise to all forms;
yet although it gives rise to all forms,
it does not exist outside of space.
Only emptiness acts as form;
form and emptiness are unimpeded,
merging into a state without dual characteristics.
The cultivation of the mind is likewise so.
There is no obstruction between principle and phenomena. Principle is the mind.
The "matter" is the body.
From the very beginning,
form and mind have been non-dual.
Thus, with body and mind unimpeded,
it is called the Mahāyāna; the Tathāgata preaches this Dharma-gate of non-obstruction.
The Tathāgata Pañcabodhi dwells in the seat of enlightenment that is signless (animitta),
and is able to expound the Dharma-gate of signlessness.
The Sūtra says:
"The four great elements have no master;
the body likewise has no self."
This state, free from the characteristics of subject and object,
is called the Buddha-body.
For one who contemplates the mind in this manner without interruption:
When one contemplates the sphere of the mind's activity and finds it to be perfectly endowed with the true mark (dharmatā),
this is called Bodhi-Tathāgata.
Because all sentient beings are themselves the characteristic of bodhi,
they are the six actualities of the Tathāgata.
Abiding in the bodhimanda of the boundless,
he is able to expound the dharma-gate of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
namely: when one perceives a small object with one's own eyes.
That object enters into the interior of the eye;
that object is extremely subtle because it has no interior.
Thus, it contains the great characteristics of the external dharma-realm;
by this, one knows that at the moment of a single kṣaṇa of mind,
when perceiving the characteristics of objects.
In the mind of the subsequent moment,
there is no objective phenomenon,
because both the preceding mind and the subsequent moment are one's own mind.
Knowing clearly that it is unmoving yet equal in measure to motes of dust,
pervading the entire dharma-realm,
this is the limit of reality of one's own mind.
Pervading all places,
the Sūtra says:
"There is the undertaking of karma and there is the performance of action."
This is precisely the work of Māra;
the six sense faculties make no progress,
and one does not practice the various dharmas.
This is called "equanimous diligence.
The Tathāgata of the Sevenfold Suchness abides eternally at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
He is able to expound the Dharma-gate of eternal abiding;
he contemplates the mind as it travels throughout the lands of the dust-motes,
remaining profoundly still and tranquil.
This concentrated and tranquil mind,
when applied to its object,
does not lose its original essence.
For this reason, throughout the limits of the future,
one encounters conditions while remaining eternally unmoved;
therefore, it is called the "ever-abiding Dharma."
As the sutra says:
"Whether a Buddha appears or not, all phenomena, both conditioned and unconditioned,"
The nature and characteristics are eternally abiding,
without change or alteration.
Thus are the Tathāgatas of the eight realms.
Abiding in the site of enlightenment within the dharma-realm,
they are able to expound the dharma-gates of the dharma-realm.
As for "dharma":
The realm of the mind of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-citta*):
this refers to the various lands that emerge based upon this mind.
Just as all things produced from the great ocean are none other than the ocean itself,
so it is with all phenomena.
All are produced from the mind of true reality;
there is nothing that is not mind.
Therefore, one should know this.
The forms seen by the eyes and the sounds heard by the ears are all the true Dharma.
Because all phenomena are but a single phenomenon.
As the sutra says:
"All phenomena have but a single characteristic."
The ninth is Dharmatā-tathāgata,
who resides at the site of enlightenment of dharmatā and expounds the dharma-gate of dharmatā.
That which does not differentiate between ordinary and sagely, or good and evil dharmas,
is called "nature" (prakṛti).
This undifferentiated dharma is identical within the *dharmadhātu*.
Layer upon layer, inexhaustible.
Within one, one understands the immeasurable,
for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inexhaustible.
The reason one knows that all are inexhaustible is that when one enters the dharma-realm and seeks each individual condition,
nothing is found throughout the limits of the future.
Tenth: The Tathāgata Nirvāṇa resides in the place of enlightenment of quiescent extinction.
One who is able to expound the dharma-gate of quiescent extinction— that all phenomena are nirvana—
and who can grasp this meaning, [is a true disciple].
Within the sphere of activity,
one perceives the dharma of quiescence;
yet one does not depart from birth and death.
One constantly attains nirvana,
yet does not abandon the impermanent body;
one eternally attains the eternal body.
The Sūtra says:
"The suchness of sentient beings is the suchness of all phenomena."
Just as there is no arising,
so too there is no cessation; for this reason.
Lifting and lowering the feet never leaves the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
In every moment of thought, one constantly performs the work of a Buddha.
Thus, one should know that this is the penetration of a single thought-moment.
All phenomena are perfectly complete;
one realizes the single mind with clarity;
every gate is fully endowed.
Thus, boundless Buddha-activities do not transcend a single atom. Furthermore,
there is the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*).
They sit pervasively in the Dharma-nature bodhimaṇḍa;
it is the Dharma-body that sits in the bodhimaṇḍa without sitting.
The Dharma-door body,
serenely seated upon the site of enlightenment of the myriad practices;
the illusory transformation body.
Sitting peacefully in the water-moon *bodhimaṇḍa*,
the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) is itself the Dharma.
The nature (dharmatā) is that which is realized,
because it is established by the realizing wisdom.
It is the locus where realization occurs.
This is the site where the Way is attained.
As for the Dharma-body:
since the Dharma-body is devoid of subject and object, it is thus.
Therefore it is said: "It is not sitting;
it is the sitting of non-sitting.
One dwells in profound stillness and peace.
This is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Regarding the body of the Dharma-gate,
it is as when it is said that giving is the site of enlightenment.
Because one does not expect a reward, etc.,
the ten thousand practices are the place where the Way is attained;
this is the *bodhimaṇḍa*.
Regarding the "illusory transformation body," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"This body of mine now..."
This is an illusory transformation body;
the locus of the path thus attained is like the moon reflected in water.
Therefore, an ancient said:
"One cultivates the myriad practices that are like flowers in the sky,
and sits peacefully within a dharma-hall that is like the moon reflected in water."
Subduing the celestial Māra as a mirror-image,
one realizes and perfects the fruit of Buddhahood within a dream;
the meaning is that this applies to both cause and fruit.
All arise from conditions,
for they are like dreams and illusions;
therefore, whether real or illusory, [they are of the same nature].
All are of one mind;
for reality is the nature of this mind,
while illusion is the appearance of this mind.
When one realizes that the perceived characteristics are empty through their causes and perceives the nature of one's own mind,
this is the place where the Way is attained.
Therefore, it is called the "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa).
For one who understands it thus,
there is nothing that is not the site of enlightenment, even within the space between raising and lowering [the hand].
Thus, in every thought-moment, one accomplishes inexhaustible Dharma-gates,
and in every thought-moment, one fully realizes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*,
as elucidated in the Tiantai teachings.
The Lotus Samādhi consists of the fourfold "oneness":
oneness of principle and oneness of teaching.
In practice, there is one person and one [practice];
in contemplation, there is one mind and the three truths;
in principle, there is one.
The three contemplations within a single mind:
practicing the one and performing the contemplations.
The person is one;
they are able to explain and contemplate the object.
The teaching is one.
Furthermore, the Dharma-body is one in principle;
so too is Prajñā.
The teaching is one;
liberation is one;
the practice is one.
The combination of these three dharmas constitutes a provisional designation:
the person is one;
this is precisely the Tathāgata of contemplative practice.
Approximately six stages of identity;
in each stage, there are four aspects of oneness within a single thought-moment.
In every thought-moment, there are four and one;
whether it be a single form or a single fragrance,
there is nothing that is not four and one.
When one practices contemplation in this manner,
what dharma is not the Lotus Samādhi? Why is this so?
For the teachings and principles are what the mind elucidates,
and human conduct is what the mind performs;
since both do not transcend the single mind.
It is said that in every atom and every thought-moment,
there is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
Question:
Since you have already spoken of "one mind" and "one body," why do you establish various bodily forms and various Dharma-gates?
Answer: This is the source of the myriad transformations and the foundation of the single truth.
It functions in accordance with conditions,
like a wish-fulfilling jewel that manifests forms in response to objects.
It is like a great round mirror,
for it can encompass all phenomena;
it is the great treasury of the Dharma.
Birth is inexhaustible;
this is the treasury of the inexhaustible.
Sublime wisdom is infinite.
This is the treasury of great wisdom;
all phenomena are eternally as they are.
This is the Tathāgatagarbha.
Its fundamental nature is formless;
it is the pure Dharmakāya,
its essence in union with true emptiness.
This is the body of empty space;
its marks and embellishments are profound and mysterious.
This is the body of wondrous form.
His wondrous eloquence is inexhaustible;
this is the body of wisdom.
Its concealment and manifestation are unimpeded.
This is the body of response and transformation,
adorned with the myriad practices;
this is the body of merit.
Thought after thought is without obstruction;
this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of liberation.
Mind after mind is vast and empty.
This is the entrance into the dharma-gate of empty stillness;
it is the entrance into the dharma-gate of unimpeded mastery over the six sense faculties.
The non-arising of a single thought is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of signlessness.
Furthermore, this is the essential purport herein.
If they mutually support one another,
then they are solely vast and solely great,
unfolding without limit.
If they are mutually inclusive, they are then merely subtle and minute;
when investigated to the ultimate, they leave no trace.
This is precisely to transcend both existence and non-existence, yet without destroying existence and non-existence.
When one designates neither identity nor difference,
then the fires of the four extremes cannot burn,
and the defilements of the hundred negations cannot stain.
It merely manifests in accordance with conditions,
like an echo in a valley. Thus,
the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says:
For example, suppose there is a single person who possesses many skills;
when he runs, [he is swift].
Then he is called a runner;
if he collects and gathers, he is further called a gatherer;
if he prepares food and drink, [he is called a cook].
One who prepares food is called a cook;
if one works with timber,
one is called a craftsman.
When smelting gold and silver, one refers to them as "goldsmiths" or "silversmiths";
such is the case for this single person.
There are many names;
the Dharma is also like this:
its reality is one.
Yet it possesses many names;
thus we know that while they are divided into many according to their functions,
their essence remains eternally one in its profound stillness.
Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu said:
"There is only the single nature of knowing;
it is divided into many according to its functions."
It is not that, apart from the whole mind,
there exist separate numerical categories;
it is like a single piece of gold being fashioned into various vessels.
It is not that there is a separate substantial entity for the vessel apart from the gold;
rather, according to their functions, they are distinguished as sensation, perception, mental formations, and so forth,
each maintaining its own specific characteristic.
It can be said that there are numerical distinctions,
just as gold and its vessels are not without difference.
Although golden vessels are distinct,
they do not exist before or after one another in time;
the mental factors are likewise so.
If one says that it is definitely one [substance],
then at the time of the gold,
those various vessels should not exist.
If one asserts that they are definitively distinct,
then the vessel [of the world] should not be of a single substance; such would be the case regarding the identity or difference of mental phenomena and the mind.
One may know this by analogy. Therefore,
if one points only to the gold, one loses the vessel and thereby violates conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If one points only to the vessel, the gold is lost;
this is hidden within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Therefore, while its nature is pure, it follows along with defilement.
The entire substance becomes conventional;
this is the gate of arising and ceasing,
wherein the nature of defilement is eternally pure.
Originally pure and true is the gate of True Suchness (tathatā);
this is precisely defilement within purity.
Without obstructing the ultimate, one remains ever within the conventional;
this is purity within defilement.
Without destroying the conventional, one remains ever within the ultimate.
Therefore, there is no obstruction to the single mind;
the two truths are maintained simultaneously,
extending even to immeasurable clouds of bodies.
Although the immeasurable Dharma gates are divided according to their meanings,
they are undisturbed within the single mind.
Therefore, that to which all the sages have returned contains nothing that is not Dharma;
Dharma is precisely the mind.
Therefore, it is through the Dharma that one can attain Buddhahood.
The *Mahāpratītyasamutpādābhisamaya-sūtra* (Great Sūtra on Repaying Kindness) states:
"The Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher."
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"When I first attained the Way,
I contemplated whom I might revere."
It is worthy of praise;
nothing surpasses the Dharma,
for the Dharma is able to establish all ordinary beings and sages.
The Tiantai teachings state:
"If one contemplates the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground of the Tathāgatagarbha,
this is precisely contemplating the Tathāgata."
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body,
and mind suddenly and fully awaken,
and one attains the vision of Buddha-nature.
The three wisdoms manifest before one,
and the three bodies are fully perfected;
therefore, know that when unfolded, they become the myriad dharmas.
To roll it up is the one mind;
within the one is the immeasurable,
and within the immeasurable is the one.
As it is said in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Guṇākara:
O Son of the Buddha,
that which the Tathāgata has realized is but a single dharma.
How is it that you speak of immeasurable dharmas,
manifest immeasurable lands,
and transform immeasurable multitudes?
They manifest immeasurable sounds,
display immeasurable bodies,
and know immeasurable minds.
They manifest immeasurable supernormal powers,
universally shaking immeasurable worlds,
and display immeasurable, sublime adornments.
It displays boundless varieties of realms;
yet within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
these differentiated characteristics are entirely unfindable.
Then the Bodhisattva Virtue Chief answered in verse:
"The meaning of what the Son of the Buddha has asked— "
Profound and difficult to comprehend,
the wise are able to know this;
they always delight in the virtues of the Buddha.
For example, the nature of earth is one,
yet sentient beings each dwell upon it separately;
the earth has no thought of oneness or difference.
The Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise;
it is like the nature of fire, which, being one, can burn all things.
The flame is without discrimination;
such is the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
It is also like the great ocean, which is one.
Though waves and billows differ in myriads of ways,
the water itself possesses no such variety;
the Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise so.
It is also like the nature of wind,
which is one and can blow upon all things;
the wind has no thought of oneness or difference.
The Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise;
it is like a great cloud and thunder,
raining universally upon all lands.
As raindrops are without distinction,
so too are the qualities of all Buddhas; they are also like the single element of earth.
It can produce various kinds of sprouts;
it is not that the earth itself possesses any distinction.
Such is the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
Just as when there are no clouds to obscure it,
[the sun] shines universally throughout the ten directions;
its radiance has no diverse nature.
The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus;
it is like the moon in the sky,
which the world cannot fail to see.
It is not that the moon travels to those places;
such is the nature of all Buddhas.
They are like the Great Brahma King.
He manifests fully throughout the three thousandfold world-system,
