Answer: All ordinary beings [attain it].
Due to consciousness confronting its objects,
one falsely gives rise to attachment within the cycle of birth and death,
giving rise to the four inversions such as the notion of permanence.
Those of the two vehicles falsely seek liberation within nirvana, giving rise to the four inversions,
such as the inversion of impermanence and so forth.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
because both objects and consciousness are empty,
are able to transcend the eight inversions.
One attains the four pāramitās of true permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:
"Based on two kinds of dharmas..."
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata possesses the purity pāramitā.
The first is original self-nature purity,
because of its common characteristic.
Second is the purity of being free from defilement,
due to its superior characteristics.
There are two kinds of dharmas.
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body possesses the *pāramitā* of self.
First, it is far removed from the extremes of all non-Buddhists,
because it is free from the false conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of a self.
Second, it is far removed from the extremes of the śrāvakas,
because it is free from the conceptual proliferation of selflessness.
There are two kinds of dharmas.
The body of the Tathāgata possesses the perfection of bliss:
first, it is far removed from all suffering;
second, it is far removed from all afflictions and their habitual tendencies.
There are two kinds of dharmas by which the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body possesses the perfection of permanence:
first, the non-extinction of all conditioned activities.
Because it is free from the extreme of the view of annihilationism;
second, because it does not grasp at unconditioned nirvana,
being free from the extreme of the view of eternalism.
The Śrīmālā-sūtra states:
"World-Honored One, to perceive all conditioned phenomena as impermanent is the view of annihilation."
It is not right view.
To view nirvana as permanent is the view of eternalism.
It is not right view;
because it is a view based on false conceptualization, one forms such a view.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has realized only the secret treasury of the nirvāṇa possessing four virtues.
Question:
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"To perceive that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent is the view of nihilism, not the right view;
to perceive that nirvāṇa is permanent is the view of eternalism, not the right view."
How is it that within the teachings,
on the one hand, non-self is taught,
while on the other hand, self is also taught?
Is this not contradictory?
Answer: As for the discourse on permanence and impermanence—
"Self" and "non-self" are merely expressions of form and traces;
they are all skillful means.
Therefore, the *Zhao lun* states:
"The Bodhisattva, amidst those who cling to the notion of permanence,
expounds the teaching of impermanence."
Because when the Buddha first appeared in the world,
he immediately sought to expound the wondrous gateway of perfect permanence—
the Buddha-nature of the true self.
All non-Buddhists falsely cling to the notion of a self (ātman) that pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
This gives rise to the view of eternalism.
If one were to speak of true permanence, bliss, self, and purity,
there would be fear that it might be confused with false interpretations.
Furthermore, because one momentarily sweeps away the dust of emotional afflictions,
it is said that there is no permanence, no bliss, no self,
and no purity. Moreover, this applies to those of the Two Vehicles as well as provisional bodhisattvas.
Not understanding the secret intent of the Buddhas,
they cling to the gates of expedient means and hastily seek realization;
all of them take abiding in the principle of non-self as the ultimate goal.
The World-Honored One, further pitying those who have not yet attained realization,
then fully explained permanence, bliss, self, and purity. If there be anyone who,
regarding this ultimate teaching, [attains understanding...]
Clearly seeing the true self and Buddha-nature,
one perceives humans, wood, insects,
and dust with perfect clarity and without delusion.
Since they do not even abide in the Middle Way,
how much less could they be disturbed by the two views of permanence and impermanence, or self and non-self? Or,
even if they hear the names of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, [they do not realize them].
They merely form the understanding of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
following the words, they give rise to views and obscure their own true mind.
Thus, the medicine of "no-self" has become the disease of "self"; therefore,
one knows that the true self is difficult to discern.
It is not that they are not clear without being realized.
As the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says:
"For example, there were two men."
They became close friends;
one was a prince, and the other was poor and lowly.
In this manner, these two people went back and forth;
at that time, the poor man...
Seeing that this prince possessed a fine sword,
the most exquisite and pure of all,
he became greedily attached to it in his heart.
At a later time, the prince took this sword and fled to another country;
meanwhile, the poor man...
Later, while staying overnight as a guest in another household,
he muttered "knife, knife" in his sleep.
Those nearby heard it.
He was brought before the king.
At that time, the king asked him,
"As for what you call a 'sword'— "
"Where did you obtain it?
The man answered the king with all the aforementioned details.
"Now, Your Majesty, you may execute and dismember my body as you see fit."
Though one may try to divide his hands and feet,
and though one may desire to obtain a sword,
it is truly impossible to do so.
I and the prince have long been close friends; previously,
we were in one place together.
Although they have seen them with their own eyes,
they do not even dare to touch them with their hands,
let alone intentionally take them.
The King asked again:
"When you saw the sword,
what was its appearance like?"
He replied,
"Great King, as for what I have seen:"
"It is like the horn of a black sheep. Having heard this,
the king smiled with joy.
"Language! Go now wherever you wish;
do not give rise to anxiety or fear."
"In my storehouse, there are no such knives at all;
how much less could you have seen one from the Prince?"
At that time, the king immediately asked his ministers,
"Have you ever seen such a sword before?
Having spoken these words, he passed away.
He then installed his other son to succeed him on the throne and again questioned his chief minister.
"Have you all ever seen this sword within the royal archives?
The ministers replied:
"We have seen them before," they replied.
He questioned them again, asking,
"What do they look like?"
He replied, "Great King,
it is like the horn of a billy goat."
The king said, "In my treasuries,
where could there be such a sword? Then the four kings followed in succession.
They searched for him everywhere but could not find him.
After some time had passed,
the prince who had previously fled appeared.
Returning from that foreign land,
he came back to his own country and once again became king.
Having ascended the throne,
he again asked his ministers,
"Did you see the sword?"
They replied,
"Great King, we have all seen it."
He asked again,
"What does it look like?
He replied:
"Great King,
his complexion is pure,
like an utpala lotus."
Again, some replied,
"Its shape is like a ram's horn. Others said:
Its color was crimson,
like a mass of fire.
Furthermore, another replied:
"It is just like a black serpent.
At that time, the king laughed aloud and said, "None of you have seen the true nature of my sword."
Good son, it is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who appears in the world.
He explained the true nature of the self,
and having finished speaking, he departed,
like a prince holding a pure and wondrous sword.
Having fled to another country,
foolish ordinary people say:
"All have self, all have self.
Just as that poor man, while staying in another's house, muttered in his sleep, "knife, knife," so it is with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
He asked all the sentient beings,
"What marks do I have?
They replied:
I see my own form, as large as a thumb;
some say it is like a grain of rice,
or like a seed of foxtail millet.
Some say that the mark of self resides within the heart,
blazing like the sun; such are sentient beings.
Not knowing the characteristic of self is like various ministers who do not know the characteristics of a sword;
in this way, the Bodhisattva speaks of my Dharma.
Ordinary beings do not understand this;
they engage in various conceptual discriminations and falsely construct the notion of a self.
It is like asking about the characteristics of a knife and answering that it resembles a sheep's horn;
such are all ordinary worldlings.
False views arise in successive continuity;
in order to sever such false views,
the Tathāgata manifests himself.
He speaks of non-self,
just as a prince says to his ministers,
"In my treasury there is no such sword."
"Good son, that which the Tathāgata has today taught as the true self is called the Buddha-nature."
Such is the Buddha-nature;
in my Buddha-dharma, it is likened to a pure blade,
O son of good family.
If there is an ordinary person who can skillfully explain [this],
they are thereby in accord with the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.
If there is one who is well able to analyze and proclaim it in accordance [with the truth], [they likewise follow the path].
These should be understood as the characteristics of a bodhisattva.
Question:
Regarding the gate of the equality of emptiness.
Regarding the essential purport of the One Mind:
since both beauty and ugliness are boundless,
both ordinary beings and sages are equally perfected.
Why, then, is there a difference in the moisture they receive,
such that suffering and pleasure are not equal? Answer:
The myriad affairs are summoned by oneself;
the single principle of the mind alone remains unimpaired.
Beauty and evil arise solely from one's own thoughts.
From where else could the retribution come?
As the Dharma Master Chuan’ao said:
"It is simply because there is evil karma within."
Thus, if one externally encounters malevolent spirits and demons,
it is because internally one has given rise to unwholesome thoughts; if internally one gives rise to a wholesome mind, then externally one will meet with the Buddhas.
This shows that good and evil reside within oneself;
how could they depend on others?
Therefore, it was because of Xi Shi’s beauty that the river was loved.
That Mǔmǔ was dissatisfied with her mirror was truly a sign of folly. Furthermore,
the gentleman seeks [the cause of his condition] within himself.
One does not resent Heaven or blame others;
how much more so for a bodhisattva?
If one can have deep faith in this teaching, [one will attain liberation].
Thus, one can empty the mind and sever all conceptualization,
entering suddenly into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
Therefore, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says:
There may be sentient beings who lack the power of roots of goodness;
they will then be deluded and disturbed by various māras, non-Buddhists, ghosts, and spirits.
These beings may manifest forms within their midst to terrify them.
If forms such as handsome men or women appear,
one should contemplate that these are merely objects of the mind;
then they will cease.
In the end, it will not cause affliction;
thus we know that the noble one is correct.
When the mind is upright, one is a sage;
thus it is said that an upright mind can ward off evil,
just like the sun and the moon.
When it is truly midday,
the grasses and trees cast no distorted shadows;
thus we know that this mind is the abode of both the ordinary and the sage.
The root of the sense faculties and their objects is simply that ordinary beings cling to the ālayavijñāna,
thereby creating the cause for the suffering of birth and death.
The noble ones realize that this is the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind and receive the fruit of the permanence and bliss of nirvāṇa;
yet, it is called the *ālayavijñāna*.
Thus, there is name but no substance;
for one clings to existence through emotional attachment and fails to reach the ultimate realization.
When one realizes the state of sainthood,
that name is immediately relinquished;
yet it is called the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*.
Thus, it possesses both name and substance;
for its fundamental existence is not a grasping,
and it continues uninterrupted until the limits of the future.
It is like fashioning a ring from gold:
the appearance of the ring is empty,
while the substance of the gold is revealed.
The Tathāgatagarbha acts as the ālayavijñāna;
when the characteristics of the ālaya are empty,
the nature of the Garbha manifests.
Nowadays, because sentient beings cling to their own emotional attachments with such intensity,
they mostly identify with the ālayavijñāna and do not believe in the existence of the tathāgatagarbha.
Because of this lack of faith,
they not only treat themselves with contempt but also disparage and destroy others.
No transgression of slandering the Dharma exceeds this fault;
moment by moment, one remains oblivious to the nature of the Tathāgata’s Dharmadhātu.
At every step, one creates the causes for the karmic fruits of sentient beings;
evil karma renews daily,
and the conditions for suffering are inexhaustible.
While dwelling in a state of security,
one gives rise to a mind of decline and affliction toward liberation.
They undergo the fruit of bondage,
receiving the body of a flame-mouthed being with a needle-throat,
where they are scorched by the fires of hunger for an entire kalpa.
Taking on bodies with fur and horns,
one encounters entanglements and fetters at every turn,
or falls into the Avīci Hell.
They endure intense suffering while constantly dwelling within the wheel of fire;
or they may be born in the palaces of the asuras.
Thus it begins.
In constant strife, swords and blades fall like rain;
or if they briefly dwell within the human realm,
for a mere kṣaṇa they are tormented by the convergence of the eight sufferings.
Or, though they may happen to dwell in celestial palaces,
they suddenly fall into the five signs of decline;
thus they sink forever into the three obstructions.
They do not transcend the four māras because they all fail to know the mind of the Tathāgatagarbha and lose the wondrous nature of Vijñaptimātratā.
He has turned his back on his true father and hired himself out in foreign lands;
he has abandoned the Great Wise King and sought refuge in another country.
For this reason, the Buddhas were startled and entered the burning house;
the Patriarch came from the West across the mountains,
pointing toward the true home yet not returning there.
Though one demonstrates right view, it is not seen;
for all is the locus of perfuming within the ālayavijñāna,
which has been firm and enduring since beginningless time.
Their attachments are so profound they resemble ten thousand layers of icy cliffs;
their roots of doubt are so deep they seem like a thousand-layered dark chamber.
Now, I shall extensively search for the profound mysteries.
Without wearying of prolixity,
he harmonized the subtle words of a thousand sages and penetrated the secret doctrines of a hundred schools.
There is not a single dharma that does not accord with it,
capable of establishing the gateway of filial piety and righteousness;
there is not a single thought that is not harmonious.
When all is the path of non-contention,
then the six sense bases are a hollow village;
ultimately, there is no person.
Within the house of the five aggregates,
there is sudden, vast emptiness and stillness;
therefore, internally there is nothing to be done.
Externally there is nothing upon which to rely; externally there is nothing upon which to rely.
The myriad existences cannot fetter one.
Internally there is nothing to be done;
even a thousand deliberations cannot stir it.
Thus, one attains stillness at the borders of the Buddha’s realm.
He eradicated a single speck of dust that caused disorder and rectified the state's territory;
there was not a single region that did not submit.
It may be said that their innate natures were united at this time,
such that no other kind [of relationship] could exist;
their status as father and son was settled this very day.
This is simply our family tradition.
As stated in the Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra:
"One constantly enjoys all the pleasures of humans and devas."
The excellence of one's lineage is entirely perfected;
this arises from hearing and knowing.
Because all sentient beings possess the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding treasury;
this applies even to those sentient beings of the past, future, and present.
Within the five destinies,
with incomplete limbs and joints,
they transmigrate through birth and death.
They undergo all suffering because they treat the Tathāgatagarbha with contempt.
Question:
One merely realizes the single mind and seeks no other dharmas,
thereby upholding and flourishing the Triple Gem.
Question: "By practicing for oneself and transforming others, can one attain the stage of perfect, wondrous enlightenment?
Answer: [Yes.]
When the awakened mind is unchanging,
one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; once the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened, [one realizes it].
Nothing hidden remains unseen;
this mark of non-duality is what is perceived by the Buddha-eye.
The Way of the Single Reality is that which is known by the Buddha’s wisdom;
it illuminates to the very limits of the Dharma-realm.
Thoroughly penetrating to the very bottom of the true source,
they achieve Buddhahood above and transform sentient beings below.
There is nothing that does not derive from this for the mutual benefit of self and others.
Indeed, one who wishes to practice correctly cannot do so without returning to the Mirror of the Source.
All fall into erroneous cultivation,
or remain stagnant in the provisional and inferior vehicles.
This is the correct meaning of the Mirror of the School.
All Buddhas of the ten directions in the past have already perfected this through complete cultivation;
all Buddhas of the present are currently accomplishing it.
All Buddhas of the future shall accomplish it;
all Bodhisattvas of the past have already studied it;
and all Bodhisattvas of the present are currently studying it.
All bodhisattvas of the future should study this.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* clarifies that one must first correctly contemplate the dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The *Shibikshao* states:
"It means that all gates of practice arise from True Suchness."
Because these practices are merely superficial,
they do not flow from the ultimate truth; without such a flow,
one cannot accord with the truth.
How could there be a practice that accords with reality that does not arise from reality?
For this [reality] is the very root within the dharmas that are objects of faith.
Thus, while the myriad conditions arise, their arising originates from True Suchness; when one comprehends these conditions,
that which is entered is True Suchness.
Entering into suchness,
the bodhisattva who has resolved their mind first contemplates suchness.
When a bodhisattva gives rise to faith,
they first believe in *tathatā* (suchness);
this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
It also accords with and realizes suchness (tathatā).
He asked again:
"What are the characteristics of faith in suchness?"
Answer: Not believing in any phenomena is the characteristic of faith in True Suchness (tathatā).
Because within the principle of suchness,
all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent;
yet, one might perceive these phenomena as being existent.
This person believes in all phenomena but does not believe in True Suchness (tathatā).
Consequently, they lack the causal conditions for having previously planted the seeds of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) of vast bodhicitta.
It is ultimately difficult to give rise to faith.
Thus, the Patriarch said in a verse:
"When great conditions unite with faith."
Those who are able to enter the Mirror of the School (Zongjing) know that this is no small cause.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
"One who embraces the Mahāyāna embraces all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas."
To embrace all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas,
and Śrāvakas is to embrace all sentient beings;
to embrace all sentient beings is [to embrace the Dharma].
This is the upholding of the true Dharma.
To uphold the true Dharma is to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
One for whom the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed is able to fully understand the attainment of the sublime entrance;
having understood the attainment of the sublime entrance, [one realizes it].
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas always attain transformation birth.
They establish the Mahāyāna and the ten powers of mastery.
Manifesting in various forms and images,
they thoroughly understand the physical types, aspirations, and afflictions of sentient beings,
and preach the Dharma in accordance with reality.
That which is suchness is not otherwise; that which is suchness is suchness.
The characteristic of neither coming nor going;
wherein all fabrications cease—
this is called "as-it-is."
It is further said:
The Buddha stated,
"Simply awaken to the fact that [all things] are the manifestation of one's own mind."
Delusive thoughts do not arise;
there is peace, security, and happiness,
and worldly affairs are forever stilled.
That which is peaceful and blissful is the sublime, eternal tranquility; therein,
all worldly affairs are forever stilled.
Then, as all攀緣 (pān-yuán; objective attachments/mental proliferations) have been severed,
one may be said to have encountered a perfect treasury of jewels,
where all seeking is suddenly cut off.
One arrives at the eternal bliss of nirvana and goes nowhere further;
this is the boundary between the ordinary person and the sage.
It is like reaching one's hometown;
having already exhausted the root, it serves as the basis for both delusion and awakening.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
The Vajra Treasure Store is without deficiency or diminution.
As a verse in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
With various transformations and immeasurable powers,
equal in number to the atoms of all worlds,
they desire to fully comprehend that these arise from the mind.
The Bodhisattva initiates the mind [of enlightenment] by means of this.
The *Pao-tsang lun*, in the "Chapter on the Original Limit" (*Ben-ji pin*), states:
"Therefore, the original limit is nameless."
Names exist within the nameless;
the ultimate limit is without marks.
Names exist within the markless.
Once names and forms are established,
delusive confusion consequently arises,
and the principle of true oneness sinks into obscurity.
The essence of the Way is hidden;
thus, the uncarved block of namelessness pervades all things.
It is ineffable and beyond the limits of measure;
it is a single essence without duality.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"The myriad phenomena of the universe and all things are the seal of the One Dharma."
This is precisely the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
However, the principle of the primordial limit is neither self nor other.
Neither one nor different,
it encompasses the single vital breath and pervades all existence.
Furthermore, if there is a person whose self-nature is pure,
who is born endowed with this [nature], and who harbors no deluded thoughts within, [they shall attain liberation].
This refers to the noble ones (ārya).
Yet, within the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi),
there is not even so much as a speck of dust of a "noble dharma" that exists with any differentiation.
Furthermore, if there is a person whose self-nature is pure,
born containing [this nature], yet who possesses delusive thoughts within the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Those who are naturally turbid and disordered are called ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); yet,
within the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), [this is not so].
Furthermore, there is not even so much as a speck of dust’s worth of difference between the dharmas of ordinary beings [and those of Buddhas].
Therefore, a sutra says:
"The Buddha-nature is equal."
Vast and immeasurable,
it is non-dual for both ordinary beings and sages, perfectly complete and encompassing all things down to the grasses and trees.
Pervading everywhere,
from ants down to the finest motes of dust and a single hair,
there is not one that does not contain the One within it at its birth.
Therefore, it is said that by being able to comprehend this one thing, all matters are completed.
For this reason, all sentient beings are born by riding upon this one;
hence, it is called the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
If one is deluded, they are different;
if one is awakened, they are one.
Therefore, it is said that the preceding thought is that of an ordinary person.
The subsequent thought is itself the sacred;
it is also said that in a single thought one knows all dharmas.
Therefore, one is all, and all is one;
hence it is said that by means of this single dharma.
When the work is accomplished, the myriad phenomena manifest.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
"If all things possess a mind..."
This is immediately delusion regarding all things;
it is as if there were no mind.
Because it immediately pervades the ten directions,
the true One is differentiated into ten thousand.
The myriad differences are truly one.
It is like the ocean surging with a thousand waves;
the thousand waves are themselves the ocean.
All things are without any difference.
Even down to the myriad phenomena, they arise containing the One;
thus, those myriad phenomena are themselves the One.
Why is this? Because the root is one, the branches are not different.
It is like a sandalwood tree producing sandalwood branches.
It is not the *chūn* tree.
Therefore, a verse in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions..."
There is only the Single Vehicle Dharma.
The Single Vehicle is precisely the One Mind.
All phenomena throughout the ten directions of space are manifested from the seeds of the single mind of True Suchness (tathatā).
Just as a sandalwood tree produces sandalwood branches and a orchid produces orchid leaves,
so it is from beginning to end and from center to periphery.
There are no other characteristics;
therefore it is said: "One is all."
All is one. If one can understand it thus,
why worry about not reaching completion?
If one can thus achieve ultimate and perfect penetration,
there will be no further phenomena that are not fully understood; consequently,
there will be no principle that remains unilluminated.
There is no phenomenon that is not exhausted,
because a single dharma can accomplish all dharmas.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary* states:
If one enters this method of contemplation,
then wisdom will be in accord with the mind;
therefore, one should train by means of the mind.
Fruits are accomplished by the mind;
objects appear through the mind;
and understanding arises from the mind.
The supernormal powers of various states are mind;
the creative activity of functional power is mind;
the manifestation of discrimination is mind.
Having resolved that this is mind,
they proceed to seek out a teacher and travel to the Buddha-fields.
All these are but the mind;
nothing can be apprehended apart from the mind. What is there to doubt?
Therefore, know that when the mind is defiled, the Sahā world manifests;
when the mind is pure, the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha) encompasses space.
Through these transformations, the wheel of consciousness perpetually arises.
Interwoven yet not separated, they form a net of the mind;
thus, Sāgaramegha did not arise from his meditative absorption,
extensively performing the gateway of Buddha-activities throughout the ten directions.

The method by which Sudhana does not leave the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) yet traverses one hundred and ten cities is such that Mañjuśrī is the sublime wisdom capable of realizing this within one's own mind.
When Sudhana reached Maitreya,
after he had fulfilled the fruit of Buddhahood with single-minded devotion,
Maitreya then led him back to see Mañjuśrī.
When the stage of the causal position is about to reach its culmination,
one is led to reflect back upon the source of the mind,
wherein there is no longer any difference.
Because he has never stirred a single thought;
as for not seeing Mañjuśrī’s body upon returning to visit him,
it is because one has only realized that one's own mind is the emptiness of prajñā.
This is the true vision of Mañjuśrī;
Samantabhadra is the inexhaustible, wondrous practice of the Dharma-realm realized within one's own mind.
Although Sudhana has traveled throughout the Dharma-realm to visit all his spiritual friends, [he has not yet met them].
If one wishes to see Samantabhadra,
there is no need for a separate indication;
he is right there at the place where [the Buddha] first attained enlightenment during the initial assembly.
Before the Tathāgata’s seat,
one should give rise to the thought of seeking him; as soon as one recollects him,
Samantabhadra appears before the Tathāgata.
From the beginning, there was no movement or shifting.
This precisely reveals that when one contemplates the mind, one immediately perceives extraordinary signs;
thus one sees, hears, realizes, and enters [the truth].
By beholding the aforementioned signs,
one perceives the mind itself;
therefore, the physical form of Samantabhadra is like space, pervading all places.
Therefore, although the Bodhisattva Universal Eye and others entered hundreds of thousands of samādhis in search of Samantabhadra, they did not see him;
this was simply because they had departed from thought to enter meditative absorption,
and were weary of phenomenal objects while seeking the truth.

the Middle Way of ultimate truth is likewise understood to be empty as well.
If one enters the provisional from emptiness, [one proceeds accordingly].
Not only is conventional reality known to be provisional,
but true emptiness and the Middle Way are likewise understood to be provisional.
If one enters the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, [this realization occurs].
It is not merely that the Middle Way is the middle;
both the conventional and the ultimate are likewise the middle.
Thus, when one is empty, all are empty.
There is neither the provisional nor the middle,
yet it is not empty;
where there is one provisional, there is the provisional of all.
In non-existence there is no emptiness,
yet it does not depend [on anything else].
In one, all are contained within one.
Neither provisional nor empty,
yet not being midway;
it is simply designated by the name of "One Contemplation."
There is no aspect of the mind that is not understood through this realization.
Regarding the "threefold one-mind and threefold contemplation":
it is the knowledge that the single thought-moment is ungraspable and ineffable.
And yet, one is able to perfectly contemplate the three truths.
As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"To know all dharmas in a single thought-moment is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)."
Because it accomplishes all-encompassing wisdom,
it exists within the objective realm as one truth that is simultaneously three truths.
In the mind, it is one contemplation yet three contemplations;
in the fruit, it is one wisdom yet three wisdoms—
like a single perfect sphere.
The characteristics of the jewel are a metaphor for existence;
the jewel’s transparency and purity are a metaphor for emptiness;
and its perfect luminosity is a metaphor for the Middle Way.
The three are without before or after;
this illustrates how one truth is three truths.
If one were to observe them with a clear mirror, [they would appear as such].
Upon the jewel,
these three meanings manifest simultaneously and instantaneously;
this serves as a metaphor for how a single contemplation encompasses the three contemplations.
If one examines the pearl within the mirror,
the pearl and the mirror are neither identical nor distinct;
this serves as a metaphor for the mind and its objects, which are dual yet non-dual.
This constitutes true awakening.
As for "sublime contemplation," it means taking the single thought-moment as the object of observation.
Reflect inwardly upon this mind:
from where does it come,
and to what place does it go?
Pure as empty space, it is called the contemplation of emptiness;
the observed object is vivid and distinct.
This is called the contemplation of nominal designations: though they appear vividly distinct,
their nature is eternally empty of itself.
Yet, object and contemplation remain distinct and clear;
this is called the Middle Way,
which is three yet one.
It is one yet three; whether speaking or remaining silent, walking or standing still,
it is neither born nor extinguished.
Neither permanent nor discontinuous;
neither identical nor different;
neither coming nor going.
Neither existent nor non-existent;
neither abiding nor clinging;
neither defiled nor pure.
Neither loved nor grasped;
neither empty nor real;
neither bound nor liberated.
These are all different names for that which is neither born nor extinguished;
their meaning is no different.
This is emptiness itself, yet it does not abide in emptiness.
To not abide in the provisional while within the provisional,
and to not abide in the middle while within the middle—
this is called the Middle.
Why is this? Because it is emptiness itself.
What is there in emptiness that can be dwelt upon?
They are merely provisional,
like illusions, transformations,
or reflections; how, then, could they abide?
Since the two extremes cannot be dwelt upon,
how could one dwell in the middle? Therefore,
it is said that the three truths are without dwelling.
This is called the middle way;
it must be practiced in this manner.
Within emptiness there is no emptiness; do not merely [cling to] emptiness.
Within the provisional there is no provisional; simply do not cling to the provisional.
Within the middle there is no middle; simply do not cling to the middle.
One should contemplate in this manner.
Within illumination there is no illumination; simply do not illuminate.
If you perceive this principle, you will see that all things are inherently empty.
These three contemplations constitute the inconceivable realm; if even one contemplation is lacking, [the realm remains unmanifest].
Since neither object nor wisdom is established,
it is called "inconceivable.
It fully encompasses all phenomena.
Although all things are numerous,
they are fully encompassed within the ten dharma realms;
since these are already fused and integrated, [they are one].
First, one [dharma] possesses ten, thereby completing a hundred dharma-realms.
One realm, in turn, possesses ten suchnesses.
One suchness, moreover, possesses three kinds of worlds.
That is to say: the five aggregates,
sentient beings,
and the land.
The thousand suchnesses constitute the three thousandfold world,
which is termed the inconceivable provisional.
This provisional is itself emptiness and itself the Middle Way.
If the intermediate [realm] did not exist,
the principle of inclusion would not be universal;
if the ten realms did not exist, [the same would follow].
The matters of inclusion would not be exhaustive;
if there were no "ten suchnesses," cause and effect would not be complete.
If these three kinds of worlds did not exist,
the dependent and the primary would be incomplete;
therefore, one knows the true mark.
They encompass all phenomena in their entirety;
they are infinitely layered and inexhaustible,
harmoniously integrated and unimpeded.
It is like the net of Indra;
this is called the inconceivable realm.
This principle is common to both ordinary beings and sages.
Therefore, it is said that one's own three thousand worlds pervade those three thousand worlds; each and every one of those three thousand worlds [is thus pervaded].
The same applies to their mutual pervasiveness;
thus, the reliance and the supported remain brilliantly manifest throughout the day,
without any conceptual discrimination.
The Dharma-realm is profoundly luminous;
to manifest this realm, it is therefore said: "contemplating the inconceivable realm."
As stated in the Verse on the Three Contemplations:
"In the contemplation of emptiness, the nature is ungraspable;
in the contemplation of the provisional, phenomena encompass the dharma-realm."
The principles of the extremes, the middle, and the essence are non-dual;
though they are one, the three are ever distinct.
Furthermore, this is the contemplation of emptiness.
First, because all phenomena are understood to lack intrinsic nature;
second, the contemplation of the provisional,
because this sphere of emptiness contains all phenomena.
Among the three, the Middle Way has no distinct substance from emptiness and the provisional,
for it is solely the single true mind.
Since emptiness is the nature of the mind,
it is ultimate emptiness (zhēnkōng), not merely a void.
Since this provisional nature is the characteristic of the mind,
it is the wondrous provisional,
not the biased provisional.
The nature and characteristics are divided into three, yet they are not three;
the true mind is merged in oneness, yet it is not one.
While it is not one, the three contemplations are perfectly manifest.
It is not three, yet as one, the mind is unmoving;
it is precisely one, yet its three aspects are distinct,
just as the substance of a mirror is one, yet possesses the distinct characteristics of luminosity and reflected images.
Though they are three, they are a single essence without distinction,
like reflections and their radiance,
both being one and the same mirror.
Furthermore, an ancient commentary on the meaning of the three contemplations states:
"When a single thought-moment arises,
its arising is without the characteristic of arising."
Utterly and solely empty;
quiescent throughout the three periods of time;
fundamentally unattainable.
It is without the marks of seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing;
it is without the marks of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
This is the contemplation of emptiness.
When a single thought arises,
there are the manifestations of three thousand worlds:
one thousand worlds of the physical realm.
The mountains, rivers, great earth, sun, moon, and stars are it.
The world of the five aggregates is one thousand;
all defiled and pure forms and mind are it.
The thousandfold world of sentient beings consists of the six mundane realms and the four noble ones; these are provisional manifestations based on substance.
They arise from a single thought-moment of the mind.
When the three thousand natures and appearances arise simultaneously,
with the extinction of a single thought-moment,
the three thousand natures and appearances extinguish simultaneously.
Contemplate that outside of mind there is not a single hair’s breadth of a dharma to be found,
and outside of dharmas there is not a single hair’s breadth of mind to be found.
This nature of mind is perfectly luminous.
One yet capable of being many;
small yet capable of being great;
defiled yet capable of being pure.
Thus, that which exists can become non-existent; therefore,
each and every form [is thus].
In each and every fragrance,
in each and every thought—
in the slightest flicker of a mind that arises.
This refers to the three thousand worlds.
One perceives many in a single place;
one perceives a single thing in many places.
A single thought-moment is many eons;
many eons are a single thought-moment.
They manifest within one another in infinite layers.
It is likened to the net of Indra’s jewel;
this is the provisional contemplation.
When a single thought-moment arises—
Arising yet without arising;
the three periods of time are quiescent.
Without arising, there is arising.
The nature and characteristics of the three thousand realms are neither empty nor provisional;
they simultaneously illuminate both emptiness and the provisional.
This is the Middle Way.
Although it is spoken of as having three names,
when illuminating [reality], one does not form a conceptualization of them as being three, one, or both.
Simply maintain moment-to-moment awareness of the nature of one's own mind;
it spontaneously is neither three nor one,
and there is no need to dismantle or eliminate the body and mind.
Furthermore, there is no need to establish objects or contemplations as points where thought and perception are severed;
at all times, the mind spontaneously and constantly abides in the three contemplations.
Ordinary people lack the perfect capacity;
they say of themselves, "I am a vulgar and defiled being," and "I am full of afflictions."
"My wisdom is inferior;
I am a person bound by birth and death.
This is like a cataract-afflicted eye seeing flowers in the sky."
In emptiness, there are truly no flowers.
When a person of perfect realization contemplates luminosity,
they find that every encounter is entirely identical to the ancient Buddhas.
It is not that they are identical in nature.
Why is this? Because the principle of the perfect dharma-nature (dharmatā) is such.
The three virtues and the three bodies are but a single thought-moment,
for they cannot be divided.
This perfect principle is likewise devoid of sequential stages;
yet because people are unable to observe it spontaneously and constantly,
their observation is characterized by interruption.
Because my own nature has not yet been destroyed,
and because it has been destroyed but not yet exhausted,
the six stages are divided into forty-two positions.
Pointing to emptiness to guide them toward the state of non-cultivation;
or it may be said that ordinary beings possess only the Buddha-nature of the Dharma-body,
yet have not yet attained the meritorious functions of the Reward-body and Transformation-bodies.
This is the interpretation within the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
In the Perfect Contemplation, the three— afflictions, karma, and suffering— are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature and are entirely identical to the Three Virtues (triguṇa).
The three virtues fundamentally have no place of abiding;
they abide within afflictions, karma, and suffering.
Thus are the three bodies and the three paths.
All these are merely provisional designations;
within ultimate emptiness,
they are utterly unfindable.
There is no evil to be abandoned and no Way to be realized;
were one to perceive even a hair’s breadth of principle upon which to rely or rest, [it would be a delusion].
This is precisely the delusory realm that draws forth the mind;
it is because the three contemplations are not clear.
The student loathes greed, anger, and ignorance.
One applies mental attention to eliminate it,
yet fails to realize that this mind of aversion is itself a delusion.
If one perceives its arising at the very moment it occurs—
One immediately illuminates the place where this arises;
being devoid of intrinsic nature, it cannot be grasped or abandoned.
This is the clarity of the threefold contemplation.
If one were to separately cultivate remedies,
separately form an understanding of the true mark of suchness,
and separately conceive of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
To separately direct the body and mind with the thought that they pervade the Dharma-realm is not the meaning of "round" (yuan).
One who is "round" simply maintains mindfulness while being without mindfulness.
If it is claimed that the consciousness which is capable of cognizing distinctions is the mind,
this is merely the sprout of the mind;
it is not the nature of the mind itself.
Therefore it is said: "Movement is the sprout of the Dharma King;
stillness is the root of the Dharma King.
As for the nature of the mind:
This is precisely when the three contemplations are clear.
When the three contemplations are clear,
one perceives neither sentient beings nor insentient things.
The Buddhas and sentient beings,
whether their transgressions or their merits,
are within the scope of my contemplation.
Whether I contemplate the external or contemplate the internal,
neither is tenable.
If one does not understand the three contemplations,
one will falsely imagine that Buddha-nature resides within the body or that it pervades all plants and trees.
In the sutras, this is termed the "imagined nature" (parikalpita-svabhāva).
It is the doctrine adhered to by non-Buddhists and is not subsumed within the four teachings.
How much more so for the understanding of one who has attained the Perfect [Teaching]?
Now, the Middle Way is difficult to clarify,
and the Perfect Understanding is subtle and profound.
Generally speaking, that which is called "the Middle" has two kinds:
first, the mere middle (but-chung).
Regarding the two kinds of perfection:
as the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* clarifies the meaning of the "eight returns," if one analyzes the external objects before one.
Seeing that there is no place from which it returns,
the nature of seeing is uniquely wondrous;
it is simply the Center.
The seer and the objects of seeing are fundamentally the wondrous,
pure, and luminous essence of bodhi.
How is it that within this there is "is" and "is not"?
This is the Middle Way of Perfection.
Furthermore, emptiness and the conventional are themselves the Middle.
It is simply the Middle.
The Middle is itself emptiness and the provisional.
It is not merely the Middle.
This refers to the Perfect [Teaching] (Yuan).
For example, the two teachings of the Treasury (Zang) and the Penetrating (Tong) are merely emptiness (but-kong).
That is, one analyzes the substance of form and its objects until they return to the emptiness that is their fundamental nature,
as in the Separate and Complete Teachings.
This is the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*),
which fully embodies the principle of the Middle Way and the non-empty Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
Master Fu’s verse states:
It is solitary and refined;
in truth, it transcends sound and name.
Through the three contemplations within a single mind, it harmonizes all phenomena.
"Where do the thickets of thorns grow?
The commentary states:
If one can inwardly contemplate and reflect back upon oneself, refining the mind alone.
How could it be reached by the expressions of words?
Therefore it is said that its reality transcends sound and name;
one must thoroughly understand this single thought-moment.
The point of origination cannot be apprehended;
this is called the contemplation of emptiness.
Precisely within that state of emptiness, [one abides].
Because the dependently arisen phenomena appear as if they were existent,
it is said that "all phenomena" [are empty].
These are all dharmas;
they do not exist within a state of non-existence or formlessness,
yet there is neither attainment nor form.
This is called the contemplation of the provisional.
Seeking emptiness, one does not find emptiness;
seeking the provisional, one does not find the provisional.
Neither empty nor provisional—
it is entirely the one mind;
this is called the Middle Way.
In every thought-moment one is endowed with the method of the three contemplations;
in every dust mote lies the gateway to the Buddha-wisdom.
Thus it is said: "The three contemplations within a single mind harmonize all phenomena."
Thus, the afflictions are thorny brambles;
the five aggregates are a dense forest;
and birth-and-death is the root-stump.
From what further source does the great mound of self-conceit arise?
Therefore it is said: "From where do the thickets of thorns grow?"
The *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states:
"Regarding the ten gates of cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*),
the first is the practice of the single mind in accordance with principle."
Gathering the distracted mind is called *śamatha* (calm abiding).
These two forms of *śamatha* do not stagnate in quiescence,
nor do they obstruct the activities of *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Third, because principle and phenomena interpenetrate, they necessarily coexist;
this enables the unimpeded simultaneous operation of tranquility (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).
Fourth, because principle and phenomena mutually negate one another, both are exhausted.
Therefore, with both calming (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) extinguished, one transcends all dependence;
this is the realm where the five aspects are severed and principle and phenomena are unimpeded,
and it accords with the mind in which the cessation of calming and the observation of insight are non-obstructive.
They are two yet not two;
therefore, they do not obstruct the mind and its objects, but are of a single flavor.
Because they are not two yet two.
The sixth [point] is that the mind and its objects do not disrupt the single flavor,
because all phenomena are subsumed within the very nature of reality.
That is, one observes by ceasing [the distraction] and sees everything as well,
because these seven things are identical to those things.
It causes cessation and contemplation to see that this mind is precisely that mind.
Eighth, because of the preceding six [reasons], the one and the many interpenetrate such that they are not one;
seventh, the one and the many are identical such that they are not different.
These two are non-dual, being the same single dharma-realm;
through the wisdom of the non-duality of śamatha and vipaśyanā,
one suddenly sees and immediately enters both gates.
They are of one and the same dharma-realm without any distraction or movement.
Ninth, in terms of phenomena, they are layered upon one another and inexhaustible;
both śamatha and vipaśyanā likewise illuminate all universally with the eye of samantabhadra.
Tenth, because this wisdom of the Universal Gate (samantamukha-jñāna) serves as the sovereign,
when it suddenly illumines the dharma-realm of the Universal Gate,
it necessarily encompasses all things as its attendants.
Inexhaustible, inexhaustible.

Regarding the gate of contemplation (*guanmen*), there are briefly two types: first, that which relies upon the Chan school and the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) for those of the highest faculties.
Directly contemplate the nature of the mind.
Do not establish subject and object;
do not form conceptual thoughts.
Contemplating both concentration and distraction,
with the internal and external being entirely equal,
this is contemplation that is itself without contemplation.
Numinous awareness is quiescent and illuminating;
second, based on the gate of contemplation,
one contemplates the mind as appearing like a present object.
Although provisional and conventional characteristics are established,
they all arise from the transformations of the mind,
as described in the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
The *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* establishes sixteen visualization gates, such as the visualization of the sun and the visualization of water,
as well as the visualization of Maitreya’s inner court within the Tuṣita Heaven palace.
The *Zhuzhang chao shi* states:
"Regarding the statement 'contemplating a single character,' there are two kinds of principle."
First, looking; second, examining.
Regarding the first, looking:
Just as the first five consciousnesses take the five sensory objects as their conditions,
they gaze directly at these objects before them,
appearing with vivid clarity.
Because it is free from conceptual investigation and because it is subsumed under the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
one next examines it.
It is directed toward one's own consciousness,
establishing a mental model by investigating and searching for the specific boundaries and portions of the object.
Now, the gate of contemplation is established;
this corresponds to the second observation,
which is conducted in terms of the observing mind.

There are four ways of establishing the essential nature [of wisdom]. First, establishing the essential nature by its specific character: it is exclusively the discernment (*prajñā*) among the mental factors associated with specific objects.
This wisdom is able to discern and eliminate distraction, defilement, the indeterminate, and so forth,
because it selects and retains the objects transformed by what is wholesome and pure.
Second is the essence of that which induces and that which is induced.
Because concentration induces wisdom,
its essential nature consists of the three [mental] factors;
it comprises the five aggregates, excluding form.
The fourth is the substance of the retinue,
which includes the five aggregates of form.
Question:
Regarding the four associated aggregates— the mind-king and its mental factors—
which of these takes [the object] as that which performs the observation? Answer:
First, the mind-kings (citta-rāja) are analyzed;
next, the mental factors (caitta) are elucidated.
As for the eight consciousnesses as mind-kings:
Only the sixth is taken.
Question:
Do not the first five, as well as the seventh and eighth, all possess the capacity for cognitive apprehension?
Why are they not taken?
Answer: First, regarding the five sensory consciousnesses.
In the state of being with outflows (sāsrava), [the first seven consciousnesses] perceive only the five real objects of the sensory fields through direct perception (pratyakṣa);
as for the eighth [consciousness], it perceives only three objects through direct perception.
The seeds, the root-body, and the objective world of the vessel-environment are by nature exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).
This is so within the seventh [consciousness] during its state of being with outflows (sāsrava).
It constantly takes the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object;
it is subsumed under non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Now, this is the observing mind.
Based on scriptural teaching, one can infer that the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) arises through transformation;
because this is an object of inference (*anumāna*) and is subsumed under the category of "well-characterized solitary images" (*svalakṣaṇapratibimba*),
only the sixth consciousness possesses this functional capacity.
Question:
How many types of the sixth mind-king are there?
Answer: In terms of their meaning, there are four types.
First, the clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The mental consciousness within the two meditative absorptions takes the five sense objects as its objects in common with the first five consciousnesses, perceiving them with distinct clarity.
Having induced the higher meditative absorptions,
there arise within those states three types of solitary, non-concentrated mental consciousness.
It does not share the same object as the preceding five [consciousnesses].
To distinguish it for the sake of clarity,
the name "solitary" (*mānasa*) is established.
Furthermore, because it does not arise within meditative concentration,
it is termed "distracted" (*vikṣipta*);
for it arises exclusively during the state of distraction.
Fourth is the mental consciousness within dreams;
for this consciousness arises during the state of sleep.
Question:
Among these four, which is the mind capable of observation? Answer:

Regarding those who have attained superior concentration: because they observe through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within that state of concentration.
For one who has not yet attained meditative concentration,
the solitary, distracted mental consciousness alone can serve as the substance of contemplation.
Next, to clarify the mental factors (*caitta*),
there are fifty-one dharmas,
which are divided into six categories in total.
Furthermore, to explain generally those mental factors associated with the various consciousnesses in their impure (sāsrava) state:
each of the first five consciousnesses is associated with thirty-four mental factors,
namely the five omnipresent (sarvatraga) factors.
The five object-specific [mental factors],
the eleven wholesome [factors], the three root afflictions— greed, hatred, and delusion—
the two intermediate derivative afflictions, and the eight major derivative afflictions.
The sixth consciousness pertains to the three realms and the three natures;
whether in a state of concentration or distraction,
it is generally discussed as being associated with all fifty-one mental factors.
The seventh consciousness is associated with eighteen mental factors:
namely, the five omnipresent factors and the four root afflictions.
Self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), and self-love (*ātma-sneha*).
Among the eight universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), wisdom (*prajñā*) is one;
the eighth consciousness is associated exclusively with the universal mental factors.
If these eight types of consciousness become untainted (anāsrava),
they are associated with only twenty-one mental factors (caitta).
This refers to the universal, object-specific, and wholesome mental factors.
Here, in clarifying the mind capable of observation,
it is shown that this mind possesses exclusively a wholesome nature.
Regarding the sixth consciousness,
its associated mental factors are explained in accordance with the mind-king.
Within the state of meditative concentration (samādhi), there are only twenty-one mental factors (caitta).
These consist of the five universal factors (sarvatraga) and the five object-specific factors (viniyata).
The eleven wholesome [factors],
or by taking any one factor from among vitarka and vicāra,
there are twenty-two.
Vitarka is coarse and vicāra is subtle;
because they do not arise simultaneously,
they involve shallow and deep investigation, respectively.
Its essence is the wisdom born of reflection.
If it is associated with the mental king (citta) in a state of distraction,
there are twenty factors.
Because pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is excluded from the aforementioned wholesome factors;
for the single factor of pliancy is induced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
and there exists a body supported by concentration.
Only then does it become harmonious and flowing; thus, it carries the meaning of *praśrabdhi* (pliancy).
Alternatively, there are twenty-one [factors].
Because one takes up either vitarka or vicāra from among them.
Question:
Regarding the mind capable of observation, among the three types of objects—
What is the objective realm of this? Answer:
In both the states of meditative concentration and non-concentration, it is exclusively an object consisting of a mental image.
Because it is a transformation of a false appearance.
This false appearance-part arises from the seeds of the perceiving seeing-part;
it has no seeds of its own.
Therefore, it is called "solitary reflection" (ekacchāyā),
as it differs from objects of a different nature which are real matter (rūpa) and mind (citta).
Each has its own mode of arising,
such as when visual consciousness takes form and so forth as its object;
furthermore, it does not involve an object that carries its own substance.
Because when the mind takes the mind as its object, there must necessarily be a substantial basis;
thus, the intermediate image-part arises from that substantial basis.
Regarding what are called "solitary-shadow" objects,
there are two types: first, those with a substantial basis (*sanimitta*).
This very contemplation of the mind relies upon that [external object] as its substance; both [the internal and external] are without substance.
Regarding the example of tortoise hair and so forth:
Question: Since that substance already exists, [why is it not perceived?]
Why is it not "with a substantial basis"?
Answer: There are two types of "with a substantial basis."
The first is the "true-with-a-semblance" (zhen-daizhi),
wherein the mind takes the mind as its object,
such as when the seventh consciousness takes the eighth as its object.
The sixth [consciousness] takes other consciousnesses as its object;
these two are "with a semblance of a substantial essence" because the mind takes form as its object.
This very object of observation,
because it bears that substance, is generally categorized as "bearing a substance" (sābhāsadravya).
Question: Regarding the two states of concentration and distraction,
they both rely upon that objective condition.
What kind of seeds are perfumed?
Answer: Only the seeds of the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mind and mental factors that are capable of observation are perfumed.
The image-aspect (nimittabhāga) is provisional and does not perfuse;
it is the mind of impure contemplation.
It does not perfume the substance-seeds of the untainted (anāsrava).
Question:
Among the three types of valid cognition (pramāṇa)...
What is its measure? Answer: It is subsumed under the category of direct perception (pratyakṣa) within the state of meditative equipoise.
It is subsumed under inference during the state of dispersion;
it does not extend to non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), because it is not correct contemplation (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*).
Question:
Among the three natures, which nature is it? Answer:
Because it is exclusively of a virtuous nature.
Question: What are the four conditions? What is their respective conditionality?
Answer: All four conditions are complete;
this includes the sixth mental faculty (citta) along with its actual mental concomitants (caitta).
All arise from seeds.
This causal condition is the objective referent (ālambana) by way of its provisional aspect (nimitta-bhāga).
As for the condition:
the preceding moment inducing the succeeding moment is the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
There are two types of predominance:
first, the concordant;
second, the discordant.
There are two types of conformity with the superior:
first, powerful conformity;
when performing this contemplation, [it is the former].

This is the dwelling place of those who have realized that the dharma-realm is without differentiation;

it is the dwelling place of those who know that all dharmas are unborn.
This is the dwelling place of those who do not cling to anything in the world;

this is the dwelling place of those who take no pleasure in any village settlement.
This is the dwelling place of those who do not rely on any objective sphere;
this is the dwelling place of those who are free from all conceptualizations;
this is the dwelling place of those who know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
This is the dwelling place of those who have severed all conceptual activities;
it is the dwelling place of those who are free from all perceptions, mind, mentation, and consciousness;

This is the dwelling place of those who enter all profound *prajñāpāramitā*;

This is the dwelling place of those who have extinguished the fires of all afflictions;
it is the dwelling place of those who,

This is the dwelling place of those who sport in the arising of all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, superknowledges, and clarities;

This is the dwelling place of those who abide in the presence of all Tathāgatas.
By means of this, one kalpa is entered into all kalpas,

This is the dwelling place of those who do not destroy their own characteristics;
therefore, they enter all lands into a single land,

This is the dwelling place of one who does not destroy their own characteristics;
therefore, they enter all phenomena through a single phenomenon,

This is the dwelling place of one who does not destroy their characteristic marks.
Therefore, one sentient being enters into all sentient beings,

This is the dwelling place of those who do not destroy their own characteristics.
Therefore, one Buddha enters all Buddhas, and all Buddhas enter one Buddha.
It is the dwelling place of those who do not destroy its characteristics;
it is the dwelling place of those who, within a single thought-moment, know all of the three periods of time.

When the essence reaches its ultimate limit, it becomes spirit.
When the essence is at its ultimate limit, it is no longer something that can be depicted through fixed forms.
Therefore, the Sage speaks of it as a wondrous entity.
Even those with superior wisdom are still unable to definitively ascertain its essential nature and characteristics.
To exhaust its profound subtlety:
that which we call the spirit responds universally without a presiding subject.
Subtly exhaustive and nameless,
it moves in response to things and proceeds by means of the numerical principles.
It responds to things yet is not a thing;
therefore, though things undergo transformation, it does not perish.
It employs numbers yet is not a number.
Therefore, though their numbers reach their limit, they are inexhaustible.
Those with feelings can be moved by things;
those with consciousness can be sought through calculation.
Because numbers have degrees of refinement and coarseness, their natures differ;
because wisdom has degrees of clarity and dullness,
its illumination varies accordingly.
Inferring from this, we know that transformation arises through emotional resonance,
and the spirit is transmitted through transformation.
Sentiment is the mother of transformation;
spirit is the root of sentiment.
Sentiment possesses the way of meeting with external objects.
The spirit possesses the power of mysterious transformation;
yet those who attain thorough awakening return to the source.
Those who are deluded regarding principle merely pursue external objects;
they may even congregate or disperse within a single transformation.
Not to contemplate that the divine Way possesses the spiritual essence of wondrous things,

It is like fire being transmitted to kindling,

Those who are deeply deluded—
Seeing that the physical form decays within a single lifetime,

This means that when this life finally ends, it is simply exhausted;

Just as when fuel is exhausted the fire is extinguished,

Those conditions will arise again in another life.

The *Anuttarāśrayasūtra* states:
The Buddha told Ānanda:

there are four kinds of difficulties."

the *saṃskāra-bhava* (birth-and-death) arising from the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
The suffering of birth and death arising from the causal conditions of the ground of ignorance is like the difficulty of afflictions within the triple world;
it is like the difficulty of karma within the triple world.

which is as difficult to exhaust as the retributive births within the three realms.

Ānanda, you should understand that the faults within the three realms are likewise difficult to overcome.
Because the four kinds of birth and death have not yet been eliminated,

the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

their conjunction is great suffering.

The first is:

the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.

As for the five turbidities (pañcakaṣāya):
First is the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). During this time, the four defilements intensify and converge:
malice increases and weapons of war arise.
When greed increases, famine arises;
when delusion increases, pestilence arises.
Thus, the three calamities arise.
Afflictions flourish doubly;
various views blaze ever more fiercely;
coarse and debased are both form and mind.
Ill repute and foul reputation destroy one's years and diminish one's lifespan;
the various turbidities converge and flow together.
It was like water rushing toward a dark abyss;
wind and waves surged in fury,
while fish and dragons were thrown into turmoil.
There was nothing with which to take pleasure or rely upon;
it was simply the nature of the time,
like when beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven first fell to earth at the beginning of the kalpa.
It causes the earth to become desirous,
just as when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven enter the Rough and Astringent Garden (Karkaśavana),
the garden gives rise to thoughts of contention.
This is called the characteristic of the kalpa-turbidity.
As for the affliction-turbidity,
it is like an ocean of greed that receives all flowing streams.
Never satiated, these venomous serpents of anger drink poison and incinerate all the worlds.

Regarding the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*):

The sixteen types of knowledge-and-view, the sixty-three views,
and so forth, are like a net.

entangling and winding such that one cannot escape.

As for the turbidity of sentient beings,

Wandering through the six realms of existence,
taking birth in every place, they are as destitute as the poor and as afflicted as those with leprosy.
To be known for one's long life and wealth—
this is the characteristic of the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). As for the defilement of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*):
Born in the morning and perishing by evening;
appearing at dawn and setting at dusk;
shifting like waves and swirling like mist.
It flickers and does not remain still;
this is the characteristic of the turbidity of life.
Dwelling in such a time of turbid disorder, [one must practice].
Obstructions intensify;
the objects of perception drift like flames that incinerate the roots of goodness,
while karma stirs like the wind of the mind.
They blow away the pure Dharma,
clinging to the demonic realm of the ghouls of anger,
and falling into the net of the rākṣasas of delusion.
Imprisoned by the king of craving and driven into servitude by the lord of Māra’s enmity—
