For example, there are non-Buddhists who unilaterally cling to permanence;
these include the four types of theories on universal permanence and so forth.
This constitutes the extreme of the view of eternalism.
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who exclusively adhere to annihilationism;
this refers specifically to the seven theories of annihilation.
This constitutes the extreme of the view of nihilism.
Second, regarding the two extremes of the provisional and the real within the Hīnayāna:
there are some Hīnayāna schools that exclusively adhere to the provisional,
namely the Ekavyāvahārikas and others.
To hold that all phenomena possess only provisional names and lack substantial reality is to cling to the extreme of the provisional.
Furthermore, there are those of the Hīnayāna who unilaterally cling to reality,
namely the Sarvāstivādins, the Vātsīputrīyas, and others,
who maintain that all phenomena are substantially real.
This refers to clinging to the extreme of substantiality.
Third, regarding the two extremes of emptiness and existence in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna:
this refers to the Sarvāstivāda and other schools of the Hīnayāna.
To grasp that there are phenomena external to the mind is the extreme of eternalism;
this is [the view refuted by] the Mahāyāna masters such as Bhāviveka.
To dismiss both bodhi and nirvana as entirely non-existent is to cling to the extreme of emptiness.
There are two ways of manifesting the Middle Way.
First, the provisional middle way;
second, the ultimate middle way.
There are three aspects to the ultimate middle way.
First, that which can realize the dependent nature of the pure portion is its wondrous existence.
When wisdom arises and delusions are exhausted,
it is called "True Emptiness.
This wondrous existence is True Emptiness.
First, it correctly abides in the Middle Way; second,
it is able to realize the conditioned.
This is its wondrous existence;
the true principle realized therein is called "empty reality" (śūnyatā).
The wondrous existence is true emptiness;
it correctly abides in the Middle Way.
These are the three.
It is only regarding the dharmakāya that its primordial, true nature is called "wondrous existence" (miāoyǒu);
this very true nature is [what is meant].
This is precisely true emptiness.
True emptiness is wondrous existence.
It abides exactly in the Middle Way.
Regarding the middle way as a provisional designation:
this is that which the Buddha provisionally designates within his subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
There are also three kinds:
first, the Middle Way that is neither annihilated nor eternal.
That is to say, within the Buddha’s sūtras,
it is taught that there exists a maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) which serves as the sovereign lord of the collective retribution;
as soon as this aggregate (*skandha*) ceases, [the next arises].
Those aggregates then arise;
thus, it is not annihilation.
This refutes the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism held by non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, it is said that arising and ceasing are not fixed;
this is termed "impermanence," which is precisely "non-eternality."
Second, regarding the Middle Way that is neither provisional nor unreal:
this refers to [the teachings] within the Buddhist sutras.
To say that all form and mind arise from seeds is precisely to claim they do not depend [on external conditions];
it is based on this state.
If there is any reliance on appearances or forms, it is not true;
speak only in accordance with reality.
It correctly abides in the Middle Way;
this refutes the two extremes of the Lesser Vehicle regarding the provisional and the real. Thirdly:
The Middle Way of neither existence nor non-existence is precisely what the Sūtra describes as the pervasive conceptualization of self and phenomena;
this is "non-existence."
Relying on the perfect and wondrous existence is precisely not non-existence;
it is free from both existence and non-existence.
It correctly abides in the Middle Way;
this refutes the two extremes of emptiness and existence in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Therefore, it eliminates the attachment to these two extremes.
This immediately turns one's back on the principle of the Middle Way;
as soon as one offers an interpretation based on the four propositions,
one loses the gateway to the One Vehicle.
One must know that the middle does not exist apart from the extremes,
nor is the middle identical to the extremes. If one seeks the middle by departing from the extremes, [it cannot be found].
If extreme views have not yet been extinguished,
then even if the middle were identical to the extremes,
the conceptualization of a "middle" would still persist.
For this reason, it is difficult to understand and difficult to know;
only the profound Prajñāpāramitā,
which one should grasp as if it were a great mass of fire.
Its four sides are untouchable;
when one realizes this, it is like a cool,
refreshing pond, and all the gates may be entered.
Therefore, one should know that dharmas have no fixed characteristics;
they revolve according to the mind,
and attachment to them results in error.
To penetrate this is to be without fault.
This is like the fourfold dharma:
"penetration" and "obstruction" are like people.
The names of phenomena are called the four propositions;
awakening and entry are called the four gates;
false conceptualization is called the four attachments.
Defaming the Dharma is called the four types of slander.
One who knows these four propositions remains unshakable;
gain and loss arise from emptiness.
Although there is no difference in the single Dharma, beings naturally diverge in their ascent or descent.
Furthermore, the *Weixin jue* (Secret Instructions on Mind-Only) refutes one hundred and twenty types of views, stating:
"Some harmonize the spirit and cultivate the vital breath to preserve spontaneity."
Some crush their physical forms through ascetic hardship to attain the ultimate Way;
some cling to non-attachment while remaining fixed before external objects;
and some seek meditative concentration to subdue the deluded mind.
Some carve away their emotions and extinguish phenomena to fixate on emptiness;
some cling to shadows and conditions to embrace external forms;
and some lose the true illumination of the primordial source of the spirit.
Either the primary cause for the Buddha-seed is extinguished,
or one’s consciousness and spirit become purely unified,
receiving retribution in an insentient realm.
Some clarify the mind and dissolve form,
abiding in the fruit within the heavens of the eight difficulties;
others cling to existence and guard a city of dry sands.
Some negate [all existence] and are thus like the horns of a rabbit;
some sever all seeing and dwell in a dark room;
others establish illumination while maintaining that which is known.
Some recognize that having awareness is the true form of the Buddha;
others imitate being without knowledge.
They are of the same category as wood or stone;
yet some, grasping at delusion, take it to be the ultimate fruit,
as if the mud itself were the jar.
Some forget the conditions for entering the gate of liberation,
like striking the waves while seeking the water;
others race outward, falsely giving rise to dream-like affairs.
Some maintain internal vigilance while dwelling upright, embracing their ignorance;
some revere the One, wherein all phenomena and forms are identical to suchness;
and some perceive differences, each establishing their own dharma-realm.
Some cling to ignorance,
regarding non-discrimination as the Great Way;
others hold fast to views of emptiness.
They reject good and evil while claiming to practice true cultivation;
some interpret the inconceivable nature as a dull void, while others take true,
wondrous, and sublime forms to be substantially existent.
Some cultivate a sunken faculty and sever all thought,
becoming like those in the heavens of outflows;
others study through vitarka and vicāra, engaging in contemplation.
They fall into the realm of emotional cognition;
some fail to exhaustively investigate the nature of delusion and instead conceive of it as a primordial darkness,
while others remain ignorant of its illusory essence.
Establishing the doctrine of emptiness and non-existence,
some take the reflected image to be real,
while others abandon the illusory to seek the real.
Some designate the nature of seeing and hearing as a living entity;
some point to illusory and transformed objects as being insentient;
and some give rise to conceptual intentions that deviate from quiescent awareness.
Some sever mindfulness and thereby impair the Buddha’s function;
some are deluded regarding the qualities of intrinsic nature and give rise to the view of a physical body;
or some rely upon ultimate emptiness.
Consequently, they give rise to a mind of annihilationism;
some cling to the Great Principle while abruptly discarding adornment,
while others are deluded by the teaching of gradualism and engage exclusively in conditioned activity.
Some cling to the nature of solidity based on the substance while remaining detached from conditions;
some forget and obliterate all things while guarding their own ignorance;
and some are certain that persons and phenomena are inherently so.
Thus, one falls into the view of causelessness;
or else, one clings to the conjunction of object and cognition,
giving rise to the view of their commonality.
Some maintain that mind and objects are conflated,
thereby confusing the distinction between subject and object;
others cling to the conceptual differentiation between the ultimate and the conventional.
They are bound by the ignorance of the cognitive obscurations;
some cling to a single, unchanging reality and thus fall into eternalism,
while others are fixed on being transmuted by the four characteristics and thus sink into nihilism.
Some cling to the notion that there is no cultivation and thus discard the stages of sagehood;
some claim there is realization yet turn their backs on the natural truth;
some indulge in attachment to the environment and its inhabitants, thereby following the cycle of worldly rebirth.
Some, weary of birth and death, lose true liberation;
some, deluded regarding ultimate emptiness, revere causes and become attached to fruits;
others, ignorant of the limit of reality, rejoice in the Buddha and loathe Māra.
Some cling to what was spoken according to specific circumstances and hold the literal words to be the truth;
others lose sight of the true nature of sounds and voices.
They abandon words in search of silence;
some follow the religious vehicles while detesting the concentration on intrinsic nature,
or they propagate meditative contemplation while rejecting the explanations of the definitive meaning.
Some vie in eccentricity while regarding only their own personal liberation,
only to sink suddenly into the ocean of ignorance;
others cultivate purity while seeking only the profound and esoteric.
Conversely, one falls into the city of the aggregates (skandha);
or, though giving rise to extraordinary understanding and insight,
one treats the flesh as a wound.
Some abide in the original purity of their own nature,
yet they cling to medicine as if it were a disease;
others seek out the literal text and gather its meanings, thereby drinking the water of a guest.
Some dwell in stillness and sit idly amidst the dust of dharmas;
others give rise to a mind of attainment while discoursing on the signless Mahāyāna.
Some employ schemata and conceptual calculations to explore the profound principles beyond mundane things;
others abandon verbal exposition to give rise to a vision that transcends words.
Some cling to the means of expression, like those who grasp at the pointing finger;
some recognize only active functioning, remaining within the root-source of arising and ceasing;
and some focus exclusively on memory, dwelling at the limits of consciousness and conceptualization.
Either one's deliberate arrangements lose the nature of Perfect Enlightenment,
or one's unrestrained indulgence impairs the gateway for entering the Path;
or perhaps one gives rise to physical and mental diligence.
Yet they stagnate in conditioned phenomena;
or, while maintaining a state of natural spontaneity and non-action,
they sink into the fetters of wisdom.
Some, through single-minded calculation and diligent reflection,
lose right concentration;
others imitate unimpeded mastery.
They either abandon their practice,
or they rely on the emptiness of their own nature while following along with their fetters and afflictions,
or they cling to their entanglements and hindrances while falsely attempting to eliminate them.
Some cherish [the teachings] and thus give rise to attachment to dharmas;
some treat them with contempt and thereby destroy the causes for Buddhahood;
some strive and seek after them while deviating from their original resolve.
Some regress and fall into negligence;
some contradict the evidence of their own words, thereby impairing the ground of reality;
and some treat essence and function as separate entities, thus deviating from the Buddha Vehicle.
Some rejoice in stillness and dwell in emptiness,
thereby losing the nature of great compassion;
others obliterate conditions and grow weary of the provisional.
They violate the gateway of suchness:
some are attached to the view of self and remain oblivious to the emptiness of persons;
others are deluded regarding direct perception and stubbornly cling to the reality of phenomena.
Some understand without possessing faith, thereby nourishing false views;
some possess faith without possessing understanding, thereby fostering ignorance;
others claim that while the person is correct, the Dharma is not.
Some claim that while the object is profound, the wisdom is shallow;
some grasp at it and thus become deluded regarding the nature of things;
others abandon it and thereby deviate from immediate reality.
Either they separate [the cause] and contradict the cause,
or they identify [the effect] and lose the effect,
or they treat what is not as such and slander reality.
Some disparage skillful means;
some loathe ignorance and turn their backs on the gateway of immovable wisdom;
some detest diverse objects and destroy the samādhi of the dharma-nature.
Some, relying on a commonality of principle, give rise to overweening pride;
some disparage specific characteristics and thereby destroy the gateway of skillful means;
and some, mistaking [the provisional] for Bodhi, slander the True Wheel of Dharma.
Some disparage the true body of the Buddha because it is not a sentient being;
some cling to fundamental wisdom while rejecting expedient wisdom;
and some are confused about the primary teaching while adhering to the provisional gateways.
Some are stalled by principles, drowning in the pit of non-action;
some cling to phenomena, casting themselves into the net of illusion;
some sever all extremes and obliterate all traces.
This violates the gate of dual illumination;
alternatively, by preserving the ultimate while remaining within the provisional,
one loses the intent of the skillful means.
Some, through the biased cultivation of either concentration or wisdom, scorch and wither the sprouts of the Way;
some, through the solitary arousal of practices and vows, sink and bury themselves in the Buddha-way;
or they perform conditioned or unconditioned deeds.
They cultivate conditioned bodhi,
or they cling to a mind of non-clinging,
and study a semblance of prajñā.
Some pursue the appearance of purity while remaining deluded regarding the true nature of defilement;
some abide in the stage of correctness while losing sight of the fundamental emptiness of the conventional;
and some establish the contemplation of signlessness while obscuring True Suchness.
Some give rise to the knowledge of the awakened mind while contravening the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
others cling to the true teachings while giving rise to views based on words.
They consume the nectar of immortality and yet meet an early end.
Or, by adhering to perfect principles, one may give rise to a mind of attachment,
drinking the *amṛta* (clarified butter) and turning it into poison.
The above is a brief enumeration of one hundred and twenty types of views.
All of these are delusions regarding the fundamental tenets and losses of the essential meaning;
they turn their backs on profound stillness and deviate from the truth,
like pressing upon the eyes to see floating flowers.
To mistake one's head for its reflection is like striking ice to seek fire,
or climbing a tree to seek fish.
Fearing one's shadow while fleeing into emptiness,
feeling for the wind and grasping at lightning—
suffering is not the fruit of sweetness.
How could sand ever be the cause of rice?
None of these can be harmonized through the single principle of the permeation of the dharma-nature.
They exhaust themselves in delusive expedients and entirely enter the entanglements of views;
they fail to reach the true essence of the teaching.
All are cast into the net of views;
so dense and intricate it is difficult to escape,
like a crooked tree dragged through a thick forest.
His momentum is fierce and his strength is powerful,
like the Gaṅgā River sweeping away a fragrant elephant; therefore,
the celestial Māras and those of external paths [cannot withstand him].
Originally there was no such seed;
through the loss of mindfulness in practice,
its source has consequently branched out.
Therefore, know that as long as there is something held as weighty or something relied upon to establish knowledge and understanding,
even the slightest trace of such a standpoint remains unextinguished,
and one becomes a follower of external paths.
As a verse in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"Because phenomena lack intrinsic nature,
there is nothing that can be fully known."
To understand all phenomena in this way is ultimately to have nothing to understand,
because phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
Upon what basis could one form an understanding?
It would be like debating the size of a rabbit's horns or discerning the length of a tortoise's hair.
When both principle and phenomena are empty,
one may be ridiculed by the world; when the dust of emotion creates its own separation, [the truth remains obscured].
In truth, one loses the Way before one’s very eyes.
As the *Huayan lun* says: "To see [it] as being right here is to remain an ordinary person."
When emotions cease, one is the Buddha.
The Patriarch said:
"There is no need to seek the Truth."
One must simply cease all views.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"This Dharma cannot be understood through discursive thought or conceptual discrimination."
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:
"If one uses the conceptualizing mind to measure and fathom the realm of the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment..."
It is like attempting to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly;
it can never catch fire.
All such [attempts] are the minds of conditioned worldly beings.
How could one possibly fathom the intent of transcending the world through non-action?
As the former masters have said:
"Worldly affairs..."
It is not only the wielding of the plow or the handling of the axe that is called worldly business;
even sitting idly while racing toward the five sensory objects and the six desires constitutes it.
To be preoccupied with worldly affairs while also single-mindedly contemplating emptiness, signlessness,
and wishlessness is likewise a worldly affair.
Furthermore, to keep in mind that the common people are submerged in suffering and to compassionately console and rescue them is also a worldly concern.
If one can, in every thought-moment, abide in non-thought—
neither thinking nor non-thinking—
one awakens within the single mind.
This is not a worldly matter.
Therefore, even those who have truly awakened to the fundamental principle cannot attain it.
There is neither view nor understanding;
how could one further follow words and cling to their meaning,
thereby giving rise to views and understandings?
As stated in the *Mahādharmanirhāra-sūtra*:
"If bodhisattvas grasp the meaning according to the literal expression..."
Because they do not investigate phenomena through correct reasoning,
twenty-eight types of false views arise;
these are what are called the "initial views regarding characteristics."
That is to say, having heard what is taught in the Mahāyāna sūtras regarding all phenomena (dharmas).
All are devoid of intrinsic nature;
they are without arising and without cessation,
being primordially quiescent.
Expressions such as "naturally extinguished" (prakṛti-parinirvṛta) do not possess an underlying intentional meaning;
they merely follow the literal sense of these words.
He then gives rise to resolute conviction,
thinking: "All phenomena spoken of by the Buddha are certainly devoid of intrinsic nature."

To be fixated on such characteristics as "the certainty of non-arising" and so forth, or on characteristics such as "the nature of non-existence," is called the view of characteristics (*lakṣaṇadṛṣṭi*).
When they cling to such characteristics as the non-existence of nature and so forth,
they then slander the three natures.
That is to say: the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Thus it is known that if one slanders these three natures,
one then negates all phenomena, including both the ultimate and conventional truths;
this is why the two views of existence and non-existence arise.
It is the root of all views;
if one can sever all views,
one will naturally accord with the Mirror of the Fundamental Principle.
The *Huashou jing* (Sutra of the Flower-Handed One) says:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra.
"What is meant by 'right view'? Śāriputra," [the Buddha said].
As for right view,
it is without high or low;
it contemplates all phenomena with equanimity.
Furthermore, one who possesses right view has no views at all. Why is this?
Whatever views one may have are all false views;
there is no view at all.
This is precisely right view.
The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states:
The Buddha said:
Śāriputra, all views arise from false conditions.
If one forms the thought,
"This is right view," that person is, in fact, possessed of wrong view.
Śāriputra, within the Noble Dharma,
one uproots and severs the very foundation of all views.
They completely sever all paths of verbal expression,
just as a hand meets no resistance or obstruction in empty space.
All the dharmas of the śramaṇas should be thus.
It is further said:
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra, the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas..."
It is of but one meaning, namely: detachment.
What is meant by detachment?
One is free from all desires and views.
"Desire" is none other than ignorance;
"view" is none other than recollection.
Why is this? Because all phenomena have mindfulness as their foundation.
All conceptual thoughts are themselves views;
such views are themselves erroneous.
Therefore, if one can be free from views,
one immediately becomes a Buddha,
to whom the ten directions bow their heads.
The myriad species take refuge [in him].
As it says in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*:
"Gautama, the Great Holy Lord..."
Out of compassion, you have taught this Dharma that completely severs all views;
I now prostrate to you in homage.
Furthermore, regarding the one who remains in the Middle Way by distancing themselves from the two extremes,
according to the explanation based on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
Briefly stated, four types are enumerated to represent all others.
The first is defilement and purification, categorized according to afflictions (*kleśa*).
Second, bondage and liberation,
which pertain to both afflictions and karma;
third, existence and non-existence.
It penetrates both principle and phenomena.
Fourth is identity and difference,
which is determined in relation to mind and object.
Why is this so? It is because upon attaining Bodhi, one is already free from subtle thoughts and delusive afflictions have been exhausted.
Thus, the wisdom of the dharmakāya is revealed as being purely immaculate.
If one holds this view:
It cannot avoid being a limitation.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
"If there is one who perceives the Perfectly Awakened One..."
Liberated and free from all outflows,
unattached to any world—
this is not the realization of the eye of the path.
Now, having realized that the essence of delusion is fundamentally empty,
