The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states:
"Regarding the eighth consciousness, its meaning as the 'capable store' and the 'stored-in' is as follows:"
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "store" (ālaya): it refers to this consciousness as the substance that stores;
it is the locus where the sense organs, the body, the seeds, and the receptacle world are stored.
Because the sense organs, the body,
and so forth are the objective-image (nimitta-bhāga) of this consciousness,
they are like objects and images within a storehouse.
It is like being inside a room and wishing to find the *ālaya-vijñāna*;
it resides solely within form and mind.
If one wishes to seek the maṇi jewel,
it is found right within the blue and yellow;
this is next, the meaning of concealment.
This means that all phenomena, such as the sense faculties and the physical body,
are stored within the collection of consciousnesses.
Like images within a pearl,
if one wishes to seek all dharmas,
they are all contained within the ālayavijñāna.
If one seeks all images,
they are entirely contained within the mani jewel;
thus, the preceding meaning functions as both subject and object.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The existence of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is established by means of eight kinds of arguments."
1. The characteristic of being based on appropriation;
2. The characteristic of initial origination;
3. The characteristic of having clarity.
4. The characteristic of possessing the nature of seeds;
5. The characteristic of the differentiation of karmic functions; 6. [The characteristic of the differentiation of maturation].
7. The characteristics of the distinctions between bodily experience; 8. The characteristics of the mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) in seven locations;
9. The characteristics of the timing of the end of life.
Furthermore, regarding the ancient masters’ interpretation based on the treatises to prove the existence of the eighth consciousness,
the treatise states:
"This eighth consciousness..."
This is not an object perceived by worldly direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
it relies solely upon authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*) and authentic reasoning (*yukti*).
And knowing that it exists,
he cites seven sūtras as proof.
There are two verses in the Abhidharma-sūtra:
The first verse states:
"The realm existing from beginningless time is the equal support for all phenomena."
From this arise the various realms of existence as well as the realization of nirvāṇa;
that which has been the element (dhātu) from beginningless time.
The term "dhātu" (element) signifies the meaning of "cause," referring to the eighth consciousness.
From beginningless time until now,
it is able to maintain the seeds of all phenomena— both tainted and untainted, including form and mind—
and is further able to provide power to those tainted and untainted seeds.
It causes [the seeds] to arise as actual manifestations;
thus, the eighth consciousness serves as both the supporting basis (*āśraya*) and the cause of origination (*samutthāna-hetu*) for all seeds.
"All phenomena equally rely [upon it]" means that "rely" has the sense of "condition";
this refers to the eighth consciousness.
It is capable of transforming itself into the body and the environment,
serving as the support for sentient beings and acting as the basis for all defiled and undefiled manifest phenomena.
Because it is able to grasp and maintain the body of the five material sense-faculties,
serving as their simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) for the first seven consciousnesses,
the eighth consciousness is thus able to provide [support] for all currently manifest phenomena, such as matter and mind.
It serves as the dominant condition and support.
It is by virtue of this that the various realms of existence and the realization of nirvāṇa come to be.
This eighth consciousness does not only serve as the support and basis for the contaminated phenomena of saṃsāra;
it also simultaneously functions as the support for all uncontaminated phenomena conducive to the cessation of suffering.
It serves as the function of support and maintenance.
The second verse states:
"Because it contains all phenomena."
Because it is the consciousness of all seeds,
it is called the ālaya. This is what I,
the Victorious One, have expounded.
That is to say, the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the eighth consciousness is called the "seed-consciousness" because it is capable of maintaining the seeds.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states in verse:
"The ādāna-vijñāna is profound and subtle;
containing all seeds, it is like a torrential stream."
I do not reveal this to the foolish and ignorant,
fearing that they would conceptually grasp it as a self.
As for "ādāna" (appropriation)...
This is called "grasping and maintaining" (*upādāna*).
It is because this consciousness is able to grasp and maintain the seeds of all phenomena,
as well as being able to grasp and maintain the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
Furthermore, because it is also able to grasp the sense faculties and their bases, and thereby effect the continuity of rebirth,
this consciousness is so described.
It is named *ādāna*.
Regarding "all seeds like a torrential stream," this refers to all the seeds within the eighth consciousness.
If it encounters conditions such as being struck by a drum,
the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) arise in actual manifestation;
or else, the seeds undergo arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
It does not cease;
it is like a torrential stream.
As a verse in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
It is like the great waves of the ocean,
which arise from a violent wind;
the vast billows surge across the depths of the sea.
There is no time of interruption;
the ocean of the storehouse consciousness abides eternally,
stirred by the winds of objective realms.
The various waves of consciousness surge and arise in succession.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* of the Hīnayāna states:
There is a fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) which is the support for all these consciousnesses.
This fundamental consciousness...
This is precisely the eighth consciousness,
because the eighth consciousness is able to initiate the preceding six evolving consciousnesses.
Second, the Theravāda school asserts the existence of the *bhavanga-vijñāna*,
which is precisely the eighth consciousness.
The substance of this bhavāṅga-vijñāna is eternally uninterrupted and exists throughout the three realms.
"Existence" refers to the three realms of existence (*tribhava*).
"Cause" has the sense of a factor;
thus, it refers to the cause of the three realms of existence.
All [these] arise from this consciousness.
Within the Saṃmitīya school, it is taught that there are "aggregates for the exhaustion of saṃsāra" (saṃsāraparyantaskandha).
Taking these as their object, the eighth [consciousness] pervades the three realms and nine stages.
Because it exists eternally,
wherever there is birth and death,
it is always and universally present as the basis.
Because they are only relinquished when afflictions are exhausted at the end of the Mahāyāna Vajra-mind stage,
they are called the "aggregates that exhaust saṃsāra."
If it were the various evolving consciousnesses that possessed this capacity, it would not be so,
because the substance of the sixth consciousness is frequently interrupted.
When one enters the five states of mindlessness,
the six consciousnesses are all interrupted and do not function;
at such times, one should no longer be designated as a sentient being.
Because it would lack the sustaining power of consciousness,
it would immediately rot and decay. (4)
The Sarvāstivādins call this consciousness the *ālaya*.
There are four kinds of *ālayas*: that which is characterized by craving, delight, and joy.
Craving is the general term;
it takes all three periods of time as its object in general.
The remaining three are the specific terms.
They take the three time periods as their respective objects:
joy pertains to the present,
while delight pertains to the past.
This joy is future;
it is this very eighth consciousness,
which all sentient beings constantly grasp as their internal self.
This is the locus of true attachment;
therefore, it is named *ālaya*.
There are ten points regarding its true principle.
First, the mind that maintains the seeds (*bīja*).
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
As it is said in the Sūtras:
"Because it is the place where the seeds of all defiled and purified phenomena are gathered and arise,
it is called 'mind' (citta)."
If this consciousness did not exist,
that mind which maintains the seeds would not be possible;
for it is said that the various evolving consciousnesses are absent in states such as the meditative attainment of cessation.
Because they are subject to interruption;
and because categories such as the faculties, objects, mental attention,
and the wholesome and so forth arise with ease.
Like a flash of lightning and so forth,
because they do not abide firmly,
they cannot be perfumed.
Neither of these can maintain seeds,
because they are not the locus where defiled or pure seeds are accumulated and arise.
Second, the resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
As it is said in the sūtras,
there is a maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*).
Regarding the statement: "It is produced by the maturation of wholesome and unwholesome karma;
for if this consciousness did not exist, that resultant mind would not be possible."
This refers to the eighth consciousness;
that is to say, in a previous life,
it took wholesome and unwholesome karma as its cause.
The eighth resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*) acquired through karmic attraction in this present life is the fruit.
The treatise states:
"One must certainly admit the existence of a true resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*)."
Recompensing for the projecting karma,
it transforms pervasively and without interruption into the physical body and the vessel-world.
It serves as the support for sentient beings;
for it is logically impossible for the body-vessel to exist apart from the mind.
Regarding the essence of the realms, destinies, and births of the three worlds,
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
"The Sūtra says..."
Sentient beings transmigrate through the five destinies and four modes of birth;
if this consciousness did not exist,
the substantial basis for those destinies and births would not be possible.
One must believe that there exists an eighth consciousness which serves as the substance of the three realms, the nine stages, the five destinies,
and the four modes of birth.
If this consciousness did not exist, then no sentient beings could possibly exist at all.
The fourth is "appropriated" (*sopādāna*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
Furthermore, a sūtra says:
The body possessing the sense organs is subject to appropriation;
if this consciousness were absent, [it would not be so].
Because it would be impossible for that [intermediate state] to possess appropriation;
those sentient beings in the form realm possess the five material sense faculties.
As well as the five internal sense objects,
these are the eighth consciousness’s immediate *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect),
which only the eighth consciousness can grasp and maintain (*upādāna*).
If it were any other consciousness, it would lack this capacity; [for it is said:
"The five are life-force, warmth, and consciousness."
There are three proofs for the existence of the eighth consciousness.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Furthermore, a sūtra says:"
Vitality, warmth, and consciousness mutually support one another so that they may continue to abide;
if this consciousness were absent, [they would not].
Because it is capable of sustaining vitality and warmth so that they endure for a long time,
consciousness must exist; therefore,
there is mind at the time of birth and death.
The existence of the eighth consciousness is established by scriptural authority. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Furthermore, a sūtra says:"
When sentient beings undergo birth and death,
or when the mind abides in a state of distraction or enters a mindless meditative absorption,
if this consciousness did not exist, [these states would be impossible].
Because the mind at the time of birth and death should not exist [as a continuum];
furthermore, at the moment of death,
by virtue of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
The sensation of cold gradually arises in the upper and lower parts of the body;
if this consciousness were absent,
that phenomenon would not occur.
The seventh is the citation of the basis of dependent origination as proof for the existence of the eighth consciousness.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
consciousness is conditioned by name-and-form,
and name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness.
These two dharmas depend upon one another in turn,
like a bundle of reeds.
They function simultaneously;
for if this consciousness did not exist,
the intrinsic nature of those [other] consciousnesses would not be possible.
The Hīnayāna says:
"I take the six consciousnesses to be the support for name-and-form."
Why is the eighth [consciousness] necessary?
The treatise refutes this, stating:
"The evolving consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth..."
It is subsumed within "name.
If this consciousness did not exist, what would one designate as "consciousness"?
The Master of the Treatise says:
The six consciousnesses, beginning with the visual consciousness,
are already included within "name" (nāman).
For the sake of the aggregate of consciousness,
it is necessary to have the eighth [consciousness] as the external branch of consciousness,
which serves as the basis for name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Furthermore, just as when a person is born in this realm,
the mind of the intermediate state (antarābhava) grasps [the new existence] at its first moment of conception.
Since the first six consciousnesses have not yet arisen,
they are included within the aggregate of consciousness; thus, name-and-form consists of only three aggregates.
Upon what do these three aggregates called "name-and-form" depend for their abiding in a single moment?
Therefore, one knows that the eighth consciousness exists;
this is called the external branch of consciousness,
which serves as the support for name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
The eighth is the *āhāra* (nutriment) that leads consciousness [to rebirth]. This proves the existence of the eighth consciousness.
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"All sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment."
If this consciousness did not exist,
the substance of that consciousness-food would not be possible;
therefore, the Buddha said to the non-Buddhists:
It is the correct awakening and the correct teaching that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment.
Others cannot know this. You,
O outsider, who starve your own body,
will ultimately derive no benefit from it.
"Food" has the meaning of providing nourishment and sustenance; it consists of nine [types].
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that the existence of the eighth consciousness is proven by the mind present during the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Specifically, it says: [text follows].
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"For one who abides in the meditative attainment of cessation,
the activities of body, speech, and mind are all without exception extinguished."
Yet his life-force does not perish,
nor is he separated from warmth,
and his faculties do not undergo transformation or decay.
Consciousness does not depart from the body;
for if this consciousness were absent, one who dwells in the meditative attainment of cessation would [not exist].
"Consciousness does not depart from the body,
because it would then cease to exist.
Thus says the Master of the Treatise.
In an Ārya who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti),
all activities of body, speech, and mind are entirely extinguished,
including even inhalation and exhalation.
This is the application of the body;
feeling and perception are the application of the mind.
Vitarka and vicāra are the preparatory stages of speech;
these three preparatory stages are associated with the sixth consciousness.
Because all [mental factors] are extinguished within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
yet life-force (*āyus*) is not extinguished,
it resides upon the seeds of the eighth consciousness.
There is a function that maintains the continuity of the physical form and mind of a single rebirth without interruption;
this is called "life-force" (*āyus*).
As for the statement "it is also not separate from consciousness":
The sensation of heat is the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of the eighth consciousness;
these two phenomena are both inseparable from the eighth consciousness.
Since one is within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
the six groups of consciousness, as well as the preparatory activities of body, speech, and mind, are all entirely inactive; yet,
vitality (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*) remain present.
It is clearly known that this [consciousness] serves as the support for life-force (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*);
this is the eighth consciousness. Tenth, ten citations regarding defiled and pure minds prove the existence of the eighth consciousness.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
Furthermore, a sūtra says,
"Because the mind is defiled..."
Sentient beings are defiled because the mind is defiled; sentient beings are purified because the mind is purified.
If this consciousness did not exist,
those defiled and pure minds would not be possible;
for it is said that defiled and pure phenomena take the mind as their basis.
It arises because of the mind,
abides in dependence on the mind,
and receives its perfuming.
Because it sustains those seeds,
that which takes the mind as its basis refers to all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, whether defiled or pure.
All take the eighth consciousness as their root.
That which dwells in dependence upon the mind refers to the active manifestations of the preceding seven consciousnesses.
All abide in reliance upon the eighth consciousness.
As for the statement "receiving their perfuming," it means that the eighth consciousness receives the perfuming of those preceding seven consciousnesses.

Regarding the phrase "that which maintains those seeds," this refers to the eighth [consciousness], which is capable of maintaining the seeds of the three natures— both defiled and pure— of the preceding seven [consciousnesses].
Thus, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states:
This body is like a reanimated corpse,
and also like a mirage in the heat;
it revolves according to the conditions of its causes and actions.
Neither false nor real,
it is led by sensation;
its nature is empty and devoid of self.
The mental consciousness and its associates are cognized by the mind;
they arise simultaneously with it,
and the five consciousnesses further depend upon them.
Consciousness arises based on these causes;
in this manner, at all times,
the great earth functions simultaneously with them.
The ālayavijñāna is perfumed by craving and thereby increases;
having increased of its own accord, it [continues].
Furthermore, they increase other consciousnesses,
continuing in succession without interruption,
just like a well-wheel.
Because the various consciousnesses exist,
the manifold realms of existence arise;
within these various realms, [beings are born].
Consciousness further undergoes increase;
consciousness and worldly phenomena serve as mutual causes for one another.
It is like the flow of a river,
uninterrupted from beginning to end;
it is also like a sprout and its seed.
They arise in continuous succession;
each distinct in its own characteristics,
they manifest through conceptual differentiation.
The activity of consciousness is also like this:
having already been a conjunction of the three,
it then undergoes a further conjunction.
They arise with distinct characteristics;
thus they circulate in transmigration,
never ceasing for a moment.
All phenomena, both internal and external,
arise because of this; the deluded do not understand that they are but mind-only.
"You all should observe with diligence.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"O son of good family..."
The accumulation of all false karmas is called the mind (citta);
the manas deliberates, and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) discriminates.
The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, perceive objects differently;
yet foolish worldlings are unable to realize this.
Fearing old age, sickness, and death, they seek entry into nirvana;
yet they recognize neither saṃsāra nor nirvana.
They falsely give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding all objects,
and furthermore, by means of the future sense faculties.
When the objects of the five sensory realms are severed and extinguished,
foolish and ignorant people take this to be nirvana.
When all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas realize awakening for themselves,
they transform the ālayavijñāna into the wisdom of primordial awareness (mūla-bodhi-jñāna).
O son of good family!
All ordinary, ignorant people are deluded regarding the Buddha’s skillful means;
they cling to the existence of three vehicles and fail to understand the triple world.
Arising from the mind,
they do not understand that all Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time are the manifestation of one's own mind.
Seeing the five external sense objects,
they grasp them as truly existent,
just like cattle or sheep.
Unable to attain awakening,
there is no means of escape from within the wheel of birth and death.
"Good son, the Buddha has taught that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation,
and that they likewise do not exist within the three periods of time."
Why is this? Because the objects of the five sensory realms appear as manifestations of one's own mind.
Because they fundamentally do not exist;
because all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, are fundamentally unarisen.
The Noble One has realized this for himself;
such is the nature of the objective realm.
O son of good family!
Ignorant ordinary beings give rise to false discrimination,
grasping at existence within that which is non-existent.
Grasping at existence while clinging to non-existence,
they apprehend the various phenomenal aspects of the ālayavijñāna and fall into the two views of arising and ceasing.
Failing to understand one's own mind,
one gives rise to conceptual discrimination,
O son of good family.
One should know that one's own mind is itself the dharma of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
for by knowing one's own mind as the Buddha-dharma, [one realizes it].
Thus, one is able to purify all buddha-fields and enter all kalpas; for this reason,
the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) suddenly transforms into the sense organs, the body, and the receptacle world.
It is of an extremely profound meaning,
such that it cannot be measured by either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).
Furthermore, because it is immeasurable and limitless,
as a verse in the sutra says:
"The dharma-realm is not finite."
Nor is it the immeasurable;
the Muni has completely transcended both the measurable and the immeasurable.
Therefore, know that the nature of consciousness is difficult for those of shallow wisdom to clarify;
it is only through ultimate penetration that one reaches full understanding.
Only the Buddha can fully comprehend it;
for this reason, the *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the Source) extensively cites these passages,
as they are subtle, profound, and difficult to understand.
Question:
The correct principle of Vijñaptimātra is for the purpose of destroying the two attachments to self and dharmas.
It reveals the principle of the two kinds of emptiness and realizes the one true mind. How so?
Both worldly convention and the various sacred teachings [attest to this].
Question: It is said that there is a self and dharmas. Answer:
This is merely a conventional designation.
It arises solely based on the transformation of consciousness.
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Verses on Representation-only) states:
"By means of conventional designations, there are the self and phenomena."
There are various modes of transformation;
these depend on what is transformed by consciousness.
This transforming [consciousness] is of only three kinds.

That is to say: the ripening consciousness, the deliberating consciousness, and the consciousnesses that discern objects; so it is stated in the worldly scriptures and the teachings of the noble ones.
The teaching that there is a self and phenomena exists merely as a conventional designation;
it does not possess the nature of substantial reality.
"I" refers to a sovereign controller; "dharmas" refer to that which maintains its own characteristics and serves as a norm. ...
[The text continues] until: how should one understand that external objects do not truly exist?
There is only internal consciousness arising in the semblance of external objects,
for a real self and real dharmas cannot be found.
How is it that a real self cannot be found?
Briefly stated, there are three types of selves that are clung to.
First, they cling to the notion that the self is eternal, all-pervasive,
and equal in extent to space.
Because one creates karma and experiences pleasure and pain in various places;
second, although the substance of the grasped self is eternal, [it is not so].
Furthermore, its measurement is not fixed,
for it expands and contracts according to the size of the body. Thirdly:
They grasp at the self as being eternal and extremely subtle,
like a single atom,
because it secretly moves within the body to perform its activities.
The first [position] is initially unreasonable. Why is this so?
Because it maintains that the self is permanent, omnipresent, and equal in extent to space.
It should not experience suffering, pleasure, and so forth in accordance with the body.
Furthermore, because it is permanent and omnipresent, it should be devoid of movement; how then could it follow the body to perform various karmas?
Even the middle position is unreasonable.
Why is this? Because it maintains that the essence of the self is permanent.
It should not expand or contract according to the body;
since it does indeed expand and contract,
it is like the wind from a bellows.
It should not be permanent;
this applies even until the end, for it would likewise be illogical. Why is that?
My measure is so small;
how could I quickly traverse the body like a whirling firebrand?
Because it undergoes movement,
the self as it is grasped is neither unitary nor permanent;
thus, there is coming and going.
Because it is neither constant nor unitary.
Furthermore, there are three types of the self as it is conceived.
First, that which is identical with the aggregates; second, that which is distinct from them.
Third, it is neither identical to nor separate from the aggregates.
To claim that the self is initially identical to the aggregates is logically untenable;
for the self would then, like the aggregates, be neither permanent nor unitary.
Furthermore, internal forms are certainly not a real self,
just like external forms.
Because they possess resistance,
the mind and mental factors are also not a real self.
It does not continue in a constant succession,
because it depends upon various conditions;
this applies to other formations and other forms as well.
Nor is it a real self,
like space and so forth,
because it lacks the nature of sentience.
The principle that there is a self separate from the aggregates is likewise untenable;
it would then be like space.
Because there is no experience of non-action,
the subsequent claim that [the self] is not-self is also logically untenable.
It is admitted that [the self] is established in dependence upon the aggregates (skandha), neither being identical to nor separate from them,
just like a jar or similar objects.
Because it is not a real self.
Furthermore, since it cannot be described as either conditioned or unconditioned.
Furthermore, it should also be impossible to say that it is either "self" or "non-self";
therefore, the real self as they conceive it is not established.
This applies to everything up to what has been stated thus far.
All forms of self-grasping [regard] the aggregates external to one's own mind as either existing or non-existing.
All things exist within the aggregates of one's own mind;
therefore, the grasping at a self always takes as its object the characteristics of the five impermanent appropriated aggregates.
One falsely clings to them as a self;
however, the characteristics of the aggregates arise from conditions.
This exists like an illusion;
the self that is falsely grasped is so only because of arbitrary conceptualization.
It is definitively non-existent.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Bhikṣus, you should know."
All views of self held by any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas in the world arise based upon the five aggregates of clinging.
Question: If,
apart from the mind,
there is no real self and no real dharmas, [how can this be so?]
Then the provisional dharma would also not exist,
because the provisional dharma is established in dependence upon the ultimate reality. [The opponent] replies:
Now, that which is designated by means of dharmas is merely provisional;
it appears as if existent while it functions.
It certainly does not rely on the true suchness (*tathatā*).
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* says:
Someone raises this objection:
"If there are no real selves or dharmas apart from consciousness,
then even the conventional (prajñapti) should not exist."
This means that a designation (prajñapti) must necessarily be established based on a real entity (bhūtavastu), a similar entity (sādṛśyavastu), and their common characteristics (sāmānyadharma). ...
[omitted] ... Furthermore, it is answered:
"Moreover, a designation must necessarily be established based on a real entity."
This is also unreasonable;
"real" refers to the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), whereas conceptual cognition and its designations are conventional.
Because both are not objects [of direct perception].
That is to say, conventional cognition and its designations cannot apprehend specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
It functions solely with respect to the common characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of all phenomena;
nor is there any other means apart from this for the designation of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
It serves as the basis for designations;
however, the expression of conceptual cognition necessarily arises in dependence upon sound.
Where sound does not reach,
this [process] does not proceed; thus,
there is no relation between the signifier and the signified.
Since both are not self-characteristics,
we know that metaphorical designations do not rely on real entities; therefore,
they function solely by relying on things that resemble [real entities].
It appears as if it were an augmentation,
yet it does not possess the characteristic of real existence;
sound functions based on an augmented semblance.
Therefore, it cannot be said that the provisional must necessarily depend upon the real.
Question:
Regarding this eighth consciousness—
How many types of transformative consciousnesses are there that cause the various consciousnesses to arise, grow, and manifest? Answer:
There are two types of transformative consciousness:
first, the transforming consciousness as cause;
second, the transforming consciousness as result.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"There are two kinds of transformative capacity (*pariṇāma*). First, the transformative capacity of the cause (*hetu-pariṇāma*)."
This refers to the two types of causal latencies within the eighth consciousness: those of uniform outflow and those of maturation.
The outflowing habitual tendencies are caused to grow by being perfumed by the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral [states] within the seven consciousnesses.
The ripening habitual tendencies are perfumed and caused to grow by the tainted wholesome and unwholesome [states] within the six consciousnesses.
Second, the resultant transformative consciousness.
This refers to [the transformation] by the power of the two aforementioned types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The eight consciousnesses arise,
manifesting various appearances due to the causal conditions of the habit-energies of their outflow.
The eight consciousnesses arise with distinct characteristics and natures;
this is called the "result of outflow" (niṣyanda-phala),
because the result resembles its cause.
The ripening habitual tendencies act as the dominant condition to induce the eighth consciousness,
thereby recompensing the force of the projecting karma.
Because it is constantly continuous,
it is designated by the name "ripening" (*vipāka*).
That which brings about the six preceding consciousnesses is what repays and fulfills the karma.
That which arises from maturation is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*),
but it is not itself called "maturation" (*vipāka*).
Because there is an interruption,
that which is the aforementioned maturation and that which is born of maturation is called the "fruit of maturation."
Because the fruit differs from its cause,
this section shall first explain the resultant consciousness that undergoes transformation, which is the storehouse of self-clinging and the repository for the seeds of all defiled phenomena.
It is called "maturation" (vipāka).
Question:
The eighth consciousness is vast, all-encompassing, and pervasive.
It is the root source of all phenomena;
both the sūtras and the śāstras unanimously extol it,
and thus it is called "the foremost."
How is its subtle nature to be indicated? Answer:
This essence is ineffable;
it is subtle and most difficult to know.
It pervades the entire dharma-realm, yet the mind dwells nowhere.
It sustains all things without manifesting any signs;
it is like a bird flying through the sky:
though it comes and goes, soaring and wheeling, its tracks cannot be found.
Like a child within the eye,
it can reflect the myriad phenomena of the universe, yet the eye itself never sees;
it is as if the moon contains a single hue.
It manifests the forms of ten thousand images in their entirety,
equaling the sun in its thousand rays as it shines universally upon the four continents below.
Like a maṇi jewel that rains down treasures without thought,
it extensively saves all living beings;
like a magnet that moves others without awareness, it draws them forth.
Circulating through the six realms of existence,
the *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* verse states:
"The storehouse consciousness sustains the world."
Just as beads are strung on a thread,
and as a chariot possesses wheels,
so too do they revolve according to the winds of karma.
As a potter turns his wheel with a staff,
vessels are formed according to their intended use;
so too are the storehouse consciousness and the various realms.
Through combined power, nothing remains unaccomplished;
throughout all internal and external worlds,
it pervades and encompasses everything completely.
Just as the various constellations and celestial forms are arrayed in the void,
sustained by the power of the wind.
Its operation is constant and never ceasing;
like the tracks of a bird in the sky,
it cannot be seen even when sought.
Yet the bird does not leave the void;
it soars and descends as it advances and retreats.
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is likewise.
Not separate from one's own body or the bodies of others;
like waves surging from the sea,
like the sky containing all myriad forms.
The storehouse consciousness is also like this,
storing all habitual tendencies;
it is like the moon reflected in water.
And as for the various lotus flowers,
they are never separated from the water,
yet they are not defiled by the water.
The storehouse consciousness is likewise;
habitual tendencies cannot defile it.
It is like having a film on the eye.
The eye ultimately cannot see itself;
the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) dwells within the body, storing all seeds.
Pervasively sustaining life-force, warmth, and consciousness,
like clouds covering the world,
its karmic activity never ceases.
Sentient beings are unable to see it.
It further says:
"O virtuous ones!"
All various forms are associated with the seeds of form within the ālayavijñāna;
they manifest as if appearing as those very characteristics.
It does not possess a separate substantial entity;
it is identical to that which is falsely discriminated by the ignorant.
O virtuous ones!
All sentient beings—
whether sitting or lying down,
whether walking or standing.
From torpor and sleep,
up to madness and wandering,
there is nothing that is not the ālayavijñāna.
Even as the power of a magnet causes iron to move,
though it has no mind,
it appears as if it possessed a mind.
The ālayavijñāna is likewise thus:
it is sustained by the phenomena of birth and death.
Wandering through the various realms of existence,
it is not the self, yet resembles the self;
it is like an object within water.
Although it lacks thought or awareness,
it follows the water,
flowing without ceasing.
The ālayavijñāna is likewise; although it is devoid of discrimination, [it functions in this manner].
It functions in dependence upon the body;
furthermore, if one is able to correctly observe this,
one will know all worlds.
All these are one's own mind;
they are views born of discrimination,
which are all then transformed and extinguished.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"That which can sustain the causes of the world is what is called the ālayavijñāna."
The eighth is the consciousness of the Great Being, which moves all things,
just as a wheel turns many jars.
Just as oil pervades sesame seeds,
and as there is a salty taste within salt,
so too is the nature of impermanence.
It is omnipresent throughout all forms.
Question:
This consciousness is all-pervasive.
The realms of both ordinary beings and sages are universally to be abandoned; apart from these,
there exists a true nature.
"Are they identical? Answer:
"Neither identical nor different."
It receives this name of "consciousness" because it unites with that which is not united,
thereby fulfilling its meaning as a "storehouse."
This ālayavijñāna is precisely the true mind that does not abide in its own nature,
following along with conditions of either defilement or purity.
That which unites what is not united,
and is able to contain and store all realms of both the ultimate and the conventional,
is therefore called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).
Just as a clear mirror does not unite with its reflections yet contains them—
this is explained from the perspective of the meaning of "conjunction" (saṃyoga).
If it does not accord with the meaning [of conditioned phenomena],
its essence is eternally unchanging; therefore,
it is termed True Suchness (Tathatā).
Based on whether they are conjoined or not,
these two meanings are distinguished;
fundamentally, there is only the one true mind.
It is profoundly still and unmoving.
If there is one who does not believe in the ālayavijñāna,
it is precisely the tathāgatagarbha.
To seek the principle of True Suchness apart from [phenomena] is like seeking a mirror apart from its reflection;
this is indeed a mark of impaired wisdom.
Because they have not yet understood the meaning of "the unchanging following conditions" and "following conditions while remaining unchanging," they give rise to two types of grasping.
Question:
What is the meaning of the transformation of the eighth consciousness?
Answer: "Transformation" refers to the substance of consciousness transforming and appearing as two divisions.
The commentary states:
The treatise clarifies that the essence of the various consciousnesses is precisely the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).
It arises by transforming into two parts, resembling the image and the seeing;
this refers to the essence of consciousness,
which is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The transformation appearing as the two external aspects— the object and the subject—
is not non-existent;
it is also the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
Based on these two divisions,
one clings to the reality of the two graspers;
the Noble Ones declare this to be non-existent.
It is not that these two parts do not exist within the dependent nature;
for the treatise states that there are only two [natures], namely the dependent nature.
This refers to the wisdom that takes reality as its object.
Because it takes true suchness as its object;
since it is partless and signless,
all others possess signs.
No, that is not so. How then could it be called "knowledge of others' minds" (paracittajñāna)? It would merely be subsequent knowledge (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) and the like.
Because there is no grasping from without,
and because it is admitted that the two natures of the image (nimitta) and the seeing (darśana) exist,
the seeds of the image and the seeing are spoken of.
They may be either identical or different.
If they are of the same kind,
they are then a single consciousness-essence.
It arises by transforming into the appearance and function of two parts,
just as a single snail manifests and produces two horns.
This explains that the appearance and seeing of the reflected image are devoid of substantiality and possess no separate nature apart from it.
This is because it is the function of consciousness.
If one says that the aspect and the seeing are of distinct seeds,
then the seeing would be its own self-substance.
Because they are divided according to their functional meanings,
there are no distinct seeds apart from consciousness;
they are simply the single substance of consciousness itself.
It arises through the transformation of the function of discerning the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga),
taking consciousness as its support;
it arises from the seeds of the transformed image-part (nimitta-bhāga) as something resembling that image.
Because they differ in their activities and their natures are each distinct,
they arise from different seeds with distinct characteristics.
This is superior from the perspective of principle;
therefore, it is said that the substance of consciousness transforms and appears as two parts.
This dependent nature is non-existent yet appears as existent.
In reality, it is not divided into two parts;
however, because it resembles the imagined duality of the perceived object (*nimitta*) and the perceiving subject (*darśana*),
it is designated with the term "resembling" (*pratibhāsa*).
If the characteristics are distinct from the seeds,
why are they called transformations of consciousness?
Because they are not separate from consciousness.
When internal consciousness undergoes transformation,
the objective aspect arises subsequently;
this reveals the two divisions of the subjective and objective aspects of the transforming consciousness.
If the substance [of consciousness] exists as something distinct,
for what reason does it further state that consciousness arises appearing as two parts?
The treatise states that both the seeing-part and the seen-part arise based upon self-cognition;
if self-cognition were absent,
these two would certainly not arise.
Just as when there is no head,
horns certainly do not exist,
and when there is no mirror.
The objective aspect does not arise independently,
as it manifests its characteristics entirely upon consciousness; therefore,
it is said that the two divisions arise based on the substance of consciousness.
Furthermore, it is not only the two divisions of the perceived and the perceiver that arise based on the substance of consciousness;
this extends even to the bodies of ordinary beings and sages.
Pure and impure lands both manifest from consciousness,
as Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
The Tathāgata Candrasūryapradīpa instructed me to practice the samādhi of mind-only consciousness and enter into samādhi.
Throughout kalpas past,
they have served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with this samādhi,
yet they have sought after a mind for worldly fame.
It ceased and vanished.
Upon the appearance of Dīpaṃkara Buddha in the world,
I finally attained the unsurpassed, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the mind of consciousness.
Even unto the exhaustion of the Tathāgata’s lands throughout space—
whether pure or defiled, existent or non-existent—
all are manifestations produced by the transformations of my own mind.
World-Honored One,
because I have thus realized that it is solely mind and consciousness,
the nature of consciousness flows forth as immeasurable Tathāgatas.
Now I have received this prediction that I shall next succeed to the Buddha’s place.
I ask the Buddha about the perfect penetration of the Way.
I have observed with clarity that the ten directions are solely consciousness;
the mind of consciousness is perfectly luminous, entering the state of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Distant from the dependent nature and the imagined nature,
one attains the patience regarding non-arising.
This is the foremost. Therefore,
the pure and impure lands throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions are all manifested from within my own mind.
All is my own dwelling;
truth and falsehood follow the mind,
while skill and clumsiness depend on wisdom.
For the sake of the great bodhisattvas,
he elucidates that pure method;
for the sake of inferior sentient beings, he provides a provisional resort.
Manifesting this defiled land,
the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are all those who have flowed forth from within my own heart.
An ancient commentator said:
"They are like bubbles on the sea,
each arising at a different time."
Through observation by means of a discriminating mind,
there is "this" and "that," yet the substance of the water is one.
One immediately knows that when a single Buddha appears,
all buddha-fields appear simultaneously,
because they are free from the marks of self and other.
However, wherever sentient beings exist,
the Tathāgatas of the ten directions manifest in various bodies to assist in their transformation;
it is not that the Tathāgata alone encompasses this single meaning.
All sentient beings are also my emanations.
Question:
Transformation.
Regarding the transformation and manifestation: what is the meaning of their identity or distinction? Answer:
An ancient commentator said:
"There are those that undergo transformation alone,
but do not manifest through transformation."
The term "transformation" (pariṇāma) applies to both seeds and manifest phenomena;
manifest phenomena can, moreover, perfume the seeds.
The seed producing a seed and the seed giving rise to actual manifestation are both termed "transformation."
The term "manifestation" refers solely to the manifestation of the mind and its associates, which are capable of giving rise to the perceived object and the perceiving subject.
This is termed "transformation" (vikāra).
It does not apply to the seeds, the characteristics, or the differentiated forms of matter and so forth.
Question:
Question: Regarding the eighth storehouse consciousness and the fruits it produces, are they identical or distinct? Answer:
It is neither identical nor different.
The treatise states:
"Within the fundamental consciousness, that which directly produces its own fruit..."
The distinction of its functional capacity [is such that] it [stands in relation] to the fundamental consciousness and the fruits produced therefrom.
They are neither identical nor different;
for it is logically necessary that their essence and function, as well as cause and effect, should be thus.
The commentary states:
"The fundamental consciousness is the substance;
the seeds are the function."
The seed is the cause;
that which is produced is the fruit.
These two phenomena—
In principle, it should be thus: neither identical nor different.
This applies when considering the fundamental consciousness in relation to its seeds within the context of establishing their essential nature.
Subsuming characteristics into their fundamental nature,
they are all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The seeds arise from active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
When viewed from the perspective of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and functions (*vṛtti*) are discussed separately; therefore,
it pervades all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
If they were identical,
it could not be said that there are dharmas of cause and effect,
nor that there are entities and dharmas.
If they were entirely different,
then rice, wheat, and so forth would be able to produce beans and the like,
because you assert that cause and effect are entirely different.
This is not so; otherwise,
the function would only exist when the entity has already ceased,
because you admit that the essence and the function are entirely distinct.
Because their substance is similar,
their vital energy and influence must be the same;
because cause and effect are similar.
Their functions and appearances can correspond with one another;
they are not invariably different.
Question:
With how many mental factors (caitta) is the ālayavijñāna associated? Answer:
The *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* states:
"It is always associated with contact (*sparśa*) and attention (*manasikāra*)."
Feeling, perception,
and volition.
It is associated with the ālayavijñāna from beginningless time.
Until it has ceased to function,
it is always associated with these five mental factors throughout all its stages.
Because it is subsumed under the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*),
first, regarding contact (*sparśa*),
the treatise says:
It refers to the transformation resulting from the conjunction of the three;
its nature is that which causes the mind and mental factors to contact their objects,
and its function is to serve as the basis for feeling, perception, volition, and so forth.
The commentary states:
Because these five types are,
in essence, subsumed within the category of omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitta*).
It is definitively associated;
though it does not increase,
it likewise cannot be diminished.
Contact is so named because it arises and ceases simultaneously with concentration and is called "universal."
The so-called "conjunction of the three" refers to the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness;
their distinct natures are designated as "the three."
Not being contradictory and instead mutually interpenetrating is called "conformity.
This is the root.
It can serve as a basis;
it can serve as an object; it can be grasped.
The three consciousnesses arise from these;
they rely upon the sense faculties to apprehend their respective objects. Upon these three—
All possess the functional capacity to give rise to all mental factors (caitta) in accordance [with their conditions];
this is termed "transformation" (vipariṇāma),
which is the function of discrimination (vikalpa).
This is the functional capacity of contact (*sparśa*). That is to say, upon contact,
there exists a transformative functional capacity that resembles the three preceding [causes] and is conducive to the arising of mental factors (*caitta*).
It is called "discrimination" (vikalpa).
Discrimination is precisely the experiencing of what appears as a distinct name.
Just as a son resembles his father,
he is called a "discriminative father.
Question:
Why is it that, among the threefold conjunction,
the sense faculty alone is preeminent? Answer:
First, by virtue of being the master:
that which possesses superior capability is designated as the "master."
Second, by virtue of proximity,
it is able to give rise proximately to the mind and its mental factors.
Third, by virtue of its pervasiveness:
it is not merely a mental factor,
as it is also capable of producing the mind.
Fourth, by way of continuity:
it exists as a constant succession,
whereas the object and consciousness are not so.
Although the objective sphere (ālambana) can indeed give rise to the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta),
it is not the primary agent.
Furthermore, because it is not proximate,
it lacks two meanings and is therefore not called "superior."
Although the mind is the sovereign,
it cannot produce the mental factors that arise immediately from it.
Because it is not sovereign,
it is not pervasive;
it lacks one essential characteristic.
Therefore, it is not superior;
both object and consciousness do not continue.
Consciousness.
Because it arises with an object,
it lacks the meaning of continuity; thus,
it does not receive the superior name [of "acquisition"].
Only the faculties are preeminent.
Question: What is the intrinsic nature of contact?
Question: Is this real or is it provisional?
Answer: This is the enumeration of contact.
Concentration is truly existent,
because it has the nature of the four nutriments.
Second, regarding mental attention:
The treatise states:
"Attention (manasikāra) has the nature of being able to arouse the mind."
Its function is to direct the mind toward its respective object.
The commentary explains:
"Attention (manasikāra) alerts the mind."
There are two types of functional power:
first, causing the mind that has not yet arisen to arise;
second, causing the mind that has already arisen to proceed toward its object.
Therefore, it is said that "alerting" refers to the arousal of the seeds of the mind,
which leads them to move toward their objects.
Regarding the three feelings,
the treatise says:
"Feeling."
It has the nature of experiencing the objective aspects that are favorable, unfavorable, or neutral, and its function is to give rise to craving.
As for the fourth, perception (*saṃjñā*): [it is the grasping of the specific characteristics of an object].
The treatise states:
Perception (saṃjñā) has the nature of grasping the image of an object.
Its function is to establish various conventional designations;
that is to say, it is only by establishing the specific characteristics of the boundaries of objects that one can subsequently give rise to various conventional designations.
The commentary states:
"In this context, 'establishment' (an-lì) is a synonym for 'grasping images' (qu-xiang)."
To establish a demarcation by determining its characteristics— such as "this is blue" or "it is not blue"—
is called "establishment" (prajñapti).
Based on this grasping of images,
one then gives rise to names and expressions,
such as "this is blue," and so forth.
Because their natures and categories are manifold, they are called "various.
As for the five types of volition:
The Treatise says:
Volition (cetanā) has the nature of causing the mind to engage in formative activity (abhisamskāra).
Its function is to employ the mind toward virtuous categories and so forth;
that is, it can apprehend the characteristics of the correct causes and conditions of objects and direct the mind itself to perform virtuous and other such deeds.
These five sections are subsumed under the universal [mental factors].
Therefore, they are necessarily associated with the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
These five, beginning with contact (sparśa),...
Although its mode of activity differs from that of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*),
it shares the same time, basis,
and objective referent.
Therefore, it is called "associated.
The aspect of this consciousness is extremely indistinct.
It is unable to differentiate between favorable and unfavorable objects;
it is subtle and uniform,
corresponding exclusively with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Furthermore, this associated feeling is exclusively a maturation (vipāka),
evolving in accordance with previously projected karma.
It does not depend on present conditions,
as it proceeds solely by the power of the influence of wholesome and unwholesome karma; therefore,
it is exclusively neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
The two feelings of suffering and pleasure are born of maturation (vipākaja),
yet they are not actual maturation (vipāka).
Because it depends on present conditions,
it is not associated with this [consciousness].
Furthermore, because this consciousness is eternally without transformation.
Sentient beings constantly grasp [this] as their internal self;
when it is associated with the two feelings of pleasure and pain,
it undergoes transformation.
One would rather grasp it as a self;
therefore, it is associated only with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
The commentary states:
Although these five factors, such as contact and so forth, differ from the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) in their modes of activity (*ākāra*),
they are identical in terms of time, basis (*āśraya*), and the objects (*ālambana*) and entities (*vastu*) they apprehend.
It is called "concordant" because it is so by virtue of the fourfold equality;
thus it is designated as concordant.
That is to say: equality of object,
equality of location,
and equality of time.
Regarding the basis and so forth:
now, with respect to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), it constitutes the aspect (*ākāra*);
with respect to the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), it constitutes the object-condition (*ālambana*).
"Self-nature," "named entity," and so forth.
Regarding the meaning of "similarity":
their essential natures are each unique,
yet their objective aspects are similar.
Therefore, the objects of focus are all termed "equal" by virtue of the five characteristics,
such as contact and so forth.
They arise based on the characteristics of the fundamental consciousness;
since their objects of perception are similar,
they are called "equal."
Taking Consciousness-Only as its tenet,
it does not designate the "substantial essence" as the object-condition (*ālambana*),
nor does it designate the "reflected image" as the mode-of-apprehension (*ākāra*).
"Time" means that [the moments] are necessarily identical in terms of the same world-moment (*kṣaṇa*).
"Basis" means that they coexist with the sense-faculties without any interval.
"Only associated with neutral feeling" means:
This has five meanings.
First, it is extremely indistinct; this is the characteristic of the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
If it is a feeling of suffering or pleasure,
it must be clearly discerned; therefore,
it is "feeling."
In total there are five:
first, sorrow;
second, joy.
Three are suffering;
four are pleasure;
five are equanimity.
In this context, sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and joy (*saumanasya*) are included within suffering (*duḥkha*) and pleasure (*sukha*);
they are distinguished according to the three doors of feeling (*vedanā*),
and thus sorrow and joy are not mentioned separately.
Second, being unable to distinguish between agreeable and disagreeable objects,
one perceives neutral objects; this is the characteristic of the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
If it refers to other feelings,
they arise from grasping at objects that are either disagreeable or agreeable;
thirdly, by way of subtlety.
If it were any other feeling,
its mode of activity would necessarily be coarse.
Fourth, by way of being of one kind.
If it were any other feeling,
it would necessarily be easily relinquished; thus,
the characteristic of this [feeling] is fixed.
Therefore, they constitute a single category.
Five [types] proceed as a continuous succession;
if it were any other feeling, [it would not be so].
There must necessarily be interruptions;
this [state], however, is constantly continuous.
Therefore, it consists solely of neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
If one can differentiate between the characteristics of favorable and unfavorable objects,
it is not true maturation (*vipāka*).
As for that which is maturation:
Because it is fixed upon its object;
if it were coarse and mobile,
it would be like other states of mind.
It is not the primary agent of maturation;
this indicates that its mode of activity is difficult to discern,
distinguishing it from other forms of consciousness.
Because these five meanings necessarily exist,
it is able to receive perfuming, maintain seeds, and continue in succession.
Furthermore, it is explained that this consciousness is extremely indistinct and has never possessed wisdom or mindfulness.
Because the mental aspect of wisdom and mindfulness is extremely clear,
one is unable to differentiate between the characteristics of favorable and unfavorable objects.

This demonstrates that it is exclusively the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), and not associated with either suffering or pleasure; furthermore, it distinguishes it from being associated with the wholesome, the defiled, and so forth.
They proceed in continuous succession,
manifesting that there is no desire,
yet there is now hope.
Just as there is a desire to arise,
because of this continuity,
there is no [separate] desire.
By means of these five points,
the second point specifically clarifies the reason why it is exclusively associated with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*);
the remaining four points [clarify this as well].
Because it is distinguished by its object and other such factors,
it is associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Question:
Since this consciousness is associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*),
how can it also be the maturation (*vipāka*) of unwholesome karma? Answer:
The treatise states:
"Because the sensation of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā) does not conflict with either the wholesome or unwholesome categories,
it is like indeterminate (avyākṛta) phenomena."
"Both good and evil bring about [results].
The commentary explains:
"Since the indeterminate (avyākṛta) is quiescent..."
What constitutes the fruit of evil karma?
Although abandonment is quiescent,
it does not contradict these two.
One will obtain evil fruits;
it is not like the tranquility of meditative concentration,
for this [state] is incapable of accomplishing anything.
Therefore, it is universally associated with the maturation of unwholesome karma;
even if the other seven evolving consciousnesses give rise to suffering or pleasure,
this consciousness is always concomitant with them.
Because equanimity does not conflict with the categories of suffering and pleasure;
for if suffering and pleasure were not simultaneous,
[this would apply] among humans and devas.
One should not experience bitter fruits [of karma],
because they are contradictory;
this applies to the three evil destinies.
One should not experience the fruit of pleasure,
as that too would be contradictory.
In this context, suffering and pleasure—
These are all separately summoned;
therefore, their abandonment does not constitute a transgression. Question:
Question: Why does the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) not associate with the five mental factors of specific objects (viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa) and so forth?
Answer: The treatise states:
Because they are mutually contradictory,
it functions as a desire for the attainment of what one seeks and hopes for.
This consciousness functions in accordance with karma without any expectation;
it proceeds by way of resolute conviction and the definitive apprehension of an object.
This consciousness is dull and indistinct, lacking any stable support;
its function is solely to clearly record and revolve upon previously experienced matters.
This consciousness is dull and inferior, unable to clearly remember;
concentration,
however, can cause the mind to focus single-pointedly on a single object.
This consciousness functions spontaneously, discerning each object moment by moment;
wisdom, however,
functions by means of selective discrimination regarding matters such as acquisition.
Because this consciousness is subtle and indistinct, it lacks the capacity for discernment;
therefore, it does not associate with the object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-viniyata*).
Furthermore, because this consciousness is exclusively of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*).
The wholesome, the defiled, and so forth are likewise not associated with it.
As for the four factors such as remorse (*kaukṛtya*) that are of indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*):
Because it is interrupted,
it is certainly not a maturation (vipāka).
The commentary states:
Concentration is indeed able to cause the mind to focus one-pointedly on a single object.
Although this consciousness spontaneously perceives different objects moment by moment,
and although the image-aspect (nimittabhāga) arises anew in each moment, concentration remains focused.
At the time of preparatory application, the essential nature that is observed is an object to which one continuously and constantly focuses throughout its preceding and succeeding moments;
this consciousness functions spontaneously.
Without applying effort to focus on the essential nature,
one constantly takes as an object the present mental image.
However, they arise anew and anew;

Deeply grasping and focusing,

this consciousness is superficial and unstable.
The mode of activity (*ākāra*) is not thus;
therefore, it is not a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*). As for the term "spontaneous" (*svarasa*):
These, such as regret (*kaukṛtya*) and so forth, which follow the transformation of karma,
are certainly not of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*).
It is not a true maturation,
yet it does not preclude the arising of maturation.
There are also [mental factors] such as remorse (*kaukṛtya*),
because they do not persist in a continuous stream at all times; therefore,
they are not associated with this [state].
Thus we know that the eighth true consciousness is eternally like the aspect of equanimity,
functioning through the conditions of spontaneous spontaneity.
It accords with the path of permanence;
it is not defiled by impure dharmas,
and is instead governed by pure dharmas.
It is not that which is bound by birth and death,
nor can it be stilled by nirvana; therefore,
it is called the lord of consciousness.
Therefore, it is called the "King of the Mind.
Subsequently, due to a single thought of ignorance,
the waves of the seven consciousnesses arise.
Consequently, mental factors arise and the fundamental mind-king is lost;
all this is due to the forceful awakening of cognitive clarity.
By distinguishing the means of proof from the object of proof,
one gives rise to clear understanding;
the mind and its objects become vividly manifest.
The emotions of discrimination are set in motion;
self and other appear distinct.
From this, within the minds of sentient beings...
Following after hatred and love, one binds together enemies and kin;
within the realm of insentient objects,

Consequently, externally, mulberry fields were transformed into oceans and oceans were transformed into mulberry fields;
internally, one's own kin became the source of enmity.
Enmity is the seed of intimacy;
they alternate between superiority and inferiority,
reciprocating with one another in turn.
From this point on, karmic fruits will perpetually renew,
and the conditions for suffering will remain unceasing. Therefore, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "This delusion of clarity is not caused by another;
the fault lies in the awakening-clarity itself."
Once what is falsely imagined has been established,
the clear principle does not exceed it;
for these reasons and conditions.
Hearing does not transcend sound;
seeing does not transcend form;
and so on, until there is only killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
These three are the root.
By these causes and conditions,
the fruits of karma continue in succession.
Pūrṇa, these three kinds of inverted continuities are all the nature of awareness—
clear, luminous, and fully cognizant.
Because they arise from the manifestation of conditions,
they are born from deluded vision;
these include the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all other conditioned phenomena.
Successively migrating and flowing,
because of this delusion,
it ends and begins again.
Therefore, if one wishes to return to the source and revert to the root,
and to turn away from delusion to merge with the True,
it requires nothing more than the non-arising of a single thought.
The past and future limits are severed;
the discriminating mind is extinguished;
and the karma of saṃsāra perishes.
When the roots are exhausted, the branches wither;
when the cause is empty, the fruit perishes.
Thus, the afflictions of the sensory objects and consciousness, which have persisted since beginningless time, are brought to an end.
All conceptual thoughts should be completely dissolved;
the primordial Buddha-eye and eternal body manifest instantaneously in accordance with reality.
