"Measurement" (pramāṇa) means the act of measuring;
for it is by means of analogical measurement that one knows [the object] exists.
This is called inference (*anumāna*). Regarding that which is not a valid means of cognition (*apramāṇa*):
it refers to when the mind takes an object as its focal point.
Deluded regarding objects,
one engages in false conceptualization and is unable to know correctly.
When an object does not accord with the mind,
it is termed "non-valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*).
As the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
Direct perception has three characteristics: first,
the characteristic of not being non-manifest.
Second, the characteristic not formed by conceptual construction;
third, the characteristic not seen through error.
First, regarding the characteristic not being non-perceptually evident:
Furthermore, there are four kinds that should be known:
namely, by virtue of the sense faculties being unimpaired.
When attention manifests,
there is the arising of similar types and the arising of dissimilar types.
There is no obstruction;
it is not extremely distant;
and those born of the same class [perceive it].
That is to say, the faculties of the desire realm with respect to objects of the desire realm;
and the faculties of the higher realms with respect to objects of the higher realms.
That which has already arisen,
and so forth— whether it be arising or having arisen—
is called "arising of the same kind" (sabhāga-utpāda).
Regarding "arising from a different category":
this refers to the faculties of a higher stage [engaging] with objects of a lower stage,
whether they have already arisen or otherwise.
This is called birth in a different class.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of those who are without obstruction.
First, it is not obstructed by concealment;
second, it is not obstructed by hiding;
third, it is not obstructed by overshadowing.
Fourth, it is not obstructed by the hindrance of delusion.
Regarding that which is obstructed by the hindrance of concealment:
this refers to the darkness of ignorance and the gloom of nescience.
"Obstructed by what is not pure and clear,
and hindered by concealment" refers,
for instance, to the power of medicinal herbs.
Whether obscured by the power of incantations or concealed by the power of supernormal faculties,
those who are hindered and obstructed.
This means that because a small thing is overwhelmed by many objects,
it cannot be seen; or, as in the case of food and drink, and so forth.
It is eclipsed by various poisons; or else,
at the tips of the hair,
it is eclipsed by other coarse objects.
Such categories as these are immeasurable and boundless; for instance,
it is like a small light being eclipsed by a great light.
It cannot be seen; that is to say,
it is like sunlight eclipsing the stars and moon,
or as the antidote overpowers and supplants that which is to be remedied.
It renders them unobtainable;
that is to say, the contemplation of impurity eclipses and supersedes the perception of purity.
The contemplation of impermanence, suffering,
and non-self eclipses the characteristics of permanence, bliss, and self through the power of the contemplation of signlessness.
"Overpowering all appearances and being obstructed by delusive hindrances" refers to that which is produced through illusion.
Either through differences in appearance,
or through similarity,
or through internal activities such as dizziness, stupor, or dreams.
Those who are agitated and intoxicated by wine,
those who are heedless and insane,
and others of such a kind.
These are called the obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
If one is not hindered by these four obstacles,
it is called being without obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*).
"Not extremely distant" means it is not any of the three kinds of extreme distance;
first, extreme distance of location.
Second, extreme distance in time;
third, extreme distance through analysis.
These collectively are termed "not non-perceptible."
Because it is not non-apparent,
it is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Second, as for the characteristic of not being produced by conceptual construction:
This refers to establishing the objective sphere;
as soon as one grasps the supporting object, it is established.
It is not produced by conceptual construction;
therefore, it is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Third, as for the characteristic of what is seen without error:
There are seven kinds:
first, error of perception;
second, error of counting.
Third, confusion of form;
fourth, confusion of manifestation;
fifth, confusion of karma.
Sixth, confusion of mind;
seventh, confusion of view.
As for confusion of perception:
This refers to giving rise to the perception of a certain characteristic with respect to that which does not possess that characteristic,
such as perceiving the shimmering heat haze as the characteristic of a mirage.
One gives rise to the perception of water.
Regarding "erroneous counting," this refers to counting fewer [instances] than there actually are.
They give rise to much overweening pride,
like one with cataracts who perceives two moons where there is but one.
Regarding the seeing of many lunar images with distorted shapes,
this refers to [seeing them] in other forms.
One gives rise to the overweening pride (*abhimāna*) of perceiving another form,
just as one sees the shape of a wheel in a whirling firebrand.
To manifest error means to give rise to overweening pride regarding one visible form by taking it to be another visible form.
It is like when the visual faculty is impaired by jaundice (kāmalā),
such that one perceives everything that is not yellow as having a yellow appearance.
Regarding the confusion of karma:
it refers to the overweening pride of conceiving that there is karma where there is actually no karma.
Just as one who runs while clutching a scroll perceives trees as rushing torrents,
so it is for one whose mind is deranged.
That is to say, one who perceives error gives rise to joy and delight toward the five kinds of objects that are mistaken.
That is to say, regarding those five kinds of objects of error,
one endures them, proclaims them,
and establishes them as precious and weighty.
To be stubbornly attached to such false imaginings is not what is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which refers instead to that which is not seen through such erroneous confusion.
It is further stated:
"Direct perception (pratyakṣa) refers,
for example, to the dharmas of form consisting of the five sense objects."
This is the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) transformed by the eighth consciousness.
When the first five evolving consciousnesses and the clearly manifest mental consciousness take this as their object, [they arise].
Initially encountering an object,
before discrimination has arisen,
it is not accompanied by names or expressions.
The wisdom that takes it as its object directly realizes the essence of the realm and attains the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
This is called direct perception (pratyakṣa) that apprehends specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
As for the first five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness, at all times...
All of these are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*) that apprehend the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena,
without discriminating between cause and effect, or between the states of being with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
It is the same for all of them. When the sixth consciousness takes those five sensory objects as its objective conditions, [it is likewise].
Regarding that essence of phenomena, one gives rise to conceptualizing thoughts and engages in verbal expression;
such is the reach of verbal expression.
It cannot be personally realized;
because it is an object of conceptual cognition,
it is termed the "attainment of the common characteristic."
Without distinguishing between the causal stage and the resultant stage,
whenever one gives rise to a conceptualizing mind toward the essence of an object,
or when one employs verbal expressions, [this occurs].
All are said to attain the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*),
because when the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) takes objective phenomena as its domain,
it gives rise to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Because it arises from verbal expression,
it is also a conventional cognition;
it does not apprehend the actual substance of those phenomena characterized by commonality.
However, this refers to the meaning of their shared characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore,
relying further upon the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*),
I shall explain the meaning of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
According to the *Yinming shu* (Commentary on the Nyāyapraveśa), there are briefly two interpretations.
The first is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
which refers to the first five consciousnesses.
Depending on its supporting faculty (*indriya*),
it takes the presently existing object as its condition in the present world;
the faculty also illuminates the preceding object together with consciousness.
Because they possess the function of generating consciousness,
the meaning of "faculty" (indriya) is preeminent;
thus, they receive the designation of "manifest."
Although it illuminates objects,
because its essence is matter,
it lacks the function of cognitive apprehension and is thus incapable of measurement.
There is only the sense of "manifestation," but it does not receive the name "valid cognition" (pramāṇa).
Only the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) measure their objects.
The function of objective apprehension increases;
its essence possesses the meaning of manifestation and also has the capacity for limited objects.
Now, based on the sense faculty that gives rise [to cognition],
the consciousness produced by it is designated as "direct perception" (pratyakṣa).
This is an *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
The second [type], "present direct perception," refers to a portion of the clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Excluding other distracted mental consciousnesses as well as those that arise independently,
this also includes the mental consciousness associated with meditative concentration.
Furthermore, the eighth consciousness has a perceiving aspect (darśana-bhāga) that directly perceives present objects, and its functional activity is manifested;
yet the substance of its supporting mental faculty (manas-indriya-dhātu) remains [unmanifested].
Because it does not manifest,
it is not grasped; rather, [the analysis] proceeds solely with respect to the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) which serves as the apprehending subject.
"Manifestation is itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Furthermore, the ancient masters asked:
If one follows the previous explanation,
that which is expressed by conceptual cognition merely attains the meaning of a common characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
One cannot share in the essential nature of phenomena;
for example, when one speaks of "form" with the mouth,
the mouth itself should be obstructed [by that form].
Since the essence of that form has resistance as its intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
and it is not itself obstructed by other forms,
we know that one does not apprehend its essence, but rather apprehends its meaning.

Furthermore, for instance, when the eighth consciousness, the visual consciousness, and the clearly discerning mental consciousness give rise to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and take fire as their object:
Since it is said that direct perception (pratyakṣa) apprehends the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of phenomena,
why would it not burn the mind? If it were not burned, [it would be no different from] delusion.
One must not perceive the intrinsic characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of fire;
how, then, could it be called an object of direct perception (pratyakṣa)? If you grant that it is being burned, [then it cannot be its own characteristic].
If, at the very time fire is perceived by the world,
the eye were not impaired,
there would be the fault of contradicting worldly direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The answer is:
Although it is not burned,
its own characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is nonetheless obtained.
This is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Why is this so?
Because the mind is subtle while form is coarse.
The mind is subtle and formless;
matter is coarse and possesses form.
Therefore, when one takes that fire as an object, [it is perceived as such].
Although one apprehends the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), yet it is not burned;
this is also called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, even that coarse matter cannot actually destroy subtle matter,
let alone mental phenomena.
Just as when a fire disaster arises,
the fire disaster of the desire realm burns only the desire realm.
However, it cannot burn the material realms of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
because their matter is exceptionally sublime and subtle; rather,
a fire arises spontaneously within those form realms themselves.
It burns its own level.
Question:
Since it has been said that the mind is subtle while matter is coarse, when the mind takes fire as its object, [how does this occur]?
Regarding "the mind not being burned":
it is like an arhat who transforms fire to incinerate his own body; as the body is consumed, the mental consciousness perishes accordingly.
How is this to be reconciled?
The answer is:
he transformed fire to incinerate his body.
It merely burns the dust that supports the roots;
it does not burn the five kinds of pure material faculties,
nor the mind and its mental factors.
Those five kinds of pure material faculties,
along with their associated mental consciousnesses,
lack any supporting substrate or objective field.
When conditions are lacking, [a phenomenon] does not arise;
thus, it attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Although this is a definitive fire, [it is so called].
Nor can it burn [the body],
because they differ in their coarseness and subtlety;
although the fire of meditative concentration is subtle and refined compared to worldly fire.
It is still relatively coarse compared to the mind,
because these material phenomena possess form and substance.
As for inference (*anumāna*):
This, moreover, is of five kinds:
first, characteristics;
second, essence.
Third, the three karmas;
fourth, the four dharmas;
fifth, cause and effect.
First, inference based on comparison (*upamāna-anumāna*) refers to that which follows from the characteristics and their associated relations,
or from the present as well as from what was previously inferred regarding an object.
Just as one infers the existence of a chariot by seeing its banner,
or [infers fire] by seeing smoke.
Inference based on analogy, such as inferring the existence of fire and so forth, is an inference of two natures,
because it proceeds from the direct perception of their essential nature.
One infers the nature of an object that is not currently perceived by analogy with it,
or one infers its other parts by analogy with a portion of its own nature that is currently perceived.
Just as one uses the present to infer the past and future,
so too is there inference based on the three types of karma.
That is to say, one infers the basis of an action by means of its activity;
for example, seeing that a distant object is motionless while birds gather upon it.
By means of such matters as these,
one infers that it is a stump;
if there are matters such as movement and so forth, [one infers otherwise].
This is the knowledge of persons and so forth.
As for the fourfold inference (*anumāna*),
it refers to all phenomena that are interconnected and associated.
One uses one instance as a comparison for the rest;
for example, just as [something] is known to belong to the category of impermanence, so too is it inferred to exist because it exists.
Because it is associated with suffering,
it is compared to emptiness and selflessness;
because it is associated with birth.
There is the phenomenon of aging;
because it belongs to the category of aging.
There are likewise the phenomena of death and so forth.
The fifth is inference by way of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇa-anumāna*).
This refers to inferring the cause through the effect;
for example, seeing the movement of an object.
When there is that which has arrived, one sees that which has arrived;
prior to this, there was movement.
If one sees someone serving the king in accordance with the Dharma,
one may infer that they shall obtain vast rank and emolument;
seeing such great rank and emolument, one knows this to be so.
Having previously understood that one serves kings and others in accordance with the Dharma,
the three measures and the differentiation of the eight consciousnesses consist of the first five evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
This is exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because the first five consciousnesses manifest and realize their objects without engaging in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Because it attains the intrinsic nature of phenomena and functions spontaneously,
the sixth consciousness, which pervades all three types of valid cognition, has two aspects.
First, the clearly manifest mental consciousness (manovijñāna) shares the same objects as the five [sensory consciousnesses] and encompasses all three types of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
The first moment of cognition apprehends the intrinsic nature of the five sense objects;
this is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
From the second moment onward, until the time of the conceptualizing mind (*vikalpa-citta*), [it is inferential].
If the object of cognition is not erroneous,
it is inference (anumāna).
If the mental factor does not accord with the cognition of the object, [it is not valid].
This is therefore not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
There are three types of independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*): first, the independent [consciousness] in the state of distraction (*vikṣiptāvasthā*).
It also encompasses the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For the most part, it is inference (*anumāna*) rather than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, if it takes direct perception as its object, it is [direct perception].
This refers to the solitary, distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises following the five sensory consciousnesses;
it is said to occur in the first moment,
taking as its object the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that were previously perceived by the five consciousnesses.
To apprehend its own nature is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Second,
there is that which occurs independently within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
These are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Third, those occurring independently within dreams are exclusively invalid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*).
If one considers [the consciousnesses], the objective aspect (grāhyāṃśa) is exclusively non-perceptual (anumāna),
while the two internal aspects (dvayantarāṃśa) are perceptual (pratyakṣa).
As for the seventh manas:
Within the state of being subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), this [consciousness] is exclusively non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*),
falsely grasping the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] as a self.
Because it is for the sake of the Dharma, the original eighth consciousness's seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is pure-white and indeterminate (avyākṛta).
However, it is not the self;
now, it is falsely grasped as the self by the seventh [consciousness],
which does not accord with the cognition of its object.
Therefore, it is called "non-valid cognition" (aprāmāṇya).
If the seventh [consciousness] has two internal divisions,
it is exclusively direct perception (pratyakṣa).
The eighth ālaya-vijñāna is identical to the five types of direct perception (pratyakṣa),
as has already been explained previously.
Question:
Question: How is it distinguished from what merely resembles direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*)? Answer:
The ancient Śākyas maintain that there are two types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):
first, the real;
second, the apparent.
True direct perception (pratyakṣa) consists in essence of the five groups of sensory consciousnesses and the mental consciousness that arises simultaneously with them.
All self-verifying portions (svasaṃvitti-bhāga),
all concentrated minds (samāhita-citta),
together with the eighth consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
These various minds and mental factors are termed "manifest" (*pratyakṣa*) by virtue of six meanings.
First, they exist manifestly.
"Excluding tortoise hair, etc.
refers to the present,
thereby excluding the past and future.
Third, it is the manifestation [of the object],
which distinguishes it from the seed because it lacks causal activity.
The fourth is the manifestation of the illumination of detachment;
this is called "manifestation," referring to the mental aspect (ākāra) of the cognizing mind.
Because it is far removed from all conceptual constructions;
that is to say, because it is free from the various modes of conceptualizing mind, such as recollection, discursive estimation, and the categories of conventional designations.
The *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* states:
"In this context, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*)."
The commentary states:
This reveals the aspect of the cognitive faculty (*ālambana-ākāra*),
which neither deliberates nor evaluates.
Spontaneous and conformative,
it illuminates in accordance with the objective realm;
"fivefold manifestation" refers to clear manifestation.
This means that when the mind in meditative concentration is limpid and tranquil,
it clearly realizes and witnesses whatever object it encounters.
That which clearly realizes various objects is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"Sixfold direct perception" refers to immediate manifestation.
That which is directly proximate is the self-substance itself.
If all distracted states of mind were directly proximate to their objects, they would be clearly distinct from the self-substance.
All are termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The fifth clarifies manifestation;
the sixth is immediate manifestation.
These two meanings distinguish [the true object] from various forms of erroneous cognition,
such as the vision of flowers in the sky or floating hairs by one with diseased eyes.
Although it functions spontaneously without conceptual discrimination,
it cannot clearly realize all objects nor directly intimate its own essence.
Therefore, it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As for that which resembles direct perception,
according to reason:
There are five kinds of cognition,
all of which are termed "pseudo-perception" (pratyakṣābhāsa).
The first is the mind in a distracted state taking the past as its object.
Second, the solitary mind takes the present as its object;
third, the distracted mind takes the future as its object;
fourth, the wisdom of doubt takes the three periods of time as its object.
The five conditions resolve the various present delusions;
these various minds are able to take objective aspects as their objects because they possess deliberation.
Because none of these take their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object,
and because they arise through conceptualization (*vikalpa*) following what was previously experienced,
they are called "resembling direct perception" (*pratyakṣābhāsa*).
However, there are two kinds.
The first is those with non-discriminative minds,
namely, the class of ignorant people.
Furthermore, when one spontaneously perceives things such as flowers in the sky,
although there is no conceptual discrimination,
the object is not clearly realized but is instead apprehended in a dim manner.
These are termed "pseudo-perception.
Second, there is conceptual cognition,
which currently carries names and expressions.
Failing to apprehend the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena,
one falsely claims to have clearly attained the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the object.
It is called "pseudo-direct perception.
Furthermore, it says:
"men, women, heaven, earth, and so forth."
To perceive a unified whole is called a semblance of direct perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*);
this is because it arises from the conjunction of various conditions.
Just as one gathers various subtle particles to form matter,
or combines the five aggregates to form a person,
this is called a "composite mark."
Seeing in this manner is discriminative cognition;
it functions differently from the actual object.
Therefore, it is called "pseudo-perception.
As for true perception,
it is like the appearance of a unified whole.
Characteristics cannot be apprehended.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"The Tathāgata speaks of a 'unified characteristic' (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*)."
It is not a unified whole,
because it arises from the conjunction of conditions and thus lacks intrinsic nature.
The nature of the absence of intrinsic nature is the principle to be realized;
one who knows it thus—
This is the arising of right knowledge;
it functions as its own characteristic mark and is called true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, one sweeps away the traces of both the subject and object of realization to constitute true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That is to say, if there were a cognition distinct from suchness that were to unite with suchness, [it would not be true direct perception].
If there is still something attained,
it is not a true realization; only when both subject and object have perished is there true realization.
Only then is it truly manifest.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* says:
"When, with respect to the object..."
When wisdom perceives nothing at all,
it then abides in consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra),
because it is free from the characteristics of the two graspings.
The Sūtra states:
"Furthermore, there is no wisdom external to suchness that can realize suchness;
this alone constitutes true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
Therefore, the actions performed by all Buddhas are entirely within the scope of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As stated in the *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*:
The Tathāgata fully knows the exhalations and inhalations, as well as the various kinds of food and drink, of all those sentient beings.
Various requisites, various appearances,
and various faculties.
Various modes of conduct and understanding;
various dispositions of mind;
dying here and being born there.
The momentary flow and the continuous succession of arising and ceasing—
all such things as these, the Tathāgata knows completely.
It is obtained through direct perception (pratyakṣa),
not known through inference (anumāna).
What is direct perception?
That is to say, with an unmoving mind,
one knows things as they truly are;
it is not a flowing, discursive mind.
Entering into the past,
he thus knows the time;
his wisdom is fully perfected.
Question: He expounds the Dharma in various ways according to the minds of sentient beings.
The fundamental consciousness transforms into what appears as the sense organs, the body, and the receptacle world;
is this a transformation through its own power alone,
or is it a collective transformation?
Answer: There are four propositions regarding this.
First, that which undergoes transformation within the commonality of the collective.
1. Common transformation within the common; 2. uncommon transformation within the common; 3. uncommon transformation within the uncommon;
4. common transformation within the uncommon.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"That which is called 'common transformation' refers to the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*)."
By the power of the maturation of seeds of common characteristics, consciousness appears as the aspect of the vessel-world (bhājana-loka), such as form and so forth;
that is to say, the external primary elements (mahābhūta) and their derived matter (upādāya-rūpa).
Although the transformations produced by various sentient beings are distinct from one another,
they are similar in appearance and occupy the same location without difference.
It is like the light of many lamps,
each appearing as if it were one.
The commentary says:
The meaning of this statement is as follows:
by virtue of its own seeds acting as causes and conditions,
the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) transforms into the appearance of the receptacle world (bhājanaloka).
Only external non-sentient things;
these consist of both the primary elements and the derived matter that exist among the external bases.
Therefore, it is said that they are external primary elements,
not dharmas external to the mind.
Furthermore, there are generally two kinds of seeds.
First is the common characteristic;
second is the uncommon characteristic.
What is the common characteristic?
Because it is perceived by many people,
although one knows that the transformations of each individual are distinct,
it is called "representation-only" (vijñaptimātra).
However, there is a sense of being similarly experienced in common, which is designated as the "common characteristic" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa);
in reality, it does not arise through one's own transformation.
He is able to employ it. If he can so employ it,
this is precisely what is called "taking external phenomena as objects" (ālambana).
However, this object of mine serves as a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) that allows many people to enjoy it together; thus,
it is called "common."
Regarding [the analogy of] mountains, rivers, and so forth:
as for their specific characteristics, if one follows the principle of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), [they are merely mental constructs].
That which is a transformation of one's own mind alone is called the "unshared characteristic" (asādhāraṇa-nimitta);
everything else is a transformation of others.
It is a thing belonging to others;
one cannot use it for oneself.
This is also called the "unshared characteristic" (asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa).
However, for the time being, we shall consider it from the perspective of one's own person alone; because others cannot utilize it,
it is termed "unshared" (*āveṇika*).
It is like slaves and so forth.
Another explanation states:
"The 'shared' [karma] is of two kinds."
They are collectively and simultaneously active,
like mountains, rivers, and so forth;
they do not function as a single, unified stream.
It cannot be used by those in other realms.
Furthermore, the *Weishi yi jing* (Mirror of the Meaning of Consciousness-Only) states:
"Among the common [objects], there is that which is common to all."
When many consciousnesses undergo transformation together,
it is termed "common"; once the consciousnesses have transformed, they function in common.
It is further termed "common" (sādhāraṇa).
Moreover, the *Weishi chao* states:
"This refers to the matter transformed by the consciousnesses of sentient beings belonging to many realms of existence."
Abiding in the same place,
they mutually interpenetrate,
their characteristics being identical.
To enjoy [it] together is called "common within the common.
This refers to the first instance of the word "common" (共).
The subsequent word "common" (sādhāraṇa) refers to the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya);
it refers to the predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
This refers precisely to things such as mountains and rivers that have no owner.
If they were to have an owner,
they would be subsumed under either the "shared" or the "unshared."
Second, there are those that are both common and uncommon,
such as one's own fields and houses,
as well as objects like the fierce fires seen by spirits and others.
Humans perceive it as water;
because it cannot be utilized by those in other realms or by other persons, it is among the non-common characteristics (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
There are also two kinds:
first, those that are uncommon among the uncommon,
such as the eye and other sense organs.
It functions solely as the support for its own consciousness and not for others; thus,
it is both uncommon and common.
Just as one supports one's own sense faculties and their objects,
others likewise partake of them; therefore,
these are called seeds of common characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa-bīja*).
This is precisely the case of being both within and among,
like the light of many lamps,
each of which pervades everywhere while appearing as one.
This explanation concerns the coexistence of common fruits in a single location without mutual obstruction; that is to say,
the characteristics of the external vessel-world.
It is like many lamps and lights together in a single room,
each illuminating the entire room.
Each is distinct from the others,
yet they resemble one another in appearance;
their locations are no different.
How is it known that each [lamp] pervades everywhere?
When one lamp moves away,
its light remains constantly pervasive.
If they were a single unity,
then once one lamp had been taken away,
the remaining light would not be pervasive.
Furthermore, because they interpenetrate one another without mutual obstruction,
they appear as if they were a single entity once many lamps have been placed there.
Furthermore, because there are many human figures,
it is also said:
"Among the uncommon [phenomena], there is that which is uncommonly transformed."
Just as with the five faculties such as the eye,
there is only the eighth [consciousness] itself;
within this, there is the final mind.
First thought: at the moment of being entrusted with the physical body of one's parents,
the name is transformed into "The Unshared."
Because it transforms solely from the eighth [consciousness],
and because it is experienced solely by oneself,
it is further termed "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*).
Just as visual consciousness arises based solely on the eye faculty, so too do the other consciousnesses,
up to tactile consciousness, arise based on the body faculty and the others.
Second, the common transformation within the uncommon [seeds],
which refers to the internal sense-faculties that support the sensory objects (*nir-māṇa-rūpa*). The former (the sense-faculties) is transformed solely by one's own eighth consciousness.
It is called "unshared," "transformative," and "arising after birth."
Others also have the sense of being experienced;
therefore, it is further called "common.
Question:
If it is admitted that one experiences the atoms supported by others,
how can this be called "consciousness-only"?
It would be the grasping of dharmas external to the mind.
Answer: When one experiences the sensory particles supported by another,
one's own consciousness first transforms into a single layer of objective images (nimittabhāga).
When it is experienced in another person,
if it is experienced at the time of enjoyment,
one is still experiencing one's own *svabhāga* (specific portion).
There are no phenomena apart from the mind;
thus, the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) is established. Question:
If it is said that one experiences [the result] through one's own *svabhāga* (objective aspect),
why does killing another person result in the sin of hell?
It is because one has killed one's own *svabhāga*.
Answer: One's own objective part and another's objective part both exist in the same location within the other person's body.
It destroys its own objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*) and is also able to cause the objective parts of the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) of others to be severed and extinguished;
therefore, one incurs the offense.
Third is that which undergoes transformation in common among many;
for example, mountains, rivers, and the great earth,
which are transformed by the collective karmic power of all people.
Furthermore, it is "shared" because it is received and utilized together. Question:
Why is it called "shared" when many people transform it together?
It is like a single tree that twenty people transform together;
there are twenty layers of shared appearances.
Suddenly, a person cuts down this tree;
since the mutual distinction no longer exists,
it may be called "consciousness-only."
The remaining nineteen persons would likewise lack the division of marks;
consequently, they would not be mere consciousness, because they do not cut themselves.
Answer: The objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of the person who strikes is that which is followed;
the objective aspects of the other nineteen persons are those that follow.

Since that which conforms to the objective aspect must necessarily depend on that which it conforms to for its existence, and since that which it conforms to is already non-existent, [the conforming aspect cannot exist either].
That which is capable of following [the object] is also extinguished. From this perspective,
it is also termed "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra).
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Karma arises as something similar [to its cause],
and it evolves in accordance with that karma."
That is to say, when the collective karma of the multitude undergoes transformation, it is termed "similar karma";
the individual portions of the many are then experienced by a single person.
This is called "evolving in accordance with karma.
Furthermore, because it is transformed and experienced collectively,
among the four types of commonality, this refers to that which is not common in its transformation.
Just as fields, houses, wives, and children are transformed by many people and a collective eighth [consciousness],
they are termed "common."
When they are used, only the first six themselves may enjoy them;
it does not extend to others.
This is precisely what is called "unshared.
Furthermore, it is like a single body of water that corresponds to four types of minds;
according to their karma, each perceives it differently.
Question:
Do the various consciousnesses each transform their own sense organs,
or do they also transform the sense organs of others?
Answer: It merely transforms to resemble the locus of another's sense organs,
because those sense organs have no utility for oneself at all.
The verse of the treatise states:
"Consciousness arises and transforms, appearing as objects,
sentient beings, a self, and cognition."
This object does not truly exist.
Since the object is non-existent, consciousness is non-existent.
The commentary states:
Regarding the eight consciousnesses arising and transforming to resemble objects:
these are the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). "Object" (*artha*) refers to the sphere of experience (*viṣaya*).
Because dependent phenomena appear as if they were substantially existent,
that which transforms into the semblance of sentient beings refers precisely to the five sense faculties, which are phenomena categorized among the number of sentient beings.
Sentience itself is the faculty;
it is called *sattva* because it transforms into what appears as a self.
This manas is that which undergoes transformation and that which cognizes;
the six consciousnesses are that which conditions and that which cognizes.
That is to say, the eighth [consciousness] takes both the sense faculties and their objects as its two types of form;
the seventh takes the self as its object;
and the six consciousnesses take the dharmas and meanings cognized by the six sense objects as their objects.
The treatise states:
There is an interpretation that [the sense-faculties] can only transform into something resembling their own bases, because the sense-faculties of others are not utilized by oneself.
Regarding the appearance of the five sense faculties as belonging to one's own or another's body,
the statement that the consciousnesses of oneself and others each undergo transformation refers solely to the transformation of the other's sense faculties and their bases.
Since the male organ is of no use at all to oneself,
if it were to undergo transformation despite being useless,
why would the seven consciousnesses not also transform?
Because it attains its object despite lacking the function of cognitive apprehension.
If that is so, then it is said that the sense faculties of oneself and others are manifest.
How can this text be reconciled?
It states that the ālayavijñāna of oneself and others each transforms itself into the sense organs.
It is not the case that one's own [consciousness] transforms the sense organs of another. First, it would be useless; second, it would not transform the sense organs of another.
Furthermore, because it is stated indistinctly that "one's own fundamental consciousness transforms the sense organs of another."
This cannot serve as proof.
Question: If form (rūpa) arises through the transformation of consciousness (vijñāna),...
The formless realm is without form.
How, then, can it be said to undergo transformation? Answer:
That which is perceived by sentient beings of the lower realms is the matter of karmic fruition; that which appears as an object in the formless realm is [the same].
This refers to the "matter resulting from meditative concentration" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), which, like [other forms of matter], is not separate from the mind. Ci'en says:
Regarding the transformation of another's body through meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The gods of the form and formless realms..."
Manifesting in ten trillion forms,
they together stand upon the tip of a single hair;
this is the mind of equality.
Since the formless realm lacks supernormal powers,
it consists solely of the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
The olfactory faculty of a bodhisattva perceives the fragrance of the palaces of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
As the *Āgama* Sūtra states:
When Śāriputra entered nirvana,
tears fell like a fine spring rain within the celestial palaces of the realms of form and formlessness.
When Mahāprajāpatī entered parinirvāṇa,
the gods of the form and formless realms stood by the side of the Buddha.
Furthermore, regarding that which is the object of meditative concentration within actual matter,
it is the power of the transformed object that constitutes the continuity.
It is interrupted;
if the internal body is largely continuous,
it is only slightly interrupted.
Because one may pass away at the very moment of being born,
or like the mayfly and other such creatures.
Because once born, one must die; however, if it refers to the transformation of the external vessel-world,
it generally lasts for a long period of time.
Because it transforms spontaneously according to the power of karma.
Question:
Upon what phenomena does the fundamental consciousness necessarily depend as its object?
Answer: Consciousness takes real dharmas as its object;
it does not take provisional dharmas as its object.
Cien asked: "Does the fundamental consciousness not take the four types of form—such as 'extremely subtle' and so forth—as its objects?
He replied:
Because it is provisional, it does not serve as an object-condition,
just like the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*).
As the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
The "extremely concise" (*paramāṇu*) and the "extremely remote" (*dūre-dūra*) are objects of the sixth mental consciousness alone,
because they can be analyzed into atoms (*paramāṇu*).
The eighth is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Among the matter derived from volition (*cetanā-ākṣipta-rūpa*), this refers to the matter associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahagata-rūpa*) and the matter associated with the Path (*mārga-sahagata-rūpa*).
This very [consciousness] does not take that as its object,
because its essence consists solely of manifest volition; thus,
it is the form arising from pervasive conceptualization.
These are merely mirror-images and the moon in water; they,
too, are not [ultimately] perceived as objects,
because they arise solely from the pervasive conceptualization of the sixth consciousness.
Furthermore, among the forms produced by meditative concentration,
such as the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
one likewise does not take conceptually constructed forms as an object.
Therefore, this treatise takes only substantial form (*rūpa*) as its object,
not a provisional one (*prajñapti*),
because the object of the eighth consciousness must necessarily have functional utility.
That has no practical utility;
the eighth [consciousness] does not take it as an object.
However, such is the nature of all phenomena.
First is existence; second is non-existence.
For what reason does the eighth [consciousness] not take non-existence as its object?
This is spontaneous engagement because it is non-conceptual and free from deliberation.
Because subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and the like possess deliberative investigation,
and because the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) and the like possess conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), it is known by this that [the ālayavijñāna is distinct].
The substance of the eighth consciousness does not take the self as its object;
it is the eighth consciousness that undergoes transformation.
Transformation must have utility;
therefore, it does not depend on what is useless.
They are useless;
therefore, they do not take us as their objects,
because they lack both essence and function.
Within the category of existent phenomena (*bhāva*),
there are briefly two kinds:
first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The second is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Why does this consciousness not take the unconditioned as its object?
If it were truly unconditioned, [it would not be an object].
Because it has not yet been realized;
and if it were a conventional unconditioned,
it would lack both essence and function.
None of these can serve as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Question: What about the transformation of consciousness that is with outflows (*sāsrava*)?
How many kinds of transformations are there? Answer:
Briefly, there are two kinds.
First, transformation through causal conditions;
second, transformation through conceptualization. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) states:
The transformation of contaminated consciousness is,
in brief, of two kinds: first,
that which transforms due to the force of causes and conditions.
"Second, it transforms due to the power of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*).
The commentary explains:
"That which arises from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*)."
This means that by virtue of the seeds of prior karma and the seeds of names and expressions,
which must be potent, there is solely the spontaneously occurring mind.
The mind arises not through volitional attention;
it refers to the five and eight consciousnesses.
Taking the dominant ripening cause as its condition and the seeds of names and phrases as its cause,
it thus transforms the object.
"Discriminative transformation" refers to the mind produced by attention;
it is the mind that deliberates.
That is to say, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses;
because they arise following their own respective conceptual mental engagements (*manasikāra*),
when these sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] take [an object] as their condition, [they do so].
The image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) has no substantial reality and does not necessarily possess functional utility.
Initially, that which undergoes transformation according to causes and conditions must necessarily possess substantial reality and function;
this refers precisely to the objects transformed by the five [consciousnesses] and the eight [consciousnesses], and so forth.
Subsequently, they transform according to conceptual discrimination;
they can merely serve as objects,
but do not necessarily possess functional utility.
This refers to the seventh consciousness and so forth.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that initially it refers solely to the eighth consciousness.
Because it is the primary factor for maturation,
because it is the locus of perfuming,
and because it can maintain the seeds.
Transformations must necessarily have practical utility;
however, the subsequently transformed objects such as visible form and tangibility by the remaining seven consciousnesses are all devoid of practical utility.
It functions like an essential nature,
such as light within a mirror;
among the three types of objects, it is a neutral object that does not conform to the mind.

Those [images] produced by causes and conditions are subsumed under "transformation"; those that are "solitary images" and "those accompanied by a real object" are all transformations of conceptual construction.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"The transformation of the ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna) occurs solely in accordance with causes and conditions."
The transformed objects such as form and so forth must possess actual utility; however,
if they were to transform into mind and so forth, they would lack actual utility,
because the mind and its associated factors within the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) are incapable of taking themselves as objects.
It is shown that the manifested changes of color and so forth arise from actual seeds; therefore,
these manifested phenomena [are derived from them].
There must necessarily be both essence and function;
for example, the objective aspects (nimittabhāga) of mind and mental factors are like the mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta), and so forth.
Therefore, one does not take them as objects;
if they were taken as objects, [the practice] would be useless.
(From the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*)
It is said:
"All transformative minds lack a mind that is self-dependent."
There is a mind that depends on others.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"There is no mind that possesses a self-referential, substantial entity as its object of cognition."
There is a mental aspect that resembles the faculty of deliberation, which arises as a transformed image-part (nimittabhāga) following the seeing-part (darśanabhāga),
like light within a mirror;
this is what is called "discriminative transformation."
Regarding the fourfold analysis: first,
transformation through causes and conditions,
not transformation through conceptual discrimination.
That is to say, the five consciousnesses along with their associated mental factors,
as well as the eighth consciousness as the mind-king,
constitute the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) that serves as the object-condition.
Because they arise from their own seeds,
these two are transformations of mere conceptualization and not transformations of causal conditions.
That is to say, the seventh consciousness with outflows,
along with the five mental factors of the eighth [consciousness],
constitute the transformed objective aspect (nimittabhāga).
Because it arises solely from the discriminating mind, these three are the "concurrent" (sahabhū) factors; that is,
the sixth consciousness with outflows (sāsrava).
And the eight untainted consciousnesses (*anāsrava-vijñāna*),
because they can universally take both provisional and real phenomena as their objects;
the four [remaining categories] are neither.

That is to say, they are non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). This is because they lack substantial reality and because they do not arise as being of the same kind as that which possesses the cognitive capacity (*ālambaka*).
Question:
Regarding this consciousness,
[is it] wholesome, unwholesome, or obscured-neutral?
Regarding the unobscured-neutral [dharmas],
among the four kinds of dharmas,
by which dharma are they subsumed?
Answer: The treatise states:
"This consciousness is exclusively non-obscured and neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta)."
Because it is of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*). If maturation were of a wholesome or defiled nature,
the process of saṃsāra and its cessation would not be possible.
Furthermore, this consciousness is the basis for both the wholesome and the defiled;
if it were either wholesome or defiled,
they would be mutually contradictory.
It should not serve as the support for both [the wholesome and the defiled] simultaneously.
Furthermore, since this consciousness is of a nature that is perfumable (*bhāvyatva*), if it were [itself] wholesome or defiled, [it could not be perfumed].
Just as with extreme fragrance or stench,
[the mind] should not be perfumed,
because there is no perfuming.
The causes and effects of both defilement and purity are equally not established.
This is exclusively undefiled-neutral;
"defilement" (āvaraṇa) refers here to defiled phenomena.
Because it obstructs the Noble Path,
and because it can veil the mind, causing it to become impure.
This consciousness is not defiled;
therefore, it is unobscured and indeterminate.
That is to say, it refers to the wholesome and the unwholesome, which have results that are either desirable or undesirable,
as well as a distinguished personal existence.
Because it cannot be definitively classified as either wholesome or unwholesome,
it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
Contact and the other [factors] are likewise.
That is to say, just as the ālayavijñāna is comprised solely of the nature of being non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta), so too is contact (sparśa).
Mental attention,
feeling, and perception.
The same applies to volition and all associated mental factors.
"Because it must be of the same nature.
The commentary explains:
"If the maturation were of a wholesome or defiled nature..."
If it were the case that the process of transmigration and its cessation could not be established,
then since the happy realms are wholesome,
unwholesome states would never arise there.
Because they constantly give rise to goodness,
there is no longer any sense of wandering through the evil realms.
Through karma, the stream of birth and death flows;
through suffering, birth and death revolve.
The same applies, conversely, to the miserable destinies.
Since evil would thus constantly arise, there should be no cessation;
yet, by means of the Path it returns,
and by means of Cessation it is extinguished.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "this consciousness is the basis for both the wholesome and the defiled":
since this consciousness is the master of retribution (vipāka),
it is eternally wholesome.
One should not rely on evil,
for that is evil;
likewise, one should not rely on good either.
Because they are mutually contradictory;
if one were both wholesome and defiled, it would be like something that is both extremely fragrant and foul-smelling.
That which should not be perfumed is this consciousness, which is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta) and capable of receiving perfuming.
Since there is no perfuming,
there are no seeds; if seeds are absent, [what could arise]?
This is precisely the absence of a cause.
Since the cause is absent,
its effect is likewise non-existent.
This is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
There are three types of indeterminate:
first, the associated indeterminate (*saṃprayuktāvyākṛta*).
This refers to all indeterminate minds, mental factors,
and the two types of dissociated indeterminate phenomena.
That is to say: indeterminate form (rūpa),
dissociated factors (viprayukta-dharma),
and the three types of ultimate indeterminacy (paramārtha-avyākṛta).
This refers to space and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, there is an extensive analysis of the four types of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
first, the indeterminate of transformative manifestation (*pariṇāma-avyākṛta*).
That is, it is the neutral mind and its mental factors;
both are neutral as they are transformed from [the two].
These are the various material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) and their seeds,
which constitute the neutral state of the three stages.
That is to say, among the twenty-four dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*),
it refers to those established as provisional (*prajñapti*) indeterminate states;
these are the four ultimate indeterminates (*paramārtha-avyākṛta*).
That is to say, it is the unconditioned [state] of space and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, within the first transformation, which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
there are additionally four kinds of indeterminates.
First, the ripening;
second, the deportment;
third, the skillful arts.
Regarding the four types of transformation:
as for that which is indeterminate by way of maturation (*vipāka*), "maturation" (*vipāka*) means:
They are distinct;
that is, they differ in their causal natures.
The cause may be either wholesome or unwholesome.
The fruit is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
"Matured" means fully ripened.
This refers exclusively to the fruit;
when cause and fruit are spoken of together,
it is termed "maturation" (vipāka).
Regarding the "indeterminate" (avyākṛta):
that which cannot be distinguished as having a future fruit is called indeterminate.
Alternatively, that which cannot be designated as either wholesome or unwholesome is termed "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
This karma produces a truly indeterminate matured result (vipāka).
This refers to the eighth consciousness.
"Karma" refers specifically to the two types of volition: wholesome and unwholesome.
"Feeling" (gan) means the accumulation of meaning and the summoning of meaning.
This present active volition is capable of producing the seeds for the five fruits— such as the *ālayavijñāna* that constitutes the collective retribution (*vipāka*) to be experienced in the future;
furthermore, it can also bring about the manifest fruit of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of future maturation (*vipāka*).
Therefore, it is called "the result of karma.
As for the term "true," it means "real."
Furthermore, although the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is a maturation (*vipāka*),
it is also conventional (*prajñapti*). Moreover,
as for the ultimate (*paramārtha*):
It is eternal.
Its substance is eternally continuous,
never again interrupted.
That which exists throughout the realms and stages is called the truly matured neutral (*vipāka-avyākṛta*). Furthermore,
if the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is itself a maturation, [it is also so termed].
It arises from the maturation consciousness (vipākavijñāna) and continues without interruption throughout all realms and stages.
It is called true maturation (*vipāka*),
and it is also called born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
If the essence of a phenomenon (*dharma*) is maturation, [it is so designated].
That which arises from the ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna) but is subject to interruption,
and does not pervade all realms or stages,
is merely termed "born of ripening" (vipākaja).
It cannot be called a true maturation (vipāka).
This specifically excludes the six consciousnesses;
for if their substance were not maturation, [it would not be so named].
Furthermore, it is intermittent and does not pervade all realms or stages;
although it arises from the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), [it is not identical to it].
These are not called true maturation (*vipāka*),
but are merely termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
This applies to those such as deportment, craftsmanship, and transformations.
Although it has the capacity to act, it does not bring about results such as wholesome or unwholesome fruits;
therefore, it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
Question:
If the ālayavijñāna were permanent,
it would be without transformation.
If it is severed,
it will not continue;
how then can this be reconciled?
This accords with correct reasoning.
Answer: They are neither identical nor different.
Neither annihilated nor eternal;
only then does one accord with the correct principle of dependent origination and consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
This consciousness is neither annihilated nor eternal,
because it is perpetually evolving. "Perpetual" means...
This means that from beginningless time,
this consciousness has been a single, continuous stream, eternally uninterrupted.
This is the realm, the destiny, and the birth;
because it is the fundamental basis for designation,
its nature firmly maintains the seeds.
It transforms so as not to be lost.
This refers to this consciousness which has existed since beginningless time.
Moment by moment they arise and perish;
they undergo change from beginning to end;
as the cause perishes, the effect arises.
Because it is neither permanent nor unitary,
it can serve as the basis for the perfuming of seeds by the evolving consciousnesses.
The term "constant" (nitya) serves to exclude [impermanence], while "transforming" (pariṇāma) expresses that it is not constant;
it is like a torrential stream.
The nature of cause and effect is such that it is like a flowing torrent:
neither discontinuous nor permanent.
Just as there is drifting and drowning over a long duration of continuity,
this consciousness is also like that.
From beginningless time, arising and ceasing have continued in succession,
being neither permanent nor annihilated.
They cause sentient beings to drift and drown,
preventing them from attaining liberation;
they are like a torrential flood.
The wind and other elements strike and stir up various waves,
which flow on without interruption.
This consciousness is likewise:
although it encounters various conditions to give rise to visual consciousness and the rest,
it remains constantly continuous.
Furthermore, it is like a torrential stream that carries fish, grass, and other objects up and down;
they follow the current without being left behind.
This consciousness is likewise;
it constantly evolves in conjunction with internal habitual tendencies and external factors such as contact.
Through such analogies for these dharmas,
the intent is to clarify that this consciousness represents a beginningless causality,
which is neither subject to annihilation nor eternalism.
That is to say, this nature of consciousness,
from time immemorial, undergoes the arising of effects and the cessation of causes moment by moment.
Because the fruit arises, it is not annihilation;
because the cause ceases, it is not eternal.
Thus, it is neither annihilated nor eternal.
This is the principle of dependent origination;
therefore, it is said that this consciousness perpetually revolves like a flowing stream.
The commentary states:
"A single category" means the sense of being eternally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
"Continuity" means the sense of never being interrupted.
"The basis of realms, destinies, and births" refers to...
It is precisely because one relies on this consciousness that the three realms,
the five destinies, and the four modes of birth are established;
for it is the projecting cause.
Consciousness is the root of the realms, destinies, and births;
because the cause perishes while the fruit arises, it is neither permanent nor unitary,
due to its nature as cause and effect.
To exclude the non-self [is to do so] because it possesses arising and ceasing;

The Sūtra states that there are four kinds of nutriment.
The first is edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra),

Those bound to the desire realm— namely,
the three objects of fragrance, flavor, and tangibility—

Because of this, the sphere of visible form is not included within edible food,

The second is the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*).
Its characteristic is the contact with objects;
it consists of the moment when tainted contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*) first apprehends an object.

Although this contact is associated with all consciousnesses,

Regarding that which belongs to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the sense of "nutriment" (*āhāra*) is predominant,
