[This would apply to] past and future factors that are dissociated from mind.
They do not possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
as this has already been fully established; such is the case with all phenomena, including form (*rūpa*) and the rest.
Apart from consciousness, nothing exists;
for it has already been refuted that [anything else] can receive perfuming or maintain seeds.
This should be understood to apply analogously even to states such as the realm of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*).
Furthermore, regarding those states such as the meditative attainment of cessation that are termed "mindless," it is not necessarily the case that they are entirely devoid of mind.
As the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* states:
The mind is of two kinds. First is the mind that accumulates and gives rise [to phenomena],
because it is the locus where immeasurable seeds accumulate and arise.
Second, there are two kinds of minds,
because they function with distinctions in their objects and modes of activity;
in states such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the second mind is absent.
It is called "mindless," just as a horse with only one leg is so designated because it lacks one leg.
It is also called "the footless.
Question: When those of the Hīnayāna enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti),...
Why is it that one cannot manifest their majestic demeanor?
Answer: In the Hīnayāna, this matter is extinguished.
The Mahāyāna is the cessation through principle (*li-mie*).
As the *Qingliang shu* states:
"The samādhi-wisdom-penetration of the extinction of all phenomena."
This refers to the fact that all phenomena comprised within the five aggregates are, in their very essence, quiescent;
this is what is meant by "extinction in principle" (li-mie).
Unlike the cessation attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in other schools,
which merely clarifies the cessation of phenomena,
this [attainment] extinguishes only the six or seven minds and mental factors.
The eighth consciousness and so forth are not extinguished; however, because their objective referents have been extinguished,
they cannot be immediately determined and employed.
Because one realizes the principle through its cessation,
concentration and distraction are unimpeded;
this is because the principle is inherent within phenomena themselves.
Therefore, it does not obstruct cessation;
being principle itself within phenomena,
it does not obstruct function.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Although one enters [cessation] in every thought-moment,
one does not abandon the bodhisattva path," and so forth.
Nor is it that the mind is fixed while the body initiates activity;
nor is it merely a case where concentration and distraction are both transcended.
Rather, it is because phenomena and principle are unimpeded.
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:
"Although one practices within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
one does not realize it as a final attainment."
One is able to enter moment by moment and also arise moment by moment;
as stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*:
Not arising from the meditative absorption of cessation while manifesting all modes of dignified conduct—
this is precisely that meaning.
Furthermore, ancient masters have said:
"If the Mahāyāna cessation-attainment possesses the five aggregates," [it is not a true cessation].
There exists the eighth consciousness,
as well as the seventh pure portion of manas and the wisdom of equality,
which are capable of giving rise to various modes of deportment.
In the Hīnayāna, there are only the two aggregates of form and formations;
the first six consciousnesses have already ceased.
This is based on the manifest deportment and activities of the Hīnayāna practitioners.
It must first be initiated by mental consciousness;
since mental consciousness is absent,
there is no function of application.
It differs from the Mahāyāna.
Question: What are the distinctions between the Great and Small Vehicles?
All postures and deportments arise from the mental consciousness;
since the sixth mental consciousness is that which is to be abandoned in the meditative attainment of cessation,
the sixth mental consciousness is already absent.
Even if there were a seventh consciousness, the Wisdom of Equality,
it would not be the consciousness that initiates physical postures; furthermore,
although the eighth consciousness is admitted to sustain and perceive [objects], [it does not initiate them].
Furthermore, it is not that which can initiate deportment (*īryāpatha*). How, then, can it be said to initiate deportment? Answer:
An ancient commentary states:
At the very moment of entering the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), although there is no mental consciousness, [the life-faculty continues].
However, before it has been extinguished,
within the mind of preparatory application,
one makes a vow.
After I have entered parinirvāṇa,
if there are sentient beings who are destined to hear my teaching of the Dharma or behold my majestic deportment, [they shall do so].
"I shall bring them to spiritual maturity. Because of this vow,
after entering meditative absorption, he...
It activates the seeds of the transformed aspects within the fundamental consciousness,
causing them to arise as actual manifestations by means of the wisdom of equality.
Yet it is able to manifest the deportments;
however, although the wisdom of equality does not correspond with the deportments manifested by the sixth consciousness through its aspirational delight, [it nevertheless manifests them].
If one wishes to give rise to impartial transformation,
one must rely on the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
The above has been an analysis according to the aspects of activity (*ākāra*).
If one discusses this according to principle,
deportment is itself concentration,
and concentration is itself deportment.
Since form and mind have existed for such a long time,
it is asked:
among the enumeration of the hundred dharmas, [how are they categorized]?
Although there are distinctions in names and meanings,
when one traces them back to their origin and root,
they are but a single consciousness.
In the Sūtra,
why is it said that within the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) there are three factors: vitality (āyuḥ), warmth (uṣman), and consciousness (vijñāna)?
Answer: Although it is a single consciousness,
it is explained as threefold according to its distinct meanings.
The treatise states:
"In terms of their distinct meanings, three are taught,
as in the case of the four right efforts and so forth."
The commentary states:
This refers to the matter (rūpa-dharma) within the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of the ālayavijñāna;
that which is apprehended by the body-faculty (kāyendriya) is termed "warmth" (uṣman).
The seeds of this consciousness are called "life-span" (*āyus*),
because they are able to sustain the consciousness;
the manifest consciousness is simply "consciousness."
Therefore, it is said that there are three dharmas; these are explained according to their distinct meanings,
not because they possess separate intrinsic natures.
In this case, when the body abandons warmth,
the other two [faculties] need not necessarily be abandoned,
as in the case of birth in the formless realm.
Just as when the other two [faculties] are relinquished, "heat" (*uṣmagata*) must necessarily be relinquished along with them;
however, these three are now explained separately according to their specific meanings.
However, they constitute a single entity.

For example, although the four right efforts (samyakpradhāna) are taught as having four distinct entities based on the different meanings of the two categories of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas— those already arisen and those not yet arisen—
they are nonetheless a single essence.
However, they constitute a single essence;
for example, regarding the four right efforts, although the wholesome and unwholesome dharmas— both those already arisen and those not yet arisen—
are explained as having four distinct essences based on their specific meanings, [they are in fact one].
However, it is merely a numerical category of diligence.
Question:
Is the seed of consciousness itself the life-faculty (jīvitendriya)?
In what sense is it considered the root?
The treatise answers: [as follows].
However, based on the seeds that directly produce this consciousness,
the duration of their abiding is determined by the specific functional capacities induced by karma.
The provisional establishment of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
The commentary states:
"As for the word 'this'..."
It produces the seeds of other consciousnesses;
the term "consciousness" is used to distinguish these from the seeds of associated mental factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*).
Because it grasps only consciousness,
the term "seed" is used to distinguish it from active manifestations (*pravṛtti*).
The eighth [consciousness] is not taken as manifest,
because formations serve as the life-faculty;
this is what is excluded by that [statement].
It is not all [of these] that constitute the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Here, we take the term "seed" (*bīja*) in its primary sense;
it refers to the specific capacity for maintaining the body, which is projected and sustained by the karma of previous lives.
It causes the physical form, mind, and so forth to abide with certainty;
based on this functional capacity,
it is designated as the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
This does not mean that the manifesting consciousness arises through grasping;
rather, because this seed functions as the power of karma,
it possesses the specific capacity to maintain a body of a single lifetime.
This causes [the body] to attain stability;
if this seed lacked this capacity,
the body would simply decay and disintegrate.
The ālayavijñāna manifests; by virtue of these seeds, it is able to take objects as its cognitive support.
Furthermore, that which sustains the dharmas such as the eye is also called "the sustainer";
this seed is precisely what sustains the manifesting consciousness.
If it were not so, the functioning consciousness would not exist, nor would there be anything capable of sustaining the dharmas of the other faculties and so forth.
By virtue of this functional capacity,
consciousness sustains the body through the power of manifest activity and internal seeds.
Birth and the dharmas that serve as its conditions and support are not called the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
Because it is not the root;
because it arises from seeds;
and because these seeds do not exist by virtue of manifest activity.
Because the seeds are the root of all phenomena,
and because the manifesting consciousness is that which is supported by them; it is spoken of from the perspective of that which is supported.
The consciousness capable of maintaining the seeds is called the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
The dharma of the life-faculty maintains its own substance.
It is not the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
because at the time when the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) abide,
they are determined; therefore, the seed is the life-faculty.
Other currently manifest phenomena, such as matter and mind, are not the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
because they do not continue in an uninterrupted stream and are not projected by karma.
However, when karma is actually drawing forth [its result],
it draws forth only this seed;
only then can the seed produce the manifest activity (pravṛtti).
It is not because the manifest state is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*);
rather, only the seed is the faculty.
Furthermore, as for the life-faculty:
It is conceptually established in dependence upon the mind; life is the dependent,
and the mind is the basis.
Master Sheng said:
"The fire from burning wood,
when whirled around, forms a wheel."
A wheel must grasp fire to produce illumination;
the emotions are likewise so,
for they must rely upon the mind to function.
Life depends on the mind,
just as feeling depends on the mind.
Question:
Are the various mental factors and so forth distinct from one another,
or are they non-distinct?
Answer: The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is without differentiation; it is only in terms of their characteristics (lakṣaṇa) that there are distinctions.
Although there are differences,
they do not contradict one another.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Just as with all mental factors,
although there is no difference in the nature of these mental factors,
they are nonetheless distinct by virtue of their characteristics.
In this way, the ālayavijñāna and the various evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñānas) arise simultaneously within a single body.
One should know that within a single body they operate simultaneously, and furthermore,
they do not contradict one another.
It is like a single torrent with many waves;
or again, like a single clear mirror surface.
There are many images that arise simultaneously,
without contradicting one another.
In this way, within a single ālayavijñāna,
many evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) evolve simultaneously;
it should be understood that they do so in mutual relation to one another.
Nor is this contradictory;
it is just as, for example, a single visual consciousness [operates] at one time.
Regarding a single objective sphere,
one perceives only a single type of non-distinct color-form;
or, at a single time.
It simultaneously apprehends the various kinds of color-forms,
as well as the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, and body,
up to and including the discriminating mental consciousness.
At one time, it may grasp the aspect of a single object,
or it may grasp various aspects of many different objects.
This should be understood as not being contradictory; furthermore,
the manas also always functions simultaneously with the ālayavijñāna.
It is always associated simultaneously with the four types of afflictions, such as the innate and spontaneous *asmimāna* (conceit of "I am").
Question:
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"From the root of non-abiding,
all dharmas are established."
The root of non-abiding is precisely the ālayavijñāna.
Why is this consciousness said to be the root of all dharmas?
Answer: This consciousness establishes sentient and insentient beings,
and gives rise to defiled and pure phenomena.
If there is knowing and perceiving,
then the realm of sentient beings arises; if there is no ideation and no reflection, [the realm of sentient beings does not arise].
Thus, the realms of existence arise through dependent origination;
by means of defiled dharmas, one revolves within the six destinies,
while by following pure dharmas, one ascends through the four stages of the noble ones.
This may be called the root of both the ordinary and the sage,
the source from which the physical vessel arises.
To thoroughly understand the origin of this consciousness—
What dharma is not realized?
It is this very nature of mind that is realized. What realm is not true? It is this very nature of mind that is realized.
This may be called the gateway to the cessation of study and the locus for the settling of the spirit.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
The ālayavijñāna is the root of all defilements. Why is this so?
By means of this consciousness,
it is the fundamental basis for the arising of the world of sentient beings,
and it is capable of producing the various sense faculties.
Because it is the locus upon which the faculties depend and the basis for the evolving consciousnesses and so forth,
it is also the fundamental cause for the arising of the vessel-world (bhājana-loka).
Because it is capable of giving rise to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*),
it is also the fundamental basis for the mutual arising of sentient beings;
thus, all sentient beings are related to one another.
Because they serve as mutual dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Why is this so?
Because there is no instance where sentient beings do not see one another and so forth.
Suffering, pleasure, and so forth do not arise;
they are mutually experienced. By this principle.
One should know that the realms of sentient beings act as mutual dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another.
Furthermore, it is precisely this *ālaya-vijñāna* which is able to sustain the seeds of all phenomena.
In the present world, this is the essence of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*);
it is also the cause for the arising of the truth of suffering in the future,
and furthermore, it is the cause for the arising of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) in the present.
Thus, because it can produce the world of sentient beings and because it can produce the receptacle world,
it is even maintained by the ālayavijñāna.
The seeds of wholesome dharmas such as the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
as well as visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and so forth.
Regarding the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), the Sūtra says:
"The simile of the cluster of akṣa fruits."
Because there are multiple realms within the ālayavijñāna.
Question:
If one is endowed with the ālayavijñāna...
Is the evolving consciousness also accomplished?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold analysis (catuṣkoṭi).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"There are those who possess the ālayavijñāna but not the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)."
That is to say: being asleep without consciousness,
being unconscious due to fainting,
or having entered the meditative attainment of non-conception.
They enter the meditative attainment of cessation,
are born in the Heaven of No-Thought,
or possess the evolving consciousnesses.
It is not the ālayavijñāna;
namely, [it belongs to] arhats or those who are pratyekabuddhas.
Non-retrogressive bodhisattvas and all Tathāgatas abide in the stage of having a mind.
Or there may be those who achieve both,
namely other sentient beings abiding in the state of having a mind.
Or there may be those who achieve neither.
That is to say: Arhats,
Pratyekabuddhas, and non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas.
And all Tathāgatas enter the meditative absorption of cessation and abide in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Question:
The Most Holy One has bestowed his compassion;
the Awakened King has manifested his traces.
With the mark of a broad and long tongue,
he utters subtle words of truth from within the realm of namelessness and signlessness.
He spreads the inconceivable ocean of the teaching,
explaining it through provisional names and marks,
and expounds the inexhaustible principles of its essential doctrine.
Furthermore, for instance, the eighth consciousness has no name or characteristic in its fundamental state;
it is given designations according to its various stages.
The name is derived from grasping;
at what stage or level is this designation of "falsity" abandoned?
Answer: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The eighth consciousness..."
Although all sentient beings fully possess [these qualities],
various names are established according to their distinct meanings.
That is to say, it is called "mind" because it is accumulated through the seeds perfumed by various phenomena.
It is called *ādāna* because it grasps and maintains the seeds and the material sense faculties so that they do not perish;
or it is called the "basis of the knowable."
Because it serves as the basis for all knowable phenomena, whether defiled or pure,
it is called the seed-consciousness.
Because it is able to universally sustain the seeds of all mundane and supramundane phenomena,
these various names apply throughout all stages.
It is also called the *ālaya-vijñāna*,
because it stores all phenomena belonging to the category of defilement (*saṃkleśa*) so that they are not lost.
Because it is apprehended as a storehouse for the grasping at a self and so forth, and is taken as one's own internal self,
this name applies only to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*).
It is not the stage of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), nor that of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas,
because it possesses the sense of being a storehouse for afflicted phenomena (kliṣṭadharma-ālaya).
It is also called "maturation" (*vipāka*),
because it is the maturation fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karma that leads to birth and death.
This designation applies only to ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.
The stages of the various bodhisattvas are not the stage of a Tathāgata,
because they still possess dharmas that are maturation-born and indeterminate.
It is also called the "stainless consciousness" (*amala-vijñāna*),
because it is the basis upon which all the most utterly pure,
untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena depend.
This name exists only in the stage of the Tathāgata;
in the stages of the bodhisattva, the two vehicles, and ordinary beings,
there exist contaminated seeds that are susceptible to being perfumed.
Because the eighth consciousness has not yet been attained in its pure state,
as stated in a verse of a sutra:
"The Tathāgata’s stainless consciousness..."
This is the pure, untainted realm,
liberated from all obstructions,
and associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
The name "ālayavijñāna" is abandoned first because its faults are grave.
In this context, the substance of the maturation consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is specifically discussed;
it is abandoned by the Bodhisattva when he is about to attain enlightenment (*bodhi*).
When Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas enter the nirvāṇa without remainder, they relinquish the essence of the immaculate consciousness (amala-vijñāna).
There is no time of relinquishment,
because there is no time when the benefit and happiness of sentient beings is exhausted,
and because the mind and so forth are all-pervasive.
It should be explained according to its meaning.
The commentary states:
it has the sense of accumulation.
This is the meaning of "mind.
This is the meaning of "arising and gathering.
This is the meaning of "mind."
Because it is capable of gathering and producing various seeds;
or because it can permeate seeds within this consciousness,
thereby being able to accumulate them.
Furthermore, because it gives rise to all dharmas,
this consciousness is explained as having the meaning of "mind" (citta).
As for "appropriating" (ādāna):
This is called "sustaining" (upādāna),
because it sustains the various material sense-faculties (rūpīndriya). This [consciousness] is common to both ordinary beings and noble ones (ārya).
Regarding the "basis of the knowable":
the three natures serve as its basis;
thus, it is called the "basis of the knowable."
Furthermore, an ancient master said:
"The *ālayavijñāna* is named for its meaning of 'storehouse' (*ālaya*)."
This is because the true mind does not abide in its own nature;
following the influence of conditioning, it enters into combination,
appearing as if it were unitary and eternal.
Therefore, all the ignorant take that which is similar to be real,
and grasp it as an internal self.
Because it is subsumed by the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*),
it is called a "store" (*ālaya*);
furthermore, it can conceal its own essence within all phenomena.
Furthermore, when it can conceal all dharmas within its own body and the two types of self-view never again arise,
it loses the name "ālaya."
Furthermore, it is said:
regarding the name of the eighth consciousness,
from the eighth bhūmi upward, the name "ālaya" no longer applies.
There is only the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
The seventh [consciousness] merely clings to the ripening consciousness as its object.
Furthermore, the eighth consciousness originally did not possess the name "ālaya."
Because the seventh [consciousness] clings to the perceived aspect (nimittabhāga) of the eighth as a self,
it causes the eighth to receive the name *ālayavijñāna*.
If it did not so cling, [it would not].
It is simply called the "ripening consciousness" (vipākavijñāna), or the "eighth," or "mind" (citta),
because it accumulates the seeds of various phenomena.
Therefore, it is called "mind" (citta).
Although it receives perfuming and maintains seeds,
it is named "mind" based on the meanings of accumulation and arising.
It is solely the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).
It is likened to a storehouse, for it is capable of containing all things and can maintain all seeds.
Subsequently, it causes seeds to give rise to manifest activity;
thus, it serves as both the support and the cause for the arising of seeds.
This makes it known that the eighth consciousness receives perfuming and maintains the seeds.
It is called "mind" (citta).
Because it maintains both new and old seeds within the causal state,
it is named "mind."
Because the state of fruition maintains all previously existing untainted seeds,
it is called "mind" (*citta*).
This is also termed the "mind that maintains seeds."
It is also called *citta*,
which refers to the conditioned mind;
it is also called *muhūrta*.
This is called the "mind of steadfast reality," which is precisely suchness (tathatā).
This is the unconditioned mind.
It is also called *ādāna*, which is translated here as the "appropriating consciousness" (*zhíchí shì*).
The meaning of "arising as a continuity" refers to its capacity to maintain the seeds, the root-body,
and the sense of the realms, destinies, and births.
This [vitality] pervades all stages.
Its functions are threefold:
first, it sustains the physical body so that it does not decay or disintegrate.
2. It maintains the seeds so that they are not lost or dispersed.
3. It grasps and takes up the continuity of rebirth.
That is to say, when a sentient being in the intermediate state (antarābhava) reaches its final moment,
at the very first instant of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) undergoing rebirth,
there occurs the sense of grasping (*upādāna*) and the continuity of linking existence (*pratisaṃdhi*).
"Knot" (kṣema) means binding;
it means attachment.
In a single thought-moment, one takes birth within the mother’s womb;
because one is immediately bound to it,
it is like a lodestone attracting iron.
The iron is like the two drops of the parents' semen and blood;
the eighth consciousness is like a lodestone;
in a single kṣaṇa—
It then grasps and remains;
simultaneously, the seeds of the faculties, objects,
and so forth also arise as actual manifestations from within their respective consciousnesses.
It is so called because it grasps and links to rebirth.
Regarding the five stages within the womb:
during the first seven days, it is termed the "impure mass" (kalala).
Its appearance is like thin curd.
The mingling of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood is called "mixed";
its inherent impurity is called "foul."
Within the second week, it is called a pustule (*piṭaka*),
resembling a pea-sized boil;
the surface and interior of this pustule are like curd.
Because the flesh has not yet formed,
the period within the first twenty-one days is called "coagulation," meaning the form is slightly coagulated.
Just as when blood has coagulated,
within four weeks it is called "congealed and thickened," gradually becoming firm and hard.
Within five weeks it is called the stage of form;
blown by the internal winds,
the various sense organs and physical forms are produced.
The single body has four limbs;
because of the distinctions in their arising,
it takes thirty-five days for these to develop.
When its five sense organs are all fully developed,
within six or seven days it is called the stage of hair, body hair, nails, and teeth;
within seven weeks it is called the stage of possessing the sense organs.
With the five sense faculties complete,
consciousness gradually arises; at this stage,
the conditions such as space and light have not yet been fully assembled.
It is also called the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*).
Question:
What is the difference between this consciousness and the meaning of "mind" (*citta*)?
Answer: The meaning of "seed" (bīja) is distinct from that of "mind" (citta);
it refers specifically to the active manifestation (pravṛtti) of the eighth consciousness.
It is also called a seed;
it is simply a seed because it is capable of producing actual manifestations (*samudācāra*).
It is called the seed-consciousness.
When this consciousness manifests,
it is able to give rise to the preceding seven consciousnesses.
Thus, from the perspective of the functional capacity to produce the seeds of dharmas,
the eighth consciousness is termed the "seed-consciousness."
Regarding the preliminary statement on "mind" (*citta*):
it is named "mind" in the sense of being an accumulation and that which arises through accumulation.
Furthermore, this refers to the eighth consciousness.
However, according to its various meanings, it is established under various names;
it is sometimes called the "fundamental consciousness" (mūlavijñāna) or the "cause of transmigration" (pravṛttihetu).
It is the cause for returning to cessation;
it is the substance of the realms, destinies, and modes of birth;
and it is the sovereign lord that projects the total retribution of the fruit.
Ālaya is here translated as "the storehouse of self-love and grasping.
As for the vipāka-vijñāna (retribution-consciousness):
This is the stage of the fruition of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Because it takes the fruition of wholesome and unwholesome karma as its cause,
it is that which is summoned and attained as this projected fruit (*ākṣepa-phala*).
Karmic actions from previous lives serve as the cause;
depending on whether these causes are wholesome or unwholesome,
one experiences the eighth consciousness in this present life.
This is an indeterminate maturation.
Because the fruit is distinct from its cause,
it is called "maturation" (vipāka).
Furthermore, it possesses four meanings:
first, reality;
second, permanence.
Third, it is pervasive;
fourth, it is unmixed.
This is called the true ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Question:
How is the eighth, the truly resultant consciousness (vipākavijñāna),
designated as that which "draws forth" the fruit?
Answer: Wholesome and unwholesome karma act as the projectors,
while the eighth [consciousness] is that which is projected.
Because it can induce the fruit of a household, it is called "inducing fruit" (ākṣepa-phala); therefore,
it is the sovereign lord of the collective retribution.
The first six consciousnesses are called "fulfilling fruits" (*pūrṇa-phala*),
because they are fulfilled by the arrival of partial retributions for good and evil.
These are what are summoned by fulfilling karma (*pūrṇa-karman*).
It is termed "born of maturation," but it is not true maturation,
as it does not possess the four characteristics.
Only the eighth consciousness is the projecting fruit;
it is the true maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna),
because it possesses four characteristics.
This [consciousness] is common to ordinary beings and persists up through the tenth stage;
it bears the name *vipākavijñāna* until the very end of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*).
In a single kṣaṇa, it is forever relinquished.
Within the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga),
it immediately becomes the stainless consciousness (amala-vijñāna).
It is named Amala,
which is the eighth consciousness within the fruit;
it is purely untainted (anāsrava).
Because it does not contain the seeds of all defiled phenomena,
and because it does not serve as the basis for the seeds or manifestations of affliction,
it is associated exclusively with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
It is named the immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*).
Furthermore, there are six alternative names for the mind (*citta*):
first, it is called "mind" because it arises from the accumulation [of seeds].
It belongs exclusively to the eighth [consciousness],
because it gathers all seeds and gives rise to manifest activity;
secondly, it is called "mind" (*citta*) because of its accumulation.
It belongs to the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses,
because they are able to perfuse and accumulate the seeds of all phenomena;
alternatively, its initial accumulation and arising belong to the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses.
Because it arises from seeds perfumed by the simultaneous gathering of present activities,
the subsequently accumulated state is called "mind" (*citta*), which belongs to the eighth consciousness;
for it contains and accumulates the seeds of all phenomena.
Although both of these preceding interpretations each possess the sense of that which accumulates and that which is accumulated,
for now we take only "that which accumulates" to mean *citta*.
This should be reflected upon according to reason.
Third, that which cogitates is called "mind" (*citta*),
because it is capable of cogitating its own respective objects.
Fourth, it is also termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
It is called "vijñāna" (consciousness) in the sense of discerning; it is also called "manas" (mind) in the sense of being the immediate antecedent condition.
Sixth, it is also called "mind" (*citta*).
To explain this further:
first, that which arises through accumulation is called "mind."
This refers to the eighth consciousness,
because it gathers all seeds and gives rise to manifest activities.
Regarding the statement "the collection of all seeds":
this refers to the seeds of all phenomena— whether form or mind, human or celestial, belonging to the three realms, and whether outflowing (sāsrava) or non-outflowing (anāsrava)—
all of which are collected by the other, the eighth consciousness.
It is like the storehouse of people in the world.

Regarding the phrase "because it gives rise to active manifestation," this refers to the manifestation of all contaminated and uncontaminated forms and minds within the three realms and five destinies.
All arise from the eighth consciousness; that is,
the eighth consciousness is that which is capable of collecting and giving rise to all seeds of form, mind, and so forth.
This is that which is accumulated and produced.
Now, we take only that which is capable of accumulating and producing as "mind" (*citta*).
Specifically, we now take the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the eighth mind-king (*cittarāja*).
It is called the "mind that accumulates and arises.
The image-aspect (nimittabhāga) is form;
the seeing-aspect (darśanabhāga) is function.
Because the self-witnessing aspect (svasaṃvittibhāga) follows after [the object],
it serves as the self-witnessing aspect;
it is capable of gathering the seeds of all phenomena.
It ensures that [the seeds] are not lost or scattered,
and furthermore enables the capacity for various types of manifest activities to arise,
remaining uninterrupted from beginningless time.
It possesses only the meaning of "collecting and arising";
that is to say, it is known that the eighth self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) serves as two causes for the seeds within consciousness.
This refers precisely to the two meanings of "accumulation" (*saṃgraha*) within this context:
first, it serves as the causal basis of support (*ādhāra-hetu*),
which is the meaning of "accumulation."
Second, it provides the power that causes [the seeds] to arise;
this is the meaning of "arising.
Second, that which is accumulated is called "mind" (*citta*).
Furthermore, because it maintains the seeds of all three realms and five destinies within the eighth consciousness,
the eighth consciousness is named the "repository" (*ālaya*) and the "accumulator."
That is the eighth, the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvittibhāga),
which can maintain the old seeds; therefore,
it is called "accumulation" (caya).
Furthermore, because it can also accumulate new perfumings,
it is called "accumulation" (cita).
Thus, one understands that the mind is characterized by accumulation and origination through such gathering.
The eighth consciousness alone is designated as "mind" (*citta*) for the sake of establishing the correct meaning.
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
Because it is able to universally sustain the seeds of all mundane and supramundane phenomena,
this is the meaning of the *ālayavijñāna*; that is,
the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).
It is that which is able to sustain and accumulate all seeds; it is that which is sustained.
Regarding that which is accumulated:
the first seven are called *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses),
where "evolving" (*pravṛtti*) means to undergo transformation.
This is not fixed; because the three natures,
the three means of valid cognition, and the three objects are easily discarded and indeterminate,
they are properly termed "transforming consciousnesses" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
Now, the eighth [consciousness] is exclusively of one type, which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Furthermore, because it perceives only objective entities (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) and functions solely as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is called the "non-transforming consciousness" (*aviparīta-vijñāna*).
Furthermore, that which is termed "mind" (*citta*) by virtue of its accumulation also belongs to the seventh *pravṛtti-vijñāna*.
"Accumulation" refers to the gathering of the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the preceding seven consciousnesses.
As for "arising," it refers to the seven aforementioned active manifestations,
each of which possesses its own power.
The generation of new seeds by the perfuming agent is called "arising.
For instance, when visual consciousness perceives a form,
it necessarily relies upon the simultaneous mental consciousness.
The seeds of mutual perfuming are accumulated;
the same applies to the other four consciousnesses.
Question:
If the clearly discerning mental consciousness (manovijñāna) arises together with the five [sensory consciousnesses] sharing the same object, it is termed "collective gathering" (saṃnipāta).
For instance, when the independent mental consciousness takes the eighteen elements (dhātus) as its object.
Since it does not share the same object-condition (*ālambana*) with other consciousnesses, nor does it perfuse (*vāsayati*) and give rise to seeds,
how could there be any sense of "collecting together"?
Answer: It is by virtue of the seventh consciousness serving as the support that the sixth consciousness subsequently arises and perfumes the seeds.
It is also called "common gathering.
Regarding the third point— that which takes objects as its cognitive focus is called "mind" (*citta*)—
this means it is able to take its own respective objects as its cognitive focus.
That is, the eight consciousnesses each have the capacity to cognize their respective objective spheres. "Cognizing" (yuan) refers to apprehending and maintaining [the object].
"Discernment" (lǜ) refers to deliberation.
If one uses discernment as the object to liberate the mind,
it is a general term.
The first five consciousnesses perceive only the five sense objects;
these are their respective domains,
except in cases where the various faculties function interchangeably.
And at the stage of Buddhahood,
the sixth consciousness takes as its objects the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) and the phenomena of the three periods of time,
as well as all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena, both mundane and supramundane.
It takes its own sphere as its objective field.
The seventh consciousness takes the seeing-division (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth consciousness as its own sphere as its objective field.
The eighth consciousness takes three objects as its objective conditions;
these are its own-referential objects (*svabhūmika-viṣaya*). It takes these three objects simultaneously and continuously.
The eighth consciousness is common knowledge because its objects are ever-present; thus,
it differs from the first six consciousnesses, which are subject to interruption.
Furthermore, the objects of focus are not permanent.
As for its eighth true meaning:
if it pertains to the realm of desire (kāmadhātu),...
That which takes the faculties, bodies, and the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) of the desire realm as its own sphere (sva-bhūmi) conditions them as its objective field; if it is the seeds,
it universally conditions the three realms as its own sphere.
The same applies to the two upper realms;
they likewise cannot take [the uncontaminated] as an object, with the sole exception of the uncontaminated seeds,
because [they consist of] both contaminated and uncontaminated seeds.
Because they are not mutually concordant,
it is therefore able only to sustain [the object] but cannot take it as an object of cognition;
this is because the meaning of "sustaining" is pervasive.
The meaning of "condition" (pratyaya) is narrow.
It is like a person with red eyes holding a torch,
or like carrying an object upon one's head.
One merely maintains it without mental engagement;
one simply maintains it so that it does not scatter,
for it is not separated from consciousness.
The fourth is called the consciousness that cognizes; that is,
the seeing-aspects (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses,
all of which are capable of cognizing their respective objects of perception.
That is, visual consciousness is able to discern visible forms,
and so on, up to the eighth consciousness, which is able to discern the sense organs, the body, the vessel-world, and seeds; thus,
discernment is the defining characteristic of consciousness.
The eight consciousnesses are collectively termed "vijñāna" (consciousness).
If one understands consciousness as the discernment of coarse objects,
then it applies specifically to the six evolving consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*).
The fifth is called "mind" (*manas*) because it is the immediate antecedent; that is,
the eight consciousnesses of the preceding moment.
It serves as the support for the eight consciousnesses of the subsequent moment;
thus, we take the name "manas" (mind) for the eight consciousnesses of the preceding moment.
If the mind of the preceding moment were not to cease, [the subsequent would have no support].
The subsequent thought arises without a [simultaneous] cause;
it arises only after depending on the location where the preceding thought has ceased. This occurs within the state of immediate succession (*samanantara*).
When minds of the same category are not separated by an interval,
it is called "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*).
In the Mahāyāna, there are two types.
First is the *manas* of deliberation,
which is the sevenfold consciousness;
second is the *manas* of immediate succession.
It penetrates the eight consciousnesses.
"Intention" (manas) has the meaning of being the basis of support.
Just as the seventh [consciousness] is called "mind" (*manas*) because it serves as the support for the sixth,
so too is it understood as "mind" when it functions as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The eight consciousnesses are collectively termed "manas" (mind).
If "manas" is understood in the sense of "cogitation," then the seventh consciousness alone is designated as "manas."
The sixth is called *citta*;
alternatively, the eighth is called *citta*,
and the seventh is called *manas*.
The sixth is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This designation "sixth" is given in accordance with its preeminence.
That which accumulates and arises is understood as "mind" (*citta*);
the eighth [consciousness] alone is named "mind.
That which cogitates is understood as "intellect" (*manas*).
The seventh alone is named "mind" (manas),
which is explained as consciousness (vijñāna) because it discerns coarse objects;
the preceding six alone are named "consciousnesses."
Regarding the eight consciousnesses,
each possesses both a general and a specific name;
the eighth [consciousness] is called "mind" (*citta*) because it possesses these two meanings.
First, the sense of accumulation and origination;
second, the sense of objective reference.
The seventh [aggregate] also has two [meanings].
First, the sense of deliberation;
second, the sense of immediate succession.
The first six are also called consciousnesses, and these likewise have two [meanings].
First, the meaning of discernment;
second, the meaning of discerning coarse objects.
Possessing these four meanings, it is termed "coarse."
The first is easily understood,
even by children. The second is commonly accepted as existing.
This is accepted by all three vehicles.
The three aspects are coarse because they are intended to clarify the specific aspects.
Fourth, the objects of focus are coarse;
that is, the five sense-objects are coarse realms.
Furthermore, the nine consciousnesses are generally divided into four sections.
Each category is individually established with ten names.
First, regarding the ten names of the sixth consciousness:
the first is named after its corresponding sense organ.
These are called the six consciousnesses.
Second, that which is able to deliberate upon right and wrong is called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Third, it is able to engage with the realms of sensory objects;
this is called the "object-apprehending consciousness" (*ālambana-vijñāna*). Fourth, it is able to universally apprehend the five sense-objects.

The consciousness that wanders through former acquaintances is called the consciousness of recollecting the past. The consciousness whose five perceptions flow and disperse is called the wave-consciousness.
Sixth, that which can discern external objects is called the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*).
Seventh, that which exists to destroy others.
The consciousness of the named self is called the *ālayavijñāna*.
That which is drawn forth by the karma of the eight cravings is called the consciousness of the four abodes (*catur-vihāra-vijñāna*).
Ninth, that which prevents correct understanding from arising is called the consciousness of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa-vijñāna*).
Tenth, that which brings the exhaustion of karmic retribution to completion.
The distinction between mind and mental factors is called the consciousness of death in the realm of segmented existence.
Second, regarding the ten names of the seventh consciousness:
16. Subsequently attained, it is called the seventh consciousness. 2.
The faculties and their objects do not meet.
This is called the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
Third is the habit-energy of non-awakening;
suddenly, thoughts arise.
That which is named "discriminative consciousness" arises and ceases without interval; that which is named "continuous consciousness" is its uninterrupted succession.
The five hindrances obscure the principle;
this is called the consciousness of ignorance.
The six [sense bases] repeatedly lead to delusion away from the correct.
Being able to sever the afflictions of the four abodes is called "liberated consciousness.
The seventh [consciousness] traverses the profound path.
The arising of goodness in accordance with principle is called the consciousness of practice;
it liberates one from the cycle of birth and death within the three realms.
All is my own mind; there are no external dharmas.
This is called the consciousness of fearlessness.
The ninth consciousness clearly and distinctly illuminates,
like a mirror manifesting images;
it is called the *xiàn-shí* (manifesting consciousness).
Once these ten dharmas have falsely arisen,
one harbors pride in one's own wisdom,
which prevents the true nature from manifesting.
It is called the consciousness of the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa-vijñāna*). Regarding the third [point], the eight consciousnesses have ten names:
the first seven are designated as "subsequently attained" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
These are called the eight consciousnesses.
When the two— true and false— are intermingled,
it is called the synthetic consciousness (*saṃvṛti-vijñāna*).
The three aggregates that accumulate all phenomena are called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).
The fourth is that which sustains and initiates [them].
The perfuming of names transforms consciousness;
when the five ordinary states become the state of a sage,
it is called the "consciousness of birth."
The essence of the six treasuries is uninterrupted;
it is called adamantine wisdom-consciousness (*vajra-jñāna-vijñāna*).
Seventh, its essence is neither still nor turbulent.
It is called the consciousness of quiescent extinction.
Among the eight [consciousnesses], that which is real and not provisional is called the consciousness of essence.
The substance of the nine repositories is not delusion;
it is called the consciousness of original enlightenment.
The ten merits are perfected.
It is named the consciousness of all-aspect wisdom (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*).
Regarding the names of the four [consciousnesses], the ninth, and the tenth:
first, its essential nature is non-false.
It is called true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*).
Its two natures are neither existent nor non-existent;
it is called the signless consciousness (*animitta-vijñāna*).
The three modes of activity remain unchanged;
this is called the consciousness of the dharma-nature.
Fourth, true awakening constantly abides.
Its essence is neither hidden nor manifest;
it is named the Buddha-nature, the true consciousness.
Its five natures transcend all falsity and artifice.
The consciousness of the limit of reality is named such;
the six great elements functioning without fixed direction is named the consciousness of the Dharma-body.
The seventh is the non-defiled consciousness that follows along with the outflows,
called the consciousness of intrinsic purity (*svabhāva-viśuddha-vijñāna*).
The eighth is the *amala*-consciousness.
In this translation, it is called the "Stainless Consciousness" (amala-vijñāna).
Its substance is neither identical to nor different from the nine [consciousnesses];
it is called the "Tathatā-consciousness."
The ten [stages] are supremely sublime and beyond comparison;
they are designated as "Ineffable" and "Beyond Cognition.
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Jiejing) states:
The Buddha told Bodhisattva Vighuṣṭamati:
"This consciousness is sometimes called the ādāna-vijñāna. Why is this?"
Because this fundamental consciousness is able to grasp and maintain the body,
it is sometimes called the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Why is this? Because this fundamental consciousness is constantly hidden within the body,
as it shares in its formation and destruction.
Or it is called *vijñapti*.
Why? Because this consciousness cognizes forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and so forth.
Because it arises from the growth of all objects,
O Broad Wisdom,
this is the fundamental consciousness.
This aggregate of consciousness arises;
that is to say, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.
Depending on consciousness and the eye faculty,
one takes external visible objects as an object-condition.
Visual consciousness arises;
simultaneously with the visual consciousness, there arises a conceptualizing mental consciousness that shares the same object.
If a single visual consciousness arises,
at that time a certain mental consciousness (manovijñāna) arises,
sharing the same object as the visual consciousness.
This visual consciousness may arise together with two,
or three, four, or five other consciousnesses.
At that time, a single conceptual mental consciousness arises together with the five sensory consciousnesses to take an object as its focus,
like a great flow of water.
If a single cause capable of producing a wave arrives,
then a single wave arises;
if two or many causes capable of producing waves arrive, [then multiple waves arise].
Then many waves arise;
this water flows constantly,
without ceasing or interruption.
Furthermore, within the surface of a pure, circular mirror,
if a single cause capable of producing a reflection arrives,
then a single reflection arises.
If two or many causes capable of producing reflections arrive,
then many reflections arise;
yet the surface of a round mirror does not turn to follow them in order to produce those reflections.
Nor is it subject to destruction.
This fundamental consciousness is like a flowing stream,
a mirror surface, and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states:
"There are two kinds of mind: first, the mind that accumulates and initiates (*saṃcetanika-citta*)."
Because it is the place where immeasurable seeds arise and accumulate,
the second is called the "variegated mind" (*citra-citta*),
because it functions with distinctions in its objects and modes of activity.
The *Tiantai Jingming shu* states:
"Regarding the various names for a single dharma:
the various sūtras employ different names to describe true nature (*tathatā*) and the reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)."
Some speak of the single ultimate truth;
some speak of the intrinsically pure mind;
and some speak of the tathāgatagarbha.
Some call it suchness (tathatā);
some call it the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
and some call it the prajñā of the true mark (lakṣaṇa-prajñā).
Some say it is the One Vehicle; some say it is the Śūraṅgama;
others say it is the Dharma-nature.
Some speak of the Dharma-body;
some speak of the Middle Way;
and some speak of ultimate emptiness.
Some speak of it as the "causal Buddha-nature" (正因佛性) or "nirvana of intrinsic purity" (性淨涅槃);
such are its various different names.
Since these are all alternative designations for the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*),
a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Prajñā is a single dharma."
The Buddha speaks various names;
according to the different classes of sentient beings,
he establishes diverse designations for them.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says:
"For example, Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
has a thousand names."
Liberation is likewise;
it has many names.
It is also said:
The Buddha-nature has five names; thus,
all of them are intended to accord with the capacities of sentient beings and to benefit them.
This is for the purpose of establishing alternative names;
yet the essence of the dharma is one,
never having been different.
It is like the thousand names of Śakra;
although the names differ,
they all ultimately refer to the Lord of Devas.
How could one hear a different name and yet claim it is not the principle of the true mark?
It would be like a person making offerings to Śakra.
To disparage Kauśika is to disparage Śakra;
to offer worship to Kauśika is to offer worship to Śakra.
Making offerings in such a manner does not necessarily result in merit;
the same applies to those who propagate the Dharma in the final age.
Some rely on the self-nature of the mind as being intrinsically pure,
yet disparage ultimate emptiness;
others believe that ultimate emptiness is a mere nothingness.
They disparage the *ālayavijñāna* and the intrinsically pure mind;
some claim that the *prajñāpāramitā* clarifies the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*),
while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* clarifies the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
None of these constitute the Buddha-nature.
In seeking such blessings,
how can one fail to consider the impending calamity?
If one knows that names are distinct while their substance is one,
then the merit of rejoicing will pervade the entire dharma-realm.
What is there to dispute?
Furthermore, within the various sūtras, [the Buddha] employs different names according to the conditions and capacities of his audience.
Established everywhere,
it is designated as an "ocean" by virtue of its vastness and its limits.
Because its perfect luminosity reveals the principle,
it is called a "jewel";
because it is that upon which all phenomena rely, it is so named.
They call him "King" because he is able to give birth to all things;
they designate her as "Mother."
Yet it is the true meaning of that which is without meaning;
it is neither many nor few.
It is the true mind of that which is without mind.
"Unity is also not unity.
Thus, the *Huayan siji* states:
"This refers to the meaning of decisive resolution."
In terms of wisdom, it refers to that which is capable of growth;
in terms of the earth, it refers to the ground.
Regarding its loftiness and prominence,
it is described by way of the mountain;
regarding its depth and vastness, it is likewise described.
Speaking in terms of the ocean,
it is taken for its roundness and purity;
speaking in terms of the jewel, [it is taken for its brilliance].
The aforementioned categories are merely those with names;
they are already innumerable.
Furthermore, there are those without names.
How could it ever be measured?
As stated in the *Mahādharmolkā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*,
the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas:
"You all must not say that heaven is fixed as heaven,
or that humanity is fixed as humanity."
The hungry ghosts are certainly hungry ghosts.
This is just as a single thing may have various names,
or as a single person may have various names.
Just as there is one "heaven," so too,
up to the realms of hungry ghosts and animals,
there are various names.
It is also like this; furthermore,
there are many hungry ghosts who have no names at all,
appearing in the mere space of a finger-snap.
They transform their bodies into various forms;
likewise, these sentient beings manifest immeasurable physical bodies in a single moment.
How could one possibly call them by name?
Even for those such as hungry ghosts,
who have names for their places of birth.
The names of their received food and the names of their lifespans;
as for those hell-beings who have no names or places of birth, [they likewise receive these].
Thus, their forms are also not fixed;
because the causal conditions for their evil karma therein have not yet been exhausted,
they manifest various transformed bodies within a single thought-moment.
The commentary states:
As it is within the hells,
during a single day and night.
Ten thousand births and ten thousand deaths;
furthermore, within the Avīci Hell,
there is no interval between each successive body.
Each fills the entirety of eighty-four thousand yojanas of hell without obstructing one another,
like a pure and wondrous Dharma-body amidst the clouds.
It is profoundly still yet responds to all things.
People of the present age, however,
assume that this refers to the Dharma-body of the Buddhas.
Capable of dividing and pervading,
he inspires faith in sentient beings;
likewise, his single body is an infinite body.
Because the karmic fruits of sentient beings are inconceivable,
a sutra states: "The realm of the Buddha is inconceivable."
The realm of sentient beings is likewise inconceivable.
