Compiled by Chan Master Yanshou, Chief Administrator of Yongming Temple, Huiri:
Now, names are established based on characteristics, and characteristics are manifested through names. Names have already been extensively analyzed; how, then, should one understand characteristics?
Answer: That which expresses and invokes [an object] is termed a "name" (nāman).
Its manifestations are observable;
it is designated as "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa).
The sixth, the discerning consciousness of objects (viṣayavijñaptivijñāna), is its name.
The defiled mind that grasps objects is the aspect (nimitta);
the seventh manifest consciousness is the name (nāman).
The deluded mind perfumed by ignorance is the aspect.
The eighth storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the name;
the purity of mind is its characteristic.
The ninth true consciousness (tathatāvijñāna) is the name.
That the essential nature does not change is its characteristic.
All of these are names for the nameless and characteristics for the characteristicless.
Why is this? Because names and characteristics do not emerge from the mind or its objects;
therefore, the mind has no intrinsic nature.
They arise dependent upon objects;
yet objects have no intrinsic nature.
They exist dependent upon the mind.
Thus, when the mind expands, there is no realm external to the mind;
when the realm expands, there is no mind external to the realm.
If they mutually negate one another, both vanish.
When both mind and objects are extinguished, they vanish;
yet if they support one another and stand side by side,
mind and objects remain vividly present.
This is emptiness through the absence of intrinsic nature;
it is empty yet not empty,
and devoid of intrinsic nature yet existent.
Existence that is non-existence;
the existence of non-existence.
Existence reveals the single suchness (ekayāna).
The emptiness of non-emptiness: through this emptiness, the myriad virtues are perfected.
It may be said that all phenomena are subsumed within the emptiness of their intrinsic nature.
"Dang" (蕩) signifies being entirely devoid of anything ultimate.
Furthermore, the *Yuishiki Shuyō* (Essentials of the Pivot of Consciousness-Only) states that there are two interpretations for the phrase "arising from the marks of one's own mind."
The first says:
it is the characteristic of the reflected image. The second says: [it is the characteristic of the mind].
That is, although the apprehended characteristic lacks substantial reality,
it appears to the mind.
It should be understood that all explanations regarding the characteristics of the mind follow this same principle.
The commentary states:
Regarding the characteristic of reflected images:
all phenomena are the reflected images of the mind.
Regarding the characteristic of grasped objects:
All objects lack intrinsic nature;
they arise according to grasping and are produced from one's own mind.
It further functions as a characteristic of the mind.
Question:
Regarding the ālayavijñāna—
By what cause is it named?
Does it arise from its own intrinsic nature,
or does it exist through a combination of factors?
Answer: If one says that [ignorance] arises from itself,
that is the self-arising of ignorance.
If one says it arises from another,
that is the delusion of "other-nature.
If one says it arises through a combination [of causes], [that is likewise a delusion].
This is the delusion of commonality.
If one says that [arising] occurs apart from self and other,
this is the delusion of causelessness.
Now, I shall speak according to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and the skillful means of the established tenets (siddhānta):
just as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), when conjoined with ignorance (avidyā),
gives rise to all dharmas, it is like a sleeping mind that, upon encountering a dream, perceives all manner of objective realms.
This fundamental consciousness is established from the gate of arising and ceasing;
it derives its name from the conjunction of the real and the false.
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"The gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind refers to the transformation of the arising and ceasing mind based upon the Tathāgatagarbha."
The non-arising and non-ceasing is in conjunction with arising and ceasing;
being neither identical nor different,
it is called the ālayavijñāna.
This consciousness has two meanings:
namely, it can encompass all phenomena and it can give rise to all phenomena.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of meanings:
first, the meaning of awakening;
second, the meaning of non-awakening.
As for the meaning of "awakening" (bodhi),
it refers to the ultimate nature of the mind,
which is free from all characteristics of delusive thought.
Because it is free from all marks of deluded thought,
it is equal to the realm of empty space,
pervading everywhere without exception.
The single characteristic of the dharma-realm is precisely the equal dharma-body of all Tathāgatas.
It is upon this dharma-body that [all things] depend.
It is taught that all Tathāgatas are the original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi),
which is established as such in relation to the initial enlightenment (ādi-bodhi).
However, at the time of initial awakening,
it is precisely the original awakening;
no separate awakening arises.
Regarding the establishment of initial awakening (ādikṣaya-bodhi): it means that based on fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) there is non-awakening (abodhi),
and based on non-awakening it is said that initial awakening exists.
Furthermore, because one awakens to the source of the mind,
it is called ultimate awakening; because one does not awaken to the source of the mind, [it is called non-awakening].
This is not ultimate awakening;
even up to the point of "not awakening to the meaning" refers to [this state] from time immemorial.
Because they do not know the true Dharma as it truly is— namely, that it is one—
they fail to awaken to the arising of the mind and thus give rise to deluded thoughts;
these thoughts themselves lack any real characteristic.
It does not depart from original enlightenment;
it is like a person who has lost their way,
who becomes confused because they rely on the directions.
Delusion has no intrinsic characteristic and does not exist apart from the directions;
sentient beings are likewise.
Because there is awakening,
there is non-awakening;
through deluded thought, confusion arises.
However, that [unawakened state] is not itself aware;
it lacks its own true nature,
yet it does not depart from original awakening.
Furthermore, one waits for non-awakening so that true awakening may be explained; once non-awakening is no longer present, [true awakening is realized].
Even true awakening is discarded.
An ancient master explained it thus:
"The mind that is neither born nor extinguished."
Regarding the statement that it is "in union with arising and ceasing,
neither identical nor different":
this is because the seven consciousnesses and their defiled phenomena constitute arising and ceasing.
Because the pure dharmas of the Tathāgatagarbha are neither arising nor ceasing,
yet the entire substance of this non-arising, non-ceasing mind is in motion,
the mind does not depart from the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
Since the characteristics of arising and ceasing are none other than the resolution of the spirit,
arising and ceasing do not depart from the characteristics of the mind.
It is because they are thus inseparable.
The synthesis [of these factors] is designated as the *ālayavijñāna*.
Because it is a synthesis,
it is neither identical to nor different from them.
If they were one,
there would be no conjunction;
if they were different...
Furthermore, there is no conjunction;
because they are neither identical nor different,
conjunction is attained.
Furthermore, the Tathāgatagarbha, the pure mind,
and its activities of arising and ceasing are inseparable from one another.
Therefore, it is said that they are "harmoniously united.
This does not mean that there are separate arising and ceasing that come to unite with the True [Nature];
rather, it refers to the mind of arising and ceasing.
Because the arising and ceasing of the mind is without marks,
the arising and ceasing of the mind is brought about by ignorance.
The mind of arising and ceasing originates from fundamental awakening,
yet they possess no dual nature.
They are not separated from one another;
therefore, they are called "harmonious integration," like the waters of the great ocean.
Due to the wind, the water moves;
the characteristic of the water and the characteristic of the wind are not separate from one another.
If arising and non-arising were one and the same,
then at the time when the characteristics of the consciousness of arising and ceasing are extinguished, [non-arising would also be extinguished].
The substance of the mental consciousness would also perish accordingly,
falling into the extreme of nihilism. If, on the other hand,
they were different, [the same fault would follow].
When stirred by the wind of ignorance,
the essence of the tranquil mind should not follow along with conditions.
One would then fall into the extreme of eternalism.
Free from these two extremes,
it is neither identical nor different.
Furthermore, regarding the awakening and non-awakening mentioned above,
these two dharmas mutually permeate one another,
thereby constituting defilement and purity.
Since it lacks intrinsic nature,
it is entirely a single awakening. Why is this so?
Due to ignorance, non-enlightenment is established;
because the meaning of non-enlightenment perfumes the original enlightenment,
all defiled phenomena arise.
Furthermore, because fundamental awakening (mūlābodha) perfumes non-awakening,
all pure dharmas arise.
Based on these two meanings:
Because it universally produces all things,
it is said that consciousness has two meanings.
It gives rise to all phenomena.
Question:
Regarding the ālayavijñāna.
What serves as its cause?
What serves as its condition?
What constitutes its essence?
Answer: The *Xiányáng lùn* (Exposition of Manifestation) states:
"As for the ālayavijñāna..."
It has as its essence all the seeds produced by the maturation [of karma],
with the karma and afflictions accumulated in previous lives serving as conditions and the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) from beginningless time serving as the cause.
This consciousness is able to grasp, apprehend, and discern the material sense faculties,
the bases upon which those faculties rely,
and conceptual proliferation.
Due to these perfumations, at all times,
the single category of birth and death cannot be fully understood.
Furthermore, it can maintain and discern the external container world;
it is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation and is consistently unobscured-neutral.
It acts as the causal basis for the evolving consciousnesses and so forth.
As the Sūtra says:
Enveloped by ignorance and bound by the fetter of craving,
the fool brings about the acquisition of a conscious body.
This statement reveals that there exists the maturation-consciousness, the ālayavijñāna.
Question:
Regarding the ālayavijñāna...
Its essence as suchness is its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
its responding to the causes of good and evil is its characteristic as fruit (*phalalakṣaṇa*);
and its receiving perfuming and maintaining seeds is its characteristic as cause (*hetulakṣaṇa*).
Since the eighth [cause] is characterized by both cause and effect,
to which of the six causes does it belong,
and among the five effects, to which effect does it correspond?
Answer: Among the six causes, four possess the sense of being able to maintain seeds.
This is the cause that maintains the seeds.
If the cause and the seeds exist simultaneously,
it is a co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
If it is considered in relation to its own kind of seeds that mutually induce one another across time,
it is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); if it is considered in relation to simultaneous mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth, [it is a concomitant cause].
This refers to the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
As for the absence of the other two causes:
the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is of a wholesome or unwholesome nature.
This consciousness is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
If it were associated with universal causes (sarvatraga-hetu)—
namely, views, doubt, ignorance, and so forth— it would be defiled (kliṣṭa).
This consciousness is not defiled;
among the five fruits, it possesses four,
excluding only the fruit of disjunction.
In relation to its own seeds,
it is an outflowing fruit (niṣyanda-phala);
in relation to mental factors such as attention (manasikāra) and so forth, [it is a dominant fruit].
This is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*);
with respect to the seventh consciousness,
it is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding the observation of the causes of good and evil,
these are the ripened fruits (*vipākaphala*).
Question:
Among all forms of consciousness,
which consciousness is stable and not tossed about by various conditions?
Answer: There is not a single phenomenon in the world that does not arise from conditions.
Such phenomena are dependently originated.
All are entirely impermanent;
only the fundamental mind does not arise from a prior limit.
It does not abide in the middle limit,
nor does it cease in the future limit;
it is truly the foundation of all existence.
This is the dwelling place of all Buddhas;
therefore, it is likened to a mirror,
by which one may clearly discern the beautiful and the ugly.
Profound, cavernous, and subtle;
we look up to it as our source,
like a vast ocean receiving all rivers.
The Great Void contains all forms.
The *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states:
"The mind has eight kinds."
Alternatively, there are nine [factors] that coexist with ignorance and serve as the cause for the world.
The entire world is a manifestation of mind and mental factors;
these mind and mental factors,
as well as the various sense faculties.
The fundamental mind undergoes transformation through arising and ceasing, and through the flux of transmigration,
being altered by ignorance and other such factors.
Firm and immovable,
the causal conditions of the world consist of twelve links.
Whether it be the faculties or their objects,
that which produces and that which is produced perish in each moment.
From the Brahma-world up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception,
all arise through causes and conditions.
Only the Tathāgata is free from all causes and conditions,
both internally and externally, within the world.
Whether moving or stationary,
all phenomena are like jars and other such objects;
their nature is that of disintegration and cessation.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"O you sons of the Buddhas,
why do you not see or hear?"
The essence of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is pure;
it is the support for all bodies,
or it possesses the thirty-two marks.
Whether as the marks of a Buddha or as a wheel-turning monarch,
or in various other forms,
they are seen by all in the world.
Just as the pure moon in the sky is surrounded by a multitude of stars,
so too are the various consciousnesses centered upon the ālayavijñāna.
Thus he dwells within this body,
like the Lord of the Desire Realm,
attended by his retinue as he wanders through his jewel palace.
The various deities of the rivers, seas,
and so forth exercise mastery within the waters; likewise,
the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) dwells within the world.
One should know that it is likewise so:
just as the earth gives rise to all things,
this mind manifests many appearances.
It is like the Son of Heaven, the Sun,
resplendent as he rides his precious palace,
circling Mount Sumeru.
Circulating throughout and illuminating the world,
all the devas and people of the world see him and pay him homage with reverence.
The characteristics of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) within the Buddha-ground are likewise thus;
it performs the various practices of the ten stages.
Revealing and proclaiming the Mahāyāna Dharma,
universally bestowing happiness upon all sentient beings,
and constantly praising the Tathāgata.
Abiding within the body of a bodhisattva,
one is thus named a bodhisattva;
so too are the Buddhas and all the bodhisattvas.
All these are names for the ālayavijñāna;
the Buddhas and the sons of the Buddhas have already received, or will receive, the prophecy [of their enlightenment].
The vast ālayavijñāna becomes manifest as perfect enlightenment for those practitioners of the Guhyasamāja Samādhi in the Śrī-maṇḍala.
In conjunction with sublime meditative concentration,
one is able to clearly and distinctly perceive the ālayavijñāna.
The Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas,
Śrāvakas, and those of other paths—
whoever perceives the truth— is a person free from fear.
All that is observed is this very consciousness;
the various objects of all cognitions are all transformations of the mind.
Objects such as jars and garments—
of such a nature they all lack inherent existence;
they all depend upon the ālayavijñāna.
Sentient beings perceive through delusion;
due to various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
the grasped and the grasper continue to revolve.
This nature is not like an illusion,
a mirage, or a mass of floating hairs;
it is neither produced nor unproduced.
Neither empty nor existent,
like long and short and so forth;
apart from one, all are non-existent.
The wise person contemplates illusory phenomena;
these are all merely magical illusions.
Not a single thing has ever truly existed.
Arising together with illusions,
they are perceived through the conjunction of mirages, firebrands, and the appearance of falling hairs.
Apart from these, there is no combination;
nor do the past and future exist. They are like illusions, hair-tufts [seen by those with cataracts], and so forth.
The various characteristics of all things that appear here and there are all transformations of the mind;
they have neither substance nor name.
People deluded within the world have minds that lack self-mastery;
they falsely claim there exists the power of illusion.
A magician creates various objects;
the many kinds of things produced by the magician, such as bricks, tiles, and so forth.
Whether various things come or go,
all such views are unreal;
it is like iron [being attracted] because of a magnet.
Just as it shifts according to where it is directed,
so too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna);
it evolves in accordance with conceptual discrimination (vikalpa).
Throughout all worlds,
there is nowhere he does not pervade,
like the sun or a mani jewel.
Without thought or discrimination,
this consciousness pervades all places;
to perceive it is called transmigration.
Neither dying nor being born,
it is fundamentally not a phenomenon of saṃsāra;
the one established in meditative concentration should observe this with diligence.
Birth and death are like a dream;
at that moment, one undergoes the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), which is called liberation.
This is the supreme teaching and principle of all Buddhas,
which thoroughly examines all phenomena.
It is like a scale, like a clear mirror;
it is also like a great bright lamp,
and like a touchstone for testing gold.
Free from annihilation,
it is the defining characteristic of the Noble Path for those who practice sublime meditative concentration.
Reaching the cause of liberation,
forever free from all defilements,
it manifests through the transformation of the basis.
Question:
The fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is in conjunction with the various consciousnesses,
arising and ceasing together with them.
Upon reaching the stage of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), all afflicted consciousnesses cease,
and only the fundamental consciousness remains.
How are the differences between that which is extinguished and that which is not extinguished distinguished?
Answer: The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
If the fundamental consciousness and the non-fundamental consciousness arise and cease together,
they are like water and milk mixed together.
How is it that the fundamental consciousness does not cease? It is not that the fundamental consciousness ceases;
it is like [the reflection] in water.
Regarding "the milk drunk by the goose," the commentary states:
For example, although water and milk may be blended together, [they can still be separated].
When the geese drink,
they drink only milk and do not drink water.
Therefore, although the milk is exhausted,
the water does not run dry;
it is the same with the fundamental consciousness and that which is not the fundamental consciousness.
Although they are combined,
one ceases while the other remains.
Question:
This fundamental consciousness,
being called the essence of all phenomena,
is also said to be:
It is eternally abiding and immovable.
Just as with the myriad dharmas,
they exist precisely because of this mind.
If it exists apart from this mind,
or if it is identical to this mind,
then the myriad phenomena would undergo constant change and transformation.
How can this mind be called eternally abiding?
If it were apart from this mind,
how could it further serve as the essence of all phenomena?
Answer: Opening and closing follow conditions;
they are neither identical nor separate.
They unite because conditions converge;
they separate because conditions disperse.
This opening and closing is merely due to conditions.
Rolling up and unfolding have no substance;
conditions merely open and close,
yet conditions themselves are fundamentally empty.
Mutually unknown, both subject and object are quiescent.
As a verse in the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says:
For example, gold, stone, and the like originally possess no characteristic of water;
yet when they are brought into conjunction with fire, [they appear as such].
Just as water is in constant motion,
so too is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna);
yet its essence is not a phenomenon subject to transmigration.
The various consciousnesses are associated together;
they evolve in tandem with mental factors,
just as iron is attracted by a magnet.
They revolve and shift about;
both are devoid of volition,
yet their appearance is as if they possessed conscious awareness.
One should know that the ālayavijñāna and the seven consciousnesses are likewise so;
they are bound by the ropes of habitual tendencies.
Though without a person, it is as if there were one;
it pervades the bodies of all sentient beings and circulates throughout all aggregates and realms of existence.
It is like iron and a magnet;
they do not know one another reciprocally.
Question:
Question: How many types of the eighth storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) are there? Answer:
The *Śikṣāsamuccaya-ṭīkā* (Shì mōhēyán lùn) states: "The ālayavijñāna,
in total, comprises ten types."
Why is this? Because they are explained individually in the sūtras. First:
It is called the Great Sovereign Ālaya-vijñāna;
that is to say, it is the Great Cognition of universal characteristics,
the meaning of which is as previously explained.
The second is called fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*),
which is established separately as the *ālayavijñāna*.
Therefore, regarding these ten kinds of false conceptualization, it is stated thus in the Sūtra:
"The consciousness of King Kṣatriya-daṇḍin."
These are indeed false dharmas;
they are unable to fully comprehend the essence of the single dharma-realm,
which is all defiled phenomena.
Taking the ālayavijñāna as its root,
it is born and grows.
There is no time of interruption.
If King Māra’s consciousness and its dark retinue do not exist, [then...]
It is forever without dependence,
for it cannot grow or develop;
such is this ālayavijñāna.
By what definitive determination is this subsumed?
In the fundamental treatise,
it is stated as follows:
What is meant by the meaning of "non-awakening" (abodha) is this:
because one does not know, as they truly are, that the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) is one,
the mind arises in non-awakening and possesses conceptualization (saṃjñā).
...and so on, as explained at length. Third,
it is called the pure fundamental awakening, the ālayavijñāna.
That which is called natural fundamental wisdom is separately established as the *ālayavijñāna*; therefore,
in the *Mūlapratibhāsajñānasamādhi Sūtra*, it is said:
He spoke thus: "The Buddha’s own ālayavijñāna is pure in its essential nature and is fully endowed with untainted, perfect merits."
It is eternal, constant, and definitive;
it possesses no characteristic of being perfumed and no characteristic of transformation.
The essence of wisdom is immovable and fully endowed with all pure qualities; therefore,
it is called the solitary, pure consciousness.
Therefore, within this treatise, under which section of the definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) should this ālayavijñāna be subsumed?
Thus it is said. Furthermore,
regarding the essential characteristics of awakening,
there are four kinds of great meanings.
It is equal to space, like a pure mirror;
as explained at length, and so forth.
The fourth is called the *ālaya-vijñāna* of the fundamentally awakened nature of defilement and purity;
it is what is known as the *dhāraṇī*-wisdom that does not abide in its own nature.
Therefore, it is established separately as the ālayavijñāna.
Thus, in the sūtras concerning the fundamental dependent origination:
When he had spoken thus,
the youth Prabhāketu immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
Venerable sir,
for what reason is it difficult to enter this unprecedented assembly?
It is thus said:
The wisdom of the *dhāraṇī* that arises in accordance with other conditions is called the consciousness of the King of Laṅkā.
Why is it called the King of Laṅkā?
It is used as a metaphor to demonstrate the wisdom of the *dhāraṇī* of dependent origination to them.
Thereupon, the Venerable One addressed Kāśyapa:
"Young man, this is King Laṅkā."
He constantly dwells on Mount Malaya in the great ocean,
leading a retinue of one hundred and six thousand spirits and deities as his followers.
In this manner, these retinues,
riding in palaces of flowers,
travel through various buddha-fields.
All those hosts of spirits and ghosts are able to roam about only by relying entirely upon that King of Laṅkā.
They spoke these words:
"We, the host of deities,
possess no majestic power."
Lacking physical strength,
he has no capacity for any activity.
"As it suits Your Majesty,
we shall provide whatever capability is required from among our ranks."
That King of Laṅkā,
according to that very time,
bestowed upon him superior power.
They do not separate from one another,
but evolve together; this,
O King of Laṅkā, is what is meant.
Although he does not manifest as divided bodies,
he is able to pervade all the hosts of spirits,
causing each of them to perceive him as being the size of his entire body.
At all times and in all places,
they function together without ever being separated.
The wisdom that does not abide in its own nature is likewise able to receive all immeasurable and boundless defiled phenomena of affliction.
The various perfumes of ghosts and spirits do not depart from one another,
for they evolve together.
For this reason, it is difficult for me to enter therein;
thus have I spoken.
The evolving cognitive wisdom is called the consciousness of King Laṅkā;
therefore, this is the ālayavijñāna.
By what definitive determination is this subsumed?
In the root treatise,
it is stated as follows:
The intrinsically pure mind,
stirred by the wind of ignorance,
becomes associated with ignorance.
Both are devoid of form and characteristics;
they are not separated from one another,
as is explained at length.
Fifth, it is called the "characteristic of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*), which is the *ālayavijñāna* as the fundamental characteristic of karma (*mūlakarmalakṣaṇa*).
And because the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) is separately established as the *ālaya*,
it is stated in the *Prakṛti-jñāna-sūtra*:
It is stated thus:
"The ālayavijñāna has no capacity for cognitive discernment."
It is without anything produced through conscious effort; it cannot be analyzed,
nor can it be differentiated.
Because it has the sense of being subtle and flowing while being stirred by activity,
it is called *kaṇḍa*;
therefore, this is the *ālayavijñāna*.
By what definitive determination is this subsumed?
In the root treatise,
it is stated as follows:
Furthermore, based on non-awakening,
three kinds of marks arise,
which correspond to that non-awakening.
They are associated and inseparable. What are the three?
First is the karma-aspect of ignorance.
Because it relies on non-awakening, the mind moves;
this is designated as karma.
When there is awakening, there is no movement.
Movement leads to suffering,
because the fruit does not depart from its cause. Sixth:
It is called the *ālayavijñāna* as the evolving characteristic of evolving consciousness;
that is to say, it is the aspect of being able to perceive objects and the evolving consciousness itself.
It is established separately as the *ālaya*.
Therefore, it is stated in the *Mahāpramāṇa-sūtra*:
"The *ālayavijñāna*..."
Because there is the transformation of the vision of seeing and the arising of the vision of non-seeing, this is the ālayavijñāna.
By what definitive determination is this subsumed?
In the root treatise it is stated thus:
"The second is the characteristic of being able to see."
Because one can see by depending on movement;
without movement, there is no seeing. Seventh:
It is called the ālayavijñāna as the manifestation of signs;
that is to say, the signs of objects and the manifesting consciousness.
It is established separately as the *ālaya*.
Therefore, it is stated thus in the *Tattvanirdeśa-sūtra*:
"Diverse and diverse."
In the stage of Presence (Abhimukhī), there is the transformation of the characteristics and their distinctions;
it proceeds as the fulfillment of practice.
For this reason, it is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Furthermore, this *ālaya-vijñāna* is truly a dharma that is maturation (*vipāka*) and morally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because its characteristics are pure and white,
it is also called "accomplishment.
Therefore, this is the ālayavijñāna.
By which determination is it subsumed?
In this treatise, it is stated as follows:
Third is the characteristic of the objective realm (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*).
Because it depends upon the perceiving subject (*darśana*),
the objective realm appears as a delusion.
Because when free from views, there are no objective realms.
The eighth is called the fundamental nature of suchness, the principle of the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
This refers to the pure *tathatā* realized through correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).
Because it is established separately as the *ālayavijñāna*,
the *Sarvadharmasamatā-sūtra* states as follows:
There is consciousness;
this consciousness is not subsumed under the category of consciousness-consciousness.
That which is called the suchness-ālayavijñāna:
under what category of definitive determination (*viniścaya*) should this ālayavijñāna be subsumed?
This is because it is subsumed within the true suchness (*tathatā*) that is the objective realm of pure prajñā.
Ninth, it is called the pure initial awakening (*ādi-prativedha-bodhi*) of the ālayavijñāna.
That which is called the originally existent, pure, and white *ādi-bodhi* (primordial awakening) wisdom is separately established as the *ālayavijñāna*;
therefore, the fruition is perfected.
In a sūtra it is stated thus:
The Buddha addressed the King of the Bodhi Tree, saying,
"The *ālayavijñāna* is the spontaneous initial awakening."
One should always remain inseparable from the pure fundamental awakening (viśuddha-mūla-avabodha).
The pure fundamental awakening should always remain inseparable from the pure consciousness of initial awakening (ādi-avabodha-viśuddha-vijñāna).
It exists following that; it exists because of that;
or it is not of the same kind.
Alternatively, because it is not of a different kind [from consciousness],
under which category of definitive analysis (*viniścaya*) should this ālayavijñāna be subsumed?
In this treatise, it is stated as follows:
"The meaning of original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) is..."
For one who has attained initial enlightenment (ādi-bodhi),
it is identical to original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi). Tenth:
It is termed the *ālayavijñāna* of the initial awakening of defilement and purity;
that is to say, the *prajñā* of initial awakening that accords with conditions is established separately as the *ālaya*.
Therefore, the fruit is perfected.
Thus it is said in the Sūtra:
"Furthermore, O King of Trees."

First, that which is associated with the view of a self as a person (pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi);
second, that which is associated with the view of a self in phenomena (dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi).
It is associated with the third wisdom, the Wisdom of Equality;
it initially pervades the mental continuums of all ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles who are still in training.
Prior to the seventh bhūmi, for a certain class of bodhisattvas in the state of a mind with outflows (sāsrava-citta),
they take the ālayavijñāna as their object.
The view of a self as a person (pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi) arises;
subsequently, it pervades the mental continuums of all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas,
as well as all bodhisattvas during those stages when the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna-phala) has not yet manifested.
Taking that maturation-consciousness as its object,
it gives rise to the view of a self in phenomena (dharmātman);
subsequently, it pervades the mental continuums of all Tathāgatas.

The stage at which the fruit of the knowledge of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna-phala) becomes manifest during the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (darśana-mārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).
Taking that stainless maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and so forth as its object,
it gives rise to the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
Question:
The two types of grasping—grasping at persons and grasping at phenomena—arise together.
Why, then, do their states differ according to their sequence? Answer:
The grasping of persons (pudgala-grāha) necessarily arises based on the grasping of phenomena (dharma-grāha).
Furthermore, the self of phenomena (dharma-ātman) is universal, whereas the self of persons (pudgala-ātman) is restricted.
The treatise states:
"At the stage when the view of a person (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) arises,
there is that view of a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*)."
It must also necessarily manifest before one.
The grasping at a self necessarily arises based on the grasping at phenomena,
just as one must first be deluded regarding a tree stump or the like [to mistake it for a person].
Because it refers to persons and so forth.
The commentary states:
"This now clarifies the initial stage."
It must include the subsequent stage because the initial one is short; this refers to the stage of the person-self (pudgala-ātman).
There must necessarily be a self of phenomena (*dharmātman*), because the self of persons (*pudgalātman*) necessarily arises based upon the self of phenomena.
The self of persons...
This is because [the self] functions as a sovereign controller and agent;
and because the "self of phenomena" (dharma-ātman) possesses its own intrinsic nature and superior functions.
That is, the dharma-self is universal,
while the person-self is limited.
Question:
Regarding this seventh consciousness:
how is it that it possesses a distinct self-substance apart from the visual and other [sensory] consciousnesses?
From which scriptural passage is this derived? Answer:
The Treatise states:
The sacred teaching and correct reasoning serve as valid authorities;
that is to say, in various sūtras, the Blessed One has stated:
It is taught that there are three distinct meanings for mind (citta), mentation (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna).
That which arises through accumulation is called "mind."
"Reflection" is the meaning of *manas*;
"discernment" is the meaning of *vijñāna*.
These are the three distinct meanings.
Although these three meanings apply to all eight consciousnesses,
they are manifested according to their predominant characteristics.
The eighth is named "Mind" (*citta*),
because it gathers the seeds of all phenomena and gives rise to all phenomena.
The seventh is called the mind (manas). It takes the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and so forth as its objects,
constantly and thoroughly deliberating upon them as being "self" and so forth.
The remaining six are called consciousnesses (*vijñāna*),
because they function by discerning (*vijñapti*) six distinct objects that are coarse, mobile, and intermittent.
As stated in the verses of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
"The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is called 'mind' (*citta*); that which has the nature of reflection is called 'intellect' (*manas*)."
That which is able to discern the characteristics of all objects is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The commentary states:
Although all eight consciousnesses are equally termed "mind," "intellect," and "consciousness," they are designated according to their predominant manifestation.
The eighth is called the mind (*citta*).
It serves as the locus for the perfuming and accumulation of the seeds of all dharmas that manifest,
and it takes these manifestations as its support.
Because the seed-consciousness acts as the cause that is able to produce all phenomena,
it gives rise to all dharmas.
The seventh is called "mind" (manas);
it exists within the state of outflows (sāsrava) and takes only the self as its object.
The eighth [consciousness] has uncontaminated objects and suchness as its objects;
this is because it is admitted that at the stage of fruition, it takes all phenomena as its objects.
The remaining six consciousnesses are called "vijñāna" (cognition).
Among the six object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyatālambana*), their nature is coarse and mobile,
and they are phenomena characterized by interruption.
Because it functions as discernment,
that which is easily discerned is called "coarse" (audārika); because it changes and fluctuates, it is called "mobile" (cala).
Non-continuity is called "interval.
Each possesses this excellence,
and thus each receives its distinct name.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"The Sūtra speaks of 'unshared ignorance' (āveṇikī avidyā)."
Subtle and constantly active,
it obscures reality; if this consciousness did not exist, [it could not do so].
That [self] should not exist;
that is to say, throughout all parts of the present life.
It constantly gives rise to the uncommon ignorance that deludes one regarding the principles,
obscuring the true meaning and obstructing the eye of supreme wisdom.
As it is said in a verse:
"The true meaning arises in the mind;
at all times, [ignorance] acts as its obstacle."
It accompanies all factors;
that is, it is the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*). Therefore, the Sūtra says:
It is said that ordinary beings dwell perpetually throughout the long night.
Blinded by ignorance, their minds are shrouded in stupor and intoxication;
they have never once awakened.
If, during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there were a time when this ignorance did not temporarily arise;
This would contradict the meaning of the sūtra,
which states that in the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), there is ignorance regarding the principles of reality (*tattva*).
There is [the case of] practicing and not practicing;
for it would not accord with reason.
Based on these six consciousnesses,
none can be established;
it must be interrupted here.
Because it is constantly present as an object,
the existence of the manas is admitted;
thus, this fault does not arise.
The commentary states:
As in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*,
there are four types of ignorance (*avidyā*).
First, manifestation;
second, the two types;
third, correspondence.
Four are non-associated;
some are both conditioned and associated.
Regarding "unshared" and so forth:
that which is now called "unshared" refers to this subtle, constant activity.
Its modes of activity are difficult to discern;
it conceals the principle of non-self and obscures untainted wisdom.
It is called "obscuring the reality.
There are two kinds of reality:
first, the principle of selflessness.
Second, regarding the two types of untainted vision (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*), there are two meanings for the term "object" (*artha*):
first, it refers to the sense of "objective sphere" (*viṣaya*).
Because it perceives objects through its aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*). "Two" refers to the object and the principle;
suchness is the principle itself.
Question:
The defiled manas is always associated with the four afflictions.
How is "unshared ignorance" (āveṇikī avidyā) explained?
The treatise says:
It should be said that among these four,
ignorance is the primary factor; although all three arise together, [ignorance is predominant].
It is also called "unshared" (āveṇika),
for from the beginningless limit,
it has been constantly inwardly deluded.
They have never examined this,
because delusion predominates;
even to the point of claiming that the seventh [member] is associated with ignorance (*avidyā*).
Operating perpetually from beginningless time,
it obstructs the wisdom that realizes ultimate reality;
such is its superior function.
It is absent in other consciousnesses and exists only in this consciousness;
therefore, it is called "unshared."
Furthermore, there are two general types of non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*): first, the ever-active non-common [ignorance];
and second, the occasion-specific non-common [ignorance].
What other consciousnesses lack— namely,
these two types of independent and non-common [factors]—
this consciousness does not possess.
The commentary states:
"Lord" (*prabhu*) has the meaning of sovereignty;
it has the meaning of being the cause and the basis.
Because it serves as the basis for that [ignorance],
it is called "unshared.
Why is this so regarding ignorance?
It is called "unshared," meaning that from the beginningless limit,
it has manifested as constantly arising throughout the long night.
Constantly inwardly muddled and deluded,
they fail to understand the principle of emptiness at all times and have never engaged in self-examination.
This demonstrates that ignorance constantly clings to a self and never turns back;
this meaning generally reveals the sense of ignorance as the sovereign master.
First, regarding those that are constantly active and unique:
these are all associated with this consciousness;
it is concerning these that we now discuss.
Other consciousnesses do not possess them.
As for those that function independently and are not shared,
they arise in association with anger and other such afflictions.
It is called "acting alone" because ignorance arises without being accompanied by other [defilements],
being deluded regarding the principles of the Truths in isolation.
This consciousness does not exist.
Furthermore, regarding "unshared ignorance," it is because ignorance is the primary factor.
It is called "unshared" because its subject matter has the sense of being unshared.
It is unshared.
This is the meaning of being "solely" (eka).
That is to say, ignorance (avidyā) has the sense of darkness; it refers to the ignorance that co-exists with the [other] seven [factors].
Constantly active and uninterrupted;
this is the meaning of "long darkness.
Because of this long darkness, [it is called so].
It is called the "long night";
this ignorance alone constitutes the essence of the long night.
All other dharmas lack the sense of "long night," whereas this alone possesses it; therefore,
it is called "unshared" (āveṇika).
Apart from these, other phenomena possess the characteristic of a certain type of prolonged continuity,
yet they lack the characteristic of darkness.
There may be a certain class [of phenomena] that,
while possessing the sense of darkness,
lacks the sense of long-term continuity.
One should analyze this through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First, there are those that are long but not night,
such as the three [mental states] beginning with greed associated with the seven [universal factors], as well as mental states associated with the two wisdoms of the excellent and the even.
Second, there is that which is darkness but not long,
such as the ignorance associated with the first six consciousnesses.
Third, there is that which is both long and darkness.
The seventh is ignorance (avidyā);
the fourth is neither long nor night.
The first six consciousnesses exclude ignorance.
It takes up the remaining [afflictions] such as greed,
as well as the wholesome states and so forth within the causal stage,
together with their results.
It observes the accomplishment of the matter within.
It consists of mental states associated with the two types of wisdom and so forth.
Now, this ignorance coexists with these seven factors.
According to this principle, it not only does not coexist with other consciousnesses,

but furthermore does not coexist even with its own associated factors, such as greed and so forth. That is to say, although it arises simultaneously with greed and the like within the same aggregate, [it does not share their specific characteristics].
However, greed and the like do not have the meaning of "long-term darkness.
Greed and the like take "attachment" and so forth as their meaning,
whereas this [term] takes "long-term darkness" as its meaning.
It differs from those [other afflictions],
and is therefore called "unshared" (*āveṇika*).
Here, it is designated as "unshared" because it is a state of constant delusion and darkness throughout the seventh [consciousness].
Among the six consciousnesses,
there is no sense of permanence;
they possess only the quality of arising independently.
It is called "unshared.
Question:
It is associated with the ever-active unshared ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
How many meanings are there?
Answer: There are four meanings.
An ancient worthy said:
"The one is the host;
that is to say, the ignorance of the first six consciousnesses is the guest."
Because it is subject to interruption;
the seventh, ignorance, is the primary factor because it is uninterrupted.
Second, those that constantly manifest:
they arise and manifest continuously during the state of being with outflows (sāsrava).
Because it is uninterrupted,
it is called "constantly active.
Third, regarding the "unshared" [factors]:
It is called "unshared" because it differs from the sixth consciousness acting independently; thus,
the sixth consciousness is not unshared [in this sense].
However, it does not arise simultaneously with the other nine afflictions;
therefore, it is called "unshared" (āveṇika). If the seventh [consciousness] were called "unshared," [it would be so for a different reason].
Because it is superior to the obscuration of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas,
and because it functions constantly without interruption.
Fourth, when the first six consciousnesses operate through minds of the three natures (*trividha-citta*).
This consciousness and ignorance both arise as manifest activity;
that is to say, when the preceding six consciousnesses are of a wholesome nature.
Those who cannot eliminate the signs of giving and so forth all possess the seventh ever-present, unique ignorance that internally clings to a self;
this causes the six consciousnesses and so forth to proceed with giving.
They are unable to realize the emptiness of the three spheres,
and furthermore, they are constantly hindered by the presence of uncommon ignorance (*āveṇikī-avidyā*).
Furthermore, it causes the non-arising of the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that ought to arise;
because this ignorance coexists with the seventh consciousness,
it has not been abandoned until now.
Therefore, it is called "co-arising.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The eye and visible forms serve as conditions."
Visual consciousness arises;
and so on, up to: with the mind and mental phenomena as conditions, mental consciousness arises.
If this consciousness did not exist,
that mind would not exist;
the eye-faculty and the object-form serve as the two conditions.
The [object] capable of inducing the arising of visual consciousness,
up to and including the mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*) capable of inducing the arising of mental consciousness, serves as the two conditions for the arising of mental consciousness.
If the seventh consciousness did not exist,
then the sixth consciousness would have only a single category of object as its objective condition,
and it would lack a supporting sense faculty as its basis.
Since there exists that which is a simultaneous root (*sahabhū-indriya*),
it is clearly understood that this refers to the seventh consciousness acting as the simultaneous root for the sixth consciousness.
The Hīnayāna school says:
In our school, we maintain that the physical mass of flesh serves as the support for the sixth consciousness; why, then,
must one insist on the existence of a separate seventh consciousness?
The author of the treatise refutes this, saying:
It cannot be said that the sixth [consciousness] depends on form;
rather, the sixth must necessarily depend upon the mind (manas).
It is said that the mind (manas) is not of the nature of form (rūpa).
Furthermore, it is said that the sixth [consciousness] possesses three types of discrimination:
recollective discrimination (anusmaraṇa-vikalpa), conceptualizing discrimination (abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa), and intrinsic discrimination (svabhāva-vikalpa).
If it were granted that the sixth [consciousness] abides in dependence upon form,
it would be identical to the first five consciousnesses,
lacking the two types of discrimination: recollective and conceptualizing.
Jiū said: "In my school,
the five consciousnesses [arise] with the sense organs first and the consciousnesses subsequent."
That is to say, the five sense faculties of the preceding moment give rise to the five consciousnesses of the succeeding moment.
The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying:
As for that which possesses roots:
it is like leaves arising in dependence upon seeds;
the sprout and the seed exist simultaneously.
The shadow arises dependent upon the body;
where there is a body, there is a shadow. Consciousness issues forth depending upon the sense faculties; where there are faculties, there is consciousness.
In principle, they must be simultaneous;
for there is no preceding momentary faculty that gives rise to a succeeding momentary consciousness.
Since the five consciousnesses possess simultaneous bases (*sahabhū-indriya*),
it must be proven that the sixth consciousness likewise possesses a simultaneous base;
this is precisely the seventh consciousness.
Regarding the proof by means of an inferential principle:
that which is described in the scriptures as possessing "deliberation" (manana) is precisely the seventh consciousness.
The Hīnayāna states:
Only the sixth [consciousness], the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
is designated as the "investigating mind" (*manas*).
Why is it necessary to specifically designate the seventh [consciousness] as the *manas* that cogitates?
The author of the treatise refutes this by saying:
"For instance, when the sixth *manovijñāna* is present..."
If the mind that serves as the equal-and-immediate antecedent has already ceased and lacks substantial existence,
how can it possess the function of cogitation to be designated as "mind" (manas)?
Furthermore, for example, as for the sixth consciousness:
although it possesses mentation when abiding in the present, [it does not possess the nature of self-reflection].
It is always designated as "consciousness" (vijñāna) and not as "mind" (manas); therefore,
it must depend upon the past.
Because it is precisely that which is named "manas," one must believe in the existence of a seventh consciousness,
which possesses constant and thorough deliberation.
Only then can it be called "the meaning of intention.
"Intention" (manas) has the sense of being a basis or support.
If it is the immediately preceding mind (samanantara-manas),
it is metaphorically designated by the name "seventh" because its function is to cogitate (manana) based upon this [storehouse consciousness] as its simultaneous support (sahabhū-āśraya).
Furthermore, the seventh consciousness is associated with the four afflictions and is termed "defiled.
It constantly and thoroughly engages in deliberation.
It is called "mind" (manas).
Because it possesses a constant, ever-present activity that is unique to it—
namely, the ignorance of defilement— it is termed "defiled."
This is precisely the nature of being obscured;
that is, it obscures the meaning of the true object-condition and veils pure, wondrous wisdom.
"Constantly and scrutinizingly deliberating" distinguishes this [manas] from the eighth consciousness and the first six consciousnesses.
"Constantly" means:
It is uninterrupted.
It is "thorough" because it resolutely clings to a self and to phenomena.
Question:
The eighth [liberation] is also uninterrupted,
and the sixth is definitive.
Question: Since there is deliberation (*manana*), why is it not called "mind" (*manas*)? Answer:
There are four propositions.
First: constant yet not discerning.
The eighth [consciousness] is constant and uninterrupted.
Because one does not carefully deliberate upon my Dharma.
Second, [the mind] is careful but not constant;
this is the sixth.
Although it involves deliberative reflection,
because it is not constant,
it is not called "mind" (manas).
The first five are neither;
they are neither constant nor deliberate.
The seventh encompasses both.
Because it is constantly and continuously discerning,
it alone is called "mind" (manas).
Question:
Question: What dharma does the seventh [consciousness] contemplate?
Answer: It grasps the eighth [consciousness], its seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*).
Because it involves deliberation regarding the existence of a self and dharmas,
the two vehicles in their state of no-more-learning lack the grasping at a personal self;
however, because they still involve deliberation regarding the grasping at a self in dharmas, it is called "manas."
In the state of Buddhahood, both the grasping at a self (*ātman*) and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely absent.
It constantly and thoroughly deliberates upon the principle of non-self;
thus, the seventh consciousness in the state of Buddhahood is also called *manas*.
Question:
Does the seventh [consciousness] possess volition as its own intrinsic nature,
or is it the volition included within the universal mental factors associated with the seventh?
Question: Is it called "mental deliberation" (manasikāra) because it takes up what the mind deliberates upon? Answer: It is so called because it takes up that which the mind deliberates upon.
If all eight consciousnesses possess [this],
why does volition (*cetanā*) belong exclusively to the seventh?
Question:
If it were the case that the mind itself possesses volition (*cetanā*) by its very nature,
then what would be the purpose of including volition among the mental factors (*caitta*)? Answer:
It possesses two meanings:
first, it has associated deliberation;
second, its own essence is also deliberation.
Now, that which possesses the nature of deliberation is designated as "mind" (manas).
Question:
Regarding the mental factors (caitta) and the mind-king (cittarāja):
One type [of person] constantly and repeatedly deliberates,
grasping the eighth consciousness as the self. Why,
then, is it not stated that the mental factors (caitta) constitute the mind-base (manas)?
Answer: The meaning of "basis" (āśraya) refers to the sense of "relying upon."
Although mental factors (caitta) are always and continuously engaged in deliberation,
they are not primary;
they are subordinate phenomena.
Because it is not that which is relied upon,
it is not called "mind" (*manas*).
Second, the consciousness of its own essence possesses deliberation (*manana*).
It serves as the basis for the other seven consciousnesses;
taking only the mind-king (citta-rāja) as its referent,
it is termed "manas" (the mental faculty).
Question:
If it is said that the mind (manas) is defined as that which possesses the nature of deliberation,
then the seventh consciousness must possess four parts.
What portion is called "the mental state of deliberation"?
Answer: There are two interpretations.
The first aspect, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), is called "conceptualization" (*manasikāra*);
the two internal aspects are not called conceptualization,
but are simply termed "mind" (*manas*).
The objective aspect (viṣayabhāga) is not called "mind" (manas),
because it possesses the function of cogitation (manana).
It is the faculty of reflection that contemplates self and non-self.
The two internal [faculties] cannot contemplate self and non-self;
they are merely termed "mind."
Because it has this as its essence,
the second part, the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), is characterized by deliberation (*manana*). As for "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*):
Regarding its essence and characteristics:
its internal two parts are of the nature of mentation.
Thus, both the internal and external are termed "mind" (manas);
all three parts involve deliberation, with the exception of the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect).
The image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) is the object of cognition.
Question: How is this known?
The three divisions of internal and external are all merely conceptualization.
Answer: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) states:
Its nature and characteristic consist of mentation (*manasikāra*).
Its internal two divisions constitute its essence;
it is called the nature of mentation.
The external aspect of perception is the characteristic of deliberation;
it is the function.
One kind is deliberation itself.
All three parts are termed "mind" (manas).
Specifically, the part that does not grasp at signs is termed "cognition" (saṃjñā),
because it lacks the functional capacity of an objective referent.
Question:
The seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) takes self and phenomena as its objects because it cogitates upon a self.
It may be called "investigation" (vitarka).
Since the self-witnessing division (svasaṃvittibhāga) does not take the self-characterized division (ātman-viṣayabhāga) as its object,
how can the self-witnessing division also be called "investigation"?
Answer: It is realized by the self-witnessing division (svasaṃvittibhāga),
because that seeing division (darśanabhāga) involves the conceit of "I" (ahaṃkāra).
It is also called "deliberation" (manana).
Question:
Does the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) deliberate upon the self?
This is not subsumed under valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
it is realized by the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), which conceives of that seeing-portion (*darśanabhāga*) as a self.
Is the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) also non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*)? Answer:
The seeing-division (darśana-bhāga) conceives of a self;
because the seeing-division falsely grasps [this],
it is termed non-valid cognition (aprāmāṇya).
Self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is the internal realization of the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*), because it is erroneously grasped [as a self];
the essence of self-cognition is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Thus, both its essence and its function are acts of deliberation (*manana*).
Thus, the two internal divisions are also called *manas* (mind) and also called *vijñāna* (consciousness);
the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) is also called *manas*.
It is also called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*),
because it is the function of the mind (*manas*).
Discernment is its function.
The mind (*manas*) is the substance;
"deliberation" (*manana*) is precisely the mind.
This is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Question:
The seventh consciousness takes only the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth consciousness as its object, perceiving it as the self.
Why does it not take its image-part (nimitta-bhāga)?
As for the two internal parts and so forth,
the answer is:
the image-part (nimittabhāga) is discontinuous.
Furthermore, this is an external condition.
The functions of the two internal parts are submerged and difficult to discern;
thus, they are not grasped.
Because the seeds lack functional activity,
they are not grasped as a self;
whereas the aspect of seeing (darśana-bhāga) manifests through its functional activity.
Question:
Regarding the seventh consciousness, how are its three types of valid cognition (pramāṇa) distinguished as being either conventional (prajñapti) or real (dravya)?
Answer: Regarding the ancient explanation of the differentiation of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
the seventh [consciousness], the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), is not a valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
Because the object does not accord with the mind,
that eighth seeing-part is fundamentally not the self.
Now, the seventh [consciousness] falsely clings to it as a self;
thus, it does not accord with its actual nature.
Furthermore, it does not directly perceive or attach to the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth [consciousness].
The objective aspect (nimittabhāga) that arises as a transformation is not originally the self.
Seventh, it is further clung to as the self;
furthermore, it does not accord with the aspect of the object-part (nimittabhāga). Thus, there are two instances of non-correspondence with the object.
Therefore, it is known to be non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Regarding the distinction between the provisional and the real:
the seventh [consciousness] takes the fundamental substance (*mūla-vastu*) of another as its object.
The eighth [consciousness] does not cling to the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga),
but merely takes as its object the intermediate, provisional aspect of the self (ātman-bhāga); thus,
the object is provisional and not real.
Question:
Is the intermediate aspect (ākāra) necessarily merely provisional?
Question: Does it also apply to the real? Answer:
The seventh, the intermediate aspect (nimitta-bhāga), is provisional.
There is no production from real seeds;
rather, this objective aspect arises solely from the two poles.
It nevertheless possesses both natures.
If half of it arises from its essential nature,
it is of an unobscured nature.
This then belongs to the essential nature.
If half [of it] arises from the seventh seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga), which is its own object-condition,
it is identical to the seeing-portion.
This is of an obscured nature;
however, when two mental factors arise simultaneously,
they form a single objective aspect (nimittabhāga).
Now, as for the statement that the object is provisional,
this is said solely in reference to the portion of the self-characteristic that follows the deluded mind.
Question:
If it is argued that the seventh consciousness’s objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is merely provisional,
arising from both ends and encompassing both natures:
Within the objective aspect (ālambana-bhāga) of the self-characteristic of the seventh [consciousness],
half should be considered obscured (nivṛta) and half unobscured (anivṛta).
"Half is me; half is not me. He replied.

The non-obscured (anivṛta) nature of the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) that arises upon the eighth consciousness’s perceiving portion (darśana-bhāga) is secretly merged as one with the objective aspect of the deluded seventh consciousness, which acts as the subject that perceives it through pervasive conceptualization (parikalpa).

If it is the seventh [consciousness], it merely grasps its own delusory arising of the pervasive conceptualization (parikalpa) as a concealed (nivṛta) and provisional objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga),
taking it to be its own internal self;
although these are secretly unified in a single location.
Furthermore, one does not incur the fault of [the self] being pervaded by two natures within the self that is grasped;
it is like the taste of salt in water,
yet one merely grasps it as "water."
One does not grasp at the salt.
Water and salt are fundamentally inseparable.
Question:
The seventh [consciousness] possesses its own objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).
Why does it not take its own objective aspect as its object,
rather than taking the objective aspect of the eighth [consciousness], the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), as the self?
Answer: An ancient master said:
"The term 'conditioning the seeing-part' (ālambana-dṛṣṭi-bhāga) used here [refers to the following]."
This refers to remote conditions (*parokṣa-pratyaya*).
If one says they are direct [conditions],
then where does the meaning of "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) lie?
He asked again:
"Even if it were granted that the eighth consciousness serves as a remote condition,
upon what phenomena does the seventh consciousness itself give rise to grasping?"
Answer: One gives rise to grasping toward the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) of one's own consciousness.
Furthermore, he asked:
Question: What is the distinction between these two views?
Answer: If we discuss external objects, [the distinction is as follows].
The characteristics and the seeing are entirely distinct;
yet, if one speaks from the perspective of the mind,
there is no difference between the characteristics and the seeing.
Marks are themselves views.
Thus, a sutra says:
"The mind manifests as marks."
It is seen as the basis for the mind.
Question:
If the manas does not exist, [how can this be so?]
What fault would there be?
The answer is:
if the seventh [consciousness] did not exist.
Then there is no ordinary being to be weary of,
and no sage to be delighted in;
neither the ordinary nor the sage are established.
Both the defiled and the pure would be lost.
The treatise says:
"Therefore, it must certainly be that there is this distinct intention."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Within a single lifetime, sentient beings in the realm of non-conception..."
The mind and mental factors cease.
If this consciousness did not exist,
they would be without defilement.
This means that for a long period of time, those [beings] lack the six evolving consciousnesses;
if this manas were absent,
the grasping at a self would likewise be non-existent.
Therefore, there must exist a distinct afflicted manas that constantly gives rise to the grasping of a self within the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva).
For this reason, the noble ones alike condemn and loathe it;
furthermore, a sutra states:
When ordinary beings possess wholesome, defiled, or neutral states of mind,
they are always accompanied by the grasping of a self; if this consciousness did not exist, [such grasping would be impossible].
That [attainment] should not exist for those of the class of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) at the time when their minds are of the three natures (trividha-svabhāva).
Although various karmas arise externally,
one constantly clings to a self internally; because of this internal clinging to a self, [the cycle continues].
This causes the giving and other virtues arising within the six consciousnesses to be unable to transcend conceptual signs; therefore,
the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
The defiled manas serves as the support for consciousness; as long as it has not been extinguished, [consciousness persists].
Bound by the discernment of signs,
one does not attain liberation;
once the manas has ceased, [liberation is attained].
There is bondage by signs and liberation from them.
What is called "bondage by signs" refers to being conditioned by the characteristics of objects.
Being unable to fully comprehend that [consciousness] is like an illusory phenomenon and so forth,
one is thereby constrained by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*),
and fails to attain mastery.
Therefore, it is called the "bondage of name and sign. Based on this meaning,
there is a verse that says:
In this way, the afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas) is the support of consciousness;
as long as this mind has not been extinguished, [consciousness continues].
"Consciousness remains bound and is never released.
The commentary states:
"In the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva)."
Because the grasping at a self arises constantly,
the noble ones alike revile and loathe it.
There is a seventh [consciousness] that gives rise to the grasping of a self toward those [objects],
because they are ordinary worldlings;
this occurs after they have emerged from meditative absorption.
They sink again into birth and death and give rise to various afflictions;
thus the sages and worthies rebuke them.
If there were no seventh [consciousness],
one would not criticize that [state] as being a fruit without fault.
Because of the grasping at a self,
the acts of giving and so forth that arise within the six consciousnesses are unable to transcend conceptual signs;
this self is an external condition.
The modes of activity [of these consciousnesses] are coarse and mobile; they do not arise from the seventh [consciousness],
because of the nature of the seventh.
The sixth [category] arises from this;
it is entirely due to seven births,
as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Within the sixth consciousness,
the substance of the self-grasping is intermittent and pervades minds of all three natures.
Because it arises intermittently,
and because the seventh consciousness does not arise by taking external objects as its objective support.
The above is a brief record concerning the seventh manas-consciousness.
All teachings have the same purport,
and all sages provide joint exegesis.
For those who have newly entered the Path:
This point must be clarified:
this is the cause for the arising of both ordinary beings and sages;
its essential nature should be thoroughly investigated.
Thus, one establishes the foundation for resolving delusion and attaining enlightenment;
one may investigate its root source.
To be deluded regarding it constitutes the human dharma.
To grasp [them] is ignorance;
to awaken to them is to realize the wisdom of the nature of equality.
Within all consciousnesses...
It alone attains the name "mind" (manas);
within the realm of outflows,
it acts as the sovereign of ignorance.
Without interruption or cessation,
the state of non-ideation is treated but not eliminated;
it is ever-examined and eternally constant.
The four deities of the Ārūpyadhātu withdraw and arise again;
although they possess concealment, it is indeterminate (avyākṛta);
they do not grasp externally but take the internal as their object.
Constantly arising and manifesting,
they are able to obscure reality and obstruct the Path; thus,
they are designated as "unshared" (āveṇika).
It merely results in defilement and moistens rebirth. Therefore,
if one wishes to penetrate through the dust and toil of worldly existence,
one must know the essential path.
When about to administer a wondrous medicine,
one first waits to ascertain the origin of the ailment;
if one investigates with meticulous care, [the cause will be found].
If you settle the mind in contemplation and investigate deeply, what defilement will not emerge [into clarity],
and what ailment will not be dispelled?
This gateway for severing delusions is of paramount importance.

53. *Zongjing lu*, Scroll 53, Compiled by Chan Master Zhijue, Abbot of Huiji Yongming Temple, Yan-shou. Part Three: The Third Transformative Consciousness.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Wei shi lun) verse states: "The next is the third transformative consciousness; its distinctions..."
There are six kinds.
Their nature and characteristic is the discernment of objects;
they are wholesome, unwholesome, or neither.
These three transformative consciousnesses are consciousnesses that discern objects;
their self-verifying aspect (svasaṃvittibhāga) is the nature of discernment itself.
The seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is the aspect of discernment;
it is obscured and indeterminate consciousness.
Since its intrinsic nature consists in the cognition of objects,
and it further employs that very [cognition] as its mode of activity (ākāra),
then that which cognizes the object—
This is the intrinsic nature of consciousness;
it is also its mode of activity.
The mode of activity is its function.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Because the types [of objects] corresponding to the six sense organs differ."
Alternatively, they are named after their respective objects, from "consciousness of form" (rūpa-vijñāna) up to "consciousness of phenomena" (dharma-vijñāna).
Because it accords with the meaning of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
That is to say, the discernment of the six objects is called consciousness.
The five consciousnesses, such as that of form and so forth, perceive only form and its like;
the consciousness of phenomena (dharmavijñāna), however, is capable of comprehending all phenomena.
Alternatively, because it alone can discern phenomena (dharma), it receives the specific name "consciousness of phenomena" (dharmavijñāna);
thus, there are six consciousnesses.
There is no fault of confusion.
Question:
If there is no real form external to the mind, [how is this so?]
If so, the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, would have no objects of perception (*ālambana*).
To this, the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* replies:
Although it is not formless,
it is nevertheless a transformation of consciousness;
that is to say, when consciousness arises.
Through the power of internal causes and conditions,
[consciousness] manifests as if appearing in the forms of the eye, visible objects, and so forth; it is precisely by means of these manifestations that [the process occurs].
They serve as the objective conditions for the support;
however, the sense organs such as the eye are not apprehended through direct perception.
Because it can give rise to consciousness,
one infers that it exists; this, however,
is merely a functional capacity.
Since it is not produced by external factors,
and the principle that external,
resistant form exists is already untenable.
Therefore, it must be merely the manifestation of internal consciousness.
The commentary states:
"Although the eyes and so forth have forms that serve as their supports and objects, [they do not exist externally]."
Rather, these are manifested by consciousness;
they do not exist externally to the mind as separate atoms.
This constitutes the sense faculties and their objects;
however, when the eight consciousnesses arise,
it is through the power of internal causal conditions, such as seeds and so forth.
The eighth consciousness transforms into what resembles the five sense organs and the five sense objects; the five consciousnesses,
such as the visual consciousness and so forth,
rely upon those transformed organs.
Although it does not directly apprehend its objective sphere as its essential nature,
it must depend upon that [sphere] for its arising.
In reality, upon the objective realm of form within the fundamental consciousness,
there arise transformations appearing as the five sensory objects;
these then take those five sense organs as their support.
Taking both those and these two kinds of five objects as objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
if the five consciousnesses were not to rely upon what is transformed by the eighth [consciousness], [they could not arise].
Consequently, there would be no object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
because within the category of object-conditions,
there is a distinction between the proximate and the remote.
However, as for the sense organs such as the eye,
which are not apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
there are the five objects, such as visible form.
These are commonly perceived by the world and are obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): namely,
the five sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth.
It is not apprehended by direct perception,
except for the eighth consciousness as its object and the cognition of Tathāgatas and the like.
This is obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It is not commonly spoken of in the world;
[it occurs] in other states of distracted mind.
It is not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It merely possesses the functional capacity to give rise to consciousness;
it is known to exist on that basis.
This consists merely of functional capacity;
it is not a form produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) that exists separately outside of the mind.
This refers to the term "functional capacity."
This is precisely the arising of the functions of the five consciousnesses;
one contemplates the function to know the essence,
just as one contemplates the sprouting of a seedling.
From this, one knows that the substance of the seeds exists.
Thus, a verse in the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says:
"With the eye, forms, and so forth as conditions..."
Thus consciousness arises,
just as fire blazes because of fuel;
the arising of consciousness is likewise so.
Objects arise following the deluded mind,
just as iron pursues a magnet;
they are like a city in the sky or a mirage.
That which is grasped by the ignorant through thirst has no creator within;
it merely undergoes transformation according to the mind.
Furthermore, like those in a city of Gandharvas,
whose coming and going are entirely unreal,
so too is the body of sentient beings.
All movements and stillnesses are not real;
they are like what is seen in a dream,
which no longer exists once one has awakened.
One falsely perceives phenomena such as the aggregates;
yet upon awakening, they are fundamentally quiescent—
a mere collection of the four great elements and subtle particles.
Apart from the mind, nothing is to be found.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the youth Īśvaraguhya said to Sudhana:
"Good son, I further possess excellent knowledge of the eighteen arts and crafts and various technical skills."
Together with the sixty-two vidyā-mantras and their retinues,
as well as all methods such as the inner science (adhyātma-vidyā),
they treat the internal afflictions.
What are called the internal afflictions of the body?
There are four causes and conditions:
the first is the eye faculty.
First, by grasping at the objects of form;
second, by the habitual tendencies of attachment from beginningless time;
and third, by the intrinsic nature of that consciousness itself.
Fourth, there is the mental attention and aspiration toward the object of form.
By the power of these four kinds of causal conditions, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) undergoes transformation.
The waves of consciousness arise like a torrential stream,
continuing in an uninterrupted succession.
Good son, just as visual consciousness arises,
so too do all the sensory consciousnesses arise within every pore of the atoms of the sense organs.
Their simultaneous birth is likewise like this; it is,
for example, like a bright mirror.
Just as various images appear all at once,
so too do the various consciousnesses;
sometimes they manifest simultaneously.
Good son, it is like a fierce wind blowing upon the waters of the great ocean.
The waves do not cease;
driven by the winds of sensory objects,
they toss the ocean of the tranquil mind.
The waves of consciousness arise,
continuing in an uninterrupted succession;
causes and conditions act upon one another.
They are neither separated nor abandoned;
they are neither one nor different,
like water and its waves.
Due to the characteristics produced by karma,
