and without consciousness, the object cannot be cognized.

Just as all worlds arise and perish depending upon space, so too [all phenomena] depend upon the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).
There are sense-faculties that arise and perish;
fire does not burn empty space,
for it is impossible for it to do so.
In this way, old age, sickness,
and death cannot burn away the Buddha-nature;
the earth rests supported by water.
Water, in turn, depends upon wind;
wind depends upon space; but space does not depend upon earth or the other elements.
In this way, the aggregates, elements,
and faculties abide within afflictions and karma;
these various afflictions and karmas likewise [abide therein].
Abiding in unwholesome reflection and practicing unwholesome reflection,
one dwells within a pure mind.
The intrinsically pure mind does not abide in those phenomena; the aggregates,
bases, and elements are like the earth.
Afflictions and karma are like water;
improper mindfulness is like the wind;
the pure realm of mind is like space.
Based on the nature, false thoughts arise;
from the arising of thoughts, afflictions and karma are produced,
which are able to give rise to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Based upon the five aggregates, the elements,
the sense bases, and all other phenomena,
there arise and cease the various faculties.
Just as the world undergoes formation and destruction,
the pure mind is like space;
it has no cause and no conditions.
Furthermore, there is no meaning of combination,
nor is there arising, abiding, or ceasing;
it is like the pure mind that is like space.
The eternal luminosity is unchanging;
it is defiled by adventitious afflictions through false conceptualization.
Furthermore, the five sensory consciousnesses are immovable;
it is only the mental consciousness that discriminates.
As the Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The nature of consciousness has no source;
it arises falsely due to the six kinds of faculties and objects."
Now you should survey this assembly of noble ones;
let your eyes range over them,
looking about in every direction.
It is simply like a mirror, wherein there is no separate analysis;
yet within it, your consciousness sequentially identifies and points them out.
"This is Mañjuśrī; this is Pūrṇa; this is Maudgalyāyana."
These, Subhūti, these, Śāriputra,
and so forth, are like the five types of direct perception (pratyakṣa).
It surveys all around,
like a mirror reflecting images without discrimination,
as if it were the sixth mental faculty.
That is, they are distinguished sequentially;
it is not like the five sensory cognitions which perceive simultaneously.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
"Consciousness moves while seeing is clear" means that "seeing is clear" refers to the five types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) consciousness.
Discrimination is movement.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
"Originally, there is nothing from which [it] comes."
This consciousness-mind is originally profound and still;
it is not obtained through cultivation.
It is fundamentally serene and quiescent.
The five types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-vijñāna*) are likewise so.
Question:
Regarding the extent to which the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes objects as its conditions: there are three types of objects and three types of cognitions.
How are these to be distinguished?
Answer: An ancient master said:
"The sixth consciousness."
This is inference (*anumāna*).
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to take as its objects phenomena of the three time periods and phenomena of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The phenomena of the three realms,
such as the one hundred dharmas and so forth,
are by their very nature all objects of the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
There are two types:
first, the manifest;
second, the independent.
Furthermore, those who are clear-sighted perceive only the five sensory objects within the gates of the five sense faculties.
When this initial moment of thought shares the same object as the five [sensory consciousnesses],
within that state of sudden arousal (*sateru-citta*),
it is exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Taking the five sensory objects as its objective conditions,
if the subsequent moment has already passed,
it does not preclude its being classified as either inference (*anumāna*) or non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*).
When one forms a conceptual understanding by taking its length and other such qualities as objects,
this is inference (*anumāna*);
or when one gives rise to grasping with respect to the five sense-objects.
This is non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*);

it is the clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). It is admitted that this [consciousness] may pertain to all three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) across its preceding and succeeding moments.
Among the three types of objects:
when one takes the real dharmas of the five sense-objects as an object-condition,
this is a "nature-object" (svabhāva-viṣaya).
If, at a subsequent moment, the mind of practice and understanding takes as its object a provisional form such as length,
it is a true "solitary reflection" (pratibimba-mātra) that appears as if it were "with a substantial basis" (sadravya).
There are three types of independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The first is the independent [consciousness] within dreams;
it also takes the eighteen spheres (*dharmadhātu*) as its object.
These are exclusively solitary shadows and lack reality;
these objects within the dream are subsumed solely under the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Nor does it have an intrinsic nature.
Second, the waking *mukhyamātra* (solitary) [consciousness] takes all phenomena as its object.
With outflows and without outflows;
conditioned and unconditioned;
mundane and supramundane.
Whether possessing substance or lacking substance,
like flowers in the sky or the horns of a rabbit—
so are all phenomena throughout the three periods of time.
All are attained through conditions.
Question:
Regarding this waking mental consciousness—
When a single moment of thought takes the eighteen realms as its object,
how many are image-aspects (nimitta-bhāga) and how many are substantial entities (svabhāva)?
Question: How many are the seeing-parts? Answer:
The fundamental essence and the image-part.
Each has eighteen divisions;
the perceived portion is one alone.
Question:
How can there be eighteen aspects?
Answer: There are eighteen aspects.
Arising from the eighteen essential natures,
there are eighteen objective-image portions (*nimitta-bhāga*),
just as within a single mirror.
When observing the reflections of immeasurable people,
there are eighteen actual people on the outside,
while the mirror itself is but one.
Just as eighteen person-images appear upon a mirror,
so too is it with the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*);
a single seeing-part is able to take and apprehend eighteen object-parts (*nimitta-bhāga*).
If the shadow-substance exists as eighteen [elements],
then there is no fault, as it serves as the object of perception.
If a single moment possessed eighteen aspects of seeing,
there would be the fault of multiple minds; [this applies] to the independent [consciousness] within the three meditative absorptions.
It also takes as its objects the eighteen realms,
the one hundred dharmas,
and past and future spheres.
And because both the provisional and the real— including such things as *tathatā* (suchness)—
can all serve as objects of cognition.
Regarding the differentiation by the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
if it is the clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
its preceding and succeeding moments all pertain to the three means of valid cognition.
Solitary [cognition] within a dream is exclusively non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*),
because it does not correspond to its object.
Upon awakening, it accords with the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
When it takes an existent entity as its object, [it is direct perception].
Because taking the five objects and so forth as conditions is universally direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If, however,
it takes the five sense-faculties (*indriya-dhātu*) as conditions...
The seven mental elements (cittadhātu) and so forth are objects of inference (anumāna),
as are [objects such as] empty flowers or past and future realms.
It is comprised of inference and non-valid cognition; however,
if it occurs within meditative concentration,
it is exclusively direct perception.
Although they take conventional phenomena as objects,
because they do not falsely grasp them,
they are free from conceptual construction.
Therefore, it is exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, the "solitary mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) is precisely the solitary, scattered mind that arises independently.
The gateway of the reflected image (*pratibimba*).
As for the "reflected image," it refers to all atoms (*paramāṇu*).
These two types of form— extremely remote and extremely subtle—
are both merely shadow-forms that exist only within the observing mind.
By analyzing gross matter down to the limit of matter,
one conventionally designates the "ultimate atom" (paramāṇu).
One observes only the images of the mind,
which possess no substantial reality whatsoever.
