Now, regarding the matter of form within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), how many kinds are there in total? Answer: There are five kinds. First, the ultimate...

Briefly stated, there are three types of form: first, form derived from the ultimate limit of space; second, form derived from the ultimate limit of distance; and third, form derived from what is acquired through volition.

Fourth, pervasive conceptualized form; fifth, form as the result of meditative concentration. First, extremely condensed form: [The text continues: "What is extremely condensed form? It refers to the form that is the object of the first dhyāna, which is produced by the mind through the synthesis of many atoms. It is called "extremely condensed" because it is condensed from the most subtle [atoms]. It is called "form" because it is the object of the eye-consciousness. It is called "object" because it is the basis for the arising of consciousness. It is called "produced by the mind" because it is produced by the power of the mind. It is called "produced by synthesis" because it is produced by the synthesis of many atoms. It is called "the object of the first dhyāna" because it is the object of the first dhyāna. It is called "produced" because it is produced by the power of the first dhyāna. It is called "mind" because it is the nature of the mind. It is called "power" because it is the capacity of the mind. It is called "synthesis" because it is the gathering together of many atoms. It is called "atoms" because they are the most subtle particles. It is called "gathering together" because they are collected into one place. It is called "one place" because they are not separated. It is called "not separated" because they are contiguous. It is called "contiguous" because there is no space between them. It is called "space" because it is the absence of matter. It is called "absence of matter" because it is not a substance. It is called "not a substance" because it has no intrinsic nature. It is called "intrinsic nature" because it is the essence of things. It is called "essence" because it is the fundamental reality. It is called "fundamental reality" because it is the ultimate truth. It is called "ultimate truth" because it is not subject to change. It is called "not subject to change" because it is eternal. It is called "eternal" because it is unconditioned. It is called "unconditioned" because it is not produced by causes and conditions. It is called "not produced by causes and conditions" because it is beyond all phenomena. It is called "beyond all phenomena" because it is the realm of the Tathāgata. It is called "realm of the Tathāgata" because it is the state of liberation. It is called "state of liberation" because it is free from all afflictions. It is called "free from all afflictions" because it is the cessation of suffering. It is called "cessation of suffering" because it is the end of the cycle of birth and death. It is called "end of the cycle of birth and death" because it is the attainment of nirvana. It is called "attainment of nirvana" because it is the final goal. It is called "final goal" because there is nothing further to be attained. It is called "nothing further to be attained" because all aspirations have been fulfilled. It is called "all aspirations fulfilled" because the mind is at peace. It is called "mind at peace" because it is free from agitation. It is called "free from agitation" because it is tranquil. It is called "tranquil" because it is undisturbed. It is called "undisturbed" because it is immutable. It is called "immutable" because it is the nature of the Dharma. It is called "nature of the Dharma" because it is the true reality. It is called "true reality" because it is the ultimate nature. It is called "ultimate nature" because it is the source of all wisdom. It is called "source of all wisdom" because it is the foundation of all practice. It is called "foundation of all practice" because it is the basis for all virtues. It is called "basis for all virtues" because it is the ground of all beings. It is called "ground of all beings" because it is the refuge of all. It is called "refuge of all" because it is the protector of all. It is called "protector of all" because it is the savior of all. It is called "savior of all" because it is the deliverer of all. It is called "deliverer of all" because it is the liberator of all. It is called "liberator of all" because it is the path to enlightenment. It is called "path to enlightenment" because it leads to the realization of Buddhahood. It is called "realization of Buddhahood" because it is the perfection of all qualities. It is called "perfection of all qualities" because it is the fulfillment of all vows. It is called "fulfillment of all vows" because it is the completion of all practices. It is called "completion of all practices" because it is the culmination of all efforts. It is called "culmination of all efforts" because it is the attainment of the supreme state. It is called "attainment of the supreme state" because it is the ultimate fruit. It is called "ultimate fruit" because it is the end of the journey. It is called "end of the journey" because there is no further travel. It is called "no further travel" because all destinations have been reached. It is called "all destinations reached" because the mind is fully realized. It is called "mind fully realized" because it is the state of omniscience. It is called "state of omniscience" because it knows all things. It is called "knows all things" because it perceives all phenomena. It is called "perceives all phenomena" because it sees the nature of reality. It is called "sees the nature of reality" because it is the vision of the Buddhas. It is called "vision of the Buddhas" because it is the eye of wisdom. It is called "eye of wisdom" because it is the light of truth. It is called "light of truth" because it dispels all darkness. It is called "dispels all darkness" because it illuminates all worlds. It is called "illuminates all worlds" because it reveals the way of liberation. It is called "reveals the way of liberation" because it shows the path to peace. It is called "shows the path to peace" because it leads to the city of Nirvana. It is called "leads to the city of Nirvana" because it brings about the cessation of suffering. It is called "brings about the cessation of suffering" because it is the medicine for all ailments. It is called "medicine for all ailments" because it heals all wounds. It is called "heals all wounds" because it removes all pain. It is called "removes all pain" because it is the balm of compassion. It is called "balm of compassion" because it is the heart of the Buddhas. It is called "heart of the Buddhas" because it is the essence of love. It is called "essence of love" because it is the root of virtue. It is called "root of virtue" because it is the source of merit. It is called "source of merit" because it is the accumulation of goodness. It is called "accumulation of goodness" because it is the foundation of the path. It is called "foundation of the path" because it is the support for all beings. It is called "support for all beings" because it is the vessel of the Dharma. It is called "vessel of the Dharma" because it holds the teachings. It is called "holds the teachings" because it preserves the truth. It is called "preserves the truth" because it upholds the lineage of the Buddhas. It is called "upholds the lineage of the Buddhas" because it ensures the continuity of the Dharma. It is called "ensures the continuity of the Dharma" because it maintains the light of wisdom. It is called "maintains the light of wisdom" because it dispels the darkness of ignorance. It is called "dispels the darkness of ignorance" because it awakens the mind of sentient beings. It is called "awakens the mind of sentient beings" because it leads them to the shore of liberation. It is called "leads them to the shore of liberation" because it is the boat of the Dharma. It is called "boat of the Dharma" because it carries beings across the ocean of suffering. It is called "carries beings across the ocean of suffering" because it is the bridge to the city of peace. It is called "bridge to the city of peace" because it connects this world to the next. It is called "connects this world to the next" because it is the path of the Bodhisattvas. It is called "path of the Bodhisattvas" because it is the vehicle of great compassion. It is called "vehicle of great compassion" because it is the power of the Buddhas. It is called "power of the Buddhas" because it is the strength of the Dharma. It is called "strength of the Dharma" because it is the majesty of the Sangha. It is called "majesty of the Sangha" because it is the assembly of the noble ones. It is called "assembly of the noble ones" because it is the community of practitioners. It is called "community of practitioners" because it is the field of merit. It is called "field of merit" because it is the source of blessings. It is called "source of blessings" because it is the ground of cultivation. It is called "ground of cultivation" because it is the place of practice
It has the atom as its substance;
it is merely the analysis of those five sense organs and five sense objects.
The four great elements,
as the matter resulting from meditative concentration, reach the state of ultimate atoms; it is these very ultimate atoms [that constitute such matter].
This refers to the most subtle form-substance.
Second, "extremely remote form" refers to the six types of coarse forms, namely space, light, shadow, brightness, darkness, and so forth.
Now, by analyzing these six kinds of coarse matter down to the level of the ultimate atom (paramāṇu),
one apprehends this subtle matter.
It constitutes the essence of the color of extreme distance;
furthermore, it is that which is seen as the upper and lower spatial realms.
Blue, yellow, red, white, light, shadow, brightness, and darkness—
these are collectively termed the "single manifest color of space," as are those appearing within the openings of doors, windows, and crevices.
This is collectively termed "distant color" (prātibhāsika-rūpa).
Regarding "form derived from the three feelings" (vedanā-samudgata-rūpa):
as for "feeling" (vedanā)...
This has the meaning of "experiencing.
As for the "matter that is induced," it refers to the capacity to prevent or incite [actions] existing within the seeds and manifest states of volition (*cetanā*).
This is called "matter induced by names.
The meaning is that it is received through the instruction of a teacher.
That which has the capacity to prevent the arising of volition (cetanā) in both its latent seeds and its manifest state is called "derived matter" (nairmāṇika-rūpa).
Furthermore, because this very capacity to prevent the arising [of unwholesome states] cannot be manifested to others,
it is also called non-informative matter (avijñaptirūpa).
It takes non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) as its essence.
Fourth, pervasive conceptualization of matter refers to the pervasive conceptualization of the deluded mind.
The five types of matter resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) refer to the objects manifested within meditative absorption.
These constitute the five kinds of matter within the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
These are divided into three sections:
first, the section on images;
second, the section on non-informative matter (avijñapti).
The Section on the Fruits of the Three Concentrations.
Regarding the first, the Section on Images: as for "image" (chāyā), it refers to...
The meaning of "flowing type" (*jāti*) is that of a "likeness" (*pratibimba*),
which signifies similarity.
That is, the perceived aspect (nimittabhāga) which is transformed is of the same category as the original object and is similar to that original object.
Therefore, it is called a "reflected image.
Those that possess atoms are precisely the two types of matter: the extremely condensed (*saṃhata*) and the extremely remote (*dūre*).
This is merely an observation of the mind;
by analyzing the coarse into the subtle,
one provisionally establishes the "extreme atom" (paramāṇu).
There is only the observation of the mental image;
it has no substantial reality whatsoever.
As for the arising of solitary, distracted thoughts:
This refers specifically to the discerning mind within meditative concentration and the clearly manifest mental consciousness; here, however,
we take only the independent, obscure mental consciousness occurring in the state of non-concentration.
When this dispersed consciousness apprehends objects— such as the moon in water or reflections in a mirror— through the five sense organs and their five objects—
it gives rise to the imagined aspect of the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) through the transformation of the mind.
This is provisional and not real.
Together with the "extremely concise" [perception] and others,
they are established as a single gateway of images.
Question:
Furthermore, for example, the moon in water and the image in a mirror are also objects perceived by visual consciousness.
How can it be said that [this] is merely a conventional designation (prajñapti) perceived solely by the mental consciousness (manovijñāna)? Answer:
The moon in water and images in a mirror are solely the objects of phenomena;
they arise merely by taking water and mirrors as conditions.
The mental consciousness then falsely discriminates that there is a moon and an image;
these are not the objects of the visual consciousness,
and they are likewise subsumed under the category of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
Furthermore, pervasive conceptualization is the deluded mind,
while extreme brevity and so forth are the contemplative mind;
this is because both are equally false images.
Therefore, the second category, the gate of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), is established in general.
First, regarding the informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) of restraint (*saṃvara*):
This refers precisely to the time when one receives the precepts in the presence of a teacher;
it is by means of this informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) that the seeds of wholesome volition (*kuśala-cetanā-bīja*) are subsequently perfumed and acquired.
Because it possesses the capacity to prevent [unwholesome actions] from arising,
non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is established.
Second, regarding the informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
It is precisely at the moment when one applies the blade to kill and creates karma that this occurs;
it is by means of this manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) that the seeds of unwholesome volition (*akuśala-cetanā*) are subsequently perfumed.
Because it possesses the capacity to prevent and initiate [unwholesome action],
one establishes the existence of unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa). This applies even in cases where manifest form (vijñapti-rūpa) is present.
It is precisely at the time of performing prostrations to the Buddha and walking in meditation,
as well as when driving away, striking, or reviling others,
that there exists unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) arising from these actions.
Once the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome volitions have been perfumed,
they also possess the capacity to prevent [unwholesome states] from arising;
it is for this reason that non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is established.
Question:
If the moon in water and images in a mirror are objects of the conceptualizing mind of the sixth consciousness, [how can they be considered non-existent?]
These are merely conventional designations.
As for length, shortness, squareness, and roundness being subsumed under form (*rūpa*),
this is because the clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes the object-field of form as its condition.
How is it that the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is subsumed under the perception of imagined form?
Answer: If one is a wise person.
When one realizes that these aspects of seeing and form are merely provisional,
they are subsumed within the sphere of visible objects;
if the deluded do not understand this, [they remain bound].
The false attachment to [the object] as real gives rise to a reflected image;
this provisional *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) is subsumed solely within the category of *parikalpita-rūpa* (imagined form).
It is subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Question:
What is meant by the statement that the reflected image is an object of perception for two [senses]?
Answer: First, the relative is the reflected image.
"Coarse" refers to the primary object (*bimba*).
First, the reflected image (*pratibimba*) is explained.
Regarding the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
it refers to the fact that the various image-aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving seeing-aspects (*darśana-bhāga*) are inseparable in their essence.
That which is relied upon and supported by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is the object of deliberation;
that which is thus supported is termed the "condition" (*ālambana*).
That which is contemplated is called the "object" (ālambana).
These are the two meanings of this term.
This is called the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Furthermore, this image has four names:
first, "image" (pratibimba).
2. The aspectual division (nimitta-bhāga);
3. That which is internally relied upon as the object of thought;
4. The immediate condition as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Next, to explain the essential nature:
if it is separated from the substance of the cognitive subject,
it is a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*).
Because they are separated by their respective aspects,
the essential nature and the perceiving seeing-aspect are essentially distinct; therefore,
they are called "separated."
Question:
Since they are mutually separated,
how can they be called "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya)?
Answer: Because the substantial entity (dravya) is able to give rise to the appearance-aspect (nimittabhāga),
"arising" is predicated here with respect to the appearance-aspect.
Because it causes the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) to have something to contemplate,
and because the essential nature (svabhāva) arises as the object-conditioned (ālambana),
it is also called the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Because it serves as a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for that which is its immediate object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
it is also designated as an object-condition;
that is, because it gives rise to the object.
It also has three names:
first, "essence" (svabhāva);
second, "that which is externally relied upon as an object of cognition" (ālambana).
The third is the "object-condition as that which is sparsely perceived" (ālambana-pratyaya). This serves as the substantial essence capable of giving rise to the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga),
and the objective aspect gives rise to the subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga).

The seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) gives rise to the self-verifying-part (svasaṃvitti-bhāga); the self-verifying-part is able to give rise to the verifying-the-self-verifying-part (saṃvitti-saṃvitti-bhāga),
which serves as the objective basis for its arising.
Because it relies upon its own deliberations by entrusting itself to the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect),
the primary object (*mauladharmin*) is also called the "object-condition" (*ālambanapratyaya*).
Furthermore, as for the dharma-consciousness that is able to cognize all phenomena,
it is precisely the sixth mental consciousness.
There are five types in each case,
all of which take dharmas as their objective realm:
first, the independent manovijñāna within meditative concentration.
It takes the object of meditative concentration as its condition. Within that object of concentration,
there is both principle and phenomenon.

Among these entities, there are the forms included in the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) that are extremely subtle, extremely remote, or produced by the mastery of meditative concentration; secondly,
those occurring independently during the state of distraction,
which are projected by the impressions of feeling (*vedanā*).
And the form of the objective bases of all phenomena arising from conceptual construction,
which is like perceiving flowers in the sky,
rabbit horns, or reflections in a mirror.
Those produced by the conceptualization of water-moons are all subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Third are those occurring independently within dreams.

The four types of clearly manifesting mental consciousnesses take as their objects the dharmas of form that are the locus of pervasive conceptualization, which are based upon the objects experienced within dreams.
Relying on the gates of the five sense faculties,
it shares the same objects as the first five consciousnesses in perceiving the five sensory realms with clarity.
The first is called the clearly manifest mental consciousness;
the five are the distracted mental consciousnesses, which constitute the scattered mental consciousness.
It arises in a state of derangement within the five faculties,
yet it does not share the same objects as the five consciousnesses,
much like one suffering from a feverish illness.
To see blue as yellow is not the function of the visual consciousness; rather,
it is due to this [defiled] condition.
Taking the color-form of the thoroughly imagined nature as its object;
furthermore, if the clearly manifest mental consciousness [arises] at the gates of the five sense faculties.
Because they share the same objects as the five [sensory consciousnesses]— namely, the five sensory domains—
they should take the five consciousnesses as their co-existent supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*),
with the exception of those that arise independently (*mukha-pravṛtta*).
As for those that arise independently,
there are four types in total. First:
This refers to that which arises independently within meditative concentration, taking the object of concentration as its focal point,
and not sharing the same focal object as the five sensory consciousnesses.
Second, the independent [consciousness] within dreams,
which takes the objects of the dharma-realm as its conditions and perceives the various signs within dreams.
It is also that which arises from pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita).
Third, the independent [consciousness] in the state of distraction.
Constructing the appearance of an object,
these four distracted mental consciousnesses take as their objective support the form produced by pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
It may also be known as "independent" (*mukhyaka*).
Question:
With how many mental factors (*caitta*) are the six consciousnesses associated?
Answer: The verse of the treatise says:
These mental factors consist of the universal,
the object-specific, the wholesome, the afflictions,
the secondary afflictions, and the indeterminate.
All [of these] are associated with the three feelings.
These six evolving consciousnesses,
in their totality, are associated with the mental factors (caitta) of the six stages.
That is to say, the universal [mental factors] and so forth always arise based upon the mind and are associated with the mind.
They are called mental factors (caitta) because they are bound to the mind,
just as objects belong to a person.
Establishing the designation of "mine," the mind,
with respect to its object, apprehends only the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
The mental factors also apprehend distinct characteristics therein,
assisting in the accomplishment of the mind's activities.
It receives the name "mental concomitants" (caitta),
just as a master painter and his apprentice work together to create a model and fill it with colors.
The Yogācāra treatises state:
consciousness (*vijñāna*) is able to discern the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of an object,
while attention (*manasikāra*) discerns those characteristics not yet discerned by it.
That is to say, it is the specific characteristics apprehended by the various mental factors (*caitasika*).
Contact (*sparśa*) is able to cognize these characteristics, such as being agreeable;
feeling (*vedanā*) is able to cognize these characteristics, such as grasping (*parigraha*).
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is able to discern the characteristics of the causes for such verbal expression;
volition (*cetanā*) is able to discern the characteristics of the primary causes and so forth. Therefore, attention (*manasikāra*) and the others [are established].
This is called a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*).
This indicates that mental factors also take general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as their objects.
Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere:
Desire also comprehends the characteristics of things that are pleasurable;
resolute conviction likewise comprehends the characteristics of things that are certain.
Mindfulness can also discern the characteristics of habitual tendencies;
concentration and wisdom likewise discern characteristics such as gain and loss.
By means of these, one gives rise to wholesome, defiled, and other states with respect to objects.
All mental factors (caitta-dharma) apprehend both the general object and its specific characteristics.
Regarding the distinctions among these six stages:
That is to say, there are five universal [mental factors],
five object-specific ones,
and eleven wholesome ones.
There are six primary afflictions (*kleśa*),
twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),
and four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*).
Thus, these six stages comprise fifty-one [mental states] in total,
as they are invariably obtainable within all minds.
Because they arise with respect to distinct and specific objects;
because they can only arise within a wholesome state of mind;
and because their nature is subsumed under the root afflictions.
Because they are exclusively of the nature of afflictions and other defilements,
and because they are indeterminate with respect to both the wholesome and the defiled,
this applies even to these six evolving consciousnesses.
Because they are easily displaced and unstable,
all of them can be associated with the three types of feeling (*vedanā*).
This is because they all experience objects that are agreeable, disagreeable, or neither.
That which perceives the characteristics of favorable objects and brings gratification to body and mind is called pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
That which opposes the characteristics of the objective field and oppresses the body and mind is called the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhā vedanā*).
One perceives the characteristics of the intermediate sphere,
which is neither oppressive nor pleasant to the body and mind.
This is called the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
The commentary states:
"The above three lines are the verse."
The preceding line provides the general name for the six categories of mental factors;
the following line correctly explains the category of feeling (*vedanā*).
Regarding the mental aspect of activity:
the mind apprehends the general characteristics of an object;
it merely apprehends them in their generality.
There is no separate discrimination;
as when one says "perceiving blue," it merely takes blue in its entirety.
There is no further discrimination;
because the mental factors apprehend both general and specific characteristics therein,
the word "also" is used.
It is like a master painter and his apprentice working on a model and filling it with colors;
"master" refers to the teacher,
and "apprentice" refers to the disciple.
Just as when a master has finished drawing a form using a mold,
the disciple fills it with colors;
the colors are applied according to the mold.
Because it does not depart from the mold;
it is like taking up the general form when applying colors.
It causes the charming and beautiful to emerge;
likewise, it apprehends the specific characteristics of the mind and mental factors.
The apprehension of objects is likewise:
consciousness is able to discern the general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) of things,
but it is not said to apprehend their specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
Because it is the master; if one were to take its specific characteristics,
it would then be a mental factor (caitta).
A single mental attention (*manasikāra*) alone is capable of discerning numerous distinct characteristics;
for it is through mental attention that the power of the mind and its mental factors to apprehend objects becomes preeminent.
There is this general grasping of the specific characteristics of multiple phenomena.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"With attention as the primary factor..."
This treatise takes contact as the first [topic],
because its conjunction is preeminent; each [point] is established according to a specific meaning.
Contact can grasp three types:
namely, the agreeable,
the disagreeable, and the neutral.
Regarding the characteristic of being contrary to both:
within sensation (*vedanā*), there are those that are beneficial, harmful, or contrary to both, and so forth.
As for perception (*saṃjñā*), it is able to discern the characteristics that serve as the causes for verbal expression.
Because it can apprehend the specific characteristics of objects,
that is, by discerning that "this is blue" and "not non-blue," one subsequently gives rise to verbal expression.
Therefore, the characteristic of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is the cause for verbal expression;
it discerns the correct cause from the erroneous cause.
The "concordant and discordant" and so forth refer to the characteristics of correctness, incorrectness, and so on regarding the object;
these are the causes of karma.
That which can certainly be found within all minds is the universal [mental factor];
this holds regardless of what kind of mind it may be.
However, since that which arises must necessarily have a cause,
those other distinct objects by which [the mind] is produced are the five specific objects (pañca-viṣaya-viniyata).
It can only be obtained within a wholesome mind.
Regarding "because it arises":
this refers to the eleven wholesome dharmas.
Only the wholesome mind possesses [these roots];
their essence is fundamental and capable of producing all delusions,
namely the six beginning with greed.
Regarding those that are indeterminate with respect to both wholesome and defiled minds, these are the four indeterminate [mental factors];
that is, they occur in relation to the three natures of mind: wholesome, defiled, and neutral.
Because all are indeterminate.
Regarding the statement that these six evolving consciousnesses are easily detached and indeterminate:
indeed, these six consciousnesses...
They are not like the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses],
whose natures are all easily detached because they are constantly indeterminate.
"Easy to abandon" means that it is subject to interruption and transformation;
it is not fixed.
Because these practices of joy, sorrow, and equanimity arise alternately,
they all pertain to the three types of feeling.
Question:
What is the state in which the six consciousnesses manifest?
The answer is given in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā*:
Depending upon the fundamental consciousness,
the five consciousnesses manifest according to conditions;
they may arise together or not.
Just as waves depend upon water,
the mental consciousness constantly manifests,
except when one is born in the Heaven of Non-conceptualization.
And the two mindless attainments,
as well as sleep and fainting;
these are the fundamental consciousness.
The *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness) is so called because it is the fundamental source from which all defiled and pure consciousnesses arise;
thus, it is the "basis."
This refers to the aforementioned six evolving consciousnesses,
which take the fundamental consciousness as their common support.
As for the five [sensory] consciousnesses:
This refers to the first five evolving consciousnesses;
because they are similar in kind,
they are spoken of collectively.
The phrase "manifesting in accordance with conditions" indicates that it does not arise constantly.
"Conditions" refers to conditions such as mental attention (*manasikāra*), the sense faculties (*indriya*), and their objects (*viṣaya*).
This refers to the five groups of sensory consciousness. Internally dependent upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*),
and externally conditioned by the harmony of various factors such as mental attention (*manasikāra*), the five sense organs, and their respective objects.
Only then do they manifest before one.
Consequently, they may arise either simultaneously or not simultaneously.
Regarding the convergence of external conditions,
there is both suddenness and gradualness,
like waves upon water.
According to the conditions encountered,
the five evolving consciousnesses possess coarse and active modes of activity and depend upon a multitude of external conditions.
Because the conditions are frequently incomplete,
the moments of arising are few,
while the moments of non-arising are many.
Although the sixth consciousness is also coarse and active,
the conditions upon which it relies are never absent.
Due to adverse conditions,
they do not arise at times.
The modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are subtle.
Since the various conditions upon which it depends exist at all times,
there is no obstruction of conditions that could cause them all to cease functioning.
Furthermore, the five groups of consciousness are incapable of deliberation;
they operate solely toward external objects and arise depending upon many conditions.
Therefore, the period of cessation is long,
while the period of active manifestation is short;
the sixth consciousness is capable of independent reflection.
It functions through internal and external doors,
not depending on many conditions,
except for five specific stages.
Because it is constantly able to manifest,
the time of its cessation is brief while the time of its manifestation is long;
for this reason, it is not said that this [defilement] manifests according to conditions.
The commentary states:
"That which relies" refers to the six preceding evolving consciousnesses.
Regarding the fundamental consciousness as the common support:
these preceding six consciousnesses take the fundamental consciousness as their common support.
This refers precisely to the manifesting fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*),
because all consciousnesses share it as their basis.
As for the "direct support":
This refers to the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*), because each possesses its own distinct seeds.
As for the similarity in type among the first five evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*):
There are five [characteristics].
First, both rely upon the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
Second, they both take material objects as their objective conditions (*ālambana*).
The third [category] takes only the present as its object;
the fourth is obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
the fifth involves interruptions.
Because their types are similar,
they are explained collectively.
This is like waves on water, which vary in quantity according to conditions.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states:
"It is like a great torrential stream;
if the conditions for the arising of a single wave are present,"
There is only the turning of a single wave,
until the conditions for the arising of many waves manifest before one.
There are many surging waves;
the various consciousnesses are likewise,
like the flow of a torrential stream.
"By depending on the ādāna-vijñāna,
up to the point where the various consciousnesses undergo transformation," etc.;
this refers to the five sensory consciousnesses.
The waves are a metaphor for the fundamental consciousness; the torrential stream is a metaphor for the ālayavijñāna.
The five groups of consciousness cannot engage in deliberation,
because they lack vitarka and vicāra.
It cannot arise by itself;
it depends on being induced by another,
namely, the sixth consciousness.
It is capable of independent reflection and operates through both the internal and external doors,
with the sole exception of the Heaven of Non-conceptualization.
The attainment of non-perception,
the attainment of cessation, and sleep.
Because the five stages, such as fainting and so forth,
can constantly manifest;
furthermore, the ancient commentary states:
First, it is like many waves:
based upon a single great ocean, many waves arise.
Second, it is like a reflected image.
Relying on a single large mirror, many images arise;
these two factors— the sea and the mirror—
serve as metaphors for the fundamental mind-consciousness.
The surging waves are a metaphor for the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Within a single thought-moment—
There are four types of karma:
first, the karma that differentiates the vessel-world;
second, the karma that differentiates the basis.
Third is the discernment of the self;
fourth is the discernment of objects.
These are the various forms of discernment.
They are observed to arise simultaneously at every moment;
therefore, within a single consciousness,
in a single instant, [multiple factors coexist].
There are such distinctions in the functions of karma.
As a verse in the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says:
"Like a flash of lightning or drifting clouds..."
All are false and not real;
they are like pots crafted by a craftsman,
produced through conceptual construction.
O Benevolent Lord, you should listen attentively:
all sentient beings in the world have their minds constantly shrouded by habitual tendencies.
Various conceptual proliferations arise;
the manas and the mental consciousness,
together with all the other consciousnesses, continue in succession.
The five dharmas and the three natures,
along with the two kinds of selflessness,
are always in constant association.
Just as wind strikes a torrential waterfall,
causing the waves of the various consciousnesses to arise;
once these waves are born, their flow never ceases.
The ālayavijñāna is likewise:
the various habitual tendencies from beginningless time are like that torrential stream.
Stirred by the winds of objects,
the waves of various consciousnesses arise,
never ceasing for even a moment.
The eight kinds of flowing minds,
though lacking multiple distinct entities,
may arise instantaneously according to conditions.
Sometimes they arise gradually;
the apprehension of objects is likewise.
There is a distinction between the gradual and the instantaneous.
The mind revolves within dwellings,
the sun, moon, and stars, and the branches,
leaves, flowers, and fruits of trees.
In mountain forests, among military hosts,
and in such places as these,
they are all able to arise both gradually and instantaneously.
It often causes [the object] to appear suddenly,
or to arise gradually with distinctions;
this occurs when, within a dream, [it manifests].
One perceives the objects previously experienced,
from the initial arising of conceptualization up to old age and death.
Calculating numbers and various objects,
investigating the meaning of phrases,
and contemplating diverse literary expressions.
Experiencing various excellent foods and drinks,
one gradually comes to understand such objects of perception.
Or at times they arise all at once;
yet that which can apprehend them is the nature of the mind, which is fundamentally pure.
It is inconceivable;
it is the wondrous treasury of the Tathāgata,
like gold existing within ore.
The mind-born arises from the storehouse consciousness;
the same applies to the other six.
Consciousness is of six kinds or more.
The distinctions within the three realms consist of the ālayavijñāna, the perfuming agents,
and other mental factors and phenomena.
Although the various seeds of defilement and purity coexist without being defiled,
the Buddha-lineage is likewise so.
Concentration is neither fixed nor eternally pure;
it is like the ocean water which remains constant,
while the waves shift and flow.
The ālayavijñāna is likewise;
according to the distinctions of the stages (bhūmi),
its cultivation is categorized as inferior, middling, or superior.
Abandoning defilement, it becomes manifest.
As explained extensively above, the mental faculty (manas) perceives objects and performs discrimination.
Among all consciousnesses, the mind is the most powerful;
thus, all that is good and evil is preceded by the mind as its guide.
The mind arises with great swiftness;
the mind precedes speech.
When the mind is wholesome, the Dharma is correct.
If the mind is evil, then the environment is perverse;
it is like a single breath:
if one inhales it, it is warm.
If blown upon, it immediately becomes cold,
appearing like water;
if chilled, it immediately solidifies.
If warmed, it immediately melts;
how much more so when unified by the single mind?
If left to run wild, it becomes ordinary.
To expand upon this is itself the sacred;
though the transformations differ,
the true nature remains without deficiency.
As stated in the Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra:
"The mind precedes all phenomena;
the mind is supreme, and from the mind they arise."
If one speaks or acts with a mind of pure faith toward the Dharma,
happiness will follow of its own accord.
Just as a shadow follows a form,
I spoke this verse for the sake of those of the Śrāvaka vehicle;
my intention was as follows:
This refers to the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
If the mind is intrinsically pure,
that mind is the *tathāgatagarbha*.
It surpasses all phenomena.
All phenomena are produced by the Tathāgatagarbha,
as well as the dharma of the mind of pure faith.
Because all afflictions have been severed,
and because the realm of the self has been perceived,
one possesses pure faith that there is a *tathāgatagarbha* within oneself.
Thereafter, whatever one speaks or does will be such that,
upon attaining Buddhahood,
one will likewise speak and act accordingly.
Delivering all the worlds,
one sees the Tathāgatagarbha as a person sees a reflection.
It is also like this. Therefore it is said that they follow one another like a shadow;
mental phenomena (dharma) precede the mind.
The mind is supreme; from the mind arises all that is mental.
It is the mind that makes deeds either good or evil, whether one speaks or acts.
Various sufferings pursue one from within,
like a wheel following its tracks.
This verse explains the meaning of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Those whose minds and mental objects are evil are shrouded by immeasurable afflictions and commit various misdeeds.
Therefore, it is called "evil.
The naturally pure *tathāgatagarbha* enters into the state of immeasurable afflictions.
Thus, because of this restless and turbid state that does not cease,
whether one speaks or acts.
All manner of sufferings constantly follow without ceasing,
like a wheel following its tracks;
thus do all evils accumulate.
The cycle of birth and death revolves;
all sentient beings [suffer] within the three evil realms.
Just as a wheel follows its tracks,
it is for this reason that it is said: those who are slow in accumulating merit find their minds delighting in unwholesome dharmas.
The commentary states:
In a single moment of mental purity,
one perceives the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Able to deliver oneself and others,
one experiences the bliss of nirvana,
following the body like a shadow.
If for a single thought-moment the mind is evil,
one enters the net of worldly toil and falls into the various realms of existence.
They undergo the suffering of birth and death like a wheel following its tracks;
this is illustrated by the analogy of a shadow following its form.
This is because it is never separated from them.
As for the analogy of the wheel’s tracks,
it is because they revolve with great speed.
Therefore, good and evil follow the mind without ever ceasing.
If one perceives this clearly, [one will understand].
Liberation occurs right where one is.
Thus, the Mahāyāna-nyāya-prakāśa-sūtra states:
"For this reason, the bodhisattva contemplates the five hindrances."
From what cause does it arise?
How is it to be abandoned?
A bodhisattva should first contemplate these matters.
Sensual desire is like the moon reflected in water;
as the water moves, the moon moves.
When the mind arises, phenomena arise;
it is the same with the mind of craving and desire.
Moment by moment they do not abide;
they arise swiftly and perish swiftly.
The *Mahāyāna-mūla-jātaka-citta-bhūmi-darśana-sūtra* says:
A pure mind serves as the root of wholesome karma; an unwholesome mind [serves as the root of unwholesome karma].
It is the root of evil karma;
because the mind is pure, the world is pure.
Because the mind is defiled,
the world is defiled.
Within my Buddha-dharma...
The mind is sovereign.
Among all phenomena, there is nothing that does not arise from the mind.
For this reason, it is as when Jyotiṣka was born amidst a raging fire,
yet the fire could not harm him.
The Buddha said:
"This is the karmic retribution of this child;
it was not created by me.
Therefore, one knows that it is produced by one's own mind."
If one does not shift from relying on the power of others,
then the path between ascent and descent is not far off;
the retribution of black and white karma is thus certain.
Although the retributions for good and evil differ,
they all manifest from the mirror of the deluded mind.
As a verse in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
Just as an image in a mirror,
though seen, does not exist, so too is the mind seen through the mirror of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Ordinary beings speak of duality;
not knowing that it is but mind-only, they perceive it thus.
Therefore, they discriminate between two.
When one knows the mind as it truly is,
conceptual discrimination does not arise; therefore,
know that this is the true consciousness of the mind.
Just as one sees the reflection of one's own face in a mirror and never again gives rise to false grasping toward external objects, so too,
once the bondage of signs is understood, [one is liberated].
The ocean of karma is entirely dried up.
As stated in the *Kṣema-kalpa-samādhi-sūtra*:
"It extinguishes and eliminates all existing karmas."
To perceive the fundamental nature of the faculties of all sentient beings is called wisdom.
Question:
Regarding the five states in which mental consciousness does not arise:
what are the characteristics of these five states that cause mental consciousness to not arise?
Answer: The *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* states:
"As for the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*):"
That is to say, by cultivating that meditative concentration and through the power of aversion toward coarse perceptions,
one is born among those devas.
Contrary to the constantly active mind and mental factors,
it is characterized by the cessation of perception as its primary feature; thus it is called the Heaven of No-Perception (asaṃjñisattva).
And the two meditative attainments without mind refer to the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation.
Because both lack the six consciousnesses,
it is called "mindless.
As for the attainment of non-conception:
This refers to an ordinary person who has suppressed the craving for the Subhakṛtsna realm but has not yet suppressed the defilements of the higher realms,
and who takes the mental attention of the perception of renunciation as a precursor.
It causes the cessation of those mental states and mental factors that do not function constantly;
because the cessation of perception is primary,
it is designated by the name "non-perception."
Because it causes the body to be peaceful and harmonious,
it is also called "concentration" (samādhi).
As for the "attainment of cessation" (nirodhasamāpatti):
That is to say, there are those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa), or noble ones still in training (śaikṣa),
who have already subdued the afflictions and are free from craving for the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
The higher [attainments] are not fixed as to their objects of craving. By taking the mental attention to the perception of cessation as a precursor,
they cause the cessation of the non-perpetually active and perpetually active defiled minds and mental factors.
It is given the name "cessation" because it causes the mind to become tranquil and harmonious;
for this reason, it is also called "concentration."
Regarding those who are mindless in sleep or in a state of fainting:
this refers to cases where there is such profound sleep or fainting that the first six consciousnesses no longer manifest.

Among these five stages, there are four types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), excluding those in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). As for the noble ones (*ārya*): [they are present in all].
Only the latter three;
among these, only the Tathāgata and the sovereign Bodhisattva possess one.
Because there is no drowsiness or distress.
The commentary explains:
"Those in the Heaven of No-Thought who have grown weary of the power of coarse perception."
This means that the various non-Buddhists take perception (*saṃjñā*) to be the cause of birth and death,
and thus they exclusively cultivate revulsion toward it.
Only the perceptions of the first six consciousnesses are [intentional];
they are not those of the seventh or eighth.
Therefore, it is called "coarse perception."
Because subtle conceptualization still persists,
the six consciousnesses are extinguished;
the seventh and eighth are subtle.
Because they cannot know it,
it is not extinguished. As for those who suppress the craving of the Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna) realm through the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti):
This means that it does not exist in the third dhyāna;
from the fourth dhyāna upward,
greed has not yet been subdued.
This reveals the state of being free from desire.
As for the "perception of renunciation," it reveals that the perception itself constitutes the perception of nirvāṇa.
"Those that cease when not constantly active" indicates the number of consciousnesses that are ceased.
"One enters meditative absorption by suppressing defilements through attention" [indicates the method of entry].
One should contemplate [the body] as a disease, as an abscess,
and as an arrow; thus, one should dwell in aversion toward whatever various perceptions arise.
"Only" means that the state of non-perception is tranquil and sublime;
within this state of non-perception,
one maintains the mind and abides therein.
In this way, by gradually departing from all objects of perception,
the mind becomes tranquil and ceases;
this is the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
Regarding the phrase "those who possess the state of no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa*) and so forth: this refers to noble ones (*ārya*) on the path of learning (*śaikṣa*),
excluding those who have attained the first two fruits.
The body-witness non-returner is among those in training who have attained the third fruit.
Because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are excluded;
because they are free from craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); and because craving for the higher [realms] does not obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is because the attainment of cessation arises solely based on the sphere of nothingness.
This statement regarding "separation" refers to those who first cultivate the two vehicles;
for Bodhisattvas, they subdue but do not separate from craving.
This is also called the "attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception.
Among these five states, ordinary beings possess four,
excluding the attainment of cessation.
The Noble Ones possess only the latter three [attainments].
Only the Buddha and Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (bhūmi) onward possess only one type of extinction attainment (nirodha-samāpatti).
There are no two states of sleep and fainting,
because due to unwholesome dharmas,
they merely appear as if there were sleep.
Because they do not truly exist,
even those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) of the two vehicles may likewise fall into a state of fainting or stupor.
Question:
Regarding the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñisamāpatti).
Both are termed "mindless.
What is the distinction between these two meditative attainments? Answer:
There are four points of difference.
An ancient commentary states:
first, they differ with respect to the persons who attain them.
The attainment of cessation is acquired by noble ones;
the state of non-conception is acquired by ordinary persons.
These two differ in their respective aspirations.
One who enters the attainment of cessation does so by forming the perception of perfect tranquility and seeking its merits; [this is distinct from] the attainment of non-perception.
It constitutes an entry into liberation.
Thirdly, there is the distinction between those that induce results and those that do not;
the attainment of non-conception is contaminated (*sāsrava*).
It can induce the specific retributive fruit of the Heaven of Non-conception;
the meditative attainment of cessation is untainted (anāsrava) and does not induce fruits within the three realms.
Fourth, there is a difference in the extent to which consciousness is ceased. In the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), consciousness is ceased to a greater degree,
as it also ceases the defiled portion of the seventh manas.
In the attainment of non-conceptualization, consciousness is diminished; in the attainment of cessation, the first six consciousnesses are extinguished.
Question:
For instance, in states such as the attainment of cessation where there is no mind, [how does this occur]?
Since they are without mind,
why do they not transcend the three realms? Answer:
As for "mindlessness," it refers to merely suppressing the coarse minds of the preceding six consciousnesses;
this is also termed "mindlessness."
The seventh and eighth consciousnesses still remain;
it is not that the mind is entirely absent.
As the *Siddhiviniścaya-śāstra* states:
The mind is of two kinds. First is the mind that accumulates and gives rise [to phenomena],
which contains immeasurable seeds.
Because it is the locus of accumulation,
there are two kinds of mind: the mind as object and the mind as aspect.
Because they function differently,
[these factors] are absent in states such as the meditative attainment of cessation.
The second mind is called "mindless," like a horse with only one leg.
Because one foot is missing,
it is also called "footless.
Question:
The five faculties and the four great elements constitute all internal and external phenomena.
Which phenomenon possesses the "great"?
Which dharmas possess seeds?
The answer is:
the ancient commentators analyzed this by means of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
First is that which is great but not a seed-element;
this is space (*ākāśa*),
which is all-pervasive.
Therefore, it is great;
because it is not born,
it is not a seed.
Second, there are seeds that are not great,
namely the five sense faculties and so forth,
which are productive.
Therefore it is called a "seed.
Because it is not pervasive,
it is not a "great" element.
The third [category] is both seeds and great;
that is, earth, water, and so forth,
whose substance is vast and extensive.
It is called "Great" (mahat) because it is so designated; it is called "seed" (bīja) because it serves as the basis for derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
The fourth is neither great nor a lineage;
this refers to the śrāvakas who seek tranquility.
Question:
The six sense faculties are divided into seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing.
In total, how many such capacities do they possess? Answer: [They possess all six.]
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): first, direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*);
second, inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*).
Third, the authority of scripture (*āptāgama*).
The treatise states:
"The three authorities establish the six sense faculties."
Based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the eye faculty and its associated mental states and mental factors are called "seeing" (*darśana*).
Based on the other five faculties, such as the ear, the associated mental states and mental factors are called "knowing" (*jñāna*).
Based on inference (*anumāna*), the associated mental states and mental factors are called "cognizing" (*buddhi*).
Based on the authority of the ultimate teaching (*āptāgama*), the mind and mental factors are called "hearing" (*śruta*).
Furthermore, it is said:
"That which is seen or known is verbal expression."
This is based on direct perception (pratyakṣa);
if one conceptualizes through verbal expression,
this is based on inference (anumāna).
If one hears such an exposition,
one should interpret it according to the authority of the ultimate teaching (āptāgama).
Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) refers to the direct realization of an object as it appears before one;
that which clearly and distinctly realizes [the object] is called valid cognition.
The eye, mind, and mental factors are called "seeing.
When the five faculties, such as the ear, along with their associated minds and mental factors,
cognize their respective objects through direct perception (*pramāṇa*), [they constitute seeing].
Collectively, these are termed "cognition.
The mental faculty (*manas*), the mind (*citta*), and its associated mental factors (*caitta*) discern objects through inference (*anumāna*); this is termed "discernment" (*buddhi*).
It is like seeing a horn through a wall and,
by means of inference, knowing it is an ox;
this is the process of inferential investigation.
It resides solely in the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
Based on authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) are termed "hearing" (*śruta*);
that is, the verbal instruction of the Noble Ones (*ārya*).
It is called "the authority of the ultimate teaching" (āptāgama-pramāṇa),
also known as "the authority of the noble verbal instruction. This is a term used in the Western Land [of India] to distinguish specific categories of dharma.
One must possess these three measures.
Question: Regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Among the six sense faculties, which one is primary?
Answer: The mind is primary.
Because the four great elements and so forth lack intrinsic nature,
they have no power or function independently;
they exist only through the mind.
Therefore, they are called "lords.
The *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching* says:
"As for these five faculties..."
The mind is its sovereign.
This clarifies the beginning of the entrustment to the womb;
the mind stands at the forefront of all the sense faculties.
It is designated as the "master.
However, although it serves as the master for the duration of a single lifetime,
it is nonetheless not fixed.
The Tiantai teachings clarify that the mind cannot control the various sense faculties;
the mind serves as the general gateway for receiving [sensory data].
If the body is ill, the mind also becomes ill;
how then can it be considered the master?
At times, the proponent and the opponent may argue with one another:
for instance, earth possesses the four subtle elements and is thus dull,
being constrained by water.
Water consists of three atoms and is thus constrained by fire; fire,
however, consists of only two atoms.
It is constrained by wind;
wind has a single atom,
which is in turn constrained by the mind.
Because the mind has no substance,
it attains mastery;
yet it is further afflicted by the four great elements.
Since no doctrine is established,
there is no primary subject.
Furthermore, if the four great elements each maintained their own nature, [the body could not exist].
Earth, maintaining its nature of solidity, should not move;
water, maintaining its nature of moisture, should not ripple;
fire, maintaining its nature of heat, should not flame.
The wind element, being mobile by nature, should not be maintained;
because its original nature is lost, it is unreal.
Because it is unreal, it is empty.
The *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-samantamukha-parivarta* states:
"Earth has no nature of solidity."
The nature of water does not abide;
fire arises from conditions;
the nature of wind is unimpeded.
Each and every one enters the limit of reality as it is.
Furthermore, the mind is not fixed;
good and evil contend with one another, and the karma that has reached maturity exerts its pull.
The *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* states:
"Citta, manas, and vijñāna are different names for a single dharma."
That which is reckoned is called "mind" (citta);
that which is capable of producing [thought] is called "intellect" (manas); and that which discriminates is called "consciousness" (vijñāna).
Furthermore, that which arises first is called mind (*citta*);
that which arises next is called intellect (*manas*); and that which subsequently cognizes is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Or, although the mind in this life may practice virtue,
if the maturation of evil karma from previous lives has already reached its time, it will manifest.
They immediately receive their evil retribution;
thus, they are dragged away by the maturation of their karma.
Or, even if one has lived a life where the mind occasionally performed evil deeds.
At the time of death, when the wholesome mind is intense and powerful,
one immediately ascends in accordance with that goodness;
thus, one is drawn away by the force of this potent karma.
Because one knows that there is not a single dharma in the world that possesses a fixed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
but rather all things evolve according to conditions,
being ungraspable from moment to moment.
One must not dogmatically adhere to a single gate and thereby give rise to grasping or rejection;
for each and every phenomenon is devoid of intrinsic essence or function.
Being without self-mastery,
and being ungraspable in every moment,
one then enters entirely into the limit of reality as it is.
Within the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
both name and referent cease;
it is like the four eyes merging into the Buddha-eye.
The ten knowledges enter into true wisdom,
and all names and designations are lost,
like an object cast into honey.
Like rivers converging into the sea,
every distinct flavor becomes neither sweet nor salty.
Just as the myriad dharmas return to the Mirror of the Source and together follow the One Path.
Question:
The designation of the six consciousnesses is established according to their respective objects;
this is explained based on the state where the five material sense-faculties have not yet attained mastery.
In the state of mastery, however, [the situation is otherwise].
How are they distinguished? Answer:
If within the state of sovereignty.
Then the various faculties function interchangeably,
as clarified in the Lotus Sūtra:
the faculty of the nose is able to see forms.
Regarding "contemplating the mind" and so forth,
the treatise states:
"If one attains mastery..."
The various faculties function interchangeably;
from a single faculty, consciousness arises,
perceiving all objects.
One may simply follow the faculties [of the practitioners],
so as to avoid the error of confusion;
this is even stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*.
The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done discerns the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings and initiates transformations through the three types of action.
Regarding the four types of categorical answers and so forth:
if [the mind] did not take all things as its object,
it would lack this capacity.
The commentary states:
There are ten types in total regarding the transformation of the three karmas.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that there are three types of bodily emanation (*kāya-nirmāṇa*): first,
the emanation that manifests supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Second is the transformation manifesting as birth;
third is the transformation manifesting as the fruit of karma.
There are likewise three types of verbal transformation.
First, transformation through words of consolation;
second, transformation through words of skillful means;
third, transformation through words of eloquence.
There are four types of mental transformation:
first, mental transformation through discernment;
second, mental transformation through volitional activity.
Third is transformation through the arousal of intention;
fourth is transformation through the acceptance of intention.
Regarding the four types of responses within transformation through acceptance:
First is the categorical response;
second is the analytical response;
third is the response by counter-question.
Fourth is the "record by remaining silent.
The above are the characteristics of the six consciousnesses,
which collectively constitute the gateway of the three karmas.
Within the state prior to the transformation of the basis,
one follows the flow and pursues objects,
thereby generating the seeds of affliction.
They bind the roots of birth and death;
they give rise only to the hindrances and entanglements, and merely entwine the suffering and its accumulation.
Turning one's back on the pure nature of awakening,
one unites with the delusive objects of the sense bases and elements,
thereby erecting the walls of the three realms of existence.
It creates the waves of the four currents; upon reaching the stage of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
it merges with reality and returns the flow.
It proceeds in accordance with wisdom,
constitutes untainted goodness,
and is subsumed within the Truth of the Path.
In accord with right principle,
he manifests the mind of wondrous observation and decisively cuts through the web of doubts regarding the four modes of birth.
It constitutes the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done,
arising as the source of the transformative manifestations of the three wheels;
if one investigates this within the mind, [one realizes its true nature].
The afflictions are the wondrous function of bodhi;
yet, missing the essential meaning,
one constantly delights in creating the painful wheel of birth and death.
Therefore, know that defilement and purity do not come from another;
gain and loss depend on oneself,
like the turning over of one's own hand.
It is like a person waking from intoxication. Why?
Because even the opposite is still the hand.
Covering is also a form of hand-gesture;
however, it occurs at the time of turning over, not at the time of covering,
and at the time of covering, not at the time of turning over.
Yet in both cases, they do not leave the hand.
One who is intoxicated is also a human being;
one who is sober is also a human being.
Essentially, the time of intoxication is not the time of sobriety,
and the time of sobriety is not the time of intoxication;
yet, there is no sobriety apart from intoxication.
Nor is being intoxicated itself awakening.
Just as delusion is the mind,
so too is awakening the mind.
Essentially, the time of delusion is not the time of awakening,
and the time of awakening is not the time of delusion;
yet, delusion and awakening are not distinct.
At that time, there is a difference in the seasons;
it exists solely within the Prajñāpāramitā,
transforming according to the occasion.
The single essence does not shift;
yet the myriad differences naturally diverge.
To be deluded by this is to suffer pointlessly in the depths of samsara.
In every thought-moment one becomes an ordinary person;
yet awakening is fundamentally perfect and luminous.
In every mind one realizes sainthood.
Question:
All phenomena arise dependent upon conditions.
Question: Among the eight consciousnesses, how many conditions does each possess for its establishment? Answer:
The eye possesses nine conditions.
First is the condition of space (*ākāśa-pratyaya*),
which means that there is no obstruction from objects before it due to its empty and vacuous nature.
This means it is unobstructed,
because it induces and gives rise to the consciousness that takes it as its object;
furthermore, it is because there is cognition of what is separated [from the senses].
Second, the clarification of the objective condition (*ālambana*). "Clarification" refers to luminosity,
because it is free from the characteristic of darkness.
It is clearly manifest,
for it opens up and guides the cognizing consciousness. Three.
The condition of the faculty (indriya-pratyaya) refers to its having its own eye-faculty as its support. The condition of the object (viṣaya-pratyaya) refers to the four [types of] objects.
Because they serve as the objects of the cognizing consciousness,
and because they draw forth and induce that cognizing consciousness,
there are five types of attention as objects.
It is called "arousing the mind" because it is capable of generating [the mind] within the state of the seeds of the mind.
The faculty of mind causes [the object] to arise and manifest;
in its state of active engagement,
it leads the mind toward the object.
The six fundamental conditions refer to the eighth consciousness and its relationship with the visual consciousness and the other sensory consciousnesses.
Because it serves as the root and fundamental basis,
and because it acts as the support for the preceding seven consciousnesses, it is the condition for the seven types of defiled and pure states.
This refers to the seventh consciousness;
because it serves as the basis for both defilement and purification for all six preceding [consciousnesses],
the eighth is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This refers to the sixth consciousness,
because it clearly discerns and distinguishes preceding objects.
It is the ninth seed-condition.
This refers to the seeds of visual consciousness;
because they are capable of producing the manifest [consciousness],
they are also called the "proximate conditions that directly accomplish their own results."
The actual manifestation of one's own consciousness, established and brought forth by its conditions,
is called its own fruit.
This is the case when the auditory consciousness takes a direct sound as its object.
It possesses only the previous eight conditions,
excluding the condition of light;
this applies even in the dark.
Because they can also be heard.
When the three consciousnesses of the nose, tongue, and body take fragrance, flavor, and tangibles as their objects, [they likewise arise].
There are only seven conditions;
the two conditions of space and light mentioned previously are excluded,
because these three pertain to cognition within conjunction.
It does not depend on the condition of emptiness.
When the sixth consciousness conditions all objects,
it possesses only five conditions.
First, the root; second, the object-condition of the roots;
third, attention.
The four seeds and the five objective conditions,
excluding space.
Elucidating the four conditions for discernment, defilement, and purification.
Furthermore, among the four types [of mental activity], the sixth consciousness may be either concentrated,
dreaming, or solitary and distracted.
These three possess five conditions.
If it is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
it follows the preceding five consciousnesses.
Or seven, eight, nine, and so forth,
depending on the number of conditions present.
This applies when the seventh consciousness is in its impure (sāsrava) state.
When taking the eighth factor, the view-division, as the self,
there are only three conditions:
first, the fundamental condition.
Namely, the eighth consciousness;
second, attention;
and third, seeds.
When the eighth consciousness takes seeds, the body with its sense organs, and the receptacle world as its objects,
it possesses only four conditions: first,
the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
That is, the three aforementioned objects are the conditions for the two faculties;
that is, the seventh consciousness.
The three seeds,
the four mental attentions,
and if one adds the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya).
Upon each of the aforementioned eight consciousnesses,
one further condition is added; thus,
the eye-consciousness, for example, possesses ten conditions.
Question:
Do the eight consciousnesses collectively exist within the three realms?
Answer: [They do.]
Incomplete. An ancient commentary states:
Regarding the presence or absence of the eight consciousnesses within the three realms and nine stages:
In the single stage of the desire realm,
there are eight types of consciousness.
In the first dhyāna of the form realm, there is one stage.
There are only six consciousnesses;
the two consciousnesses of the nose and tongue are absent from the second dhyāna upward.
Up to and including the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
there are only the latter three consciousnesses;
the first five consciousnesses do not exist.
The four destinies of the desire realm— humans, devas, pretas, and animals—
all possess the eight consciousnesses.
Within the destiny of the hells specifically:
In the Avīci Hell, there are no first five consciousnesses;
there are only the latter three consciousnesses,
or perhaps even the sixth is absent.
Because one has already entered a state of extreme heavy delusion.
Question:
How are the various consciousnesses universally conceptualized as existing or non-existing?
Answer: An ancient master said,
"The five [sensory] consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness are without grasping."
Because it changes due to causes and conditions,
it is solely direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Now, as for those who hold [to this]:
There is the position that there must be forced conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) and so forth;
for it is held that only the sixth and seventh consciousnesses possess pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa-vikalpa*).
That is to say, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses possess grasping (*sagraha*).
Furthermore, there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): first.
It is pervasive yet non-conceptual;
it is the sixth, independent manovijñāna (mental consciousness),
which universally takes all things as its object.
Because it does not involve conceptual grasping.
Second, that which conceives but is not pervasive refers to the seventh consciousness.
Because it arises by taking only the ālayavijñāna as its object and engaging in conceptual construction,
the third [consciousness] is both pervasive and conceptualizing.
As for the sixth consciousness, during the causal stage...
There are those that are pervasive and conceptualizing;
four are neither conceptualizing nor pervasive;
that is, the five consciousnesses take only [their respective objects] as their conditions.
Regarding the five sensory objects:
because they lack discursive calculation,
the first five consciousnesses spontaneously realize their objects.
It is not associated with names and conventions,
because it is purely direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The eighth [consciousness] is likewise.
