Externally.
It refers to that which exists externally to each individual body,
serves as the basis for the five objects such as form, is comprised of warmth and heat,
and is of a non-appropriated nature.
Furthermore, there is a superior accumulation,
namely: setting villages or cities ablaze,
or drilling wood and striking stone.
Seeking it in various ways,
one finds that this external essence of fire is subject to transformation and decay as it is consumed.
Their function is to counteract and nourish.
There are four winds,
which are also of two kinds.
First, the internal;
second, the external; third, the internal.
This refers to the five sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth,
belonging to each individual body, as well as their respective bases of support,
which are comprised within the category of lightness and mobility.
It possesses the nature of being appropriated,
and there is further superior accumulation,
namely, moving upward, downward, and horizontally.
The inhalation and exhalation of breath and so forth constitute the substance of internal wind;
its function is the activity of movement and the experience of sensory objects.
"External" refers to that which exists outside of each individual body,
serving as the basis for the five objects of the senses, such as visible form and so forth.
It is comprised of lightness and mobility;
it is non-appropriated in nature;
furthermore, there is superior accumulation.
That is to say, they shatter mountain cliffs and uproot forests; once these have been dispersed and destroyed,
[the beings are likewise cast down].
It is tranquil because it is without support.
If one seeks wind, one moves one's garment or shakes a fan.
It is unwavering; because there are no conditions, it ceases.
Such are these [teachings].
This is the external nature of wind;
its functions are to serve as a support,
to be experienced, to act as an antidote, and to provide nourishment.
The five eyes are that which are sustained by the ālayavijñāna containing all seeds;
they take as their objective domain the matter derived from the four great elements.
It is the support for consciousness that takes form as its object;
it has pure matter (*rūpa*) as its essence and is subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The nature of being non-visible and possessing resistance;
the sixth is the ear;
the seventh is the nose.
The same applies to the eight tongues and the nine bodies.
The distinction here is that each functions with respect to its own object and serves as the basis for the cognition of its own object.
The ten material [bases].
That is to say, the objective domain of the eye and the focal object of visual consciousness.
It is derived from the four great elements,
is subsumed within the aggregate of form,
and possesses the nature of being visible and resistant.
The eleventh is sound.
It refers to the objective domain of the ear and the focal object of auditory consciousness.
It is derived from the four great elements,
has audible sound as its essence,
and is subsumed within the aggregate of form.
It is non-visible and possesses resistance.
There are twelve types of odors,
which are the objects of the nose's range.
The object of olfactory consciousness consists of odorous substances produced by the four great elements as its essence.
It is included within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha);
it is invisible and possesses resistance;
there are thirteen tastes.
It refers to the objective sphere traversed by the tongue and the focal object of tongue-consciousness;
it is derived from the four great elements.
It has the nature of being tasted as its substance;
it is comprised within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and possesses the quality of being invisible yet obstructive (anidarśana-sapratigha).
The fourteen types of tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*).
These are the objective sphere traversed by the body and the focal object of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
It is composed of the four great elements;
its essence consists of tangible objects;
it is subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
It is non-visible and possesses resistance.
It consists of fifteen types of matter included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
which at all times constitute the objective domain of the mind.
It is subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and possesses the nature of being invisible and non-obstructive.
Furthermore, according to the *Śatadharma-vidyāmukha-śāstra*, there are eleven types of form.
These are the so-called five faculties and six objects.
Regarding the five faculties,
the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
It has derived matter as its substance;
there is one primary creator,
namely the four great elements.
Earth, water, fire, and wind;
the two derived [elements] are the four subtle particles (tanmātra).
Visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
Regarding the six objects:
first, visible form.
There are thirty-one [types].
Regarding visible color (*varṇa*), there are thirteen:

first, blue; second, yellow; third, red; fourth, white; fifth, light; sixth, shadow; seventh, radiance; eighth, darkness; ninth, cloud; tenth, smoke; eleventh, dust; twelfth, mist; and thirteenth, the visible color of space.
There are ten types of shape and color:
first, long; second, short; third, square; fourth, round; fifth, coarse; sixth, fine; seventh, high; eighth, low; ninth, regular; tenth, irregular.
There are eight types of manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*):
first, taking up; second, laying down; third, contraction; fourth, extension; fifth, walking; sixth, standing; seventh, sitting; and eighth, lying down.
There are five types of form belonging to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*).
1. Extremely remote form; 2. Extremely condensed form; 3. Form produced by mastery over meditative concentration; 4. Form induced by sensation; 5. Form grasped through conceptual construction.
The five sense organs have the primary elements as their substance. Within the objective sphere of the *dharmāyatana*,
they have the "extremely remote" (*parama-pratibhāsa*) and the "extremely subtle" (*parama-sūkṣma*) as their substance.
The four types of form, such as form derived from sensation (vedanā-samādāna-rūpa) and so forth, which are conceptually constructed (parikalpita),
are not derivative form (bhautika-rūpa).
Because they lack intrinsic nature,
they are provisional and not real.
Furthermore, with the exception of the four colors— blue, yellow, red, and white— which are real, [all else is provisional].
The twenty-seven kinds, such as long and short, are all conventional designations (*prajñapti*),
because they are established upon the four real forms (*rūpa*) and are established through mutual comparison.
Regarding the second, sound,
there are eleven types: first,
sound produced by great elements that are appropriated (*upātta-mahābhūta*).
"Condition" (hetu) has the meaning of "relying upon"; that is,
relying upon that eighth consciousness.
It refers to sounds produced by the four great elements that are appropriated,
such as the sound of circulating blood and pulses;
these are sounds produced by sentient beings through the internal four great elements.
Because all [of these] are appropriated, there are two causes that are non-appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*): sound is one such case;
the sound of the four external great elements is another.
There are sounds produced by three causes from both appropriated and non-appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
such as when the external four primary elements directly produce those sounds.
The hand itself is the internal four great elements that directly produce the sound as their fruit.
The four external great elements serve merely as auxiliary conditions,
collectively producing a single sound.
The sounds commonly established by the world—
such as worldly speech, teachings, books, and the arts of yin and yang—
are called "sounds commonly established."
Humanity, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and sincerity—
these five are sounds produced by the [wisdom] of accomplishment, or they are produced by the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
The teachings cited are precisely those of the Tathāgata’s six types of pleasing sounds.
That which is desired and liked by the mind;
seventh, unpleasant sounds,
which are not desired or liked by the mind.
Eighth is the sound of mutual contradiction.
That which is neither pleasant nor unpleasant is called the sound of mutual contradiction.
Ninth, sounds that are conceptually imputed,
which refers to the verbal teachings established by non-Buddhists.
Tenth, sounds subsumed under authoritative testimony (*āptavāda*).
Eleven sounds not included within authoritative verbal testimony (*āptavacana*);
three odors; and six [tastes].
First is the "excellent" [aspect].
This is explained in terms of mental states;
it follows the transformations of one's own consciousness.
That which accords with one's own mind and so forth is properly called a "good fragrance. There are two types of evil [fragrances].
Third, the three types of equality,
which are neither good nor evil.
Fourth, the innate [fragrances], such as agallochum and sandalwood.
Arising together with the substance,
the five elements combine;
various fragrances and so forth merge to form a single fragrance.
Sixth is transformation.
The state prior to ripening, when there is no fragrance,
is called transformation.
There are four tastes, which comprise twelve types:
first, bitter; second, sour; third, sweet; fourth, pungent; fifth, salty; sixth, bland; seventh, agreeable.
That is to say, they are agreeable because they accord with one's feelings; the eight disagreeable ones are those that do not accord with one's feelings.
Nine are mutually contradictory;
the latter two are opposites;
ten are co-arising.
It exists simultaneously with its substance;
it is the combination of eleven [factors] and the gathering of various flavors.
There are twelve types of transformation;
after ripening, there is a transformation of taste.
Regarding the aforementioned five contacts,
there are twenty-six [types].

1. Earth; 2. Water; 3. Fire; 4. Wind; 5. Smoothness; 6. Roughness; 7. Lightness; 8. Heaviness; 9. Softness; 10. Slackness; 11. Tension; 12. Cold; 13. Hunger; 14. Thirst; 15. Satiety; 16. Strength; 17. Weakness; 18. Dullness; 19. Itchiness; 20. Stickiness; 21. Illness; 22. Old age; 23. Death; 24. Fatigue; 25. Respiration; 26. Vigor.
The first four—earth, water, fire, and wind—are real;
the remaining twenty-two, which are established based on the distinctions of these four great elements, are conventional.
Question:
How many meanings does the category of form-dharmas have? Answer:
There are four meanings.
In the *Śata-dharmā-megha-śāstra*, it is stated:
"First, matter as the basis for consciousness belongs exclusively to the five sense organs."
Second, the objects of consciousness as form belong exclusively to the six sense-fields.
Third, speaking in terms of general characteristics.
Matter (rūpa) is defined by its characteristic of resistance;
speaking in terms of their specific characteristics,
there are briefly two kinds.
First is the resistant [matter].
According to the Sarvāstivāda school,
it is composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
In the Mahāyāna, it is formed from the primary derivative matter (upādāyarūpa).
Second, it is non-obstructive (apratigha) and is not composed of atoms (paramāṇu).
This refers to the matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
such as the aforementioned earth, water, fire, and wind,
and all other material phenomena (*rūpadharma*).
Causes and conditions appear to exist,
yet both their essence and function are empty. Why is this so?
Both self-nature and other-nature are entirely empty of intrinsic nature;
so too are the subjective perceiver and the objective perceived.
Neither possesses independent power,
for it is established through its own cause and the other,
while the other arises through its own cause and itself.
He is both self and other;
the self is the other-self.
They mutually establish and mutually negate one another.
Both the fixed nature and the coexistence are absent;
furthermore, that which is established by means of a reason, and that from which the probans proceeds, [are likewise non-existent].
If the subjective capacity lacks power, it enters into the objective field;
if the objective field lacks power, it enters into the subjective capacity.
Thus they mutually encompass and mutually support one another.
All are merely provisional designations;
when conditions assemble, they appear to exist,
but when conditions disperse, they return to non-existence.
Because that which is sustained by consciousness ultimately returns to emptiness,
as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
Furthermore, if earth were permanent,
it would possess the characteristic of solidity.
One should not abandon its characteristic,
which is like solidified butter, wax, or honey.
When resin melts,
it abandons its solid characteristic.
They fall into the state of moisture;
the same applies to gold, silver, copper,
iron, and so forth.
Just as water has the characteristic of moisture,
yet when cold it transforms into the characteristic of solidity,
so too are there various [other] such cases.
All these characteristics are entirely abandoned.
Furthermore, among the various masters of treatises,
there are those capable of making [something] non-existent.
There is no one capable of causing existence,
whether among the noble sages or those who practice seated meditation.
It can cause earth to become water and water to become earth;
such are these various phenomena.
All are capable of transforming into one another because they lack a fixed essence;
they manifest through transformation in accordance with conditions.
One must not cling to existence or cling to non-existence, as this contradicts the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). This is the fourth category:
formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma*).
There are twenty-four.
These are the non-associated formations.
As for the associated [formations]:

This is consistent with the meaning [of the term]. For example, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) are not "appropriating" (*upādāna*), because they are not capable of being cognitive objects (*ālambaka*).
That which does not associate with mind or mental factors is called "dissociated. Furthermore,
acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth do not possess the quality of being material or obstructive.
It is not associated with form,
and it possesses arising and ceasing;
it is not associated with the unconditioned.
To distinguish it from the four categories of phenomena,
it is called "non-associated"; the first is acquisition (*prāpti*).
It refers to the nature of the continuity and differentiation of the arising of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) when they are comprised within their seeds and function with mastery.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"It refers to the increase or decrease of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena."
It is provisionally established that one attains and accomplishes dharmas that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
"Manifesting the basis" refers to [the basis] whether increasing or decreasing; "manifesting the essential nature" refers to the self-substance.
Why is this? Because there is an increase [in their intensity],
they are said to be "endowed with superior faith" and so forth.
Because of this deficiency,
it is said that they possess only a low degree of faith and so forth.
Second, the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
That is to say, one who has already abandoned desire for the realm of purity (śuddhāvāsa), but has not yet abandoned desire for the higher realms,
[is reborn] in the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva).
One gives rise to the perception of renunciation.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"It refers to the cessation of the non-perpetually active mind and mental factors."
The so-called "attainment of non-conception" is comprised of the non-constantly active evolving consciousnesses;
that which ceases [is as follows].
It refers to the temporary cessation of those minds and mental factors that are induced by meditative concentration and do not manifest continuously.
Third is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

This refers to one who has already become detached from the desire for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
It is not the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, it is said:
"One desires to transcend the Peak of Existence."
Forming the perception of cessation,
with mental attention as the precursor,
[one applies it] to those minds and mental factors that do not function continuously.
Furthermore, the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is conventionally established based on the cessation of a portion of the constantly active mind and mental factors.
Regarding this, the reason why it is not stated that one must have already abandoned desire for the higher realms is as follows:
This is to demonstrate that even Arhats and others, having abandoned desire for the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
also attain this meditative absorption (samādhi).
The first category consists of those who constantly practice;
this refers to that which is comprised within the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) and the four heavens of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*).
This refers to attaining the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) in this world,
by virtue of which one is subsequently reborn among the non-conceptualizing beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) in the heavens;
therein, the non-continually active mind and mental factors cease.
The designation of the maturation of non-conception and the five life-faculties refers to the homogeneous class of beings.
Induced by prior karma,
its duration is determined;
it is conventionally designated as "life-span."
The "homogeneity of the group" (nikāyasabhāga) refers to the continuity of the aggregates throughout a single lifetime;
it is that which determines the duration of that stay.
For such a duration,
it causes the commonality of the group (nikāya-sabhāga) to remain constantly stable,
whether for a hundred years, a thousand years, or more.
Due to the specific functional capacities induced by karma,
and furthermore, based on the seeds of the eighth consciousness induced by karma.
That which causes the continuity of form and mind is called the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and the homogeneous character (nikāyasabhāga) of the six classes of beings.
That is to say, such and such sentient beings are similar to one another in their various types of individual existence.
The designation of "homogeneity" (nikāya-sabhāga) is established.
The seventh is the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva),
which refers to the nature of initiating [actions] according to their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
Furthermore, due to the seeds of the two obscurations,
there are distinctions among the various destinies and eight types of births.
That is to say, regarding the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga),
the nature of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) being non-existent previously and now existing is conventionally designated as "arising" (jāti).
The ninth is difference (anyathātva).
This refers to the nature of transformation within the continuity of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) across a given homogeneous class of beings (nikāya-sabhāga).
Provisionally established as "difference," it is also called "aging.
This constitutes the tenth stage.

That is to say, the nature of the non-disintegration and non-alteration of the continuity of conditioned phenomena within a particular homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga) is conventionally designated as "abiding" (sthiti).
Eleventh is impermanence,
which refers to the nature of the disintegration following the arising of conditioned phenomena within a common life-span (nikāya-sabhāga).
The designation of the characteristic of impermanence.
The twelfth is the "name-body" (nāmakāya),
which refers to the superimposed verbal expression regarding the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
The provisional establishment of the collection of names (*nāmakāya*) and the collection of phrases (*padakāya*),
which refers to the increased verbal expressions regarding the distinctions among phenomena.
The provisionally established group of phrases (*pada-kāya*) and the fourteen groups of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*),
which refer to all the syllables that serve as the basis for those aforementioned two [groups of] phrases and phonemes.
The provisional designation of "syllable-groups" (vyañjana-kāya) consists of fifteen types of transmigration,
which refers to the uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect.
The provisional designation of "cyclic flow" (pravṛtti).
Sixteenth, "distinctness" (pratiniyama),
which refers to the various distinctions between causes and effects.
It is provisionally established that they are distinct.
They are associated in seventeen ways;
namely, the cause and effect of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
The nature of correspondence.
Eighteen types of rapidity:
namely, the nature of the swift flow of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Nineteen is succession (*anupūrvī*),
which refers to the nature of the successive flow of each individual conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskāra*).
Twenty is time (*kāla*).
This refers to the nature of the successive arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
The twenty-first aspect refers to the nature of the pervasive demarcation of all material phenomena (*rūpa-saṃskāra*).
The twenty-two enumerations refer to the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and so forth,
each having its own distinct continuity.
The nature of the flow of essential characteristics consists of twenty-three types of conjunctions; that is to say,
the nature of the convergence of conditions for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Twenty-fourth is non-concordance (*apratisaṃyukta*),
which refers to the nature of the discordant conditions of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). This is a factor dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Although it does not associate with the mind-king,
mental factors,
or form-dharmas.
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and so forth correspond to four states;
however, all of these are merely temporal phases of the mind.
Nor is it apart from the transformation of the mind,
nor does it transcend the true nature of consciousness-only;
it is so because it is distinguished according to the phenomenal aspects of a single lifetime.
As stated in the *Śataśāstra*:
"The objects perceived through the conceptualization of one's own mind are,
in fact, one's own mind."
However, as the seeds of various formations ripen through dependence on conditions,
one's own mind manifests various states;
these are transformations of one's own mind.
Since there is no substantial entity or characteristic,
what is the purpose of diligent effort?
It is merely the establishment of a distinct phenomenon.
One should simply have faith and accept that all phenomena are mind-only.
Question:
The wondrous purport of the single mind;
the true source of the eight consciousnesses;
within the gateway of the conditioned.
Since it has already been clarified that [the King] resides within the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas,
how can he be pointed out or described?
Answer: This sets forth the fifth [category], the unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma), as well as the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and the unconditioned.
Because all arise through the transformation of a single mind,
and because they do not depart from the nature of the single mind.
Question:
Regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned,
how many types are there for each,
and what are their respective modes of activity?
How are they distinguished? Answer:
Conditioned phenomena, in brief, are of three kinds.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is briefly of six kinds.
First, conditioned phenomena that are universally established do not exceed three types.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"First, phenomena known through direct perception,
such as form, mind, and so forth."
Second are objects of enjoyment in the present,
such as jars, clothing, and so forth.
These are the two types of phenomena.
These three types of phenomena that possess functional activity are known by common worldly consensus; they do not depend on [further] logical proof for their existence.
Just as with the eye, ear,
and so forth, their existence is established through their respective functions.
The commentary states:
"That which is like matter, mind, and so forth" refers precisely to the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).
The object of the knowledge of others' minds consists of the five sense objects, such as form,
as well as mind and mental factors.
This refers to the aggregate as a whole,
not distinguishing its individual components.
To what consciousness does this serve as an object?
That which is known through direct perception is not known as an object,
such as a jar, a garment, or the like.
Although this is currently perceived as being experienced,
it is not an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because it is a conventional (*prajñapti*) phenomenon.
However, these are objects experienced in the present life.
Question:
Within this context, to which [cognitive] measure (*pramāṇa*) is the mind that takes a jar and so forth as its object subsumed?
Answer: It is not subsumed under direct perception (*pramāṇa*),
because it does not directly apprehend the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the dharma.
Because it is not a matter of inference,
it is not subsumed under direct perception (*pramāṇa*),
such as the eye, ear, and so forth.
These five material sense-faculties are not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
nor are they known by anyone in the present world.
These [faculties], such as the eye and ear,
are each inferred to exist by virtue of their respective functions of producing consciousness.
"Realization through knowledge" refers to the principle of logical proof;
it is established by means of perceiving the result directly.
Because there is a cause for this,
there is a fruit;
that is to say, the mind and mental factors that are produced.
The existence of the various pure material sense-faculties is known through inference;
this is not known through direct perception or through the knowledge of others' minds.
However, the object of the eighth consciousness in the Mahāyāna is likewise apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) when the Buddha’s wisdom takes it as its cognitive object.
It is also established by direct perception;
with the exception of the Buddha,
it is accepted as a treatise by all.
This is not commonly known in the world;
therefore, it is simply stated that this knowledge exists.
Next, [this will be discussed] in reference to various sūtras and śāstras.
There are six kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
According to the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*:
First, the unconditioned phenomenon of space (*ākāśa*).
The ultimate truth revealed by being free from all obstructions of form,
mind, and mental factors is called unconditioned space (*ākāśa-asamskṛta*).
There are three kinds of space.
First is the space that is a transformation of consciousness;
this refers to the conceptualizing mind (*vikalpa-citta*) arising within the sixth consciousness.
First, because it arises as the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) within empty space.
Second, the dharma-nature of empty space is the essence of suchness (tathatā), which is free from all obstructions.
Therefore, it is named "empty space.
This empty space of the three matters is precisely the insentient emptiness that is perceived.

Second is the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). By means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one gives rise to discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) and thereby extinguishes all obstructive defilements.
Because it is the suchness (tathatā) revealed by that [cessation],
there are three. The third is the unconditioned state of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
There is a dharma that, without relying on the power of analytical discernment,
gives rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) for investigation,
and is pure by its very nature.
This is precisely the nirvana of intrinsic purity;
it is the very nature of *tathatā*,
free from all obstructions and defilements.
It is not through the arising of wisdom that afflictions are severed, for its essential nature is inherently pure.
This is the fourth unconditioned state: immovability.
The fourth dhyāna is free from the eight afflictions and the three calamities;
it realizes the unconditioned state of immovability and the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling.
From the fourth dhyāna upward,
down to the sphere of nothingness,
the sensation of equanimity does not function.
Furthermore, when even coarse perception is absent,
the manifestation of suchness is termed the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling.
The six types of unconditioned true thusness (ṣaḍ-asamskṛta-tathatā) are twofold: first,
those that receive their names by way of being correlative counterparts.
This refers to the principle of *tathatā* (suchness),
which receives its name in contrast to phenomena (*dharma*). Second, as for distinguishing it from other phenomena:
That is, True Suchness (tathatā) is distinguished from the imputed nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) and is free from arising and ceasing.
As for its essential substance:
In the Mahāyāna, space is merely provisionally designated as existing based on the transformation of the mind into its objective aspect (nimittabhāga);
it is not that space exists externally apart from the mind.
If one says that the essence is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
it does not depart from being a transformation of consciousness.
Question:
If one speaks of the transformation of consciousness into the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) and calls it unconditioned (asaṃskṛta),
this is merely the characteristic of a phenomenal mark.
If it follows consciousness,
how can it be unconditioned? Answer:
This is said to be the transformation of consciousness;
it is provisionally called "unconditioned," but in reality, it is not unconditioned.
Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is an eternally abiding dharma,
that which here relies upon the essence of the unconditioned takes only the "image-part" (*nimittabhāga*)— which is a solitary reflection following consciousness— as its essence.
Because they are similar before and after,
without change, and consist solely of a single category of characteristics such as emptiness,
they are conventionally designated as "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta).
These six unconditioned phenomena,
as transformations of consciousness for bodhisattvas prior to the stages,

Question:
How many meanings does the mental factor (*caitta*) possess?
Regarding the section on establishing the mental factors (*caitta*), the answer is as follows:
An ancient master explained it thus:
The meaning of mental factors (caitta) is threefold:
first, they always arise in dependence upon the mind;
second, they are associated with the mind.
Third: they are bound to the mind;
the mind-king takes the general characteristics as its object.
It is like a painter making a model;
the mind universally perceives both general and specific characteristics,
just as a disciple [works] within a model of general characteristics.
It is filled with various colors; that is,

this is its general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); one does not further engage in manifold modes of cognitive construction.
Regarding the specific characteristics of the mental objects of the mental factors (*caitta*): for example, among the five mental factors,
attention (*manasikāra*) has the specific characteristic of alerting the mind and directing it toward its object.

constructing various mental images; this is the universal cognition that takes both general and specific characteristics as its objects.

First, it can act as the sovereign;
second, it can act as the support;
third, its mode of activity is general.
The four [mental factors] are constant and determinate;
they are not like the mental concomitants (caitta),
which are sometimes indeterminate.
Furthermore, if one relies on the truth of manifestation as the primary essence and function,
then the mind-king (*cittarāja*) constitutes the essence and the mental factors (*caitasika*) constitute the function.
This refers to the fact that essence and function are neither identical nor separate.
If one relies on the ultimate truth (paramārtha),
this is the truth of the differentiation between cause and effect.
Thus, the king and [his subjects] are mutually cause and effect;
it is the nature of things that they are not separate.
If one relies on the third [reason], one realizes the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
Regarding "that which is based on the expressive designation":
if one speaks in terms of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) as the expressive designator, it is not identical [to the expressed].
If explained according to the principle of the two kinds of selflessness that are expressed,
then the king is not separate from what is [expressed].
This refers to the fourth, the ultimate of ultimates (paramārthaparamārtha-satya).
Setting aside the means of expression to discuss the ultimate meaning,
one neither says they are identical nor that they are separate;
this is precisely the single true dharma-realm.
It is beyond words and transcends all signs,
for the principles of both the King and the [Buddha] ultimately converge in the single True Suchness (tathatā).
Question:
Regarding the mind-king (citta-rāja) and its mental factors (caitta),
how are they explained in terms of being provisional (prajñapti) or substantial (dravya)? Answer:
That which arises from seeds is called "real" (dravya);
that which is established based on others is called "provisional" (prajñapti).
Mental factors (caitta-dharma) exist only as real entities.
Among the mental factors (*caitta*),
those that are universal (*sarvatraga*) and those with specific objects (*viniyata*) are exclusively substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
As for all other phenomena,
they are either provisional or substantial,
or they are suchness and the unconditioned.
Although it does not arise from its own seeds,
it is nonetheless called "real," because it does not depend on anything else.
Alternatively, for all phenomena, both name and referent are conventional;
only the single category of unconditioned *tathatā* (suchness) has a conventional name but a real essence.
Because it is beyond verbal expression.
Question: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
To say that consciousness alone encompasses the mental factors (caitta) implies that True Suchness (tathatā) and consciousness are not like the mental factors.
Why is it not taught?
Answer: Because it is the true nature of consciousness.
Because it coexists with consciousness; because it exists;
and because it is not separate from consciousness.
Because it is not based on my own teachings,
I speak only of consciousness and do not speak of *tathatā*.
Therefore, one knows that true suchness is consciousness,
and consciousness is true suchness.
Question:
True Suchness is consciousness;
consciousness is True Suchness.
Furthermore, True Suchness is not that which is manifested by consciousness.
How is it established as *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)? Answer: Although it is not a transformation of consciousness, [it is so established].
Because it realizes the true nature of consciousness,
it is also called "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra).
True suchness (tathatā) is beyond words.
It is neither identical to nor different from the cognizing consciousness;
unlike form and other such phenomena, it cannot serve as a basis for the arising of grasping.
Therefore, it is not the basis for grasping;
this is not mentioned herein. If one looks from afar with a broad perspective, [it is not so].
It may also be said that those who study the final teachings rely upon the grasping of phenomena.
Because attachment arises based upon it.
Furthermore, since True Suchness (tathatā) is not something transformed by consciousness,
it should not be "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra).
It is not because of transformation that it is called "consciousness-only"; rather,
it is because nothing exists apart from consciousness.
The correct designation is "Vijñaptimātra" (Cognition-Only). Question:
Among the one hundred dharmas, [which are included?]
Do ordinary beings and sages possess [these] in common?
Answer: If one is at the stage of an ordinary being...
Generally speaking, the seeds of the nine stages within the three realms all possess one hundred dharmas;
this is also the case for the stage of the fruition of the Buddhas.
It consists exclusively of sixty-six factors.
Excluding the six root afflictions, twenty secondary afflictions, four indeterminate factors, and four factors among the dissociated formations,
a total of thirty-four factors are excluded.
Question:
Since the mind encompasses all things,
why are only the gates of the five categories and one hundred dharmas designated?
Answer: Although the hundred dharmas are set forth as the essential framework,
the sequence of these five categories already encompasses them all.
The inexhaustible Dharma-gates do not transcend this. Why is that?
The Cloud of One Hundred Dharmas. First, the clarification of mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*):
this refers to these eight types of mind-kings (*citta-rāja*).
Because this is the most supreme among conditioned phenomena,
it pertains to both the mundane and the supramundane.
There is nothing that is not created by the mind.
Second, it clarifies the mental factors (caitta) which,
together with this mind-king (cittarāja), [constitute all phenomena].
Because they are constantly associated [with the mind], they are called "associated dharmas" (*samprayukta-dharma*).
This is in relation to the preceding mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
This is precisely what is inferior;
it was superior before and becomes inferior afterward.
For this reason, it is explained next.
The three types of form are reflections manifested by the mind-king and its associates;
that is to say, these forms cannot arise of themselves.
This is because it relies on the manifestations of the preceding two [types of] mind-kings and mental factors;
since these manifestations do not directly apprehend [the object], the term "reflection" (chāyā) is employed.
Alternatively, it may refer to the essential nature;
the first two transformative consciousnesses are that which transforms, while this [essential nature] is that which is transformed.
The subjective precedes the objective;
therefore, the four non-associated formations are explained next.
That is to say, these twenty-four factors, such as acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth, cannot arise by themselves;
they are provisionally established based on the distinctions of the preceding three stages.
These three preceding [stages] are real.
This is precisely the conventional (prajñapti).
It is real first and conventional later;
therefore, it is explained next.
The five unconditioned dharmas are profound in their essential nature;
if one does not clarify the unconditioned by means of the dharmas, [it cannot be understood].
Because it cannot be manifested on its own,
it is revealed by means of the preceding four [factors] which, through the elimination of defilement, achieve purity;
these preceding four are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It exists first and then ceases;
for this reason, it is explained last.
Furthermore, the *Chao* (Excerpts) provides an extensive explanation of the first point, "because the mind-dharma is most supreme.
A verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
The mind is like a skilled painter;
it can paint all worlds.
Within all worlds, [it is the creator].
Regarding "there is nothing that is not created":
this sovereign of the eight consciousnesses is most preeminent,
being like a master painter.
One can paint the forms and images of all beings in the five destinies, including humans and devas,
as well as the forms and images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth; however,
the sūtras employ analogies to illustrate this.
The Buddha merely took a small portion;
for the painter could only paint the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha),
but was unable to paint the other four aggregates.
If, within the Dharma, these are the eight consciousnesses,
they are collectively capable of producing the five aggregates.
For instance, take the sixth consciousness.
Associated with non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*),
as well as other afflictions (*kleśa*)— both conceptual (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*)—
if one performs and acquires karma that results in the general and specific retributions of the hells.
One should immediately draw for oneself the five aggregates of the hells;
likewise, if one has created the collective or specific karmic retributions for humans and devas,
one should immediately draw the forms of humans and devas for oneself.
If one fully cultivates the ten thousand practices and attains the two fruits of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti),
one will immediately draw for oneself an image of the form of Buddhahood.
Therefore, one should know that all five aggregates, both mundane and supramundane,
are painted by one's own sixth consciousness.
Without distinguishing between the environment (the retribution of the basis) and the individual body (the retribution of the principal), all are transformations of the mind;
therefore, they are mental phenomena.
It is uniquely designated as the most excellent because it is associated with this second category: the mental factors (caitta).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* briefly explains association through five meanings.
First, as for simultaneity:
it refers to that which arises at the same time as its sovereign.
Second, the basis (āśraya) refers to the same sense-faculty (indriya) upon which the king relies.
Third, the conditions (pratyaya).
That is, it is the same object of focus as that of the king.
As for the "four types of practitioners," they refer to the three measures (pramāṇa) of the king.
The modes of activity (*ākāra*) are identical in both cases. As for the five things:
they are the respective self-attesting portions (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) that constitute the essential substance of each king.
The third is the category of form-dharmas (rūpa-dharma),
because it consists of two kinds of manifested images.
As for "manifested":
It is a transformation.
It manifests as eleven kinds of forms,
all of which are mind.
It is a mental factor (caitta), because it is a manifestation [of the mind]. It is a reflection (chāyā).
This refers to "images" (pratibimba), which means that which is similar in kind;
it refers specifically to these eleven types of objective aspects of form.
This is a category of essential nature;
it resembles essential nature. If there were no essential nature, [it would not exist].
Because it resembles the internal mind,
it is called a "reflection.
Its transformation does not directly perceive [the object].
Therefore, the term "image" (nimitta) is employed because all eight consciousnesses possess the sense of transforming into an objective aspect (nimittabhāga) as their object.
For example, when the first five consciousnesses perceive the objects of the five sensory realms, [they transform into those images].
The sixth consciousness takes the transformed images as its objects;
it also takes the eighteen dhātus as its objects by transforming them into objective parts (nimittabhāga).
When the seventh consciousness takes the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness as its object and regards it as the self,

it likewise transforms its own image-part to take that as its object. If the eighth consciousness takes the "floating dust" (the physical body) of another person as its object, [it likewise transforms its own image-part].
Furthermore, when the matter resulting from meditative concentration (*samāpatti-phala-rūpa*) and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) arise,
they likewise transform as objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*). These objective images, in relation to the eight consciousnesses, [are their objects].
That is the direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*).
With respect to the eight consciousnesses, the primary object (*bimba*) is the indirect objective condition (*paramparā-ālambana-pratyaya*).
What has been explained above is stated with reference to those cases where there is a substantial object that casts a shadow. If, however,
there is only the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) without a substantial basis (svabhāva), [the following applies].
That is to say, the eighth [consciousness] takes its own three objects as its sphere;
it is the mental consciousness in meditative concentration that takes the form produced by its own concentration as its object.
Regarding the phrase "because of the differentiation of the fourth state": [it refers to the distinction between the various stages].
These twenty-four dharmas, such as acquisition (prāpti) and so forth,
are dependent on others;
they are conventionally established upon the seeds and manifestations of the first three stages.
The fifth [category] reveals the nature of reality;
it consists of the five unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), as previously explained.
Furthermore, the first eight types of mind-kings are the most excellent gateways for cognition;
the second are the mental factors (caitta-dharma).
Associated with the mind;
this is the common, superior, and shared objective-condition gate.
This is the third category of material phenomena.
The mental image is the gateway of the objective sphere;
it is the fourth category of dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
This is the gate of establishing [dharmas] by way of their states;
the fifth is the gate of revealing the true nature, which consists of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
As manifested above, the superior and the inferior are established through the mutual interaction of subject and object;
they are evaluated through the provisional and the real.
Existence and non-existence, concealment and manifestation,
and so forth, are able to manifest inexhaustible dharma-gates.
These inexhaustible dharma-gates.
These do not go beyond the five categories and one hundred dharmas.
The five categories and one hundred dharmas,
in turn, do not go beyond the two dharmas of form and mind.
To subsume the branches and return to the root is nothing other than the single dharma of Mind-Only.
Question:
The true source of the eight consciousnesses is where the myriad dharmas find their abode;
if one examines its essential nature, it is as follows.
How many types are there?
The answer is:
as explained throughout the sūtras and śāstras.
There are three kinds of nature.
Distinguished according to the subject and object of defilement and purification, they are spoken of as three in accordance with their respective phenomena.
Even though there may be contraction and expansion,
neither departs from the nature of consciousness;
when unified, they are of one essence without distinction.
When opened, the three characteristics are distinct;
as the three characteristics are distinct,
they are deployed according to their functions.
The single essence is without differentiation;
it is through its nature that they are perfectly interfused,
while their sequential arrangement is established according to specific meanings and applications.
If there is perfect interfusion, one accords with the nature and enters profound stillness;
yet if there were no sequential arrangement, there would be nothing for perfect interfusion to interpenetrate.
Just as without false conceptualization true wisdom cannot be established, so too,
when defilement and purity are both lost, [reality is obscured].
The two truths are not established [as separate entities].
Therefore, one must fully comprehend that the true is distinguished from the false through their respective modes of manifestation (*ākāra*).
Tracing the traces back to the source,
one employs provisional causes and conditions to bring forth illumination;
this is the Dharma-gate of the three natures.
It encompasses the realms of both the ordinary and the sagely;
there is no phenomenon that is not exhausted,
and no principle that is not fully penetrated.
Now, regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*),
they are established collectively based on the sūtras and śāstras:
first, the nature of imaginary construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Second is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
Third is the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
As for the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva):
That which is grasped by foolish commoners through pervasive conceptualization—
the aggregates and so forth as being real persons and real phenomena—
is called the "imagined nature" (parikalpita-svabhāva).
There are two [types].
First, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*):
the general grasping that all phenomena possess a real intrinsic nature.
Second, regarding differentiation:
they separately grasp at permanence, impermanence,
and so forth as having a truly existent intrinsic nature.
Or one may conceptually construct an object based on its name,
such as when one has not yet recognized a cow but hears the word "cow."
He then reasoned: "By what principle is it called 'ox'?"
Either one conceptually constructs a name based on a meaning,
or one perceives a physical object without knowing its name.
One then falsely conjectures,
"What is the name of this object?
just as when one does not yet recognize an ox, one collectively conjectures about it.
"Are they ghosts?
Are they beasts? These are all mere conceptual constructions."
In terms of their essential nature, they do not exceed the two natures of person and phenomena;
in terms of their grasping, they do not exceed the two types of name and meaning;
furthermore, there is one [type of] pervasive non-grasping.
Just as with the various untainted minds,
so too do tainted wholesome consciousnesses have the capacity to take objects extensively and universally.
It is not a conceptual construction; rather,
it refers to the untainted minds,
which are the untainted wisdom of the noble ones.
Having realized that all phenomena are empty,
there is no phenomenon that is not pervaded;
thus, there is no conceptualization or grasping whatsoever.
This is termed "non-conceptualization.
It consists solely of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and contaminated wholesome consciousness (*sāsrava-kuśala-vijñāna*).
This refers to bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi), who,
even within a state of mind characterized by outflows (āsrava),
are able to practice the contemplation of non-self (anātman).
Furthermore, one is able to contemplate that all things are devoid of self;
this is both universal and free from conceptualization.
The other two involve conceptualization and are not universal.

Just as the seventh consciousness with outflows constantly takes the seeing-part of the eighth consciousness as its object and gives rise to the two types of grasping— grasping at a self and grasping at phenomena—
when one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons from the sixth consciousness, [the seventh consciousness likewise ceases].
Within the seventh consciousness,
it still takes the seeing-division (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth consciousness as its object and gives rise to the grasping of dharmas (dharma-grāha).
Thus, one should know that *vitarka* (applied thought) is not pervasive;
the third [factor], however, is both pervasive and *vitarka*,
namely the defiled mind of sentient beings.
The four that are neither pervasive nor conceptual are the five contaminated sensory consciousnesses and the eighth ālayavijñāna.
Each is cognizant only of its own respective domain;
it is not pervasive and is devoid of conceptual construction.
Because it is a conceptualization arising from recollection,
it is not the Ālaya-vijñāna.
It takes as its objects only seeds,
the root-body,
and the receptacle world.
Because it has three kinds of objects,
it cannot even take the seven preceding manifest states as its objects; thus,
it is neither pervasive nor conceptualizing.
The contaminated seeds are able to sustain and take as objects the uncontaminated seeds.
If one maintains [the mind] without even taking that as an object,
how much more so regarding other objects?
Furthermore, an ancient master said:
It should be understood that within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
the defiled minds of sentient beings harbor two kinds of grasping at the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The first is "concomitant awakening," which refers to manifest grasping.
The second is "habituation."
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are precisely the grasping seeds;
this is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Arising through the combination of other various conditions,
like a magical illusion,
it is called the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*):
it is the perfect accomplishment of the single flavor of suchness (*tathatā*).
Question:
What is the principle by which the nature of pervasive conceptualization is established?
Answer: According to Dharmapāla, it is as follows.
Those mental states of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses that grasp at a self and phenomena are capable of universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*),
because it is taught that only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of universal conceptualization.
Question:
What is the principle of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)? Answer:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Compendium of Ascertainment) states: "This is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
because it is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the mind and mental factors of universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*)."
Cien says: Among the three natures, this is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

That which is called the "object-condition" (ālambana) must necessarily be an existent phenomenon; it is the object of the mind and its mental factors that engage in pervasive conceptualization (parikalpa).
Taking this as the condition,
that which possesses the aspect of the real (sākāra) must necessarily depend on the other.
It does not take the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) as its object,
because it is not similar [to it].
Question:
Among the three natures, the imagined nature is mere false conceptualization;
it is non-existent.
The dependent nature belongs to causes and conditions.
"Does this exist?
He replied,
"These two natures arise from the interaction between the producer and the produced."
Both lack intrinsic nature.
Why? Because names and characteristics are established based on conceptual construction.
It is because of names and marks that causes and conditions are established.
If false discrimination does not arise,
how could names and marks exist?
Names and characteristics do not exist;
causes and conditions are themselves empty,
for all phenomena do not transcend names.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* verse says:
"For example, as in the practice of cultivation,
a single [nature] appears as various [forms]."
"In that [state], there are no various [phenomena];
such is the nature of conceptual construction.
The commentary explains:
This is the refutation of the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
For example, when those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) practice various contemplative exercises (*vipaśyanā*),
if they perform a visualization (*bhāvanā*) of the color blue:
Heaven, earth, and the myriad things—
there is none that is not blue. It is by means of that which is not blue that one perceives the blue.
Because of the transformation of the mind,
there are various differences regarding a single objective form.
It is like an ordinary person’s deluded perception of birth and death;
it is likewise a deluded perception of birth and death where there is no place for birth and death.
Furthermore, a verse in a sutra says:
Just as various kinds of cataracts cause manifold forms to appear through false imagination,
yet the cataracts themselves are neither form nor non-form.
The failure to realize dependent origination is thus [the error].
This refutes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) based on causes and conditions,
which is like what is seen by one with cataracts in the eyes.
The distinctions are not the same.
Those [distinctions] are truly not dharmas arisen from conditions;
they are, rather, the empty essence of conceptual construction.
The absence of intrinsic nature in causes and conditions is precisely the ultimate single dharma of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
It is like a person with clear vision.
One perceives the pure void;
how much more so the single true mind,
which has nothing else whatsoever.
Question:
Among these three natures,
how many dharmas are provisional?
"How many dharmas are real?
Answer: The *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* states:
The thoroughly imagined nature may be said to be conventional, because it is falsely established.
Because it lacks the characteristics of intrinsic nature,
it is neither provisional nor real;
this is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
There are both the real and the provisional,
because they are of the nature of aggregates, continuities, and specific states.
It is said to be conventional because mind, mental factors,
and form arise from conditions.
It is said that they exist as real entities; if there were no real dharmas,
then even conventional dharmas would not exist.
Because the imputed nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is designated based on real causes,
the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is exclusively truly existent.
Because it is designated without depending on other conditions.
The commentary explains: "universal imagination" (parikalpa).
Having a name but no substance,
established by deluded sentiment,
it may be said to be "provisional."
Regarding its essential nature:
since it possesses no marks,
it is neither provisional nor substantial.
It is not like the horns of a rabbit or similar things that can be described as either conventional or real;
it must necessarily depend upon dharmas— whether general or specific— that possess substantial existence.
Because they are established as either provisional or real,
the dependent nature has three types of provisionality.
First, the conventionally designated entity as a collection:
such as a jar, a basin, a sentient being, and so forth. This is it.
The nature of aggregation:
because many factors are accumulated and integrated simultaneously,
although that which performs the aggregation is real.
That which is produced is provisional.
Second, the provisional nature of continuity refers to such things as the past and future time periods.
Only cause and effect possess this nature of continuity across many phenomena and over a long duration.
One establishes a conventional dharma,
as the Buddha said:
"In the past, there was a king of deer."
This very body of mine is it;
although the five aggregates upon which it depends are substantially real, they perish moment by moment.
Based on the continuity of these many dharmas,
one conventionally designates a "sentient being";
because it has persisted until the present day.
The provisional entity of the three stages is like the non-associated formations; it is such.
Because they are of a nature consisting of temporal states, they are all merely provisional designations established upon a single dharma at a single moment.
For example, with respect to a single form,
it is designated as "outflow-tainted" (sāsrava) and "visible" (sanidarśana).
There is resistance (sapratigha),
which is also called form (rūpa) and so forth;
both refer to a single dharma.
Because it is a conceptual designation. If it were real,
it would necessarily have multiple entities.
All such states as anger and resentment are subsumed under this [category] of the provisional;
they consist of mind, mental factors, and form.
Because they arise from causes and conditions,
they are said to be real.
Furthermore, regarding the three natures:
This is precisely the single nature.
The single nature is itself the absence of nature. Why is this?
The imagined nature is signless;
the dependent nature is unarisen;
the perfected nature is without intrinsic being.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states:
"A person with cataracts is like the parikalpita (imagined nature)."
Appearing as blue or yellow,
like [an object] depending on others,
it is seen by pure eyes.
Regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is like a snake."
The dependent nature is like the vine;
if a person were to analyze this vine by taking it as the object of four elemental qualities.
One perceives only the four characteristics;
one does not perceive a separate creeper,
for it consists merely of the characteristics of color, fragrance, taste, and tangibility.
The vine is not substantially existent;
for apart from the four types of atoms,
there is no separate vine that exists.
Therefore, a verse in the treatise says:
"The cognition of a snake arises with respect to a vine;
upon seeing the vine, the [external] object is absent."
If one knows the parts of the vine,
the knowledge of the vine is like the knowledge of a snake;
if one knows that the nature of the parts of the vine is empty, [the knowledge of the vine is likewise empty].
This is, for example, like the false conception of a snake arising upon a vine.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The Bodhisattva does not perceive external objects."
One merely perceives mental verbalization and discrimination,
and thereby realizes the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
How is this realization distinguished?
This phenomenon,
if separated from causes and conditions,
cannot arise of itself.
The faculties and their objects serve as causes and conditions;
since the faculties and objects are not established,
these phenomena lack causes and conditions.
How is birth attained?
By relying on the initial true contemplation, one enters the nature of dependence on others (paratantra-svabhāva).
Through the second true contemplation,
by eliminating the dependent nature,
the ideation of "representation-only" ceases.
The manifestation of mental verbalization and conceptual discrimination appears as all objects heard and reflected upon,
even up to appearing as the mere ideation of consciousness-only.
None of these can arise.
There are two conditions for arising:
namely, the nature of conceptualization (parikalpita-svabhāva).
Furthermore, once the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) has been purified and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) has already ceased, the dependent nature can no longer arise.
Since there are no two objects,
all meanings— even those that appear as the notion of representation-only— are likewise [non-existent].
None of these can arise;
even the perception of consciousness cannot yet be produced,
let alone other conceptualizations through mental discourse.
In what does the bodhisattva abide?
He abides solely in non-conceptualization,
in the state of perfect equality regarding all names and referents.
Furthermore, it is based on two kinds of equality,
namely, that of the subject (the grasper) and the object (the grasped). The subject is non-conceptual wisdom.
Because wisdom is non-conceptual,
it is called "equanimity.
Its object of focus is the realm of suchness.
The object is likewise without discrimination;
