the second is the absence of a self-existent nature;
and the last is due to being far removed from the former two.
The nature of the self and phenomena as they are grasped—
this ultimate reality of all phenomena— is also precisely suchness.
Because it is always as its own nature,
it is the true nature of consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātratā).
This refers to the three natures previously explained.
He establishes the three kinds of non-nature mentioned in the latter teaching, namely: the non-nature of characteristics, the non-nature of arising, and [the non-nature of ultimate reality].
Because they lack intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense,
the Buddha spoke with intentional meaning.
All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; it is not that their nature is entirely non-existent—
this is spoken with intentional meaning.
This reveals that it is not of definitive meaning;
that is to say, although the latter two natures exist, they do so without having an intrinsic essence.
Fools superimpose upon them and falsely cling to them,
[asserting] that there is a real self-nature of persons and phenomena.
This is precisely what is called the "thoroughly imagined" (parikalpita).
In order to eliminate this attachment, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, [taught as follows].
Regarding existence and non-existence,
they are collectively described as being without intrinsic nature. On what basis is this said?
And those three [natures] are established:
namely, based on this first [nature], the imagined (parikalpita), the naturelessness of characteristics (lakṣaṇaniḥsvabhāvatā) is established.
Because this intrinsic nature is ultimately non-existent,
like a flower in the sky,
one next establishes the lack of nature in terms of arising based on the dependent nature.
This is like a magical illusion;
it arises dependent upon a multitude of conditions,
for it is falsely grasped as having an inherent nature.
The absence of nature is spoken of metaphorically;
it does not mean that nature is entirely non-existent,
for this is based on the subsequent perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The establishment of the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature means that it is the ultimate itself,
because it is free from the previously mentioned nature of the self and phenomena as they are conceptually constructed.
It is conventionally described as being without intrinsic nature, yet it is not that its nature is entirely non-existent,
like the great empty space.
Although it pervades all colors,
these various colors are manifested as being without intrinsic nature;
thus, even in the sūtras, the term "without intrinsic nature" is spoken.
This is not of ultimate meaning;
those who possess wisdom should not rely upon it to categorically deny all phenomena.
They are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
As a verse in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:
"The characteristic, the arising, and the ultimate lack intrinsic nature."
Thus have I fully revealed all this.
If one does not understand this secret intention of the Buddha,
one will lose the right path and be unable to proceed.
"Characteristics" refers to the parikalpita (imagined nature); "arising" refers to the paratantra (dependent nature).
This is the dependent nature;
this is the ultimate;
this is the perfected nature.
Regarding "lack of intrinsic nature":
with respect to these three natures,
there is no false attachment to a self or phenomena as having an imagined, independent intrinsic nature.
If a person does not understand the Buddha’s intentional meaning (*abhiprāya*),

[they may fail to realize that] the three absences of nature (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) are taught in relation to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) in order to refute the self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) of non-Buddhists and followers of the Hīnayāna.
If one then dismisses both bodhi and nirvāṇa as being entirely non-existent,
such a person has lost and destroyed the right path and will be unable to reach its destination.
This statement regarding the three natures and the three absences of nature does not mean that the dependent and perfected natures are also non-existent; rather,
it means that the falsely imagined self and phenomena are absent.
Therefore, it is called "the absence of intrinsic nature.
Thus, the three natures are boundless;
following any one of them, all are fully subsumed.
Truth and falsehood are mutually integrated;
essence and appearance are without obstruction.
Such is the teaching of the Tathāgata throughout his entire lifetime.
The infinite gateways of meaning and the underlying intentions are all subsumed within the framework of the three natures.
The ultimate and the conventional,
the root and the branches, are all comprehensively gathered at once to reveal the correct principle of Vijñaptimātra.
There is no other path;
for the dependent nature is the very essence of consciousness-only.
From the dependent nature, there arises conceptual construction;
from the dependent nature, one realizes the ultimate reality.
This is precisely the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Due to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
one portion constitutes birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
By virtue of reality,
one part constitutes nirvāṇa; one realizes that the nature of conceptual construction is empty.
Thus, birth-and-death becomes nirvāṇa;
when one is deluded regarding true reality,
existence becomes birth-and-death, and nirvāṇa becomes birth-and-death.
All are a single Dharma that accords with conditions;
the revealed meanings form three,
yet these three are not three, for the one principle is perfect.
Though it is neither one nor many, the three natures are fully present;
in its unfolding and rolling up, nothing is lost;
in its concealment and manifestation, it is ever as it is.
Neither one nor three;
it merges essence and appearance within the ground of reality,
yet remains both three and one.
The radiance of practice spreads throughout the Dharma-realm;
as for summarizing the ultimate destination,
nothing precedes this essential principle.
Question:
The characteristics of the three transformative consciousnesses have already been detailed and presented.
How should the manifested marks be explained? Answer:
There are three types of transformation:
namely, the ripening consciousness, the mentation consciousness,
and the consciousness that discriminates objects.
This consciousness is the self-substance of the transformer;
that which is transformed consists of the two parts: the seeing and the perceived.
Because it is that which is transformed by the self-substance portion (svabhāva-bhāga),
and because it is the function of the self-substance portion,
it is called "self-substance."
This is the basis for these two divisions.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) asks: How should this be understood?
Based on what is transformed by consciousness,
the self and phenomena are provisionally designated;
they do not exist as separate, real entities.
Is it therefore the case that all this is merely consciousness?
The verse says:
These various consciousnesses undergo transformation.
The grasper and the grasped— by this,
both are non-existent; therefore,
all is representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).
These various consciousnesses refer to the three transforming consciousnesses previously mentioned,
as well as their associated mental factors.

All [of these] are able to transform and manifest as the two divisions of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*); thus, they are designated by the term "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
As for the transformed seeing-part:
It is called "discrimination" because it can grasp images; it refers to the image-aspect (nimittabhāga) that is transformed [by consciousness].
It is called the "object of conceptualization," because it is the object apprehended by views.
By this correct reasoning, [it is established].
Those [entities], such as the self and dharmas,
which are distinct from what is transformed by consciousness,
are all certainly non-existent.
Because there is no distinct entity apart from the grasped and the grasper,
it does not exist as a real substance.
Because it is free from these two characteristics,
all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena—
whether real or provisional— are likewise [free from them].
All [phenomena] are not separate from consciousness.
The word "only" (kevalam) is used to exclude the existence of real entities apart from consciousness.
It is not that [these] do not exist, nor are they separate from consciousness, mental factors,
and so forth. Alternatively, "transformation" refers to the various internal consciousnesses transforming and appearing as a self and phenomena.
The manifestation of external objects is this very capacity for transformation;
it is precisely what is called "discrimination."
Because its intrinsic nature is false discrimination,
it refers to the mind of the three realms.
Together with the mental factors,
these objects of grasping are called the "discriminated."
That which is thus falsely grasped as the real nature of self and phenomena undergoes transformation through this discrimination, appearing as external objects.
The characteristics of the provisional self and dharmas—
the real nature of the self and dharmas as they are conceptually discriminated—
definitively do not exist at all.
Since the scriptural citations and principles previously adduced have already been extensively refuted, therefore, all [of them]...
All are merely consciousness;
they exist as false discrimination,
because this is universally established.
Since it is not the case that phenomena not separate from consciousness are excluded,
such things as *tathatā* (true thusness) also possess substantial existence.
By this, one remains far removed from the two extremes of increase and decrease;
thus the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is established, and one accords with the Middle Way.
The commentary states:
"Regarding 'the transformation of these various consciousnesses,' 'transformation' (pariṇāma) carries the meaning of alteration."
That is to say, the single substance of consciousness transforms and arises as two aspects,
which are distinct from its own substance.
That is to say, the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) possesses the function of grasping,
while the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) possesses the function of objective resistance;
this is due to the self-substance of consciousness.
Because it arises as a transformation capable of grasping and because it possesses resistance,
it is the perceived aspect (darśana-bhāga) that is transformed.
It is called "discrimination" because it is able to grasp the characteristics [of objects] within that which was previously transformed.
The transformed seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is called "discrimination" (vikalpa);
it is the nature of dependence on others (paratantra-svabhāva).
Because it can grasp the dependent *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) that it itself has transformed,
it gives rise to various conceptualizations of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
these are transformations of the substance of this consciousness.
Because it is able to differentiate through its function,
it is called "differentiation."
The dependent nature and characteristics transformed by the essence of that consciousness are divided [into two].
That which resembles the apprehended aspect (nimittabhāga) is called the "object of discrimination" (vikalpya),
because it is the aspect apprehended by the preceding subject-aspect of discrimination (darśanabhāga).
It is not meant that the intrinsic nature of consciousness itself is able to perceive;
rather, what is called "discrimination" refers to the arising of discriminative views.
This is the function of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because both the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) arise based upon self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*),
and because "only" (*kevala*) does not exclude nor depart from phenomena that are consciousness.
If you argue that *tathatā* (suchness) and so forth are also existent entities,
[we reply that] the word "only" (*mātra*) does not exclude phenomena that are not separate from consciousness.
This refers to *tathatā* and the mental factors (*caitta*).
Nor are they separate from consciousness;
therefore, their substance exists in all cases.
Now, in this state:
It merely negates the existence of that which is conceptually constructed apart from consciousness;
it does not negate the existence of suchness and so forth, which are not separate from consciousness.
This should be understood according to the principle.
Since this manas possesses both the evolving discriminating consciousness and the dependent *paratantra* aspect of the object it evolves,
there exist the objects discriminated by it, such as external real dharmas and so forth.
It is determined that these do not exist at all;
there are only such dharmas as true thusness (*tathatā*) and mental factors (*caitta*),
all of which are not separate from consciousness (*vijñāna*).
It is also substantially existent.
That which is free from the two extremes of superimposition and denial is so because there are no phenomena external to the mind.
It excludes the extreme of superimposition because of the existence of the false mind and so forth;
it avoids the extreme of deprecation.
Because it avoids the extreme of deprecation,
it excludes the denial [of reality] as taught by Bhāviveka and others, who are like the sky;
because it avoids the extreme of superimposition.
The various attachments of the Hinayana schools to the existence of phenomena external to the mind are eliminated; thus,
the doctrine of Consciousness-Only is established,
harmonizing with the Middle Way.
Because it is free from partiality and attachment.
Furthermore, according to the explanations of various masters,
there are generally four aspects of meaning.
1. The objective part (nimittabhāga).
2. The subjective part (darśanabhāga).
3. The self-verifying part (svasaṃvittibhāga).
Fourth is the self-witnessing division (svasaṃvittibhāga).
There are four aspects (nimittabhāga): first, [the aspect of the object].
The names and marks of the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) have as their essence suchness (tathatā),
because they are the true characteristic.
Second, the characteristic of the object is called "characteristic" because it serves as the objective field for the sense faculties and the mind. Third,
the characteristic of the mode of appearance is called "characteristic."
These are exclusively conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*),
because they possess characteristics;
this applies to both reflections and their substantial bases.
These are solely transformations of consciousness.
The four meanings consist of the characteristics (*nimitta*) and the names (*nāman*);
that is, the expressed meanings corresponding to the expressing [names].
Regarding the "objective aspect" (*nimitta-bhāga*): among the four types of aspects mentioned above,
only the latter three aspects are taken as the objective aspect.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of objective aspects (nimitta-bhāga): first,
that which is suddenly transformed by consciousness,
which is the primary object (maulika-vastu).
The two types of consciousness and so forth take objects as mere transformations of images;
they do not apprehend the actual essence.
Regarding the second, the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*),
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"With respect to its own object of cognition..."
It has the function of discernment.
This aspect of seeing (darśana-bhāga) is of five types.
First, that which realizes [the object] is called "seeing."
This refers precisely to the "seeing-division" (darśana-bhāga) of the three fundamental wisdoms.
The term "illumination" (āloka) is used for this seeing;
it extends to both the sense faculties and the mind.
Because they all possess the sense of illuminating,
the three that are capable of taking an object are called "view" (*darśana*);
this thus encompasses the three internal parts [of consciousness].

Because both are capable of taking [the object] as their cognitive support, the four applications of mindfulness are termed "view," since they are that which is expressed by the term "application of mindfulness."
5. Inferential deliberation is called "view" (dṛṣṭi);
it is the mind of inference (anumāna).
Because it speculates upon all objects,
among these five types of views, the five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are excluded.
Including the two internal parts,
all others are subsumed under the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga).
There are three self-witnessing-parts (svasaṃvitti-bhāga).

The fourth is the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvittivijñāna*), because it is capable of acting as the witness that personally realizes, without error, that its own seeing-division (*darśanabhāga*) takes the image-division (*nimittabhāga*) as its object.
This means that because the third self-cognizing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) directly realizes the seeing division (*darśana-bhāga*) without error,
it derives its name from that which is realized.
Such is the meaning of these four divisions.
In general, this is illustrated by the analogy of a mirror.
The mirror is like the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvittibhāga).
The clarity of the mirror is like the seeing-portion; the mirror-image is [like the seen-portion].
The image-part (nimittabhāga) is like the handle behind the mirror;
the self-cognizing part (svasaṃvittibhāga) is like the mirror itself.
Regarding these four parts,
there are the established doctrines of four masters.
The first is the Bodhisattva Sthiramati.
Establishing one part as the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"This self-cognizing portion..."
Because it arises from conditions,
it is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva);
therefore, it is said to exist.
The perceived aspect and the perceiving aspect do not arise from conditions;
they are caused by the mind of pervasive conceptualization.
They exist through false attachment.
Thus, these two aspects are existent in terms of mental perception but non-existent in terms of ultimate reality.
Only the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvittibhāga) is of the nature of dependence on others (paratantrasvabhāva);
it arises from seeds.
Because these [aspects] exist substantially,
the two parts— the perceived and the perceiving— are non-existent and arise through further transformation.
The two attachments to self and dharmas are also non-existent;
they are like non-existence because they are non-existent.
If one follows the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla,
this means that existence is treated as if it were non-existence;
he holds that the two parts— the perceived (nimitta-bhāga) and the perceiving (darśana-bhāga)— possess substantial reality.
The transformation arises because the two types of grasping— grasping at a self and grasping at phenomena— are without intrinsic substance.
Sthiramati quotes the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as follows:
The contaminated minds and mental factors within the three realms are all false conceptualizations,
because they constitute its intrinsic nature.
Therefore, one should know that the two divisions of subject and object within the eight consciousnesses are all merely false attachments of pervasive conceptualization; thus,
there exists only the single division of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*).
This is the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature),
because it exists substantially.
As a verse in the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says:
What is discriminated by the foolish—
external objects— does not exist at all in reality;
it is the mind that is agitated and turbid by habitual tendencies.
Therefore, it arises as if resembling that [object].
Thus, one should know that this is merely the deluded conceptualization of fools arising upon the basis of the truly existent self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).
Because it manifests as two parts that appear to have no substance,
in reality these two parts lack any actual essence.
However, because foolish people do not understand this and falsely cling to it as being real,
the treatise says:
Ordinary beings cling to existence;
noble ones realize non-existence.
Question:
If one says that the two parts of the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) are merely provisional,
then consider, for example, the great earth, mountains, and rivers;
these are subsumed under the perceived aspect.
If it is directly perceived as real,
how can you say it is merely conventional? Answer:
Although one perceives mountains, rivers, and so forth as real,
these are fundamentally false attachments to the existence of external mountains, rivers, the great earth, and so on;
this is the truth when discussed according to principle.
Because none of them are apart from the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga).
Thus, a verse in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
"Due to attachment to one's own mind..."
The mind manifests as external objects;
what is seen therein does not exist.
Therefore, it is said that there is "mind-only."
Therefore, one should know that apart from self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*),
there are no real divisions of the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) and the object-part (*nimittabhāga*). Second, the master Nanda...
Regarding the establishment of the two divisions as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*): first,
the statement of the thesis is that all minds arise.
All [cognitions] possess both the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) and the aspect of the perceived (*nimitta-bhāga*). These two aspects, the seeing and the perceived,
constitute the twofold objective conditions of the subject and the object.
If there were no image-part (nimittabhāga) to draw forth the mind,
mental factors would have no basis for arising;
if there were no perceiving seeing-part (darśanabhāga), [the same would follow].
Who would have known that there exists an objective aspect (nimittabhāga) as a focal object?
Thus, the existence of objects and the existence of mind together establish the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra).
The seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is that which undergoes transformation; the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) is that which is transformed.
Thus, the subject and object are established.
It must possess two parts: the seeing part (darśana-bhāga) and the image part (nimitta-bhāga);
these constitute the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
At times it takes as its object a solitary image (pratibimba),
arising from the same seed;
at times it takes as its object that which possesses substance (sadravya).
It arises from a distinct seed;
because it arises from a seed,
it is not a mere conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).
If this were not admitted,
the Buddhas would not manifest various images such as their bodies and lands. Thus,
Sthiramati raises an objection.
If you establish the existence of the image-aspect (nimittabhāga),
how could there not be an object external to the mind? How, then,
can it be called "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra)?
Nanda said: "The *bhāga* of subjectivity (*darśana-bhāga*) is the cognizing faculty (*ālambaka*), while the *bhāga* of objectivity (*nimitta-bhāga*) is the cognized object (*ālambana*)."
That which is subsumed by the object is still merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
Furthermore, if you claim that there is no objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), [then...]
In that case, one part of the established thesis—that all is representation-only (vijñapti-mātra)—would not be proven. Why?
Because Sthiramati maintains that the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) exists as a product of false attachment.
It is the seed of the *nimitta-bhāga* within the objective aspect (*ālambana*) of the eighth consciousness;
it is subsumed under the objective aspect.
That is to say, this seed is capable of producing the manifestation of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*).
Regarding the dharmas of direct causes and conditions:
if the aspect of the seed-characteristic is a product of deluded perception,
what prevents the self-verifying aspect of the manifest activity that it produces from being likewise so?
This is also a false conception;
it does not contradict the principle of the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*).
If one does not allow that the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is a false conception, [then...]
The seeds that are capable of producing [results] are also substantially existent;
thus, both cause and effect are real.
This proves that the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is also substantially existent.
Since the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) exists, the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga) must also exist; thus,
the relationship between subject and object is established.
Thus, the two divisions establish the nature of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

Furthermore, the five sense-faculties are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness. If the *nimitta-bhāga* were [exclusively] the product of *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), [then the sense-faculties would not be real].
How could there be a thoroughly imagined faculty capable of producing the five consciousnesses?
Sthiramati says:
The five consciousnesses do not arise by depending on the five sense organs;
rather, they each arise from their own respective seeds.
Question:
If [the five consciousnesses] were not produced by depending on the sense faculties but arose solely from seeds,
you would have to admit that the seeds of the five consciousnesses [exist independently].
"Is this the eighth [consciousness's] objective aspect (nimittabhāga)?
He replied,
"I grant that it is the eighth [consciousness's] objective aspect."
Difficult.
If that is so, then the seed itself is the parikalpita (the imagined nature).
That which can produce the five consciousnesses is also a form of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*).
Sthiramati offers this defense:
The seed is merely a functional potency (vāsanā) upon the eighth consciousness;
because it possesses the capacity to produce manifest activity (pravṛtti),
it is metaphorically designated as a "seed."
However, these are merely different names for habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
they are not real. [Objection: This is difficult to maintain.
In the various holy teachings, that which arises from seeds is called "real," while that which is established based on others is called "provisional.
How could there be a case where a provisional seed gives rise to a real manifest activity?
If it were a provisional seed,
how could it directly produce its own fruit?
If the seed were a provisional phenomenon, [how could it do so]?
Consequently, the meaning of the eighth consciousness undergoing transformation through causes and conditions within the causal state would not be established.
If it were not a transformation through causes and conditions,
it would contradict everything.
An-hui’s defense is utterly refuted.
Since there exist both the subjective and objective conditions,
all of these must be the truly existent dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
This refers to the characteristic of knowing and seeing as it truly is.
As for the citation of evidence:
The *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* states:
"All things exist only as cognition;
the objects of cognition are entirely non-existent."
The subject that perceives and the object perceived each turn spontaneously.
The commentary states:
That "everything is nothing but cognition" refers to *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
That "the objects of cognition are all non-existent" means:
That is to say, the falsely grasped external objects as real are non-existent;
as for the division into the "subject that perceives" and the "object perceived," the subject that perceives is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the aspect of real seeing.
That which is perceived is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the aspect of the real; each evolves spontaneously.
As for the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), it arises from the seeds of the mind.
The image-aspect arises from the seeds of the image-aspect;
therefore, one must know that both aspects must be established for consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) to be fully realized.
Regarding the contradiction:
Sthiramati raises the objection, "If that is so..."
How are the two preceding passages from the *Ghanavyūha* and the *Laṅkāvatāra* to be reconciled?
To reconcile them correctly:
The preceding scriptural passage does not serve as proof for a single portion [of the self],
but merely negates the attachment to the notion that there exists a real self and its attributes external to the mind.
Nor does he deny that the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is not separate from the mind.
The third [position] was established by the Bodhisattva Dignāga as having three aspects;
it is not the view of the former masters.
Sthiramati establishes one part [of consciousness],
which possesses only substance but lacks function;
Nanda establishes the two parts of seeing and the seen.
There is only function and no substance;
all are mutually insufficient.
This is the principle established by the proponent.
This refers to the meaning of the result established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The treatise states:
"The cognizer (*pramātṛ*)."

Because the object of cognition (*prameya*), the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the fruit of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) are distinct; and because the characteristic (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) must necessarily have a substratum as their essence.
The image-part (nimittabhāga) is the object of cognition,
and the seeing-part (darśanabhāga) is the means of cognition;
this requires the self-verifying part (svasaṃvittibhāga).
That which serves as the means of cognition (pramāṇa) is the result of cognition (pramāṇaphala). It is,
for example, like using a measuring rod to measure silk cloth.
Silk. It is that which is measured.
The person with the cubit.
The cognition that performs the measurement is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the wisdom that records the count is called the result of the measurement (*pramāṇaphala*).
Now, it is seen that there is no error in the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) taking the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) as its object,
because both are produced by the self-witnessing-part (svasaṃvitti-bhāga). Thus,
when the seeing-part of visual consciousness takes blue as its object:
It certainly does not take yellow as its object.
For example, when the subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga) takes as its object something never before seen,
and suddenly takes the object of yellow as its focus—
That is to say, in meditative concentration, it does not take blue as its object.
If there were no self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*),
the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) would be unable to remember itself.
Therefore, one must establish three parts.
If the self-verifying part (svasaṃvittibhāga) did not exist, then both the image-part (nimittabhāga) and the seeing-part (darśanabhāga) would likewise not exist.
If one asserts that there are two parts,
then it must necessarily be established that there is a self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*);
this self-verifying part is analogous to the head of an ox.
The two horns are used as a metaphor for the two parts of the aspect of the perceived object (*grāhya-bhāga*).
As the *Pramāṇasamuccaya-kārikā* states:
"That which resembles the object is the object of cognition (*prameya*)."
Regarding "the apprehending aspect is self-cognized," the commentary explains:
"That which resembles the objective aspect is the object of cognition."
That is to say, the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) appears as if it were an external object.
Regarding "the grasper-aspect and self-cognition":
the "grasper-aspect" refers to...
This is precisely the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*),
because it is able to apprehend the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*).
This is precisely the essence.
Fourth, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla established four divisions.
Regarding the establishment of the thesis:
if one were to analyze the mind and mental factors in detail,
there should be four parts.
Regarding the establishment of the principle: if there were no fourth member,
with what dharma would the third member constitute the fruit of the means of valid cognition?
As for your establishment of the three parts, Dharmakīrti,
it is because the seeing-part possesses the function of cognizing objects as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore,
the self-cognizing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is taken as the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
Since your own self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) also possesses the capacity to cognize and illumine the object,
what dharma would you then designate as the result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) for that self-cognizing part which acts as the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
One must then take the fourth part, the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*),
as the third part, the fruit of cognition. This is supported by scriptural evidence.
A verse from the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says:
"The minds of sentient beings possess two natures,
comprising all internal and external divisions."
The entanglements of the grasped and the grasper manifest as various distinctions;
such is the duality of the mind.
That is to say, the two internal divisions constitute one nature;
the two divisions of the seeing and the seen constitute the second nature;
that is, the two natures of the internal and external of mind and object.
The "enveloping grasper" (grāhakaparyavasthāna) refers to that which is capable of objectifying coarse movement;
it is the objective-seeing aspect (darśanabhāga).
The "entanglement of the grasped" refers to the bondage of signs and the bondage of the object of cognition.
Regarding the observation of various distinctions:
the observation of the divisions is common to the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is the meaning.
Therefore, it is said that various distinctions are perceived.
Neither of the two preceding masters is entirely incorrect.
The third master, Dignāga, [posits] three parts which appear to have both substance and function;
if these were established as valid means of cognition (pramāṇa),...
The reasoning therein remains insufficient;
one must further establish a fourth division:
the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) as the object of cognition (*prameya*).

The aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) is taken as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is taken as the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). Alternatively,
if the aspect of seeing is taken as the object of cognition (*prameya*), [the self-cognizing aspect remains the fruit].
If the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what other phenomenon could serve as the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*)? Therefore,
it is known that the self-cognizing aspect itself is taken as the result of valid cognition.
This refers to the "square foot.
Seeing that external conditions are empty and sparse, it is understood through inference (*anumāna*) rather than the two [other] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) is not taken as the fruit of self-cognition; rather,
the two internal portions are exclusively direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Therefore, there is no fault in their being mutually results.
Now, that which functions as the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) must be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Only then does it constitute the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). This is not [the case] by analogy (*upamāna*).
Concentration is not the fruit of valid cognition; it is like a guarantor,
who must be upright and honest.
This shall serve as the proof.
If one were to omit the guarantor, they would be unable to fulfill the role of a surety.
Furthermore, regarding the first five consciousnesses:
Although it is direct perception (pratyakṣa) together with the eighth [consciousness] and its seeing-part (darśana-bhāga), it is [considered such] because of external objects.
It is therefore not the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). For that which is the result of valid cognition must necessarily have an internal object-condition (*ālambana*).
This alone constitutes the fruit of valid cognition.
Furthermore, although the seventh consciousness is an internal object-condition, it is nonetheless an object-condition.
This is not a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor can it be the fruit of a valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
For that which constitutes the fruit of a valid cognition...
It possesses two meanings:
first, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
second, internal cognition (*antarālambana*).
Furthermore, although the subsequently attained seeing-part within the fruit is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), when it internally takes [the fruit] as its object, [it is not so].
Because it is a transformation of reflected images and conditions, it is not the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It must, therefore, possess three characteristics.
Furthermore, although the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the fundamental wisdom within the fruit directly realizes suchness, it does not produce a mental image (pratibimba),
because it is non-transformative.
Because this is the function of the mind,
it is not the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); rather, it must necessarily possess the substance of the mind.
It must possess four characteristics:
first, direct perception;
second, internal conditions.
The first three do not project an image;
the fourth is the essence of the mind,
which alone constitutes the fruit of valid cognition.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"These four divisions may be subsumed into three."
Fourth, they are subsumed under the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti*).
Alternatively, they are subsumed as two,
because the latter three are all of the nature of being cognitive subjects (*ālambaka*).
All are subsumed under the category of "seeing.
This term "seeing" carries the meaning of that which is capable of cognition.
Alternatively, they may be subsumed as a single entity because there is no distinction between them.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"Due to the attachment of one's own mind..."
The mind appears as external objects;
what is seen therein does not exist.
Therefore, it is said that there is "mind-only."
Thus, in various places,
it is taught that there is only one mind;
this refers to the expression "one mind."
This is also because it includes the mental factors (*caitta*).
The commentary explains:
"In this way, in each and every instance, there is only a single mind."
Because external objects do not exist,
there is only the single mind; yet,
due to internal grasping, [this delusion arises].
It manifests as if it were external objects;
yet there are certainly no external objects,
for we maintain that there is only one's own mind.
Because they are not separate from the mind,
they are collectively termed "one consciousness.
Mental factors (caitta) are associated with the mind (citta).
Form-dharmas are transformations of the mind;
True Suchness is the actual nature of consciousness.
Furthermore, both are not separate from consciousness.
These are both termed "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*).
Furthermore, the *Qingliang ji* (Record of Qingliang) cites the *Śāstra* to explain the fourth [part], the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).
If this did not exist,
who would realize the third [moment]? Since the mental factors are identical, [how could there be realization?]
Because they should all be realized.
The commentary states:
the aspect of seeing (darśana-bhāga) is a part of the mind (citta).
There must be a self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).
Since the self-cognizing is a portion of the mind,
there ought to be a fourth cognition to cognize it.
The treatise further states:
"The self-verifying portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) should have no result,
for it is that which performs the act of measuring."
Because all possess results.
The commentary states:
the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is the means of cognition.
There must be a fruit of self-realization;
the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) of the measure of self-realization must have a fourth fruit.
Fearing that the opponent might claim that the "seeing-part" (darśana-bhāga) is instead used as the third fruit,
the subsequent treatise states:
The seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) should not be regarded as the third fruit,
because the seeing-part is sometimes subsumed under non-valid cognition (apramāṇa).
For this reason, the seeing-part does not realize the third [fruit].
The realization of its own essence must be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore,
the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) are common to all three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The three means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are:
direct perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna).
It is not a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). That is to say, at the time of clearly seeing the characteristics of the object-condition,
it may be either a valid cognition or not a valid cognition.

It is not possible for a phenomenon that is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to be the result of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor can it be seen as having the characteristics of its conditions.
This is an inference; furthermore,
with respect to self-reflexive awareness,
it is also direct perception.
Therefore, self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is the essence of the mind;
it serves as the fruit for both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
The objective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), however, is not the essence of the mind.
Because it cannot serve as the result of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*) with respect to its own self-cognition;
nor can the aspect of seeing be cognized in a third [moment].
As for that which realizes its own essence:
Because it must be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Since the third quarter is indeed direct perception, [it follows that the other three quarters must also be so].
Therefore, mutual proof is established,
and there is no fault of infinite regress.
The intended meaning is as follows:
If the seeing-part is taken as the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),
then even three parts would suffice. If the seeing-part is taken as the object of cognition (*prameya*), [then four parts are required].
The fourth must necessarily be the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
If one applies this as a general analogy:
the silk cloth is like the object of measurement (*prameya*).
The measuring instrument is like the capacity to measure;
wisdom is the result of measurement,
which is the self-verifying aspect (svasaṃvitti).
If the foot-rule is that which is employed,
and wisdom is that which employs it,
then what is the thing that uses wisdom?
This refers to the person (*pudgala*).
Just as in the case of the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*),
the person is able to employ cognition.
Wisdom enables one to act as a person;
thus, one is able to further realize [the truth].
It is also like a bright mirror.
The reflected image is the characteristic;
the clarity of the mirror is the seeing;
the surface of the mirror is like self-realization.
The back of the mirror is like self-witnessing self-witnessing;
the face depends upon the back,
and the back in turn depends upon the face.
Thus, they can mutually verify one another;
furthermore, copper can serve as a witness for self-verification,
for the mirror depends upon the copper.
Copper [mirror] relies upon the mirror.

Compiled by Chan Master Yanshou, Chief Administrator of Yongming Temple, Huiji:

Regarding the essence of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya), what constitutes its fundamental nature? Answer: Its fundamental nature consists of the perceived objects (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the transformed matter (*rūpa*), which are the mind itself.
If the three internal [factors] take the currently active mental factors (*caitta*) as their essence,
a question arises:
Within the state of fruition, one directly realizes suchness,
for which there is no objective sphere.
However, when the four wisdoms take objects as their conditions:
"Does it possess four parts?
He replied:
"It certainly possesses the aspect of seeing (darśana-bhāga), because it illuminates the preceding object."
There is the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) which universally illumines and perceives the perceiving portion (darśana-bhāga);
there is also the portion that verifies the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvitti-saṃvitti-bhāga).
Because it illuminates the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*). Regarding the image-portion (*nimittabhāga*),
the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Regarding these four mental states associated with wisdom as described above:
do they possess the image-part (nimittabhāga) and the seeing-part (darśanabhāga), or not? If they do not, [how can they function]?
It would have no object of cognition;
it should not be called "knowledge. Answer:
The category of untainted consciousness directly illuminates the object before it, because it is free from obstruction.
There is no following after mental transformations;
rather, with an untainted mind, one perceives appearances similar to the objects before one.
It is called "signless" because it is non-conceptual;
furthermore, it is said that its objective referent is inconceivable. According to one interpretation:
In truth, the category of uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) also possesses the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).
All minds and mental factors are termed "conditions" because it is their inherent nature to manifest as resembling their objects;
this is not like a pair of tongs or similar tools that grasp an object through physical movement.
It is not like a lamp and such, which illuminates objects by radiating light;
nor is it like a clear mirror and such,
which illuminates objects by reflecting images.
Because it appears as if it were an object and clearly illuminates it,
it is called "unobstructed."
Not grasping and not calculating is called signlessness;
it is also without distinct clarity.
Its wondrous function is difficult to fathom;
it is called "inconceivable.
It is not that it does not manifest its reflection.
If one says it is signless,
then there would be no division of signs; if one says it is non-conceptual, [then there would be no conceptualization].
There should be no seeing-part;
one would perceive a non-existent seeing,
which would be like space or a rabbit's horns.
It should not be called "wisdom," because it is devoid of conceptual clinging;
it is said to be without the characteristics of a grasper or a grasped object.
It is not that there is no functional capacity for the illumination and perception of an object resembling [the external world].
If it were an uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*),
it would entirely lack the aspect-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).
The Buddhas should not manifest various images, such as their bodies, lands, and so forth;
even up to such conceptual distinctions.
This is merely according to the principles of conventional discourse;
if one were to approach it from the perspective of ultimate truth,
it transcends words and is beyond thought.
Since there is no mutual perception,
it cannot be described as mind or mental factors;
it is free from all conceptual proliferation.
It is inconceivable. There is a sense in which it is non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna).
Because it is non-conceptual,
the suchness that is its object is not separate from its essence.
Just as it illuminates its own substance,
there is no separate objective aspect;
this is non-conceptualization.
If it transforms its objective aspect (nimittabhāga),
then with respect to the object of suchness (tathatā), it would not be a direct realization (sākṣātkaraṇa).
If it is subsequently attained wisdom,
because it possesses conceptual discrimination,
its objective referent is as follows:
Alternatively, because it is separate from the entity,
as with a contaminated mind,
there appears an image resembling the object.
Clearly illuminating by means of conditions is called "taking the preceding object as a condition. Therefore,
this is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
It is certain that there is an objective aspect (nimittabhāga). Question:
As for Sthiramati, for instance...
It speaks of one part and does not establish the characteristics of "view" (*darśana*) and so forth;
now, when Dharmapāla subsumes the four [parts] into this one part.
Furthermore, since the logical force of the argument is identical in not establishing a separate category for the "aspect of seeing" (darśanabhāga),
why do you say that this is not known by masters such as Sthiramati?
Answer: At first glance they appear the same,
but upon careful examination their principles differ.
For instance, Sthiramati establishes only the self-cognizing portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) and does not mention the self-cognizing-of-self-cognizing portion (svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga) at all;
although he does speak of the two portions of the seeing and the seen (darśana-ākāra-bhāga).
Nevertheless, it is consistently determined to be of the nature of the purely imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).
This is but one part among the four parts;
since a part cannot exist without the whole, it exists nominally but lacks substantial reality.
That too is non-existent;
there is only the establishment of a single dependent self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).
Now, although Dharmapāla subsumes the four under one, [the opponent argues that]...
However, it is not called the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*);
rather, it is collectively termed "one mind.
Although these are collectively described as portions of one mind, [they are distinct].
Yet it does not lose the meaning of the four aspects, such as self-realization;
rather, because it is not definitively separate from the mind,
it is collectively designated as "one aspect."
The meaning of establishing the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) separately from those [other portions] is distinct;
even when subsuming the four into the three,
the two internal portions [remain].
Although they take one another as objects,
their functions are each distinct;
nevertheless, that which is taken as the object—
Because it does not lose its own essence,
it is simply termed "self-realization" (svasaṃvedana). Although it is generally termed self-realization, [it is so called for this specific reason].
Furthermore, the meaning of the two parts being mutually conditioned is not lost;
they are not identical.
Dignāga’s self-cognition consists solely of the self-cognition that cognizes the self-perceiving portion;
it lacks the self-cognition that cognizes the self-cognizing cognition.
For this reason, it is not the knowledge and vision of the various teachers.
Question:
Among those [objects] that are transformed, these are the matter of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect). Why, then,
do various masters state that the manifest consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) is called "matter-consciousness" (*rūpa-vijñāna*)?
Answer: The ancient masters say that the manifest consciousness (khyāti-vijñāna) is called the consciousness of form (rūpa-vijñāna).
This statement regarding "form-consciousness" (rūpa-vijñāna) is named after its object;
it is so called because the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) of consciousness transforms and appears as form.
It is called "form-consciousness," yet its essence is actually consciousness,
because it is able to transform into form.
Therefore, it is called "consciousness of name-and-form.
This takes the seeing-portion of consciousness as its substance,
because it is able to take form as its object.
Alternatively, it is called "consciousness of form" because it can transform into form;
furthermore, it is because the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) of form is not separate from consciousness.
It is called "consciousness of form.
This takes the form of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) as its essence;
however, the form of the *nimitta-bhāga* is not actually consciousness.
Because it arises from the transformation of consciousness and is not separate from consciousness,
it is called "form-consciousness" (*rūpa-vijñapti*); alternatively, the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is termed "form."
The seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is called consciousness (vijñāna). This [consciousness] has as its essence both the consciousness itself and its object,
because the seeing-part and the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) belong to the same seed.
This asserts that the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of a preceding moment of consciousness serves as the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for a subsequent moment of consciousness;
that is to say, the objective aspect of the preceding moment of consciousness [is so].
It becomes the object of a subsequent moment of consciousness;
that is, it arises within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) by means of the arising of a function that constitutes its own fruit.
That is to say, the objective aspect (*nimitta*) of the preceding moment of consciousness serves as the reason for the object of the subsequent moment of consciousness;
this is because it takes the focal object (*ālambana*) of the preceding moment as its cause.
It further perfumes the seeds;
by virtue of these seeds, the present thought arises and continues through successive transformations.
To trace the merit back to its source is to recognize that the object of the preceding thought serves as the condition for the present consciousness.
The "self-result" refers to the manifestation of the objective aspect (nimittabhāga).
The "functional capacity" refers to...
It is the seed. This means that because the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the preceding moment of consciousness acts as the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*),
it perfumes and induces the production of its own seed.
Within the foundational consciousness (ālayavijñāna),
the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) of form and so forth that arises as the subsequent moment of consciousness serves as the object for that subsequent consciousness.
From the seeds perfumed by the characteristics of the preceding moment,
the objective characteristics of the succeeding moment arise;
this is called the "objective part" (*nimittabhāga*) of the preceding moment.
It serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the subsequent consciousness.
Question:
How does the preceding characteristic-seed (*lakṣaṇa-bīja*) give rise to the present consciousness?
Answer: Because the aspects and seeds of the views are identical.
Question:
If that is so, why not state directly that the seed is the condition? Answer:
The seeds are causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*),
not object conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the ancient masters asked:
For example, when the sixth consciousness takes such things as a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horns as its objects,
does this perceived object exist or not?
If one says that it exists,
then the holy teachings should not point to this as an analogy for the non-existence of the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).
If one says that it does not exist, then...
Being without object and without substance,
it is not an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); thus, the mental consciousness conditioned by this is deficient.
Regarding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), how can it arise?
If one were to say that this mind has no object-condition, [how could it arise?]
Why does the treatise state that the direct object-condition (sākṣātālambanapratyaya) exists for all cognitions?
If turtles originally have no hair, how could it be produced?
A rabbit fundamentally has no horns;
taking this fundamental non-existence as an analogy illustrates the nature of that which is grasped [as real].
Because both the self that is grasped and the dharmas that are grasped are fundamentally non-existent.
When that cognizing mind is about to take such non-existent phenomena as its objects,
due to [beginningless] time since the past...
By the power of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*),
when [the cognition] arises based on its seeds,
it emerges from the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvedanabhāga*) of consciousness.
The transformed arising of the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) such as the hair of a tortoise,
and the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga) that takes this hair of a tortoise as its object—
these objective and subjective aspects.
It arises from the same seed as the self-verifying portion of consciousness;
since it arises based on a seed,
it is of the nature of dependence (paratantra-svabhāva).
It is not that its essence is entirely non-existent,
for it differs from the hair of a tortoise, which has been non-existent from the very beginning; therefore, it can function as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Therefore, this mind that takes these as its objects can also be said to arise from four conditions;
this applies even to cases such as the conceptualization of a real self or real dharmas apart from the aggregates.
It is likewise so:
apart from the nature of the aggregates,
there is absolutely no real self.
Furthermore, there is no determinate, real dharma;
it is merely that sentient beings falsely cling to its existence.
When investigated through reasoning, [it is found to be non-existent].
They lack any intrinsic nature;
thus, they are like the hair of a tortoise, which has been without essence from the very beginning.
Nevertheless, there remains the clinging to self and phenomena.
At this time when the mind takes these as its object and clings to them,
it likewise, by the power of beginningless false habitual perfuming,
transforms and gives rise to the appearances of a provisional self and dharmas.
This image (nimitta) is of the same seed as the seeing (darśana) and so forth;
it is also dependently originated (paratantra) and constitutes the objective condition (ālambanapratyaya).
Therefore, the treatise says:
"In this way, the grasping at a self [consists in] the aggregates external to one's own mind."
Whether some things exist or do not exist,
all are contained within one's own mind.
All things exist [therein].
The internal aggregates within one's own mind are precisely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect).
If it is said that objects consisting of mere images (*pratibimba*) are of the nature of universal imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), [then...]
Its substance is non-existent,
just like the hair of a tortoise; thus,
this specific portion, the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), is non-existent.
How can the treatise state that all [phenomena] exist within one's own mind?
The above are all the views of Dharmapāla.
As for Sthiramati:
The perceived aspect and the perceiving aspect are of the nature of pervasive conceptual construction;
their essence is non-existent.

Now, it is commonly maintained in the traditional lineage that "solitary images" (pratibimba) are of the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) and are not objective conditions (ālambana-pratyaya).
This is the position of Sthiramati;
according to Dharmapāla, all four parts are the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
Among these, that which is falsely grasped as being determinate and real is precisely what is termed the "thoroughly imagined nature" (parikalpita-svabhāva),
even extending to the "perfected nature" (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
Furthermore, if one stubbornly clings to the nature of the five sensory objects as being real,
this is also termed the "thoroughly imagined" (parikalpita).
However, things such as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit, which are fundamentally without essence,
do not confront a grasping mind and thus are not of the nature of parikalpita (imagined).
Nowadays, there are many who mistakenly identify such things as "tortoise hair" and so forth as the nature of parikalpita;
this is incorrect.

The Difficulty Concerning the Contradiction Between Dream and Waking. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "If, during the waking state, all forms are like dream objects and do not depart from consciousness..."
Just as upon waking from a dream one knows that it was merely mind,
why is it that during the waking state one does not likewise [know] one's own material objects [to be so]?
Not knowing [the doctrine of] Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra). Answer:
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
Just as one who has not yet awakened from a dream cannot know it for themselves,
[it must wait] until the time of awakening.
Only then can one subsequently awaken;
it should be understood that the same applies to objective forms at the time of awakening.
This remains so until the stage of true awakening.
One cannot know this for oneself;
only upon reaching the time of true awakening can one subsequently realize it.
Not yet having attained true awakening,
one constantly dwells within a dream;
therefore, the Buddha describes this as the long night of birth and death.
Because of this failure to understand that the objective realm of form is representation-only,
the seventh [consciousness] becomes the root of the long night of birth and death;
it is capable of causing the arising of afflictions and the creation of karma.
Within the cycle of the three realms,
one must reach the stage of true awakening before realizing that all things are but consciousness-only.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (The Essential Points of Consciousness-Only) asks:
"When various consciousnesses arise appearing as a self and phenomena,

It is also not due to them. If it were due to both,

When the fruit arises, it should not resemble those two.
If it does not [resemble them],

Answer: Both interpretations are acceptable.
That both derive from "understanding" (or "interpretation") is as follows:
All contaminated phenomena (sāsrava) are associated with the seventh consciousness and its two types of discrimination;

Second, because they are led by discrimination,
when subsequent fruits arise,
they all resemble the self and phenomena.
Regarding that which does not arise from understanding:
this refers to the sixth root,

Because they give rise to the various consciousnesses and cause them to be perfumed,
when the subsequent fruits arise,
they manifest in the likeness of the marks of a self and dharmas.
Or, that which is not external appears as if it were external,

This is the eighth external difficulty: knowing the minds of others.
If the Master of the Treatise says that external forms do not truly exist and are merely objects of internal consciousness, then...
That may be so. Furthermore,
for example, if the mind of another person is truly existent,
is it not an object of one's own mind?
The Master said:
"Furthermore, if the minds of such people were able to directly perceive the mental attachments of others,"
That is to say, apart from this person’s mind,
there is a separate mind that serves as the object.
If this person’s mind does not become attached while taking another person’s mind as its object, [then it would follow that they do not perceive it].
Thus, there is an object-field, yet it is not apprehended;
for if it were apprehended,
it would contradict the principle of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra).
If one does not cling to the object of perception,
how then can the knowledge of others' minds be established?
The Master of the Treatise replies:
Although it is said that the minds of others are not the objects of one's own consciousness,
this does not mean they are not direct objective conditions (*ālambana*).
The intended meaning is that while the minds of other persons are said not to be the objects of this person’s [consciousness], they are nonetheless direct conditions.
If this person personally takes another's mind as an object,
they do not attain it;
if they rely upon another's mind as a pledge, they do not attain it.
There is also the knowledge of others' minds that takes as its object a transformed image-part (nimitta-bhāga); however,
this occurs only when it transforms an image-part to take it as its object.
One does not actually apprehend the essence of another;
rather, it is called "knowing another's mind" because the image of another appears upon one's own mind.
One immediately knows that the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of another's mind does not depart from one's own mind,
and is likewise merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
The meaning is this:
when this person’s mind takes another person’s mind as its object,
it transforms and gives rise to a *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect).
In reality, the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) lacks any actual functional activity;
it does not grasp objects in the manner that hands or similar things do.
Nor is it like the sun radiating light that directly illuminates its object;
for when one takes another person's mind as an object, [it does not function in that manner].
It is merely like a reflection in a mirror,
appearing as if it were an external substance;
it is an image within the mirror.
Nor does it possess any real activity;
when taking another person's mind as its object, it is likewise so.
It is not because it lacks the essence of another's mind that it is called "knowing another's mind"; rather,
it is not through direct perception that it knows.
That which is cognized by the subject refers to that which has been transformed by itself.
Furthermore, an ancient master asked:
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds:
it means that since there exists another person's mind, it is known by one's own mind;
that is to say, it is distinct from one's own mind.
If there are the minds of others that serve as objects for one's own mind,
how can it be said that there are no external objects and only consciousness exists? Answer:
That is to say, it takes as its object the color-form of the *nimitta-bhāga* (reflected image) of the sense-faculties supported by external matter;
furthermore, this is not directly apprehended, but is merely based upon that [external matter] as a substantial substrate (*ālambana*).
Just as when one's own visual consciousness takes the color of the vessel-world transformed by the eighth consciousness as its object,

As for the four consciousnesses, such as the ear-consciousness,

furthermore, the ear itself is a transformation of the eighth consciousness, which serves as its substantial basis.
Now, in relation to the five consciousnesses,
it is called "image-consciousness" (*pratibimba-vijñāna*).
Just as the five consciousnesses and others take the objective reality (*bhūta-artha*) transformed by the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) as their object.
Nor is it directly apprehended;
although it does serve as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it constitutes only a remote object-condition.
If knowing things as they truly are is the domain of the Buddha,

"The two types of knowledge [operate] with respect to their objects."
Each, being shrouded by ignorance, does not know the sphere of the ineffable that is the range of the Buddha's conduct.

it is the wondrous principle of True Suchness (tathatā).

these two types of knowledge.
