there are immeasurable types of the "highest mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*).
If even the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is thus,
how much more so the rest?
It is like complying with the perceptions of the blind.
Various [people] point to milk;
yet the blind, hearing different descriptions, dispute over its white color—
how could that be the milk itself?
The various masters did not comprehend this meaning;
each adhered to a single passage and gave rise to disputes based on their own views.
They mutually assert what is right and what is wrong;
they believe one thing and disbelieve another.
How vast and chaotic this is!
It is not known which of these is correct.
Regarding the three worldly views and those who refute them,
there is scriptural evidence.
If all such judgments are based on the two truths according to worldly sentiment (*sāṃvṛta-satya*),
and there is no textual evidence to support them,
they are entirely false views.
This means that they are the same as those non-Buddhists;
they are not subsumed within the two truths.
As for "those who follow conventional wisdom":
"Sentiment" refers to the two truths;
both are conventional. If one awakens to the principle of the truths, [they are no longer such].
Only then can it be considered true;
what is true is singular.
It is like the five hundred bhikṣus, each of whom spoke of the cause of the body.
The causes of the body are manifold,
whereas the correct principle is singular.
As the Sūtra says:
What is perceived by the minds of worldly people is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
What is perceived by the minds of those who have transcended the world...
This is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
To speak in this manner is precisely to accord with the two truths of conventional sentiment and wisdom (*jñāna*).
Regarding "following wisdom":
when a noble one awakens to the principle,
they do not merely perceive the truth.
It is also able to comprehend the conventional,
just as when the eyes are cleared of cataracts,
one sees both forms and space.
Furthermore, it is like one who has entered meditative absorption:
at the time of emerging from contemplation,
the body feels light and the mind feels expansive.
Like light clouds gathering in the sky,
it is already different from the distracted mind;
how much more so for one who has realized the truth yet does not comprehend the conventional?
The Abhidharma states:
"Small clouds produce obstruction;
great clouds produce obstruction."
The untainted [wisdom] becomes ever more profound,
and mundane wisdom becomes increasingly pure.
Thus, a verse in the Sūtra says:
Ordinary people move through the world without knowing the true nature of the world;
the Tathāgata moves through the world [knowing it].
To clearly understand the characteristics of the world—
this is the two truths according to wisdom.
If one understands these three meanings, [one attains realization].
Although various [teachings] are explained in the sūtras and śāstras,
with respect to each individual truth (satya), they are as follows.
All [of these] fully possess the three meanings.
Regarding the second point, which correctly elucidates the two truths,
I have summarized the essential meaning for the sake of brevity.

It is sufficient for the purpose of the meaning to take the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and ignorance and the twelve links of dependent origination as the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
However, people are coarse and shallow;
they do not perceive its profound subtlety and must further expand their understanding.
Thus, the treatise discusses seven types of the two truths;
each of these two truths is further divided into three kinds.
There are twenty-one varieties of the two truths in total.
If one employs the first set of the two truths,
all erroneous views are refuted.
That is to say:
all attachments are utterly exhausted,
like the conflagration at the end of an eon.
Not even a single mustard seed is left behind;
how much more so the various truths laid out thereafter, which emerge beyond the scope of the text and are no longer within the reach of worldly estimation.
Regarding what are called the seven kinds of two truths:
first, that which exists substantially is the conventional truth,
and the cessation of that which exists substantially is the ultimate truth.
Second, illusory existence is the conventional;
the emptiness of that illusory existence is the ultimate.
Third, illusory existence is the conventional.
Thus, the emptiness and non-emptiness of illusory existence together constitute the truth.
Fourth, illusory existence is the conventional;
illusory existence is itself both empty and non-empty.
All phenomena take emptiness and non-emptiness as their ultimate reality.
Fifth, that which exists like an illusion and that which is illusory existence are both empty; these are all termed the conventional.
Non-existence and non-emptiness constitute the ultimate reality.
Sixth, that which is illusory existence and illusory existence as emptiness are both termed the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
That which is neither existent nor empty—
that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) tend toward this neither-existence-nor-emptiness— is the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Seventh, that which exists as an illusion and that which is empty as an illusion are both conventional.
That all phenomena tend toward existence and tend toward emptiness,
yet tend neither toward non-existence nor toward emptiness, is the ultimate.
Regarding the two truths of reality: the aggregates (skandhas),
bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus),
and so forth, are all real dharmas.
The myriad phenomena, formed from substantial dharmas,
are therefore called the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). This refers to the cultivation of the path through skillful means.
Only after extinguishing these conventional [distinctions] can one attain the realization of the ultimate truth.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
Emptiness is form, and form is emptiness.
Because form is extinguished,
it is termed "emptiness-form."
Because one does not extinguish form,
one regards it as the emptiness of form;
this is like having no medicine within an illness.
Within words there is no bodhi; this is the meaning of all [teachings].
This constitutes the characteristics of the two truths in terms of ultimate reality.
In terms of this, there are likewise three meanings— such as those corresponding to sentiment, wisdom, and so forth—
which may be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the two truths of the illusory existence and emptiness:
This refutes the previous position.
Why? Because in reality, time exists while the True [Nature] does not.
If cessation exists while the conventional does not,
the meaning of the two truths cannot be established. If one clarifies that [things] exist as illusions, [then the two truths are preserved].
That which exists as an illusion is the conventional;
that the existence of an illusion cannot be apprehended is the ultimate within the conventional.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Form itself is emptiness;
emptiness itself is form."
The identity of emptiness and form establishes the meaning of the two truths;
this is called the two truths of the illusory existence.
In terms of this, there are also three meanings: that which accords with sentiment, that which accords with both sentiment and wisdom, and that which accords with wisdom alone.
One should distinguish them according to the degree of wisdom.
What are they? There is indeed wisdom that conforms [to reality].
Illuminating the ultimate truth is no different from this;
it differs only in that it illuminates the conventional according to wisdom.
Why is this? Because the person of comprehensive understanding is skillful in entering contemplation of the ultimate,
and is likewise skillful in the localized illumination of the conventional.
Just as the hundred rivers converge in the ocean,
their flavors become indistinguishable; yet when they are again confined and return to their sources, they are distinct once more.
Rivers and streams differ;
these are worldly phenomena.
To perceive their differences is not a cause for doubt.
This is indeed the principle of the Dharma;
it cannot be otherwise. It simply proceeds from those who have attained thorough understanding to manifest in provisional forms.
Furthermore, these differ from person to person and can be understood through one's own insight;
this may be illustrated by way of the Tripiṭaka.
Emerging from the provisional should also be understood in this way.
Regarding the two truths of the emptiness and non-emptiness of illusions:
The conventional is no different from before;
however, the ultimate consists of three distinct types.
First, the conventional conforms to the three ultimates.
This immediately constitutes three kinds of the two truths.
What are their characteristics?
As explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, they are neither outflows (*āsrava*) nor non-outflows (*anāsrava*).
The first person says: "It is neither outflow (āsrava) nor mundane;
it is not non-outflow, for it dispels attachment. Why is this so?"
The practitioner gives rise to attachment by taking the untainted as an object,
just as one gives rise to latent tendencies by taking cessation as an object;
having thus broken his mind, he returns to enter the untainted.
This constitutes one set of the two truths.
Next, when a person hears that it is neither outflowing nor non-outflowing,
they consider this to be the avoidance of the two extremes.
This separately reveals the Middle Way;
as the Middle Way is the truth,
this is yet another formulation of the two truths.
Furthermore, when a person hears that something is neither with-outflows nor without-outflows,
they immediately understand this "double negation," which directly reveals the Middle Way.
The dharma-realm of the Middle Way possesses vast power and function,
equal in extent to empty space.
All dharmas tend toward that which is neither with outflows nor without outflows.
This is yet another instance of the two truths.
As the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says:
Śrāvakas perceive only emptiness; they do not perceive non-emptiness.
The wise perceive both emptiness and non-emptiness;
this is precisely the intended meaning.
The followers of the two vehicles are said to be attached to this emptiness;
in order to shatter their attachment to emptiness,
it is therefore called "not empty."
If emptiness is attached to or destroyed,
one merely perceives emptiness and does not perceive non-emptiness.
To benefit others, it is said that "not empty" refers to wondrous existence;
thus, one speaks of "not empty.
When those to be benefited hear of "not empty," they take it to mean the *tathāgatagarbha*.
All phenomena tend toward the Tathāgatagarbha;
when categorized according to the empty and the non-empty,
there are thus three kinds of two truths.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "all dharmas tend toward that which is neither outflowing nor non-outflowing," which reveals three distinct types of persons:
first, when a person hears that all dharmas tend toward that which is neither outflowing nor non-outflowing, [they attain realization].
All phenomena do not depart from emptiness;
they circulate throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
yet remain as the suchness of the jar.
Furthermore, when a person hears of the "approaching" (āya),
they understand the principle herein:
that all formations (saṃskāra) must come and approach in order to give rise [to consciousness].
Furthermore, when one person hears of all destinies,
it is neither with outflows nor without outflows, yet it is endowed with all dharmas.
For this reason, it is called this single conventional reality.
It evolves according to the three truths;
it may correspond to a single truth,
or it may correspond to multiple truths.
Alternatively, facing the inconceivable reality,
he manifests immeasurable forms and postures,
skillfully adapting to the capacities of sentient beings.
Appearing and disappearing to benefit sentient beings,
each instance possesses both that which accords with their emotions and that which accords with their wisdom.
Regarding the three meanings, such as wisdom (*jñāna*):
if one follows the realization of wisdom,
the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) turns in accordance with that wisdom.
When wisdom realizes the partial truth,
it immediately becomes pervasive of the two truths;
when wisdom realizes the non-empty truth, it likewise becomes pervasive.
This constitutes the distinct entry into the two truths; through wisdom,
one realizes that all destinies are the non-empty truth,
which constitutes the perfect entry into the two truths.
The three types of persons differ in their entry into wisdom;
furthermore, they differ in their limited illumination of the conventional.
For what reason do these three persons hear the two truths in the same way?
As for the fact that their understandings differ,
this is the uncommon *prajñā* (wisdom),
which is taught in common with the two vehicles.
This is merely a distinction of depth and shallowness.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"There are bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds [on enlightenment]."
Corresponding with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*),
there are bodhisattvas who, having first resolved their minds [on enlightenment],
sport in supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Purifying the Buddha-lands:
there are bodhisattvas who, upon first generating the mind of enlightenment,

This is precisely that meaning.
That which is illusory existence is the conventional (samvṛti),
while that which is neither existent nor non-existent is the ultimate (paramārtha).
Because existence and non-existence are dual, they constitute the conventional;
the Middle Way, which is neither existent nor non-existent and is non-dual, constitutes the ultimate.
Upon hearing of this conventional and ultimate, the followers of the Two Vehicles—
None understood it at all;
thus they were like the mute and the deaf.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
I and Maitreya were discussing conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) together with five hundred śrāvakas.
This refers to the teaching of the ultimate truth;
this is precisely the intended meaning.
Even with respect to this, there is that which accords with conventional sentiment.
Regarding "affection and wisdom":
as for the three meanings such as "wisdom" and so forth,
they perfectly enter into the two distinct truths.
The conventional is the same as the distinct;

For others, the distinct is not empty.

to manifest this principle,
one must rely on the skillful means of cultivation.
Therefore, it is said that all dharmas tend toward non-emptiness.

Because there is no deficiency or omission,

Regarding the Two Truths in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao):
it directly expounds the inconceivable Two Truths,
wherein the True is itself the Conventional.
The conventional is itself the ultimate.
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel;
the jewel is used as a metaphor for the ultimate.
This is used as a metaphor for the conventional;
thus the jewel is the function,
and the function is the jewel.
Though non-dual, it is divided into two;
this merely distinguishes the ultimate and the conventional.
From this perspective, there is also that which accords with worldly sentiment.
Regarding the three meanings of emotion, wisdom,
and so forth, the verse by Śāriputra says:
"The Buddha, through various conditions..."
Using skillful metaphors and eloquent speech,
his mind is as tranquil as the ocean;
having heard this, my net of doubts has been severed.
This is precisely its meaning.
Question:
The ultimate and the conventional should be mutually relative.
In what way are they not the same?
Answer: This should be explained by means of four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
The conventional is different, while the ultimate is the same; the ultimate is different, while the conventional is the same.
Thus, the ultimate and the conventional are different yet mutually relative.
The ultimate and the conventional are not different, yet they relate as opposites;
the Tripiṭaka and the Shared [Vehicle] are identical in their ultimate truth, yet differ in their conventional truth.
In the two [truths], the ultimate is different while the conventional is the same; in the distinct [two truths],
both the ultimate and the conventional are different yet stand in relation to one another.
Perfectly round:
the ultimate and the conventional are not different, yet they appear as opposites;
they are not the same, yet they are identical.
If they do not interpenetrate,
then the ultimate and the conventional would be distinct and merely relative;
thus there would be seven types of two truths.
The detailed explanation is as previously stated. To summarize:
the characteristics within the realm are mutually identical.
They do not interpenetrate.
Within the realm beyond, they interpenetrate;
they do not interpenetrate.
The four types of the two truths:
the Separate Teaching’s connection with the Shared is the fifth;
the Perfect Teaching’s connection with the Shared is the sixth.
The *Yuanjie* (Perfect Integration) follows the seven distinct [treatises]. Question:
Why does it not integrate the *Zangzang* (Tripitaka)?
Answer: The Tripitaka pertains to the realm within and is not immediately realized;
it is that which the followers of the Hinayana take as their realization.
A person whose faculties have perished is therefore not considered for reception;
the remaining six are gates of the Mahāyāna.
If one wishes to advance,
one may indeed go; for this reason,
one is received [into the path].
Question:
If there is no meeting when there is no encounter, what is the answer? Answer: [As follows].
"Being grafted" is not the same as "meeting";
even before they have met,
one is already said to be being grafted.
Regarding the discernment of the coarse and the subtle:
in reality there are two truths,
the dharma-gate of the "half-syllables."
To lead those of dull faculties,
one clears away the dung of conceptual proliferation; thus,
the meaning of the two truths is not established.
This dharma is coarse; it is like an illusion, pertaining to the two truths,
and belongs to the gateway of the full letters.
For the sake of teaching those of sharp faculties the true reality of all phenomena,
these three types of persons attain it together.
Compared to what precedes it, this is superior;
one sees that all is merely empty.
Compared to what follows, this is still coarse.
By entering the universal through the particular,
one is able to perceive that which is not empty;
this is what is called "wondrous."
When the teachings discuss principles without their full integration,
they are therefore considered coarse;
by entering the Universal through the Perfect, they are considered subtle and wondrous.
The subtle [truth] does not differ from the subsequent inclusion of the provisional means;
therefore, it is considered coarse.
It is distinct from the two truths that do not include the provisional means.
Therefore, it is subtle.
When the teaching discusses principles without integration,
it is consequently coarse.
The perfect entry is distinct;
its principle being harmonious is subtle,
while being accompanied by distinct expedient means is coarse.
Only the two truths are perfectly complete;
directly and straightforwardly, he has set aside expedient means and taught only the unsurpassed path.
Therefore, it is considered sublime.
Next, regarding the determination of the coarse and the sublime based on the correspondence between [the teaching] and the emotions or the wisdom,
we shall first consider this in terms of the Tripiṭaka.
Upon first hearing the two truths according to their conventional designations,
they grasp true speech as false speech because they give rise to views regarding speech.
Birth and death are vast and boundless;
they lack the influence of the Buddha-dharma.
If one can diligently cultivate the foundations of mindfulness, [one may transcend them].
When the four roots of goodness (catvāri kuśalamūlāni) arise,
at that time both conventional truths (saṃvṛtisatya) according to worldly sentiment are termed "conventional" (sāṃvṛta).
When one gives rise to the untainted [wisdom],
both truths that are illuminated are called "the Real."
From the perspective of those who have attained the four fruits [of the śrāvaka], the true and conventional natures are illuminated by untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna).
These are all termed the two truths according to wisdom.
According to worldly sentiment they are coarse;
according to wisdom they are subtle.
It is like the churning of milk:
it first becomes curd, and once it has become curd, [it proceeds further].
With mutual trust in the nature of the mind,
one enters and emerges from it without difficulty;
thus, one immediately attains the equality of sentiment and wisdom, and of wisdom and wisdom.
By explaining the distinct entry into the universal and the perfect entry into the universal,
he causes them to feel shame for the Lesser Vehicle and to aspire to the Great Vehicle.
Lamenting his own ruined seed,
he thirsted for and yearned for the Supreme Vehicle;
at that time, it was as if curd were being transformed into fresh butter.
As his mind gradually became open and serene,

[the Buddha] accordingly taught him the distinctions between the Separate and Perfect Vehicles, as well as the entry into the Separate Vehicle, in accordance with his disposition, his emotions, and his wisdom.
He clearly explained the uncommon Prajñāpāramitā and commanded him to take charge of the family estate,
including its gold, silver, and precious treasures.
In all matters of coming and going, taking and giving,
he ensures that everyone knows; once they have known these things, [he instructs them].
It is just as when fresh butter is processed into clarified butter;
after a long time, the Buddhas must necessarily speak the truth.

That is to say, according to the dispositions [of sentient beings], there are the conventional and ultimate truths, as well as the conventional and ultimate wisdoms; these are explained as the two perfect truths,
like the transformation of refined butter into ghee.
These are the six kinds of two truths;
though they ripen sentient beings and achieve four flavors, [they remain within these categories].
Therefore, it is considered coarse;
the single flavor of ghee is what is considered sublime.
Furthermore, they are categorized as coarse or subtle.
Although the first two teachings contain elements that accord with wisdom (*jñāna*),
they are entirely based on worldly sentiment (*saṃtīraṇa*).
Because it expresses the thoughts of others,
it is called "coarse";
it enters specifically and proceeds universally.
Although there are [distinctions] such as "according to sentiment" (*anuvṛtti*), they are consistently grouped together as "sentiment" (*anuvṛtti*) and "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
Wisdom is said to be speech that expresses one's own or another's intention.
Therefore, it is both coarse and subtle.
Although the two truths of the Perfect [Teaching] include aspects that accord with worldly sentiment and so forth,
they are invariably in accordance with wisdom.
It is called "sublime" because it explains the Buddha’s own wisdom and expresses the Buddha’s own intentional words.
Question:
Regarding the first two pairs of truths,
they are exclusively in accordance with worldly sentiment.
"One should neither see the Truths nor attain the Path. Answer:
Because they cannot attain the Middle Way,
they are said to follow their own emotions.
Thus it is with all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Amoghasiddhi’s teaching of the Dharma,
although not the Middle Way,
is nonetheless the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
They do not fail to provide the benefits of the three *siddhāntas*.
To judge them in general terms, they all belong to the level of "coarse" [teaching], as they are established according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Next, regarding the clarification of the three truths:
they excel over the previous two types of two-truth systems because those do not clarify the middle way.
Based on the treatise on the middle way attained through the five kinds of two truths,
there are likewise five kinds of three truths, categorized according to the distinction between the specific and the general.
It is neither with outflows nor without outflows; thus,
the meaning of the two truths is established.
That which is with outflows (sāsrava) is the conventional; that which is without outflows (anāsrava) is the ultimate;
that which is neither with nor without outflows is the middle.
In the *Śāstraviniścaya*,
it is merely different from emptiness;
there is no effort within the Middle Way.
Regarding "not being incomplete in all dharmas" and "perfectly entering and penetrating the three truths":
the two truths are no different from what preceded.
It is neither with outflows nor without outflows,
and it possesses all dharmas;
this differs from the preceding [category].
Regarding the differentiation of the three truths:
that conventional truth constitutes two truths,
while in contrast to the ultimate truth, it serves as the middle truth.
It is simply the Middle Principle.
Regarding the Perfect [Teaching] entering the three truths of the Distinct [Teaching],
the two truths are no different from those previously mentioned.
To manifest the true Middle Way is to be fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma.
To perfect the Three Truths is...
Not only is the Middle Way fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma,
but the same is true for the Truths of Reality and the Conventional; the three truths are perfectly interfused.
1331. Regarding the judgment of the coarse and the subtle:
the Separate and Perfect [Teachings] enter into the Common [Teaching].
Because it involves the provisional means of the Shared [Vehicle], it is considered coarse;
because it is distinct and does not involve the Shared, it is considered subtle.
It enters the distinct through the perfect.
That which involves separate expedient means is coarse;
that which is perfect and devoid of expedient means is most sublime.
Regarding the teachings of the five flavors:
The Milk Teaching explains three kinds of the Three Truths:
two are coarse and one is subtle;
the Curd Teaching regards only the coarse as subtle.
Fresh butter and processed butter both consist of five kinds of the three truths;
four are coarse and one is subtle.
This sutra possesses only one kind of threefold truth,
namely the wondrousness of mutual relativity (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This refers to opening up the coarse to reveal the wondrous.
It decisively subsumes all preceding coarse [teachings] into one sublime [truth].
The three truths have nothing upon which they depend;
this is what is meant by the "sublime beyond dependence."
Furthermore, regarding the elucidation of the single truth,
the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra states:
"As for what is called the two truths..."
In reality, it is one;
it is spoken of as two through skillful means, like a drunkard who sees the sun and moon revolving as they vomit.
That is to say, there are days when the sun moves and days when it does not move;
yet those who are awake perceive only the non-moving [sun].
Non-activation is not seen;
activation of the two is coarse,
while non-activation is subtle.
The entire Tripiṭaka is merely a transformation of the two [vehicles],
similar to that intoxicated person;
so it is with all the Mahāyāna sūtras.
The two [vehicles] involve turning back, while the one does not turn back.
Now, this sutra directly abandons expedient means and speaks only of the unsurpassed path.
It does not deviate from the single reality;
therefore, it is sublime.
As for the fact that the various truths are inexpressible:
All dharmas, from the very beginning,
are eternally of the nature of quiescence;
how then could there be any truths?
In this state of chaotic mutual obstruction,
even the Single Truth does not exist;
how then could the various truths possibly exist?
Each and every one is ineffable;
it can be described as coarse,
but it cannot be described as sublime.
It is ineffable and yet ineffable;
it is sublime and yet sublime,
for the path of language has been severed.
If one were to speak of them collectively as "inexpressible," then arising and arising would be inexpressible,
up to and including non-arising and non-arising being inexpressible.
The former cannot be described as coarse;
that which is non-arising and non-non-arising cannot be described as sublime.
If the coarse were different from the sublime, [it would not be so].
When mutual dependence is not fused,
the coarse and the subtle are non-dual;
this is precisely the wondrous state that transcends all relativity.
Question:
For what reason do both the Great and Small Vehicles equally discuss the non-existence of truth? Answer:
The *Śāstra* states:
"One does not destroy the nirvāṇa attained within the minds of the sages for the sake of those who have not yet attained it."
To cling to nirvana is to give rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Just as one might take "non-arising" as an object, this [clinging] acts as a fetter; therefore, it is refuted by stating that there is no truth in such [proliferation].
Question:
If that is so, then regarding the Lesser Vehicle, is there attainment or non-attainment?
Since both are equally refuted,
whether the Mahāyāna is attained or not attained,
it too should be refuted.
Answer: This is not comparable to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna),
where there are still distinct afflictions remaining to be eliminated.
A separate principle can be revealed;
therefore, although it must be refuted once attained,
this is not the case for the Middle Way.
How is it refuted?
Question: If that is so, then...
The Middle Way should have only one true reality;
one should not say that there is no truth. Answer:
For those who have not yet attained [realization],
delusions arise from grasping at the middle;
therefore, there must be no truths.
That which is truly attained exists;
that which consists of conceptual proliferation does not exist. Furthermore, this is according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Regarding the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional, four layers are opened,
forming eight truths in total.
As for the four conventional truths:
First is the conventional truth that lacks substantial reality,
such as jars and basins;
these exist merely as conventional designations.
Yet they lack substantial reality;
they are called "truths" (satya) because they are spoken of by means of designating expressions.
Second is the truth of differentiation according to phenomena,
which refers to the aggregates, elements, and so forth,
in accordance with their respective entities.
The dharmas such as the aggregates are established;
the truths, such as suffering and its origin, are established through three skillful means.
Because they are established by virtue of being realized through reasoning,
the four conventional truths are non-established truths.
This refers to the principle of the two kinds of emptiness;
based on that gateway of emptiness,
it is taught as the true nature.
Because that true nature is the object of internally realized wisdom and is inexpressible,
it is called the suchness of the two emptinesses.
It is merely a conventional designation.
Regarding the four ultimate truths:
first, the truth of the manifestation of essence and function.
That is to say, the aggregates, elements,
and so forth possess substantial reality,
which exceeds the first level of conventional truth.
It is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
According to the distinctions among phenomena,
it is designated as the aggregates (skandha) and so forth.
Therefore, it is called "manifestation.
Second is the truth of the distinction between cause and effect,
namely suffering, its origin, and so forth.
The distinctions between wisdom, abandonment, realization, and cultivation; the distinctions between cause and effect;
and the manifestation of the ultimate truth through the three bases.
It refers to the principle of the two kinds of emptiness;
because it transcends the conventional and is realized through direct realization, it is called the ultimate (paramārtha).
One can realize [the ultimate] by relying on emptiness,
thereby manifesting the reality; therefore,
it is called the "gate of reliance."
The fourth is the truth of the ultimate meaning beyond linguistic expression;
it refers to the single, true *tathatā*,
whose essence is subtle and transcends words.
That which has already been designated as the ultimate (paramārtha) is not truly real in itself;
it is called "real" only in dependence upon the conventional (saṃvṛti).
That is to say, the aforementioned three truths are also described as conventional;
the conventional does not become conventional by itself.
Because the conventional depends upon the ultimate,
the latter three types of the conventional are also called "ultimate."
The profound mystery of the ultimate truth is further verified herein.
Moreover, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
Approximating their circular number,
they are established as the ten truths and so forth,
even down to each individual dharma.
Perfectly interfused and inexhaustible.
Engraved on woodblocks at the Bureau for the Supervision of the Tripitaka in the year Wushen (768).
*Zongjing lu*, Scroll Sixty-Eight.
Compiled by Chan Master Yanshou, Chief Abbot of Yongming Temple:

Now, since it is said that these are provisionally established according to conventional truth, both mind and objects are presented together; when opened, they are divided into two, but when merged, they are of a single flavor.
Now, according to the meaning of "opening," they arise mutually;
there has never been a state of mind devoid of objects.
There has never been a mind without an object.
Generally speaking, across both ordinary beings and sages,
how many objects are there in total?
Answer: Generally, there are three types of objects.
The verse says:
The objective realm does not follow the mind;
the solitary image arises solely from the seeing-part;
the image with substance pertains to both the mental object and its basis.
Regarding the phrase "the nature-seed and so forth according to their respective applications;
as for the objective realm that does not follow the mind":
the "objective realm" (性境) refers to—
"Nature" (svabhāva) means "reality.
It refers to the real sense organs, objects, and the four great elements,
as well as the objective spheres of the image-aspects (nimitta-bhāga), such as the matter resulting from meditative concentration.
Regarding the statement that [consciousness] does not follow the mind:
it is because these aspects of the faculties, objects,
and so forth all arise from their own actual seeds.
Because it does not arise following the seeds of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the cognitive faculty,
that which is "solely a shadow" arises only from the seeing;
here, "shadow" refers to a reflected image.
This is another name for the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect).
For this reason, the provisional *nimitta-bhāga* has no seeds as its accompaniment.
Because it exists only as a solitary [mental image],
it is called a "solitary shadow" (duoying),
such as a flower in the sky or a rabbit's horn.
All phenomena that are provisional images of the past and future arise solely from this.
It arises as a transformation of the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) that serves as its cognitive object; because it is of the same seed as the seeing-part,
it is called "sole-image" (kevala-chāyā).
Regarding the statement that "only from seeing" and "the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) which carries the substantial [object] and penetrates both the mental state and its basis":
this refers precisely to the image-aspect.
Half [of the self-witnessing aspect] is of the same genus as the essence (svabhāva),
and half is of the same genus as the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga); therefore,
it is said to "pervade both the mental object and the essence."

"Affection" (*qing*) refers to the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), which is the subjective faculty; "the fundamental" (*ben*) refers to the objective essence (*svabhāva*), which is the perceived object.
Regarding the phrase "nature-seeds and so forth, as appropriate," it means that they correspond to their respective conditions.
"According to what is appropriate" is not a fixed definition;
it means that among the three types of objects, one acts according to what is appropriate for each.
There are existence, seed,
and realm-attachment.
The three categories,
such as maturation and so forth,
have indeterminate distinctions.
Furthermore, the extensive explanation states:

"As for the objective realm of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), it is that which possesses a real substance and has its own distinct aspect; this is termed the objective realm of intrinsic nature."
These are the five sensory consciousnesses, the eighth mind-king,
and all real forms perceived by the sixth consciousness through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
One apprehends the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object,
unaccompanied by names and concepts,
and devoid of any discursive deliberation.
Only this object is termed a "nature-object" (svabhāva-viṣaya).
Furthermore, when fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) takes suchness (tathatā) as its object,
that too is a nature-object.
Because it functions spontaneously through non-conceptuality,
it is said that "it does not follow the mind.
There are five kinds of such non-following in total.
Regarding "one nature does not follow":
its objective-cause aspect (ālambana-bhāga) and its subjective-seeing aspect (darśana-bhāga) both pertain to all three natures.
The objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) that serves as the focal object is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta);
it does not follow the three moral natures of the subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga), which is the perceiving faculty.
Regarding the two types of non-conformity:
the seeing-part arises from its own seed of the seeing-part,
and the image-part arises from its own seed of the image-part.
Because it does not arise following the seeds of the mind’s perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*),
it is called "seeds not following.
Regarding "affiliations with the three realms not following":
For example, when the clearly discerning mental consciousness takes fragrance and taste as its objects,
those two objects— fragrance and taste—
are exclusively bound to the desire realm.
The clearly manifest mental consciousness (vijñāna) does not follow [the seeds] into the higher realms.
Furthermore, when the eighth [consciousness] in the desire realm takes seeds as its object,
that which acts as the perceiver— the eighth [consciousness]— is exclusively bound to the desire realm.
The seeds of the objects of perception thus pertain to all three realms;
they consist of the six, the eight, and the two consciousnesses.
Regarding those that are bound to the realms but do not follow [the aggregates],
and those that do not follow the four or three categories:
first, as for those that do not follow the five aggregates—
For example, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the five consciousnesses is subsumed under the seeds of those consciousnesses,
while the five objects as their image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) are not.
It is subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
It does not follow the classification of aggregates;
it does not follow [the classification of] the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

The seeing-division (darśana-bhāga) of those five consciousnesses is subsumed under the sphere of mind (manāyatana); the image-division (nimitta-bhāga) of the five sense objects [is subsumed under the spheres of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch].
It is subsumed within the five sense-sphere bases (*pañca-āyatana*). It does not follow the classification of "bases" (*āyatana*),
nor does it follow the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*).

The seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of those five consciousnesses is subsumed under the five consciousness-elements (*vijñāna-dhātu*); the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), which consists of the five sense-objects, is subsumed under the five object-elements (*viṣaya-dhātu*).
It is subsumed within the five objects of experience (*pañca-viṣaya*). This does not follow the three categories.
Regarding its not following the five maturations (*pañca-vipāka*):
For example, the eighth [consciousness] has the nature of maturation (*vipāka*);
its objective referent (*ālambana*) is the aspectual-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) consisting of the five sense objects.
It is not of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*).
It is called "non-conforming to maturation.
Regarding the object consisting of a solitary image (*kevala-pratibimba*):
This refers to cases where the image-part (nimittabhāga) and the seeing-part (darśanabhāga) arise from the same seed;
such is called "solitary shadow" (kevala-chāyā), which arises solely from the seeing-part.
This is, for example, like the sixth consciousness perceiving empty flowers, rabbit horns, or the past and future.
As well as those conditioned by transformation or reflection, those conditioned by the unconditioned, those conditioned by the earth element, those conditioned by dharmas,
or those conditioned by the fruits of meditative attainment.
Extremely remote objects, extremely subtle objects,
and so forth, are all merely provisional images;
these arise solely through the transformation of the seeing-division (darśana-bhāga).
That which lacks its own seed is called "arising from [erroneous] views.
There are two types of "solitary images" (pratibimba).

The first is the "solitary shadow without substance," which refers to the objective aspects (nimitta-bhāga) transformed by the sixth consciousness when it takes as its objects empty flowers, rabbit horns, or the past and future.
This is so. Its objective aspect (nimittabhāga) arises from the same seed as the sixth consciousness's subjective aspect (darśanabhāga).
First, there are those without a real substrate, such as flowers in the sky;
second, there are those with a real substrate that are mere mental images,
namely the sixth consciousness apprehending the seeds and manifestations of the five sense organs.
Since all of these arise by depending upon a substrate,
their objective aspect (nimittabhāga) likewise arises from the same seed as the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga).
It is also called the "solitary shadow" object.
Third, the "conveying a substance" [object] refers to the mind taking the mind as its object.
For example, when the seventh consciousness takes the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth consciousness as its object,
its image-part (nimitta-bhāga) does not arise from a separate seed;
half of it arises from the same seed as the objective essence (ālambana-svabhāva).
Half arises from the same seed as the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) that takes it as an object;
that which arises from its own essential nature (svabhāva) is of an unobscured nature (anivṛta).
That which arises from the seeing-part (darśanabhāga) as its cognitive object is of an obscured nature;
this is because both ends are subsumed within the indeterminate.
Therefore, it is called "penetrating the fundamental nature of feeling.
"Substance" refers to the seventh consciousness's perceiving aspect (darśana-bhāga),
while "fundamental" refers to the eighth consciousness's perceived aspect (ālambana-bhāga).
Furthermore, there is a fourfold analysis:
first, those that are exclusively of distinct seeds and not of the same seed.
That is the objective realm (viṣaya).
Second, they are exclusively of the same kind (sajātīya),
not of different kinds (vijātīya).
The "sole-image" object corresponds to the "three-together" category;
the "object with substance" corresponds to the "with-substance" category.
The fourth is "neither of the two," which refers to fundamental wisdom taking suchness as its object;
for suchness does not arise from the seeds of the seeing-part.
Their names do not belong to the same category.
Furthermore, the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) itself is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta),
yet it is manifested through realization.
Because it is not a phenomenon produced by generative causes,
it is called "not a distinct seed.
Regarding the statement that the nature-seed (prakṛti-bīja) is "according to what is appropriate":
"Nature" refers to the objective realm (*viṣaya*).
"Kind" refers to the category (*jāti*).
This means, among the three types of objects:
Each has its own distinct categories;
now, all must be explained according to their respective applications.
Furthermore, if one distinguishes them by way of the eight consciousnesses:
The first five evolving consciousnesses are,
at all times, exclusively objective realms (svabhāva-viṣaya),
regardless of whether they function reciprocally or not.
Between the two kinds of transformation,
it is only the transformation of causes and conditions;
furthermore, it is of the same kind as the five sense organs.
The sixth consciousness consists of four types.
The first is the clearly manifest consciousness,
which also operates across all three types of objects.
When these five [consciousnesses] share the same objects, they truly take the five sense-objects as their domain;
in the initial moment of sudden engagement (*saṃrambha-citta*), these are real objects (*dharmatā-viṣaya*).
However, if subsequent moments take the five sense-objects as their domain, they then apprehend conventional forms (*prajñapti-rūpa*) such as square, round, long, or short.
These are the "substantial" (saviṣaya) and the "solitary shadow" (kevala-chāyā),
also termed "seemingly with a substantial basis" (sadṛśa-sadviṣaya).
Second is the solitary manovijñāna occurring in the state of distraction (vikṣipta).
It also extends to three types of objects;
for the most part, these are "solitary shadows" (duoying),
as they universally take as their objects dharmas of the three time periods, whether possessing a substantial basis or lacking one.
When taking as its object the currently active mind and mental factors within one's own continuum,
it is an object with a substantial core (sadravya-viṣaya); when taking as its object the five sense faculties within one's own continuum, [it is likewise].
Furthermore, when taking the minds and mental factors of others as objects,
these are solitary images;
they are also termed "objects that appear to carry a substantial essence."
Furthermore, the independent manovijñāna (mental consciousness) takes the five sense objects as its object during its first moment;
it partially takes actual matter as its object.
It is also called the "objective realm" (svabhāva-viṣaya).
Within the three meditative absorptions, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) likewise extends across all three types of objects.
Because it universally takes as its object phenomena of the three time periods, whether possessing substance or lacking substance,
it is an object consisting solely of mental images (*pratibimba*).
Furthermore, it can take as its object the currently active mind and mental factors within itself.
This is the "境 with a substrate" (sābhāsālambana).
Furthermore, in the states of meditative concentration (samāhita) involving outflows (sāsrava) prior to the seventh stage,
the five consciousnesses can also be induced.
Because they take the five sense objects as their conditions,
these are objective realms (svabhāva-viṣaya).
Fourth, the mental consciousness within dreams.
The seventh consciousness has only images-without-substance as its objects; the eighth consciousness has only images-with-substance as its objects.
The mind-king (cittarāja) possesses only the nature-object (svabhāva-viṣaya),
because it undergoes transformation through causes and conditions.
The five mental factors associated with it, such as attention (manasikāra) and so forth, [also possess this].
These are similar to the "object with a substrate" (sābhāsālambana) and the "true solitary reflection" (kevalapratibimba).
Question:
What constitutes the essence of these three types of objects?
Answer: The first is the objective realm of nature;
its substance consists of the five real sense objects.
Because it is accomplished by being endowed with eight factors.
These eight factors are the four great elements.
Earth, water, fire, and wind;
the four subtle elements;
and form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
Speaking in terms of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*):
if one can take as an object [the states] within the contaminated (*sāsrava*) stage,
with the exception of the seventh consciousness.
The remaining seven [objects] all take their own mind and mental factors as their substance.
The second, the object consisting solely of a reflected image (*pratibimba*),
takes the provisional aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the sixth consciousness as its substance.
The objective condition (ālambana) consists of one's own mind and mental factors as its essence.
The third [type of object], the "object with a core" (sadravya),
consists of the provisionally established intermediate image-part (nimitta-bhāga) that arises through transformation.
If it can take as its object, within the state of being with outflows (*sāsrava*),
only the mind and mental factors of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses as its substance,
the *Weishilun shuyao* (Essential Points of the Treatise on Consciousness-Only) records:
True form and true mind are both objects of cognition;
the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) manifested by them is both termed the "objective realm" (svabhāva-viṣaya).
Alternatively, that which is capable of being the object-condition for the mind, yet is not a false attachment, conceptualization, or mental construction,
is called the true mind.
Only when the true mind takes those true objects, such as true form and so forth, as its conditions,
and the resulting image-part (nimitta-bhāga) manifests,
can it be called a "real object" (svabhāva-viṣaya).
If the mind takes as its object the aspect (nimitta-bhāga) manifested by the mind itself,
that aspect lacks substantial reality.
However, because it possesses a substantial basis,
"nature" (xing) refers to the essence (ti).
That whose essential nature is real is called an objective sphere (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).
As for "sole reflection" (*pratibimba-mātra*):
"Solitary" means "single.
It is single in having a reflected image.
Since it lacks an essential nature,
its characteristic is termed "solitary," just like the characteristics of a tortoise's hair or a barren woman's son.
Alternatively, although there may be a substantial image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*),
it cannot permeate the seeds of that substance; thus,
in relation to the substance, it lacks efficacy.
There is only a provisional reflection,
which is also called "solitary," just as the discriminating mind takes the marks of the unconditioned as its object.
The same applies to the mental factors associated with the eighth consciousness;
the others should be understood accordingly.
As for objects that possess a substantial core:
As for "substance" (*zhì*),
the *Zhouyi* says it refers to "form and body."
As for the "sash" (dai),
the *Shuowen Jiezi* calls it the "girdle" (shen);
the girdle refers to that which binds.
Furthermore, according to the local dialect,
"dai" (帶) means "to proceed. Thus, what is now called "dai-shitsu" (帶質) [is explained as] "proceeding toward the essence."
The meaning applies to both cases.
According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*,
it refers to the sense of "clinging to" or "adhering closely."
It is like a sash that binds.
If one follows the local dialects,
the shadow arises dependent upon the substance.
Just as a path exists only because one travels upon it,
so too does this objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) exist.
Although there are perfuming agents, as well as the seeds of their own nature and substance,
they lack practical efficacy, just like the mental images that serve as objects of cognition.
The mind of the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) has no deliberative function; thus,
it penetrates the fundamental nature of feeling.
"Sentience" refers to the seeing-division (darśana-bhāga);
"original" refers to the objective essence (bimba).
This reveals the manifested images (nimitta) that have been transformed.
The determination of lineage is made according to what is observed and its essential nature;
these two meanings are not fixed.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of objects:
first, the objects of the imagined nature of sentient beings,
which are perceived as phenomena external to the mind.
This is termed "objective realm.
Second is the objective realm of the wisdom of the sovereign powers and functions of all the noble ones;
it is so called because it manifests from the mind.
It constitutes the sphere of wisdom of its wondrous function.
Furthermore, there are two [types]:
first, the sphere of partial demarcation.
Because it is vast and boundless;
second, because only a Buddha can exhaustively know the objects of cognition.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the mind and its objects,
because they are manifested solely by the mind.
When the mind is extended, there is no realm external to the mind;
when the realm is extended, there is no mind external to the realm.
This is because they constantly contain a single flavor.
The second is the realm of the objective sphere.
This refers to the non-obstruction between mind and objects,
wherein concealment and manifestation occur simultaneously.
Essence and function mutually complete one another;
principle and phenomena manifest simultaneously.
Question:
There is no object outside the mind;
there is no mind outside objects.
Why, then, do you speak of "mind" and "objects"?
Answer: This has already been explained at length above;
why is it necessary to insist upon it again?
The one mind has four aspects;
principle and teaching do not differ.
There is the objective realm and there is the mind.
Only then is it established as *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
For example, when the mind takes an object as its condition,
there must necessarily be an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Just as when a mirror reflects a face,
there is an image of the face. The formal argument (*prayoga*) states:
The mind taking an object as its condition is a functional entity;
it must necessarily carry an image of that object upon itself.
This is the thesis and the reason.
The mind faces external objects,
analogous to the way a mirror reflects a face.
Question:
If the objects of wisdom and their respective domains are each singular, how can they be divided into many kinds? Answer:
Wisdom is differentiated according to its objects;
thus, there is the distinction between the ultimate and the conventional.
Objects are established based upon wisdom.
While the distinctions between ordinary beings and sages are marked by their diverse functions,
when one investigates their fundamental essence, they are ultimately one.
As the *Qixinlun chao* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith) asks:
"Are the object and wisdom one or different?
It answers:
The essence of wisdom is non-dual,
and its object is likewise non-dual.
As for the non-duality of wisdom:
It is simply a single wisdom;
its meanings and functions differ according to the point at which truth is known.
That which is called true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) is designated as conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) insofar as it cognizes the conventional realm.
Regarding "the object has no duality":
this means that form itself is emptiness as the ultimate object,
and emptiness itself is form as the conventional object.
Therefore, when one realizes the ultimate truth, one necessarily penetrates the conventional;
when one penetrates the conventional, one necessarily realizes the ultimate. One understands that the conventional has no intrinsic nature.
This is precisely true emptiness;
how could there be before or after?
Moreover, there are no objects external to the mind.
How could there be a mind directed toward anything external?
This is precisely the state where the mind and its objects are blended into a single,
undifferentiated dharma-realm.
Question:
The single mind and the two truths;
principle and phenomena are not false.
Realizing the nature of reality constitutes the ultimate truth;
examining the facts of phenomena constitutes the conventional truth.
Both possess the sense of being "thoroughly established."
Without undermining the gateway of the two truths,
both the Great and Small Vehicles are established together.
What is the meaning of "thoroughly established" (*prasiddha*)? Answer:
That which is established as definitive and cannot be altered.
Following the ultimate truth and following conventional truth each have their own underlying principles.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
First, there is the reality established by worldly consensus;
second, there is the reality established by reasoning.
Regarding the reality established by worldly consensus:
That is to say, all worldly people,
in relation to various things,
apply conventional designations in accordance with them.
Worldly convention and the object perceived by realized wisdom are of the same nature;
that is to say, earth is simply earth.
It is not fire and so forth;
even up to suffering, it is only suffering and not pleasure and so forth.
Pleasure is exclusively pleasure;
it is not suffering or anything else. To state it briefly:
This is exactly so; it is not otherwise.
This is precisely thus.
It is not otherwise;
it is the object of activity determined by resolute conviction.
All the worlds have been transmitted from their original limit through successive succession.
It is a conceptual construction established through mutual consensus;
it does not arise from reflection, deliberation, or investigation.
Only then does one take [it];
this is called the "truth established by worldly consensus.
As for the "truth established by reasoning":
Relying upon direct perception and inference,
up to the point of the knowledge of decisive discernment resulting from thorough investigation and comparison,
it concerns the objects that are practiced and known.
The meaning established and designated by means of the principles of proof is called the reality universally established through reasoning.
Question:
To claim that form exists apart from consciousness is false both in its words and its meaning.
There are no objects external to the mind;
this is established by both scripture and reasoning.
Yet, alas, there remains the habitual perfuming of names and concepts.
The worldly view is tenacious;
unless it is minutely analyzed and exposed,
it will be difficult to establish perfect and correct faith.
As for external forms,

Knowing that its essence is empty,

Answer: Both coarse and subtle forms are transformations of consciousness.
Since external forms are entirely empty once they arise from consciousness,

The nature of form is itself empty;

This is said for the sake of those who have not yet understood.
One must further break down and analyze [the object] until reaching the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*),

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"How is it that the various dharmas, such as form and so forth, which are clung to by other vehicles as being real and existing apart from consciousness, do not exist?"
The form, non-associated formations, and various unconditioned phenomena that they grasp.
Because it does not exist in principle,
the form (rūpa) that is clung to is,
for the time being, of two general kinds.
The first is with resistance,
composed of atoms;
the second is without resistance.
It is not composed of atoms;
that resistant form is certainly not substantially real.
The atoms that constitute [matter] do not exist as substantial entities;
that is to say, all atoms...
If it possesses resistance,

conventional and not real.
If it were devoid of resistance,

Furthermore, if atoms possessed spatial dimensions,

It would then not be substantially existent.
If it lacked spatial dimensions,
it would be like that which is non-material.
Even though they are not formless,
they are transformations of consciousness;
that is to say, when consciousness arises.
Through the power of internal dependent origination,

Because it can give rise to consciousness,

Since it is not produced by external factors,

This serves as the basis for the arising of the visual consciousness and so forth.
These visual consciousnesses and so forth...

It serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
meaning that it can induce the arising of a consciousness resembling itself;

The manifestations of one's own consciousness, appearing with the characteristics of form and so forth,
serve as the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya);
the subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga) arises in dependence upon them.
Because it arises bearing that characteristic;
however, when consciousness undergoes transformation,
it conforms to the magnitude of the object.
It manifests instantaneously as a single appearance;

For those who cling to the notion that coarse matter possesses a substantial reality,

It is not meant that the various forms (rūpa) actually exist as atoms (paramāṇu);

One gradually analyzes and deconstructs coarse material forms until reaching that which is no longer analyzable.
Although these atoms are conventionally designated as such, they still possess spatial dimensions and yet cannot be further divided.
If one further analyzes it,

Therefore, it is said that the atom (paramāṇu) is the limit of form (rūpa).
From this, it should be understood.
All material forms that possess resistance are manifestations of consciousness;

The remaining non-obstructive forms (apratigha-rūpa), being of this same category,

Alternatively, because it is non-obstructive,

All resistant forms manifest as having the characteristic of form; yet when investigated through reasoning, [they are found to be devoid of such characteristics].
If even consciousness does not exist,
how much less so can there be non-resistant form?
It currently lacks any manifestation of formal characteristics.
And it may be described as a truly existent material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*).

conditioned phenomena perish.
Because it does not depend on causes.

If one says there is a form that is neither manifest color nor shape,

rather, it has the mind as its cause.
It causes the color-forms of the hands and so forth, which are transformations of consciousness,

Because it appears to involve movement and expresses the mind,

Vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) is also not substantially existent as the nature of sound,
because a single momentary sound lacks the capacity for signification.
Because a succession of many mental moments is not real,
external resistant form [is likewise not real].
This has already been refuted previously.
However, because of the mind, consciousness transforms and appears as sound.
The continuity of arising and ceasing appears as if it were indicative; thus,

This does not contradict reason.
Since the manifest [action] is truly non-existent,

Nevertheless, it is not logically contradictory to provisionally establish non-informative matter (avijñapti) based on the limits of the wholesome or unwholesome nature of one's intention and vow.
Question:
The sūtras state that there are three types of karma,

Without conflating the ascending and the sinking,

Answer: It is not denied as being non-existent;
rather, it is for the purpose of manifesting consciousness.
When its lack of substantiality is investigated,

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"It is not denied as being non-existent;

Volition that can move the body is called bodily action;
volition that can produce speech [is called vocal action].
It is called verbal action because it consists of two types of volition— deliberative and decisive—
which are associated with the mind.
Because it functions with intention,
it is called mental action (manas-karma).
It gives rise to volitions (cetanā) of body and speech.
That which is performed is called karma,
because it is the sphere traversed by volition that is definitive and decisive.
Because it universally produces the maturation fruits of suffering and pleasure,
it is also called a "path" (*mārga*).
Alternatively, it refers to bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*).
Because it arises from something distinct,
it is metaphorically designated as "action" (karman);
because it is that which volition (cetanā) traverses.
This is called a path of action.
From this, one should know that there is,
in reality, no external form.
There is only internal consciousness,
which transforms and appears as form.
Question:
Are the dissociated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra) substantially existent? Answer: [They are not.]
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) are likewise not substantially existent."
Why is this so? Because acquisition, non-acquisition,
and so forth are not like matter, mind, and the various mental factors.
Its essential nature and characteristics can be apprehended;
it is not distinct from matter, mind, and the various mental factors.
Its functional activity can also be apprehended.
From this it is known that [the self] is certainly not substantially existent;
it is merely a provisional designation based upon the states of form and so forth.
This meditative absorption does not possess a substantial entity or function distinct from matter, mind, or mental factors.
Question:
Regarding the two mindless absorptions...
The maturation of non-conception (āsaṃjñika-vipāka) must possess a real intrinsic nature (svabhāva) distinct from matter, mind, and so forth;

It should not be able to prevent the mind and mental factors from arising in the present. Answer:
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"If there were a distinct, real dharma in the state of non-consciousness that differs from form,
mind, and so forth, and which is capable of obstructing the mind, it would be called the 'meditative absorption of non-consciousness'."
There must exist a distinct, real dharma at the time of formlessness,
different from matter, mind, and so forth,
which is capable of obstructing matter and is termed the "formless absorption" (ārūpya-samāpatti).
Since that is not the case,
how could this be so? Furthermore, it obstructs and impedes the mind.
What need is there for real dharmas?
Even conventional designations, such as embankments and the like, are capable of providing obstruction.
This means that when practicing meditative concentration,
one feels aversion toward the coarse movement of the mind and mental factors during the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for concentration.
One generates the sublime aspirational vow,
restrains the mind and mental factors, and maintains mindfulness of the mind and mental factors.
Becoming gradually subtler and more subtle,
at the time of the extremely subtle mind,
it perfumes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
One accomplishes various types of extremely superior states of aversion and so forth;
because these damage and subdue the seeds of the mind and other factors,
coarse agitation and the like do not manifest for a time.
Based on these states, two meditative absorptions are provisionally established;
because this seed is wholesome.
This meditative absorption is also called "wholesome" because,
prior to it, one seeks the fruit of non-conception; thus,
seeds are perfumed and established therein.
It summons that resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*),
and based upon it, coarse and active perceptions and so forth do not arise;
within this state, [the mind remains].
The designation "non-conceptualization" (asaṃjñi) is established based on maturation (vipāka);
thus it receives the name "maturation."
Therefore, these three dharmas are also not substantially existent.
Question:
The world is established based on conceptualization;
all conditioned phenomena are empty.
Conventional truth arises from the activities of consciousness.
The gateway of non-substantiality exhausts all falsehood.
For instance, according to the sacred teachings,
words and phrases are capable of expressing meaning.
This is proclaimed by the mark of the broad and long tongue and expounded by the wisdom of wondrous observation.
How can both be said to be unreal?
"Are they all empty?
He replied,
"The various sages expound their teachings through verbal explanations."
This relies upon conventional words and letters;
therefore, the Buddha told those studying the Three Vehicles that they should rely solely on the meaning and not on the words.
One provisionally relies on the teachings to clarify the mind;
therefore, both words and letters lack intrinsic nature and likewise arise through the transformation of consciousness.
The *Śata-śāstra* states: "However,
all worldly phenomena arise in accordance with the transformations of one's own mind."
That is to say, there are various syllables that combine to form a name;
furthermore, various names combine to form a phrase.
These refer to such names and phrases.
That which is capable of signifying and that which is signified are both transformations of one's own mind.
All these transformations of the mind exist for sentient beings but are non-existent in principle; regarding them,
the Noble Ones [perceive] as follows.
To know and see according to reality.
How does one know and see?
It refers to those phenomena.
All these are produced by the discriminative activity of the deluded and false consciousness-mind of ordinary beings;
they are provisional and not real,
existing conventionally but non-existent in truth.
In accordance with worldly convention,
it is provisionally said to exist.
Question:
Sounds can be heard;
the dust of form possesses resistance;
thus it may be said that these are transformations of the mind.
If time and phenomena are without marks,
they ought to be substantially existent. Answer:
Since that which possesses characteristics is already empty, how could that which lacks characteristics exist?
Even time has no substantial essence.
Extension and contraction depend on the mind;
beginning from a single thought-moment,
they culminate in the formation of an eon.
If mindfulness does not arise,
then time and kalpas are fundamentally empty;
there is only the temporal measure of beginning, middle, and end.
This is the time when all is merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*).
The *Śataśāstra*, in the "Chapter on Refuting Time," states:
"Furthermore, this implies that everything—whether conventional or ultimate—"
All are established based on conventional designations of provisional characteristics.
Why, then, do you all dogmatically cling to all phenomena as being real?
All are substantial entities.
[Objection:
If all phenomena...
Since none of these are substantially existent,
how can they be clearly perceived as manifest before one? Answer:
Like reflections in a mirror, the moon in water,
a city of the gandharvas,
a dream, and a magical illusion.
The second moon and so forth can be seen clearly;
how could they truly exist?
All that is seen in the world is devoid of reality;
how then can the Dharma realized through direct perception be considered true?
All that is seen during the waking state is not real;
it is the object-conditioned by consciousness.
Like what is seen in a dream—
what is seen by the dreaming mind—
is certainly not real.
The objects perceived by a disturbed consciousness are like a second moon;
thus, although there is no real ontological essence, they appear.
Yet it is able to serve as an object that gives rise to a mind of direct perception; through this,
in turn, recollection is produced.
Since both the preceding and succeeding moments take [the same object] as their condition, it is not a truly existent objective realm;
therefore, one cannot give rise to recollection [of it].
The realization of the Dharma is true;
yet if the Dharma itself is not true,
how can that time be real?
Difficult.
If one takes delusive objects as conditions,
inverted views will arise.
[Objection: "The object may indeed be false, but the seeing must be real.
[Response: Answer.
Since the object is illusory,
