It is just as in a dream.
This refers to the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth;
when perceiving objects such as forms,
one realizes at the time of awakening that both of those things are non-existent.
The deluded objects and inverted minds are likewise thus;
the foolish claim they exist.
It is difficult for the Noble One to know non-existence,
because there exists a perverted state of mind.
Both of these two types are false;
both the non-erroneous object and the mind [perceiving it] should be real.
Answer: This may be so from the perspective of conventional truth,
but it is not so from the perspective of ultimate truth.
Because in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), the mind is beyond verbal expression.
If the mind is beyond verbal expression in the ultimate sense,
how can it be repeatedly said that the objects of the mind are empty?
In order to destroy the grasping at reality,
one speaks provisionally of "emptiness. Once this grasping at reality is eliminated, [the provisional designation is no longer required].
Even emptiness does not exist.
Whether real or empty,
both are intended to dispel attachment.
This is spoken according to conventional truth;
it is not from the perspective of ultimate truth.
Regarding the term "ultimate truth":
This, too, is a provisional designation;
it is established to overturn conventional reality and does not possess a fixed, definitive expression.
This is difficult.
One can say that the mind and its objects, being directly perceived, are non-existent.
Regarding the mind that recollects an object:
how could it not exist? Answer:
If it is not even perceived in the present,
how could it exist in memory? This is difficult to explain.
If all phenomena are entirely non-existent in reality,
how is it that people in the world currently perform good and evil deeds?
If there were neither good nor evil,
there would likewise be no suffering or pleasure;
this would then be a repudiation of all causes and effects.
If one were to deny cause and effect,
there would be no wrong view;
would one not then fear the transgression of such wrong view?
Answer: How strange is this world!
It is so deluded that it is difficult to awaken.
They only know to fear transgressions,
yet do not recognize the causes of transgression; they are ignorant of all that is wholesome and unwholesome.
The causes and effects of suffering and pleasure both exist conventionally;
they do not exist in the ultimate sense.
Relying on the ultimate truth,
I say that [things] are unfindable;
yet I do not negate the conventional.
How does this constitute a wrong view?
It is by grasping at that which exists conventionally as being ultimately real.
Not to accord with correct principle is what constitutes wrong view;
this is the case here.
To destroy the attachment to [the notion of] time,
the various phenomena are briefly explained:
they exist conventionally and are non-existent ultimately.
Furthermore, an ancient commentary states:
Whenever the Tathāgata preached the Dharma during the three periods,
it was sometimes referred to as "at one time."
The three periods of time, the ten periods of time, and so forth,
all arise from the mind that undergoes transformation;
externally, there are no objects belonging to the three periods of time.
Apart from one's own mind,
all phenomena have no intrinsic nature,
as the Blessed One said regarding Maitreya becoming a Buddha.
Immediately, for the listener, there arises a transformation of the past objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) upon their own mind;
the World-Honored One replied:
"From now, after twelve years,
you will certainly attain rebirth there.
These words were heard upon the hearts of those who listened.
Furthermore, the evolving consciousness arises by transforming into the aspect of the future;
the evolving consciousness itself is the present.
In this past time, there was no actual objective realm;
everything arose as a transformation of the mind.
It merely arises as long or short durations according to the limits of the mind; therefore,
time is established based on the mind.
There is no fixed nature;
it is because of the present that there exist the past and the future.
Causes may be extended or abbreviated;
within a single thought-moment there may be a great eon.
If there were no present mind, [these would not exist].
Wherein are the past and the future established?
The seventh fascicle of the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
"In the past, there was a hermit."
He built a thatched hut to withdraw from the world,
extensively studied the arts and crafts,
and investigated the ultimate mysteries of the divine principles.
He was able to transform rubble into jewels and change the forms of humans and animals,
yet he was still unable to command the winds and clouds.
Accompanying the celestial carriage,
I examined ancient charts and antiquities,
further seeking the methods of the immortals.
He then obtained a method for seeking immortality which stated:
"One who wishes to seek immortality must construct an altar and summon a brave warrior."
Grasping his long sword,
he stood at the corner of the altar,
holding his breath and remaining silent.
From dusk until dawn,
the seeker of immortality sat within the altar.
Grasping the long sword,
reciting the divine mantra,
withdrawing the gaze and turning the hearing inward.
He ascended to immortality at dawn.
Having obtained this method,
he was unable to find a worthy hero for several years.
Later, he encountered a man who had previously worked as a hired laborer for five years, enduring great hardship.
Once he failed, he was subsequently subjected to flogging and humiliation,
and gained nothing at all.
Wailing piteously, he traveled along the roads.
A hermit saw him and bestowed upon him a generous gift.
The heroic man desired to repay this kindness.
The hermit said,
"I have wandered for many years,
and it is by good fortune that we have met."
That his extraordinary appearance accords with the ancient diagrams is not due to any other cause;
I only wish that he would remain silent for a single day.
The knight said,
"I would not even decline death;
how much less would I refuse to speak."
Thereupon, the hermit established an altar and received the methods of the immortals;
he relied upon these matters and practiced them accordingly.
After sunset, each reflected upon their own affairs;
the hermit recited mantras.
The knight of chivalry rested his hand upon his sword,
awaiting the break of dawn.
Suddenly, the knight let out a great cry.
At that time, fire descended from space,
with smoke and flames rising like steaming clouds;
the steadfast man quickly led this person away.
He entered the pond to take refuge.
[The father] asked,
"I instructed you to remain silent."
"Why do you cry out in alarm?
The knight replied,
"Since receiving my mandate..."
When night fell and he was in a state of drowsy confusion as if dreaming,
he saw his former master come personally to his side.
Feeling his profound kindness, he remained silent; yet,
struck by the master's violent rage,
he was brought to harm.
He was then seen to be entrusted with rebirth into the family of a great Brahmin in South India;
he underwent birth and so forth, until his emergence from the womb.
He underwent all manner of suffering and hardship;
yet, bearing her grace, he remained silent.
This continued until he was invested with the crown and fathered a son.
Every time he recalled his former kindness, he would reflect on it in silence;
consequently, all the members of his family and relatives found him strange.
He was over sixty years old and had a single son;
his wife said to him:
"If you do not speak,
I shall kill your son;
this is my own firm resolve."
"Now that we have been separated by rebirths, I have but this one son; how could I bear to let him be killed?
Because of this, he stopped his wife.
He then uttered these words.
The hermit said,
"It was my fault."
Harassed by the Māra,
the valiant man was moved by indignation at this matter and died in a fit of wrath.
Thus one knows that what is seen in sleep and dreams,
as well as in the waking state, is solely the mind;
so too are long and short durations of time.
It does not depart from a single thought-moment;
therefore, it cites the time of dreaming to clarify the state of awakening.
Furthermore, in the "Peaceful Practices" chapter of the Lotus Sūtra,
it is said that he dreamed of entering a bronze wheel,
attaining enlightenment, and delivering sentient beings.
After an immeasurable period of time,
it was merely the mind of a single night's dream;
therefore, the verse in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says:
While dreaming, one may think years have passed;
yet upon waking, it is but a brief moment.
Thus, although time may seem immeasurable, [it is relative].
Subsumed within a single moment,
it can be realized that the listener’s own mind undergoes transformations of both long and short durations.
In reality, these are exclusively the present mind and mental factors.
Thus, the *Yìhǎi* (Ocean of Meaning) states:
"For example, at the time of seeing an object..."
This is manifested by a single thought-moment.
At the time of this single thought-moment,
it is entirely composed of hundreds of thousands of great kalpas.
Why is this? For hundreds of thousands of great kalpas are fundamentally formed by means of a single thought-moment.
Since the great kalpas are established through mutual dependence,
they all lack intrinsic nature,
extending even to distant and near worlds.
The Buddhas, sentient beings,
and all phenomena of the three periods of time—
all without exception— manifest within a single thought-moment.
Why is this? Because all phenomena arise in dependence upon the mind.
Since mindfulness is unimpeded,
phenomena likewise dissolve accordingly;
therefore, in a single thought-moment—
Thereupon, the phenomena of the three periods of time are clearly perceived.
Thus, a verse from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons."
Without going, without coming, and without abiding—
thus one understands the matters of the three times.
Transcending all skillful means, one accomplishes the ten powers.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"From the first thought-moment until the completion of an eon,
all arise from the mental conceptions of sentient beings."
The oceans of all lands and their kalpas are boundless;
yet by a single skillful means, they are all purified.
Furthermore, a verse says:
Or they arise from the ocean of the mind;
they abide according to what the mind understands.
Like an illusion, they have no fixed location.
All is conceptual construction;
thus we know that it horizontally encompasses the oceans of lands and vertically penetrates through the kalpas.
All are the single thought-moment,
wherein the past and future limits are severed;
since there are no lands of greater or lesser size, [how could there be coming or going?]
Furthermore, there is no time of extension or contraction;
by means of the single expedient of the gateway of mind-only,
he causes the realms of sentient beings to become entirely pure.
Why is this? Because one knows that objects are merely the conceptual constructions of deluded consciousness,
the mind does not arise.
Because the mind does not arise,
delusive objects do not appear.
Delusive objects not appearing—
In the dharmas of defilement and purity, there is no dependence; coarse conceptualization does not arise, and distinctions of long and short duration are naturally severed.
As for the measures of kalpas—whether extended or abbreviated—as taught in the scriptures:
All of these are skillful means adapted to the capacities of sentient beings;
for those who are timid and weak,
it is taught that attaining Buddhahood occurs in a mere instant.
Or, for the sake of indolent sentient beings,
he explains that the principle of attaining Buddhahood requires passing through incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
In their ultimate unity there is no difference;
the explanations of extension and brevity all return to provisional wisdom.
Furthermore, an ancient commentary states:
"The first expedient means is precisely the realization that all is mind-only."
A single thought-moment and an eon are both produced by the conceptualizing mind; when the conceptualizing mind does not arise, they cease to exist.
Wherein do length and shortness reside?
Being neither long nor short—
this is called purity.
If one does not destroy appearances,
then kalpas as vast as the ocean are boundless;
thus one knows all dharmas.
All lack intrinsic nature;
none are solid or stable;
they arise solely from conceptualization.
If one clings to these as being real,
it is merely a perversion.
Thus, the *Vaipulya-prabhāsa-viśuddha-sūtra* states:
Mañjuśrī said to Ānanda,
"Foolish and ignorant people conceive of the sun as being the day."
Because of a lack of wisdom. Why is that?
If one were to cause this day—
This is the reality;
this is the eternal;
this is the steadfast.
There should be accumulation;
there should not be the past;
there should be only the day.
There should be no night.
Question:
Regarding these three periods of time:
Since it arises from the transformation of the mind,
among the eight consciousnesses,
which consciousness takes it as its object?
Answer: An ancient commentary states:
"It is exclusively the object of the mental faculty."
That is to say, the dharma of "time" is merely a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*).
The first five [consciousnesses] and the eighth cannot take it as an object;
furthermore, the seventh consciousness constantly takes the internal aspect of the eighth consciousness as its object, perceiving it as the self (*ātman*).
Furthermore, because it is non-conceptual,
only the sixth [consciousness] can take it as its object.
Moreover, among the four types of mental consciousness:
Only the clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is unable to take time as its object,
because time is a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*). This refers to the state within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The dream state,
the solitary state, and the state of distraction— these three are all capable of taking objects as their cognitive conditions.
If categorized among the three types of objects,
this is an object consisting solely of mental images (*pratibimba*). Question:
Among the conditioned phenomena within the formations dissociated from mind,
those that appear to possess functional activity should not be separate from consciousness.
Just as the six kinds of unconditioned phenomena lack functional activity,
they should exist as real entities independent of matter, mind, and so forth.
Answer: All phenomena, whether existent or non-existent,
arise through the transformation of consciousness.
The five unconditioned phenomena, such as space and so forth,
all depend upon the transformations of deluded consciousness;
the unconditioned phenomenon of true thusness (tathatā) is different.
This is the nature of pure consciousness;
it is also not separate from consciousness,
even regarding existence and non-existence, or the true and the false.
All natures and characteristics,
apart from the true nature of consciousness-only,
do not exist at all.

Indeed, the Awakened King, in accordance with worldly conventions and by conforming to the capacities of sentient beings, first elucidates the principle of having marks in order to reveal the gate of marklessness;
through skillful means, he opens the way to the ultimate reality.
To provisionally posit activity while realizing non-arising does not accord with the original intention;
it is merely a provisional, intentional teaching.
Within the four conventional truths,
the second— the truth of differentiation according to phenomena—
is established by teaching the three categories of the Dharma-method.
That is to say, the aggregates, bases, elements,
and so forth. Now, wishing to demonstrate that their ultimate convergence is emptiness,
one should first establish them and subsequently refute them.
One must first understand the den before one can overturn the entire nest;
this is precisely what is addressed in the initial section on the five aggregates.
What is the meaning of the "primordial beginning of the four great elements"? Answer:
"Skandha" means "aggregate" (karaṇḍa);
it is also called the "five heaps" (pañca-skandha).
"Skandha" (aggregate) means "to cover.
It refers to the concealment and storage of delusive seeds.
It obscures the true mind.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"As for the aggregates (*skandha*):"
The meaning of accumulation (*caya*).
Furthermore, they are called aggregates (*skandha*) because they bear the burden of affliction (*saṃkleśa*),
just as one carries a load upon the shoulders.
This is explained according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
If one discusses ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
there is not a single dharma that can be aggregated.
Because each lacks intrinsic nature and also lacks functional activity,
the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"You should skillfully understand the four great elements and derived matter.
How does a bodhisattva skillfully understand the four great elements and derived matter?"
Mahāmati, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva trains in this manner.
That which is the ultimate truth is that the four great elements are unarisen;
within those four great elements, there is no arising.
One should conduct such an investigation.
Having completed the investigation,
one discerns the limits of names, signs, and conceptual constructions.
The differentiation of what is manifested by one's own mind,
up to and including, Mahāmati,
those four great elements.
How is derived form produced?
It is said that the moistening delusive great elements produce the internal and external water element.
The great element of the conceptualization of capability gives rise to the internal and external fire element;
the great element of the conceptualization of agitation [gives rise to the wind element].
The internal and external wind elements arise,
severing the great elements of the false conceptualization of form;
the internal and external earth elements arise.
The commentary states:
"The delusion of capability" refers to the calculation that the fire element possesses the nature of being capable of maturing all things.
As for those who sever the false conceptualization of form,
they reckon the nature of being severable as the earth element; yet,
since the four great elements are empty, [this too is negated].
The five aggregates have no master;
therefore, one first contemplates the aggregate of form,
which is composed of the four great elements.
They arise through a succession of mutual causes.
Since there is no sovereign within the four great elements,
who could assemble them to form matter?
Viewed in this way, the aggregate of form is itself emptiness; since the aggregate of form is empty,
[so too are the other aggregates].
What exists within the four aggregates?
One who has well studied the True Reality possesses the foremost pure mind.
Not abiding in a single characteristic,
there are no four great elements that can arise.
Therefore, one knows that all things are nothing other than true awakening.
Thus, awakening to one is awakening to all,
for there is nothing that is not awakened within the encompassing unity of the single mind.
External phenomena are fundamentally devoid of names and characteristics.
All perceived objects and divisions are merely the measure of the mind;
through prajñā, one illuminates that the five aggregates are all empty.
Since the color of the mass of foam is already empty,
how can there be the sensation of a water bubble?
The perception of a mirage is not real.
The movement of the plantain tree is purely empty;
illusory consciousness suddenly has no support.
The great emptiness is profoundly still and unmoving.
When one exhaustively investigates the fundamental source of the four great elements,
even their nature and characteristics do not exist; how much less so, then, can the branches and twigs— the six sense faculties— be said to exist?
What influence could there be?
Since the view of a self-body is not established,
deluded consciousness likewise has no source.
The single true mind;
the divine nature is independent;
it contains the ocean-treasury of the sands of Ganges.
The gateways of immeasurable meanings are all encompassed within this ultimate destination;
herein the principle reaches its consummation.
Without arising for even a single thought-moment,
both person and phenomena are empty.
As the *Dharaṇīśvara-rāja-paripṛcchā Sūtra* says:
The Buddha said:
"All ordinary persons,
regarding the phenomena of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing..."
They calculate this as the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) and become greedily attached to the existence of mental recollection.
Such persons are greedily attached to the phenomena of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Bound by the aggregate of consciousness,
they value what is known, for mind,
intellect, and consciousness are bound together.
Therefore, they run back and forth;
that is to say, from this world to that world.
From that world to this world,
all are bound by the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).
One is unable to know the aggregate of consciousness as it truly is.
The aggregate of consciousness is illusory and unreal,
associated with perversion.
They arise due to the phenomena of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing;
herein there is no truly existent consciousness.
If one cannot contemplate in this way as it truly is, [one remains deluded].
Either a wholesome consciousness arises,
or an unwholesome consciousness arises,
or a consciousness that is both wholesome and unwholesome arises.
This person constantly follows the movements of consciousness;
they do not know the place where consciousness arises,
nor do they know the true nature of consciousness as it really is.
Lokadhara, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should contemplate this correctly in such a manner.
The aggregate of consciousness arises from false discernment;
that is to say, it is produced by various causes and conditions within the phenomena of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
This is because one perceives the notion of a phenomenon where no phenomenon exists.
Because one is greedily attached to the aggregate of consciousness,
one knows that all aggregates do not transcend the mind of the emptiness of dharmas within a single thought-moment.
Therefore, the *Yongjia ji* says:
"To clearly recognize the five aggregates within a single thought-moment" means to perceive them with vivid and distinct clarity.
This is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha).
That which is experienced within the mind is precisely the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha).
The mind taking this principle as its object is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha);
the mental formations (saṃskāra) operate upon this principle.
This is precisely the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), which defiles the true nature;
this is precisely the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).
These five aggregates,
in their entirety, are but a single thought-moment.
As for this "single thought-moment":
The entire body is composed entirely of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
One clearly perceives that within this single thought-moment, there is no sovereign master.
This is the wisdom of the emptiness of persons;
seeing [all things] as like illusions and transformations is the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena.
Therefore, the *Sūtra of the King of Supreme Victory* states:
The Buddha told the goddess Bhadradattā,
"The five aggregates can manifest the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)."
The dharma-realm is precisely the five aggregates.
Question:
What is the meaning of "base" (āyatana)?
Answer: The treatise states that it has the meaning of being the gateway for the growth of consciousness.
One should know that the meaning of "seed" encompasses the meaning of the differentiation of all phenomena;
it is also the meaning of "basis."
Question:
What is the meaning of "dhātu" (element)? Answer:
This is the meaning of establishing the divisions of the realms (*dhātu*),
because they are established by setting each in opposition to the internal, external, and intermediate.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"The meaning of the seeds of all phenomena refers to the seeds of all phenomena within the ālayavijñāna."
It is called a "dhātu" (element).
"Dhātu" has the meaning of "cause," and it also carries the meaning of "maintaining its own characteristic."
Furthermore, it can maintain the meaning of the nature of cause and effect;
furthermore, it sustains the meaning of the differentiation of all phenomena.
Question:
For what reason are the five aggregates said to be exactly five?
Answer: The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
In order to clarify the five kinds of "self-entities" (ātma-vastu):
first is the self-entity of the body's possession,
which refers to that which is comprised within the internal and external aggregates of form (rūpa-skandha).
Second is the basis for the self as experiencer,
which is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). Third is the basis for the self as speaker.
That is, the four formations of the aggregate of perception;
all phenomena, non-phenomena, and the objects of the self—
this refers to the aggregate of formations.
Fifth is the entity of the self as that which is relied upon,
namely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). This is the referent for the characteristic of a self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) as the basis for the body, its faculties, and so forth.
Sentient beings in the world mostly conceive of the aggregate of consciousness as the self,
and conceive of the other aggregates as belonging to the self.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)? Answer:
The characteristic of transformation is the characteristic of form (*rūpa*).
This is threefold: transformation through contact and transformation through impairment.
That is to say, when touched or encountered by hands, feet, or even mosquitoes and snakes,
it immediately undergoes transformation and decay.
Second is that which is manifested by way of direction;
that is, it can be indicated by means of spatial location.
Question:
What is the characteristic of the aggregate of feeling? Answer:
The characteristic of experiencing is the characteristic of feeling.
Due to this feeling,
one experiences the various results of maturation obtained from pure and impure karma.
If it is pure karma, one experiences its ripening as pleasure;
if it is impure karma...
Purifying and non-purifying karma results in the maturation of suffering; [purifying and non-purifying karma] results in the maturation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Why is this so? Because it is through pure and impure karma that the resultant ālayavijñāna is brought about.
It is always associated with the sensation of equanimity;
this sensation of equanimity alone is the actual substance of maturation (*vipāka*).
The two feelings of suffering and pleasure arise from maturation; therefore,
they are metaphorically designated as "maturation."
Question:
What are the characteristics of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha)? Answer:
The characteristic of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is the characteristic of constructing images.
By means of this conceptualization, one constructs various types of images of phenomena according to the objects as they are seen, heard, sensed, or known.
Various verbal expressions arise.
These various verbal expressions refer to the elucidation and discrimination of meanings.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the aggregate of formations? Answer:
The characteristic of volitional construction is the characteristic of formative activity (*saṃskāra*).
It is by virtue of this formative activity that the mind performs its volitional constructions.
This refers to the driving and directing of the mind within the categories of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate. Question: [What is this?]
What is the characteristic of the aggregate of consciousness? Answer:
The characteristic of discerning is the characteristic of consciousness.
By means of this consciousness,
one discerns various objects, such as forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
Question:
For what reason are there only twelve bases? Answer:
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"It is solely by means of the body and its requisites that one can provide for the enjoyment of the six modes of activity in the future."
It is for the sake of being the gateway for growth;
that is to say, just as the sixfold objects of experience in the past and present are sustained by the eye and the other faculties.
The future sixfold activity of experience likewise has the faculties and their objects as its gateways of growth.
The twelve bases (āyatana) are established solely on the basis of the sense faculties (indriya) and their objects (viṣaya),
and not on the basis of the sixfold consciousnesses characterized by experience.
Question:
What is the characteristic of the bases (*āyatana*)?
Answer: It should be understood as being the same as that of the elements (*dhātu*).
According to what is appropriate:
namely, that the eye shall see forms,
as well as their seeds and so forth.
This should be explained according to the meaning.
Question:
For what reason are there only eighteen elements (*dhātu*)?
Answer: The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"By means of the body, its equipment, and so forth."
It is so called because it can maintain the nature of experiencing the six modes of activity of the past and present.
"Body" refers to the six faculties, namely the eye and so forth.
"Endowed with" refers to the six objects, such as form and so forth.
"Experiencing through the six modes of activity" refers to those of the past and present.
This refers to the six consciousnesses.
That which is able to sustain them refers to the six faculties and the six objects.
Because it can maintain the support and the object-condition for the six consciousnesses;
that is, the past and present six consciousnesses, as the experiencers, are maintained by it because they do not abandon their own characteristics.
One should know that there are eighteen;
they are called "elements" (dhātu) in the sense that they are able to maintain their own characteristics.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the eye-element? Answer:
It refers to the eye having previously seen forms,
as well as the ālayavijñāna which is the ripening of the accumulated seeds of that [seeing].
This is the characteristic of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*).
Regarding "the eye having previously seen form," this means it possesses the capacity to maintain the past consciousness that experienced [form].
To manifest the nature of the elements:
that which is presently perceived as form means it is capable of sustaining the object of experience for present consciousness.
To reveal the nature of the elements (*dhātu*) and that which is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the accumulated seeds— the ālayavijñāna—
this refers to the seed of the eye.
Or it is merely accumulated for the purpose of drawing forth the future eye-faculty.
Or it has already matured for the sake of producing the present faculty of the eye.
These two types are called the "eye element" because they are the causes for the arising of the eye,
according to the characteristics of the eye element.
The characteristics of the realms of the ear, nose, tongue, body,
and mind are likewise so.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the form realm? Answer:
It consists of all forms that have been previously seen by the eye.
Furthermore, that which exercises sovereignty over the eye-element is the characteristic of the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Regarding the predominance of the eye-faculty (cakṣur-dhātu) therein:
it means that external objects arise by the predominant power of the material sense-faculties (rūpīndriya).
As it is with the characteristic of the realm of form,
so it is with the characteristics of the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch,
and mental phenomena.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the visual consciousness element? Answer:
It refers to the discernment of forms as resembling form based on the eye and conditioned by forms,
as well as the ripening ālayavijñāna in which the seeds of this [discernment] are accumulated.
This is the characteristic of the visual consciousness element.
As it is for the visual consciousness element,
so it is for the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness elements.
It is likewise. Therefore,
in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) there is no existence, yet in the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) there is no non-existence.
If one is deluded, the emotions of "one" and "two" arise;
if one awakens, essence and appearance are without obstruction.
Thus, the former masters said:
Both the ultimate and the conventional are simultaneously extinguished,
yet the two truths eternally persist;
both emptiness and existence are equally absent.
The single flavor is constantly manifest.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
"One who contemplates the true Dharma..."
Furthermore, how does one contemplate the teachings concerning the aggregates in accordance with correct reasoning by means of the mode of weighing?
This refers to investigation by means of the four principles. What are these four?
First, the principle of dependence.
2. The principle of efficacy;
3. The principle of logical proof;
4. The principle of natural law.
What is called the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*)?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of dependence:
first, dependence regarding origination (*utpatty-apekṣā*).
Second is the dependence of designation.
Regarding the dependence of origination,
it refers to the power of various causes and conditions.
The arising of the aggregates occurs;
this arising of the aggregates must depend upon causes and conditions.
Regarding the designation of dependence:
this refers to [dependence] by means of the group of names (nāmakāya) and the group of phrases (padakāya).
The body of letters (vyañjana-kāya).
The designation of the aggregates (skandha-prajñapti); this is the designation of those aggregates.
One must rely upon the sets of names, phrases, and syllables;
this is called the reliance regarding the arising of the aggregates and the reliance regarding their designation.
That is to say, the aggregates arise in dependence upon origination and in dependence upon designation;
they are designated through origination and designation.
This is called the method of yoga through reasoning;
therefore, it is termed the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*).
What is meant by the principle of efficacy (*kāryakāraṇa-yukti*)?
This means that once the aggregates have arisen,
they possess their own specific functions by virtue of their respective conditions.
Each is distinct: that is to say, the eye can see forms,
and the ear can hear sounds.
The nose can smell odors;
the tongue can taste flavors;
the body can perceive tangibles.
The mind can cognize dharmas;
visible form is the object of the eye and the sphere of the eye's activity.
Up to and including phenomena as the objective domain of the mind,
as the range of the mind, or whatever other such categories there may be.
It should be understood that the distinct functions regarding those various phenomena are likewise so.
This refers to the principles, yogic methods, and practical applications regarding the individual functions of these various phenomena.
All of these are called the principle of efficacy (*kāryakāraṇayukti*).
What is called the principle of logical proof (*upapattisādhanayukti*)?
It refers to the fact that all aggregates (*skandha*) are impermanent.
Arising from a multitude of conditions,
it is suffering, empty, and without self;
this is established by means of the three measures of valid cognition.
One observes according to reality;
that is, by means of authoritative scripture and by means of direct perception.
By means of inference.
Through these three types of valid cognition,
the principles are verified.
All those who possess wisdom correctly grasp it with their minds,
establishing and maintaining it.
That is to say: all aggregates are impermanent by nature,
dependently originated by nature,
suffering by nature, and empty by nature.
And the nature of selflessness—
such as these are called the principle of logical proof (*upapattisādhanayukti*).
What is called the principle of natural law (*dharmatā-yukti*)?
It refers to the causal conditions by which those very aggregates (*skandha*) possess such a nature.
By what causes and conditions are the various receptacle worlds thus arranged?
Earth has solidity as its characteristic;
water has moisture as its characteristic;
fire has warmth as its characteristic.
Wind has light movement as its characteristic.
For what cause and condition [is this so]?
All aggregates are impermanent;
all phenomena are selfless; nirvana is peace.
For what reason does form have the characteristic of transformation and decay,
and sensation have the characteristic of experiencing?
Perception has the characteristic of conceptualizing;
volitional formations have the characteristic of conditioning; consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing.
This is because those phenomena are such by their fundamental nature;
they are such by their own intrinsic nature.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) ought to be thus;
this very suchness (dharmatā) is called "reason" (yukti).
The skillful means of yoga may be just like this,
or it may be otherwise than this.
Or it may not be thus; rather,
everything relies upon the nature of things (dharmatā),
and everything returns to the principle of the nature of things.
It causes the mind to abide in peace and causes the mind to understand clearly;
this is called the principle of natural law (dharmatā-yukti).
In this way, by relying on the four principles to examine the discourses associated with the aggregates,
one comes to know that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inherently so.
All things are thus;
there is not a single dharma that acts as an obstruction.
To realize this is to be without fault.
The affliction of grasping arises;
it exists merely in dependence upon relative observation and functional activity.

they extensively set forth refutations and establishments.
To reveal the principle of true emptiness,
one first clarifies the origins of illusory existence,
ultimately pointing the way back to the ocean of the single mind.
Question:
Regarding worldly phenomena within the body composed of the five aggregates.
What kind of views constitute the tenets of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika),
and how are they reconciled with the tenets of the Buddha-dharma? Answer:
The non-Buddhists do not understand that all phenomena are composed of the aggregates through the harmonious combination of causes and conditions;
whatever they do is entirely the aggregate of consciousness.
Consequently, one clings to the aggregates as having a real self that possesses sovereign control over experience.
It is called the "divine lord" (īśvara).
Within that which appears to be permanent and appears to be a single continuum,
one speaks of a divine nature.
This is the doctrine of the non-Buddhists.
If one understands that [all things] are formed through the causes and conditions of the conjunction of the internal and external,
and are merely transformations of consciousness.
That which appears as an object is the eighth consciousness itself, which maintains its continuity without interruption; thus,
it appears to have a continuous succession.
This is precisely the meaning of the Buddha-dharma;
the non-Buddhists do not understand it and take it to be truly existent.
Deluded regarding the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature,
they are ignorant, clinging to the view of a self.
Question:
Previously, the five aggregates,
the six sense bases,
and the eighteen elements were refuted.
If the seven great elements and the meaning of consciousness are both non-existent,
how can one establish the doctrine of Consciousness-Only?
Answer: First, consciousness is established in order to dispel the [notion of an external] object. Why is this?
If it were not dependent on consciousness,
how could objects be established?
If it did not manifest consciousness, [how could they be known]?
Why does it dispel objects?
Second, because there is a mind of discursive thought (*vikalpa*),
one is able to know names and meanings.
Why is this? If there were no delusion, one could not manifest the truth;
if there were no truth, one could not destroy delusion.
Therefore, one knows that refutation and establishment depend upon oneself;
defilement and purity arise from the mind.
As the *Treatise on the Three Non-natures* states:
Now, in order to establish this dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva),
the principles of its proof are explained;
this nature does not have mere verbal expression as its essence.
Why is this? Because verbal expression must have a basis;
it does not rely on the categories of distracted consciousness.
It is impossible for designations to be established [in that way]. If it were not so,
[it would be impossible].
Since the categories of the basis do not exist,
the verbal designations that are spoken cannot be established. If this is so, then...
Thus, there is no duality of nature.
Because there is no duality of nature,
there is no category of delusion.
Because there would be no distinction between those who are deluded and those who are not, two faults would follow:
first, that [liberation] would not depend on effort.
Spontaneous liberation.
Second, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa cannot be manifested.
Since these two faults do not occur,
one should therefore understand this.
There definitely exists the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
Because this nature exists, it is established as conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
If conventional truth is not established,
ultimate truth cannot be attained either. Why is this?
Because one realizes that the conventional has no intrinsic nature,
it immediately becomes the ultimate truth.
If one were to conceive of two truths, they would not be such.
This is a perverted grasping of false emptiness;
it does not skillfully penetrate correct principle.
Furthermore, if there were no basis in ultimate truth, [the conventional would be untenable].
Why do you manifest the traces of conventional truth?
Although the fundamental and the manifested differ,
they are one in their inconceivability.
As in the *Fahua xuanyi*,
the extensive explanation of the "original and trace" (benji) establishes six types of the original: first,
the principle-original (*li-ben*).
This is precisely the single ultimate path of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
As for "traces," these exclude the true mark of all phenomena.
All other various [phenomena] are termed "traces. Furthermore,
there are both principle and phenomena.
All are termed the "Fundamental";
whether explaining principle or explaining phenomena,
all are termed the "Traces of the Teaching."
Furthermore, the teachings on both principle and phenomena constitute the "root," while receiving these teachings and practicing them is termed the "trace.
It is like a person relying upon a dwelling place.
Thus there are tracks;
by following the tracks, one finds the place.
Furthermore, practice is able to realize the essence.
The essence is the fundamental;
based on the essence, function arises.
Function is the manifestation.
Furthermore, that which truly attains essence and function is called the "root" (ben);
that which expediently manifests essence and function is called the "trace" (ji).
Moreover, that which is revealed this day constitutes the root.
That which was previously explained constitutes the "trace" (jì).
Based on these six meanings, the relationship between the fundamental (běn) and the trace (jì) is elucidated.
Furthermore, regarding the clarification of the fundamental and the manifested in terms of principle and phenomena:
from the fundamentally non-abiding source,
all dharmas are established.
The principle of non-abiding is precisely the true reality (bhūtatathatā) and ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) of the original state of all phenomena. All dharmas...
This is precisely the myriad phenomena of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) from the original time;
by virtue of the true reality (bhūta-lakṣaṇa) as the fundamental source,
they descend into the traces of the conventional world.
By investigating the traces of the mundane,
one immediately reveals the true source;
though the source and the traces differ, they are fundamentally one.
First is the inconceivable.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Contemplate all phenomena as empty."
It is according to its true nature:
it exists merely through causes and conditions,
arising from inversion.
Regarding the second point, clarifying the fundamental and the manifested through principle and teaching:
this refers to the two truths illuminated during the original time,
both of which are ultimately ineffable.
All are termed "the fundamental.
This was taught by the Buddha through skillful means;
it is precisely the teaching of the two truths.
The teaching is termed the "trace.
If there were no foundation of the two truths,
then there would be no two kinds of teaching.
If there were no manifestation of the traces,
how could the essence of the Truths be revealed?
Although the essence and the traces differ, [they are not separate].
The inconceivable is one.
A verse in the sutra says:
"This Dharma cannot be shown."
The characteristics of words are quiescent;
yet, by the power of skillful means,
he spoke for the sake of the five bhikṣus.
Third, regarding the classification by teaching as the basis for the provisional and the real:
taking the teachings received from the Buddhas of the past as the basis,
there arises the practice of cultivating causes to bring about the realization of the fruit.
Through the teaching that elucidates principle, practice arises;
through practice that accords with the teaching, principle is manifested.
Although the fundamental and the derivative differ, [they are one].
The inconceivable is one.
A verse in the sutra says:
"All phenomena, from the very beginning..."
Always possessing the mark of inherent quiescence,
the Son of the Buddha, having practiced the Way,
shall become a Buddha in a future age.
Fourth, regarding the clarification of the fundamental and the manifested in terms of essence and function:
because one originally practiced in accordance with the principle in the past,
the realization of the Dharma-body constitutes the fundamental.
Because one initially attains the fundamental dharmakāya,
the function of the nirmāṇakāya arises from that very essence;
it is by means of the nirmāṇakāya [that this occurs].
Thus the Dharmakāya is revealed;
although the fundamental and the manifested differ,
they are one in their inconceivability.
The Sūtra says:
"Since I attained Buddhahood,
it has been an exceedingly long time."
It is thus; he speaks in this way solely as a skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings.
Fifth, regarding the clarification of the fundamental and the manifested through the provisional and the real:
as for the real,
it refers to the beginningless and remote past.
The actual attainment of the Dharma and the two bodies are both termed the "fundamental"; between these,
there is the repeated proclamation of birth and the proclamation of extinction.
The various provisional teachings manifested in accordance with the two bodies are therefore called "traces" (jì);
they are not the original source of the Dharma manifested in accordance with the fundamental [body].
Thus, there are no intermediate dharmas corresponding to its traces;
it is through the traces that the fundamental reality is revealed. Although the fundamental and the trace differ, [they are one].
The inconceivable is one.
The Sūtra says:
"This is my skillful means."
The same applies to all Buddhas.
Sixth, regarding the discussion of the fundamental and the manifested based on the present:
the preceding teachings have already explained both principle and phenomena.
Even the provisional and the ultimate are all merely traces.
What is now taught in this sutra concerns the principle and phenomena of the long eon.
As for the provisional and the real,
these are all termed "the fundamental";
however, they are not the fundamental origin from long ago that is clarified here.
There is no way to transmit the traces of what has already been said; for if they were not the traces of what has already been said,
how could they manifest the present text?
Although the fundamental and the manifest differ,
they are one in their inconceivability.
As a verse in the sutra says:
After a long time, the Buddhas must speak the truth.
Question:
In the world, there is not a single phenomenon that does not arise from conditions.
How many causes and conditions must be present to give rise to the myriad phenomena?
Answer: Never has there been a phenomenon external to the mind that can serve as a condition for the mind.
However, it arises from one's own mind and,
in turn, serves as a characteristic for that mind.
The *Yìhǎi* (Ocean of Meaning) says:
To clarify dependent origination:
it is like seeing an object;
this object is a manifestation of one's own mind.
Manifesting from one's own mind,
it serves as a condition for that very mind;
through the presence of these conditions, [the manifestation occurs].
Because mental phenomena then arise,
they are called "dharmas arisen through conditions" (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
As the Sūtra says:
All phenomena arise from conditions;
without conditions, they do not arise.
Thus, one comes to know the essential nature of objects.
Emptiness is non-existent.
Now I realize that conditions are not conditions;
there is no arising that is not wondrous.
Yet the essence of dependent origination is quiescent;
its arising is eternally non-arising.
To penetrate this essence is to follow conditions.
That which does not arise yet constantly arises—
seeing it in this way is called knowing and seeing in accordance with reality.
What is meant by "knowing and seeing in accordance with reality"?
If one perceives conditions but does not perceive their essence,
this is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
If one perceives the substance [of phenomena] but does not perceive their conditions,
this is the view of annihilationism.
Now, one perceives the nature [of phenomena] through causes and conditions.
Thus, one does not fall into permanence;
arising dependently within true nature,
one does not fall into nihilism.
This is called "knowledge and vision according to reality.
The reason for extensively analyzing the characteristics of causes and conditions is that one reveals the principle by means of specific phenomena.
This ensures that principle is not isolated;
through principle, affairs are accomplished, and affairs are made to harmonize with and coincide in principle.
However, according to the sūtras and śāstras,
there are four causes and conditions established in accordance with conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Established as conventional designations internally and externally,
they are not without objective aspects (*ākāra*).
As for the single causal condition (*ekapratyaya*):
The treatise says:
First is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*),
which refers to conditioned phenomena directly producing their own effects.
This substance has two types: first, seeds;
second, active manifestations.
The commentary states:
If all seeds of the afflictions have already been suppressed by the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*),...
It never possesses the activity of manifesting as a current state;
although the seed is a phenomenon that functions as a cause and condition,
it cannot produce a manifest state.
It cannot be called a causal condition (*pratyaya*).
Furthermore, it is like taking a mental seed and hoping for the manifestation of form;
this too cannot be called a causal condition.
If the mental seed gives rise to the manifestation of mind,
and the material seed gives rise to the manifestation of matter, and so forth,
these are all dependent origination (pratyaya).
Because this pair applies to both the new and the two types of seeds.
Second, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
This refers to the eight manifest consciousnesses,
along with their associated mental factors,
as the preceding group.
Thereafter, within its own category, it leads and guides [the subsequent state] with uninterrupted continuity and equality.
This causes that [consciousness] to definitely arise.
The commentary states:
"The eight manifest consciousnesses and their mental factors."
The substance of the object-condition is seen only as self-cognition;
this is the general name for the objective consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*).
Excluding matter,
the non-associated [formations], and seeds.
The unconditioned is not of this nature of conditions;
so says the treatise.
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is spoken of only with reference to all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*),
because it is comprised of the opening and guiding [of the way] by what has arisen previously.
"Opening" means the sense of avoiding and the sense of being apart from that place.
"Guide" (nāyaka) means the sense of leading or attracting;
that is, going forward to avoid that place.
"Drawing forth subsequent dharmas so that they arise" means that the preceding aggregate acts as a condition for the subsequent one;
this excludes those that are simultaneous or subsequent from being considered prior conditions.
Because they do not act as an opening or guiding [condition].
"Of its own kind" indicates that it does not have another consciousness as its condition.
"Immediate" (ānantarya) indicates that although what precedes serves as the condition for what follows immediately,
it is not the case that there is an interval between them; it must be immediate.
The phrase "and so forth" indicates the meaning of conditions (*pratyaya*). As for "opening and guiding," it reveals the sense of being a condition.
This causes that certainty to arise,
which clearly manifests the subsequent fruit,
even though it may have passed through a vast duration of time.
As it is said in the sutra: "Even across eighty thousand kalpas,
a preceding visual consciousness serves as the condition for a subsequent one."
Because that subsequent fruit is certain to arise;
this specifically excludes the final moment of consciousness upon entering the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*),
for which no subsequent fruit is certain to arise.
Therefore, this is not a condition;
for although there is the sense of opening,
it lacks the power of attraction.
Question: Since the mind and mental factors are not of the same category,
[how can they be considered homogeneous?]
Just as the eight kinds of consciousness always evolve simultaneously,
their substance and function are each distinct.
How can it be that those arising simultaneously stand in relation to subsequent [moments] and mutually function as conditions for one another? Answer:
The treatise says:
Although the mind and its mental factors always arise together, [they do not necessarily share the same object].
Because they are associated,
they are harmoniously combined as if they were one;
it is impossible to designate them as separate or distinct.
They can mutually serve as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
That which is "harmonized as if one" means they share the same object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, they share the same basis, arise simultaneously,
and are subsumed within the same nature.
They cannot be separated or made distinct from one another;
they do not differ in their modes of activity (*ākāra*), objects of perception (*ālambana*), or bases (*āśraya*) as do the eight consciousnesses.
Because they are each unequal,
they do not serve as mutual conditions for one another.
Furthermore, this excludes only those who have entered the nirvana without remainder.
All other minds and mental factors are equal-immediate conditions,
because their functional efficacy is equal.
Because there is no interval between its own kind.
Third, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):
that is, if there is a phenomenon...
This is associated with its own characteristics, mind,
or mental concomitants.
Regarding that which is entrusted and relied upon, this entity has two aspects: first, the relative; second, the ultimate.
First, the relative.
Second, the remote [object].
If it is not separate from the substance of the perceiving faculty,
it is that which is internally relied upon as the object of consideration by the visual division (*darśana-bhāga*) and so forth.
One should know that this is the direct objective condition (*sākṣātālambanapratyaya*).
Even though it is physically separated from the nature of the cognizing subject,
it serves as the substantial basis (*viṣayabhūta*) that enables the arising of internal mental objects of cognition.
It should be understood that both the remote objective condition and the immediate objective condition exist for all cognizing subjects.
Because it will certainly not arise apart from what is internally relied upon and depended upon,
it is the remote object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭālambanapratyaya*).
The cognitive object may exist,
for consciousness can arise even when it is devoid of an external basis upon which it depends.
The commentary states:
"That which is said to 'exist' refers to that which is not the parikalpita-svabhāva (the imagined nature)."
That which is grasped has no substantiality and cannot produce the cognizing consciousness; therefore,
it is not an object-condition (*ālambana*).
That which serves as a condition must necessarily depend on others;
now, this [condition] must necessarily exist as a substantial entity in order to function as a condition.
"Carrying its own characteristic" refers to the mind and so forth that take [an object] as their focus;
it means these carry the characteristic of this form and so forth as their own.
"Carrying" (dài) means to carry on one's person;
"characteristic" (xiàng) means—
The nature of the essence (svabhāva) does not mean having a formal characteristic (nimitta);
that is to say, when right knowledge and so forth arise.
It arises as the essential nature and characteristics of True Suchness (tathatā),
neither identical to nor different from True Suchness;
it is neither a characteristic nor not a characteristic.
If that which grasps the object of cognition as its own self were to be taken as the objective aspect (*nimitta*), then because it is an object of cognition,
if one speaks of "aspect" (*lakṣaṇa*) as meaning "substance" (*svabhāva*), [it would follow that the subject is itself the object].
There is, moreover, the simultaneous nature and characteristics of the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta),
which also exist as being carried along by the mind. As for these "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa):
The meaning of differentiation, or the meaning of essence and characteristics;
suchness is also termed "characteristic."
The mark of the signless.
Thus the Sūtra says:
"They are all of one and the same mark."
Regarding what is called "the object of direct perception" (pratyakṣālambana) as being without marks (animitta):
if it is not essentially separate from the seeing-part (darśanabhāga) and so forth, [it is the object of direct perception].
This excludes what is transformed by other consciousnesses,
as well as the distinct objects of each of the eight consciousnesses themselves;
it refers exclusively to that which is internally apprehended and relied upon by the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving portion).
This is of two kinds: first,
the conditioned, which is that which is transformed by consciousness.
The first is called that which is internally relied upon for reflection;
the second is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The essence of suchness (*tathatā*) is not separate from consciousness.
That which is named "the object of concern and reliance" refers,
for example, to the self-cognition that takes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and so forth as its object;
all such cases are illustrations of this.
This explains the direct object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The remote object-condition consists of those phenomena that are separated from the cognizing mind.
This refers to that which is transformed by the consciousness of another,
as well as that which is transformed by a distinct consciousness within one's own continuum,
and which serves as the objective basis (ālambana-pratibimba).
Furthermore, that which is the directly perceived object (sākṣātālambana) refers to the seeing-part (darśanabhāga);
it is that which carries its own image (nimitta).
Within this remote [object], it is precisely the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) that constitutes the objective support (ālambana), because it bears the essential nature (svabhāva). Therefore,
it is called the "object of cognition."
Furthermore, the directly perceived object-condition (sākṣātālambana-pratyaya) exists in all minds that are capable of cognition.
Because all minds and mental factors necessarily do not function apart from the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) upon which they internally rely and depend.
Now, within the Mahāyāna,
if one takes a non-existent dharma as an object,
the mind does not arise.
Regarding the condition of the distant object (ālambana-pratyaya):
the cognizing dharma may either exist or not exist.
Because these are external phenomena relative to the mind,
they are like the grasping at a real self or phenomena;
although they lack an underlying essence.
Nevertheless, since the mind also arises apart from those factors,
the *Ālambanaparīkṣā-kārikā* states:
Internal matter appears as if external;
it serves as the objective condition for consciousness.
It is maintained that its aspect resides within the consciousness.
Furthermore, because it can produce consciousness,
the form transformed by one's own internal consciousness serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva),
because it is a dharma possessing substantial reality,
and because it does not take as its object a non-existent entity grasped outside of the mind.
The Treatise says:
"Seeing relies upon that for its arising;
it arises bearing the aspect of that."
To see that birth is entrusted to those [conditions] is precisely the meaning of "condition" (pratyaya).
However, when the mind arises...
Arising while bearing that image is called the "object-condition" (ālambana).
"Bearing" (dai) carries the meaning of "clinging to" or "adhering to."
The Hundred Dharmas Cloud states:
Dharmapāla clarifies that this object of cognition is like seeing a mark.
There is no portion of fixed characteristics,
because fundamental wisdom directly realizes the essence of suchness and does not grasp at characteristics.
Because it is in profound union with the essence of suchness,
it is the mark of being markless;
it is simply the mark of possessing the essence.
This is the meaning of "carrying along" (挟带).
It is also the object-condition (所缘缘). An objection is raised as follows:
If there is a perceiving aspect (darśana-bhāga),
then there is a conceptualized characteristic;
how, then, can it be called a non-conceptualized characteristic?
Furthermore, it is asked:
"Is there no grasper?
The answer is:
Although it possesses the aspect of seeing, it is devoid of conceptualization and lacks a grasper;
right cognition takes suchness as its object.
Because they are intimately embraced and attached to the body as mutual conditions,
there is no further characteristic of characteristics;
thus it is said.
Regarding the aspect of signlessness (*animitta-bhāga*):
the statement that there is no grasper means that there is no conceptual construction falsely adhering to a real grasper.
It is not that there is no internal part capable of being the object-condition for the seeing-part.
Furthermore, it is difficult to maintain [your position]: if you say that there is no image-part (nimitta-bhāga), then...
The *Ālambanaparīkṣā* states:
"It arises depending upon that [object] and bears its image."
Therefore, it is called the "characteristic of the object-condition" (*ālambana-nimitta*). If there were no aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā*) as an objective part,
there would be no object-condition at all.
Hufa said: "There is also the sense of an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya);
although one perceives the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga)."
However, it can arise as something possessing characteristics such as being "conjoined," because it is not separate [from the fundamental wisdom]; that is,
it is the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) of fundamental wisdom.
Because it directly carries the essence and characteristics of suchness (tathatā) as they arise,
it is called the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
It is like the self-witnessing division (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) which directly carries the seeing division (darśana-bhāga).
It is called the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya).
This case should be understood in the same way;
in reality, there is no sense of [the cognition] undergoing transformation or assuming the form [of the object].
Only that which is "carried along" (as an accompaniment) is called an object-condition (ālambanapratyaya); therefore,
it is distinct from the subsequently attained [wisdom].
If it were to take the transformed aspect (nimittabhāga) as its object,
it would not be direct realization,
just like subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna).
There must be a distinction; since it differs from the subsequently attained [cognition],
it is clearly understood that there is a seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) and no image-part (nimitta-bhāga).
Furthermore, all aspects of the subjective vision (darśana-bhāga) possess the sense of "carrying" the objective image (nimitta),
because the image is not separate from the vision.
This refers to the meaning of being "conjoined" (*sahagata*).
There are two types of non-separation:
first, the conditioned aspect (*saṃskṛta-nimitta-bhāga*).
Looking toward the consciousness that is capable of transformation itself,
their bloodlines are connected,
just like father and son.
Therefore, it is called "not separate.
Second, objects such as *tathatā* (suchness), although not transformations of consciousness, [are nonetheless not separate].
However, because these are the substantial entities of consciousness and so forth,
they are said to be "not separate.
Question:
The *Ālambanaparīkṣākārikā* states:
"Internal matter appears as if external;
it serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness."
It is admitted that those characteristics reside within consciousness and are capable of producing consciousness; therefore,
although external objects do not exist, [consciousness arises].
There is internal form that appears as if it were an external object,
serving as the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Since the external aspect exists within consciousness,
it arises simultaneously with it;
for the aspect exists [within it].
How, furthermore, can it produce consciousness and act as a condition for consciousness? Answer:
Just as the visual consciousness and others arise bearing the images of those [objects],
even though they are simultaneous.
There is no obstruction between the preceding and the succeeding,
for they form the principle of the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) through their mutual dependence.
The treatise asks:
Since these internal objective aspects are not separate from consciousness, [how can they be said to exist externally?]
How can that which arises simultaneously serve as a condition for consciousness?
The verse answers:
Because they are determined to follow one another,
they act as conditions simultaneously; or else,
the preceding acts as a condition for the succeeding.
Because it draws forth that functional capacity;
for the objective aspect and consciousness are necessarily concomitant.
Although they arise simultaneously,
they also serve as conditions for consciousness;
yet this is not the case for external phenomena.
Since it is not logically existent,
one must necessarily admit that this faculty's function resides in consciousness and nowhere else.
Together with the objective forms of the external realm,
they have served as reciprocal causes from beginningless time.
In this way, these various consciousnesses take only the internal objective aspects as their object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
The principle is well-established.
Question:
Regarding the "concomitance" that has been clarified.
Regarding this "condition as an object of direct perception" (ālambanapratyaya), does it encompass both the essence (svabhāva) and the function (vṛtti)? Answer: [It encompasses both].
One should apply a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, regarding that which takes a substance as its object while itself being a substance: this refers to the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) taking the verifying-of-self-verifying portion (*sākṣāt-svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) as its object.
The self-witnessing division (svasaṃvittivijñāna) takes the witnessing-of-self division as its object; this is it.
Second, regarding the "function encompassing function":
This refers to the seeing-parts (darśana-bhāga) of the eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (citta-caitta),
which take their own respective direct image-parts (nimitta-bhāga) as objects.
Regarding "the third using the body as its support":
this refers to the fundamental wisdom's seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) taking True Suchness (tathatā) as its object. This is it.
Regarding "the four bodies functioning in conjunction," this refers to the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) taking the seeing portion (darśana-bhāga) as its object.
Question:
Regarding the meaning of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), how are its degrees of intimacy and remoteness distinguished among the eight consciousnesses? Answer:
The *Śata-dharma-megha-śāstra* explains that this refers to the eighth mind and its associated mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
This chapter is thus named.
Whether it be cause or fruit,
the existence or non-existence of the remote object-condition (*pariṣkāra-ālambana*) is indeterminate.
If, within the causal state, the eighth consciousness relies upon the sensory objects of others' bodies, the fine particles,
and the environment of the physical world.
When they take as their objects the transformed image-aspects (*nimittabhāga*) of themselves, they can mutually enjoy one another; thus,
there is the sense of a remote objective support (*parokṣālambana*).
If it were the sense of being a condition for both self and other,
then the five faculties and their seeds would not mutually transform as conditions.
Thus, there is no such thing as a remote object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, where there is the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), there is also the "sustaining dust" (*phu-ch'en*).
The receptacle world may be mutually [related];
thus, the supporting atoms (upādāya-rūpa) constitute a distant object-condition (parokṣālambana-pratyaya).
This is not the case in the formless realm.
Because there is no form (rūpa) that can serve as a support,
there is consequently no sense of the "distant object-condition" (viprakṛṣṭālambanapratyaya).
This is the case when the eighth consciousness itself takes its own three objects as its objective conditions.

This is a detailed analysis within the context of the causes;
however, when one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, [the situation differs].
The eighth consciousness,
when taking its own objects as its objective support, as well as when taking True Suchness (tathatā) as its objective support.
Furthermore, when taking as objects all dharmas of the past and future that lack substantial existence,

This is also the case when taking the bodies and lands of other Buddhas as objects.
It takes the transformed image as its object;
there is also a sense of remoteness.

This applies to the eighth consciousness and its five mental associates within both the causal and fruitional states.
All [of these] possess a distant objective condition (*viprakṛṣṭālambanapratyaya*).

The treatise states:
"In the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),

Because it must support the external substance,
there is also necessarily a distant objective condition (*viprakṛṣṭālambanapratyaya*) during the stage of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
This does not exist determinately,
because it takes suchness as its object and lacks an external substance.
Now it is said:
"Regarding this seventh consciousness in its impure state,
its substance is innate."
Being spontaneously devoid of power,
it must necessarily rely upon the eighth consciousness as its external substrate,
for it only transforms and perceives images based upon that.
Thus, there definitely exists a remote object-condition (*parālambanapratyaya*).
If one considers the state of being untainted (*anāsrava*),
it is precisely the remote object-condition.
Existence and non-existence are not fixed.
If it is the mental state associated with the seventh fundamental wisdom,
it takes true suchness as its object.
Thus, there is no indirect condition.
If subsequently attained wisdom takes suchness as its object,
then there is an indirect condition.
If the seventh [consciousness], when untainted (*anāsrava*), takes the past, the future, or various non-existent phenomena as its objects,
