Question:
For what reason must the seventh [consciousness], when giving rise to grasping within the outflowing realm (*sāsrava*),
rely upon and depend on a substantial entity (*bhāva*) as its objective basis?
For that which constitutes grasping is produced through conceptual construction (*parikalpa*).
That is to say, it does not arise by depending on external matter.
Answer: There are two types of grasping.
First, there are those who give rise to attachment through forceful volition, conceptualization, and deliberation;
for them, the external substance upon which they rely is indeterminate as to its existence or non-existence.
The first is the solitary, scattered mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), such as that which arises independently.
The second is that which arises spontaneously with grasping;
this is the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭamanas*).
The seventh consciousness and its mental factors are co-emergent and spontaneous;
they lack the power to arise by themselves and must depend upon external objects as their basis.
This arises from one's own adherence to a particular position.

Therefore, it should be understood that within the state of the seventh [consciousness] when it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), the existence or non-existence of the remote object-condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*) is indeterminate.
If it were the sixth consciousness,
this consciousness would possess a mental and physical continuum with a sharp and intense mode of activity.
In all states, one is able to exercise mastery;
the external objective basis upon which one relies may either exist or not exist.
The condition as a distant object-cause (ālambanapratyaya) is indefinite as to its existence;
it exists or does not exist depending on the state of cause and effect.
All function with mastery,
whether they arise through discrimination or are innate.
When taking all phenomena as objects,
there are those that arise by relying on a substantial basis and those that arise without relying on a substantial basis.
Because its objective sphere is the most extensive,
the remote object-condition (parokṣālambanapratyaya) is indeterminate as to whether it exists or not.
As for the first five evolving consciousnesses,

because they have not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), their observation is coarse and inferior; therefore, they must rely upon external objects as their substantial support (*bimba*).
Thus, the distant objective condition definitely exists; however,
in the state of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), this does not definitely exist.
Because objects such as the past and future lack an external substance,
within the causal stages of the first five evolving consciousnesses—
Regarding the mutual functioning of the sense faculties,
they must likewise rely upon a material basis (*rūpa*) to arise; thus,
there must necessarily be a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*).
If one reaches the stage of fruition,
their existence or non-existence is indeterminate.
Furthermore, regarding the mutual conditioning of the various consciousnesses:
The eighth consciousness serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the preceding seven consciousnesses;
that is, the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness serves as the object-condition for the five sensory consciousnesses.
The sixth consciousness takes the four parts of the eighth consciousness as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The seventh consciousness, however, relies solely upon the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object-condition;
that is, the four parts of the eighth consciousness serve as its objective essence (*bhāva*).
That is to say, the seeing-division (darśana-bhāga) of the first seven consciousnesses transforms into the object-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) as its object;
thus, the eighth consciousness serves as the objective support (ālambana) for the first seven.
Therefore, the eighth exists in relation to the seven.
That is to say, the eighth [consciousness] serves as the distant object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭālambanapratyaya*) for the preceding seven;
if the seven do not exist for the eighth,
then the preceding seven do not serve as the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the eighth.
Because the eighth [consciousness] does not take the preceding seven as its object,
and because it does not arise dependent upon the preceding seven,
it takes only its own three objects as its objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the Extensive Explanation (*Vyākhyā*) states:
Regarding the definition of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) established by the ancient Mahāyāna masters, they say:
That is to say, if there is a phenomenon (dharma),
it possesses an essential substance; such a phenomenon is termed a "condition" (pratyaya).
That which is said to "bear its own characteristics" refers to the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga);
it is called the "characteristic of the object-condition" (ālambana-nimitta).
The combination of their characteristics and substance is called the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya).
As for the phrase "bearing its own characteristic," it means:
The character "dai" (帶) belongs to the mind;
the character "ji" (己) belongs to the fundamental substance;
and "xiang" (相) refers to the objective aspect.
This refers to the cognizing mind which,
when perceiving an objective referent,
brings forth its own image-part (nimitta-bhāga) that carries the essential nature of that object.
Therefore, it is said that this carries its own characteristic (*sanimitta*).
It was thus understood by the Sāmmitīya school of the Hīnayāna and by those among the Prajñāpāda who do not establish the aspectual division (*nimittabhāga*).
He composed the *Mahāyānasaṃpradāyabhaṅgaśataka* (The Treatise in Seven Hundred Verses Refuting Mahāyāna),
in which he demolished the doctrine of the "object-condition" (*ālambanapratyaya*) held by the ancient Mahāyāna masters, stating:
"If you say that the 'already-characterized' (*jñātalakṣaṇa*) is the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*)," [he continues].
Regarding that which serves as an object of focus:
for instance, according to your Mahāyāna school,
when non-conceptual wisdom takes true suchness (tathatā) as its object, [it does so without conceptualization].
If True Suchness does not manifest as an objective aspect (nimittabhāga),
then, in relation to the seeing aspect (darśanabhāga) of the cognizing wisdom,
it would lack the status of being an object-condition (ālambanapratyaya).
If you claim that fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) takes suchness as its object and likewise possesses an objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga),
this contradicts all the sūtras and śāstras of your own school.
How can this be reconciled?
When the ancient Mahāyāna masters were confronted with this single objection,
they were left without a defense at that time.
For twelve years, no one was able to rescue the meaning of the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the Mahāyāna.
The Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty rescued it, saying:
In our Mahāyāna school, there are two meanings of "carrying along" (dai):
first, transformation-carrying (biàn-dài);
second, simultaneous-carrying (xié-dài).
If it transforms into a representation,
then a representation resembling the substrate arises;
this is the characteristic of the characteristic.
When fundamental wisdom takes suchness as its object, it is non-existent;
if it carries [the object] along with it,
it is existent.
Fundamental wisdom directly grasps and takes as its object the essence and characteristics of True Suchness (tathatā),
without further transforming them into objective aspects (nimittabhāga).
It also constitutes an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
"That is to say, if there is a phenomenon..."
Thus, True Suchness (tathatā) is a dharma that possesses substantial existence;
it is designated as the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya). It is precisely this True Suchness.
This is the object of deliberation for fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*);
it is also called the "object-condition" (*ālambana*). These two terms are spoken of in conjunction due to their mutual influence.
It is called the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya). Here, "object" (ālambana) is itself the "condition" (pratyaya);
this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
It is also like the seeing-parts (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses;
when each perceives its own respective and immediate object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*),
they all do so by "carrying it along" (*upādāya*).
This applies even to the mutual conditioning of the two internal parts;
thus, one knows that fundamental wisdom takes suchness as its object,
even though it does not transform into an objective part (*nimittabhāga*).
Nevertheless, even when one takes the essence and characteristics of *tathatā* as an object by directly grasping them,
it still constitutes an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Those ancient Mahāyāna masters who misinterpreted the meaning of the object-condition were mistaken.
Now, as for the meaning of the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya):
it is that which exists as a substantial entity (dravya-sat) that serves as the condition;
that is to say, this very existent entity itself.
Because this is the object of focus for the mind that takes it as its cognitive support,
it is termed the "object-condition" (ālambana).
Thus say the Mahāyāna masters of both ancient and modern times.
Since you claim that only the true nature (dharmatā) is divided into the object of cognition (ālambana),
you have erred greatly.
To correctly explain the meaning of the objective condition (ālambanapratyaya):
That is to say, if there is a phenomenon that bears the characteristic of having already been produced;
"if there is a phenomenon" means:
This refers to dharmas that possess substantial reality,
thereby distinguishing them from dharmas that are merely nominal and from those dharmas lacking intrinsic nature, such as the imagined aspect (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
A dharma that lacks intrinsic nature is merely an object of cognition;
it does not constitute a condition.
Now, that which acts as a condition must be a real dharma possessing substantial existence,
because it possesses causal efficacy.
That which is able to draw forth and produce consciousness is precisely the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) based upon the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva);
it is a phenomenon that possesses substantial reality.
Regarding the statement "this carries its own characteristic," there are two meanings to "carrying" (*dharana*): first,
transformational carrying (*pariṇāma-dharana*).
That is, the eight consciousnesses have a substantial object (bhāva) as their remote objective condition;
this constitutes the basis of reliance.
Taking this existent entity as its objective essence,
a semblance of that essence arises;
this is termed "transformational manifestation."
The second is "being carried along," which refers to all portions of the real nature (lakṣaṇa) of the objective conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) that are associated with the self.
This is because these portions of the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) are distinct from the cognizing mind (ālambaka-citta).
The cognizing mind directly grasps this objective aspect (nimittabhāga) while cognizing it;
this is termed "grasping by inclusion" (parigraha).
Regarding the characteristics of what has already been spoken of, there are also two meanings.
First, concerning that which is explained with respect to the remote object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) associated with transformation:
That is to say, it transforms into an appearance resembling the objective substance (*viṣaya*).
"Already" (*yi*) refers to its essence (*tattva*).
That is, the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) has already taken on the essence of the original object;
this is the characteristic of the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).
Second, regarding the explanation in terms of that which carries along the direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
It is the already-apprehended aspect (ākāra) that directly carries the objective image within the mind that takes it as its object;
this is the characteristic of the objective image itself,
and it is not the same as the remote objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
When a cognition arises bearing the aspect of an already-past object,
someone might suddenly ask:
"What is meant by saying it bears the aspect of the already-past?"
It has not yet been determined with what kind of previously apprehended characteristic (*pūrvanimitta*) the perceiving mind is endowed when it cognizes.
One should answer as follows:
If it is a remote objective condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*),
it is that which has already transformed and carried the essential nature (*svabhāva*) as its object-condition;
if it is an immediate objective condition (*pratyakṣālambanapratyaya*).
That is to say, it is the already-apprehended aspect that serves as the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for the apprehending part;
furthermore, it is the remote objective condition,
which is the aspect that carries the mental image.
That is to say, it bears an appearance resembling the substance;
if it is the direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*),
it bears an appearance that carries the aspect of the object.
Because it takes the aspect of the object as its immediate support while apprehending it.
Some say that this refers to the "already-apprehended aspect" belonging to the cognizing mind.
This person does not understand the meaning of the object of focus (*ālambana*).
Question: If it is said that [consciousness] directly carries the aspect of the object (*viṣaya-nimitta*), [how is this so]?
As for the transformation that arises with appearances resembling the substance,
which constitutes the two conditions of the proximate and the remote,
these are external material phenomena (*rūpadharma*).
It also establishes the two conditions of intimacy and distance;
for instance, when one uses a mirror to reflect a person,
upon the surface of that mirror—
Moreover, it would also be able to directly grasp the reflection of a person,
because the human image does not depart from the surface of the mirror; thus,
it should constitute a direct object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, from the perspective of the surface of a mirror, the essential nature (svabhāva) of a person outside it should constitute a remote object-condition (viprakṛṣṭālambanapratyaya). Answer:
To simplify what has been considered,
the intention is as follows:
That which acts as an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is...
Only when there is a dharma capable of being the object of cognition and that which is actually cognized can it be termed an "object-condition" (ālambanapratyaya).
Now, since the surface of the mirror is not a phenomenon capable of cognitive reflection,
it follows that both the reflected image within the mirror and the objective essence of the person outside are likewise not such phenomena.
Nor can it be called a "dharma that is contemplated.
Since it lacks the meaning of being contemplated, it does not constitute an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The opponent further objects: "If that is so,
then consider, for instance,
when the sixth consciousness takes as its object a non-substantial phenomenon such as a flower in the sky."
If there were an object of deliberation,
it would necessarily constitute an object-condition (ālambanapratyaya), because consciousness is that which is capable of deliberating.
Answer: He took the note he had been entrusted with and read its contents, which said:
When the mind takes a non-substantial phenomenon as its object,
although there is the sense of something being considered,
it lacks the sense of having a basis upon which to rely.
Since things such as flowers in the sky lack intrinsic nature,
they do not serve as a physical basis for the cognizing mind; nevertheless,
this does not prevent them from being established as objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
Thus, it does not constitute a condition.
For this reason, one must analyze it by means of the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
First: there is that which is the object of consideration.
It is not that which is entrusted;
rather, it refers to the falsely imagined and grasped self and dharmas,
because they lack intrinsic substance.
First, one is concerned about what is being done,
but not about what has been entrusted;
second, there is that which has been entrusted.
It is not something to be deliberated upon;
it is simply that which is reflected in a mirror or water, such as a person.
This merely has something upon which it relies.
And there is no deliberation,
because mirrors, water, and so forth are not capable of deliberating.
This is the third, the "conjunction" category.
That is to say, it consists of the portion of the true nature of all objects of perception (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Fourth is "neither":
this refers to everything other than what is reflected by mirrors, water, and so forth.
Those that do not take it as an object are the others.
Furthermore, "intimate object" (pratyupasthita) has the meaning of being closely attached.
"Proximate" means that it is like the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect),
which is closely and immediately adjacent to the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect).
Because there is no other intervening part,
"sparse" (sū) means "distant" (dūra).
Because they are separated by characteristics,
they are indeed the substantial dharma. Furthermore, it is the immediate object-condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*).
Each has four types. First,
there are those that have a direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*),
which arise through transformation from both the primary object and the mind.
That is to say, the objective image (*nimitta-bhāga*) perceived by the five consciousnesses when they take the five sense objects as their domain is [the first type].
Second, there is the "directly apprehended object-condition" (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*), which arises solely from the transformation of the mind itself.
It does not arise by relying on a substantial entity;

rather, it is the eighth consciousness taking the three types of objects as its objective-image (nimittabhāga). These three possess the status of being direct objective conditions (sākṣātālambanapratyaya).
It does not arise from a transformation of the mind, nor does it arise from a substantial entity;
it is precisely the suchness realized by fundamental wisdom.
Fourth, there are those that have a direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*) but do not constitute the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*);
this refers to the mutual conditioning between the two internal divisions [of consciousness].
Cien said: "If [an object] is not separate from the substance of the perceiving faculty,
it is that which is internally taken as the object of concern by the seeing-part and so forth."
It should be understood that when it is said "that is the direct objective condition (sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya)," if it is for the cognizing subject,
it refers to the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga).
"Being inseparable in essence" means being inseparable in essence from the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga).
This is what it means.
The image-aspect (nimittabhāga) is the immediate object-condition for the seeing-aspect (darśanabhāga);
the seeing-aspect is the immediate object-condition for the self-witnessing-aspect (svasaṃvittibhāga).
All of these are not separate from the essence of the self-witnessing-aspect.
This precisely excludes the distant objective condition (ālambanapratyaya),
namely the fundamental entity (mūladharma), with respect to the seeing portion (darśanabhāga) of the perceiving subject.
Because it is dissociated from the eight consciousnesses;
this also excludes the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by others,
as well as one's own eight consciousnesses.
The respective *nimitta-bhāga*s (objective images) produced by each [consciousness] are,
when compared with one another,
none of them direct [reflections].

Now, we take only the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by one's own consciousness and designate it as "direct" (*pratyakṣa*), in relation to the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) that performs the transformation.
Their essences are not separate from one another;
when there is nothing intervening to create obstruction,
this constitutes the meaning of intimacy.
Regarding the statement "that which is internally relied upon as the object of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and so forth":
the phrase "the seeing-part and so forth" includes,
by way of the term "and so forth," the self-cognizing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) and the fourth part (*caturtha-bhāga*).
Furthermore, fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) taking suchness (tathatā) and so forth as its object—
all these constitute direct objective conditions (sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya). For instance,
consider the image-part (nimitta-bhāga).
The seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) is the immediate objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for the self-witnessing-part (svasaṃvedana-bhāga); the seeing-part,
in turn, is the immediate objective condition for the self-witnessing-part.
The self-verifying part (svasaṃvittibhāga) is the immediate object-condition for the self-verifying self-verifying part;
furthermore, suchness (tathatā).
This is the direct object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Furthermore, it also includes the direct image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*),
which likewise constitutes a direct object-condition.
All of the above are instances of simultaneous association and objective apprehension.
