Now, the mind does not arise in isolation; it arises only by relying upon objects. Is there, then, any arising that does not depend upon the substance of an object?
Answer: There is.
As the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla says:
The arising of the mind does not necessarily require an essential nature.
This is the correct principle:
if it is a remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*).
Existence and non-existence are not fixed;
without depending on an objective essence,
the mind can likewise give rise to the objects of consciousness-only.
Whether it takes its own *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) as its object, or arises only by depending on an external substrate (*ālambana*), Ci'en says:
I fear that such reasoning would deviate from the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
If the existence or non-existence of the eighth and sixth consciousnesses were not fixed,
it would be as if the eight consciousnesses were functioning to perceive objects [without a consistent basis].
The first five consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness definitely possess a substantial basis (*dravya*).

As for the eighth [consciousness], when it takes as its object the *adhiṣṭhāna-indriya* (the physical support of the sense organs) of another person, the receptacle world of other realms, or the matter produced by meditative concentration (*samādhiphalarūpa*), [it likewise possesses a substantial basis].
Thus, there is an essential nature.
If it takes its own three objects as conditions,
it is exclusively a direct transformation and a direct condition.
Thus, there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
However, if the sixth [consciousness] takes the eighteen dhātus of the present as its object,
an intrinsic nature may exist.
If one takes the eighteen dhātus of the past as objects,
or takes non-existent phenomena as objects,
what then serves as the objective basis?

Therefore, one should know that the substantial basis relied upon by the six [sense organs] and the eight [consciousnesses] is not fixed as either existent or non-existent; if it were definitively a derivative form (avijñapti-rūpa), [the following would apply].
There is transformation and metamorphosis.
Regarding what is called "transformation," it refers to that which relies upon a substrate, namely, possessing an essential substance.
To say that there is transformation means it is detached from its substance; or,
in some cases, it arises conditioned by another.
This carries the sense of "transformation.
That is, relying on another as a basis,
one transforms an image within oneself.
It is like churning the great river to produce butter and curds,
or transforming the great earth into gold;
all of these have a substantial basis.
If there is one for whom [the form] arises through the power of meditative concentration,
then there is the sense of "transformation" (nirmāṇa); that is, transformation while remaining distinct from the physical basis.
That which was non-existent suddenly comes into being,
like flowers in the sky,
manifesting as pavilions, towers, the seven treasures, and other such things.
All of these are transformations produced by the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) apart from their underlying substance (*bhūta*).

One should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to distinguish whether the fundamental substance (*mūla-bhūta*), its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), and the three types of objects exist or do not exist.
First, there is the substantial image-part (*nimittabhāga*),
which is a truly existent objective sphere;
this refers to the first five consciousnesses.
This includes the first moment of the clearly discerning mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and a small portion of the independent mental consciousness (*svatantra-manovijñāna*). Second,
it possesses a substantial basis and an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).

This is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). It consists of those [objects] that have a real substance (*sadravya*) and cast a shadow, as well as those that carry a real substance as their objective support (*ālambana*).
The third, the aspect of an insubstantial object,
is provisional;
it is precisely the "solitary reflection" that lacks a substantial basis.
The fourth [category], the aspect of non-substantiality,
is the truly existent objective realm;
that is, the eighth mind-king takes these three realms as its objects.
The fundamental wisdom takes such [objects] as its conditions.
Furthermore, the *Bie xing chao* (Separate Practice Extract) states:
"As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):"
Because it is that which the mind deliberates upon,
it is called the "object-condition" (ālambana). It is precisely this objective sphere that constitutes the object-condition.
Furthermore, there is that which draws the mind forth and causes it to arise;
because it is that upon which the mind relies,
it is further called an "object-condition" (ālambana).
That which serves as the object of cognition (ālambana) acting as a condition is called the objective condition (ālambanapratyaya); "condition" (pratyaya) here refers to its essential nature.
The object-condition (ālambana) is the function.
Among the six consciousnesses,
the object-condition is simply the condition.
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Now, first to establish the correct principle:
you, Master Saṃghabhadra.
They do not understand the meaning of the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) in my Mahāyāna.
It is simply as I say in the Mahāyāna:
"that which carries the image of what has already been perceived."
There are two meanings for each of "implication" (dai) and "already" (yi).
Regarding the two meanings of "implication":
the first is "to carry along" (kyōdai).
First, direct grasping: the cognizing mind directly grasps the essence of the object while cognizing it.
Second, transformational grasping:
the cognizing mind transforms and brings forth an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) while cognizing it.
The "already-manifested" (jñāta) also has two meanings:
first, the characteristic of essence (svabhāva-lakṣaṇa) as a name-characteristic; second, the characteristic of appearance (ākṛti-lakṣaṇa) as a name-characteristic.
Furthermore, regarding the mode of apprehension that "carries along" both essence and attributes:
fundamental wisdom takes true suchness as its object by way of this mode of apprehending it while carrying along both its essence and its attributes.
This is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
It extends even to the mutual conditioning of the two internal parts,
as well as the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) taking the seeing part (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object.
Furthermore, that which carries along both the essence (svabhāva) and the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) is called the object-condition (ālambanapratyaya);
this refers to the cognizing mind.
The "two parts" within the *qinjièdài* (intimately encompassing) refer to the aspect (*xiàng*) and the characteristic (*xiāng*).
Regarding the second, the *biàndài xiāngzhuàng xiāng* (transformative encompassing of characteristic and appearance),
there are two differing interpretations.
The founder of the Chūryōshō states:
"This refers to the contaminated mind and mental factors,
as well as the seeing-division of the subsequently attained uncontaminated wisdom."
When taking an object as a condition,
one takes it by means of its transformed appearance;
this makes no distinction between that which possesses substance and that which lacks substance.
All these are instances where the "name" (nāman) is associated with transformation and the "characteristic" (nimitta) is associated with appearance;
they serve as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
The second fascicle of the *Xianyou chao* states:
"When the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses takes its own immediate object (*sva-sākṣāt-lakṣaṇa*) as its condition,
it is in every case 'encompassing' (*sahagata*)."
Although there are many such explanations,
I fear they may not be logically sound.
If that were the case:
There are three fallacies:

first, the fallacy of the lack of distinction between "concomitance" (*sahagata*) and "transformation" (*pariṇāma*); [the second is] that it directly concomits with the essence of the object as its condition.

That which is called "carrying along" (xié dài) refers to taking as an object by means of the arising of transformed image-aspects (xiàngfēn). That which is called "transformative carrying" (biàn dài) refers to taking as an object through transformation.
Now that they have already called them "mutually inclusive" (*xié dài*),
we know there is no distinction between them.
Second, there is the error of contradicting the past with the present.
In ancient times, there were some instances where the manner of wearing [the sash] slightly deviated from principle;
this was particularly so regarding the transformation of its placement.
Thus, there is no contradiction.
What is now called "carrying along by implication" (*xié dài*) was in ancient times referred to as "transforming and carrying along" (*biàn dài*).
Is this not contradictory?

[If so,] the three transformations would lose their status as having only the primary object (maulālambana) as their basis. Is it not the case that there are no image-aspects (nimittabhāga) without a primary object?
Is it not a transformation of the mind?
Now, if we infer by means of reasoning,
it is merely the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect).
Whether the object of discourse has substance or lacks substance,
all are termed "transformative and concomitant.
This is because they do not transform into the aspect-part (nimittabhāga).
To directly attach to the substance of the object is precisely what is called "carrying along" (xièdài).
This is why the Tripitaka Master of the Tang [dynasty]...
They will resort to sophistry to rescue their previous arguments,
claiming that this refers to the ancient Mahāyāna masters.
This merely clarifies the transformation and the concomitance.
Next, following the treatise, there is the refutation of the Small Vehicle’s (Hīnayāna) definition of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This section is divided into two parts.
First, in refuting the Saṃmitīya masters,
the author of the treatise states:
"Now, as for that which is the object-condition (*ālambana*) of the five consciousnesses..."
This means that the consciousness which takes it as its object arises bearing its image,
and that it possesses substantial reality,
causing the cognizing consciousness to arise by depending upon it.
O teacher of the Saṃmitīya school,
if you say that the meaning of the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) consists solely in its capacity to produce consciousness;
If it is not permitted that the eye-consciousness which takes it as an object arises bearing its image,
then it would follow that it is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The Mahāyāna proof states:
That which is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for your visual consciousness is a functional entity (*dharma*).
It should not be the object-condition for visual consciousness. This is the thesis (*pakṣa*);
the reason (*hetu*) is as follows:
Because they both possess the single characteristic of being able to produce consciousness,
they are analogous to the causal conditions for visual consciousness.
Furthermore, one may refute this by establishing a counter-argument as follows:
The causal condition for your visual consciousness is an existent phenomenon;
it ought to be the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of that visual consciousness.
This is the thesis and the reason.
It is simply because it can produce a single meaning.
For example, when the eye conditions a visible form;
the intention here is as follows:
The ancient Mahāyāna masters did not speak of "co-inherence" (*xièdài*);
thus, the claim that fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) serves as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) when it takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object is logically flawed.
If the Saṃmitīya school does not admit that [the object] imparts its form [to the cognition],
then when visual consciousness takes a visible form as its object,
the definition of the "object-condition" (ālambanapratyaya) would be untenable.
Next, regarding the refutation of the Sautrāntika masters,
the author of the treatise says:
"You, O Sautrāntika master..."
To claim that external, conventionally constructed form serves as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is incorrect;
even if it were granted, your visual consciousness would merely carry the image of that coarse form.
Even if it is permitted that [the imagined form] acts as an object-condition (*ālambana*), it cannot be called a "condition" (*pratyaya*),
because you maintain that imagined form lacks any substantial essence (*svabhāva*).
It is just as when the visual consciousness is deranged and sees a second moon;
that [second moon] has no substantial reality.
It cannot produce consciousness;
it is merely called an "object-condition" (ālambana),
but it cannot be called a "condition" (pratyaya).
The same applies to the conventional color of aggregation (*saṃghāta-rūpa*). To refute this,
one establishes the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*):
Your thesis is that "the coarse matter resulting from aggregation is an existent phenomenon.
Even if it were the object-condition (*ālambana*) of visual consciousness, it would not be its [direct] condition.
The reason (*hetu*) is as follows:
Because you maintain that this is a mere designation lacking intrinsic substance,
it is like the second moon as a concordant example.
As the *Ālambanaparīkṣā-śloka* states:
It is associated with the five consciousnesses;
even if it has an object of perception, that object is not a condition,
because its substance does not truly exist.
It is like a second moon.
The Sautrāntikas hold that it is a coarse color resulting from a combination [of atoms].
Although these are conventionally existent,
they are able to constitute each individual atom,
which is substantially existent.
Each [of these] can serve as a condition to induce the five consciousnesses;
why then would this not be possible?
The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying:
Those combined forms and so forth that constitute atoms,
even if granted to be conditions,
are not objects of cognition.
Because the visual consciousness and other such cognitions arise without bearing the characteristics of those atoms;
it is just as when visual consciousness arises.
Not bearing the characteristics of those eye-faculties,
the five faculties beginning with the eye can only produce the five consciousnesses beginning with the visual consciousness.
However, the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness,
cannot take their own respective faculties, such as the eye-faculty, as objects; thus,
the faculty is used here as a metaphor.
The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is stated as follows: Your "atoms" (*paramāṇu*), which are the functional bases for the establishment of form and so forth, are the subject (*dharmin*).
Even if they serve as conditions for the five consciousnesses, they are not their objects (*ālambana*).
The thesis and reason are stated as follows:
"Because the five consciousnesses arise without bearing the aspect of that [object],
they are like the five sense organs, which serve as the concordant example."
The *Ālambanaparīkṣā-kārikā* states:
"Even if it were granted that atoms are not the objective conditions for the five consciousnesses..."
Because that objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) does not exist,
just like the eye-faculty and so forth;
this is according to the doctrine of the masters of the eighteen schools.
Since it has already been granted that it bears those characteristics,
it is therefore not refuted.
As for the correct explanation now:
Sū states: "This means that if there is a phenomenon which bears the aspect of what has already been perceived."
Regarding what is called "the existence of dharmas," there are two interpretations.
First, the *Xianyou chao* explains it as follows:
"Existing phenomena" (dharmas) refers to phenomena that possess substantial reality;
this distinguishes them from provisional phenomena.
Furthermore, phenomena that lack intrinsic nature, such as those characterized by pervasive conceptualization,
are merely objects of cognition;
they do not constitute conditions.
Now, for something to function as a condition,
it must be a real entity possessing actual substantiality and causal efficacy.
That which is able to draw forth and produce consciousness is precisely the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) based upon the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva);
this is a phenomenon that possesses substantial reality.
The second, Longxing, says:
"That which is called 'having dharmas' refers to the two natures of the dependent and the perfected."
Because it possesses substantial existence,
it is able to draw the mind toward itself; thus,
it is called a "condition" (pratyaya).
It does not follow that it lacks an essence;
for if it were a parikalpita (imagined nature),
it would lack an essence by definition.
It merely possesses an object of cognition,
but it is not the substance of the cognitive act itself. If it were the object of cognition, [it would follow that...].
The essence itself thus pervades both existence and non-existence.
Question: Regarding the thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
Since it lacks intrinsic nature,
it cannot produce a mind; how, then,
can it be designated as an object of cognition?
Answer: An object of cognition that lacks intrinsic nature arises dependent upon a condition that possesses intrinsic nature.
Regarding phenomena that possess substantial existence,
they are falsely superimposed as being existent,
yet they are not [actual] conditions.
Between these two interpretations,
the latter is correct.
Question:
What fault is there in the former interpretation?
Answer: If the former interpretation were to involve a real entity (dharma), [it would be untenable].
Regarding the claim that only real dharmas are taken as objects of perception:
although many former masters have confirmed this meaning,
I shall now briefly investigate it.
There are three faults.
First, the fault of stubbornly contradicting the commentary:
if provisional phenomena were not to possess an intrinsic substance...
Why does the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) establish the essence of the hundred dharmas based on both the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures?
It is because the hundred dharmas encompass both the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the substantial (*dravya*).
Now, it is said that provisional dharmas lack an essence.
Is this not contradictory?

There is no fault of distinction between the two types of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), for since it is stated that the provisional phenomena based upon the dependent and perfected natures have no intrinsic substance, [the conceptualization of them is likewise devoid of substance].
How does this differ from the absence of intrinsic nature in the *parikalpita-svabhāva*?
The treatise states:
"The *paratantra* and *pariniṣpanna* [natures] are existent."
If the parikalpita (the imagined nature) is non-existent, would this not be contradictory?
There is no fault of failing to establish the analogy for the phenomena of the three realms of existence.
Regarding the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
the treatise states:
"When there is a phenomenon, one speaks of it as being exclusively real."
Regarding the nature of the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*),
the treatise states: "It is an existent phenomenon (*dharma*)."
How can it be that these are merely provisional designations?
For instance, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth— how could these be real?
If, according to the present clarification,
existent phenomena (bhāva) are taken to encompass all three types of objects— whether provisional or real—
they are simply termed "existent phenomena."
All [objects] function as objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*).
Among the eight consciousnesses, they are distinguished as follows:
for the first five and the eighth consciousness, objective spheres (*svabhāvaviṣaya*) serve as objective conditions.
Excluding all provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) and those that are purely imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
the seventh [consciousness] takes the object with its underlying substance (*saviṣaya-ālambana*) as its objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
It is merely conventional and not real;
furthermore, it excludes the sixth consciousness, which is the thoroughly imagined nature.
Taking the three objects as conditions, they function as object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
encompassing both the provisional and the real,
while excluding only the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, he establishes a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
"The various provisional objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) are the subject (*dharmin*);
they are necessarily the direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the transforming mind."
The thesis and reason are as follows:
because it is subsumed under the character "shadow" (chāyā) within the category of existence and non-existence among the sense bases (dharmāyatana);
the concordant example is like the matter of the fruit of meditative concentration (samādhi-phala-rūpa).
The thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) serves as the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*).

Alternatively, one may formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "That which possesses a substantial basis (*sālambana*) and that which consists of a solitary image (*nirālambana*) are the subject (*dharmin*)."
This is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the primary [object]. The thesis and reason are:
because it is a particularity of the reflection.
The same analogy applies as with the nature of the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Question:
Do real dharmas possess a substantial entity (*svabhāva*) that constitutes the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*)?
Question: Provisional phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
they are not object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Answer: [They are].
There are two kinds of provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*): first, those that possess a substantial basis (*sadravya-prajñapti*),
which refers to all provisional phenomena based upon the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The second is the designation of that which lacks intrinsic nature; this refers to the thoroughly imagined nature,
whether it be the self or phenomena.
Flowers in the sky, rabbit horns,
and the like are merely excluded as non-existent entities that are not object-conditions;
they are not excluded because they possess existence.
Question:
If that which is conceptually constructed (parikalpita) is not an object of cognition,
how is it that the sixth consciousness takes such things as empty flowers as its objects?
There is also the sense of being an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Is it, then, identical to having a substantial entity? Answer:
It is only with respect to that which possesses its own characteristics and functions as a distinct entity that it is considered a "conditioned object" (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
it is not with respect to things such as sky-flowers. If it were like a sky-flower or the like, [it could not serve as such a condition].
However, based upon the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga),
one falsely clings to the notion that flowers have arisen;
yet their substance is non-existent.
If the manifested image-part (nimittabhāga) has existence as its essence,
it can constitute the object-condition (ālambanapratyaya).
Question:

What scriptural teaching states that the provisional *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) of both the "substantially endowed" (*sadravya*) and "solely reflected" (*pratibimba-mātra*) objects can serve as an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
Answer: Its teachings are extremely numerous.
Below, we shall distinguish and explain the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) by way of analyzing consciousness.
The Commentary states:
"The eight exist in relation to the seven,
but the seven do not exist in relation to the eight."
The other seven [consciousnesses] are not the objective basis relied upon by the eighth, for instance.
Furthermore, when the seventh consciousness takes the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth as its object,
does this not constitute a "concrete-object condition" (sabhāga-viṣaya-pratyaya) serving as its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya)?
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"In the sixth [consciousness], the five [faculties] are absent;
in the other five [consciousnesses], those [five faculties] are present."
This is also characterized by the presence of a substantial object. The object acts as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
The directly perceived object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is invariably present in the arising of all consciousnesses.
If separated from what is internally conceived and relied upon,
it can certainly not arise;
this serves as abundant proof.
I cannot cite further examples at length.
Question:
Should not all phenomena that possess substantial existence [be included]?
It is always an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
because it is an existent phenomenon (*dharma*).
The commentary on the answer states:
This is the characteristic of "carrying along" (sābhāsagrāhin).
It means that when the mind capable of cognition takes an object as its focus,
it carries along and gives rise to the image of that object.
This existent entity is precisely the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Other phenomena that do not arise accompanied by their own characteristics,
although they are existent dharmas,
do not function as object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
For example, when visual consciousness perceives an object,
it brings forth the aspect (nimitta) of that form.
This existent entity is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the visual consciousness;
as for other things that do not arise accompanied by its [the object's] own characteristics, they are not so.
Although it is an existent phenomenon,
it is not the objective condition for visual consciousness; as it is with visual consciousness, so it is with the others.
The same applies to the other consciousnesses.
Regarding "bearing" and "having already [experienced] the aspect," each has two meanings.
Furthermore, regarding the two meanings of "carrying along" (*sahagata*):
first is "to carry along," which means that the cognizing mind directly adheres to the essence of the object while cognizing it.
Second is transformation with accompaniment (*sābhāsā-pariṇāma*),
which means that the cognizing mind transforms to give rise to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and then perceives it.
Furthermore, the term "aspect" (*ākāra*) also has two meanings.
First is the characteristic of essential identity;
second is the characteristic of phenomenal appearance.
If non-conceptual wisdom takes suchness as its object, [it perceives it in these two ways].
This is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), which takes the essence and characteristics as its concomitants,
as well as the mutual conditioning of the two internal parts.
It also self-cognizes its own objective aspect (ālambana-bhāga) and subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga);
this is "carrying along" (saṃśleṣa).
If it is the objective aspect of a contaminated (sāsrava) mind or mental factor, [it carries along its own seeds].
Furthermore, when the subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) that is free from outflows arises and its seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) takes an object as its condition,
it does so by means of manifesting and carrying a phenomenal aspect (nimitta).
This is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya);
that is to say, whatever dharma serves as a condition.
This is the characteristic of being "bound" (saṃyukta),
and this is the object-condition (ālambana);
it possesses these two meanings.
This is the meaning of the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Furthermore, regarding the analysis of the result by means of distinguishing phenomena,
first, Ci'en is cited as raising an objection:
For whom does dependent origination arise?
Who bears its characteristic?
The commentary answers:
The mind may be associated [with it].
This explains the fruit of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Taking the object as its condition.
This is the cause;
that which arises as mind and mental factors is the result.
"Mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses, the sovereign kings of mind.
"Or associated" refers to the mental factors that accompany them.
This refers to the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*).
Because they may arise or not arise as they are indeterminate,
the word "or" is used.
That is to say, one excludes matter (*rūpa*),
as well as the dissociated (*viprayukta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena,
from being the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
It is not a mental phenomenon (*citta-dharma*),
because it lacks objective referential cognition (*ālambana*). Question:
Within the objective conditions consisting of the near and the distant,
among the internal image-aspects (nimittabhāga), which ones are real?
Answer: Both are unreal. The *Weishi jing* (Mirror of Consciousness-Only) says:
Within the two parts of the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*),
the seeing part (*darśana-bhāga*) alone is real.
Regarding the perceived object part:
Suchness is real; all other characteristics of intimacy or distance are not real.
The Commentary states:
"By means of the remote object-condition and so forth,
one grasps the direct aspect."
That which is not immediately apprehended and does not function as a mode of activity is the distant objective condition (*viprakṛṣṭālambanapratyaya*).
Because the cognizing mind does not directly apprehend the primary object,
the remote object-condition is not termed an "aspect" (ākāra).
Just as when the first five consciousnesses perceive the five sense objects,
they must rely upon the five sense objects transformed by the eighth consciousness as their objective essence (*bhāva*) at the time of perception.
One merely perceives the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) manifested by one's own consciousness;
since this objective aspect necessarily carries the original essence (bimba), it is so designated.
When taking the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) as a condition, because it is a remote condition for the fundamental essence,
the remote object-condition is not identical to the direct attainment.
This is not called an aspect of activity (*ākāra*).
The objective parts (*nimittabhāga*) of the five consciousnesses are each, in relation to their own respective consciousnesses, merely provisional within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Subsuming the provisional within the real,
there are no external objects apart from the mind; therefore,
it is called "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra).
Regarding its objective essence:
in relation to the substance of the eighth consciousness, which is the transformer,
this is the objective essence.
Furthermore, because they do not exist as substantial entities,
both the proximate and remote objects are unreal. Now,
as for the meaning of the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya):
Although they apply to both the great and the small,
one cannot distinguish between the distant and the intimate;
when it comes to the intimate, [the affliction] arises by being closely attached and pressing upon them.
Like tongs grasping an object,
or like the sun radiating its light;
it personally illuminates and personally sustains.
Their substance is inseparable.
When they are distant, the transformations arise by depending upon and attaching to the shadow,
taking on an appearance that resembles the original object.
The intimacy of the aspect of detachment from characteristics does not encompass their substance;
internally, there arises a concern based on reliance.
If one realizes it in this way, distinguishing between the intimate and the distant without confusion,
only then will one know that there are no objects external to the mind.
To see dharmas is the mind.
If one is ignorant and dark, failing to distinguish between them,
then the mind and its objects appear as distinct entities.
Profoundly exhausting the nature of conditions,
one begins to sweep away the dust of the emotions;
minutely penetrating the source of views.
This clarifies the Buddha’s intent.
Regarding the fourth, the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*):
it refers to any phenomenon that—
It possesses a superior power and function that can either accord with or oppose other phenomena.
This establishes the meaning of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The commentary states:
"That is to say, if there is a phenomenon..."
It also possesses substantiality;
this excludes that which is conceptually imputed.
It is that which possesses superior power and function.
This refers to the ultimate sense;
that is, conditioned and unconditioned phenomena possess superior functional efficacy.
This efficacy is not the same as the function of bestowing results and so forth.
However, regarding the phrase "the power that does not obstruct [its own nature] can [function] with respect to other phenomena," this serves to exclude its own essential substance.
This is to show that it differs from the previously mentioned object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The phrase "whether favorable or unfavorable" indicates that both the favorable and the unfavorable can function as conditions.
It serves as a condition for dharmas that arise later,
not for those that have already ceased;
this refers to ten types of causes.
The first nine are concordant;
the tenth is discordant.
This is also because they serve as conditions for this.
Question:
Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) in terms of its strength or weakness when considered in both reverse and direct order,
how many types are there in total?
Answer: There are four traditional explanations.
Now, as for the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*):
That is to say, one must exclude the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is a phenomenon lacking intrinsic substance;
it must be a phenomenon possessing intrinsic substance that can function as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
That is to say, both the perfected nature and the dependent nature are substantial dharmas that function as the meaning of the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
If dharmas were without intrinsic nature,
then they would be identical to the self and so forth,
because they would be entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.
It arises from false attachment;
it is not a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya). It is concordant with one [of the two types].
Just as earth and water serve as concordant dominant conditions for green grass and the like,
the practice of the six pāramitās serves as the cause for the fruit of Buddhahood.
As a concordant dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
the two members of feeling (*vedanā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) serve as the concordant dominant conditions for the seeds of the five fruits.
The second is opposition (*virodha*).
This is like frost and hail acting as an opposing dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for green grass.
Furthermore, just as wisdom acts as a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) that opposes the afflictions,
so too, at the very moment wisdom arises, [the afflictions are suppressed].
Delusion is then severed.
One immediately knows that there are two types of predominance within a single thought-moment:
the first is the predominance that directly acts as an adversary to delusion.
It thus acts as a concordant dominant condition for the principle of the two emptinesses.
Third is the powerful dominant condition,
which is also called the immediate dominant condition.
Just as the five faculties give rise to the five consciousnesses and so forth,
the predominance of the four powers refers to these very same five faculties of that person.
Regarding those five consciousnesses of another person,
they lack the power of predominance and are also termed "distant predominance."
Just as when a lamp flame is in the process of arising,
all dharmas such as the great earth do not obstruct the arising of this flame;
this is called the remote sovereign condition (*viprakṛṣṭādhipatipratyaya*).
It is defined as the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) solely from the perspective of its aspect of non-obstruction.
Question:
Regarding the two meanings of "causal condition" (hetu-pratyaya) and "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda): are they identical or distinct? Answer:
An ancient worthy said:
"As for 'causes and conditions,' they follow."
The differentiation of conventional phenomena is precisely due to the mutual relation of causes and conditions.
The manifestation of the meaning of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is precisely the essence of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). This is the condition (*pratyaya*).
That which arises is compliant;
its nature is non-conceptual.
That is to say, these characteristics are mutually identical and fused,
manifesting the meaning of equality.
"Correct.
This refers to the essence of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Question:
All phenomena, whether defiled or pure,
possess causes and conditions;
the cause is proximate while the condition is remote.
The two meanings have been established.
The meaning of "condition" has already been clarified;
how then is the principle of "cause" to be understood?
The detailed and abbreviated explanations have been fully set forth.
How many kinds are there in total? Answer:
The sūtras and śāstras together establish six causes and ten causes.
First, regarding the six causes:
First is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*):
that which is capable of acting as a cause, excluding itself.
Excluding its own self-nature,
all other phenomena do not obstruct the arising of conditioned phenomena.
Collectively, these are called the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
This cause is the essence of all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
The essence possesses the function of being an agent;
this "agent" is itself the cause.
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
"Upholding" means sustaining;
"activity" refers to functional operation;
"cause" is the essence.
It is capable of performing this function;
when the function is subsumed within the essence,
it is called a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).
The second is the co-existent cause;
co-existent factors are mutually causes and effects for one another,
as is the mind.
They arise simultaneously with the mind and function in accordance with it.
When the effect and the cause coexist,
it is called the coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). This refers to those that function as effects for one another.
There are three [types of causes].
First, the four great elements act as simultaneous causes for one another.
They are mutually *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruits of human effort),
like the relationship between a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*),
wherein the characteristic serves as the cause.
The characterized is the effect;
the characterized is the cause;
the characteristic is the effect.
Regarding the three types of mental states and their associated mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*): the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is the cause,
and the mental factors are the effect.
The mental factors (caitta) act as the cause,
and the mind-king (cittarāja) acts as the fruit;
these are the three types of similar-cause (sabhāga-hetu).
That is, the cause resembles the fruit,
and the fruit resembles the cause,
as in the case of the five aggregates whose nature is defiled.
The aggregate of form can induce the aggregate of form;
the aggregate of form induces the other four aggregates,
and the four aggregates induce the aggregate of form.
Although mind and matter differ,
they share the same nature of defilement; therefore,
they are associated causes (samprayuktaka-hetu).
It is determined that the mind and its mental factors share the same basis; that is,
the mind-king and its mental factors possess five common characteristics.
First, they share the same supporting faculty;
second, they share the same objective referent;
third, they share the same time.
Fourth, they share the same object;
fifth, they share the same mode of activity.
Being endowed with five meanings is called "concordance" (yoga);
this is the cause of concordance.
Furthermore, for example, when the mental factors (caitta) give rise to the mental sovereign (cittarāja),
the mental sovereign is an associated phenomenon (saṃprayuktadharma) and is the fruit.
That which is superior is the mind; that which is inferior is the mental factors (caitta).
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound).
The five universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) are the causes for defilement within the same level;
they consist of the eleven universal proclivities (*anuśaya*).
The universal [factors] are themselves the cause.
The universal factors consist of the eleven pervasive proclivities (*paryavasthāna*).
This means that within their own substance, they possess the functional capacity to serve as causes for all five categories [of defilements].
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Sixth is the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*):
contaminated wholesome and unwholesome karma serves as the ripening cause.
The cause comprises both the wholesome and the unwholesome,
while the fruit is exclusively neutral (avyākṛta).
The maturation (vipāka) is identical to the cause.
The cause is precisely wholesome and unwholesome karma;
it possesses the function of maturation (vipāka) within its own substance.
This is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Regarding the ten causes,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Among the five sciences..."
The speech of all Buddhas is called the Inner Science (adhyātma-vidyā).
What is the Inner Science?
The treatise says:
This demonstrates the characteristics of correct cause and effect.
That is to say, there are ten kinds of causes;
one should know that these establish the non-erroneous cause.
It encompasses all causes, whether for defilement or for purification.
Or it functions with respect to various indeterminate phenomena of the world, such as agriculture and the like.
What are the ten causes? First, the cause of conventional designation (*vyavahāra-hetu*).
That is to say, all phenomena are preceded by names;
thus, they are preceded by conceptualization (saṃjñā). Conceptualization is what precedes them.
Therefore it is said:
this is called the "cause of conventional designation" (*prajñapti-hetu*) for those various phenomena.
Second is the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*).
In dependence upon this,
and with this as the cause,
one seeks or grasps at various things.
This is called its "relative cause" (apekṣā-hetu);
for example, because it depends upon the hand,
the hand serves as its cause.
There is dependence on relatives,
because one relies upon them for support and because they serve as its cause.
There is karma involving coming and going.
There are three projecting causes:
all seeds, in relation to their subsequent respective fruits.
The first is called the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
The fourth is the sustaining cause (*parigraha-hetu*), which refers to all conditions other than the seed.
The first is called the "appropriating cause.
The fifth is the "generative cause," which refers to all seeds in relation to their own initial fruits.
This is called the cause of origination (utpattihetu). Sixth is the cause of induction (āvāhakahetu),
which refers to the fruit produced from the aforementioned seeds.
The cause that draws forth the fruit projected by seeds after the passing of the expectation period is called the productive cause (*ākṣepahetu*).
The seventh is the cause of specific determination (*pratiniyamahetu*).
The various distinct categories,
each with its own specific causes and conditions,
are called the cause of fixed differentiation.
The eight causes of commonality (sābhāgya-hetu) range from the cause of conformity in expression (anuvāda-hetu) to the cause of specific determination (pratiniyama-hetu).
These various causes are collectively subsumed as one,
termed the "cause of common purpose" (*samānārtha-hetu*). There are nine types of "contradictory causes" (*viruddha-hetu*).
A cause that is able to obstruct the arising of a phenomenon is called a contradictory cause (*virodha-hetu*).
There are ten non-contradictory causes (*avirodha-hetu*).
When these causes of obstruction are absent or departed from,
they are called non-contradictory causes;
such are all these causes.
It is comprised of two causes:
first, the productive cause;
second, the instrumental cause.
It should be understood that herein, the projecting seed and the producing seed are called the generative causes.
The remaining causes are called the causes of skillful means; it should be understood that among these,
those which are capable of producing [the result] are the generative causes.
This is called the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
If it is a skillful means as a cause,
it is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the object condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) are explained solely with reference to all minds and mental factors,
it is because all those minds and mental factors [arise] from them.
Because it is sustained by the guidance provided in previous lives,
and because it is sustained by its objective referent,
it arises and evolves.
Therefore, one should know that the equal-and-immediate condition and the object-condition are subsumed within the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya).
Question:
Once the mind has been established,
the causal conditions are already complete.
What is elicited by causes and conditions must inevitably have its fruit;
this is why the Lotus Sutra...
It is said: "Such is the cause;
such is the condition."
Such is the fruit;
such is the retribution.
How many kinds of fruits are there?
From what respective locations are they obtained?
Answer: Generally speaking, this applies to both ordinary beings and sages alike.
Briefly, there are five kinds.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The first is the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*)."
This refers to the indeterminate states born of maturation (*vipākaja*) within one's own continuum,
which are summoned by tainted wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
The commentary states:
"Wholesome with outflows" (sāsrava-kuśala) is used to distinguish it from wholesome without outflows (anāsrava-kuśala).
"From one's own continuum" excludes the bodies of others and insentient things.
If one were to speak merely of "maturation," [it would be unclear].
That is, it is the retribution among the six consciousnesses,
but it is not subsumed under true maturation (*vipāka*); now, for the sake of subsuming that [retribution] in its entirety, [it is included here].
Therefore, it is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
However, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is also termed "born of maturation," because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This stage is somewhat prolonged;
upon reaching the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*),
one suddenly attains the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) across all three vehicles.
First, the truly resultant [consciousness],
which is the eighth consciousness;
second, that which is produced from maturation.
This refers to the aforementioned six consciousnesses.
They are established as the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) because they are also termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*), arising from their own seeds of maturation.
If the first six consciousnesses arise from the true ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*),
they are also termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
This is a portion of mind and mental factors that,
when taking an object as their condition, are dull, inferior, and not sharp or clear.
Because it does not perfume the seeds of the mind that leads to liberation,
it is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
There are four types of maturation (*vipāka*).
They ripen at one and the same time.
"Different" means that they are distinct from one another.
The cause of belonging.
"Mature" means to bring to full development.
This is the fruit.
While the distinct cause resides in the past,
the ripened fruit is in the present.
Therefore, it is called "ripening" (vipāka).
Second, it ripens as something of a different nature;
one has cultivated dissimilar causes in the past.
The ripening fruits of the general and specific retributions for gods and humans, which are summoned by the karma of the five precepts, the ten precepts, and so forth.
If, due to the ten unwholesome karmas,
there arises the ripening fruit of the general and specific retributions of the three miserable realms,
it is collectively of an indeterminate nature.
Third, maturation through different categories:
performing actions of one category and receiving birth in a different category.
The five destinies are each distinct;
four ripen as something other than the noble ones,
namely, the fruit of maturation (vipāka-phala).

Because it possesses the functional capacity to differentiate the various modes of rebirth within the realms of existence based upon the seeds of the two obstacles as they are conceptually discriminated,
this [capacity] no longer exists for noble ones (*ārya*).
Among the eight consciousnesses,
only the eighth possesses three meanings:
first, pervasiveness.
The first phrase, "excluding the five consciousnesses," excludes the second [type of] continuity; the second phrase, "continuity," excludes the sixth [consciousness].
The three karmas bring about [this result].
This excludes the seventh [consciousness].
Regarding the second, the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*):
"Equal," etc., means equal flow.
This refers to the categories of outflow and equal outflow;
there are two distinct types.
The first is the truly uniform outflow (*eka-sabhāga-niṣyanda*),
which takes the three natures— wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—
as its cause and produces a similar result.
Therefore, it is called the "fruit of uniform outflow" (*niṣyanda-phala*).
For example, within the eighth consciousness, seeds of the three natures each produce manifest fruits of their respective three natures.
Because the nature of the fruit is identical to that of the cause,
it is the mental seed that gives rise to the mental manifestation,
and the material seed that gives rise to the material manifestation.
Defiled seeds produce defiled manifest activities;
uncontaminated seeds produce uncontaminated manifest activities.
These are called "outflow" (nisyanda).
This has the meaning of "outflow" (*niṣyanda*).
Second, regarding "equal outflows of the conventional":
in a previous life, one caused the life-span of others to be shortened.
In this life, one's own body and life span are likewise short;
this is because it is a fruit concordant with the previous karma of killing.
Depending on the total retribution thus summoned, the eighth consciousness has varying durations of length.
It is nominally designated as a flow-on result (*niṣyanda-phala*),
but in reality it is a dominant result (*adhipati-phala*);
it refers specifically to the taking of another's life.
By causing the life-span of others to be short,
one's own life-span in this present life will also be short;
this is because there is a corresponding principle [of karmic retribution].
The conventional designation is a "flow-on" (niṣyanda) result,
whereas in reality, wholesome and unwholesome [actions] induce neutral results.
Third is the dominant result (adhipatiphala).
Increasingly superior and preeminent:
with the exception of the four fruits [of the śramaṇa], all other fruits that are attained.
All of these are subsumed under the result of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This dominant result is the most extensive,
just as the dominant condition is the most extensive among the four conditions.
Among the five views, wrong view does not distinguish between the out-flowing and the non-out-flowing,
nor between the conditioned and the unconditioned.
However, whatever fruits are attained that are not subsumed within the first four fruits are all included among the sovereign fruits (*adhipatiphala*).
This is of two kinds. First,
the dominant fruit of providing power,
as in the case of the external vessel-world, which serves as a basis for experience and has the sense of being conducive to benefit.
Second, there is the dominant fruit that is not bestowed by power,
such as the gold, silk, wife, children, and so forth of others. Furthermore,
there are two kinds [of this].
First, conformity:
as when visual consciousness obtains the condition of light.
Second, opposition.
An example is when encountering darkness and so forth.
As for the fourth, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), this refers to all agents.
The accomplishment of various activities by other things, such as vessels and so forth,
is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
A certain class [of beings], in this present life,
relies upon and engages in all various crafts and occupations,
exercising human effort.
These refer to the so-called scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants,
as well as matters such as calligraphy, arithmetic, and divination;
these constitute the functions of such gentlemen.
The accomplishment of results such as various crops, wealth,
and profit is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). Question:
Regarding the eight consciousnesses,
how does each individual consciousness possess four fruits? Answer:
An ancient commentary states:
For instance, visual consciousness arises from seeds as a manifest state.
This is the fruit of uniform outflow (niṣyanda-phala).
Because the eye-faculty serves as its basis,
it is called the sovereign fruit (adhipati-phala).
The mental attention associated with visual consciousness serves as the dominant fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*) by alerting the mind;
alternatively, visual consciousness is able to take real form and so forth as its object.
It is also a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*),
because the eye-faculty is its eighth immediate objective part (*sākṣāt-viṣaya*).
It is also a fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
The four consciousnesses, such as the auditory consciousness and so forth, are all to be treated according to this same principle.
If the seeds of the sixth consciousness produce their manifest state, [the same applies].
This is the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
The preceding moment of the mental faculty (*manas*) acts as the projector,
or it projects the first five consciousnesses.
Therefore, it is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Furthermore, that which can take as its object the internal and external realms of the three times,
by virtue of its functional activity, is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
That which is capable of producing future retributive results,
both collective and individual, is called the "ripened fruit" (*vipākaphala*), because it serves as the cause for ripening.
This is called the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*).
If the seeds of the seventh consciousness produce their manifest result as a similar outflow (*niṣyandaphala*),
the preceding moment of the seventh consciousness serves as the support for the subsequent moment.
This is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Internally, the perceiving aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] is taken as the self;
this is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
Because it can serve as the basis for the true ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*),
it is called the "ripening fruit" (*vipākaphala*).
This occurs when the seeds of the eight consciousnesses give rise to their manifest forms.
It is called "outflow" (niṣyanda) because it serves as the basis for the seventh [consciousness];
it is an "overlord fruit" (adhipatiphala).
It is able to take three objects as its cognitive conditions and to maintain seeds while receiving perfuming;
this is called the virile fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Because its very essence is true maturation (*vipāka*).
Fifth, the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) belongs exclusively to noble ones (*ārya*).
This is not attained by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Various treatises, such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*,
all state that ordinary beings [attain it] through conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Because it extinguishes all afflictions but is not ultimate,
it is not subsumed under this fruit.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The fruit of disjunction refers to the severance of hindrances by means of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*)."
Because one realizes the untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*).
When the fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) unites with suchness (*tathatā*),
it is subsumed under the fruit of dissociation (*visamyogaphala*).
If one subsequently attains the condition of true suchness (*tathatā*),
it is subsumed under the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Question:
How many fruits can the six causes produce?
Answer: The six causes collectively produce five fruits.
The efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) brings about the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala).
The associated and co-existent causes (samprayukta- and sahabhū-hetu) are both [types of] causes.

The efficient cause (purusakāra-hetu) obtains the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala). The similar-cause (sabhāga-hetu) and the universal-cause (sarvatraga-hetu) obtain the fruit of outflow (niṣyanda-phala).
The ripening cause produces the ripening fruit;
the fifth is the fruit of dissociation.
It has the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its essence.
Its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*).
It is termed the "fruit of dissociation" (*visamyoga-phala*) because it is realized by the path that is capable of severing [the defilements].
Question:
What is the distinction between the two causes, the associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu) and the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu)?
Answer: Association (saṃprayoga) pertains exclusively to the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma),
which are co-existent (sahabhū).
That which penetrates both matter and mind and attains the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) relies upon two kinds of causes.
In each of the fruits attained,
there is the functional power of a person (puruṣakāra); thus,
while the name is the same, the entities are distinct.
Question:
What is the distinction between the two causes of similar-type (sabhāga) and pervasive (sarvatraga)?
Answer: It is of the same category and pervades all three natures.
They encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). They are universal (*sarvatraga*),
whereas the specific [mental factors] are exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
The results obtained from these two kinds of causes both resemble their respective causes;
they are called "results of outflow" (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Now, the four conditions, the six causes, the ten causes, and the five fruits encompass the entire path of both ordinary beings and sages,
and they constitute the gateway through which the teachings are established.
If one omits any of these, a single dharma will not be perfected;
if one is ignorant of them, one will ultimately remain an outsider to the Way.
Furthermore, as for the four conditions:
Through causes and conditions,
they directly produce their own effects within the gateway of the conditioned.
Non-inquiry constitutes the meaning of guidance;
thus, all phenomena arise.
As for the object of perception, it is only when it possesses a basis for mental attention that it is fully established.
They are established both in terms of intimacy and remoteness;
as for predominance,
it possesses superior power.
It does not obstruct other conditions.
As for the six causes, they are the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu).
Thus, the function of karma is accomplished;
as for the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu),
its members exist simultaneously with one another.
The homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) is characterized by similarity between the initial and subsequent moments. The associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu) [is characterized by mutual concomitance].
Thus, it is determined that the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) has a single object (ālambana) and is of the same defiled category as its effect.
The ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) brings about the matured result.
As for the ten causes:
The causal condition of verbal expression is the gateway that precedes all phenomena.
The causal condition of dependence.
Having manifested the activity of its function,
the projecting cause then brings about its own fruit.
The cause of grasping can then encompass all conditions;
it is the cause of arising.
It causes the myriad classes of beings to be able to arise;
it is the productive cause that brings all effects to completion.
The cause of distinct determination results in the differentiation of categories;
the cause of common function...
Thus, the essence is universally one;
yet the causes of mutual contradiction can give rise to the gateway of obstruction.
It does not contradict the principle of dependent origination; it accords with it.
Regarding the five fruits:
the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) is that in which the fruit ripens from the arising of the cause.
They are established at different times.
As for the outflowing result (*niṣyanda*), however, the cause and effect share the same nature.
Their respective categories do not overlap.
As for "predominance," its functional power is particularly superior.
That which assists other conditions is the "virile activity" (puruṣakāra),
which is that which is accomplished through human effort.
One can obtain wealth and profit;
through detachment,
one severs hindrances and realizes the truth.
Transcending all fetters of outflows,
it comprehensively encompasses the aforementioned causes and conditions.
The five fruits of retribution are all subsumed within the true maturation of the eighth consciousness;
this is the gateway of the fruit of maturation.
They ripen at a different time.
If one gives rise to a single thought of goodness,
it is like sowing sweet seeds in fertile soil.
Or, should a single thought of evil arise—
like planting the seeds of suffering in a parched field below—
then through the convergence of conditions such as water, soil, and the proper season, [the fruit will ripen].
Then sprouts emerge and leaves unfurl, growing in successive stages;
flowers bloom and fruits form, ripening through gradual accumulation.
Such are the seeds of defilement and purity.
The same applies to maturation (vipāka):
if one performs a wholesome cause,
it plants the seeds for the happiness of the lower realms of humans and devas.
Or they may engage in evil conduct,
being born into the evil fields of the four realms of existence,
failing to give rise to either wholesome or unwholesome causes.
In the end, there will be no retribution of suffering or pleasure.
Just as one does not plant coarse or inferior seeds,
how could flowers or fruit ever grow?
Therefore, one knows that cause and effect recompense one another;
the transformation of consciousness is certain,
just as images appear in a mirror.
It is like a shadow following a form;
there is no shadow that does not follow a form,
and no mirror in which an image is not manifested.
Thus, there is no action performed that does not bring retribution,
and no fruit that does not correspond to its cause;
such is the natural law.
This is universally known to the world;
only that which is not created is such that the fruit of karma is certain and difficult to restrain.
However, for one who realizes the principle of the One Mind,
all conditions are suddenly stilled;
therefore, one realizes the truth of Vijñapti-mātra.
Having no mental application,
one ultimately does not falsely give rise to the karmic fruits of the three realms,
because the transformation of consciousness is certain.
Only those who fear karma are able to believe and accept this.
As the *Precedent Record of Determinations* states:
"Formerly, when Lord Han Hwang was in the Secretariat..."
Once he summoned an official who arrived late;
in his anger, he was about to whip him.
The official said,
"I have other duties to attend to and cannot arrive immediately."
The Duke of Jin asked,
"To whom else do the officials of the Chancellor belong?"
The official said,
"I am unfortunate; moreover,
I am subject to the Yin officials."
The Duke of Jin considered this to be insincere and said in anger,
"Since you have already been assigned to the Office of Yin."
"What do you oversee?
The official replied,
"I oversee such-and-such."
Regarding foodstuffs of the third grade and above,
the Duke of Jin said, "If that is so."
"What shall I eat tomorrow?
The official said,
"Although this is a minor matter,"
It cannot be spoken aloud;
I beg you to write it down on paper so that it may serve as verification later.
He did exactly as instructed and detained the official.
At dawn, an imperial decree was suddenly issued.
Having finished his response,
he happened to encounter the Grand Official presenting food.
There was a vessel of sweet rice porridge;
he gave half of it to the Duke of Jin.
