Furthermore, to exclude that which can act as a perfuming agent, the seven types of manifest consciousness are distinguished from the seeds they perfume by being their basis for growth and so forth;
yet these very manifest consciousnesses that act as perfumers are themselves intermittent.
There is no definitive meaning.
Question:
If there were a definitive meaning, [what would it be?]
These are the bases, namely:
the four great elements, the life-faculty,
the five sense objects, and the seeds.
All possess a definitive meaning and should therefore be the basis;
this is so when there is the occurrence of manifest consciousness.
Because there must certainly exist seeds.
Answer: To distinguish [it] from the second meaning, it is said:
There is an object-possessor (*viṣayin*). That which is called an object-possessor possesses the functional capacity to illuminate and to take objects as its conditions.
Excluding the mind and mental factors, as well as the five material sense-faculties and their consciousnesses,
all other phenomena lack the status of being objects.
This includes, for instance, the four great elements, the five sensory objects, and the life-faculty.
Although it possesses the sense of being determinate,
it lacks the sense of having an object;
therefore, it is not the basis.
Question:
If that which possesses these two meanings is designated as the "basis," [then...]
Furthermore, for instance, the five omnipresent mental factors (mahābhūmika) also possess both the sense of being determinate and the sense of having an object;
they should therefore serve as the support for the mind and its mental factors.
Answer: To distinguish it from the third meaning, it is stated that [the self] is the primary agent.
Now, although the five omnipresent mental factors (pañca-sarvatraga) possess two meanings,
they lack the meaning of "predominance" (adhipati).
Nor is it the basis. Question: If it possesses these three meanings, [why is it not the basis?]
Regarding the phrase "it becomes the support":
for instance, the manifesting eighth consciousness,
in relation to the seeds within that consciousness, [serves as their support].
Furthermore, there are three meanings— being determinate, having an object,
and being primary— which these eight consciousnesses in their active manifestation (pravṛtti) must possess in order to serve as the co-existent supports (sahabhū-āśraya) for their seeds.
Answer: To distinguish it from the fourth meaning, it is stated:
"It causes the mind and mental factors to apprehend their respective objects."
That is to say, the mind and mental factors that depend [upon it] must take their own basis as their object;
only then does it become a "basis."
Now, the eighth functioning consciousness cannot cause seeds to grasp their own objects;
therefore, it is not the support.
Now, the seeds within the eighth consciousness lack the capacity for cognitive apprehension (ālambana),
and thus cannot take their own objects as their objective support (ālambana).
The eighth is not the basis for seeds;
it serves merely as a support.
Question:
It is not yet clear which dharma possesses these four meanings such that it is fit to be called the "basis" (*āśraya*). Answer:
The five material sense-faculties and the mind-base—
these six bases possess the four aforementioned meanings.
The feet alone are designated as the support.
Question:
Are the six internal bases the simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*)?
How does this differ from the essential nature and meaning of the six sense faculties?
Answer: It is their simultaneous support (sahabhū-āśraya).
It takes up only the active manifestation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*),
not their seeds, because the latter lack the characteristic of being an objective domain (*viṣaya*).
If one speaks only of the six sense faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya),
they encompass both the seeds and the manifest states;
furthermore, these are the co-existent supports (sahabhū-āśraya).
It takes the sense of "basis" (*āśraya*).
If one speaks of the six sense-faculties,
it then takes the sense of "growth" (*niṣpatti*).
Each is discussed according to its specific excellence.
Furthermore, when the mind and mental factors arise and abide,
they are already endowed with the co-existent support (sahabhū-āśraya).
When a material phenomenon (rūpadharma) arises or persists,
it obtains its basis solely through causes and conditions;
it certainly lacks a simultaneous basis (sahabhū-āśraya).
Because material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*),
their own essence cannot be a cognizing phenomenon (*ālambakadharma*).
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Regarding the five consciousnesses, there are three supports:
first, the support of seeds (*bījāśraya*)."
Second is the simultaneous support;
third is the opening-and-guiding support.
Question:
How many levels of support are there?
Answer: There are four levels.
This refers to the five material sense-faculties and the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses;
that is, while the five consciousnesses each rely upon their own respective faculties,
as for the latter three consciousnesses:
It thus serves as the support for both [the mental consciousness] and the five sensory consciousnesses.
Question:
Regarding the five material sense-faculties and the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses—
Regarding the four bases of the four grave offenses,
what is the specific function of each?
Why is it said that if even one of them is lacking, [the offense is not established]?
Even if it does not transform.
Answer: It refers to having the same object.
Second, discrimination;
third, defilement and purity;
fourth, the fundamental [consciousness] and so forth.
Because their bases are distinct.
That which is said to have the same object refers precisely to the five material sense-faculties themselves.
Just as when the eye faculty illuminates an object that is blue in color,
the visual consciousness also takes that blue object as its objective condition,
because the blue object is common to both.
Therefore, they are said to share the same object.
This applies likewise up to the body faculty and its consciousness.
As for the term "discrimination":
That is to say, the sixth consciousness can serve as the basis for differentiation (*viniścaya-āśraya*) for the first five [consciousnesses];
for when they perceive the same object,
the sixth consciousness gives rise to conceptual differentiation.
This is the sixth [type of mind], which serves as the basis for discrimination for the five consciousnesses.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"There is that with discrimination and that without discrimination."
Because they take the same present object as their condition,
the sixth [consciousness] is called "with discrimination," while the first five are called "without discrimination."
The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra states:
"When the five consciousnesses arise,
there is necessarily a mental consciousness that takes the same object as its condition."
That which is called "defiled and pure" is precisely the seventh consciousness;
it is the seventh consciousness.
It can serve as the basis for defilement and purity for the five consciousnesses.
If the seventh [consciousness] is in a state of outflow (sāsrava),
it serves as the basis for defilement for the five consciousnesses.
When it becomes untainted (*anāsrava*),
it serves as the basis for purification for the preceding five [faculties]. Thus,
there exists this basis for both defilement and purification.
The first five rotate through the directions;
if they were absent,
rebirth could not occur.
What is called the "root" is the eighth consciousness; that is,
the eighth consciousness.
It serves as the fundamental support (*mūlāśraya*) for the first five consciousnesses,
while the first five consciousnesses are its branches.
Furthermore, the eighth consciousness is able to maintain the seeds of the first five consciousnesses.
The various modes of arising and manifestation are traced back to their source and attributed to the fundamental;
for all are accomplished from within the eighth consciousness.
This eighth [consciousness] is not only the fundamental support for the first five consciousnesses,
but is also the fundamental basis for all phenomena,
because it is able to sustain the seeds of all phenomena.
Within the stages of cause and effect,
the eighth [consciousness] serves as the fundamental basis for all four of these layers of dependence.
Each is distinct. That is, the eight consciousnesses all possess a basis (*āśraya*).
Regarding the fourfold difference in name and meaning:
Just as with the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness,
their four types of objective supports— namely, the common object and so forth—
each possess a determinate meaning.
For example, in the case of visual consciousness,
the eye faculty serves as its determinate basis for the common object,
because it determinately apprehends the same object together with that consciousness.
The same applies to the other four objects and the four faculties,
each of which is determined to apprehend its own respective object;
this is because the sixth consciousness serves as the basis for determinate discernment.
The seventh consciousness is taken as the definitive basis for defilement and purity;
the eighth consciousness is taken as the definitive fundamental basis. Furthermore, these constitute the relationship between the supported and the support.
Analysis by way of the four alternatives:
first, that which is solely the dependent and not the support,
namely the mental factors (caitta-dharma).
The second consists solely of that which is a basis but not a dependent,
namely the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriyāṇi*).
The third is the category of both.
That is, the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings;
four are "neither" (non-perceptual),
which refers to external material phenomena.
Furthermore, regarding the "basis of opening and guiding":
"opening" means avoiding;
that is, opening up and vacating a location.
"Guiding" refers to leading and inducing. It means leading and inducing [the subsequent state] to arise;
that is, at the moment when the preceding mental sovereign (citta-rāja) is about to cease.
It clears away the locus and draws forth the subsequent moments of mind and mental factors,
causing them to arise.
That is to say, the subsequent moments of mind and mental factors arise based upon the preceding moment— the mind-king that acts as an opening and guiding support—
and are thus termed the "opening and guiding support" (ākāraṇa-pratyaya).
The locus of causal dependence is the beginning of the arising of both defilement and purity;
it is the realm of karmic fruition.
When the ripening of suffering and pleasure occurs,
then the ten causes and five fruits are without discrepancy,
and the three supports and four conditions are without confusion.
All are due to that very first thought,
which turns its back on awakening, joins with the sensory dust,
and transforms into the active mind.
They manifest as various objects;
the three subtle consciousnesses arise entirely from non-awakening,
while the six coarse characteristics forever serve as their objective referents.
They enter the cycle of birth and death,
like a whirling wheel of fire,
never ceasing for even a moment.
Abiding amidst the defilements of worldly toil and the Avīci Hell,
when will there ever be a time of deliverance?
If one can clarify the origin of all phenomena and comprehend the very first moment of a single thought,
only then will one know that they arise from one's own mind.
When arising, there is no trace;
only my own mind has vanished.
When ceasing, there is no mark.
Thus, the root of suffering is forever withered;
the six realms of existence melt away like ice,
and the source of craving is suddenly exhausted.
The two deaths disperse like clouds from this point on;
the true intent of the twenty-eight patriarchs becomes clear and bright from here.
The fundamental intent of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is elucidated herein.
Question:
Prajñā is signless and does not receive even a single speck of dust;
how then can it extensively discriminate the four conditions and all causes and effects?
Answer: Now,
the Buddha-way and the True Dharma all arise from conditions.
Therefore it is said that mental phenomena arise from four conditions,
while material phenomena arise from two conditions;
if one were to insist that they do not arise from conditions, [it would be a fallacy].
None of these are the True Dharma;
they all belong to the heterodox paths and their spontaneous false views.
Furthermore, as for the single dharma of the mind:
If the first causal condition did not exist,
there would be no sense of the actualization of the fruit produced by its immediate cause;
consequently, all phenomena would fail to be established.
If there were no second equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
then there would be no sense of opening the way and leading forth subsequent births,
and there would be no continuity.
The continuity would be entirely interrupted.
If there were no third object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
then the mind would have no basis for its deliberations.
Unable to direct the mind through application,
the mind has nothing upon which to rely;
thus, both mind and objects become utterly extinguished.
If the fourth dominant condition were absent,
then even if the first three conditions were present,
without the dominant condition, [the result would not arise].
It immediately becomes an obstruction,
and the dharma does not arise,
even though the four conditions are fully present.
Only then does one truly establish the mind-dharma.
If one can clearly understand that all phenomena in the world are produced through causes and conditions,
only then will one perceive the principle of non-arising.
Because one realizes non-arising through the very phenomenon of arising. If,
even regarding the phenomenon of arising, one does not yet know its true cause,
how could one possibly comprehend the subtle principle of non-arising?
Therefore, the *Huayan shuchao* states:
"The profound meaning of dependent origination is the fundamental tenet of the Buddha's teachings."
Since ancient times, many of great virtue have said that [this] is the source of the three teachings.
The Confucians take the Five Constant Virtues as their fundamental principle;
the Daoists take spontaneity as their fundamental principle; and the Buddhists take dependent origination as their fundamental principle.
However, although Laozi says that "the Dao gives birth to One;
One gives birth to Two; Two gives birth to Three," [it does not contradict this].
The three realms give birth to the myriad things;
it appears as though there are causes and conditions,
yet they are not the true causes and conditions.
Regarding the statement that "the Way gives birth to One":
because the Way is itself non-being (xūwú) and spontaneity (zìrán).
Furthermore, it says:
Man models himself after the earth;
the earth models itself after heaven;
heaven models itself after the Dao.
The Way (Dao) accords with nature (*ziran*).
That which is empty and pervasive is called the Way;
it is simply spontaneous and natural.
Although there are causes and conditions for this,
it nonetheless fulfills the meaning of spontaneity.
Although the Buddha-dharma possesses wisdom that is not derived from a teacher, [it is nevertheless spontaneous].
Innate wisdom is the eternally abiding truth,
yet it must depend on conditions to be manifested.
This, too, is due to causes and conditions; therefore,
the teaching speaks of the three periods of time,
wherein one cultivates the cause to accord with the fruit.
It is not because there are no wholesome causes or unwholesome causes.
In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*,
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
The Buddha speaks of the eternal and the inconceivable;
yet those non-Buddhists also have their own notions of the eternal and the inconceivable.
"In what way do they differ?
The Buddha said,
"Those various non-Buddhists..."
There is no eternal or inconceivable [nature] because it lacks a cause;
I teach that the eternal and inconceivable have a cause.
Since it arises from internal realization, how could it be the same?
This, then, is true permanence.
It is also manifested through causes and conditions.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"In teaching the Dharma, it is neither existent nor non-existent."
All phenomena arise by way of causes and conditions.
As the Lotus Sūtra says:
The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings,
know that all phenomena are eternally devoid of intrinsic nature;
the lineage of the Buddhas arises from conditions.
For this reason, the One Vehicle (ekayāna) is taught.
Furthermore, a sutra says: "All dharmas..."
Conditionality is the fundamental principle.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"There has never been a single phenomenon..."
They do not arise from causes and conditions; therefore,
there is no phenomenon that is not empty.
Thus, even the true Middle Way of emptiness is also a dependent origination. If that is so, then...
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"I observe that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent."
How is this known? By means of causes and conditions.
For if all phenomena arise from conditions, [then they are empty].
Thus one knows impermanence;
among all these non-Buddhists,
there is not a single phenomenon that does not arise from conditions.
Therefore, impermanence implies that for the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), there exists a causal condition.
The commentary states:
This clarifies that the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) exist within the context of causes and conditions,
yet they cling to the characteristics of those conditions as being permanent. Therefore:
This refutes [the former view];
it merely speaks of impermanence.
Now, the clear teaching elucidates the subtle principle of dependent origination.
Since they possess both permanence and impermanence, how could they be the same?
This is all the more so for those who hold such a tenet.
Speaking from the perspective of the majority,
the reasons and conditions for this are our established tenet;
one should not harbor doubt regarding them.
Thus, one knows that this is exclusively the dharma-gate of the dependent origination of the single mind;
for phenomena lack intrinsic nature and manifest in accordance with the mind.
All phenomena that appear are entirely one's own mind; ultimately,
there are no phenomena external to the mind.
It is able to serve as a condition for the mind;
thus, from beginning to end, all things mutually encompass one another and ultimately converge within the Mirror of the Source.
Why is this? That which is internal is the root;
that which is external is the branch.
By means of the principle of "mind-only," one withdraws the external within;
the mind arises by relying upon objects.
Thus, even the branches are gathered within;
if one takes the dharma-nature as the root,
the dharma-nature is all-pervasive and interfused.
Through the mutual interdependence of conditions,
the sensory objects encompass great bodies,
and a single hair can contain entire buddha-lands.
Therefore, these are combined into one great dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Thus, we know that there may be wisdom without extensive learning,
and there may be extensive learning without wisdom.
Neither has attained the true reality;
yet they are fully endowed with the wisdom born of hearing and have truly perceived the source of the mind.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"If one wishes to study Prajñā,
one should study all dharmas."
Because form (*rūpa*) is limitless,
Prajñā is limitless.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
If one wishes to thoroughly understand the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*),
the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Regarding the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), one should study Prajñā.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* commentary explains:
It does not refute the meaning of the four conditions;
it only refutes attachment to the four conditions,
like the moon in water.
It does not refute the vision itself,
but refutes only that which is grasped;
thus we know there exists only the clinging mind of the grasper.
Thus, it is not through illusion that illusory phenomena are produced.
If one achieves the wisdom of non-apprehension,
then even illusion itself will not arise.
The attachment to mourning is a hollow emotion;
the myriad dharmas are without fault.
This is the true nature of Prajñā.
What is it that causes stagnation?
As the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra states:
"The bodhisattva skillfully understands all conditions."
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive the characteristic of form,
nor does he perceive the conditions for form.
One does not see the substance of form;
one does not see the arising of form;
one does not see the cessation of form.
One does not perceive a single characteristic;
one does not perceive a distinct characteristic;
one does not perceive a perceiver.
One does not perceive characteristics;
one does not perceive a recipient. Why is this?
Because they are understood through causes and conditions;
as it is with form, so it is with all phenomena.
Furthermore, the meanings of the ten preceding causes and four conditions are explained according to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Sarvāstivāda);
this is a brief elucidation of their functional characteristics (*ākāra*).
Now, according to the Dharma-gate of sovereign non-obstruction in the Faxing (Dharmatā) school,
I shall explain its essential nature;
this is based on the inexhaustible doctrine of the *dharmadhātu* dependent origination in the Huayan school.
There are also six meanings according to the gate of causes and ten meanings according to dependent origination.
For now, I shall explain the six meanings of the gate of causes.
The single void possesses power;
it does not depend on conditions.
This is the meaning of momentary destruction.
Because of this momentary destruction,
there is no intrinsic nature.
This is emptiness.
Because of this cessation,
resultant phenomena are able to arise.
This possesses power;
yet this cessation does not arise from conditions.
Because of its power, it does not depend on conditions;
it possesses the two kinds of emptiness and has power.
"Waiting for conditions" is the meaning of "coexistent.
It is by virtue of being coexistent [that they function].
That which is "just manifest" is "not existing";
this is the meaning of emptiness.
Because they coexist, they are able to constitute existence; this is their power.
Because they coexist, they are not dispersed.
This depends on conditions.
The three emptinesses lack power.
"Dependent on conditions" is the meaning of "dependent on conditions," because they lack intrinsic nature.
This is emptiness,
because it arises dependently through non-arising.
This is powerlessness.
The four existences possess power and do not depend on conditions.
This is the meaning of "determined," because it does not change within its own category.
It is the meaning of "existent."
However, because it produces a fruit without undergoing change,
the fruit possesses the sense of having power;
yet this [cause] does not undergo change.
Because they do not arise through the power of conditions, they do not depend on conditions; thus,
there are five kinds of existence.
It possesses power;
it awaits conditions;
and it has the sense of projecting its own fruit.
Because it draws forth and manifests its own fruit,
it has the sense of "existence," even though it arises only upon obtaining conditions.
However, the fact that it does not produce a resultant fruit through conditions is the meaning of its possessing power;
it is precisely for this reason.
This is the meaning of depending on conditions.
The six [elements] lack power.
The meaning of "constantly following and evolving" (anuvartana) refers to waiting for conditions;
it is because [the mind] follows after another [factor].
Therefore, it lacks independent power;
for this reason, it depends on conditions.
The primary cause encounters these conditions.
There are only three meanings:
first, the cause;
second, the power.
It does not depend on conditions,
because it is capable of producing [the effect] entirely by itself and because it is not mixed with the power of conditions.
Second, the cause has power when it encounters conditions.
Because they arise through mutual support,
these three causes lack power.
It awaits conditions;
because it does not act at all [independently],
it functions by means of conditions.
Furthermore, by virtue of the three aforementioned meanings,
each of the causes possesses both the sense of emptiness and the sense of existence; thus,
there are three aspects for each of the two gates.
Because there are only six [factors],
they neither increase nor decrease.
For what reason is a fourth category— not possessing power and not depending on conditions— not established?
Because it lacks the meaning of being a cause,
it is not established.
Question:
Question: Are there six meanings within the fruit?
Answer: Within the fruit, there are only two meanings: emptiness and existence.
This means that because what arises from others lacks intrinsic nature,
it has the sense of emptiness;
for it answers the [logical] reason.
This has meaning.
If explained in terms of mutual causality, at the time when it serves as the cause for another, [it is the cause].
When these six meanings are present and it functions as a fruit for another,
there are then only two meanings.
Therefore, these six meanings exist only within the cause.
"Depending on conditions" refers to depending on the three conditions— such as the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and so forth— in addition to the causal factors themselves.
If the secret meaning of dependent origination is considered,
it possesses all these six meanings.
These six meanings are:
Regarding essence and function, there are four propositions for each.
First, regarding essence, there are four propositions concerning existence and non-existence.
The first is existence,
in the sense of being determinate;
the second is non-existence.
This refers to the meaning of momentary destruction.
Third, they are both existent and non-existent;
this refers to their conjunction with that which draws forth its own fruit and with the coexistent [factors].
Non-duality is this very point.
Fourth, it is neither existent nor non-existent;
that is to say, it is both conjoined with that which constantly evolves and dependent upon various conditions.
Non-duality is precisely this. Regarding the two [aspects], they are established through four propositions.
First, because there is no duality between that which is constantly accompanying and that which depends on various conditions when they are combined.
This is not self-arisen,
because it is non-dual with that [other] momentary cessation and with the meaning of certainty.
This is not other-arisen.
Third, because that which is co-existent with it and that which induces its own fruit are non-dual when combined,
they do not arise together.
Fourth, because the meaning of "cause" is only established when the three phrases encompassing the six meanings are combined.
It does not arise without a cause.
This is according to the eight negations of the Madhyamaka, which rely on apophatic discourse (*paryudāsa*).
The six meanings pertain to direct expression (*abhilāpa*),
whereas the eight negations do not.
When principle and emotion manifest of themselves,
the six meanings rely on that manifestation; when principle and emotion vanish of themselves, [the six meanings] likewise cease.
There are these two attendants.
Regarding the opening and closing of the six meanings:
sometimes they are treated as being of a single essence.
Because the cause has no dual nature, or rather,
it is divided into two according to its meaning:
namely, emptiness and existence.
Because they lack intrinsic nature,
because dependent origination is manifest,
or categorized according to their function, they are divided into three.
First, there is that which possesses power and does not depend on conditions; second, there is that which possesses power [and depends on conditions].
Waiting for conditions;
third, lack of power;
waiting for conditions.
At the beginning, there is full power;
at the end, there is no power at all;
in the middle, there is both power and lack of power.
The fourth phrase:
lacking power and not depending on conditions.
It is not a cause;
therefore, it is not discussed.
These six meanings are based on the self-substance of dependent origination.
The six characteristics are based on the gateway of the meaning of dependent origination;
the six meanings arise from the sense of emptiness and existence.
Therefore, there is the gate of mutual identity;
because of the principle of having power and lacking power,
there is the gate of mutual entry.
Based on the meanings of "depending on conditions" and "not depending on conditions," there are the categories of "identical essence" and "different essence.
These are established through these various categories of meaning.
Therefore, it is possible for such matters as the containment of oceans of lands within a single hair-pore to occur.
As for their mutual penetration and mutual support,
these all arise from the presence or absence of power.
These two meanings cannot coexist at the same time; if both were equally powerful,
[contradiction would arise].
If there were no lack of power,
it would result in the fault of multiple effects,
because each [cause] would produce [its effect] individually.
If both are without power, or if there is no one with power,
it results in the fallacy of the absence of a fruit.
Because neither arises.
The treatise states:
"The cause does not arise, yet the conditions give rise [to the effect]."
Because conditions do not arise while causes arise;
for a single [cause] has the power to sustain many,
whereas the many, lacking such power, enter into the one.
Because many possess the power to sustain one,
and because one lacks the power to do so, it enters into the midst of the many;
thus, a single atom possesses power.
It can contain oceans of lands;
yet these oceans of lands, being powerless,
enter secretly into a single one.
Question:
What is the meaning of "possessing power" and "lacking power"?
Answer: If one considers that which possesses power,
this is the meaning of emptiness and the absence of intrinsic nature.
Because they lack intrinsic nature,
they are able to bring all phenomena into being;
this is because of the meaning of emptiness.
When all phenomena are established,
there is then one powerful factor acting as the primary agent,
with many powerless factors serving as its companions.
If one considers those with great power,
there is not a single dharma that possesses an intrinsic nature capable of existing independently;
all are established through dependence upon and in relation to a multitude of conditions.
Thus, many who possess power act as leaders,
while those who lack power act as companions;
it is for this reason that companions are established so that they may mutually support one another.
Self and other are established in mutual dependence;
without a companion, the self cannot be established,
and lacking a self, the other cannot be formed.
Furthermore, with respect to their function,
because they are mutually dependent,
they possess the sense of both power and lack of power.
These are mutual inclusion and mutual penetration;
these two are based on substance,
because they function through their characteristics.
It possesses the meaning of both existence and non-existence;
therefore, they are identical in nature and are that very nature.
As a verse in a sutra says:
All phenomena are devoid of activity and lack intrinsic nature; therefore, all phenomena—
Each is unaware of the other;
taking what is other as self,
they therefore lack intrinsic nature.
Because they are established through mutual dependence,
they lack causal activity;
this is the meaning of being powerless.

Furthermore, it is precisely because of this absence of knowledge and absence of intrinsic nature that dependent origination exists; if even a single dharma possessed a substantial essence, [dependent origination would not occur].
Then there would be no dependence on conditions;
if there were no dependence on conditions,
then all phenomena would not exist.
If all phenomena were not empty,
there would be neither the Path nor its fruit;
this is the meaning of "possessing power."
Next, regarding the ten gates of dependent origination:
this refers to the power of the mutual conditioning of characteristics,
meaning that the one and the many act as conditions for one another.
Characteristics are established through mutual dependence;
therefore, there are such things as "characteristic-identity" and "characteristic-entry. This is of two kinds.
First, regarding their function as conditions,
there are those that possess power and those that lack it;
they exist in mutual dependence and mutual reliance.
Because the whole is mutually contained within each part, there is mutual interpenetration.
Second, this is discussed in terms of the substance of conditions.
There is emptiness and non-emptiness;
the agent and the acted-upon are entirely the manifestation of its essence.
Therefore, there is mutual identity.
This constitutes the entry into two gates,
which further possess two meanings.
When distinct entities are compared with one another,

This is the subtle meaning;
it is the characteristic of distinct entities,
possessing the sense of concealment and manifestation.
Second, because they possess virtues within a single identical substance,
there is both unity and multiplicity, as well as breadth and narrowness;

because they are of the same substance and mutually identical,
there is the non-obstruction of the expansive and the narrow.
Furthermore, because the different encompasses the same,
there is the principle of the Indra’s Net within time.
Therefore, there is the meaning of the ten periods of time.
Because dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature,
there is the meaning of the non-obstruction between nature and characteristics.
Because they are mutually inclusive in this manner,

As for the meaning of the ten conditions:
1. The meaning of the distinctness of each condition.
Within the Great Dependent Origination (*mahā-pratītyasamutpāda*), the various conditions are mutually related.
It is essential that essence and function be distinct from one another and not confused;
only then does dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) come to be established.
If there is confusion and disorder, one loses the dharmas that serve as the original conditions; thus,
dependent origination is not established.

as one condition universally corresponds to many conditions, each is entirely identical with those many.
This one is precisely many ones.

As a verse in the sutra says:

one knows that because of the many there is the one.

In general, a single condition must possess the two preceding [conditions],
because it must abide within its own singularity.

to respond universally is to respond to manifold conditions.
It is many,
because the conditions are only one;
for one does not produce one by itself.
By means of many, one is made;
yet by means of many, many is not produced from itself.
By means of one, many is made.
Therefore, the one and the many are sovereign and unimpeded; or,
when the entire substance abides in its entirety,
this is what constitutes "the one."
Alternatively, it may pervade the entire body;
this is "many-ones.
Or, both may coexist.
Either both are extinguished,
or they are merged as a whole,
or they are entirely separated.
A verse from the Sūtra says:
"All phenomena have no basis;
they arise solely from conjunction."
These three gates complete the general explanation of the fundamental dharma of dependent origination.
Fourth is the meaning of the mutual interpenetration of distinct entities.
This refers to the power and function of the dharma-gates,
which mutually support one another and interact through mutual influence.
Each possesses both the sense of having full power and the sense of having no power;
because that which has power necessarily does not coexist with that which has multiple powers.
Therefore, there is nothing that does not support many.
Because the many lack power,
they necessarily do not coexist with the powerless one.
Therefore, there is nothing that exists as a plurality without entering into the one;
likewise, the many are sustained by the one as their basis.
This is the meaning of the mutual identity of the five distinct entities.
When various conditions are mutually compared,
they completely usurp one another's form; thus,
there is the sense that existence possesses a substantial body while non-existence lacks a substantial body.
Therefore, a single condition is that which can produce and can establish;
thus it possesses substantial reality.
Multiple conditions are that which is produced and that which is established.
Therefore, it lacks substantiality;
for that which possesses the substantiality of oneness can never coexist with that which possesses the substantiality of multiplicity.
Multiplicity has no intrinsic nature;
it can never coexist with a single thing that lacks intrinsic nature.
Therefore, there is no "one" that is not multiple.
Sixth: The principle of the mutual integration of essence and function, wherein there is no multiplicity that is not unified.
First, because its essence is non-obstruction,
the entire essence is fully functional;
thus, there is mutual interpenetration.
The absence of marks is precisely the meaning.
Since the two functions are not separate from the essence,
the entire essence is manifested by citing the functions.
That is to say, having only marks is itself the meaning of entering the markless; thus,
the essence and function of the Three Refuges do not obstruct one another's functioning.
The substance that fully employs [all phenomena] does not lose its substance;
unimpeded, they both coexist—
both identical and yet entering into one another.
They manifest simultaneously with sovereign ease:
the substance of the total function vanishes as substance,
and the function of the total substance perishes as function.
It is neither identical nor inclusive;
it is a perfectly interfused single flavor.
These five [points] combine with the preceding four phrases.
The same dependent origination exists unimpededly as a duality;
the first five phrases are subsumed within the sixth.
Transcending all dependence and free from words,
it is darkly identical with the ocean of the nature of reality.
These are the three preceding gates.
The exposition of the meaning within the first section on distinct entities is now complete.
Seventh is the principle of mutual interpenetration of identical entities,
which refers to the many-oneness of the aforementioned single condition.
Because its substance is no different from that single object-condition,
it is called "of identical substance.
Furthermore, because of this single object-condition, there ought to be many conditions.
First, the mutual inclusion [of phenomena] is clarified:
that is to say, a single condition possesses the power to sustain many "onenesses," while those many "onenesses" lack the power [to sustain it] and instead depend upon that single condition.
Therefore, the one can encompass the many,
and the many enter into the one;
this is the meaning of the eight aspects being identical in essence and mutually inclusive.
This means that the "many" and the "one" possessed by the preceding condition also have the meanings of both having substance and lacking substance; therefore,
they are likewise mutually identical.
Since many and one lack intrinsic nature,
and because the one is established by the fundamental [nature],
the many are indeed the one.
Because the fundamental single entity possesses a substantial nature,
it is able to sustain many ones and is entirely comprised of many ones.
Just as it is that one has many emptinesses,
so too does the many have one emptiness.
Nine: The meaning of mutual fusion and non-obstruction.
This is identical to the preceding six phrases in that essence and function are doubly fused.
These three gates have completed the exposition of their principles within the preceding second gate, the Gate of Identical Substance. This concludes the tenth section:
the Perfect Meaning of Identity and Difference.
By combining the preceding nine gates into one great dependent origination,
numerous thematic categories are established.
Simultaneously complete;
because they abide in a single [state] and respond universally,
there is the gate of mastery over breadth and narrowness.
From the perspective of their essential nature, there is mutual identity; from the perspective of their functional activity, [there is distinction].
There is mutual inclusion,
because distinct entities are mutually compatible,
possessing the gateway of subtlety.
Because distinct entities are identical in essence,
they possess the gate of concealment and manifestation;
in terms of their functional application, they are taken as manifesting mutual inclusion.
In terms of its own essence and characteristics, it is concealed;
furthermore, by means of the mutual entry of different essences and characteristics,
it carries along the characteristics of the same essence.
One enters the gate of the Indra’s net through this great dependent origination;
it is the unimpeded Dharma-realm.
There is the gate of entrusting to phenomena,
which reveals [the nature of] time;
there is the gate of the ten periods.
These are the related mutual integrations.
There is the gate of the principal and its retinue;
this is the gate of perfection.
Having completed the exposition of the principles within the third section,
the verse of the sutra says:
"The Bodhisattva skillfully contemplates the dharma of dependent origination."
Within a single phenomenon, one understands many;
within many phenomena, one understands the one.
Thus, the principles and facts unfold and merge, and the nature of conditions is harmoniously integrated.
One then attains the inexhaustible function of the single mind.

the three [aspects] are a dual fusion of essence and function;

Nevertheless, because they are established through mutual dependence, each possesses its own essence;
this refers to the meaning of the two being mutually pervasive and supporting one another.

which possesses many "ones," just as ten coins serve as the condition.

when it manifests as two, that which was originally one is then designated as such.

three should be considered as three-and-one,
and so on up to ten, which should be considered as eleven.

The second, third, fourth,
and so forth, each likewise have ten;
hence it is said:
Each and every one is fully present,
as illustrated by the analogy of ten coins.
Within this inexhaustible dharma of the differentiation of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu),...
Because each one universally corresponds [to all others],
each individual [phenomenon] possesses the distinct dharmas of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Third, regarding the meaning of the unimpeded coexistence of all three:
"One who is sovereign and unimpeded regarding the one and the many" generally clarifies the desire for multiplicity and permanence,
as well as the desire for unity and permanence.
Therefore, it is called "sovereign" (vaśitā).
First, the entire body may respond universally;
second, the entire body may remain entirely present.
Regarding "the three or all existing together":
this means that they exist together, abiding both in themselves and pervasively;
it also means that they exist together as both the single and the many.
As for the "extinction of the four pairs," it is because,
through their simultaneous existence,
they mutually cancel one another out.
Abiding in one is to respond universally;
it is not merely abiding in one.
Responding universally is to abide in one; it is not merely responding universally.
Fifth, "either combined as a whole" means that the preceding four phrases are combined to constitute the object of understanding.
Sixth, "or entirely separate."

Regarding the meaning of mutual inclusion through different aspects:
"mutual dependence and support" means...
By means of this dependent origination,
there is neither a fixed nature of unity nor plurality;
that is to say, unity does not possess a fixed nature.

for many possess fixed natures;
nor does it arise from one.
Now, because a single [entity] lacks a fixed nature,
it arises based on a plurality;
and that plurality lacks a fixed nature.
Because it arises from a single [cause],
and because of the meaning of the equality of non-nature,
it constitutes dependent origination.
If there is one that can be one,

then the manifold does not depend upon a single [cause].

If these are many, they lack power;
if this one is not by itself one,
then this one lacks power.
The powerless follow the powerful,
for the one and the many mutually encompass one another; thus,

The assembly of all Buddhas and the assembly of all dharmas are themselves the assembly of the single dharma.
Therefore, this single Dharma assembly is eternally pervasive while remaining unmoving;
it is eternally manifold while remaining undivided.
The preceding and succeeding parts mutually establish one another;
how can you not believe this?
Furthermore, it is said that when the first [moment] looks toward the many in the middle...

one is capable of encompassing many;
and one serves as the limit of reliance.

that which has a basis and support.

"Exerting full power" refers to accomplishing the aforementioned maintenance;
"lacking power" refers to...

first, there is the power of support.

because the meanings of existence and non-existence cannot coexist.

Question:
What fault is there in oneness not being identical to multiplicity?
Answer: Because there are two faults.
First, the fault of failing to establish multiplicity.
This means that since "many" is not established,

just as one does not constitute ten.
Since two, three, four, and so forth also do not constitute ten,
there is no fault of [the number] ten. Furthermore,
there is no fault of two not constituting one.
That is to say, if one does not constitute ten,
then this very one does not constitute one,

because among the ten, there is nothing that constitutes "one"; thus,

Now, among the eight consciousnesses, the truth is concealed and delusion is cultivated. Which consciousness creates karma? Which consciousness acts as the cause?
Which consciousness serves as the basis for forming these seeds of delusion?
Answer: The first five consciousnesses apprehend objects,
with the sixth consciousness acting as their cause.
The seventh consciousness conceives of a self that creates karma,
taking the eighth consciousness as its support;
thereby, the bitter fruits of birth and death are not severed.
A verse from the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
"Just as when the great flow of water is exhausted,
waves no longer arise."
"In this way, when the mental consciousness ceases,
the various forms of consciousness do not arise.
The commentary explains:
That is to say, the five consciousnesses apprehend objects and transition into the six consciousnesses;
the six consciousnesses take the recollection of phenomena as their cause.
The seventh consciousness provides the objective support,
while the six consciousnesses perform wholesome and unwholesome karma.
It acquires future birth and death,
obscuring and obstructing the eight consciousnesses so that they cannot manifest.
If the five consciousnesses do not apprehend objects,
then the sixth consciousness does not exist; because the sixth consciousness is absent, [the other consciousnesses would likewise cease].
The seven consciousnesses do not arise.
Because the seven consciousnesses do not arise,
there are no wholesome or unwholesome karmas.
Because there are no wholesome or unwholesome karmas,
there is no birth and death. Because there is no birth and death, [there is no nirvana].
The Tathāgatagarbha-mind is profoundly tranquil and eternally abiding;
this is precisely the cessation of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses,
wherein the eight consciousnesses are established.
Furthermore, regarding the eight consciousnesses serving as the support for the five, six,
or seven consciousnesses and acting as the cause for those various consciousnesses,
this refers specifically to the mind of the sixth consciousness.
All consciousnesses depend upon it;
just as when water is exhausted, there are no waves.
The six consciousnesses cease,
and the seventh consciousness likewise does not arise;
therefore, it is said that there is the wind of ignorance in a single thought-moment.
The ocean of True Suchness is stirred;
when the winds of ignorance are exhausted,
the waves of consciousness no longer arise.
Thus, the nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid; as it flows on with perpetual clarity, the source of awakening is fundamentally wondrous.
Question:
In all worlds, cause and effect repay one another.
Birth and death do not cease.
Among the various consciousnesses,
which consciousness acts as the primary agent?
Answer: The causes and conditions for arising and ceasing initially take the ālayavijñāna as their substance.
With the mental consciousness as its function,
the causes and effects of the three periods of time thus circulate without interruption.
The function lies in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). For this reason,
"mind" (*manas*) is termed the "successive consciousness" (*saṃtativijñāna*).
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing,
it means that all sentient beings revolve in dependence upon mind, thought, and consciousness."
What is the meaning of this?
It is because, based upon the ālayavijñāna,
there is the non-awakening of ignorance.
It arises as that which is able to see, able to manifest,
able to apprehend objects, and able to discriminate.
The continuity [of consciousness] is designated as "mind" (manas).
This mind, moreover, has five distinct synonyms.
The first is called the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
This means that by the power of ignorance,
the mind moves unconsciously.
The second is called the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*);
that is to say, depending on the moving mind,
it is able to perceive the characteristics of objects.
The third is the manifesting consciousness (ādarśa-vijñāna), which manifests the appearances of all objective realms,
like a clear mirror.
Just as various forms and images appear,
so too does consciousness appear,
corresponding to its five objects.
It manifests immediately upon encountering it;
there is no sequence of before or after,
nor does it depend on effort or power.
The fourth is called the consciousness of cognition (*jñāna-vijñāna*),
which refers to the discernment of various differentiated phenomena, both defiled and pure.
The fifth is called the consciousness of continuity (*saṃtati-vijñāna*).
It refers to the constant association with mental attention that is uninterrupted,
which sustains past wholesome and unwholesome karma so that it is not lost or destroyed.
It brings to maturity the retributions of present and future suffering, pleasure, and so forth,
ensuring that no transgressions occur,
as these have already been experienced in the past.
Suddenly, one recollects;
though it was never previously experienced,
one falsely gives rise to conceptual discrimination.
Therefore, all things within the three realms take the mind as their intrinsic nature;
apart from the mind, the objective realms of the six sense objects do not exist.
Why is this? Because all phenomena have the mind as their sovereign.
Arising from deluded thoughts,
all that is discriminated is merely the discrimination of one's own mind.
The mind does not perceive the mind;
no characteristic can be apprehended.
Therefore, you should know this.
The characteristics of all worldly realms are established entirely based upon the ignorant and deluded thoughts of sentient beings,
like images reflected in a mirror.
No substantial entity can be apprehended;
it arises solely from the transformation of the mind of false discrimination.
When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise.
When the mind ceases, the various phenomena cease;
therefore, the commentary states that this applies generally to the five kinds of consciousness.
All are termed "mind" (manas).
Speaking from the perspective of the fundamental source,
one takes only the karmic consciousness (karma-vijñāna).
Because it is the most subtle and serves as the basis for all consciousnesses,
such is the karma-consciousness (karma-vijñāna).
The characteristics of the seer and the seen have not yet been differentiated;
nevertheless, these bodhisattvas know that the mind is falsely stirred and that no external objects exist prior to it.
One realizes that all phenomena are nothing but the manifestations of consciousness,
thereby abandoning the prior attachment to external objects.
Because it accords with the meaning of karmic consciousness, it is called "karmic consciousness" (*karma-vijñāna*).
The mind does not perceive the mind.
That "no characteristic can be apprehended" clarifies the meaning that all phenomena are not existent.
As a verse in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
If the body, the means of subsistence,
and the environment were produced within a dream,
there would necessarily be two kinds of mind.
Yet the mind possesses no dualistic characteristics;
it is like a blade that cannot cut itself,
or a finger that cannot touch itself.
Just as the mind does not see itself,
so too is this matter. If the various things seen in a dream were truly existent, [they would likewise see themselves].
Thus, there appear the two aspects of the seer and the seen;
yet, within the dream,
these two phenomena do not truly exist.
All minds within the three realms are like this dream;
apart from the mind, nothing else exists.
There is nothing that can be differentiated;
therefore, it is said that all differentiation is the differentiation of one's own mind.
Yet, the mind cannot see itself, just as a sword blade or a finger cannot touch themselves; therefore,
it is said that the mind does not see the mind.
Since there is nothing else to be seen,
nor can it see itself, that which is seen has no existence.
The capacity to see cannot be established;
both the subjective and objective aspects are entirely unapprehendable.
Therefore, it is said that no characteristic can be apprehended.
Furthermore, because the single mind moves in accordance with ignorance,
it manifests as the five kinds of consciousness.
It is taught that the three realms are merely the transformation of mind.
This mind follows its habitual perfuming;
although it manifests as various things, they are but semblances.
Yet, when one thoroughly investigates its causes and conditions,
it is produced solely by the mind; apart from the manifesting consciousness, there is nothing else.
Then there would be no objects of the six sense-fields;
conversely, examining the six sense-fields reveals that they are nothing but the single mind.
Therefore it is said:
"Apart from the mind, there are no objects," and so forth.

Question: What are the causes and conditions for birth and extinction?
Apart from this, what serves as the cause and what serves as the condition for its arising?
Answer: The ancient masters explain that these are the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing.
The essence and characteristics are twofold:
first, the essence of the ālayavijñāna mind,
which does not maintain its own nature.
The transformation into all phenomena is the cause of arising and ceasing;
it is fundamental ignorance.
It perfumes and moves the substance of the mind,
serving as the condition for arising and ceasing;
furthermore, it is the root of all defilements within the ground of ignorance.
It gives rise to all forms of arising and ceasing;
therefore, it is said to be the cause.
The objects of the six sense-fields are able to move the seven consciousnesses.
Waves arise and perish; this is the condition for arising and perishing.
Based on these two meanings:
To reveal the causal conditions,
all phenomena characterized by arising and ceasing are produced through aggregation.
Therefore they are called "sentient beings," yet they have no separate substance; they exist solely in dependence upon the substance of the mind.
Therefore, it is said that [all things] depend on the mind;
this refers to the characteristics of the ālayavijñāna, one's own mind.
Furthermore, it is the dependent origination of the various consciousnesses through the union of the true and the false.
This is analyzed by means of four propositions.
First, the Tathāgatagarbha is exclusively non-arising and non-ceasing,
like the moist nature of water.
Second, the seven consciousnesses are subject only to arising and ceasing,
like waves upon water;
third, the ālayavijñāna both arises and ceases.
It is likewise neither arising nor ceasing,
like the ocean containing both motion and stillness;
the four inversions of ignorance are not arising or ceasing.
It is not that there is no arising and ceasing;
it is like the fierce wind that raises waves—
it is neither water nor waves.
Question:
Since the ālayavijñāna permeates both movement and stillness,
it should not be restricted solely to the gate of arising and ceasing.
Answer: It is for the sake of arising from stillness to accomplish movement;
there is no separate entity of movement.
Therefore, the nature of stillness follows after movement;
it too exists within the gate of arising and ceasing.
It is not only the ālayavijñāna that possesses both movement and stillness.
Within this process of arising and ceasing,
the Tathāgatagarbha likewise remains solely unmoving;
it is also within this very gate.
Why is this? Because arising and ceasing have no separate substance,
just as water forms waves.
Furthermore, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
ignorance is the cause, and objective conditions are the contributing factor.
The three subtle consciousnesses and the six coarse characteristics arise,
following the conditions of delusion and ignorance.
Yet they sink into the six realms of existence;
with initial awakening as the cause and the five perfections as the conditions.
Thus, according to the conditions for awakening and understanding,
one ascends to the One Vehicle.
Furthermore, it is said:
In delusion, there are false and defiled dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
these arise through defiled conditions and cease through pure conditions.
In awakening, there are pure merits and virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Thus, while the pure dependent origination is present, the defiled dependent origination vanishes;
yet this is all produced by the single mind,
with no second source.
In terms of conventional meaning, it is said that there is the pursuit of awakening and the pursuit of delusion;
in reality, however, there is neither a pursuer nor an object of pursuit.
Therefore, the Treatise says:
All phenomena arise from the mind; they are produced by deluded thoughts.
Whatever is conceptually discriminated [is likewise so].
All are the conceptualization of one's own mind;
the mind does not perceive the mind,
for no characteristic can be apprehended.
As explained by the ancient masters, the analogy of waves and water represents the two gates of the True Suchness (tathatā): arising and ceasing.
Therein, the moisture of the water is used as a metaphor for the Mind-as-Suchness (citta-tathatā).
The arising and ceasing of the mind is illustrated by the analogy of waves:
just as waves are not distinct from the movement of moisture,
so too the arising and ceasing [of the mind] are not distinct from True Suchness (tathatā).
Thus, by means of water, one distinguishes the waves;
it is the non-altering nature that constitutes dependent origination.
Water possesses no moisture distinct from its movement.
Thus, there is no such thing as a True Suchness (tathatā) apart from arising and ceasing;
it is like clarifying the waves by means of the water.
This signifies abandoning conditions below and realizing the Truth immediately.
Question:
Regarding the phenomenon of memory,
to which specific dharma does it belong, and from what does it arise?
Answer: In the Mahāyāna, it is taught that there are three ways of being able to remember phenomena.
First, the self-verifying portion (svasaṃvittibhāga),
which is able to remember the seeing portion (darśanabhāga);
second, mindfulness (smṛti) among the five object-specific mental factors (viśeṣa-viṣaya).
It is able to remember previously experienced events;
among the three types of consciousness,
its seeds are capable of unfailingly producing their own manifest activities (*pravṛtti*).
The *Weishi shu* (Commentary on the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi) states:
"Just as one who has never experienced an object can certainly not remember it."
Just as with a presently manifest form that has once been perceived by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*),
one will necessarily be able to remember it later.
If it had not previously served as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for the image-part (nimitta-bhāga),
it could certainly not be remembered at a later time; this is because [memory functions through] the perceiving subject-part (darśana-bhāga).
In the past and in the present, it takes only the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) as its object;
it has never taken itself as its own object.
The preceding mind has already ceased;
since it has passed away,
what basis is there for the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) to exist at this present time?
One is able to remember and maintain this oneself because, in the past,
one has never turned back to take the self-perceiving portion as an object.
Since it is already granted that the mind and mental factors of the present time are capable of self-recollection,
this clearly demonstrates that there must have been a self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) at the time of their past occurrence.
Because it takes the seeing-part as its object,
realizes that objective sphere,
and functions as the fruit of valid cognition.
Therefore, one is now able to recollect.
Question: Within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*),...
Within the state of outflows (sāsrava),
according to what is discussed in the teachings,
how many kinds of birth and death (saṃsāra) are there?
Answer: Briefly, there are two kinds:
first, the fragmentary [karma].
Second, regarding transformational death (*pariṇāmi-maraṇa*): the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states that one type is "segmented birth and death" (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*).
This refers to the coarse resultant fruits of maturation within the three realms,
produced by all contaminated wholesome and unwholesome karmas through the auxiliary power of the afflictive obscurations.
The length of one's physical life is determined by the power of causes and conditions;
it has a fixed limit.
Therefore, it is called "segmented" [birth-and-death].
Second is the inconceivable transformative birth-and-death,
which refers to various outflow-free (*anāsrava*) karmas involving conceptual discrimination.
The exceptionally subtle and superior matured fruit (vipāka-phala) that is experienced through the auxiliary power of the cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa),
[is attained] by the power of compassion and aspiration.
Because one’s physical life is transformed and lacks a fixed limit or duration,
it is called "transformation" (pariṇāma).
It is precisely the uncontaminated meditative concentration and vows that bring about its manifestation;
because its wondrous function is difficult to fathom, it is called "inconceivable," or alternatively,
it is termed the "mind-made body."
Because one's wishes are fulfilled according to one's will,
as stated in the Sūtra:
"Just as grasping is a condition."
With contaminated karma as the cause,
one who continues into future existence is born within the three realms of existence.
In this way, with the ground of the latent tendencies of ignorance as the condition and untainted karma as the cause, there is an Arhat.
The Pratyekabuddhas and the Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery possess the three kinds of mind-made bodies.
It is also called the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), because through the power of untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*),
it is transformed so as to differ from its original state, just like a magical creation.

The body remains for a long time;

If that [basis] does not exist,

This is created by the deluded mind of ordinary beings;

There is no rest. As stated in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,

Suppose there is a woman who enters another's house;
this woman is beautiful.
Her countenance was exquisitely beautiful,
and she adorned her body with fine necklaces and ornaments.
When the host saw him, he asked,
"What is your name?"
"To whom do you belong?
The woman replied,
"I am the Great Deity Guṇa."
The host asked, "Wherever you go, what do you do there?"
The woman replied,
"Wherever I go, I am able to provide various kinds of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli."
Crystal, pearls, coral, amber, tridacna shell, and agate.
Elephants, horses, chariots, and carriages;
male and female slaves and servants—
having heard this, the master [thought]:
My heart was filled with immeasurable joy and exultation.
"It is by virtue of my own merit that I have caused you to come."
Upon arriving at my residence,
they immediately burned incense, scattered flowers as offerings,
and paid homage with reverent prostrations.
Furthermore, outside the gate,
he saw another woman whose form was hideous.
Their clothing was tattered and worn,
covered in much grime and oil;
their skin was cracked and chapped.
Her complexion was pale white.
Having seen her, he asked,
"What is your name?"
"To whose family do you belong?
The woman replied,
"My name is Kālī."
He asked again, "For what reason is it called 'Darkness'?
The woman replied,
"It is the place where I go."
It causes all the wealth and treasures within that household to utterly diminish and waste away.
Upon hearing this, the master—
He immediately took up a sharp blade and spoke these words:
"If you do not depart, [I shall kill you]."
"I shall take your life," he said. The woman replied,
"You are utterly foolish."
He possesses no wisdom. The host asked,
"In what way is he called 'deluded and lacking wisdom'?"
The woman replied,
"She who is in your house is my elder sister."
"I have always been with my elder sister;
our every movement has been shared together.
If you would drive me away," [she said].
He should likewise drive her away.
When the master returns inside, he asks Śrīdevī:
Outside there was a woman who said,
"She is your younger sister. Is she truly so?"
Goddess Śrī said,
"She is truly my younger sister; she and I— "
They accompany one another in walking and staying,
never parting from each other,
wherever they may dwell.
I always do what is good;
he always does what is evil. I always act for the benefit [of others].
He is undergoing decline;
if you love me, you should also love him.
If one sees someone who is being honored,
one should likewise honor them.
The host then said:
"If there are such good or bad matters as these,
I shall accept neither;
you may each depart as you please."
At that time, the two women took each other by the hand and returned to their dwelling. Then the host—
Seeing him depart,
his heart was filled with immeasurable joy and exultation.

The goddess Puṇyavatī represents birth;

it refers simply to the two phenomena of birth and death in the world,

As for "the host having seen":
when the mind focuses upon an object,
it is called "seeing."

Regarding the woman’s reply:
it is called a "reply" (uttara) in the sense that the object (viṣaya) stands in relation to the mind (citta).
The Great Deity of Merit is a metaphor for the arising of these manifested signs;

Possessing the radiance of the six consciousnesses and illuminating the realms of the six sense objects,

Ultimately there is no body.
Having realized that the body is empty,
one nevertheless clings to the three phenomena of consciousness, warmth, and breath as being truly existent.
Regarding that which can bring about the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) within birth and death,
the Tiantai teachings state:
"This body is impermanent."
The body exists by grasping the three things— vitality, warmth, and consciousness;
yet the body is merely a conventional designation,
for these three things are impermanent.
There is no separate body;
the inhalation and exhalation of breath are reckoned as life.
The breath departs and does not return;
the body is like broken tiles and rubble;
how can life be preserved?
If the warmth sustains the water and the water moistens the earth,
one falsely claims that this body is permanent.
Fire arises from conditions;
when conditions disperse, the fire is extinguished,
and the body then becomes putrid and rotten.
Karmic conditioning and deluded consciousness shift from one realm to another in each moment,
yet they falsely claim, "I am eternal and sovereign."
As soon as karma is severed,
the mind immediately takes rebirth and the body dissolves and perishes.
The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states:
"From birth from the womb through the prime of youth..."
Aging and decay are all sustained by karma;
these three factors undergo arising and ceasing.
This continuity is uninterrupted;
ordinary beings do not understand it and falsely grasp at the characteristics of a body.
Unaware that their breath has ceased,
the three elements have separated;
it is just like the inhalation and exhalation of breath.
In a continuous succession of hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of inhalations and exhalations,
within each and every breath:
The body cannot be apprehended;
the mental consciousness of each moment arises and ceases in succession in infinite measure.
In each and every moment,
the body cannot be apprehended;
it neither stinks nor putrefies.
The three great elements form the skin, flesh, bones, and marrow;
examine each one individually, and they are found to be false and illusory.
The body cannot be apprehended;
apart from these three factors,
there is no separate body.
Therefore, one knows that body and life are fundamentally empty and that birth and death are eternally quiescent;
yet ordinary beings do not understand this.
They enter erroneously into the wheel of suffering;
life is like a flickering lamp in the wind,
extinguished in an instant.
The body is like a mass of foam in a pool,
vanishing in an instant;
therefore, the Sūtra says:
Understanding that nothing is not born,
one realizes that nothing does not die;
if one realizes that emptiness exists yet there is no self.
Since there is no self, who is it that is born?
Understanding that things are fundamentally non-existent, one does not arise.
Since there is no arising, who is it that dies?
Only the fundamental consciousness that maintains the seeds—
the wondrously profound true mind—
is in its essential nature perfectly luminous and clear.
It abides eternally in quiescence;
while in the state of an ordinary being,
it maintains the untainted [dharmas] and is constantly perfumed by them.
Reaching the gateway to the fruit of Buddhahood,
one continues the bodhicitta without interruption.
Furthermore, the nature of the mind is primordial.
Apart from the characteristics of arising and ceasing,
there is ignorance which deludes the nature of one's own mind.
Because it contradicts the nature of the mind and is characterized by the quiescence of signlessness,
it is able to give rise to the four signs of movement;
this occurs through the combined power of these four signs and ignorance.
It can cause the essence of the mind to undergo arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
As the Sūtra says:
"This very Dharma-body..."
Those who are tossed about by various afflictions and wander through birth and death are called sentient beings.
The *Awakening of Faith* clarifies that the intrinsically pure mind is moved by the wind of ignorance.
The four characteristics flow on,
yet there is only the dreaming mind;
one who dwells within the dream.
That is to say, they are distinguished as preceding and succeeding,
each being perceived part by part according to the depth or shallowness of one's intellectual power.
The one who has attained great awakening knows that the four marks of existence are like a dream,
and that there is only the single pure mind.
Since there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
it is impossible to distinguish between prior and posterior;
therefore, the treatise says:
The four characteristics exist simultaneously;
they have no independent existence as arising,
abiding, changing, and ceasing.
It evolves as a single mind;
the four characteristics exist simultaneously, being constituted by the mind.
Apart from this single mind, they do not exist.
Since there is no separate intrinsic nature,
it is said that they exist simultaneously;
there is nothing that exists independently.
They are fundamentally equal,
for they are one in their original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
As a verse in the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* says:
"Is there a limit to birth and death?
The Buddha said,
"Ultimately, there is none."
This cycle of birth and death is without limit;
its beginning and end cannot be apprehended.
As it is said in the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra:
Furthermore, O Paramavīra,
just as nirvāṇa is without limit,
so too are all phenomena without limit.
Why is this? Because birth-and-death has nirvana as its limit,
and nirvana has birth-and-death as its limit.
Since neither birth-and-death nor nirvana can be apprehended,
[there is no distinction between] birth-and-death and nirvana.
Since they cannot be apprehended,
all phenomena are entirely without limit.
Thus, one simply realizes the single mind of original enlightenment.
In every thought-moment, one accords with the Way of perfect permanence;
yet if one pursues ignorance with a distracted mind,
then in every dust mote, the wheel of birth and death is formed.
Success or failure depends on the person;
the Dharma has neither evil nor correctness.
Acceptance or rejection is left to one's own discretion.
The Way transcends both rising and sinking;
simply observe within yourself,
treading upon the Universal Gate to enter all at once.
One should simply rely on the right eye and tread the single path to achieve perfect completion.
Question:
Since the characteristics of the moving consciousness and the nature of the true mind are neither identical nor different,
are they further subject to destruction or indestructible?
If it were indestructible,
it would fall into the extreme of eternalism; if it were destructible, [it would fall into the extreme of nihilism].
This would then revert to the view of annihilationism. Answer:
Since it is neither one nor different.
That which is both destructible and indestructible.
The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"All characteristics of mind-consciousness..."
This is precisely the characteristic of ignorance;
it is neither identical to nor different from original enlightenment,
and it is not something that can be destroyed.
It is not indestructible;
it is like the seawater and its waves,
neither identical nor different.
The waves move because of the wind;
it is not the nature of water that moves.
When the wind ceases, [the waves subside].
The waves are extinguished,
yet it is not the nature of water that is extinguished.
Sentient beings are likewise.
The intrinsically pure mind,
stirred by the wind of ignorance,
gives rise to the waves of consciousness.
These three matters are all devoid of form or characteristics;
they are neither one nor different.
However, the intrinsically pure mind is the source of the moving consciousness;
when ignorance ceases, [the consciousness also ceases].
The moving consciousnesses perish accordingly,
yet the nature of wisdom remains unimpaired.
As for the extinction of fundamental ignorance:
This is the extinction through the wind of conjunction.
As for "the continuity is extinguished," it refers to the extinction of the karmic consciousness and so forth.
This refers to the cessation of the characteristic of movement.
"The nature of wisdom is indestructible" refers to the nature of the divine understanding of fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) as it accords with defilement.
It is called the nature of wisdom (*jñāna-dhātu*).
This conjoins with the nature of moisture and is indestructible.
Question:
The seeds of birth and death are not severed because they are all caused by the arousal of karma and the moistening of rebirth within the afflictions.
Which dharmas initiate karma?
Which dharmas moisten rebirth? Answer:
The nature of karma is fundamentally empty,
yet it forms into various types;
first, we shall discuss the characteristics of black and white actions.
The subsequent section will discuss the causes for the arousal and moistening of the faculties.
Here, first, regarding the aspects of black and white conduct,
the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, son of good family,
you should next contemplate karma."
Why is this? A person of wisdom should form this thought:
Feeling, perception, contact, and desire—
these are the afflictions that are capable of producing the karma of birth.
There is no karma that is not experienced;
in this way, the afflictions proceed together with karma.
There are two kinds:
first, those that produce birth;
second, those that experience [the results].
Therefore, the wise person should contemplate karma;
this karma is of three kinds.
That is to say: body, speech, and mind.
Good son, there are two types of karma: those of body and speech.
It is also called karma,
and it is also called the fruit of karma;
the mind is called only karma.
It is not called a fruit;
because it has karma as its cause,
it is therefore called karma.
Good son, the two karmas of body and speech are called external karma.
Mental action is called the cause;
these three types of action proceed together with the afflictions.
It constitutes two kinds:
first, the karma of birth;
second, the karma of experience.
Good son, right action is precisely mental action.
The "karma of the preliminary stage" refers to the karma of body and speech,
because it arises first.
That which is called mental karma arises from mental karma; that which is called bodily and vocal karma arises [from them].
Therefore, intentional karma is designated as "right.
Having observed karma in this way, the wise person—
Next, one contemplates the causes of karma.
As for the causes of karma,
they are precisely ignorance-contact (avidyā-sparśa).
Due to contact with ignorance,
sentient beings seek existence; this seeking of existence is the causal condition [for suffering].
This is precisely craving.
Due to the conditions of craving,
one performs the three types of karma of body, speech, and mind.
Good son, once the wise person has thus contemplated the causes of karma,
they next contemplate its retributive results.
There are four kinds of karmic retribution:
first, black-black retribution;
second, white-white retribution.
Third, mixed karmic retribution;
fourth, neither-black-nor-white karmic retribution.
Regarding black-black karmic retribution:
The karma is defiled, and its retribution is also defiled.
As for that which is pure and has a pure retribution:
It is called untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
