Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One..."
It was previously stated that the untainted (anāsrava) has no retribution;
how can it now be said [that it does]?
"Is it neither white nor black as its retribution?
The Buddha said, "Good son,"
This principle has two aspects:
first, that which is both a fruit and a retribution;
second, that which is only a fruit but not a retribution.
The black-black fruition is called both "fruit" (*phala*) and "retribution" (*vipāka*).
Because it arises from a black cause,
it is designated as a fruit; because it acts as a productive cause, it is so named.
It is also called "retribution.
The same applies to pure and mixed [karma].
As for the fruit of the untainted (anāsrava):
Therefore it is called a fruit;
because it does not act as a cause for another,
it is not called a retribution.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
this is untainted karma."
It is not a black dharma.
For what reason and by what causes and conditions is it not called white?
Good son, because there is no retribution,
it is not called white.
Because it counteracts the black,
it is called white.
I now speak of that which experiences the retribution of the fruit.
It is called "black-and-white," because it is untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) and thus does not receive retribution.
It is not called white;
it is called tranquility.
Therefore, one should know that karma is not to be performed.
The fruit cannot be escaped.
As a verse in the sutra says:
"Neither in the sky nor in the midst of the sea..."
It is not by entering among mountain rocks;
there is no place on earth where one can escape and avoid experiencing karma.
Only by not performing [an action] is there no fruit;
once the Way is attained, karma perishes,
just as the scent of a candāla vanishes when one exhales.
One may be born in the heavens despite having committed evil karma;
Aṅgulimāla attained the fruit of liberation despite having committed the crime of parricide.
Thus one knows that since receiving this body,
there has been no moment when one did not engage in action; even if one does not act in this present life, [the consequences of past actions remain].
In the past, they were all once practitioners of this school; there was none who, upon awakening to this teaching,
did not attain liberation.
By what means is one liberated?
If one enters the Mirror of the Source,
both person and phenomena are naturally empty.
When there is emptiness of persons, one does not perceive a person who is capable of performing an action. When there is emptiness of phenomena...
Thus, one does not see the place where the fruit of action is received;
it is merely because of deluded attachment to persons and phenomena that one creates karma,
and without departing from the realm of mind and objects, one undergoes calamity.
When both mind and objects are extinguished,
there is liberation right where one stands; thus,
one knows that all dharmas, whether good or evil, are likewise so.
There is no fixed characteristic;
it arises from the turning of the mind,
where gain and loss depend entirely upon conditions.
As it is said in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra:
The Buddha said,
"Good son,..."
If it were said that all karmas necessarily yield their retribution,
then there could be no cultivation of the holy life,
nor liberation, nor nirvana.
You should know that such a person is not my disciple;
they are a member of Māra’s retinue.
If it is said that various karmas are both determinate and indeterminate, as for those that are determinate:
Present retribution, retribution in the next life, retribution in subsequent lives,
and that which is indefinite.
When conditions converge, there is feeling;
when they do not converge, there is no feeling.
It is for this reason that [it is said].
There must be the holy life,
liberation, and nirvana;
one should know that such a person [possesses them].
They are true disciples of the Tathāgata and not the retinue of Māra;
it is even like the case of two people.
Both were traveling along a perilous path;
one possessed sight, while the other was blind.
One with eyes passes straight through without harm;
the blind fall.
One falls into a deep and perilous pit;
therefore, know that those who obtain the eye of the Mirror of the Source shall never again fall into the dangers of the three realms of existence.
They naturally pass straight through the pit of the five desires without doubt,
always dwelling on the ground of awakening.
Next, to explain the causes for the arousal and moistening of the faculties:
if one distinguishes them, the manifest afflictions directly arouse karma,
while co-emergent ignorance assists in arousing karma.
"Arising" (utthāna) means the sense of movement;
"action" (karma) means...
Regarding the meaning of "invoking and inducing":
innate [ignorance] can moisten birth,
while discriminative [ignorance] can create karma.
The fault of being overly weighted toward projecting rebirth is slight, while the innate capacity to moisten rebirth is heavy;
if it were the discriminative [consciousness] that produced karma for humans and devas, [the fault would be greater].
It immediately arises together with and assists [the mind],
for since the karma of humans and devas is difficult to arouse,
it necessarily depends upon that which is co-emergent.
If the projecting karma for the three miserable realms is projected by discriminative thought,
it does not require the assistance of co-emergent [karma] to project it,
because discriminative thought is sharp and intense.
Do not assist in its arising.
Question:
What are innate and conceptual [afflictions]?
What is the distinction between these two types?
Answer: According to the correct intent of the ancient commentaries on the sūtras and śāstras.
That is, the conceptualized is coarse,
while the innate is subtle.
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
The innate grasping at a self,
through the internal power of false habitual tendencies accumulated since beginningless time,
is constantly present together with the body.
Because it functions spontaneously without depending on false teachings or false discrimination,
it is called "innate" (*sahaja*).
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"From beginningless time until now, one has distantly followed along with active manifestations without applying mental attention as a condition."
It exists spontaneously,
without depending on deliberate mental application, conceptualization, or discursive thought,
just as a small child feels joy upon seeing its mother.
This is innate greed;
seeing another person weeping is innate hatred.
Because it arises spontaneously by itself without depending on the seeking of conceptualization or discursive thought through other conditions,
one knows that it is subtle and innate.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The conceptual grasping of a self also arises only through external conditions in the present world."
It does not arise simultaneously with the body;
it must await false teachings, false teachers,
and false discrimination.
Only then does it arise.
Furthermore, among these three conditions,
the first two are coarse.
The third is the subtlety of self-reflection.
The Sūtra says:
"By the power of conditions, the roots of goodness are severed."
The roots of goodness are severed by the power of causes when one is born in hell;
they are restored at the time of death in hell.
This is precisely the power of the cause consisting of one's own wrong reflection;
the other two are the power of conditions.
Therefore, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"All sentient beings revolve in the world due to two inverted, discriminative, and delusive views."
They arise in that very place;
they revolve according to karma.
What are the two views?
The first is the delusory vision of the individual karma of sentient beings;
the second is the delusory vision of the common lot of sentient beings.
What is meant by the delusory vision of individual karma?
Ānanda, it is like people in the world who have red film over their eyes.
At night, seeing the light of a lamp,
there appears a distinct circular shadow with five colors layered one upon another.
What do you think?
Is this circular halo manifested by the light of this night lamp the color of the lamp itself?
"Ānanda, when one sees form, is this form like the light of a lamp?"
If it were not a vision of one with cataracts, why would their perceptions not be identical?
Yet this circular shadow is seen only by the one with cataracts.
If seeing color were such that the act of seeing itself became the color,
then for that person with the cataract who sees the circular shadow—
What would its name be?
Furthermore, Ānanda, if this circular reflection existed separately from the lamp, [it would have to exist independently].
Then, when one stands beside a screen or curtain and observes any assembly,
a circular shadow appears; yet,
apart from this perception, there is nothing else.
It should not be visible to the eye;
how then can a person with cataracts see a circular shadow?
Therefore, one should know this.
Form actually resides in the lamp;
the perception of it as a shadow is a disease. Both the shadow and the perception are the result of a cataract.
Seeing the optical aberration is not the disease itself;
one should ultimately not say that this is the lamp or this is the vision.
Within this, there exists that which is neither lamp nor vision.
It is like a second moon;
it is neither a substantial entity nor a reflection. Why is this?
Regarding the second contemplation:
because it is produced by being squeezed,
those who possess wisdom [should understand this].
One should not say that this pressed root-element is either form or non-form,
or is apart from seeing or non-seeing.
This case is also like that;
it is produced by a cataract in the eye.
Now, whom do you wish to name as the lamp and as the seeing?
How much less could one differentiate between what is neither a lamp nor seeing?
Why, then, is this called "shared false vision"? Ānanda!
In this Jambudvīpa, excluding the waters of the great oceans,
there is level land in between.
There are three thousand continents.
The central continent,
measured from east to west, is as follows:
There are two thousand three hundred great lands in total;
as for the remaining small continents, [they are not enumerated].
Within these various seas,
there may be two or three hundred countries,
or perhaps only one or two.
As for those [islands] numbering thirty, forty, fifty,
or even fifty, Ānanda,
if among them there were even a single small island;
There are only two countries;
there is but one people.
Together they experience the conditions of evil karma.
Then, the sentient beings of that land on the small continent will behold all manner of inauspicious omens.
Some see two suns; some see two moons;
within them, there are even halos, solar spots, and crescent-shaped rings.
Comets, meteors, and flying stars;
halos, solar discs, and rainbows—
various such evil omens appeared.
It is seen only in this land;
the sentient beings of that land have never before seen it,
nor have they even heard of it.
Ānanda, I shall now for your sake clarify these two matters by advancing and retreating them together.
Ānanda, it is like those sentient beings who, due to the deluded vision arising from their individual karma,
perceive the circular shadow appearing within a lamp’s light.
Although it appears as if it were an external object,
it is ultimately produced by the visual impairment of the observer.
The visual impairment is itself the exhaustion of seeing;
it is not produced by external forms.
Yet, that which perceives the impairment—
Ultimately, there will be no fault to be seen;
consider your own experience today,
when you observe mountains, rivers, and the lands with your eyes.
As well as all sentient beings,
these are all produced by the disease of vision that has existed since beginningless time.
This includes both vision and its conditions.
It appears as a manifest object;
yet, lacking the awareness of selflessness,
one perceives the visual aberration of the object-condition.
To perceive and see is the cataract;
the originally awakened, luminous mind,
perceiving its conditions, is not the cataract.
The perceiver perceives what is perceived as a cataract;
yet the perceiver is not within the cataract.
This is truly the seeing of seeing.
What, furthermore, is meant by "awakening, hearing, knowing,
and seeing"? Therefore, you now see me and yourself,
as well as the ten classes of sentient beings in the world.
All these are simply the seeing of a cataract;
it is not the seer of the cataract who sees the true essence.
Since its nature is not that of a visual defect, it is not called "seeing.
Ānanda, [it is thus].
Just as those sentient beings share a commonality of deluded vision,
so too may one individual with a distinct karmic vocation be compared to that deluded vision,
like a single person with diseased eyes.
It is the same for that entire country;
they all see the circular shadow,
which is produced by the delusion of their visual impairment.
These inauspicious manifestations of this commonality of destiny arise from the baleful miasma within the karma of shared perception;
both are produced by beginningless false perceptions.
For example, within Jambudvīpa with its three thousand continents,
together with the four great oceans,
and throughout the Sahā world-system.
Furthermore, all the impure lands throughout the ten directions,
as well as all sentient beings therein,
are equally this enlightened, luminous, and untainted wondrous mind.
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing arise from the conditions of false and illusory sickness; through their conjunction they falsely come into being,
and through their conjunction they falsely perish.
If one can remain far removed from all conditions of conjunction as well as non-conjunction,
then one further eliminates the causes of birth and death.
The nature of Bodhi is perfect and free from arising or ceasing;
it is the pure fundamental mind,
the eternally abiding original enlightenment.
The *Lengyan jing shu* (Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) states:
"Deluded vision arising from individual karma" refers to the afflictions of conceptual discrimination.
The "common deluded vision" refers to innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*).
Seeing the fivefold circular shadows of lamp-light at night refers to...
This is a metaphor for the five views.
The aggregates (skandhas) are like the light of a lamp. These five views—
Arising upon the aggregates, it falsely gives rise to conceptualization and inference;
this is the nature of pervasive imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
While it exists in experience, it lacks objective reality.
That which appears as a shadow due to a visual disorder while the lamp itself remains real is, by analogy,
the nature of the dependent aggregates (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Dependent origination is not non-existent;
therefore it is said that form truly exists within the lamp,
while the essence of the view of self is empty.
It arises from the deluded mind;
therefore, it is said that seeing the illness is like seeing a shadow.
That "both the shadow and the seeing are cataracts" means:
Because the grasper and the grasped are both delusions of discrimination,
seeing them as such is not a disease.
When directly realizing the truth,
one understands that the essence of the parikalpita (imagined nature) is entirely empty.
Therefore it is said that seeing the cataract is not the illness;
once delusive discrimination has perished,
all is one with true nature.
Because it is free from the grasped and the grasper,
one should ultimately not say that "this is the lamp" or "this is the seeing," nor that "it is neither the lamp nor the seeing."
This immediately clarifies what was stated above regarding the time of "seeing the seeing":
that seeing is not [ultimately] seeing,
just as a second moon is neither a substantial entity nor a reflection.
Originally there was no moon;
with what, then, could form be established? Since form is not established, [how can it be perceived?]
Neither form nor non-existence;
this is not a single characteristic.
Both subject and object are extinguished.
Therefore it is said: "How much more so for that which is neither lamp nor seeing?
Furthermore, regarding the statement, "One who perceives the cataract ultimately incurs no fault of seeing":
if one knows that the cataract is simply a disease of the eye.
One ultimately does not grasp the reflection as being substantially real;
therefore, there is no fault of [erroneous] seeing.
As for "seeing and the conditions of seeing appearing as if they were present objects":
All of these arise through the transformations of the deluded mind;
they are not real external objects.
This refers to the two divisions of the seeing-part and the perceived-part.
In both cases, they are not separated from the mind;
how much more so when this parikalpita (imagined nature) is merely a reflection without a real substance?
This explains false vision.
"Originally, my enlightened awareness saw the affliction in what was perceived" refers to the primordial,
true enlightenment; for it is by means of this true capacity for awakening that delusion is perceived.
Having realized that both the deluded vision and its object are equally the result of a cataract,
one understands that the very act of perceiving is itself the cataract.
"The inherently enlightened, luminous mind perceives conditions but is not the cataract" concludes the preceding discussion on the two types of awareness—
the true and the deluded. Delusory vision is precisely the cataract.
The true mind capable of awareness is not itself the cataract;
it merely perceives those illusory conditions,
yet its essence is not the cataract.
Therefore, it is said that the object of awakening is not the cataract.
As for "the awakening that awakens to what is awakened to is the cataract," this restates that both the deluded awakening and its object are equally cataracts.
"The awakening is not within the cataract" reiterates that true awakening is not the cataract;
these constitute the two views of the real and the delusive.
Because one is simultaneously free from both the seer and the seen,
it is said that this is the true seeing of seeing;
for when the truth is realized, [this occurs].
Because these two views do not exist,
both the seer and the seen cannot be established.
What, then, is meant by "awakening, hearing, knowing,
and seeing"? Therefore, you now see me, yourself,
and all the ten classes of sentient beings in the world.
All these are simply the visual impairment, not the one who perceives the impairment;
that which perceives is the true essence of vision,
whose nature is not impaired.
Therefore, it is not called "seeing. For what reason is true seeing not called "seeing"?
Because it is free from the disease of cataracts.
It is solely due to perceiving the disease that one distinguishes between the establisher and the established;
consequently, one perceives the world as characterized by the mutual difference between self and other.
Therefore, it is said that all are immediately seen as the cataract.
To say they are "not the seeing of the cataract" means that true seeing is not the cataract itself.
Because true non-seeing cannot be established as a characteristic,
it is not called a cataract. Since it is not called a cataract, [it is not a disease].
Nor is it called "seeing.
This precisely clarifies the meaning of being free from seeing.
Therefore, where there is seeing, there is delusion.
It arises from the conceptualizing mind,
like a person with cataracts seeing the circular halo around a night lamp.
The absence of views is itself the truth;
when perfected wisdom manifests,
it is like a person with clear vision.
One perceives the purity of empty space.
Furthermore, if it is a false perception resulting from individual karma,
it is like the ripening of particularly grave evil karma.
Their physical bodies transform into snakes, tigers, and the like;
this is the general retribution for their immovability,
while they personally undergo the specific retribution.
It is transformed solely by one's own karmic consciousness;
those with different karma do not perceive it.
It is like the circular shadow on a lamp;
it is seen only by one with a visual disorder. To one who does not have such a disorder, it does not appear.
Thus, their views differ.
If they share the same deluded vision,
it is as if they have collectively created the karma for the Avīci Hell.
They share the collective retribution and undergo the same uninterrupted suffering;
this is so even if they do not share in those same evil karmas.
Then they do not see it.
It is like when the people of a single nation collectively encounter adverse conditions and collectively perceive all manner of inauspicious phenomena.
If the sentient beings of that land do not share in those same evil conditions,
then they would originally neither see nor hear them.
Therefore, one knows that suffering and pleasure have their conditions;
they consist of collective retribution and individual retribution,
arising from the conjunction of causes and conditions.
They arise in that very place;
when causes and conditions disperse,
they cease in that very place.
"There has never been a single dharma that did not arise from my own mind.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
If one can distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction,
then one will see that the pure original mind is eternally abiding.
Furthermore, if one discriminates afflictions, they arise only through coarse causes and perverse thoughts.
Co-emergent ignorance is subtle;
it arises spontaneously and constantly. Although there are textual passages that distinguish between the coarse and the subtle, [the former refers to the afflictions associated with views].
They are all equally deluded consciousness,
like those who experience individual karmic illusions;
due to a cataract in the eye, they perceive a circular halo upon a lamp.
It is like those with impaired vision who,
due to a miasmic affliction, perceive calamities and anomalies within their own country;
though they distinguish between shared and distinct realms, [the objects do not truly exist].
All of these are the deluded mind;
this can be verified within the realm of sentient beings.
All matters that are seen or heard are like the shadows of a cataract in the visual field of a single person’s individual karma,
or like an inauspicious omen shared by many people.
If one can know that the reflection of a lamp is produced by an optical aberration of the eye,
and that the perception of a calamitous object arises from a miasmic affliction,
then the double image upon the lamp will naturally vanish.
The two suns in the heavens suddenly sank;
like an unmoving single mind,
all conditions were simultaneously stilled.
Then the afflictions of the union of seeing and hearing will completely vanish through discernment,
and the calamity of fundamental birth and death [will be extinguished].
Co-arising [afflictions] are forever severed.
Question:
Within the three miserable realms (tridurgati),...
Furthermore, does it include both the conceptualized (*vikalpita*) and the innate (*sahaja*) [afflictions]?
The answer is that Dharmapāla says:
Within the three miserable realms, there is generally no discrimination,
and thus they do not initiate karma,
as is the case with species such as monkeys.
All afflictions are powerful and innate,
rather than being conceptual.
If one were to perform karma,
it would result only in individual retribution; if there were someone who could perform collective retribution through conceptual discrimination, [it would be otherwise].
Then there would be no time of emergence at all.
Question:
Since there are already seeds of discrimination, [how can there be liberation?]
"Why do they not produce collective retribution?
Answer: "Because they lack both the primary factor and its attendants."
The manifest activity is the principal;
the seeds that assist in its arousal are the companions.
Question:
If it is said that one does not create karma in the three miserable realms,
how is it that a powerful ghost struck Śāriputra on the head and he immediately entered hell?
A parrot bird heard the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and attained rebirth in heaven.
[The Buddha] replied:
These constitute distinct retributions;
this karma is powerful enough to assist the collective retribution of former lives.
Once the collective retribution has received assistance,
one is then able to descend to earth or ascend to heaven according to the force of one's karma.
Furthermore, the ancient masters [have said]:
Question:
Within the realms of humans and devas,
is it certain that karma is universally generated?
Answer: Among humans, those of the Northern Continent do not create karma that results in either collective or individual retribution.
By means of non-conceptual signs,
those in the other three continents initiate karma;
furthermore, the deluded persons of this continent do not initiate karma.
Question:
It was previously stated that there is no discrimination within the three miserable realms;
how then can one recognize one's parents and others?
Just as the filial crow returns to feed its parents,
and cats and dogs recognize humans and perceive their anger or joy.
Answer: This is not a conceptualized affliction;
it is a spontaneous conceptualization.
It is not a discrimination arising from afflictions.
Question:
Ignorance gives rise to karma.
How many kinds of ignorance are there?
Answer: There are four kinds.
First, the underlying tendency;
second, the enveloping ignorance;
third, association.
Regarding the four uncommon [afflictions]:
external ordinary beings possess all four;
internal ordinary beings exclude the uncommon ignorance.
The seventh mind of the stage of faith (*śraddhābhūmi*) and those within the stage of application (*prayogamārga*) are internal phenomena (*ādhyātmikadharma*).
Because there is regression prior to the seventh mind of the ten stages of faith,
and because it is called an "external dharma" within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).
If an ordinary person regarding internal phenomena attains sudden enlightenment, they immediately create karma;
if they attain gradual enlightenment, they do not.
In the verse, it is taught that those whose compassion increases further create [rebirth], while those whose wisdom increases do not.
This refers to the stages of the ten bhūmis, from the eighth stage onward.
Concentration does not initiate karma, because the substance of the afflictions is absent [in that state]. This applies from the seventh ground onward.
As for the stages prior to the seventh ground:
Some say that the Sage,
taking untainted clarity as a condition, does not initiate karma;
even if there were co-nascent [karma], it would not arise.
It merely assists in moistening and nourishing birth.
Furthermore, it is said that from the seventh stage onward, when [the afflictions] arise as innate, they...
They also create wholesome karma that results in individual retribution.
Question:
For what reason do noble ones (*ārya*) not create karma that results in collective retribution?
Answer: Because there are no afflictions involving conceptual discrimination,
and because it takes untainted luminosity as its condition.
Because it opposes birth and death,
it merely uses co-emergent [afflictions] to moisten the old, collective karmic retribution.
They undergo分段生死 (segmented birth-and-death) and dwell among human beings,
excluding those of the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru).
Cultivating the contemplation of non-self,
one is free from conceptual discrimination and is unable to create karma.
In this regard,
with the exception of those who are utterly deluded, [this applies] to the heavens.
Except for the gods of the Heaven of Non-conception,
who do not create karma because they lack mental activity.
The four kinds of ignorance collectively give rise to karma and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This is the seed;
the other three are the actual manifestations.
Question:
Regarding the statement that "ignorance initiates karma and craving moistens rebirth," among the afflictions:
"How many factors can moisten?
Answer: The ancient commentary states:"
That is to say, the seeds of the five factors beginning with consciousness must depend upon the nourishment and irrigation of afflictions such as craving.
Only then can one be born.
As for the afflictions and karma that arise simultaneously,
they are the six that arise simultaneously.
The ten discernments (*vitarka*) and twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) constitute these [thirty-six afflictions]. Among these thirty-six afflictions,
the single factor of greed (*lobha*) alone is purely and directly moistening (*sneha*).
The remaining five arise simultaneously;
that is, the primary [consciousness] and its auxiliaries moisten [the seeds].
If one distinguishes them into ten types:
This refers to assisting that which assists and moistening.
Furthermore, there is a fourfold analysis (catuṣkoṭi). First:
There is this craving that can moisten rebirth;
it is the craving of the sixth consciousness,
because the first five consciousnesses are not powerful.
However, it is subsumed by both [types of craving];
strictly speaking, it is only the sixth.
Furthermore, there are cases where craving exists but is unable to moisten rebirth.
This refers to the seventh consciousness;
although it possesses craving and attachment,
this is because its objects of perception are internal.
Regarding those within the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*):
the "three existences" (*tribhava*) constitute the branch of birth (*jāti-aṅga*), which is moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
This refers precisely to the branch of birth within the bodies of all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The fourth existence (*bhava*) is the branch of birth (*jāti*), yet it is not moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
because for a Bodhisattva in his final body,
the Mahāyāna teaches that this is a manifested transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
Or [it may arise] within the generative organs of a transformation body.
Question:
Is the mind the cause for the arising of afflictions?
The body is the root of the creation of karma.
How many kinds of bodies are there?
What kind of body is capable of creating karma?
Answer: The body, in general, consists of four types of existence:
first, existence as birth (*upapattibhava*).
That is, after the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and before the fundamental existence (*pūrvakālabhava*),
at the very moment of linking the continuity of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*).
The arising of the five aggregates in a single moment is called birth-existence (upapattibhava).
Second is existence-in-itself (mūlabhava):
That which exists prior to the birth-existence (upapattibhava) and subsequent to the death-existence (maraṇabhava)—
all the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) within that interval— are termed "prior existence" (pūrvakālabhava).
Because it is summoned by the fundamental karma of retribution,
the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:
"The existence of the fundamental state (*pūrvakālabhava*) precedes death."
Following the moment of birth-existence,
there are three types of death-existence; that is,
following the fundamental existence (pūrvakālabhava).
Among these, that which precedes death— the moment when the aggregates (skandhas) are about to cease and are actually ceasing—
is called the existence at death (maraṇabhava).
The fourth is intermediate existence (*antarābhava*),
which occurs after death-existence (*maraṇabhava*) and before birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
Because it exists in the interval between the two,
it is called the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* says:
Between the two states of death and birth,
the five aggregates are called the intermediate state;
they constitute the body between these two states of death and birth.
One does not immediately initiate karma because of the absence of mind;
this applies to the intermediate state and the two types of existence (the prior and subsequent existences).
One is thus able to initiate karma.
Question:
Regarding the state of the intermediate body (antarābhava):
Regarding those who abide in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and those who are about to enter birth,
what is the nature of their mental activity (*ākāra*)?
Answer: According to the twenty-four formations dissociated from mind,
the intermediate state possesses one dharma, which is rapidity of movement.
Regarding the force of velocity (*vega*),
there is the force of human effort (*puruṣakāra-vega*).
An ancient commentary states:
Regarding the speed of human effort (*puruṣakāra-vega*):
it is like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) body proceeding with great swiftness toward the place where one is to be reborn;
this is called the speed of human effort.
That which is called "the middle" receives its name in contrast to what precedes and follows it.
It exists.
Thus there exists the body of affective consciousness;
it constitutes the bodies of sentient beings within these five destinies after the state of death-existence (cyuty-bhava).
It exists prior to birth and between the two forms; therefore,
it is called the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
It also has the five aggregates of maturation as its substance,
because it is like the original body in that both are summoned by karma;
such is the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
It then takes on the form and appearance of the body one is destined to have upon birth,
just as the intermediate state (antarābhava) does for a human being.
They resemble humans and so forth;
the five destinies are likewise,
though they are only as large as children of five or six years of age.
Although its physical dimensions are small,
its sense faculties are sharp and keen,
just as they were in its original body.
They are capable of performing various activities;
yet toward their parents, they give rise to perverted perceptions,
thereby producing attachment and aversion.
Among these, this intermediate state body is seen only by those of its own kind and by those with the pure divine eye.
Within that intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
they subsist solely on fragrant odors while remaining in the intermediate state.
As for those with a neutral intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that is neither virtuous nor non-virtuous,
they remain in the intermediate state for an extremely long time before taking birth.
It does not exceed forty-nine days.
Within this period, there are none for whom the conditions do not converge.
This applies whether one is extremely good or extremely evil during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Regardless of distance,
they go to take rebirth in a single instant;
with perverted minds, they proceed toward the objects of desire.
This refers to the eighth consciousness at the gateway of linking rebirth;
within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the womb-born and egg-born,
it perceives the union of the parents.
Giving rise to perverted perceptions,
they then undergo birth; this applies to those born from moisture and those of miraculous birth during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Due to the power of past karma,
regardless of proximity or distance,
they become stained by attachment according to their desires.
One is reborn immediately upon coming into contact with the place of fragrance.
Question:
Do those of the same class perceive the intermediate state body (antarābhava) with their eyes?
It is not yet known whether the eye of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is able to see the body of the previous existence (*pūrvakālabhava*). Answer:
There are also those who see their original body;
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Or it is said that they see only a male."
Or they see only the woman.
Thus, as they gradually approach that place,
they gradually cease to see their parents or any other location.
One sees only the male or female sexual organs.
Furthermore, if one with little merit is in the intermediate state (antarābhava) and is to be born into a lowly, poor, and destitute family, [one sees only these signs].
When such a person is at the point of death or entering the womb,
they hear various kinds of chaotic and unpleasant sounds;
this occurs if they are in a state of meritorious existence.
When one is to be born into a wealthy and noble family, at that time,
one will naturally hear beautiful, exquisite, and pleasing sounds.
This applies even up to the objects of odor, taste, and touch,
which likewise possess degrees of gradation.
Question:
Among these, there are those at the final stage.
Do they all arise with craving and undergo rebirth?
Answer: [No].
Within this state,
the sixth consciousness first arises, moistened by craving,
and if it grasps, it brings about rebirth.
That is to say, only the eighth consciousness— whether it be the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a male or a female—
arouses craving for the mother and gives rise to a mind of desire.
As for the intermediate state of a female:
Based on the father, love arises and a mind of desire is produced;
having given rise to these two kinds of affectionate minds,
one then acts for the sake of one's own body.
When it comes into contact with the desired object,
the emitted impurity flows into the womb.
One considers it as one's own;
subsequently, joy arises.
Once this mind has arisen, [it persists].
The intermediate state body then vanishes,
and one undergoes birth as a body of existence.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
When that intermediate-state body enters the mother's womb,
a perverted cognition arises in the mind.
They give rise to a mind of false interpretation,
conceiving thoughts of coldness and thoughts of great wind and rain.
The visualization of clouds and mist.
Having performed this visualization,
according to the excellence or inferiority of one's karma.
Furthermore, ten kinds of false thoughts arise:
first, "I am entering a house";
second, "I am ascending a multi-storied pavilion."
Third, "I ascend the hall.
Fourth, "I ascend the couch.
Fifth, "I enter the grass hut."
Sixth, entering a thatched hut;
seventh, entering a thicket of grass;
eighth, entering a forest.
Ninth, entering through a hole in a wall;
tenth, entering through the gaps in a fence.
Having formed this thought,
he immediately entered his mother’s womb.
Question:
What is the color of the intermediate state body? The answer is given in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: [it is like the color of a flame].
For those who have committed evil deeds,
the intermediate state (antarābhava) is like the luster of a black ram.
Or, for one who performs wholesome deeds during the darkness of night, there is the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Like the radiance of white cloth,
or as on a clear, bright night.
The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* says:
The intermediate state of hell beings is like a charred stump;
the intermediate state of animals is...
Like smoke, it is like the intermediate state of hungry ghosts;
like water.
The intermediate state of humans and devas is like the radiance of white robes. Question: [What is this?]
If a human being’s body transforms into that of a snake, a tiger, or the like, does an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) arise?
Answer: Yes.
Cien says: There is no intermediate state body.
Because the retributive fruit of the collective karma (tongbao) does not undergo transformation,
it is merely a favorable retribution experienced in the present life (xianzhuan biebao). If the eighth consciousness were the collective retribution, [it would likewise not transform].
Thus, it does not transmigrate.
Furthermore, as in the hells where beings undergo ten thousand deaths and ten thousand births,
there is likewise no intermediate state (antarābhava).
Because the collective retribution does not change.
Question:
It is like taking water.
Once the leeches have been dried and ground into powder,
they are subsequently placed in water.
If each and every atom were to become a leech, would there be an intermediate state [between them]?
Answer: Yes.
This is merely because sentient beings of a similar class who share common karma,
having come together and relied upon this as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), undergo birth therein.
It is not that they transform into many insects;
otherwise, one would incur the fault of increasing the realm of sentient beings.
Question:
Does King Samatā see the intermediate state body (antarābhava)?
Answer: [He does not.]
"Not seen. He asked, "Suppose,
for instance, there is someone who has been summoned by the authorities of the underworld."
There are also those who see it.
"What kind of body is this? he asked.
He replied:
This is merely comprised within the category of the body existing from the beginning (*pūrvakālabhava*). Some say:
"Because this person possesses karma."
It is merely within one's own consciousness that one falsely perceives the ghost of King Yama and the circumstances by which this occurs.
This arises from its own transformation upon the object of solitary reflection;
apart from consciousness, there is no seeing.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* verse says:
Objects follow the transformation of karma-consciousness;
therefore, it is said that "all is but mind.
Thus, one knows that consciousness is the source of both good and evil.
The mind is the root of suffering and joy;
yet worldly people know only to follow the current and pursue the branches,
losing the root and becoming lost to the source.
Though they practice austerities, they merely fill three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
thus they deviate from reality and gradually drift further away.
Though they accumulate merit, they spend eternal eons in vain.
The Way remains distant; therefore,
when sages who have attained the fruits encounter this,
they willingly declare themselves to be beyond its reach.
Even great bodhisattvas who have emerged from the provisional realm have not yet attained realization of the ultimate truth;
how much less so, then, could those of the heterodox and confused schools?
The heretics of the primordial darkness,
the haughty officials of the Lacquer Garden,
and the dazed, mad scholars.
How could one possibly hope to believe and accept it?
Thus we know that the Mirror of the Essence is difficult to believe;
those who awaken to it are rare and extraordinary.
Not only did he grasp the essential tenets,
but he was also able to profoundly penetrate the principles of cause and effect;
therefore, it is said that he had deep faith in the Mahāyāna.
One does not slander cause and effect;
therefore, all sentient beings create the causes of good and evil solely through their own minds.
They attract the fruits of suffering and happiness;
or, while dwelling in the intermediate state (antarābhava),
they perform wholesome causes.
Those who, receiving the light of pure white,
give rise to evil causes,
perceive the color of black darkness.
Or, on the day of entering the womb,
those who have accumulated white karma ascend to the top of a palace tower.
Those who have created black karma are cast among grasses and thorns;
even when reborn in the human world, they appear as such.
The primary and secondary bodies are likewise distinguished by superiority and inferiority;
those who possess merit exhibit the features of a prominent swallow-jaw and a dragon-like countenance.
To receive the splendor of flowered halls and golden pavilions is for those of meager virtue;
they instead manifest the humble forms of the five-fold dew.
Dwelling in the humble conditions of a jar-window and a mat-door,
one may truly be said to have a wind that is harmonious and a resonance that is compliant;
when the form is straight, the shadow is upright.
When cause and effect are simultaneous and conditions converge without fail,
one should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm.
"All is created solely by the mind.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"In the Hīnayāna, the environment and its retributions are considered the existence of karma."
In the Mahāyāna, the ten thousand objects are fashioned by consciousness;
they are bestowed upon heaven and earth according to illusory karma,
and manifest as soil and grass following the deluded mind.
If one with cataracts beholds flowers in the sky,
it is comparable to the manifestation of birth and old age within a dream;
yet if one awakens to this within the mind's activity, [it ceases].
Thus, it is heard only in the Buddha-dharma.
Enshin year (846), carved at the Fenshi Dazang Dujian. *Zongjing Lu*, Scroll 75.
Compiled by Chan Master Yanshou, Chief Abbot of Yongming Temple:
Regarding the two types of retributive obstacles—collective and individual—to which specific consciousness among the eight do they definitively belong? Answer:
An ancient commentary states:
The collective retribution belongs exclusively to the eighth consciousness because it arises first; prior to that,
the seven [consciousnesses] and the material and mental factors do not exist.
All arise based on the eighth consciousness; that is,
the eighth consciousness can universally serve as the support for the preceding seven [consciousnesses], including both matter and mind.
It is termed the "collective retribution" (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*).
As for the "individual retribution" (*asādhāraṇa-vipāka*), it occurs only within the first six consciousnesses;
the experiences of this retribution are distinct and not uniform.
This is called "distinctive retribution" (viśeṣa-vipāka).
If it is collective retribution (sāmānya-vipāka), it is fixed and does not extend to the present life;
being exclusively "retribution to be experienced in the next life" (upapadyavedanīya), it is received only in the future life.
If it is a distinct retribution, it is indefinite;
whether experienced in this life or in future lives,
it is received in all cases without obstruction.
He asked again:
"Why does the seventh consciousness not differentiate the obstacle of retribution?
He replied:
This is not something summoned by karma that would release one from the obstacle of non-retribution.
Furthermore, if there is an obstacle of retribution but no obstacle of karma,
this refers to the eighth consciousness.
If one possesses both karmic retribution and the two obstacles,
these refer to the first six consciousnesses;
if one lacks both karmic retribution and the two obstacles, [they do not apply].
This refers to the seventh consciousness.
Furthermore, if there were only obstacles to individual retribution (*vyaktavipāka-āvaraṇa*) and no obstacles to collective retribution (*sāmānyavipāka-āvaraṇa*), [the following would occur].
This refers to the preceding six consciousnesses.
If there were only the general obstacle to retribution and no distinct obstacle to retribution, [the following would occur].
This refers to the eighth consciousness.
Question:
Sentient beings create the two types of karma—defiled and pure—which constitute birth and death.
The two retributions of suffering and pleasure both arise from the mind; thus,
apart from the mind, they have no substance.
Within the eight consciousnesses,
which one specifically is this mind? Answer:
Regarding this, there are two interpretations from ancient and modern times.
First, an ancient master explained it as the sixth consciousness-mind.
Through the discrimination of the conscious mind,
one performs actions and receives retribution;
the arising of retribution is due to the mind.
Therefore, one knows that there is no such thing as a real sentient being.
Because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure;
there is no separate purity.
Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled;
there is no other defilement.
Defilement and purity are obtained through the mind.
"Sentient beings are merely names.
Master Shenxian (Shen Jie) explains that "mind" refers to the eighth consciousness.
Because this consciousness internally maintains the seeds of both the defiled and the pure,
when these seeds encounter conditions,
they are able to bring about the two fruits of suffering and pleasure.
Since the arising of fruits is due to the mind,
we know that there is no sentient being.
If the ancient masters take the sixth consciousness as the defiled and pure mind, [this is their view].
For this reason, these six consciousnesses associate with the eleven wholesome mental factors and are able to produce wholesome karma pertaining to humans and devas;
they associate with the primary faculties and the secondary mental factors.
It can create the evil karma of the three miserable realms;
this is formed through both general and specific karma,
capable of summoning the two retributions of future suffering and happiness.
Therefore, it is said that defilement and purity arise from the mind (*citta*).
This is based on taking the agent of action as the mind.
As for Master Shenjiai’s interpretation of the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as the mind:
This is the sovereign of the aggregate retribution,
the truly resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Within this consciousness, it contains and stores the seeds of both wholesome and unwholesome karma.
However, as for the substance of consciousness,
in its causal state it is exclusively of the nature of non-obscured indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta),
because it serves to store the seeds of both defiled and pure karma.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that it "maintains the seeds of defilement and purity," these are the seeds of the three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*):
first, the affliction of mental defilements (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*).
This refers to the afflictions of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation,
the two types of karmic defilements,
and all wholesome and unwholesome karma that results in total retribution.
The three types of contaminated fruits are the resultant fruits of maturation (*vipākaphala*), comprising both the general and specific retributions of the three realms.
The pure [fruits] are likewise of three kinds.
First is mundane purity,
which is the path for subduing afflictions;
second is supramundane purity.
That is to say, it is the untainted,
the purity that is the fruit of what is to be abandoned by the three [paths],
namely, the principle realized.
All that has preceded constitutes the eighth [consciousness], the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) of karma.
The ancient masters designated it as "mind" (*citta*) based on the perfuming agent and the mind that performs the karma;
Master Jie designated it as "mind" based on the perfumed object and that which maintains the seeds.
Furthermore, the ancient masters explained "mind" (*citta*) in terms of its objective referent (*ālambana*),
while Master Jie explained it in terms of its accumulation and origination (*cita*).
The commentary states:
These two interpretations each represent a distinct approach.
The former takes that which can permeate and that which can construct as "mind."
If there were no perfuming agent,
the object of perfuming would be useless,
and thus the ultimate reality alone could not be established.
Neither delusion alone nor truth alone can establish this;
it is only through the conjunction of truth and delusion that such a phenomenon comes to be.
Furthermore, if there is no creator,
that which is created cannot be established either,
because it is by means of the creator that the created is established.
The Sūtra states:
"All things are created by mind alone.
Hereafter, "mind" refers to the seeds that are perfumed and sustained.
That which is perfumed is the basis;
if there were no object to be perfumed,
the perfuming agent would likewise be useless.
Furthermore, if there were no perfuming seeds,
the seeds of good and evil would disintegrate; by what means,
then, could one experience the future retributions of suffering and pleasure?
Just as an object that has nothing to contain it will inevitably be lost,
so too is subsequent liberation superior.
Because it is the root among these various consciousnesses,
the previous interpretation is not lost;
because it is the branch and the derivative.
Now, if one adopts both together,
the correct principle will be complete;
the root and the branches will support one another.
Through the union of the subject and the object,
which are neither identical nor different,
the positions of worldly defilement and purity are established.
Thus we know that birth and death arise from the conscious mind;
no sentient being can be found.
Ascension and descent belong to causes and conditions.
There is no real self to be found.
Question:
Regarding the karma of both collective and individual retribution.
How are they distinguished? Answer:
They are like observing the five precepts.
Obtaining a human body is the collective retributive karma;
it arises because within the causal stage there was anger, patience, and so forth.
Regarding the collective retribution of human beings, there are those who are handsome and those who are ugly;
this is termed "distinctive retribution karma" (*viśeṣa-vipāka-karma*). In the Vijñaptimātra school, it is also called "projecting and completing karma" (*ākṣepaka-pūrakakarma*).
Because it can summon the eighth [consciousness] and project the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala),
it is called "projecting karma" (ākṣepaka-karma).
That which is capable of bringing about the sixth [consciousness] and fulfilling the fruit of maturation is called a "fulfilling karma" (pūrṇakarma).
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* also states:
"A single karma projects a single birth."
Many karmas can bring about completion,
just as in the case of a painted image,
where one first sketches the outline.
Subsequently, various colors and so forth are filled in;
however, the volition that constitutes the projecting karma must necessarily be produced by the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
If the volition that creates ripening karma (vipāka-karma) arises from the five consciousnesses,
yet these five consciousnesses lack grasping (anupādāna).
It cannot produce moistening; therefore,
it is not a delusion regarding principles,
as it lacks investigative deliberation.
They cannot create karma;
even if they were to create full karma,
it would not be by their own power.
However, because it can only function when induced by the mind,
the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Dragon King Sāgara:
"Those who rely upon the world..."
They create various conditions;
their mental activities differ,
and their transgressions and merits vary accordingly.
For this reason, O Dragon King, there is a distinction in their births.
Furthermore, observe the various assemblies and the great ocean;
they consist of many different forms and diverse appearances.
All these forms and appearances are painted by the mind;
furthermore, the mind has no form and cannot be seen.
All phenomena are thus deceptive; they arise from delusion as mere appearances.
There is no owner at all;
each receives the results according to what they have done.
For example, it is like a painter who originally has no pre-existing image;
all phenomena are likewise thus.
Yet it is inconceivable;
it is naturally like the appearance of an illusion or a magical transformation,
all produced by the mind.
The *Saṃsāra-kuṭī-sūtra* states:
The Buddha said,
"Observe those categories of beings among the devas and humans within the three realms."
Whether one's status is high or low, tall or short,
and whether one's merit and virtue are great or small—
all depend on the inequality of one's mental application in previous lives.
For this reason, what is received by each is distinct and not the same.
The *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* states:
As a verse in the *Abhidharma* says:
The thought of guarding one's own body and speech,
as well as that which encompasses others,
has the Dharma of loving-kindness as its seed.
One is able to attain both present and future results.
What is called "reflection" refers to being able to discipline oneself.
It is far removed from what is contrary to the Dharma;
because it is volition associated with this mind,
it is called "volition."
"Gathering others" refers to giving and kind speech;
"protecting those in fear" refers to rescuing them from their terrors.
Because one is able to gather others through such means as these,
it is called "gathering others."
Loving-kindness refers to the mind;
the mind is what is called "dharma."
It is also the seed.
As for "seed," it is also called the cause.
For whom is it the cause?
It is the cause of the fruit.
What kind of fruit is it?
This refers to the results of the present and the future.
Why is the mind called the seed? Because it is capable of giving rise to the actions of body and speech.
It is called the seed.
Furthermore, as a verse in the treatise says:
"Just as the continuity of sprouts and so forth..."
It arises from seeds;
from these, the fruit is produced.
Apart from the seed, there is no continuity.
The commentary states:
This refers to the production of the stalk from the sprout,
and so forth, up to the branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so on.
Each has its own characteristic.
Although the seed perishes,
it gives rise to a continuous succession that proceeds in turn until the fruit is reached.
If apart from the seed,
the continuity of the sprout and so forth would have no circulation;
for this reason, [the seed must exist].
Regarding its meaning:
why does the verse of the treatise state that "the seed has a continuity"?
From the continuity there is the fruit;
first the seed, then the fruit.
It is neither interrupted nor eternal.
The commentary says:
Why is it not severed?
It is because the continuity of the seeds persists.
Why is it not eternal?
Because once the sprout has arisen, the seed is destroyed;
internal phenomena are likewise.
As the verse in the treatise says:
"In this way, from the initial mind,
the mental factors arise in a continuous succession."
From this, the fruit arises;
apart from the mind, there is no continuity. Commentary:
This refers to a mind of loving-kindness and a mind lacking loving-kindness;
these are called karma.
Although this mind has ceased, [its influence persists].
And it arises as a continuum.
As for the arising of this fruit of the continuum,
it is because it possesses the characteristics of being experienced as either pleasant or unpleasant.
If one were separated from the mind,
the fruit would not arise.
Now, the dharma of continuity shall be explained.
What is its meaning?
Therefore, a verse in the treatise says:
"From the mind, there is a continuity."
Because the fruit arises from the continuity [of the action], the karma precedes the fruit;
thus it is neither annihilated nor eternal.
The commentary says:
What is meant by "not being severed"?
It refers to the fact that the continuity is capable of producing its fruit.
Why are they not permanent?
Because they do not persist into a second moment.
Thus, one should know that the three types of action are difficult to guard against and must be protected with utmost care.
The mind is a mass of suffering;
the mouth is the source of calamity.
One should simply close the gates and guard the passes.
Only then is the continuity severed.
As stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*:
"That is the ground of that hell."
Seeing the messengers of Yama,
they are rebuked with harsh words in verse:
"Your mind could not be disciplined."
More fierce than a great, raging fire,
it moves with such speed that it cannot be restrained;
it drags people down into hell.
The mind is the most difficult to tame;
this fire is more fierce than fire;
difficult to restrain, it moves with great speed.
From hell to hell: if a person’s mind is self-governing,
they will wander through the hells.
If a person can control the mind,
they will not suffer affliction;
desire is the foremost fire.
Delusion is the foremost darkness;
hatred is the foremost enemy.
These three govern the world.
When you previously committed evil,
you did so through your own mental deliberation;
you originally acted out of a deluded mind.
Now one undergoes this evil retribution:
the mind delights in stealing the property of others and in secretly approaching the wives of others.
Constantly killing and harming sentient beings,
they are deceived by their own minds;
such is the sovereignty of karma.
I have brought you to this place;
it is due to your own past evil karma.
Why do you groan and moan like this?
Furthermore, a verse says:
"Evil deeds are not lost or destroyed;
all evil has its retribution."
All evils are obtained through action;
because of the mind there is action,
and it is by means of the mind that one commits evil.
Because there is the fruit of the mind,
everything is created by the mind;
everything is caused by the mind.
The mind can deceive sentient beings,
leading them toward evil places;
this is the evil place of hell.
This is the most bitter and evil state.
As stated in the scriptural passage above,
this is the bitter fruit summoned by an evil mind.
If a wholesome mind brings about a pleasant fruit,
it is further said: "Furthermore, monks..."
Knowing the retribution of karmic actions,
he observed the abode of the Mālādharas,
even unto the softness of that ground.
It is like fresh butter;
when gods and humans walk upon it,
it sinks and rises according to the movement of their feet.
Like cotton-wool,
at every place where his feet tread, the ground becomes level.
It was also as previously described:
from each jewel tree,
wondrously colored light radiated forth.
Its radiance is like that of the sun;
its light is delightful and joyful.
The flowers and leaves of the golden trees of exquisite color are ever fresh.
They do not wither or fall away;
born of virtuous karma,
they are beyond all comparison or description.
The power of the precepts is sovereign;
it is obtained through wholesome karma,
just as a seal impresses its mark upon an object.
In this way, O devaputra,
you sport in the gardens and lotus ponds,
experiencing the retribution of your own karma.
There are superior, middling, and inferior [beings],
who enjoy great theatrical delights;
their bodily forms are produced by their own karma.
The radiance is lovely;
forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes,
and textures provide pleasure at will.
Their bodies were free from illness and affliction;
they experienced neither hunger nor thirst,
and they constantly indulged in the five desires.
Never feeling satiated,
they give rise to much craving and desire;
their minds are never filled.
If a deva recollects,
whatever is obtained through that recollection cannot be destroyed by others.
Sovereign and unimpeded,
his mind is ever joyful;
he can reach any place simply by thinking of it.
The emanation body conforms to the mind;
its size is as one pleases,
and it is vast, light, and supple.
In the blink of an eye,
they can travel a hundred thousand yojanas without the slightest fatigue.
Just as the wind moves through space without any obstruction,
so too is it with the devas.
There is no exhaustion;
the majestic virtue of the celestial body arises from the mind.
Light, pure, and stainless;
in all places of activity, it possesses a radiant color that accords with one's wishes.
The sons of gods and goddesses joyfully engage in play.
The commentary states:
"Nevertheless, although good and evil arise from the mind,"
Suffering and pleasure are not equal;
this first clarifies cause and effect,
so that one may know there is no discrepancy even in a single thought-moment.
If one discusses the ultimate path,
neither of these constitutes liberation.
As the sutra says:
The Kālaya devas,
riding in palaces of Jambūnada gold,
enter the Devakrīḍa forest.
That forest was soft and supple;
the songs of its various birds were harmonious and exquisite.
After the devaputra had entered,
there was a bird named Deva-ghoṣa,
born from karma identical to that of the gods.
Due to his wholesome karma as a deva,
he spoke this verse:
"If there is anyone who can perform [this]..."
Through the wholesome karma of delighting in [virtue],
that person’s karmic fruition is accomplished as being exceedingly magnificent.
Having already obtained celestial pleasures,
if one does not act with negligence,
one will proceed from pleasure to a state of further bliss.
He will surely reach nirvana;
all pleasures are impermanent,
and must inevitably end in exhaustion.
Do not accept these celestial pleasures as your own private delight;
these celestial pleasures are impermanent.
When one's lifespan is exhausted, one must inevitably decline and pass away. Having understood this law,
one should constantly seek the path to nirvāṇa.
All phenomena are subject to exhaustion;
that which is high shall inevitably fall;
where there is union, there must be separation.
All who have life must return to death.
It is further said:
"In this way, O bhikṣu."
Having observed the celestial pleasures with the wisdom derived from hearing,
he spoke this verse:
"The five faculties are constantly full of craving and delight."
Deceived and deluded by the objects of desire,
the fire of lust has never ceased;
yet in an instant, one hears of wearying detachment.
In every single realm,
one sees celestial maidens everywhere;
such are all the most excellent realms.
The flames of desire blaze fiercely;
whether in union or in separation,
whether in speech or in recollection.
Due to the karmic conditions of the celestial maidens,
a fire arose and burned the devas;
such is the nature of fire.
Existence arises through conjunction;
without conjunction, it does not arise.
Whether there is conjunction or no conjunction, [it remains so].
The fire of desire is constantly blazing;
because the causes and conditions do not coincide,
the fire does not burn when it is distant.
The fire of desire knows no distance;
it constantly burns those beings who cherish it,
fueled by the power of the wood of conceptual thought.
Driven by improper mental attention,
one casts the oil of craving into the fire of desire,
which burns the foolish person.
Therefore, once it is known that suffering and pleasure arise from the mind and that external phenomena are not ultimate,
[one realizes this truth].
One should sever the notion of firewood, which is craving; the oil is the fuel;
and the wind is the thought that stirs it.
Extinguish the fire of desire,
restrain the mental ground,
and always accord with True Suchness.
It brings to perfection the sublime fruit of constant bliss, which is Bodhi.
Thus, a verse in the Sūtra says:
"If one possesses a mind that is correct and virtuous..."
Constantly observing in accordance with the Dharma,
one is not driven by transgressions,
just as sunlight dispels darkness.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"It is better to take the mind as one's teacher than to take the mind as one's master."
If one takes the mind as the teacher,
one will follow the six realms of existence without returning; therefore,
take the Dharma as the teacher.
Thus, one darkly unifies with the One Way and constantly returns to it,
as Gengsangzi said: "The mind is impartial and upright."
Not being enticed by external things,
it is said that being pure and able to endure leads to clarity;
being clear and able to endure leads to emptiness.
When empty, the Way is complete and one dwells within it.
Thus, the *Aksayamatinirdesa-sutra* says:
"Always rectify your mind."
One does not esteem other forms of learning.
For the mind is always upright and straightforward;
it is fundamentally profound and empty.
The Way is entirely mind;
mind is entirely the Way. It is because of a failure to realize this that [confusion arises].
Following the discursive mind,
one is constrained by external conditions and disturbed by internal fetters.
Thus, one is commanded that the will must return to the One and not esteem other studies;
when emptiness and luminosity manifest spontaneously,
this is what is meant by "returning to the source."
Such an instruction may be called "taking the practitioner by the hand."
Until reaching the ocean of sarvajñā (all-knowledge),
one will certainly not be left alone;
this applies to those who believe and accept it.
This may be called "remaining unmoved amidst worldly afflictions while suddenly attaining perfect enlightenment.
Question:
Consciousness arises in the body,
and the body depends upon consciousness.
When the sense faculties perish, it is said that consciousness has departed.
Having abandoned this current body and received another physical form,
what are the characteristics of the consciousness that has departed and that which is yet to come?
This intent is difficult to clarify;
the whole world is deluded by it,
like a treasure hidden within a storehouse.
"No one knows it.
He replied,
"This principle is subtle and profound."
This can be understood according to the provisional teaching.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-sūtra* (Xian-shi jing) states:
The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:
The circulation, transformation, cessation, coming, and going of consciousness is like the element of wind:
it is without color and without form.
It cannot be manifested,
yet it can impel all things and display their various forms.
Some shake and stir the forest trees,
crushing and splitting them to produce great sounds;
others manifest as cold or heat.
It touches the bodies of sentient beings,
producing suffering and pleasure;
wind has no hands, feet, face, eyes, or physical form.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla, there are no colors such as black, white, yellow, or red;
the element of consciousness is likewise.
It is without form and without shape;
it has no luminous manifestation,
yet by way of causes and conditions, it exists.
Just as various distinct functions are manifested,
one should know that the dharma-realm of sensation and perception is likewise so.
It is formless and shapeless;
yet, by means of causes and conditions,
it is manifested.
"Kauśika, when sentient beings die, their functional activities cease."
This feeling, perception, mental phenomena,
and consciousness element are all detached from the body.
Consciousness conditions sensation;
the dharma-realm experiences other bodies.
It is like the element of wind blowing various exquisite flowers; though the wind blows,
the flowers remain right here.
The fragrance flows to a great distance;
yet the nature of the wind does not grasp the fragrance of the exquisite flower.
This applies to the nature of the fragrance, the nature of the wind, and the faculty of the body.
Both lack form and color,
yet it is not by the power of wind that the fragrance reaches far.
Bhadrapāla, when the bodies of sentient beings die,
consciousness maintains the perception of the dharma-realm.
Thus, even unto future lives,
consciousness takes up residence therein by reason of the conditions provided by the parents.
The sensation-perception dharma-realm that can follow after consciousness is also like this;
it is as if from the superior power of a flower.
The nose possesses the faculty of smelling;
through the superior power of smelling,
it perceives the realm of odors.
Furthermore, it is like obtaining the color and touch of wind from the superior power of the body of wind;
it is due to the superior power of wind.
Just as fragrance can reach a great distance,
so too from consciousness arises feeling,
and from feeling arises perception.
From the awakening to the existence of phenomena,
one is then able to discern what is wholesome and what is unwholesome,
up to and including the transition of consciousness into a new body.
It is like the reflection of a face appearing in a mirror,

like the rising sun; wherever its light reaches, [it illuminates].

when the sun set and its light faded,

Darkness has no form or substance;
it is neither permanent nor impermanent,
yet one can find its locus.
Consciousness is also like this:
it has no substance and no form;
it is manifested through sensation and perception.
Consciousness resides within the body;
like darkness, it has no substance and cannot be seen even when looked at.
It cannot be grasped or held,
just as a mother carrying a child in her womb cannot know for herself whether it is male or female.
Black, white, and yellow;
whether the faculties are complete or incomplete;
hands, feet, ears, and eyes.
Whether it was similar or dissimilar food,

Engaging in speech, laughter, and conversation;
carrying heavy loads on their shoulders;
and performing various kinds of labor.
The characteristics of consciousness are fully manifest,
yet one cannot know its location;
it merely abides within the body.
One does not know its form,
O Bhadrapāla; such is the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
He enters all sense bases,
yet is not defiled by those sense bases—
the six faculties and the six objects.

through this, the functional activity of consciousness is revealed.
Bhadrapāla, it is like a wooden mechanical device that is fastened and held at a single point.

such as walking and leaping,

What do you think?
By whose power is that which is produced by a mechanical device brought about?
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying,
"My wisdom is narrow and shallow;
it is not within my power to comprehend this."
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"You should know that all this is the power of the karma one has performed.
Karma has no form; it is merely the movement of wisdom."
In this way, the mechanism of the body performs all its various activities through the power of consciousness.
Sages, gandharvas, nāgas, devas,
and humans.
Devas, asuras,
and so forth— the various realms of existence.
All karma relies entirely upon it;
consciousness can produce the body,
just as a craftsman operates a mechanical device.
Consciousness has no form or substance;
it universally sustains the dharma-realm and is fully endowed with the power of wisdom.
It even enables one to know the events of past lives.
Therefore, know that the nature of consciousness is a single unity, without abiding and without form;
it merely manifests in accordance with wisdom.
It evolves with every thought-moment;
as soon as this aggregate ceases,
that aggregate arises.
It is like the impression of a seal appearing in clay,
or like the reflection of a face confronting a mirror;

Entrusting its substance to this present life,

Like a pearl emitting radiance,

by the power of mindfulness,

"How large should it be?

The *Xiǎnshí jīng* (Sūtra on the Manifestation of Consciousness) states: The Buddha said,
"O Bhadrapāla."
Form is of two kinds:
first, internal;
second, external.

the eye is external. This continues up to bodily consciousness, which is internal.
The body, however, is external, O Bhadrapāla;
it is like one born blind.
In a dream, one sees beautiful forms;
the hands, feet, face, and eyes are of exquisite and lovely appearance.

and upon waking from sleep, he remained so.

"How is it that one can see forms within a dream?
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I pray that you will grant us an explanation."

it is not seen by the physical eye.
As for that which is seen by the physical eye—
By the power of mindfulness,
they appear for a brief moment within the dreams of the blind;
again, by the power of mindfulness.

the internal form perceived by consciousness is likewise so.

Question:
The nature of consciousness is formless and reaches the utmost subtlety.

The nature of consciousness is subtle and inconceivable;
it functions in accordance with karma.
Then beauty and ugliness are instantly distinguished;
yet because they are formless,
small and large are all equal.
The *Xiǎnshí jīng* (Sūtra on the Manifestation of Consciousness) states: The Buddha said,
"O Mahauṣadha."
Just as the element of wind has no substance and no form,

Its emergence was violent and fierce;

The three types of habitual tendencies are called "habitual tendencies" because they possess a residual influence,
