The *Qingliang ji* states:
"The meaning of the Tathāgata’s appearance is also termed 'dependent origination' (*pratītyasamutpāda*)."
It is also called "Arising of Nature" (xingqi).
If it appears through the convergence of the eight aspects and conditions,
it is therefore called "Dependent Arising" (yuanqi).
It is said that because the Tathāgata appears through great compassion, induced by the karma of sentient beings,
his manifestation of the eight phases of enlightenment proceeds from the *dharmatā*.
Therefore, it is called "Arising of Nature" (xingqi).
Now, because there is no inherent nature [independently] due to following conditions,
this very dependent origination is named the "Arising of Nature."
Furthermore, the pure dependent origination always accords with the nature;
it is also called "nature-arising" (xingqi).
Therefore, it is said that although [phenomena] arise from conditions, they should [be understood as] so.
Because they do not contradict their nature,
there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm;
this is the gate of mutual formation.
The nature of clarity is established through conditions;
therefore, this arising of nature has two meanings:
first, it is devoid of inherent nature in dependence upon conditions.
It is the arising of nature (*xingqi*).
Second, because the dharma-nature follows conditions,
it is called the arising of nature.
Because there is no non-returning [to this world] once this Dharma-body is realized,
this is the case where dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) can accomplish the nature-arising (dharmatā-utpāda);
this is precisely the gate of mutual accomplishment.
"Using the pure to displace the defiled,
because the nature itself arises" clarifies the gateway of mutual displacement.
This also serves as a general rebuttal.
That is to say, there may be one who asks:
"The *xingqi* (arising of nature) is exclusively pure."
Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is itself the arising of nature (*dharmatā-utpāda*).
Therefore, this general principle is established:
namely, that there are two kinds of arising.
First, defilement;
second, purity.
Purity refers to the great compassion of the Tathāgata.
The "ten thousand practices" and so forth of a bodhisattva are as follows:
"defilement" refers to the afflictions, karma, and so forth of sentient beings.
If one were to take the defiled to subvert the pure...
Thus it pertains to sentient beings;
therefore, it is solely dependent origination.
Now, the pure supersedes the defiled.
It belongs exclusively to all Buddhas;
therefore, it is called "Arising by Nature" (xingqi).
Thus, even the manifestation of the myriad dharmas [is included].
All are dependent arisings within the true nature.
Therefore, whatever actions a bodhisattva undertakes,
they all accord with the dharma-nature.
Because sentient beings have not yet exhausted the root of ignorance,
their self-clinging and emotional views remain undestroyed; thus,
all their actions and endeavors [are conditioned by these].
All of these contravene the nature of reality (dharmatā).
They merely establish the conditioned phenomena of arising and ceasing,
rather than establishing the gateway to the merit arising from the true nature.
As stated in the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*:
"This bodhisattva knows that the nature of phenomena is free from the characteristics of stinginess and greed."
This is the pure perfection of giving;
it accords with the practice of the *dānapāramitā*,
knowing that the nature of phenomena is detached from the objects of the five desires.
Being without the appearance of broken precepts is the perfection of pure ethical discipline;
it is the practice that accords with the *śīlapāramitā*.
To know that the nature of phenomena is without suffering or affliction and is free from the characteristics of anger and harm is the pure perfection of patience;
it is to practice the pāramitā of kṣānti in accordance with reality.
Knowing that the nature of phenomena is free from the characteristics of body and mind,
and being without indolence,
is the perfection of purification.
Practicing the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) in accordance with reality,
knowing that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is unmoving and undisturbed—
this is the purity of the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).
Practicing dhyāna-pāramitā in accordance with reality,
knowing that the nature of phenomena is free from all delusion and darkness—
this is the perfection of pure wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
By practicing in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*,

one knows that every single practice and every single action cultivated by a bodhisattva accords with the principle of true suchness (*tathatā*), the single mind, and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
It is not that there is something separate from the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that is cultivated;
because it accords with the nature of the mind,
all virtues arise in accordance with that nature.
It is inexhaustible and unconditioned;
it is neither grasped nor abandoned.
It is that which ordinary beings create through stinginess and greed.
Even up to the darkness of delusion,
all these are in opposition to reality and contrary to the nature of things,
giving rise to the mind of self-view.
Therefore, one does not arise according to [deluded] nature,
but accomplishes untainted merit; even if there were false cultivation, [it would be abandoned].
All those who perceive anything as existing separately outside of their own minds become entirely followers of external paths or celestial demons.
Conditioned phenomena arise and perish because they do not accord with True Suchness and contradict the Dharma-nature.
Furthermore, cultivation manifests nature,
and nature perfects cultivation; if there were no nature, [cultivation would not exist].
Cultivation is likewise not established;
if there is no cultivation,
the nature is not manifested.
As a virtuous elder of old said:
"That which exists fundamentally is like pure gold;
that which is produced through cultivation is like the ornaments fashioned from it."
It is through ornaments that the excellence of gold is manifested;
yet the ornaments have no intrinsic nature of their own,
being entirely composed of gold.
To illustrate these two virtues through analogies:
just as cultivation causes that which exists inherently to manifest gradually during the causal stage,
it brings that which exists inherently to full perfection during the resultant stage.
The fundamental principle is neither gradual nor perfect;
it is like the moon when first born: although its brightness gradually fills, it always retains the form of a full moon.
Because the full moon is ever-present,
the moon on the fifteenth day is thus present throughout the first, second, third, and subsequent days.
Thus one knows that the full fruit is omnipresent throughout the causal stage;
it also causes each subsequent stage to always possess all preceding stages,
and each preceding stage to always possess all subsequent stages.
From the moon on the first day until the moon on the fifteenth day;
by means of the moon on the fifteenth day.
Because it is the first month;
the correspondence with the Dharma can be understood accordingly.
For this reason, it is said:
That which is produced through cultivation is originally possessed,
because it was already perfected at the time of initial perfection.
That which is originally possessed is produced through cultivation.
Because it was already complete at the very moment of birth;
contemplate this by letting go of all thoughts.
If you cannot contemplate in this manner, [you must practice further].
Thus they lose a great benefit,
just like a destitute son who regards his own storehouse as belonging to another.
Some beg for alms while carrying a jewel within their robes;
others guard a treasury of gold yet remain in poverty.
All this is because they do not recognize the treasure of their own minds.
It has come to this state.
Furthermore, as the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says,
the Buddha declared:
All sentient beings, from time immemorial,
have been deluded by themselves regarding external objects and have lost their original mind.
Because one is turned by objects,
one perceives the great as small within this state. If one can turn objects,
however, [the situation is reversed].
Thus, they are identical to the Tathāgata;
their body and mind are perfectly luminous,
and they do not move from the site of enlightenment.
Within a single hair-tip,
they are able to universally contain all the lands of the ten directions.
Now, as for what is called "transforming objects," objects are empty and are not transformed;
one transforms only one's own mind.
Because all phenomena arise from conceptual discrimination,
are formed through perception,
and arrive in accordance with mental recollection.
Therefore, a verse in the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra* says:
"Phenomena arise from conceptual discrimination;
they likewise cease through conceptual discrimination."
One extinguishes all conceptualized phenomena;
these phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing.
Thus one knows that all dharmas are such.
All arise from the discriminating consciousness.
If one can awaken to and realize that the discriminating consciousness is empty,
then one will know that all phenomena are quiescent and extinguished.
Whether arising or ceasing,
both are conceptual constructions. If conceptual construction is extinguished, [there is liberation].
The Dharma is neither born nor extinguished.
This is also as stated in the Lotus Sūtra:
the three transformations of the land are solely transformations of the mind.
It is not that the earth itself is transformed.
The *Shoulengyan jing chao* (Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) states:
"If one can transform objects..."
That which is identical to the Tathāgata is as follows:
outside the mind there are no objects;
objects are themselves the mind.
However, when the mind is free from conceptual discrimination,
it constitutes right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). This right knowledge is itself *prajñā*,
which pervades the entire dharma-realm.
There are no obstructions;
therefore, in the land of the western direction,
the waterfowl, trees, and forests all preach the Dharma.
The place where the Dharma is taught is precisely the mind of suchness (tathatā). Therefore,
through each and every faculty-gate (indriya-mukha), the Tathāgata [manifests].
Pervading all lands as numerous as atoms,
even down to the tip of a single hair,
he preached the sublime Dharma.
Now, if one can simply be free from discursive thought,
one will immediately share the Tathāgata’s true knowledge and vision.
Formerly, there was a Zen master.
In Mianzhu County of Shu,
he practiced the Way on Mount Wúwéi.
At that time, more than three hundred households were holding a vegetarian feast.
They both requested the same preceptor;
this was entirely because their minds were free from discrimination,
allowing them to respond to circumstances without obstruction.
Question:
By what wisdom is the Dharma-realm and its manifold capacities for awakening realized?
All enter into the single mind of equality and ultimately reach the Tathāgatagarbha. Answer:
According to the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*,
there are five kinds of Tathāgatagarbha.
This is explained in the *Śīlamahāyāna-śāstra*.
Ten kinds of *tathāgatagarbha* are enumerated;
furthermore, the *Foxing lun* (Treatise on Buddha-nature) states that there are five kinds of "treasury" (*garbha*).
First, the tathāgatagarbha,
because it contains the dharmas of fruition while still enmeshed in afflictions;
second, the naturally pure garbha.
Unstained while still enmeshed in afflictions;
the treasury of the three dharma-bodies;
the basis for all qualities at the stage of fruition.
Fourth is the Transmundane Supreme Treasury,
which transcends the entanglements and surpasses both the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.
Fifth is the Dharmadhātu Treasury.
Pervading from cause to effect and externally sustaining all that is defiled and pure,
it is therefore named the Dharma-dhātu.
Because it contains within it all the inherent virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
it is called a "treasury" (garbha).
Next, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states:
The Tathāgatagarbha is of ten kinds,
as they are explained individually in the sūtras.
The first is the Tathāgatagarbha of the Great Dhāraṇī.
Because it completely encompasses all Tathāgatas,
it is stated thus in the *Sūtra on the Inexhaustible Treasury of All Buddhas*:
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
There is a Tathāgatagarbha,
named the Great Jewel, Inexhaustible, Supreme, and Perfect Dhāraṇī,
which completely encompasses all treasuries.
There is nothing it does not penetrate;
there is nothing it does not appropriately accord with.
Perfectly complete, perfectly complete.
It is perfectly equal and impartial.
Of all the Tathāgatagarbhas that exist,
there is none for which this is not the fundamental basis.
Why is this? Because this is the Tathāgatagarbha,
the King of the Tathāgatagarbhas.
The Lord of the Tathāgatagarbha,
the Deity of the Tathāgatagarbha,
and the Ground of the Tathāgatagarbha.
For this reason, it is called the "Great Jewel, Inexhaustible, Supreme, and Perfect Dhāraṇī Tathāgatagarbha.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
This refers to the revelation of the treasury of dhāraṇīs,
which serves as the general characteristic upon which the tathāgatagarbhas in other sūtras depend.
Yes. It is because it relies on specific characteristics. For what reason?
It is called the *tathāgatagarbha* because it maintains [the Buddha-nature].
Second is the *tathāgatagarbha* that is distant from transmigration and distant from bondage.
Because it is both pure and full.
Thus it is said in the *Bhūtakoṭi-sūtra*:
"O Son of the Buddha..."
The Tathāgatagarbha is nothing other than the Awakened One;
it is nothing other than Suchness (tathatā).
Free from the causes of saṃsāra,
free from the bonds of discursive thought and cognition;
pure and white in every respect.
Therefore, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It reveals what is known as True Suchness (tathatā) and the One Mind (ekacitta).
There is no cause for delusion;
there is no cause for awakening;
there is no fruit of delusion.
There is no fruit of awakening;
it is one true reality and one suchness,
for there exists only the pure and wondrous body of the Tathāgata.
For what reason is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*?
Because it is unmixed with all [defilements].
Third, there is the *tathāgatagarbha* as practice and as characteristic.
It possesses the power of saṃsāra;
because the Dharmakāya Tathāgata causes it to be concealed.
In the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra it is said:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome."
One experiences pleasure and pain together with their causes,
whether they arise or cease.
It is because it is like a performer.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It reveals that the single mind is characterized by arising and ceasing.
Regarding afflictions and power,
regarding awakening and power,
there appear the phenomena of birth-and-death and nirvana.
It is, for example, like a non-illusory illusory person who,
with respect to various illusory phenomena,
exerts power and function according to what is appropriate.
For what reason is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*?
It is because it causes [the dharmas] to be covered. Fourth is the *tathatā-tathāgatagarbha*.
It remains only as it truly is.
In the *Tathatā-samudgata-sūtra*, it is stated:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is suchness, suchness, and suchness."
Neither established nor disparaged;
neither permanent nor impermanent.
It is not that which is realized by the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*),
nor is it an object of perception for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Why is this so?
There is only principle and principle, because there is no "this" or "that.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
This refers to the revelation of the gateway of True Suchness (tathatā),
the principle of neutral true suchness, wherein the principle alone is self-contained within itself.
Because it is not that wisdom does not understand its own nature.
For what reason is the *tathāgatagarbha* elucidated?
It is because there is nothing other [than itself].
Fifth is the *tathatā* of arising and ceasing, the *tathāgatagarbha*.
It is neither born nor does it perish;
yet, because it is defiled by arising and ceasing, [it appears so].
In the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra it is said: "Mahāmati,
ignorant ordinary beings do not perceive, nor do they know."
They cling to all phenomena as being momentary and non-abiding;
falling into wrong views, they speak thus:
The untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) likewise do not abide for even a single moment,
for they would destroy that *tathatā* and *tathāgatagarbha*.
Furthermore, Mahāmati:
The Tathāgata-garbha of Vajra is the Dharma realized by the Tathāgatas;
for if it did not abide even for a single moment,
no noble ones would ever become noble ones.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It reveals the principle of the true suchness (tathatā) within the gate of arising and ceasing,
which is free from the characteristics of impermanence.
Because it is the dharma that is neither born nor extinguished.
For what reason is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*? It is because it is defiled.
Sixth is the empty tathāgatagarbha;
it is called "empty" because it conceals the Tathāgata from all [phenomena].
In the Śrīmālā-sūtra, it is stated as follows:
"World-Honored One,
the empty tathāgatagarbha..."
Whether it be "separation," "liberation," or "distinction," because it is the treasury of all afflictions—
what meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
This refers to the manifestation of all defiled phenomena within the gate of arising and ceasing,
which obscures the immeasurable qualities of the nature of self-awareness (svabhāva-āśraya-parāvṛtti) in its own essential character (svalakṣaṇa). For what reason?
All defiled phenomena are collectively termed "emptiness.
That is to say, all defiled phenomena are illusory transformations and distinctions.
Their essence and characteristics lack substantiality;
their functions are not real.
Therefore, they are called "empty."
Yet it is able to conceal and cover the true substance and real virtues of the Dharmakāya Tathāgata;
for this reason, it is called the "Tathāgatagarbha" (the Womb/Treasury of the Tathāgata),
as its name is established based on its capacity to conceal defilements.
Seventh is the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Everything is non-empty because it is defiled by emptiness.
In the Śrīmālā-sūtra, it is stated as follows:
"World-Honored One,
the Tathāgatagarbha is not empty."
Because they transcend the sands of the Ganges, are inseparable from, not distinct from, and inconceivable as the Buddha-dharmas.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It is said to reveal the intrinsically characterized original enlightenment (*prakṛti-awakening*) within the gate of arising and ceasing.
It is because it is permeated by all defiled phenomena exceeding the sands of the Ganges, despite being endowed with all merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges.
For what reason?

All pure phenomena are collectively termed "non-empty," meaning that within the very essence of all pure phenomena, their intrinsic nature is real and their functional activity is supreme and wondrous.
Being far removed from falsehood and transcending artifice and pretension,
it is therefore called "not empty."
The Tathāgatagarbha, when shrouded by defilements, is so named;
at the time of its manifestation, it is called the Dharmakāya.
When it is in a state of concealment, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Thus, its name is established based on that which is to be purified.
Eighth, it is capable of encompassing the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Because the intrinsically pure mind within the storehouse of ignorance can encompass all virtuous qualities,
it is stated as such in the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta Sūtra*.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the essence corresponding to the primordial limit,
as well as the pure dharmas;
these dharmas are suchness.
It is not false;
it is neither separated from nor detached from the inconceivable dharma of wisdom.
Since beginningless time,
this essence of the Dharma-body associated with purity has existed;
what meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
That is to say, it reveals that the intrinsically pure mind of all sentient beings has existed from time immemorial.
It is fully endowed with the three types of knowledge and perfects the four virtues,
for it is without any deficiency or loss.
For what reason is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*?
Because it is not known or realized due to the inverted mind,
its name is established based on that which can purify it.
Ninth is the Tathāgatagarbha as that which is encompassed:
once one has emerged from the storehouse of all defiled dharmas, the ground of ignorance.
Because they are subsumed within the Perfectly Awakened One,
it is stated thus in the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-sūtra*:
The Tathāgata’s essential nature is dissociated from the fundamental limit [of existence] as well as from the impure phenomena that are the entanglements of afflictions;
this fundamental limit is free from and dissociated from those impure phenomena that are the entanglements of afflictions.
Because it can only be severed by the Tathāgata’s bodhi-wisdom,
what meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It is said to reveal the fulfillment of initial awakening (ādikṣānti-bodhi) in a Buddha.
Having severed all hindrances and being endowed with all-encompassing wisdom,
the radiance of that wisdom constitutes its exterior.
Obscurations and darkness constitute the internal;
all defiled phenomena [are so designated] because they are held in check by wisdom.
For what reason is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*? It is because it "holds" [the Tathāgata].
Tenth is the concealment of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The Dharmakāya Tathāgata,
because it is obscured, hidden, and concealed by afflictions,
is described as such in the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta Sūtra*.
The Tathāgatagarbha is equal throughout the future limit;
it is eternal and the existent dharma that serves as the root of all phenomena.
It is fully equipped with all dharmas and endowed with all dharmas,
for it neither departs from nor is detached from worldly phenomena.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It reveals that the essence of the manifold mind is one,
equal to the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Pervading the three periods of time,
it is fully and perfectly endowed with all phenomena, both defiled and pure.
Because there is nothing it does not penetrate and nothing it does not reach.
Furthermore, this reveals the intrinsically pure mind within the gate of following conditions.
They are concealed and submerged within defiled phenomena because the Dharmakāya Tathāgata has not yet appeared;
this is called the tenth.
Now, I shall extract from the *Foxing lun* (Treatise on Buddha-nature),
specifically the fifth section on the Dharma-realm treasury (*dharmadhātu-garbha*),
as well as from the *Shi moheyen lun* (Commentary on Mahāyāna).
The first, the Great Universal Dhāraṇī Tathāgatagarbha:
this meaning is vast and pervasive,
encompassing all things.
By means of the wisdom of the true mark,
one shall be able to realize and enter [it],
just as the stars revolve around the North Star.
It is like the ocean gathering rivers;
it is like the great void of space,
wherein not a single speck of dust fails to enter.
If within the Mirror of the Source there is not a single dharma that does not return [to it],
it is that which all the sages ride upon.
This is the common realization of all Buddhas;
as for the remaining treasuries,
they follow the conditions of defilement and purity.
This is because, as in the two gates of arising and ceasing,
virtues and faults are respectively concealed and manifested through their mutual counteraction.
To be non-differentiated yet differentiated,
because it does not abide in its own nature;
to be differentiated yet non-differentiated.
Because its intrinsic nature is not lost,
the general and the particular share the same source,
and the beginning and the end are one and the same limit.
As it is said in a verse from the *Ratnagotravibhāga-mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra*:
"The Dharma-body is all-pervading and without distinction;
thus, the Buddha-nature truly exists in all."
Therefore, it is said that sentient beings always possess the Tathāgatagarbha.
What is the meaning elucidated by this verse?
There are three kinds of meanings;
for this reason, the Tathāgata says that at all times,
all sentient beings [possess them].
There is the tathāgatagarbha. What are the three?
First is the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.
It pervades the mental consciousnesses of all sentient beings,
as the verse states that the Dharma-body is all-pervasive.
Second, it is the essence of True Suchness (tathatā).
All sentient beings are equal and without distinction;
this is because the verse says they are "without difference. Third, all sentient beings.
All possess the Buddha-nature of True Suchness (tathatā) equally.
As the verse says: "All truly possess the Buddha-nature.
Question:
Are the wisdom that realizes and the treasury that is realized the same or different? Answer:
From the perspective of the gate of conceptual differentiation,
they are both the same and different;
yet if they are merged into a single flavor, they are identical.
Thus, there is no distinction between object and cognition;
if one speaks in terms of function,
they are identical yet different.
The objective realm cannot illuminate;
because wisdom possesses illumination,
it is called "quiescent."
They are different yet identical,
because there is no distinction between the object and the wisdom.
Because they are identical, there is no mind directed toward "this" or "that."
Because the forgetting of the mind is in perfect accord [with reality],
it is distinct [from ignorance] and thus does not lose its power of illumination;
for wisdom is distinct from wood and stone.
Therefore, the source of object and wisdom is neither separate nor united;
for if they were united, both object and wisdom would be destroyed.
If they were separate, then object and cognition would be mutually contradictory;
yet cognition cannot be established without an object,
for there is no person apart from dharmas.
Without wisdom, objects are not established,
because there are no phenomena apart from persons.
Therefore, the mind of wisdom is ever-quiescent.
Although it illuminates objects, it is without objective conditions;
though quiescent, it does not lose its illumination.
Although it is empty and still, it is constantly active.
Thus, wisdom illuminates both the object and itself;
when the object is quiescent, wisdom is also quiescent.
Quiescence and illumination are two aspects that share a single flavor.
The object and wisdom are fused and identical, yet they remain distinct;
if a dualistic sentiment arises,
one violates the true principle.
Some harbor views of sentient and insentient beings,
maintaining a sense of self and other;
others cling to minds that distinguish between the useful and the useless.
They merely fall into the net of nihilism and eternalism,
entirely because they fail to comprehend the true nature of all phenomena and the authentic essence of the Single Path.
If one penetrates this text,
all delusions are suddenly shattered.
Question:
Within the three realms and five destinies, since there is ultimately only one mind,
how can there be such differences between delusion and awakening?
Question: Regarding the ascent and descent of ordinary beings and sages. Answer:
It is solely because of the mind that one is deluded.
One awakens because of the mind;
furthermore, one becomes a sage because of awakening,
while one becomes an ordinary person because of delusion.
Ordinary beings and sages receive their names only through delusion and awakening;
yet these names are fundamentally empty.
There exists only the true mind.
It is profoundly still and unmoving;
it is only upon the single true mind that one falsely clings to the two selves of person and phenomena.
Therefore, it appears as delusion;
yet, because one realizes the twofold emptiness of persons and phenomena,
it appears as awakening.
An ancient worthy said:
"Awakening has no beginning or end;
it is because of delusion that one clings to a self."
Because of awakening, one perceives one's nature.
It is like being lost in the dark and mistaking a tree stump for a ghost;
once the light arrives, is there a ghost or not?
One is deluded and mistakes a stump for a ghost;
yet one sees that the stump has not newly come into being,
and realizes that the ghost was fundamentally non-existent.
If one realizes that the ghost was not originally non-existent—
given that one perceives only the stump and does not perceive the ghost—
one knows that the ghost was not newly non-existent.
The stump has not newly come into being;
there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
Since dualistic thoughts do not arise, [it is thus].
This is precisely true contemplation.
Why? Because when mindfulness is exhausted, the mind becomes clear and tranquil.
Because non-arising is manifested;
as it is said, "When water is clear, one obtains the true jewel," and so forth.
Furthermore, all that is seen is thus.
Whether one perceives oneself or another,
all are but the deluded mind manifesting itself—

Therefore, it is called "function.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"As for those who are icchantikas..."
By the power of the Buddha-nature in the future,
one will once again give rise to roots of goodness.
As for the power of the Buddha-nature:
Thus, through the power of the internal permeation of original enlightenment, its pure function is realized,
culminating in the attainment of the Way through the eight phases and the stages of practice of the ten bhūmis.
And these are collectively subsumed under the gate of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Question:
Above, you established the two gates of the one mind: True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Arising-and-Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).
Furthermore, through which gate does one enter so as to swiftly attain accomplishment? Answer:
One simply enters through the gate of arising and ceasing,
proceeding directly to the site of enlightenment;
without stirring the dust of worldly afflictions, one attains perfect awakening.
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"Furthermore, it is in order to cause sentient beings to enter the gate of True Suchness from the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind."
He causes [the practitioner] to observe that the characteristics of form and so forth are all unestablished.
In what way are they unestablished?
This means that one analyzes gross matter until it reaches the level of subtle atoms,
and then further analyzes these atoms by way of their spatial dimensions; therefore,
whether gross or subtle, [matter is subject to analysis].
All forms are merely images discriminated by the deluded mind;
in reality, they do not exist at all.
Investigating the remaining aggregates, one gradually arrives at the momentary;
their distinct characteristics are not uniform,
as they differ from unconditioned phenomena.
It is likewise so:
apart from the dharma-realm,
it can never be found.
In this way, one should know that all phenomena throughout the ten directions are likewise so;
they are just like a person who has lost their way and mistakes the east for the west.
In reality, it does not move.
Sentient beings are likewise;
because they are deluded by ignorance, they claim that the mind is in motion.
Yet, in reality, there is no movement.
If one knows that the moving mind is itself neither arising nor ceasing,
one immediately attains entry into the gate of True Suchness (tathatā).
Regarding the meaning of the two truths as explained above,
one must not interpret them exclusively as one,
nor must one interpret them exclusively as two.
Therefore, the *Ratnarājasūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Two Truths," states:
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One..."
Is conventional truth present within ultimate truth?
If you say it is not, then wisdom should not be twofold.
If one says that it exists,
then cognition should not be unitary;
this is the meaning of "one" and "two."
"What is that matter?
The Buddha said,
"Great King."
"In the past, within the Dharma of King Dragon-Radiance Buddha,
you already asked about this meaning;
I have nothing further to say now."
You now neither listen nor speak;
this state of neither listening nor speaking is precisely what is called "one meaning and two meanings."
"Listen attentively now;
I shall speak for you.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
The signless ultimate truth has an essence that is not produced by itself or by another;
it exists through causes and conditions like an illusion.
Nor is it created by self or other;
the nature of phenomena is fundamentally without nature,
for the ultimate truth is empty and suchness.
All phenomena that exist as illusions exist through the collection of the three types of conventional designations;
they do not exist as ultimate reality, nor are they non-existent.
Quiescence is the supreme emptiness;
all phenomena exist through causes and conditions.
Such is the meaning of existence and non-existence.
Existence and non-existence are fundamentally two,
like the two horns of an ox;
through illuminating understanding, one sees that they are not two.
The two truths are eternally not identical;
when the mind of understanding perceives them, there is no duality.
Seeking for these two, they cannot be found.
It is not said that the two truths are one;
even "one" cannot be apprehended.
In understanding, they are always inherently one.
The truths are always inherently two;
by thoroughly understanding this duality as non-dual,
one truly enters the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
The conventional truth arises as a magical illusion,
like flowers in the sky, like a shadow,
or like the appearance of falling hairs.
Through causes and conditions, illusions exist;
one perceives illusions within illusions.
The foolish call this the "truth of illusion."
A magician perceives illusory phenomena;
when examined, illusions are entirely non-existent.
If one understands phenomena in this way, [one realizes the truth].
One should immediately understand the meaning of "one" and "two," applying them universally to all phenomena;
one should practice contemplation in this manner.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* uses the metaphor of two birds flying together to illustrate that both saṃsāra—
characterized by both permanence and impermanence—
and nirvāṇa are likewise so.
The lowly and the exalted fly together and rest together;
this is the principle inherent in the very facts.
Principle is identical with phenomena;
the two truths are identical with the Middle Way, and the Middle Way is identical with the two truths.
Not being two, yet appearing as two;
thus, the meaning of their simultaneous movement is established.
As for the "two birds":
This refers to the mandarin ducks,
which fly in pairs and rest in pairs;
their flying in pairs is a metaphor for dual illumination.

The simultaneous cessation of both [extremes] is an illustration of the simultaneous negation of both; it is also the identity of essence and function, and the non-duality of principle and phenomenon,
being neither identical nor separate.
Question:
Why is the *tattvārtha* not called the *paramārthasatya*? Answer:
The "True" (tathatā) receives its name only in contrast to the conventional;
it is not yet the Middle Way.
Furthermore, it universally penetrates the selflessness of all phenomena.
However, these true expositions have not yet exhausted the ultimate nature,
nor do they penetrate both the ultimate and conventional truths.
As for the Middle Way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
it is not called "middle" by way of being separate from the two extremes;
rather, it is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
It pervades all ordinary beings and sages, as well as the sentient and the non-sentient;
therefore, it is called "foremost" and also termed "unequaled."
Because there is no dharma that can surpass it,
it is called the foremost;
because there is no dharma with which it can be compared.
Therefore, it is called "unequaled.
This is not said in reference to superiority or inferiority,
because all phenomena are identical with True Suchness and the One Mind.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings."
An ancient commentary states:
"Since all phenomena are non-existent,
there is therefore only mind."
Just as the myriad phenomena are fundamentally empty,
there is only a single mirror.
Question:
The wondrously luminous true mind pervades all places. Why,
then, does the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* say:
Question: "The Buddha-nature excludes rubble.
Answer: "The subject and the object are not the same."
One must not cling to a single [aspect].
Mind and phenomena are of one flavor;
they cannot be called different.
If nature were to follow conditions,
then the distinction between the sentient and the insentient would imply that their natures are likewise different.
If conditions are obliterated in favor of nature,
then there is neither awakening nor non-awakening;
if the two natures mutually merge, [the same follows].
Thus, there is nothing that is not awakening.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"In true suchness (*tathatā*), there is not even the slightest portion that is not awakening."
Thus, True Suchness pervades all places, whether sentient or insentient.
Since there is not even the slightest portion that is not awakened,
how could it be that the insentient are not Buddha-nature?
Furthermore, the intent of the sutra is merely to eliminate the attachment to insentient objects such as tiles and pebbles;
it does not eliminate the Buddha-nature.
Thus, this nature is omnipresent.
If one were to measure the void with a measuring instrument, could it ever be eliminated?
Furthermore, an ancient worthy said:
The nature of awakening is principle;
the act of awakening and understanding belongs to phenomena,
as is the case among insentient things.
There is only the nature of awareness,
yet no actual awareness;
it is like water that possesses only the nature of fire.
Nor is there illumination by fire.
What is now called "nature" (xing) refers merely to the fundamental principle.
Who would argue over the branches and details?
Furthermore, that which perceives and deliberates is called "sentience" (qing),
while that whose intrinsic nature does not change is called "nature" (xing).
The deluded person is confused about their nature and gives rise to emotions;
therefore, object and wisdom are not one.
The wise person realizes that emotions are the fulfillment of nature.
Therefore, things and the self are not two.
Question:
All phenomena are but mind.
The evidence for this is not singular.
A verse in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"All phenomena within the three realms, whether superior or inferior..."
I say that this is precisely the mind;
apart from all mental factors (citta-dharma),
nothing else can be found.
If the four intermediate directions, above, and below are all one's own mind,
then upon what do walking, standing, sitting, and reclining depend? If there were no environment or dwelling place to rely upon, [how could these activities exist]?
How is the primary retribution established?
Answer: It is the body possessed of consciousness.
Inanimate matter consists entirely of the internal and external four great elements,
all of which are devoid of intrinsic substance.
For instance, the earth element rests solely upon the wind-circle and is composed of a multitude of subtle atoms.
They have no intrinsic nature from the outset;
they are merely transformations of the minds of sentient beings,
and there is no other principle involved.
Every movement and gesture is tranquil and composed, all held within the mind,
like a bird soaring through the sky.
They do not depart from the realm of emptiness,
just as a fish submerged in water can never transcend its watery source.
A verse in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
"If all is but mind alone,
where does the world abide?"
Upon what dharma do going and coming depend?
How are they seen within the ground,
like a bird in the empty sky?
Moving by means of the wind of the mind,
they do not abide and do not observe;
they travel upon the earth.
In this way, all these sentient beings,
moved by the wind of conceptualization,
come and go within their own minds.
Just as a bird flying in the sky perceives the world as a vessel for sustaining life,
so the Buddha has taught that the mind is likewise.
Therefore, know that lifting the foot and setting it down does not depart from one's own mind;
it is like a bird that cannot leave the sky.
Why would they soar and fly?
If a fish were separated from water,
how could it dive and surface?
Therefore, the Indian patriarch Micchaka asked Vasumitra:
"From which direction have you come?"
"Where else has it gone?
He replied,
"It has come from the mind."
One who desires to go has nowhere to go.
Furthermore, the Master Wuxie of this land ceased eating for three days before passing away at the end of his life.
A student asked,
"Where have you gone, Master?
He replied:
There is nowhere to go.
Why does the student not see it? Answer:
It is not what is seen by the eye.
Thus, the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says:
The Buddha said:
One seeks bodhi within the four great elements and not in any other place; when seeking,
one does not perceive any phenomena whatsoever.
That which is not seen is precisely the absence of location;
that which is the absence of location—
This is precisely non-abiding.
That which is non-abiding is the very nature of all phenomena.
If all dharmas were without intrinsic nature,
that would be their true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
As for this true reality:
"Neither eternal nor annihilated" is called the ultimate joint.
The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states:
The Bodhisattva Anālaya said,
"Venerable One,
I have come from beginninglessness."
Now you have arrived at the place of no-root.
The Buddha said:
"You originally did not come from anywhere."
Even now, it does not arrive at any location.
You have attained the inconceivable fundamental benefit;
even form has no place of abiding.
Pure and nameless,
it does not enter within;
the eye has no location.
Pure and without views,
it does not go forth externally;
the mind has no location.
Pure and unsurpassed,
it has no place of origination;
pure and immovable.
There are no distinct conditions;
their nature is entirely empty and quiescent,
even unto that King of the Mind.
Fundamentally there is no place of abiding;
it is only the mind of ordinary beings that falsely discriminates and perceives.
The essence of suchness is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent;
it is the characteristic of existence and non-existence.
One perceives that there is only mind-consciousness.
Why is it without a fundamental basis?
Because it has no abiding place.
Where there is a basis, there is abiding;
where there is no abiding, there is no basis.
Thus one clearly understands the karmic destinies of sentient beings as they go and come.
The movements and stillnesses within the pure realm of all the sages:
when they come, it is the mind that comes;
when they go, it is the mind that goes.
Movement is the movement of the mind;
stillness is the stillness of the mind.
Ultimately, there is no going.
Coming, moving, and ceasing can be apprehended because they do not depart from the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Thus,
there is not a single phenomenon that is not indicated by the mind.
For this reason, Mañjuśrī transformed the youth Sudhana,
manifesting the three thousandfold world system as being filled with towers and pavilions;
Sudhana gazed upon them.
Suddenly, it vanished;
the world became entirely empty.
He then asked about the place from which the world comes and to which it goes.
Mañjuśrī replied,
"I have come from where I came;
I am returning to where I went."
They arise from within the pure dharma-realm and return back to the pure dharma-realm;
thus one knows that all phenomena are produced in this manner.
Manifested solely by the mind,
arising and ceasing, coming and going—
all are the Tathāgatagarbha.
This is the exhaustion of traces to reach the fundamental source,
seeing the Dharma and clarifying the core tenet.
Furthermore, as the Dharma Prince Vimalaprabha said:
I recall that in the past, after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges had passed,
a Buddha appeared in the world named Immeasurable Sound.
He revealed the wondrous clarity of the Bodhisattva’s fundamental awakening,
observing that this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all driven by the power of the winds of delusive conditions.
At that time, I contemplated the establishment of the elements,
contemplated the movement of the world,
and contemplated the movement and stillness of the body.
Observing the movement of the mind,
I saw that all movements are non-dual and without distinction;
at that time, I fully awakened to the nature of this multitude of movements.
Coming, they come from nowhere;
going, they go nowhere. Thus are the sentient beings throughout the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, who are subject to delusion.
They are equally false and illusory.
In this manner, even all sentient beings within a single trichiliocosm world are like a hundred mosquitoes contained within a single vessel.
They chirp and clamor in confusion,
erupting in wild tumult within the span of a mere inch. Eventually,
through my observation, I saw that the power of the wind has no basis.
Awakening the bodhicitta,
he entered samādhi,
causing the Buddhas of the ten directions to transmit to him a single wondrous mind.
This is the foremost [point].
Thus we know that the manifold movements are non-dual, being solely the wind of delusion.
This wind relies upon various conditions.
Fundamentally, there is no place of dependence.
If one can contemplate with clarity that the power of wind has no basis,
one will suddenly awaken to the fact that it is only mind, immovable.
Thus, the wondrous luminosity of original enlightenment constantly illumines the dharma-realm; therefore,
it is said that the Buddhas of the ten directions [are one].
It is merely the transmission of this wondrous mind.
Since the power of the wind has no support,
all phenomena are without a master.
Coming, it arises from conditions;
going, it pursues illusory emptiness.
There is only the mind of fundamental enlightenment.
Fundamentally, there is neither arising nor ceasing;
therefore, the Lotus Sūtra speaks only of the One Vehicle.
It is revealed here in the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras;
it is taught solely as non-duality and entrusted to this [teaching].
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
it is extensively illustrated here that the Buddha-nature is equal.
In the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
the inexhaustible Dharma-realm is manifested herein.
The boundless and wondrous purport all returns to the Mirror of the Source.
Question:
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra states:
"The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence.
Since the single mind has been established as the essence, [the following ensues].
Question: Why, then, is it said that "no-mind" is the Way?
Answer: Because the mind is taken as the fundamental principle.
This is the true mind.
This mind is neither existent nor non-existent;
it is without abiding and without reliance.
Neither arising nor ceasing,
whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha,
its nature and characteristics abide eternally.
It is the nature of all phenomena,
like the essence of empty space;
it is not any thing at all.
Yet it is able to manifest all things;
this is solely because sentient beings do not understand this eternally abiding true mind.
For the true mind has no inherent nature.
Failing to awaken, one gives rise to the mind of deluded consciousness;
consequently, one abandons this true mind and wondrous nature,
pursuing delusion through the cycle of saṃsāra.
Within ultimate sameness, they establish ultimate difference;
they single-mindedly cling to this deluded mind as being able to perceive objects and pursue external things.
To turn one's back on the Way and deviate from the Truth is to cause the cessation of that discursive, deluded mind;
if such a deluded mind does not arise, [the goal is attained].
Thus one is able to accord with awakening.
This is why it is said that "no-mind is the Way," and also why it is said that "darkening the mind merges with the Way."
Furthermore, this very mind is no-mind;
it constantly accords with original enlightenment,
and it does not necessarily require the extinction of the mind to attain realization.
Yet this results in turning one's back on the Way.
Although it is true that the mind is no-mind,
this [approach] is still not permissible.
Therefore, it arises.
This deluded consciousness arises in opposition to objects;
no substantial entity can be found.
It is like waves upon the sea,
which arise and cease according to the wind;
when the delusive winds of sensory objects do not arise, [the mind remains still].
When discrimination ceases,
the waves of consciousness do not arise.
The *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* says:
All worlds are like a mirage in the heat;
they possess the characteristic of unreality.
Though non-existent, there is false conceptualization;
awakening arises from that which is awakened to,
and that which is awakened to depends upon the awakener.
Apart from one, there is no two.
It is like light and its shadow;
where there is no mind, there is also no object.
The means of cognition and the objects of cognition are merely based upon the single mind;
it is in this way that they are discriminated.
The knowing subject and the known object are merely imagined based on the mind;
if one realizes that the known object does not exist, [the subject likewise ceases].
If that which knows is non-existent,
then that which is known is absent;
this constitutes the absence of an object.
One who is able to know non-existence is one who possesses no mind;
when the deluded mind and illusory objects are both empty, [reality is revealed].
The single path of true mind manifests of itself;
thus one knows that when the mind does not arise,
the myriad dharmas are without birth.
As soon as a thought arises,
one immediately falls into attachment.
As the *Mahādharanī-dharmolkā-sūtra* states:
The Buddha said:
"All abiding is non-abiding;
it is merely the movement of conceptual thought."
Because they arise in a continuous succession, there is birth;
this continues until, if one engages in right reflection.
All things are abidings in non-abiding.
Therefore, know that all phenomena arise from thought.
Whatever there is of thought is all wrong thought; if there is no thought, [it is right].
This is precisely right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
Therefore, it is said that if one reflects correctly,
everything is a dwelling in non-dwelling.
That which dwells in non-dwelling is the very root of all phenomena.
Question:
If it is said that the mind is identical to the emptiness of objects and is utterly ungraspable,
then consider how this infinitesimal thought arises in the present moment.
The retribution is not in vain;
with a single thought of goodness,
one may reach the fruit of Buddhahood from afar.
A single moment of an evil thought brings calamity for long kalpas;
how could it be compared to external forms or the objects before one?
Its nature is indeterminate (avyākṛta).
It exists only as a provisional designation based on the mind;
its substance is ultimately non-existent.
If it were the case that [the mind] exists simply because one directs attention toward it, then it would indeed exist. Answer:
This single thought-moment does not arise in isolation;
it exists dependently and provisionally.
Both internally and externally, all is empty.
This single thought that momentarily arises— the mind capable of awareness and cognition—
is like Ānanda’s deluded attachment to it being located within those seven locations.
The World-Honored One analyzed and deconstructed each one individually;
none had any location.
Yet, there was still a basis upon which they depended.
However, these seven [factors] are commonly adhered to by the world;
their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are firm and stable.
Were it not for the Great Sage’s meticulous investigation,
there would be no way to escape the views of the emotional mind.
Since these seven points have been refuted, [the argument is resolved].
Thus, it is absent in all places;
this can be known through present experience,
so there is no need for further attachment.
As stated in the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"It is as you have said."
It is the truly cherished cause within the mind and eyes.
If one does not know where the mind and eyes reside,
one will be unable to subdue worldly afflictions.
It is like a king who has been invaded by bandits.
He shall raise an army to suppress and eliminate them;
this army must first know the location of the thieves so that you may be set free from your wandering in saṃsāra.
"The mind and the eyes are the source of the fault. I now ask you:
is it only the mind and the eyes?"
"Where is he now? Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One," and so forth.
All ten types of ordinary beings in the world alike maintain that consciousness resides within the body;
even when they gaze upon the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes, [they do not perceive it otherwise].
"It is also on the Buddha's face.
As I now observe these four types of sensory objects of the fleshly root,
they reside only on my own face."
In this way, the consciousness-mind truly dwells within the body.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You are now sitting here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall;
look at the Jeta Grove— where is it now?"
World-Honored One,
this great multi-storied pavilion, a pure lecture hall,
is located within the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden.
"Ānanda, the Jeta Grove is actually outside the hall."
"What did you see first in the hall just now?
"World-Honored One,
while in the hall, I saw the Tathāgata first."
Next, he observed the great assembly;
looking outward in this manner,
he finally beheld the grove and garden.
Ānanda, when you gaze at the grove,
by what means do you see it?
World-Honored One,
this great lecture hall has its doors and windows wide open.
Therefore, as I am in the hall,
I am able to see from afar.
Thus, the Buddha told Ānanda:
It is as you have said:
though the body is within the lecture hall,
the doors and windows are wide open.
Looking afar at the groves and gardens,
there were also sentient beings within this hall who did not see the Tathāgata.
Regarding those who see outside the hall, Ānanda replied,
"World-Honored One."
To be in the hall and not see the Tathāgata,
yet to be able to see the forests and springs—
such a thing is impossible.
Ānanda, you are also like this.
Your mind is luminous.
All things are clearly perceived.
If this mind of yours that perceives clearly were actually within your body, [then...]
At that time, one should first thoroughly understand the internal body:
whether there are any sentient beings who first perceive [them] within their own bodies.
Later, one contemplates external objects;
even if one cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach,
one observes the growth of nails and hair.
The sinews turn and the vessels quiver;
this is truly evident and clear.
How can you not know it?
Since one certainly does not know the internal,
how could one know the external? Therefore, it should be understood.
Your claim that the mind capable of awakening and cognizing dwells within the body is impossible.
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Having heard such a Dharma-sound from the Tathāgata,
I have realized that my mind truly resides outside of my body."
Why is this? It is like a lamp burning within a room;
that lamp will necessarily first illuminate the interior of the room.
From the door of his chamber to the edge of the courtyard,
no sentient beings could see within his body.
Seeing only what is outside the body,
it is also like a lamp's light situated outside a room.
It cannot illuminate the room;
this principle must be clear so that there shall be no further confusion.
"It accords with the Buddha’s definitive meaning;
can it not be considered free from falsehood?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
These bhikṣus have just come from Śrāvastī city, where they went on alms-round for their solid food.
We have returned to Jeta’s Grove;
I have already completed my fast.
You should observe these bhikṣus.
"When one person eats, are all the people satiated? Ānanda replied, "No."
World-Honored One,
why is this? Although this bhikṣu is an arhat, [he does not yet possess such power].
"Bodies and lives are not the same;
how can one person cause many to be satiated?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
If the mind that perceives, knows, and sees were actually outside the body,
it would exist external to both the body and the mind.
Since they are not mutually related,
that which is known by the mind cannot be perceived by the body.
The sensation is at the edge of the body,
yet the mind cannot know it.
I shall now show you my hand of tūla-cotton.
"When you see with your eyes,
does the mind discriminate? Ānanda replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
If they are mutually cognizant,
how could they exist externally?
Therefore, one should know this.
Your claim that the mind which perceives and knows dwells outside the body is impossible.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
it is as the Buddha has said."
Because one does not perceive the internal,
one does not dwell within the body; thus,
body and mind know each other.
Because they are not separate from one another,
it does not exist outside the body;
this is what I now contemplate.
[He] replied, "I know it is in one place.
The Buddha asked,
"Where is that place now?"
Ānanda said: "This cognizing mind,
which does not know what is within yet is able to see what is without— "
As I reflect upon it,
it lies hidden within the sense faculties,
just as if someone were to take a crystal bowl and place it over both eyes.
Although objects may come together with it, they do not obstruct or impede it;
those faculties follow what is seen and immediately engage in discrimination.
Yet, as for this mind of mine that is aware and capable of knowing—
That which does not see internally is because it resides within the sense faculties;
that which clearly gazes externally is because there is no obstruction.
Because its roots are latent within,
the Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is as you have said."
One whose roots are submerged within is like lapis lazuli;
that person should see the mountains and rivers as if through eyes covered by a lapis lazuli veil.
"Do you see the lapis lazuli? "Yes,
World-Honored One."
"This person will have their eyes covered with a lapis lazuli cage;
they will truly see the lapis lazuli.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
If your mind were joined with the crystal as one,
you should see the mountains and rivers;
why do you not see your own eyes?
