This is like [the argument that] non-consciousness can produce consciousness. Furthermore,
it is challenged that there must be the nature of consciousness.
This is a refutation by way of concession;
[if] existence were to arise from existence, it would likewise result in simultaneous arising.
If it were non-existent, it would be identical to nothingness; being identical to nothingness, it would be like the birth of insentient matter.
Furthermore, one may question whether the nature of consciousness is one or many.
If they were one,
then that which is called "nature" could only arise later.
Consciousness and nature are one;
therefore, there is neither subject nor object.
If they were different, [then...]
If it were different from consciousness, it would be identical to external objects. Since an object can produce consciousness, it would be the same as what belongs to another;
how then could it be reckoned as one's own?
Next, regarding the refutation of other-nature:
although it is said that the mind does not arise from itself,
the mind arises because external objects exist.
The sense object is directed toward the faculty;
the sense object is termed "other.
First, one must examine this mind.
There are then three obstacles.
First, the obstacle that the object is not the mind:
if the object were not the mind, it would not be called an "object."
Second, the two types of objects are not mental;
this is because they are external, identical [to their causes], and arise spontaneously—these being the three obstacles. Third, there is the obstacle of simultaneous arising.
If dust were not mind,
it would allow for the arising of dust;
if dust were mind, [it would be otherwise].
If the mind arises from the locus of the mind,
this is called simultaneous arising,
just as when a seed gives rise to a sprout.
Then there would be subject and object;
if the son were to produce another son,
then two sons would be produced simultaneously.
What could there be of subject and object?
If the sensory objects were not mind,
they would then be equivalent to the previously mentioned position that consciousness does not exist within the sense organs.
The same applies to the intention regarding the charge.
Therefore, it is said that they are refuted as before:
that objects possess the nature of consciousness.
The preceding examples may be understood accordingly.
To refute arising from both [self and other] is to fall into the error of possessing the natures of both self and other.
This is called "arising from both.
Now it is refuted:
if there is no arising from either self or other individually, [how could there be arising from both?]
There is no combination either;
just as there is no oil in two grains of sand,
there is no combination either.
The refutation of non-causal arising is likewise.
To establish the two kinds of emptiness— of nature and of characteristics— it is simply a matter of negating the conceptualization of intrinsic nature.
This is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Once intrinsic nature has been refuted,
there remain only the internal and external marks of form and mind.
Since one does not abide in any of the four propositions regarding non-existence,
characteristics likewise cannot be apprehended;
this is called the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Regarding the statement that [the Tathāgata] does not abide within, without, or in between:
"within" refers solely to causes,
while "without" refers solely to conditions.
That which is intermediate is shared;
that which is eternally inherent is simply without cause.
Because this conceptualization does not exist,
the four natures do not exist.
These two types of emptiness—
Although the words appear sequentially,
their meaning is not of different times;
furthermore, by means of the two truths, the two kinds of emptiness are established.
If there is attachment to intrinsic nature,
then the world is not the truth; once attachment to intrinsic nature is destroyed, [the world is seen as it truly is].
This is what is called conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Therefore, it is said that conventional truth refutes intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Once the clinging to intrinsic nature has been refuted, [the ultimate truth is realized].
There are only names; what is called by these names is termed "provisional.
The provisional is itself a characteristic.
Because it is characterized by emptiness,
one contemplates the dharma-nature;
contemplating this principle, one realizes the truth.
This is called the True Truth (paramārtha-satya) which destroys all marks.
Emptiness (śūnyatā) is neither prior nor posterior;
the two truths are simultaneous.
These were spoken earlier and later for the purpose of distinguishing their essential natures and characteristics.
Furthermore, there are four stages of mental activity.
First, the stage prior to application;
second, the stage of desire for application;
third, the stage of actual application.
The four movements have already passed.
Master Fu’s verse says:
"Acting all alone."
Question: What is it that my mind clings to?
Upon investigating its four phases of activity, I find nothing arises.
How can a thousand ends and myriad entanglements bind me?
The commentary states:
The two types of mental application— the one that has not yet arisen and the one that is about to arise—
belong to the future.
Where could there be a mind in the future?
A single moment of mind that has arisen belongs to the present.
Furthermore, when it is said that the present does not abide anywhere, how can there be a mind?
Moreover, regarding the "time of arising":
the time of arising is established based on what has not yet arisen and what has already arisen.
That which has not yet arisen and that which has already arisen are both without arising;
even at the time of arising, there is no arising.
This is like [the analysis of] that which has already gone, that which has not yet gone, and the time of going.
In both cases, there is no act of going,
as has been refuted in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
This refers to a single movement of the mind that has already arisen.
It belongs to the past.
Since the past has already ceased,
where could there be a mind?
Therefore, the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra says:
"The past mind cannot be apprehended;
the future mind cannot be apprehended."
The present mind cannot be apprehended;
it is empty throughout the three periods of time. Since the single mind is thus non-existent, how can it have any being?
Since even the fundamental mind, which serves as the basis, does not exist,
how could all the myriad phenomena— the dependent branches and secondary derivatives— possibly be real?
Therefore it is said: "How can a thousand ends and ten thousand entanglements bind one?
Thus we know that once a single thought is realized as empty, all sensory objects naturally dissolve.
Since the basis no longer exists,
how can that which depends upon it arise?
It is like a stream that dries up when its source is exhausted.
The roots are perilous and the leaves have withered;
thus, although Ānanda sought support in seven locations, he found no basis.
Therefore, we know that false teachings are difficult to sustain.
The Second Patriarch sought directly beneath [the truth] yet found nothing arising;
this can be verified as proof that one must first understand emptiness before attaining awakening.
This is roughly the approach of the patriarchs and buddhas.
This refers exclusively to this school of thought:
since neither the mind that can give rise [to phenomena] is obtained,
nor the objective realm that is produced is obtained.
Because the mind cannot be apprehended, the self perishes;
because objects cannot be apprehended,
phenomena vanish.
If one can realize that both person and phenomena are empty,
the wondrous principle of the single mind is revealed;
it is merely due to the mutual confrontation of the mind and its objects.
The myriad dharmas unfold in all directions;
object and wisdom are of one suchness;
a thousand differences are instantly stilled.
In this way, one is finally able to suddenly awaken to the true mind of primordial enlightenment and numinous wisdom,
which is without abiding and without dependence,
pervading the entire dharma-realm.
The *Śata-śāstra* states:
The Sūtra says,
"There is not even the slightest dharma whose intrinsic nature can be apprehended."
There is only that which is capable of creating;
that which is capable of creating is precisely mind and mental factors.
Furthermore, it says:
"The three realms are mind-only.
Such sūtras as these are immeasurable in number.
Therefore, the principle that all phenomena are representation-only (vijñapti-mātra) is established; how could it not be certain?
However, one who clings to the view that all phenomena are truly nothing but representation-only—
This would also constitute a perversion.
If the object does not exist,
how could consciousness exist?
When the sutras speak of "consciousness-only," it is intended to cause one to contemplate consciousness so as to abandon those external objects.
Having already abandoned external objects,
the deluded mind follows the breath;
because the deluded mind ceases, [the breath ceases].
One realizes and attains the Middle Way;
thus a verse in the sutra says:
"As long as one has not reached the realization that objects are mind-only..."
Having given rise to various forms of conceptualization,
once one realizes that objects are nothing but mind,
conceptualization will no longer arise.
If one knows that objects are merely mind,
one then abandons the appearance of external phenomena;
from this, conceptual discrimination ceases.
Awakening to the equality of true emptiness,
the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* asks:
"When both object and consciousness are discarded..."
By which consciousness is it constituted?
Answer: Both object and consciousness are extinguished.
This is precisely the true nature (*dharmatā*). The true nature is the *amala-vijñāna*.
As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
The Bodhisattva Flower Adornment said:
"To give rise to duality from me constitutes duality;
one who perceives my true reality [is free from it]."
One does not give rise to dualistic dharmas.
If one does not abide in dualistic dharmas,
then there is no consciousness.
That which is without cognition is the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality; therefore,
one knows that seeing and knowledge constitute two dharmas.
Even down to the finest hair, all things belong to consciousness;
when both object and consciousness vanish together,
one enters the principle of true emptiness.
For this reason, the master Jñānaprabha established the doctrine of the medium faculties as the Dharma-character Mahāyāna.
The principle that objects are empty while consciousness exists—
that of *vijñapti-mātra*— has not yet fully entered into the equality of true emptiness;
therefore, for those of superior faculties, the signless Mahāyāna is taught.
To discern that both mind and objects are empty, equal,
and of a single flavor is the definitive meaning;
therefore, one relies on consciousness-only.
One enters the gate of the ultimate true emptiness;
to seek elsewhere apart from this is not true liberation.
The *Weishi chao* (Commentary on Consciousness-Only) asks:
Regarding the internal consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātra):
is it truly existent, or is it not truly existent?
Answer: The treatise states:
"The various minds and mental factors" refers to what was previously presented.
Because it arises dependently, it is a cause;
it is also like the analogy of a magical illusion.
It is not a phenomenon that exists truly.
Question:
If that is so, then there would be no distinction whatsoever between the mind and its objects.
Why, then, is it said that there is only consciousness? Answer:
It is in order to dispel the attachment of the non-Buddhists and others to the notion that objects exist as real entities external to the mind and mental factors.
It is provisionally stated that "there is only consciousness";
however, this expression "only consciousness" does not imply that there is any reality.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"In order to dispel the false attachment that there are real objects existing external to the mind and mental factors,
it is taught that 'there is only consciousness' (*vijñaptimātra*)."
If one holds that consciousness-only truly exists,
this is likewise an attachment to dharmas (dharma-grāha), just like holding that external objects exist.
If attachment to phenomena does not arise,
one immediately enters true emptiness.
Question:
Regarding the principle of Consciousness-Only, wherein both person and phenomena are empty:
what kind of thing is that which is presently experienced? Answer:
The dharmas that are perceived are merely the six sense objects;
they arise due to causes and conditions.
Due to causes and conditions, they cease;
it is certain that internally there is no person who can receive them,
and externally there are no sensory objects to be used.
The *Treatise on the Eighteen Emptinesses* states:
"External emptiness is also called the emptiness of that which is received."
Apart from the six external sense bases,
there is no separate dharma that can be experienced;
whatever is experienced or utilized by sentient beings [is comprised within these].
However, as for the six sense objects:
since there is no person within who can receive them,
and there is no phenomenon without that can be received.
That is, both person and phenomena are empty;
since there is only consciousness and no external objects,
it is called "emptiness of the external."
Because there is no object,
there is likewise no consciousness;
this is internal emptiness.
Up to the eighteen kinds of emptiness.
Question:
Both persons and phenomena are empty.
If consciousness is not established,
from what do this present seeing and hearing arise? Answer:
All phenomena manifested through the various sense objects arrive entirely by following recollection;
they all arise in opposition to conceptualization.
Contemplating that the objects of the breath are empty,
the mind is void and phenomena are quiescent.
Thus, a sutra says:
Perception ceases in quietude;
consciousness halts in the unconditioned.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
All Buddhas and all dharmas arise from the mind and take form therefrom.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"All phenomena are not solid;
they exist only by being established upon mindfulness."
For one who understands and perceives emptiness,
there are no conceptualizations whatsoever; thus,
one knows that seeing and hearing are merely dependent origination.
One perceives ultimate emptiness,
which is like the illusory manifestations of the world,
resembling the arising and ceasing of flowers in the sky.
Therefore it is said: "Seeing and hearing are like illusions or cataracts;
the three realms are like flowers in the sky.
For instance, the faculty of the eye attains seeing when five conditions are present.
However, this capacity for seeing consists merely of five conditions,
because there is no seer.
If it is said that consciousness arises and is able to see when five conditions are complete,
it remains unknown which specific condition definitively produces the consciousness. If it is argued that [the conditions] do not produce it individually, [then how can they do so collectively?]
If [the self] were able to produce seeing through combination,
then it would be like the case of five blind people combining;
they should likewise produce a single act of seeing.
Since the blind cannot see, how could they produce [a perception] through their combination? Therefore,
one knows that it is not produced by a separate consciousness.
Whatever is seen is simply a collection of conditions;
therefore, it is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).
Thus, a sutra says:
The eye does not see itself;
it depends upon various causes and conditions.
These conditions do not possess the nature of seeing.
The eye is itself emptiness.
Since this is the case for the faculty of the eye,
so it is for all the other faculties by analogy.
Arising is merely dependent arising;
ceasing is merely dependent cessation;
arising and ceasing are merely conditions.
Both person and phenomena are quiescent.
If one realizes this emptiness of both self and phenomena,
one immediately realizes the perfect principle.
Therefore it is said: "If one sees the dharma of causes and conditions, this is called seeing the Buddha.
Question:
Within the realm of ordinary beings, there is the discrimination of acceptance and rejection;
the mind is preoccupied with thoughts of opposition and compliance, and feelings of longing and aversion fill the heart.
Constantly bound by the six sense objects as obstructions,
how can the faculties and their objects be made to interpenetrate so that all things accord with one's will?
Answer: One merely perceives the dharma-nature and realizes great nirvana.
Since there is not even a single dharma that can be penetrated,
how could there be any dharmas acting as obstructions?
Thus, one is always as one wishes.
There is never a time when things do not accord with one's wishes.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra* states:
"What is now called 'nirvāṇa according to one's wishes'..."
All suffering and pleasure, good and evil, are none other than principle;
therefore, it is called "As One Wishes" (Yirui).
The commentary states:
There is nothing that is not principle,
for all are the principle of the True Suchness (tathatā) of the one mind;
this is because suffering and pleasure are the sensations of the mind.
Since good and evil arise from the mind,
there is nothing external that can oppose or obstruct them;
if one realizes this single mind, [all is resolved].
Is this not like having one's wishes fulfilled?
If there were even a single dharma that accorded with one's desires,
it would give rise to contention and strife.
A verse in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
"As long as there is anything established, all is delusion."
If one perceives that there is only one's own mind,
then there will be no conflict or dispute;
for when deluded, people pursue external phenomena.
After awakening, the Dharma depends on the person.
It is like a mani jewel, which has no emotional or conceptual qualities.
Furthermore, it can impartially bestow both treasures upon the multitude of sentient beings; therefore,
it is called "Wish-Fulfilling."
How much more so for the wondrous nature of the numinous mind—
how could it not be possible?
One need only return to the single mind.
Having attained great non-obstruction, it is said:
"They transform heaven and earth."
Mastery and freedom in every direction.
Question:
The Treatise says:
It is solely this one mind that is called True Suchness (*tathatā*);
"True" means it is without falsehood.
If suchness is unchanging and its wondrous form is a serene nature that is not empty,
why does the sutra further state that when the mind is empty, all dharmas are empty?
Answer: As for what is called "emptiness," it refers to the teaching that all deluded minds and defiled phenomena of the world are empty.
Because the conceptual attachments of universal imagination lack any logical basis,
they are empty; however, if it concerns the supramundane Buddha-dharma and the true mind,
then it is not empty, because it possesses logical basis.
The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"True Suchness has two aspects:
first, suchness as ultimate emptiness."
Because it can ultimately manifest reality,
it is secondly "not empty according to reality," as it possesses its own intrinsic nature.
Because it is fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharma*).
As for what is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*),
from the very beginning...
Because all defiled dharmas are non-associated with it;
that is to say, it is free from the differentiated characteristics of all phenomena,
as there is no false mental ideation.
One should know that the self-nature of true thusness (tathatā) is devoid of such characteristics as existence or non-existence, unity or difference;
this applies generally to all such descriptions.
Relying on all sentient beings,
because they possess deluded minds that differentiate from moment to moment,
none of these are in accord with reality.
Therefore, it is said to be empty;
for apart from the deluded mind,
there is truly nothing that can be empty.
That which is called "not empty" refers to the fact that the essence of phenomena has already been revealed as empty and devoid of falsehood;
it is precisely the true mind.
Being eternal, constant, and unchanging,
and being fully perfected with pure dharmas,
it is therefore called "not empty."
The *Qingliang ji* commentary explains:
"Not being conjoined with delusion is what is called emptiness."
Its nature is endowed with myriad virtues;
thus, it is called "not empty."
Upon reaching the explanation of the text,
it says: "If one is separated from the deluded mind..."
In reality, there is nothing that can be made empty;
thus, the treasury of emptiness is revealed.
It is manifested through delusion.
Regarding the "not-empty treasury," it is only by overturning defilement that the not-empty is revealed; therefore,
it is said that this serves to manifest that the essence of phenomena is empty and devoid of falsehood.
This refers to the true mind and so forth;
it is like having the virtue of generosity (dāna) inherently,
yet now being hindered by stinginess and greed.
Originally possessed the virtue of the corpse;
now one follows the five desires.
Originally possessed tranquil concentration.
Now there is disordered thought;
originally there was great wisdom,
but now there is folly.
This constitutes stinginess concealed within generosity,
and so on, up to delusion concealed within wisdom.
Therefore, the treatise says:
Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is free from stinginess and greed,
one practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) and so forth in accordance with it;
all ten thousand practices are likewise thus.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"The fundamental meaning is that there is true consciousness and cognition.
If the mind were to have movement..."
This is not true cognition;
it clarifies the movement of the deluded mind and conceals its true knowing.
Therefore, emptiness that is immanent within the delusive conceals the myriad virtues that are not empty.
Thus, a verse in the Sūtra says:
Knowing that delusion is fundamentally true,
one sees the Buddha as pure. Thus,
the Treatise says:
Because it can ultimately manifest reality,
it is called "emptiness. Thus,
one should know that the treasury of emptiness is able to contain that which is not empty.
Once the capacity to conceal is empty,
the non-empty treasury is revealed as having been inherently possessed from the beginning.
Second, the emptiness of the self-nature mind being devoid of delusion;
that which is absent therein is precisely the virtue of non-emptiness.
Just as space is without stinginess,
it manifests the presence of dāna; as space is without false movement, [it manifests the presence of śīla].
This reveals that existence is empty of intrinsic nature;
therefore, this treasury of emptiness is itself not empty.
Thus, one knows that all sentient beings possess the originally awakened Buddha-wisdom.
It is fundamentally and originally complete;
it is only because of delusion that it is obscured and one does not know it oneself.
If one realizes that delusion is empty, [one attains liberation].
True awakening manifests instantaneously,
like the moon shining brightly when the clouds part,
or like a mirror becoming clear when dust is removed.
At the moment of seeing one's nature,
it is said that it is "attained";
it is not something produced through cultivation.
On the day the three bodies are perfected,
it is also said that the myriad practices are drawn forth;
they do not come from without.
All are based on the one mind,
which is inherently and fully present;
thus, we know this is the emptiness that is not empty.
Its essence contains ten thousand virtues;
it is an existence that is non-existent,
a principle that accords with the Perfect Teaching.
Emptiness and existence mutually establish one another;
they are free from all obstructions.
If existence were divorced from emptiness, [it would be untenable].
If existence were real, it would be eternal;
if emptiness were divorced from existence,
emptiness would become nihilistic.
Now, there is that which is neither identical nor different;
it does not contradict the single intent.
Therefore, wisdom can penetrate existence.
Wisdom is able to contemplate emptiness.
If one understands existence but does not know emptiness,
then one loses the eye of wisdom.
To contemplate emptiness without reflecting upon existence is to lose the wisdom-mind; thus,
a Bodhisattva does not exhaust all conditioned phenomena.
If one does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
then when existence is exhausted, the activity of wisdom (*jñāna-karman*) will not be accomplished;
if one abides in non-existence, then the mind of insight (*prajñā-citta*) will not be luminous.
Therefore, the *Yihai* (Ocean of Meaning) states:
"If emptiness were different from existence,
then purity would not be called pure."
Because they are deluded regarding emptiness,
if there were anything distinct from emptiness,
then defilement would not be called "defilement."
Because of the grasping at existence,
that which currently exists is entirely empty;
only then is it termed the defiled portion.
Emptiness is itself the entirety of existence;
only then is it called the pure portion.
This is because emptiness and existence are without obstruction.
It is the mastery over defilement and purity.
If it is emptiness, it is existence;
if it is existence, it is emptiness.
Thus, all phenomena are mutually identical. Since they are mutually identical,
there are ultimately no phenomena such as unity and difference, or emptiness and existence.
They manifest externally to the mind;
even if they do manifest, they are all but the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of one's own mind.
Ordinary and inferior beings do not understand this;
they grasp at existence when they take up [phenomena],
and sink into emptiness when they reject them.
If one enters this gate of the Middle Way within the single mind,
one can accomplish the path of skillful means for the myriad practices.
As it is said in the *Mahāvyūha-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*:
Mañjuśrī said: "There are two kinds of skillful means:
first, not abandoning saṃsāra."
Second is non-abiding nirvana.
This, in turn, has two aspects:
first, the gate of emptiness.
Second, the gateway of wrong views.
This, in turn, has two types:
first, the gateway of signlessness.
The second is the gate of the contemplation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vitarka-vicāra*).
This, in turn, has two kinds:
first, the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
The second is the gate of aspiring for birth.
This, in turn, has two types:
the first is the gate of non-action.
Second is the practice gate of planting roots of goodness,
which further has two types:
first, the gate of non-arising.
Second is the gate of manifesting birth.
Thus, upon awakening to the fundamental principle, both the contrary and the compliant return to the same source;
upon penetrating the essence, both good and evil are transformed together.
Question:
The treatise says:
"It speaks of wisdom and the locus of wisdom."
Both are termed *prajñā*.
Since the locus of wisdom is its object,
how does it become *prajñā*?
Answer: There are two kinds of prajñā.
First, the true and eternally abiding prajñā.
Second is the wisdom of the utility of contemplative observation; as for true wisdom,
its nature pervades all places.
Quiescent yet ever-illuminating,
it is the single true mind,
undivided into subject and object.
It is not the same as the insentient objects of the mundane world that serve as its objects of illumination;
nor is it the same as the partial and inferior deluded minds that serve as its objects of illumination;
furthermore, it is also not the same as the conventionally established *tathatā* (suchness) that serves as its object of illumination.
Now, the single essence is subtly pervasive;
mind and mind illuminate one another,
for there are no external objects apart from the mind.
Nor is there a mind external to objects,
because the mind is the object-mind and the object is the mind-object.
Such melting away—how could this not be prajñā?
Therefore it is said: "Because form is boundless."
Prajñā is boundless; therefore,
one knows that apart from form there is no mind,
and apart from mind there is no form.
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"Furthermore, O Vīra,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva..."
One should practice in this way:
form is not an object of cognition. Why is that?
All phenomena are without an object of perception,
because there is not even the slightest phenomenon that can be grasped.
If they were graspable, [they would not be phenomena].
This is the object of focus.
Thus, with such vigor,
one practices formlessness within form.
Up to and including not practicing consciousness within consciousness;
O valiant one,
all phenomena are non-practicing.
Therefore, it is not seen by form,
nor is it seen by consciousness;
this extends even to its not being known by consciousness.
Nor can it be seen.
From form up to consciousness,
there is neither knowing nor seeing.
This is called Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, the Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra states:
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
when practicing the perfection of wisdom,
one does not perceive any dharma as that which should be dwelt upon.
One should not abide therein.
Nor does one perceive any characteristic of an objective realm that could be grasped or abandoned. Why is this?
Just as all Tathāgatas do not perceive the marks of the objective sphere of any phenomena,
they do not even perceive the objective sphere of the Buddhas.
How much less would they grasp at the realms of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or ordinary beings?
They do not grasp at the mark of the conceivable,
nor do they grasp at the mark of the inconceivable.
Not perceiving that all dharmas possess various characteristics,
he personally realizes the inconceivable dharma of emptiness.
Such is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Having already made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas and planted various roots of goodness,
they are now able [to practice] this profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Neither startled nor terrified.
It further says:
"Moreover, when practicing the Prajñāpāramitā..."
One does not perceive the characteristics of ordinary beings;
one does not perceive the characteristics of the Buddha-dharma;
one does not perceive any dharma as having a determinate characteristic.
This is the cultivation of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Question:
[Regarding] the mundane and the supramundane.
If it is solely this single mind,
why is it further divided into the true and the deluded,
as well as the internal and the external?
Answer: The distinctions between the real and the false, or the internal and the external,
are merely conventional classifications based on worldly terminology.
Therefore, the mind is neither internal nor external;
internal and external are the mind itself.
Its substance is neither true nor false.
Reality and delusion are the substance;
by establishing the external based on the internal,

yet they naturally give rise [to one another].
The nature of karma is likewise so.
Furthermore, it is like a skilled illusionist who, at a crossroads,
manifests various forms and appearances.
The nature of karma is also like this:
it is like a wooden mechanical figure that can produce various kinds of sounds.
That is neither self nor non-self;
the nature of karma is likewise.
It is also like the various kinds of birds.
Emerging from their shells,
their cries are each different;
the nature of karma is likewise so.
Just as within the fetal womb all the sense faculties are fully formed,
yet the substance and characteristics have no place from which they come.
The nature of karma is likewise so.
Furthermore, it is like the various kinds of suffering experienced in the hells.
They all have no point of origin;
the nature of karma is likewise.
It is like that of a wheel-turning monarch.
The attainment of the seven supreme jewels has no point of origin that can be found;
the nature of karma is likewise so.
Furthermore, just as when all worlds are consumed by a great fire,
this fire has no place from which it comes.
The nature of karma is also like this.
The *Jingye zhang jing* (Sutra on Purifying Karmic Obstructions) says:
"Contemplate all dharmas."
This is precisely the Buddha-dharma;
this is what purifies all karmic obstructions.
It is as when a student asked Master An-guo:
If one has not yet awakened, do the karmic conditions of good and evil exist?
Answer: Yes.
It does not exist.
It is like a nightmare in which one is pursued by an evil person,
or where one becomes a Brahmā king or Śakra.
Thinking that this must be existence,
one suddenly awakens to the realization that all is tranquil and devoid of affairs.
One comes to know with certainty that the three realms are fundamentally empty and are nothing other than this single mind.
Furthermore, someone asked Master Dazhu:
If one asks how the exhaustion of karma is to be known,
the answer is:
by the mind present before one.
Connecting the previous life with the subsequent life,
it is just as when one sees the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future with one's own eyes.
All phenomena arise simultaneously.
As the Sūtra says:
"To know all phenomena in a single thought-moment is the site of enlightenment."
Because one accomplishes all-knowledge,
one knows that everything arising from the mind is entirely devoid of reality.
Just as the mind in a dream is not real,
so too the objects of the dream are empty;
this is commonly known by the world.
This should be deeply believed and accepted.
Therefore, the principle is that the karmic retributions of good and evil are all empty by nature.
Not destroying dependent origination,
one constantly accords with the subtle and wondrous principle.
As the *Pramāṇa* states:
Right action is a phenomenon that exists.
That it is both existent and empty is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is stated as follows:
Because that which is dependently originated is itself devoid of intrinsic nature.
The common example is:
"like a magical illusion."
Arising from illusory dharmas and the like,
there is immediately non-obstruction within emptiness;
correct action arises from conditions.
Emptiness and existence do not obstruct one another;
therefore, we know that all phenomena arise from the conceptualizations of deluded minds and possess nothing more than empty names.
It has no substantial reality whatsoever.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"The wondrous enlightenment is profound and still."
Pervading the entire dharma-realm and encompassing the ten voids,
how could it have a fixed location?
They manifest according to karma.
The world lacks understanding and is deludedly attached to them as being caused by conditions, or as having a spontaneous nature.
All of these are merely the conceptualization and deliberation of the discerning mind;
they consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
Regarding "encompassing and exhaling the ten voids":
"encompassing" means that the single reality is unmoving,
abiding within the Tathāgatagarbha.
Emission arises based on false discrimination;
it manifests wherever it may.
Wherever even a speck of dust appears, there it is present.
All these arise from the mind itself and exist through conceptual discrimination.
If one knows that their point of origin is illusory, [they will cease].
Then one suddenly awakens to true emptiness;
when true emptiness manifests before one,
how could there remain any words or speech?
Question:
The true mind is unmoving;
throughout the three periods of time, it does not undergo change.
How is it that the mind is said to undergo transmigration?
Furthermore, what is the meaning of the cessation of transmigration? Answer:
What is called "flowing with the current" and "returning against the current" both refer, in every respect,
to the mind of sentient beings that engages in objective contemplation.
Though falsely called "transmigration," its essence is eternally quiescent;
it is simply that one does not perceive the point where even a single thought arises.
This is precisely non-flowing.
It is not necessarily that there is a thought to be severed.
The *Jizhanying* (Sutra of Wisdom Adornment) says:
Mañjuśrī said: "How does one sever the flow of saṃsāra?
By not giving rise to a past mind."
Future consciousness does not function;
the present mind does not stir;
it neither abides nor engages in discursive thought.
Without awareness and without discrimination,
one knows that by using the object to confront the object,
and the mind to treat the mind.
The dog pursues the clod and only becomes more exhausted;
the man avoids the shadow and merely suffers depletion.
If one can realize that the body is like a shadow, [one will not pursue it].
If one abandons clods of earth to follow people,
then the shadow vanishes and the tracks sink away;
thus, one may walk the Path in peace and security.
Therefore, know that all movement is lustful and entirely constitutes demonic activity.
If one knows the mind is unmoving,
then one does not follow the current.
Upon entering the Mirror of the Essence,
one forever transcends the illusions of Māra;
naturally, the mind and intellect become quiescent.
All views are extinguished.
As stated in the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Mahāgaganagañja*,
the Bodhisattva Śailaśikharasamudgata said:
It is like a place with gaps and openings where wind enters and causes objects within it to shake and move.
There is the characteristic of coming and going;
the bodhisattva is likewise.
If the mind has any interval or gap, [it is not so].
The mind then wavers; because it wavers,
Māra gains an opportunity.
Therefore, the bodhisattva guards the mind so that no interval occurs;
if the mind is without interval, [it remains protected].
Then all the marks are fulfilled;
because the marks are fulfilled,
emptiness is fulfilled.
This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of Māra.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī said:
"O Noble One."
What you have all said is entirely the realm of Māra. Why is this?
The establishment of words and letters is entirely a work of Māra;
even the words of the Buddha are likewise a work of Māra.
It is beyond verbal expression and free from all written characters;
Māra can do nothing against it.
If there is no designation,
then there is neither the view of a self nor the view of words;
this is because there is no self.
Thus, there is neither loss nor gain regarding all phenomena.
One who enters in this manner transcends the realm of Māra.
This is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Transcendence of Māra.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Great King of Teachings of the Thousand Bowls states:
The Buddha said:
The various manifestations of the delusive illusions of devas and māras obstruct the noble path of the practitioner’s mind and eyes;
they even cause one to perceive all illusory appearances and the events of birth and death throughout the succession of lifetimes.
The various signs of good and evil are illusions and delusions created by Māra;
they have no connection with right wisdom.
All manifestations are shown to be mind-only;
do not grasp at external conditions,
O practitioners who cultivate and study.
One must not, within the realm of dreams or before one's very eyes,
grasp at signs or become attached to them.
If one agitates the minds of others and causes them fear and dread,
they will be obstructed by devas, māras, and spirits.
The practitioner of right view must constantly and attentively contemplate the nature of the mind;
they shall see that the nature of the mind is quiescent.
The nature of the mind is devoid of substance;
do not grasp at these marks,
for then there will be no causes or conditions for the delusive thoughts of objective realms.
Therefore, practitioners should practice with diligent perseverance;
truly, do not regress, nor be indolent or lazy.
Then one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Excluding the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena..."
All these are the deeds of Māra for a bodhisattva.
If one realizes prajñā,
one can accord with the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
This immediately transcends the activities of Māra;
this refers to the time when one realizes the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
At the moment of direct realization, [one transcends them].
It is like a person drinking water:
one cannot describe it without having realized it for oneself. If one were to speak only of transcending Māra, [it would be like describing the taste without tasting it].
One does not depart from the realm of Māra;
if one were to transcend the realm of Māra,
both realization and speech would be utterly cut off.
Thus we know that there are certainly no external demons;
they arise solely from the mind. Why is this?
If one’s inner mind delights in birth and death,
then that body becomes a celestial Māra;
if the inner mind clings to false views, [it likewise becomes a Māra].
Then one's person becomes that of an outsider;
even to perceive phenomena as being external to the mind and to seek separately outside of principle.
All become non-Buddhists.
Question:
Ordinary beings and sages are of one mind.
Since their spiritual lineage is identical and there is no difference in that lineage,
why is it that the causes and effects they receive differ?
Question: Is there a distinction between retribution?
Answer: Although each receives the results of their own karma, [there is no such distinction].
Though there is the delusive appearance of rising and sinking,
the nature of conditions is non-arising and utterly unobtainable.
The *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra* states:
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"All sentient beings..."
Their minds are all one;
this is called the lineage (gotra).
Lineage is the meaning of the fundamental basis.
The fundamental source is eternally one,
yet sentient beings delusively give rise to distinctions between self and other,
and between ordinary people and sages, high and low.
Although distinctions arise,
the single essence remains unmoving,
because the nature of distinction does not exist.
However, because they arise falsely and lack substantial reality, a sutra states:
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī, all sentient beings are entirely without a mind that serves as a condition.
Because its intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended,
it is called "lineage" (gotra).
Furthermore, regarding all objective spheres of good and evil:
All are the radiance of the mind;
all superior and inferior enjoyments are the fruits of the mind.
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra* states in verse:
"Various radiances of mind arise;
such are the various appearances."
Because the luminous essence is not an essence,
one cannot apprehend the reality of those phenomena;
it is the manifold light of the mind.
This refers to various types of objective phenomena,
which may arise at different times,
such as desire, hatred, light, and so forth.
Or they arise simultaneously,
such as faith, energy, lightness, and so forth;
such are the mental factors in a defiled state.
In the state of purity,
mental factors possess only radiance but lack a substantial body of light;
therefore, O World-Honored One.
It is not said that those are the true Dharma.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The predominance of the momentariness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)."
As the Buddha said: "The mind leads the world away;
the mind drags the world back. It is by the power of the mind that all things are brought under control."
The world proceeds accordingly;
consciousness conditions name-and-form—
this teaching is likewise so.
Thus, one knows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the fruit of the mind.
Furthermore, regarding "that which follows purity":
purity is the mind of one in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
That person’s various activities proceed in accordance with a pure mind;
the bhikṣu who practices dhyāna is endowed with supernormal powers.
He attains mastery over his mind;
if he wishes to transform wood into gold,
he succeeds according to his will.
Therefore, one knows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the fruits of the mind.
Furthermore, regarding those who are born accordingly:
for example, sentient beings who commit transgressions.
Sentient beings who perform meritorious deeds may obtain all inferior external objects;
those who do so may obtain all excellent external objects.
Thus, one should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the fruits of the mind.
One must understand that since all phenomena take the mind as their cause, [they are likewise its effects].
The mind is also taken as the fruit;
nevertheless, although pure and impure appearances manifest differently,
they are like light and like shadows within the mirror of the mind.
It is utterly unobtainable.
Question:
One enters the gateway of Vijñaptimātra.
When one contemplates all objects,
they are naturally without marks;
what need is there to further speak of "destroying marks to reveal principle"?
Furthermore, it is said that one abandons existence to contemplate emptiness; if there is a thesis to be refuted,
then there must be a principle capable of emptying it.
If one clings to the gate of contemplation,
the previously existing empty dharmas will instead become the cause for the manifestation of marks of existence.
"How can this be consistent with the Way of Non-action?
Answer: "As for what is called 'the destruction of marks' (lakṣaṇa-bhaṅga):"
This has not yet entered into the stage of Consciousness-Only;
it merely removes false attachments, and although it speaks of "shattering appearances," [it does so from the perspective of the preceding stage].
In reality, there is nothing to be negated.
Since there is no existent thing to be negated,
there is likewise no emptiness that performs the negation.
If emotional attachments are dissolved,
both emptiness and existence are stilled;
the sensory objects before one are no longer fixed.
Destruction and establishment follow the mind;
the delusion that obscures reality does not arise,
and the reality that opposes delusion is likewise extinguished.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"All various grasping at signs is entirely false and illusory."
Just as a crystal bead changes according to the color before it and has no fixed color of its own,
so too are all phenomena.
There is no fixed characteristic;
it varies according to the mind.
Such characteristics as permanence or impermanence are likewise [subjective].
Just as one perceives this person as base due to a mind of hatred, if that mind of hatred ceases,
[the perception likewise ceases].
It arises from a mind of lustful desire;
seeing this person again as attractive,
it may also arise from a mind of arrogance.
Seeing this person, he considered them lowly and base;
yet upon hearing of their virtue,
he gave rise once more to a heart of reverence.
In this way, there is hatred and love based on reason,
as well as hatred and love without reason.
All are merely false conceptualizations;
if one removes these deceptive imaginings,
even the mark of emptiness does not exist.
It is the mark of signlessness and the mark of wishlessness,
because there is nothing to be destroyed.
Since one does not yet revere the principle of signlessness,
how could one maintain the gates of refutation and establishment,
or employ formation and destruction, or rejection and acceptance?
Since all things are one's own mind,
if one directly realizes the mind,
contemplation naturally ceases.
As a verse in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
"There is no nirvāṇa for anything;
there is no Buddha who has attained nirvāṇa."
There is no nirvāṇa of a Buddha;
it is far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened.
It is neither existent nor non-existent.
The Sage observes with tranquility, remaining detached from both;
this is the departure from birth.
This is called non-grasping;
it brings purity in this life and future lives.
There are two and a half verses [on this].
The *Dà yún jì* explains:
"The first verse realizes that all is currently one suchness."
This means that it is by means of the contemplation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is revealed.
Since there is no nirvana and no Buddha, it is "wishless."
The first phrase means that within all phenomena, such as form and mind, there is no attainment of nirvana,
because all phenomena are fundamentally suchness.
If one attains nirvana,
this is the view of annihilationism and eternalism;
for the cessation of dharmas is annihilation.
The second phrase states that this realization is permanent;
since there is no nirvana, [it must be so].
How can there be a Buddha?
Therefore, a sutra says:
"By severing the afflictions of the realm of desire, one attains Buddhahood."
This is what is called one who destroys the Buddha-dharma,
because afflictions and the Buddha-nature are quiescent.
Regarding the fourth phrase:
Because the suchness that is realized is as it is,
there is no nirvana; because the suchness that realizes is as it is.
There is no attaining Buddhahood;
transcending both the awakening and that which is awakened,
all is merged into the single suchness.
Question: Seeing,
hearing, sensing, and knowing do not transcend the mind-measure of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Question: Is true reality, which is without attainment and without arising, still within the measure of the mind?
Answer: No.
Now, as for "measurement," this refers to the cognizing mind;
it merely exists in contrast to the conventional when speaking of the ultimate.
Based on the provisional, one establishes the real;
one refutes differentiation and discusses equality.
To eliminate differentiated characteristics and establish suchness—
all of this is attained through duality.
This is called "breaking attachments and establishing the teaching.
If one can simultaneously sweep away both the ultimate and the conventional,
and cause both emptiness and existence to vanish together.
When the extremes are fully understood, they are the middle, and there are no extremes to be abandoned;
when the middle is penetrated, it is the extremes,
and there is no middle to be maintained.
Once the wisdom that realizes has ceased and the principle realized has become quiescent,
one finally transcends the realm of mental construction.
Entering the gate of absolute non-reliance:
there is both attainment and non-attainment,
as well as arising and non-arising.
All things do not transcend the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*).
As a verse in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"Free from all views."
Furthermore, being free from both the perceiving subject and the perceived object, there is neither attainment nor arising;
I describe this as the measure of mind (cittamātra).
It is neither existence nor non-existence;
it is entirely free from both existence and non-existence.
This refers to the liberation of that mind.
I teach that these are the mind-measure (cittamātra):
suchness (tathatā), the limit of emptiness (śūnyatā-koti),
nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
The various types of mind-born bodies—
I declare these to be the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*). Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
If there were even a single dharma that surpassed nirvāṇa,
I would likewise say it is like an illusion or a magical transformation,
for nirvāṇa is without marks.
If one grasps at signs,
that is merely the manifestation of one's own mind; it is not true nirvana.
The Buddha said:
"Suppose there were a Buddha who had passed into parinirvāṇa;
[one should] direct the mind toward what has been attained."
It is also established as mind-only;
all that is transformed by one's own mind is entirely illusory.
Therefore, one should know that what appears as forms and the traces of words,
which give rise to fleeting yet subtle understandings,
are all governed by the measure of the mind.
There is not a single dharma that does not concern the mind.
If one can realize that the mind is no-mind and understand that objects are no-objects, [then all is resolved].
When both principle and measure are simultaneously dissolved,
one may enter the Mirror of the School.
Question:
Now, in discussing the measure of the mind,
it does not go beyond what is seen and heard;
if we rely upon what is seen and heard, [it is as follows].
If the preceding object still exists,
how can the principle of "mind-only" (cittamātra) be established? Answer:
This is the mind-measure that is without mind;
it has no substantial reality.
Question:
If there is no substantial entity,
how are all phenomena established? Answer:
It is precisely because they lack substance and lack intrinsic nature that the myriad phenomena are established; from this,
the myriad phenomena arise.
It does not depart from true emptiness.
If one says that there is a nature,
then not a single dharma can be established.
Then emptiness is not empty of itself;
how could it possibly accommodate form?
If form were not form of itself...
Only then can one accord with emptiness.
The Mahāyāna-śāstra states:
"All dharmas revolve solely within the mind."
Regarding "no remaining dharmas":
even such mental phenomena are unattainable.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
The measure of mind that is without mind—
I call this the measure of mind.
This is based on the phrase "because the mind cannot be apprehended."
The meaning of the Great Emptiness is established;
through the phrase "the mind-measure of no-mind," the meaning of the differentiation of illusion is accomplished.
All phenomena are established by way of the meaning of great emptiness,
and by way of the meaning of the differentiation of illusion.
The principle of emptiness is thus revealed.
Question:
How can delusion conceal the truth?
It completely fulfills birth and death;
it truly can seize away delusion;
it purely manifests nirvana.
If the real and the false were separate,
they would not give rise to one another; if the real and the false were joined, [they would likewise not arise].
If the two truths are not established,
how can one reconcile them with the wondrous principle of the single mind? Answer:
The One Mind and the Two Truths are the ultimate destination of both teaching and principle; yet,
when [the truth] is disclosed, one is deluded regarding the Real.
If they were combined, they would destroy conventional reality.
Why? Because characteristics arise in accordance with the truth.
By examining these appearances, one can discern the true source:
awakening arises from delusion, yet it is precisely through delusion that one can come to know the essence of awakening.
Without delusion, awakening would have no basis to establish itself;
without truth, appearances would have nothing to rely upon.
Thus, truth and delusion are in mutual harmony.
If defilement and purity were established as functional realities, then the True [Suchness] alone could not be established.
Without delusion, with what would the True be contrasted so as to be established?
A solitary delusion cannot be established;
without the real, upon what could one rely to speak of delusion?
Both the real and the delusive lack inherent self-nature.
Names and characteristics originally share a single source;
thus, while the two truths are eternally distinct,
they always abide in a single flavor.
The nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is immovable,
yet dependent origination manifests in myriad differences.
Therefore, one knows that in reality there is not a single dharma that possesses an independent self-nature.
All arise from the conjunction of the two dharmas of reality and delusion.
As the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:
"The unborn and undying conjoin with the arising and ceasing."
Neither identical nor different,
it is called the ālayavijñāna;
it transforms and gives rise to the sense organs, the body, and the receptacle world.
The *Śīla-mahāyāna-śāstra* states:
"There are two kinds of causes and conditions for arising and ceasing.
The first is the cause and condition for arising and ceasing that are non-associated."
Second is the causal condition for the arising and ceasing of that which is associated.
The Treatise says:
"The essence of the manifest mirror-consciousness."
The six objective spheres (ṣaḍ-viṣaya) serve, in their respective order,
as the three types of defiled phenomena associated with them.
It can act as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
For this reason, it is called the "gate of coarse and heavy arising-and-ceasing causes and conditions.
Furthermore, within the essence of the manifesting consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*), there is also the sense of being an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
One should reflect upon this with careful scrutiny.
Furthermore, there are two further layers of causal conditions:
first, the fundamental pervasive causal condition.
Second is the universal cause and condition of the end.
Regarding the term "universal of the origin," it refers to fundamental ignorance and the mind of fundamental awakening.
It is expected that there is the sense of causal conditions corresponding to the six objects of the senses.
Regarding the term "subsequent pervasion" (mabien):
it refers to the manifestation of the activity of the mental factor (*caitta*),
which corresponds to the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because there is the meaning of causal conditions.
Furthermore, there are two additional causal conditions:
first, the causal condition of the upper and lower [realms].
Second is the causal condition of the lower and the higher.
Regarding the "lower and higher," ignorance is the beginning.
Karmic retribution is the ultimate end.
Whether high or low, they receive their due;
nothing exceeds its destined measure.
Because they act as causes and conditions,
the term "lower and upper" takes retribution as its starting point.
Ignorance is the end.
Below and above, they exert their power without exceeding their respective numbers.
Because they act as causes and conditions.
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena that arise and perish do not abide for even a single moment.
Because there is no cause and no condition.
Furthermore, the phenomena of causes and conditions are empty and without a master.
In fact, because self-nature is unapprehendable;
furthermore, because that which is an unapprehendable dharma is itself unapprehendable as being unapprehendable.
Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing:
this refers to the transformation of the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), and the consciousness (*vijñāna*) of sentient beings.
What meaning does this passage clarify?
This is said to demonstrate the distinction between the basis and that which depends upon it.
What is the basis? It is the mind of primordial awakening (*mūla-awakening*).
What is that which can depend [upon it]? It is sentient beings.
As for the term "sentient beings":
What dharma is it? It refers to the mind (*manas*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Why [are they so called]?
Because of the mind and mental consciousness.
It is called "sentient beings.
The mind and mental consciousness arise from the convergence and accumulation of all defilements.
Therefore, they are called "sentient beings," yet they have no separate self-essence;
they take only the mind as their essence.
Therefore, it is said that [the mind] evolves in dependence upon the mind.
Furthermore, it says:
"The characteristic of ignorance."
It does not depart from the nature of awakening;
it is neither destructible nor indestructible,
just like the great ocean.
Regarding the fact that the characteristic of wind and the characteristic of water are not mutually separated:
the great ocean is a metaphor for the ālayavijñāna, and the water is a metaphor for the mind of original enlightenment (mūlapratyavekṣaṇājñāna).
The wind is a metaphor for fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).
Being non-awakened,
it is able to activate the consciousness that involves movement and deliberation.
"Because it is like that wind,
the waves" is a metaphor for the consciousnesses of various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
The constant flux and impermanence,
wherein the characteristics of water and wind do not depart from one another,
is a metaphor for the mutual support of the true and the false.
They function in conjunction and operate in combination;
that is to say, because the mind of original enlightenment does not arise by itself,
it must rely upon the power of ignorance.
Only then can it arise;
because fundamental ignorance does not turn itself,
it must depend on the power of the true mind.
Only then can it be set in motion;
just as water does not produce waves of its own accord,
but must depend on the power of the wind.
Wind does not manifest movement by itself;
it must rely on the power of water to manifest the characteristic of movement.
The Sūtra says:
Within the great ocean of afflictions,
there exists the Perfect Tathāgata.
He proclaims the principle that the true nature is eternally abiding.
Within the reality of primordial awareness (mūla-bodhi),
there exist sentient beings obscured by ignorance.
It gives rise to waves of immeasurable and boundless afflictions.
As the sutra says:
The Buddha addressed the great assembly.
Initial awakening wisdom (*ādikṣayajñāna*) refers to the gradual emergence from the stage of being bound by all fetters,
up until the fulfillment of causal practices at the diamond-like stage (*vajropama*).
He gives rise to the ultimate path,
suddenly severing the fundamental ignorance-abiding ground;
the sun of awakening shines in its full radiance.
There is nowhere it does not pervade.
