It is simply that one does not follow [them] and does not destroy [them].
Departing from the extremes and deviance of the two views,
neither existent nor empty,

Thus, one encounters conditions without obstruction and touches upon objects without arising.

The Buddha does not say that what exists is non-existent,

as the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra* states:

Because form is boundless,
Prajñā is boundless.
It is also said:
If one studies Prajñāpāramitā,
one should study all dharmas. Why is this?
Now, Prajñā is the meaning of non-abiding;
to give rise to a thought is itself to abide in attachment.
If one does not abide in any phenomena, that is precisely prajñā;
therefore it is said: "If one studies prajñā..."
One should study all dharmas;
yet even if one abides in prajñā,
one will still become deluded and obscured.
However, since there is no abiding anywhere at all,
there is nothing that is not prajñā.
As the *Vajramaṇḍala-dhāraṇī-sūtra* says:
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there perhaps even a single dharma that a bodhisattva has practiced?"
The Buddha said: "There is a Dharma-gate of a single syllable; once a bodhisattva has attained it, they are able to enter all dharma-gates of dhāraṇīs."
One may expound ten million-word Dharma-gates,
yet this single-word Dharma-gate is likewise inexhaustible.
Having thus explained all dharmas,
they are again subsumed within the Dharma-gate of a single syllable.
The *Sūtra on the Transformation of the Female Body* states:
"If one does not perceive distinctions among all phenomena,
then one will certainly be able to bring sentient beings to maturity."
It is further said:
"If one knows that all phenomena possess the characteristic of liberation,
this is called ultimate liberation."
The commentary states:
To grasp the mind as an object is to encounter the dust of afflictions before one's very eyes.
Knowing that objects are mind,
there is nothing that is not liberation.
This is why the followers of the Two Vehicles realize only the emptiness of persons.
Merely being free from the false conceptions of the self and persons is called liberation; however,
one does not attain complete liberation until the emptiness of phenomena is realized.
Because of not recognizing the mind,
as stated in a verse from the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra:
"All phenomena lack the nature of a real entity."
Yet it is said that this is mind alone;
failing to see one's own mind,
one gives rise to conceptual discrimination.
The *Chuyao jing* (Udānavarga) says:
"One whose body is clad in the armor of precepts but whose mind lacks the sword of wisdom..."
Thus, one cannot destroy the primary root of the fetters (saṃyojana). Therefore,
it is known that if one does not contemplate the mind,
wondrous wisdom will not be accomplished.
Consequently, one cannot sever the root of ignorance.
Thus, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: "Holding the precepts or violating them merely restrains the body."
If it is not the body and has nothing to bind it,
and is fundamentally not pervasive throughout all things,
how can one attain perfect penetration?
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"In the foremost Great Way,
there is no duality."
The commentary states:
One's resolve should be focused on a single goal, the ultimate source of all dharmas,
just as a kingdom cannot have two kings.
A household has no second master.
If one departs from this and seeks elsewhere, two paths will be formed.
As it is said in the *Bodhisattvacaryā-pratipatti-sūtra*:
Now, one who seeks the Dharma does not seek it within any phenomena (*dharma*).
Furthermore, it is said:
If there is something sought, one cannot roar the lion’s roar;
if there is nothing sought, one can roar the lion’s roar.
The commentary states:
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"One who utters the lion's roar definitively declares that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature."
If one knows that one's own mind is fully endowed with buddha-nature,
how could there be any dharma outside of this nature that could be sought?
The *Nagasena-bhikṣu-sūtra* states:
The King asked Nāgasena,
"What is that which is called 'the one mind'?"
Nāgasena said:
"Among all virtues, a single-pointed mind is the most supreme.
To unify one's mind—"
"All virtues follow it.
Nāgasena said,
"It is like a staircase."
There must be that upon which one relies.
All those who follow the various wholesome paths are focused on a single mind.
The *Saṃyukta-piṭaka-sūtra* states:
King Ajātaśatru offered a precious robe to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva;
suddenly, Mañjuśrī vanished from his seat and could no longer be seen.
In this manner, they successively bestowed [the robes] upon all the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas,
and it was likewise so until they finally wore them themselves.
Nor does one perceive the body;
through this, one awakens to the Way.
The commentary states:
Now, as for the reason why the Buddhas and patriarchs established the teachings,
it was none other than to shatter the two attachments of body and mind. Thus,
the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
The Buddha said that what is not a body is called the "Great Body.
The *Pao-tsang lun* says:
The principle of pure emptiness ultimately has no body;
the mind is likewise so.
If one can directly awaken to the fact that the bodies and minds of both self and others are equally ungraspable,
and that there is no phenomenon apart from the mind.
That all ten thousand objects are empty is identical to what King Ajātaśatru realized.
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* says:
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha:
"There is a dharma-gate that can enable a bodhisattva to swiftly attain bodhi."
"Bhagavān, what is the name and title of this Dharma-gate?"
What is its meaning?
Good son, this is a single Dharma-gate.
It is named "The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings.
Bodhisattvas who wish to practice and study these immeasurable meanings should contemplate all dharmas.
From the beginningless past until now,
its nature and characteristics are empty and quiescent;
it is neither large nor small.
Without arising and without ceasing;
neither abiding nor moving;
neither advancing nor retreating.
It is just like space;
there are no two distinct dharmas,
yet sentient beings falsely and arbitrarily conceptualize them.
"This is this; that is that. This is gain; this is loss.
The commentary states:
This single dharma-gate, named "Infinite Meanings," is precisely the gate of the one mind,
which is able to give rise to infinite meanings.
Because it does not maintain its own nature,
it follows conditions to form all phenomena;
precisely at the time of following conditions, [it does so].
Nor does it lose its own nature;
it is only because sentient beings do not understand this that [the mind] merely follows the conditions for its arousal and movement.
Failing to perceive the nature of quiescence,
they recklessly conceptualize existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena.
Regarding the gains and losses of each other,
the *Tathāgata-śāsanopadeśa-vijitasena-rāja-sūtra* states:
"Great King, you should know this."
For example, suppose a man or a woman,
within a dream, [sees something].
In his dreams, he sees delightful gardens and delightful mountain valleys.
Having awakened from that dream, he beheld lovely kingdoms, cities, and various other kinds of beings.
"O Great King, all that is seen is non-existent;
such is the nature of one's national sovereignty and one's own life."
They are deceptive and impermanent;
all are like what is seen in a dream. Thus one knows that these are the realms within a dream.
The objects perceived during the waking state are seen solely by the mind;
there is nothing else besides this.
Worldly people merely believe that dream-objects are false,
yet they dogmatically cling to the objects of the waking day as real;
therefore, the Great Awakened One has compassionately descended to show them grace.
To speak by way of analogy:
one uses the unsubstantiality of what is believed to refute the substantiality of what is believed.
Causing the reality of what is believed to become identical to the emptiness of what is believed,
one suddenly awakens to the emptiness of all phenomena.
All enter the Mirror of the Fundamental Source.
The *Dharmadhātuprakṛtisvabhāvanirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"At that time, the Elder Śāriputra..."
Emerging from his own dwelling,
he went to the place where the youth Mañjuśrī was staying;
having arrived, he...
Not seeing Mañjuśrī, he immediately went to where the Buddha was;
having arrived, he...
He stood outside the entrance to the Buddha’s private quarters.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
Mañjuśrī, this bhikṣu Śāriputra is now outside the gate.
"Because they wish to hear the Dharma,
you must allow them to enter. Mañjuśrī said:
World-Honored One,
whether it be the limit of that Śāriputra,
or the limit of the dharma-realm.
World-Honored One,
as for these two limits,
could they possibly exist either within or without?
"If it were the two in the middle," the Buddha said, "it would not."
Mañjuśrī said, “World-Honored One, as for what is called ‘the reality-limit’ (bhūtakoṭi):”
Nor is it the limit of reality.
Thus, this limit and non-limit have neither interior nor exterior.
"Neither coming nor going,
World-Honored One," said the Elder Śāriputra.
This is precisely the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Śāriputra, the realm (dhātu) is precisely the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
World-Honored One,
yet this dharma-realm neither emerges nor enters.
There is no coming and no going.
From where, then, has the Elder Śāriputra come?
"Where should one enter?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,"
"If I am inside conversing with the śrāvakas while you remain outside and are not permitted to enter,
does it not occur to you to feel thoughts of suffering and distress?"
Mañjuśrī said, "No, World-Honored One."
For what reason?
World-Honored One,
whatever Dharma is taught—
It is not separate from the dharma-realm;
that which the Tathāgata teaches as the Dharma is itself the dharma-realm.
The dharma-realm is itself the tathāgata-realm.
To speak of the dharma-realm is to speak in accordance with the dharma-realm.
The realm of speech is non-dual and without distinction;
all names and speakers are not separate from the dharma-realm.
World-Honored One,
for this reason, I do not suffer.
World-Honored One,
even if I were not to come to where the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges River.
At that time, I felt neither attachment nor joy,
nor did I experience any sorrow or distress. Why was this?
If there were duality,
then affliction would arise;
the Dharma-realm is non-dual.
"Therefore, there is no affliction.
The commentary states:
"For this reason, there is no boundary between the internal and the external."
The ultimate and the conventional share a single source;
upon entering the Mirror of the School,
joy and sorrow no longer fill one’s breast.
Abiding in the state of non-duality,
increasing love leaves no attachment in the field of the emotions;
thus one knows that there is neither going nor coming.
Beholding the Buddha does not shift from the present moment;
he is neither near nor far.
Hearing the Dharma does not transcend the tip of a hair.
Only upon attaining the mind of Mañjuśrī does one come to know that this is the natural order of things (dharmatā); yet,
from this very knowledge, the views of sentient beings arise.
Having personally severed the dust of emotional defilements, the *Gambhīra-vimokṣa-sūtra* states:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas..."
That which is awakened to by the well-awakened is free from dualistic activity and reaches the state of signlessness.
They practice the conduct of all Buddhas,
attain the universal equality of all Tathāgatas,
and reach the destination that is free from obstruction.
They are able to reach the wheel of non-retrogression of all [Buddhas];
they are able to reach the inconceivable essence, the realm that cannot be overcome.
They are able to reach the equality of all three periods of time;
they pervade the bodies of all worlds;
and they arrive at the state of non-doubt regarding all dharmas.
They are able to reach the conduct of all ultimate wisdom;
they are fully able to reach the realm of doubt-free knowledge of phenomena;
and they attain all non-discriminative bodies.
They are able to answer all the questions of bodhisattvas regarding wisdom;
they are able to reach the further shore of non-dual practice;
and they are able to reach the state of the Buddhas' undifferentiated wisdom of liberation.
They are able to reach the realm of the Samādhi Without Bound or Center,
as vast as the Dharma-realm and ultimate like empty space.
"Until the end of the future.
The commentary states:
"One who has personally reached the state of certainty regarding all phenomena."
Only upon awakening the mind does one come to know;
suddenly illuminating the gate of the signlessness of all phenomena. Only upon seeing one's nature does one achieve full understanding.
This is the sphere of practice of the Tathāgata and that which is known by the Great Awakened One; therefore,
it is said to be as vast as the Dharma-realm.
Ultimately, it is like space:
without beginning and without end,
extending to the furthest reaches of the future.
The *Vajrarāja-bodhisattva-rahasya-japa-vidhi-sūtra* states:
"Sit upright with the body straightened and contemplate as follows."
All phenomena arise from one's own mind;
from the very beginning, they have never existed.
As a verse in the *Maitreya-buddhatva-sūtra* says:
For a long time I have contemplated the suffering of sentient beings;
wishing to pull them out, there was no way to liberate them.
Today I have realized Bodhi.
"Suddenly there is nothing at all.
The commentary states:
"The mental consciousness, moment by moment, clings to and is bound by sensory objects."
Lack of autonomy is itself the suffering of sentient beings;
if one realizes that objects are empty, there is no bondage.
Internal fetters do not arise;
one realizes and dwells in single-mindedness.
Both faculties and objects are quiescent.
One immediately enters the dharma-realm of intrinsic emptiness and realizes signless bodhi.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi Sūtra* says:
Without attachment and without dependence,
free from burdens and tranquil,
its intrinsic nature is like space.
This is called the Unsurpassed Way.
Furthermore, the Lotus Sūtra states:
"The Buddhas attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi herein."
It is here that all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma;
it is here that all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa.
Thus, it is here that the Buddhas manifest the eight phases of attaining enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva’s four means of integration for delivering sentient beings,
as well as the fulfillment of both self-benefit and the benefit of others, are all accomplished within this emptiness of original nature.
The *Saṃyukta-piṭaka-sūtra* states:
"For example, when two pieces of wood are rubbed together,
fire spontaneously arises from them."
It returns to burn that very wood;
the fire does not emerge from the wind,
nor does it emerge from the water.
It does not emerge from the earth;
the four Māras are likewise so.
All arise from the mind;
they do not come from without.
It is like a painter.
The painted image varies in size according to the hand; although it arises from the convergence of causes and conditions, [it remains a mere representation].
There are colors, there are boards, and there are brushes;
yet if the painter does not paint,
the image cannot be formed.
The four māras are thus.
When the mind has become firm, nothing arises.
The commentary states:
Therefore, because the mind is unmoving,
phenomena do not manifest before it.
Just as a painter does not paint because there is no form or image,
he remains unmoving in a single mind.
There is great merit.
As stated in the *Dharmapada*:
The Buddha said:
Good son, a spiritual friend possesses great merit.
It can cause you all to [be liberated] from greed, anger,
delusion, and wrong views.
Amidst the five hindrances, the five desires,
and the myriad defilements, one establishes the Buddha-dharma;
to give rise not even to a single thought possesses great merit.
It is, for example, like a person who,
holding onto a sturdy boat, crosses the great ocean with body and mind unmoving.
And thus reach the other shore.

*Zongjing Lu*, Scroll Ninety-Seventh.
Compiled by Chan Master Yanshou, Chief Abbot of Yongming Temple of Huiri:

Now that the Buddhist teachings have been clarified, it is necessary to set forth the intent of the Patriarchs. Those who attain mastery of the Buddha Vehicle will all accord with the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
As the Lotus Sūtra says:
"Whatever this person contemplates, deliberates, or speaks—
all of these are the Buddha-dharma."
There is nothing that is not true;
this is also what was spoken in the sutras of the former Buddhas.
The first verse by Vipaśyin Buddha says:
The body receives birth from within formlessness;
it manifests various forms like an illusion.
The mind-consciousness of the one who creates the illusion is fundamentally non-existent.
"Both sin and merit are empty and have no abode.
The second verse by Buddha Śikhin says:
"The arising of all wholesome dharmas is fundamentally illusory."
The commission of various evil karmas is likewise an illusion.
The body is like a mass of foam; the mind is like the wind.
These illusions arise without root and lack any real nature.
The verse of the third Buddha, Viśvabhū, says:
"Borrowing the four great elements to form a body,
the mind is fundamentally unborn, yet arises due to objects."
If the external object does not exist, the mind likewise does not exist;
offenses and merits arise and cease like illusions.
The fourth Buddha, Krakucchanda, spoke in verse:
To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha’s vision;
to understand that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha’s realization.
To realize that the fundamental nature of both body and mind is empty—this is the Buddha’s realization.
How does this person differ from the Buddha?
The fifth verse of the Buddha Kanakamuni states:
"The Buddha does not perceive a body, yet he knows himself to be the Buddha."
If one truly knows that there is no Buddha apart from cognition,
the wise are able to realize that the nature of offenses is empty;
they remain composed and unafraid of birth and death.
The verse of the sixth Buddha, Kāśyapa, says:
"The nature of all sentient beings is pure;
from the beginning, it is unborn and cannot be extinguished."
This very body and mind are born of illusion;
within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit.
The seventh verse by Śākyamuni Buddha says:
Illusions have no cause and no arising;
they are all seen as such by their very nature.
There are no phenomena that are not produced through self-transformation.
Illusions are without arising and without fear.
He further addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"I possess the pure Dharma-eye."
The wondrous mind of nirvana;
the true mark which is markless;
the subtle and sublime True Dharma.
I entrust this to you;
do not allow it to be severed.
Listen to my verse:
The Dharma is fundamentally without Dharma;
that which is without Dharma is also Dharma.
Now, at this time when I transmit the absence of Dharma—
How could phenomena ever truly be phenomena?
The Dharma verse transmitted by Mahākāśyapa, the first patriarch of India, says:
"Phenomenon after phenomenon is fundamentally the Dharma."
There is neither dharma nor non-dharma.
How could there be both dharma and non-dharma within a single dharma?
The Dharma verse transmitted by the Second Patriarch, Ānanda, says:
"Originally there was a dharma to be entrusted;
having completed the entrustment, I say there is no dharma."
Each must awaken for themselves;
once awakened, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma.
The Dharma verse transmitted by the Third Patriarch, Śaṇavāsa, says:
Neither is there non-dharma, nor is there mind;
there is no mind, nor is there dharma. When these mental dharmas are thus explained, [they are seen as empty].
This Dharma is not a mental phenomenon.
The Dharma-transmission verse of the Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, says:
"The mind is itself the original mind."
The fundamental mind is not a dharma;
dharmas possess the fundamental mind.
It is neither mind nor the fundamental dharma.
The fifth patriarch was Dhitika,
also known as Gandhamādana;
he initially entered the monastic life under Upagupta.
The Venerable One asked:
"Does one go forth by means of the mind,
or does one go forth by means of the body?"
The assembly of incense-sellers said:
"We have come to leave the household life not for the sake of seeking personal benefit for our bodies or minds."
The Venerable One said:
"If it is not for the sake of body and mind,
for whom else would one go forth?"
The assembly of incense-bearers said:
"Now, for one who has left the household life, there is no self;
because there is no self, the mind neither arises nor perishes."
The mind is neither born nor extinguished;
this is precisely what is meant by permanence. Since it is permanent, [it is thus].
The Buddha is also eternal;
the mind has no form or characteristics,
and its essence is likewise so.
The Venerable One said,
"You shall attain great enlightenment;
your mind will naturally become luminous."
According to the Buddha-dharma,
he delivered as many beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
The verse of entrusting the Dharma says:
Thoroughly penetrating the mind of this fundamental dharma,
there is neither dharma nor non-dharma;
one awakens to the realization that awakening is identical to non-awakening.
There is no mind and no dharma to be attained.
The Dharma-transmission verse of the Sixth Patriarch, Mīchaka, says:
"Without mind, there is nothing to be attained."
That which is spoken of cannot be called "dharmas.
Only when one realizes that the mind is not the mind does one begin to understand the mind and mental factors.
The Dharma-transmission verse of the Seventh Patriarch, Vāsumitra, says:
"The mind is identical to the realm of empty space;
it manifests dharmas equal to empty space."
When realizing emptiness,
there is neither existence nor non-existence.
The Dharma-transmission verse of the eighth patriarch, Buddhanandi, says:
Space has neither interior nor exterior;
the phenomena of the mind are likewise.
If one thoroughly understands space, [one understands the mind].
This is the realization of the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The Ninth Patriarch,
Vṛddhamitra, asked the Patriarch Buddhanandi in verse:
Parents are not my kin;
who is the most intimate kin?
The Buddhas are not my path.
"Who is the one most proficient in the Way?
He answered in verse:
"The one you speak of is intimate with the mind."
Parents cannot be compared [to this];
your practice accords with the Way;
it is identical to the mind of all Buddhas.
Seeking an external Buddha with attributes is not like you;
if you wish to recognize your original mind, [look within].
It is neither a union nor a separation;
through this, one awakens to the Way.
The verse of entrustment says:
Ultimate truth is originally nameless;
it is through names that ultimate truth is revealed.
Thus one receives and attains the true Dharma.
It is neither true nor false.
The Dharma verse transmitted by the Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Xie, says:
"The true essence is naturally true."
Because the true teaching possesses principle,
one realizes the authentic Dharma;
there is neither practice nor cessation.
The eleventh patriarch, Punyayasas,
was at that time the Venerable Pārśva, beneath a tree.
Pointing his finger at the ground beneath the tree, he addressed the great assembly, saying:
"If this ground should turn golden in color,
a noble being shall enter this assembly."
Not long after these words were spoken, in a mere moment,
it turned the color of gold.
The Venerable One raised his hand and saw a man standing before the assembly.
The Venerable One said:
"From where have you come? Yaśas replied,
"My mind has not gone anywhere."
The Venerable One asked,
"Where do you dwell? Yaśas replied:
"My mind does not come to rest.
The Venerable One said,
"Is your mind not settled?"
Yaśas said, "The Buddhas are likewise.
The Venerable One said:
"You are not the Buddhas.
Yaśas replied, "The Buddhas are also not [the Buddhas]."
At that time, Yaśas spoke a verse of praise, saying:
"The Teacher sits upon the golden ground,
ever expounding the meaning of ultimate truth."
The light turns back to illuminate me,
causing me to enter samādhi. Furthermore,
the verse for transmitting the Dharma says:
Delusion and enlightenment are like concealment and manifestation;
light and darkness are inseparable.
Now I transmit this dharma of concealment and manifestation.
It is neither one nor two.
The twelfth patriarch, Master Aśvaghoṣa,
transmitted the Dharma with this verse:
Manifestation and concealment are the fundamental Dharma;
light and darkness are originally non-dual.
Now I entrust this Dharma of realization.
Neither grasping nor discarding.
The Dharma verse transmitted by the Thirteenth Patriarch, Vairocana, says:
"The Dharma is neither hidden nor manifest."
This is called the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
To awaken to this dharma of concealment and manifestation is neither folly nor wisdom.
The fourteenth patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna,
traveled to South India to propagate the teachings.
In that country, many people practiced meritorious deeds.
They do not understand the principles of the Buddha;
they merely exercise petty sophistry and lack great wisdom.
Furthermore, when asked about Buddha-nature, he said,
"It is giving."
I seek meritorious deeds;
I do not understand the Buddha-nature.
You have realized the Buddha-nature.
"Tell me about it," he said.
The teacher replied,
"If you wish to study the Way..."
"First eliminate the conceit of self;
only by giving rise to a mind of reverence can one attain the Buddha-nature.
The assembly said:
"As for the magnitude of Buddha-nature," the Master said,
"it is not something you can know."
It is not a matter of speaking of "great" or "small.
If one speaks of "great" or "small," that is precisely what is great or small.
"It is not the Buddha-nature.
The assembly said,
"We wish to abandon these petty sophistries and return to the great ocean."
Nāgārjuna then preached the Dharma for him,
manifesting a miraculous sign before the great assembly:
his body became like the orb of the moon.
While seated upon the throne,
he heard only the preaching of the Dharma,
but did not behold his physical form.
Among that assembly was an elder named Deva, who addressed the multitude, saying:
"Do you recognize this auspicious omen?
The assembly replied,
"It is none other than the Great Sage."
Who could have recognized him?
At that time, Deva’s mental faculties were pure from long ago.
He also perceived its signs;
silently attuning himself to them,
he then addressed the assembly, saying:
The Master manifests the meaning of the Buddha-nature;
that which is not the Master’s body is the signless samādhi.
Its shape is like the full moon;
this is the meaning of Buddha-nature.
Before he had finished speaking—
The Master then manifested his true form and spoke a verse from his seat, saying:
"My body manifests the appearance of the full moon."
This manifests the essence of all Buddhas;
their teaching of the Dharma has no form,
and its function is to discern that which is neither sound nor color.
Furthermore, the verse for transmitting the Dharma says:
"To clarify the principle of concealment and manifestation,
one then explains the logic of liberation."
Regarding the Dharma, the mind does not realize it;
there is neither anger nor joy.
The fifteenth patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva, spoke this verse of transmitting the Dharma:
I have taught the principle of liberation to those who transmit the Dharma; yet,
regarding the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized.
There is neither end nor beginning.
The Dharma verse transmitted by the Sixteenth Patriarch, Venerable Rāhula, says:
"In the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized."
Neither grasped nor abandoned, phenomena possess neither the mark of existence nor non-existence; how, then,
could they arise internally or externally?
The Dharma verse of the Seventeenth Patriarch, Venerable Saṃghanandin, says:
"The ground of the mind is fundamentally without birth;
through seeds, it arises from conditions."
The conditions and seeds do not obstruct one another;
it is the same for flowers and fruits.
The eighteenth patriarch was Gayasata.
First, the seventeenth patriarch, Saṃghanandin,
once went to his house and suddenly saw a son.
Holding a copper mirror in his hand, he went to the Master’s place.
The Venerable One asked, "How old are you?"
The Master said,
"I shall be a hundred years old.
At that time, the Venerable One replied that he was a hundred years old.
